civs.represents: The Anglo-Saxons, that is, the English of the Early Middle Ages. The design emphasises Wessex and the late Saxon kingdom of England: Alfred, Edward the Elder, Æthelstan, Edgar and Harold II, with the burh system and the fyrd. The label “Saxons” nominally excludes the Angles (Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia) and the Jutes (Kent), and ignores the continental Saxons of Saxony, whose duchy gave Germany the Ottonian dynasty (919–1024).
civs.period: c. 449 (traditional adventus Saxonum) to 1066 (Hastings). Core of the design: c. 871–1066.
civs.verdict: It is a new civilization (The Viking Sagas) and, in its own elements, quite well documented. The Hearth Troop is the heorðwerod of Old English poetry, the Shield Wall is the bordweall of Brunanburh and Maldon, and the infantry discount per fortified centre translates the burh–fyrd link well. The repairers bonus evokes the obligation to repair fortifications, and the reinforced Longships recall Alfred's ships (896). The big conceptual error is expressing the defensive identity through castles and arrows, when castles were precisely the Norman novelty that the English lacked (Orderic Vitalis). The generic tech tree gives them crossbows, Cranequins, heavy cavalry and the Carrack, anachronistic for before 1066, although the total absence of gunpowder shows coherence. The history text has avoidable errors: Ælle “of Essex”, Middlesex as a kingdom, Alfred as “unifier” in 886, and the shield wall copied from the Vikings.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Saxons” is narrower than its subject: pre-1066 England was Anglo-Saxon, and Bede's Northumbria, Offa's Mercia and East Anglia were kingdoms of the Angles. At the same time, the name is ambiguous, because the continental Saxons fought Charlemagne (Saxon Wars, 772–804) and gave the Holy Roman Empire the Ottonian dynasty. The term “Anglo-Saxon” itself is under academic debate: the International Society of Anglo-Saxonists renamed itself ISSEME in 2019. There is direct overlap with the Britons, whose text narrates the same period and the same Battle of Hastings. In addition, the game's Huskarl still belongs to the Goths, when huscarls are an 11th-century Anglo-Scandinavian reality (the guards of Cnut and of Harold at Hastings).

elements.explanation: The Anglo-Saxons rode to get about but fought on foot (Maldon 991, Hastings 1066). In 1055, near Hereford, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (C version) relates that the English fled before a spear was thrown “because they were on horseback”, and John of Worcester adds that Earl Ralph had ordered them to fight mounted “against their custom”. The defensive identity rests on the burh system of Alfred, Edward the Elder and Æthelflæd.

elements.element: Mills, Lumber- and Mining Camps provide +35 food and +10 stone when built
elements.explanation: It can be linked to the late Saxon density of mills: Domesday Book (1086) records around 5,600 mills, most of them already in existence before the Conquest. The stone generated by lumber and mining camps is pure balance mechanics.

elements.element: Foot Soldiers cost -5% per Town Center or Castle (max -20%)
elements.explanation: It is a good abstraction. Military service was tied to land (hidage), and the Burghal Hidage fixes the men for each burh (one man per hide, four men for each pole of wall). Fortified centres were indeed the basis of defence and recruitment. Only the reference to “Castle” is anachronistic.

elements.element: Towers and Castles fire +100% base arrows starting in Castle Age
elements.explanation: Castles were the great Norman novelty. Orderic Vitalis explains the weak English resistance after 1066 precisely by the scarcity of fortifications “which the Gauls call castles”. Burhs were communal earth-and-timber enclosures defended by garrisons on foot, not archer towers, and archery was of little relevance in Anglo-Saxon warfare. Before 1066 there were only a handful of castles built by Edward the Confessor's Normans (Hereford, Richard's Castle, Ewyas Harold, possibly Clavering).

The naval part has a basis. The Chronicle (896) says that Alfred had ships built almost twice as long as the Danish ones, some with 60 oars or more, and “neither on the Frisian nor on the Danish pattern” (the name “Longship” is therefore approximate). Edgar maintained fleets, and in 1008 Æthelred imposed a naval levy (one ship for every 310 hides). The Catapult Galleons part has no foundation: there were no shipborne catapults in North Sea naval warfare.

Hearth Troop translates “heorðwerod”, the lord's household guard (Beowulf; The Battle of Maldon, where Byrhtnoth's retinue dies with him). Throwing before melee is documented: Maldon mentions darts, and William of Poitiers describes the English throwing darts, axes and stones at Hastings. What is missing is the two-handed Danish axe, typical of the 11th-century elite.

Greater conversion range is a reasonable abstraction of Anglo-Saxon missionary zeal on the Continent: Willibrord in Frisia (690s) and Boniface, the “Apostle of the Germans” (d. 754). To this can be added the monastic culture of Bede and Lindisfarne and the 10th-century Benedictine reform (Dunstan, Æthelwold). The name is generic.

The “bordweall” is attested in Old English poetry (Brunanburh, 937) and the close-packed shield formation appears at Maldon (991) and Hastings. The mechanic (more armour en masse) is a good translation. But it was not exclusive to the Saxons, as noted below regarding the history text.

It is an elegant link to the “common burdens” imposed on all land since 8th-century Mercia: service in the fyrd, repair of bridges (brycg-geweorc) and of fortifications (burh-bot). The Latin expression “trinoda necessitas”, still widely used, comes from a misreading of a spurious charter.

tree_issues.problem: This is a good call, although post-1066 and outside England. Many English exiles joined the Varangian Guard after the Conquest (Orderic Vitalis; Chronicon Laudunense), and at Dyrrhachium (1081) the Varangians, largely English, faced Robert Guiscard's Normans. The scale of this emigration is debated.

tree_issues.item: Mounted Crossbowman, Heavy Mounted Crossbowman, Cranequins, Arbalester
tree_issues.problem: They are anachronistic. The crossbow is practically absent from Anglo-Saxon England; it was the Normans who brought crossbowmen to Hastings (William of Poitiers). The cranequin is much later.
They are alien to an army that fought on foot (ASC 1055). Hussars are 15th-century Serbian and Hungarian horsemen.
The Carrack is a 14th–16th-century ship, anachronistic for before 1066. The Britons, late medieval English, do not have it.
The Castle is mandatory in the game engine, but it is the wrong fortification. A unique “Burh” building would be preferable.

tree_issues.item: No gunpowder, no Blast Furnace or Plate Barding Armor
tree_issues.problem: Coherence worth noting: the absence of Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon and Cannon Galleon is right for a civilization that ends in 1066.

history_text_issues.claim: The Saxons supposedly first sailed to England in the 5th century.
history_text_issues.problem: It ignores the earlier presence.
history_text_issues.correction: There were Saxon raids on Roman Britain from the 3rd–4th centuries (the Litus Saxonicum, or “Saxon Shore”, with its forts; the barbarica conspiratio of 367) and probable settlement of federates before the traditional date of 449.

history_text_issues.claim: Hengist and Horsa supposedly led “Saxon” mercenaries.
history_text_issues.problem: Imprecise ethnic attribution.
history_text_issues.correction: In the tradition of Bede (HE I.15) and the Chronicle, Hengist and Horsa are linked to the founding of Kent, a kingdom that Bede says belonged to the Jutes; the sources, however, use “Saxones” generically. Their historicity is doubtful: the names mean “stallion” and “horse”.

history_text_issues.claim: The Saxons supposedly founded the kingdoms of Wessex, Essex, Sussex and “Middlesex”.
history_text_issues.problem: Middlesex was never a kingdom.
history_text_issues.correction: Middlesex was a province of the East Saxons and later of Mercia. The Heptarchy included Anglian (Northumbria, Mercia, East Anglia) and Jutish (Kent) kingdoms.

history_text_issues.claim: “King Aelle of Essex” and Cerdic as a “Saxon warrior king”.
history_text_issues.problem: A factual error and a simplification.
history_text_issues.correction: Ælle was king of the South Saxons (Sussex), named by Bede as the first to hold supremacy over the other kingdoms. Cerdic, the legendary founder of Wessex, has a name of Brittonic origin (comparable to Ceretic/Caradog), which suggests mixed elites.

history_text_issues.claim: England was supposedly unified by Alfred the Great in 886.
history_text_issues.problem: Central factual error.
history_text_issues.correction: In 886 Alfred occupied London and received the submission of all the English who were not under Danish rule (ASC). He never ruled Northumbria or East Anglia. Unification was the work of Æthelstan (927). “Heptarchy” is a 16th-century historiographical term.

history_text_issues.claim: The first Viking raid was supposedly Lindisfarne, in 793.
history_text_issues.problem: Inaccuracy.
history_text_issues.correction: The Chronicle records an earlier attack at Portland (c. 789), where the reeve Beaduheard died. Lindisfarne is the symbolic landmark.

history_text_issues.claim: Burhs are said to have had walls of stone, timber or earth, and all the main ones to have been in the Burghal Hidage.
history_text_issues.problem: Generalisation and omission.
history_text_issues.correction: Most burhs had earth banks with a palisade (some received stone facing later); some reused Roman walls (Winchester, Exeter, Bath). The Burghal Hidage lists about 30 sites, mostly in Wessex, and omits most of Æthelflæd's Mercian burhs (Bridgnorth, Tamworth, Stafford, 912–915) and those of the reconquest of the Danelaw.

history_text_issues.claim: The Saxons supposedly adopted Viking techniques such as the shield wall.
history_text_issues.problem: It inverts reality.
history_text_issues.correction: The shield wall was common Germanic practice, and also late Roman and Byzantine (the fulcum of the Strategikon), predating the Vikings. The English and the Scandinavians shared it.

history_text_issues.claim: The Saxons supposedly created unique weapons to compete with the Vikings, such as the seax.
history_text_issues.problem: Anachronism and false exclusivity.
history_text_issues.correction: The seax/scramasax was common to all Germanic peoples (Franks included) from the 5th century, long before the Vikings. The etymology “Saxon” < “seax” is old but uncertain (Widukind of Corvey). The bow was secondary on the Anglo-Saxon battlefield.

history_text_issues.claim: Edward the Confessor supposedly put England back “firmly” under Saxon rule.
history_text_issues.problem: Simplification.
history_text_issues.correction: Edward was half-Norman (son of Emma of Normandy), lived in exile in Normandy and surrounded himself with Normans (Robert of Jumièges, Archbishop of Canterbury). Royal power was contested with the Godwin family.

history_text_issues.claim: Harold Godwinson supposedly “seized” the throne.
history_text_issues.problem: It adopts the framing of Norman propaganda.
history_text_issues.correction: Harold was chosen by the witan and crowned on 6 January 1066, invoking Edward's deathbed designation (ASC; Vita Ædwardi Regis). The idea of usurpation is the version of William of Poitiers and of the Tapestry.

history_text_issues.claim: Hastings supposedly ended Saxon rule.
history_text_issues.problem: It cuts the resistance short.
history_text_issues.correction: There were revolts until 1070–71 (the Harrying of the North; Hereward at Ely), and the replacement of the English aristocracy is only complete by Domesday (1086).

history_text_issues.claim: General omissions of the text.
history_text_issues.problem: A text centred on Wessex and on war.
history_text_issues.correction: Missing are Offa and his dyke, the conversion (Augustine, 597), the golden age of Northumbria (Bede, Lindisfarne Gospels), Æthelflæd, Æthelstan and Brunanburh (937), Edgar and the coinage reform (c. 973), and Æthelred, Maldon and the tributes to the Vikings.

missing_features: The huscarls and the two-handed Danish axe, the elite of the army of 1016–1066.
The fyrd and its variants: the obligation of one man per five hides (Berkshire Domesday) and the general levy; the distinction between “select fyrd” and “great fyrd” is a contested modern model.
The burh as a town: market and mint, as well as fortress.
An early administrative state: shires, hundreds, writs, and the silver penny with regular recoinages after Edgar's reform (c. 973).
The fiscal capacity of the geld/heregeld, which paid tributes and a standing fleet (lithsmen) until 1051.
Offa's Dyke (Mercia, 8th century).
Vernacular literature and manuscript culture (Beowulf, Alfred's translations, Lindisfarne Gospels).
The mounted mobility of the thegns: they rode to battle and dismounted to fight.

proposals.title: “Burh” unique building
proposals.description: Available in the Feudal Age: a cheap earth-and-timber fortification that provides population, serves as a drop-off point, trains infantry and counts towards the infantry discount bonus. It can partially replace the Castle.
proposals.historical_basis: The burh system of Alfred and Edward the Elder (Burghal Hidage) and Æthelflæd's foundations.

proposals.title: Swap the arrow bonus for a walls bonus
proposals.description: Remove “Towers and Castles +100% arrows”. Instead: Palisade and Stone Walls +20% HP and built +30% faster, and Town Centers +5 garrison.
proposals.historical_basis: Burhs were enclosures defended by garrisons on foot. Castles and wall archery arrive with the Normans (Orderic Vitalis).

proposals.title: Clear the tech tree of anachronisms
proposals.description: Remove Mounted Crossbowman, Heavy Mounted Crossbowman, Cranequins, Arbalester, Cavalier, Hussar and Carrack.
proposals.historical_basis: The crossbow and shock cavalry were not part of Anglo-Saxon warfare, and the Carrack is 14th-century or later.

proposals.title: UT “Dane Axe”
proposals.description: Hearth Troop and Militia-line gain +X attack against cavalry and +1 armour.
proposals.historical_basis: The Bayeux Tapestry shows Englishmen with two-handed axes, and Wace describes an English axe capable of felling horse and rider at Hastings.

proposals.title: UT “Fyrd”
proposals.description: Militia-line and Spearman-line cost no gold and can be trained at Town Centers.
proposals.historical_basis: Military obligations tied to land (one man per five hides) and mobilisation from the burhs (Richard Abels, Lordship and Military Obligation).

proposals.title: “Heregeld” bonus
proposals.description: Each Town Center generates a small trickle of gold, and tributes to allies pay no fee.
proposals.historical_basis: Late Saxon fiscal capacity: Æthelred's tributes (991–1012) and the heregeld that paid the lithsmen until 1051.

proposals.title: Rename Clerical Recruitment to “Boniface's Mission”
proposals.description: Keep the effect and add +10% speed to Monks.
proposals.historical_basis: The Anglo-Saxon missions to Frisia and Germany (Willibrord, Boniface, 7th–8th centuries).

contested: The scale and nature of the Anglo-Saxon migration (elite takeover vs. mass migration; 2022 ancient DNA).
The strength of the late Saxon state: James Campbell's “maximum view” vs. more cautious readings.
Whether the Anglo-Saxons ever used cavalry in battle (Richard Glover vs. Abels and Hooper).
The “select fyrd” model (C. Warren Hollister, 1962) vs. Richard Abels's critique.
Edward's designation of Harold and the alleged oath to William.
The use of the term “Anglo-Saxon” in contemporary academia.
The historicity of Hengist, Horsa and Cerdic.
The scale of the English presence in the Varangian Guard (Krijnie Ciggaar, Jonathan Shepard).

civs.represents: Two distinct entities merged under a single label. The first is the Franks proper: the 3rd-century Germanic confederation and the Merovingian (481–751) and Carolingian (751–987) kingdoms. The second is the Kingdom of France under the Capetians and Valois (987–1500). The design (heavy cavalry, castles, Ordonnance Companies) points mainly to France of the 11th–15th centuries and to Joan of Arc's campaign; only the unique unit harks back to the Merovingian Franks.
civs.period: c. 481 (Clovis) to c. 1500. The UU points to the 5th–7th centuries, the UT Ordonnance Companies to 1445.
civs.verdict: The core identity is solid: France as the cradle of the heavy knight, of chivalry as an ideal and of the stone castle. The Throwing Axeman (francisca) is one of the best-documented elements in the game, although it belongs to the 5th–7th centuries and not the 15th, and Ordonnance Companies ties in acceptably with the mounted archers of the 1445 companies. But two bonuses (Foragers, the team bonus's line of sight) are arbitrary, and the tech tree contradicts history: the Keep is missing from the land of the first stone donjons, and the Arbalester is missing from a kingdom with grand masters of the crossbowmen and francs-archers. The history text repeats the old myth of Charles Martel “converting” the Franks into cavalry to win at Poitiers, and of Poitiers as the definitive halt to Islam, and presents a thousand years of Frankish history as a teleological gestation of France.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Franks” merges the Franks and the French. After 987 (or as early as 843), the appropriate name is “French”. Even so, there is a partial defence: the Byzantines (Frangoi) and the Muslims (Ifranj, Firanja) called all Latins “Franks” during the Crusades. The Frankish kingdom gave rise not only to France but also to Germany (East Francia), Lotharingia and the Low Countries, so there is overlap with the Teutons and the Burgundians, and Charlemagne is claimed by both sides of the Rhine. The 15th-century Burgundians are a branch of the French royal house itself (Valois) and share the same institution with the Franks (ordonnance companies and coutiliers). Normandy, a French vassal duchy and the origin of the conquest of England, has no clear representation.

elements.explanation: It is faithful for France of the 11th–15th centuries: the knight as archetype and the Byzantine perception of the Frankish charge (Anna Komnene). It is plausible for the Carolingians: the capitulary of Thionville (805) required a mail shirt of anyone holding 12 manses, and there were the scarae. It does not apply to the Merovingians, whose armies were mainly infantry.
There is no identifiable historical link whatsoever.

Carolingian agrarian organisation is well documented: the bipartite estate and the polyptych of Irminon of Saint-Germain-des-Prés (c. 823–829). So is the spread of the three-field rotation and the heavy plough, although the chronology is contested. Later comes the banal mill, a seigneurial monopoly that peasants were obliged to use.

elements.element: Mounted Units +20% HP starting in Feudal Age
elements.explanation: An acceptable abstraction of the heavily armed French cavalry (gendarmes, barding).

The Loire valley was the cradle of the stone castle: Doué-la-Fontaine (c. 950), Langeais (994) and Loches (early 11th century). Fulk Nerra of Anjou was a prolific builder, and there is talk of a “castle revolution” around the year 1000 (Duby; a contested thesis). It does not hold for the Merovingians and Carolingians, who had almost no castles.

The francisca is well documented: Procopius (Wars VI.25, on the Frankish invasion of Italy in 539), Gregory of Tours, Isidore of Seville (who explains the name) and grave finds, including the tomb of Childeric I at Tournai. But it fell out of use around the 7th–8th centuries, so it is anachronistic for the medieval France that the rest of the design represents.

The institution is real: Charles VII's ordinance (1445) created 15 companies of 100 “lances”, each with a man-at-arms, a coutilier, a page and two mounted archers (some with bows, others with crossbows), plus a servant. It was the first standing army in the West. The link to mounted crossbowmen is defensible; the gold discount is a loose translation of an army paid for by a permanent tax (the taille), whose core was the heavy gendarmerie.
Chevalerie is an ideal of French origin (Chrétien de Troyes; Geoffroi de Charny's Livre de chevalerie, c. 1350). Faster Stables are a generic translation.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Knight-line +2 line of sight
elements.explanation: There is no identifiable historical basis.

tree_issues.problem: It is ironic. The earliest stone donjons in western Europe are in Franco-Angevin territory (Doué, Langeais, Loches), and Philip II spread the cylindrical “Philippine” towers (the Grosse Tour of the Louvre, c. 1190–1202). The Franks are the only civ in the group without the Keep.

France used crossbowmen en masse: the office of Grand Master of the Crossbowmen (13th century), urban crossbow militias, Genoese mercenaries and the francs-archers created by Charles VII in 1448. The idea that “the French don't shoot” is an Anglocentric stereotype born of Crécy. Curiously, the game gives them the Heavy Mounted Crossbowman and Cranequins, but not the Arbalester.
They are present, and rightly so. French artillery decided Formigny (1450) and Castillon (1453, with Jean Bureau), and Charles VIII's mobile artillery astonished Italy in 1494. It might deserve a UT.
It is appropriate: the term comes from Charlemagne's paladins (palatini, the Twelve Peers) in the Chanson de Roland. It becomes odd in civs with no connection to the Matter of France.
A minor inconsistency: the Paris guilds are codified in Étienne Boileau's Livre des métiers (c. 1268), and the Champagne fairs (12th–13th centuries) were Europe's great market.
It is defensible, but weak as an argument: many prestigious destriers came from Spain and Lombardy, although there was also breeding in France.

history_text_issues.claim: The Franks were supposedly a Germanic “tribe”.
history_text_issues.problem: Imprecision.
history_text_issues.correction: They were a confederation formed in the 3rd century, with Salians, Chamavi, Chattuarii, Bructeri and others.

history_text_issues.claim: They supposedly only began expanding into Roman Gaul in the early 5th century.
history_text_issues.problem: Chronology too late.
history_text_issues.correction: The Salian Franks had been settled as federates in Toxandria since 358 (Julian), and Frankish officers had served in the Roman army since the 4th century (Bauto, Arbogast).

history_text_issues.claim: Clovis supposedly defeated the last Roman armies, united the Franks by 509 and ruled “much of western Europe”.
history_text_issues.problem: Correct in essence, with an exaggeration and a central omission.
history_text_issues.correction: Clovis defeated Syagrius in 486 and the Visigoths at Vouillé (507), but he ruled most of Gaul, not of western Europe (Burgundy, Provence and Septimania lay outside his rule). His Catholic baptism is missing (date contested, between 496 and 508), which was decisive for the alliance with the Gallo-Roman bishops.

history_text_issues.claim: Over 1000 years, the Frankish kingdom supposedly gradually became modern France.
history_text_issues.problem: A teleological and national view.
history_text_issues.correction: The Frankish kingdom also gave rise to Germany (East Francia), Lotharingia, the Low Countries and the Kingdom of Italy. France is not its only heir.

history_text_issues.claim: By the end of the 7th century, the Merovingian kings were supposedly rulers in name only.
history_text_issues.problem: An image inherited from Carolingian propaganda.
history_text_issues.correction: The “rois fainéants” come mainly from Einhard's Vita Karoli. Paul Fouracre and Ian Wood put this image into perspective.

history_text_issues.claim: Charles Martel supposedly turned the Franks into a cavalry force.
history_text_issues.problem: An abandoned historiographical thesis.
history_text_issues.correction: Heinrich Brunner's thesis (1887), and later Lynn White's stirrup thesis (1962), have been widely rejected (Bernard Bachrach, 1970; Fouracre, 2000). Carolingian heavy cavalry developed gradually over the 8th–9th centuries.

history_text_issues.claim: His enemies supposedly called Charles “the Hammer”.
history_text_issues.problem: Unfounded origin of the epithet.
history_text_issues.correction: The epithet “Martellus” does not appear in contemporary sources; it emerges in later Carolingian chronicles, and nothing suggests that it was given by his enemies.

history_text_issues.claim: In 732, the Frankish cavalry supposedly won at Poitiers, halting the advance of Islam in the south-west forever.
history_text_issues.problem: A two-part myth.
history_text_issues.correction: First, the Franks fought on foot, in close formation: the Mozarabic Chronicle of 754 compares them to an immovable wall, like ice. Second, “forever” is an exaggeration. The date (732 or 733) is debated, and the expedition of Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi seems to have been aimed mainly at plunder. The Andalusis held Narbonne until 759, attacked Provence in the 730s and had the base of Fraxinetum from c. 890 to 973. The “saviour of Europe” reading owes much to Gibbon.

history_text_issues.claim: Pepin was supposedly made king by the pope in exchange for defending Italy from the Lombards.
history_text_issues.problem: A simplification of the sequence.
history_text_issues.correction: Pepin was elected and anointed at Soissons (751) with the assent of Pope Zachary, and anointed again by Stephen II at Saint-Denis (754). The campaigns against the Lombards (754–756) and the Donation of Pepin came afterwards.

history_text_issues.claim: Charlemagne, cultural renaissance and empire.
history_text_issues.problem: Significant omissions.
history_text_issues.correction: Missing are the imperial coronation in Rome (800), the Saxon Wars (772–804, with the Massacre of Verden in 782) and the campaigns against the Avars. The central figure of the “Carolingian renaissance” was an Anglo-Saxon, Alcuin of York.

history_text_issues.claim: Fiefs supposedly became hereditary and France was divided into independent feudal domains.
history_text_issues.problem: Uses the classic “feudal” model, now contested.
history_text_issues.correction: Elizabeth A. R. Brown (1974) and Susan Reynolds (1994) criticise the concept of “feudalism”. The capitulary of Quierzy (877) did not establish the general heritability of fiefs, although the fragmentation of power in the 10th–11th centuries is real.

history_text_issues.claim: Hugh Capet was supposedly elected in 987 because his Parisian fief was weak.
history_text_issues.problem: Misleading.
history_text_issues.correction: The Robertians were the most powerful family in West Francia: they had provided kings in 888 (Odo) and 922 (Robert I), and Hugh's father was “dux Francorum”. Part of that power had been dispersed to counts such as those of Blois and Anjou, but the election, led by Archbishop Adalbero of Reims, did not choose a weakling. The “weakness” of the royal domain is mainly a later reading.

history_text_issues.claim: The Estates General supposedly had no real power.
history_text_issues.problem: Exaggeration.
history_text_issues.correction: First convened in 1302, the Estates General tried to control taxation in 1355–58 (Étienne Marcel; Great Ordinance of 1357).

history_text_issues.claim: General omissions in the text.
history_text_issues.problem: Key milestones are missing.
history_text_issues.correction: Missing are the Crusades, largely French (1096–99; Louis VII, Philip II, Louis IX), Bouvines (1214), the Albigensian Crusade, the Gothic style (Saint-Denis, 1140s), Cluny, Joan of Arc and the military reforms of Charles VII.

missing_features: The Franks of the 5th–7th centuries: the angon (a barbed javelin described by Agathias) and shock infantry.
Carolingian institutions: capitularies, missi dominici, scarae, and the “palace school”.
The Crusades and the military orders (the Templars were founded by the Champenois knight Hugh de Payens, c. 1120).
Gothic architecture and the cathedral builders.
The Champagne fairs and 12th–13th-century trade.
The francs-archers (1448) and Charles VII's royal artillery (the Bureau brothers).
Royal administration (baillis, the Parlement of Paris, the permanent taille).
Cluny and monastic reform.

proposals.title: Split “Franks” (481–987) and “French” (987–1500)
proposals.description: The Franks keep the Throwing Axeman, a Carolingian UU and infantry and elite cavalry bonuses. The French get heavy cavalry, castles, Ordonnance Companies and artillery. Alternatively, rename the current civ to “French”.
proposals.historical_basis: They are two realities separated by half a millennium, with different armies, societies and languages.

proposals.title: Give the Keep and a “Philippine Towers” UT
proposals.description: Add the Keep to the tech tree. The UT gives Castles and Keeps +20% HP and +1 range.
proposals.historical_basis: The first stone donjons (Langeais, Loches) and the cylindrical towers of Philip Augustus.

proposals.title: Give the Arbalester and a “Francs-Archers” UT
proposals.description: The Archer-line costs -50% gold and can be trained at Town Centers.
proposals.historical_basis: Charles VII's ordinance (28 April 1448): each parish, or group of 50 to 80 hearths, had to provide an equipped archer, who trained on Sundays and was exempt from the taille.

proposals.title: “Bureau Brothers” UT
proposals.description: Bombard Cannons move +25% faster and reload +20% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: Jean and Gaspard Bureau organised the royal artillery that recovered Normandy (1449–50) and decided Castillon (1453).

proposals.title: Replace the Foragers bonus with “Champagne Fairs”
proposals.description: Market: exchange rate -X% and Trade Carts +10% gold.
proposals.historical_basis: The Champagne fairs (Troyes, Provins, Lagny, Bar-sur-Aube) were the centre of European trade in the 12th–13th centuries.

proposals.title: Carolingian UU “Scara”
proposals.description: In the separate “Franks” civ: elite cavalry in mail shirts, tough and expensive, available in the Castle Age. The Throwing Axeman can gain an angon attack.
proposals.historical_basis: The scarae of the Royal Frankish Annals and the capitularies on the equipment of horsemen (Thionville, 805).

proposals.title: Team Bonus “Oriflamme”
proposals.description: Replace +2 line of sight with “allied Knight-line and Monks +X conversion resistance”.
proposals.historical_basis: The Oriflamme of Saint-Denis, the sacred banner of the French monarchy, and the Capetian–Church bond that the text itself emphasises.

contested: The theses of Brunner and of Lynn White (cavalry and the stirrup as the origin of feudalism) vs. Bachrach and Fouracre.
The date (732 or 733), aim and significance of Poitiers.
The image of the Merovingian “rois fainéants”.
The “feudal mutation” of the year 1000 (Duby, Bois and Bonnassie vs. Barthélemy; the debate in Past & Present, 1994–97).
The date of Clovis's baptism (496, 498/99 or 508).
The speed at which the three-field rotation and the heavy plough spread.
key_sources: Gregory of Tours, Decem Libri Historiarum
Procopius, Wars; Agathias, Histories
Chronicle of Fredegar and its continuations; Mozarabic Chronicle of 754
Einhard, Vita Karoli Magni; Annales regni Francorum
Carolingian capitularies (MGH)
Bernard S. Bachrach, Merovingian Military Organization (1972) and Early Carolingian Warfare (2001)
Edward James, The Franks (1988); Ian Wood, The Merovingian Kingdoms 450–751 (1994)
Paul Fouracre, The Age of Charles Martel (2000)
Philippe Contamine, Guerre, État et société à la fin du Moyen Âge (1972) and La guerre au Moyen Âge (1980)
Jean Dunbabin, France in the Making 843–1180
Susan Reynolds, Fiefs and Vassals (1994)

civs.represents: The Valois dukes' “Burgundian State” (1363–1477): a dynastic conglomerate that joined the Duchy and the County (Franche-Comté) of Burgundy to Flanders, Artois, Brabant, Hainaut, Holland, Zeeland, Luxembourg and others. The wealth and most of the population were in the Low Countries. The name also evokes the Germanic Burgundians of the 5th–6th centuries (kingdom of Worms and later of the Rhône), with no ethnic continuity whatsoever with the Valois State.
civs.period: Design: c. 1384 (Philip the Bold inherits Flanders) to 1477 (death of Charles the Bold at Nancy). History text: 411–1477.
civs.verdict: This is a clearly researched DE design. The early economic wealth, gunpowder (ducal artillery), the Coustillier, the Flemish militia and the Pinot Noir vineyards protected by Philip the Bold all have a solid basis. The weak points are Flemish Revolution, which inverts history (the Flemish revolts were almost always against the count or the duke), and a stretched team bonus (relics generating food). The tech tree denies the Burgundians what most characterised them: crossbowmen and archers (including English ones) in the ordinance companies, and siege engineering (they lack Siege Engineers). The history text is good overall, but it has a clear error (Mary as Philip's daughter instead of Charles's), attributes Joan of Arc's capture and sale to Philip, and calls Charles the Bold's royal project a “delusion”.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Burgundians” covers more than a thousand years and four distinct realities: the East Germanic people (Worms, c. 413–436; Sapaudia/Rhône, 443–534), the Kingdom of Burgundy/Arles (888–1032, later imperial), the Capetian duchy (1032–1361) and the Valois State (1363–1477). The design represents only the last, whose subjects were mostly Dutch-speaking Flemings, Brabanters and Hollanders; some historians (Blockmans and Prevenier) therefore speak of the “Burgundian Netherlands”. The overlap with the Franks is large: the Valois dukes of Burgundy were a branch of the French royal house, fought in the Hundred Years' War, and the ordinance companies and the coutiliers existed first in France (1445). The Burgundian inheritance passed to the Habsburgs and from them to Spain (the Cross of Burgundy on Spanish flags), which links this civ to the Spanish and to the Teutons/Holy Roman Empire.

elements.explanation: Burgundian chivalric culture was real: the Order of the Golden Fleece (1430), Jacques de Lalaing's pas d'armes and the gendarmes of the ordinance companies. But Charles the Bold's armies were combined-arms forces, with English archers, Italian condottieri, pikemen and a huge artillery train. The decisive defeats came from Swiss infantry.

elements.element: Economic upgrades available one age earlier and cost -40% food
elements.explanation: A good abstraction. The Low Countries were the most urbanised and commercial region north of the Alps: Bruges, Ghent, Ypres, Antwerp. The word “bourse” is linked to the house of the Van der Beurse family in Bruges, where a branch of the Medici bank and a Hanseatic Kontor operated.
A generic reinforcement of the cavalry identity, with no specific basis.

elements.element: Cavalier upgrade available in Castle Age
elements.explanation: It suggests an “early” heavy cavalry, but the Burgundian standing companies (Abbeville, 1471) came 26 years after the French ones (1445). The possible link is the tournament culture and the wealth that paid for good equipment.

The dukes assembled one of the largest artillery parks in Europe (Smith and DeVries, 2005), with bombards such as Mons Meg (Mons, 1449), and included couleuvriniers in the ordinances. Caveats: the other great Flemish bombard, Dulle Griet, was used in 1452 by rebel Ghent against Oudenaarde, that is, against the duke; and the ducal artillery did not prevent the defeats of 1476–77, much of it being captured at Grandson.

The coutilier existed: a member of the “lance” armed with the coustille (a long knife or short sword), provided for in the Burgundian ordinances of 1471–73. But he also existed in the French companies from 1445, and was a lighter auxiliary than the man-at-arms. The “powerful charge” is a game invention.

The Flemish urban militias with goedendags and pikes defeated the French cavalry at Courtrai (the Golden Spurs, 1302), before Burgundian rule. They served the dukes (at the siege of Calais in 1436, which the Ghent and Bruges militias ended up abandoning), but became more famous for fighting them: Ghent was crushed at Gavere in 1453.

Cistercian monastic viticulture (Clos de Vougeot, linked to Cîteaux, founded in 1098) is well documented, and Philip the Bold banned the Gamay grape variety in favour of Pinot Noir by the ordinance of 1395. Wine was a prestige and export product. The caveat is that ducal revenue came mainly from the Low Countries.

The Flemish revolts were real and numerous: the Bruges Matins (1302), the peasant revolt in coastal Flanders (1323–28), Ghent under Philip van Artevelde (1379–85), Bruges (1436–38) and Ghent (1449–53). But they were directed against the count or the duke; Philip the Bold himself fought the rebels at Roosebeke (1382). They were mostly revolts of urban artisans (weavers, fullers). Giving the duke a technology that turns his peasants into militia inverts historical loyalty.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Relics generate food in addition to gold
elements.explanation: Burgundy was the heart of reformed monasticism (Cluny, 910; Cîteaux, 1098), with monasteries that were agrarian powers (Cistercian granges), and of pilgrimages such as Vézelay, with relics attributed to Mary Magdalene. The “relic generates food” link is weak.

tree_issues.item: Arbalester, Ring Archer Armor, Heavy Mounted Crossbowman and Cranequins (missing)
tree_issues.problem: Ranged infantry was essential. According to the usual reconstruction (Vaughan), the lance of the 1471–73 ordinances included, besides the man-at-arms, the coustillier and the page, three mounted archers as well as a crossbowman, a couleuvrinier and a pikeman on foot (the exact composition is debated). Charles the Bold hired large contingents of English archers, and the Flemish cities had crossbowmen's guilds (Sint-Joris). This is the most ahistorical gap in the tech tree.

tree_issues.item: Siege Engineers, Siege Ram, Heavy Scorpion (missing)
tree_issues.problem: This is inconsistent with the reputation of ducal siege engineering and artillery: the siege of Neuss (1474–75) and the campaigns against Dinant (1466) and Liège (1467–68).
Minor, but Philip the Good maintained a fleet based at Sluis and sent crusading galleys to the Mediterranean and the Black Sea (Waleran de Wavrin's expedition, 1444–45).

tree_issues.item: Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon, Bombard Tower, Elite Cannon Galleon, Paladin
tree_issues.problem: These are present and suit 15th-century Burgundy.

history_text_issues.claim: The Burgundians supposedly crossed the Rhine and became federates from 411.
history_text_issues.problem: Minor inaccuracy.
history_text_issues.correction: In 411 they supported the usurper Jovinus at Mainz. Their settlement as federates on the left bank of the Rhine (traditionally at Worms) dates from c. 413.

history_text_issues.claim: The survivors supposedly “carved out” another kingdom on the upper Rhône.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits that they were settled by Rome.
history_text_issues.correction: Aetius resettled them as federates in Sapaudia (c. 443). Only later did they expand the kingdom to Lyon and the Rhône valley.

history_text_issues.claim: Gundobad (452–516) was supposedly a devout Christian.
history_text_issues.problem: Not false, but it omits the essential point and presents a conjectural date as certain.
history_text_issues.correction: Gundobad was a Homoian (“Arian”) Christian, although close to the Catholic bishop Avitus of Vienne; it was his son Sigismund who converted to Catholicism and refounded Saint-Maurice d'Agaune (515). His date of birth is conjectural. The text also omits that he was a Roman magister militum and made Glycerius emperor (473).

history_text_issues.claim: Gundobad's code supposedly reconciled Germanic norms and Roman law.
history_text_issues.problem: Simplification.
history_text_issues.correction: There was a dual system: the Liber Constitutionum (Lex Gundobada) and a Lex Romana Burgundionum for Roman subjects.

history_text_issues.claim: Rudolph was supposedly elected “King of France” in 923.
history_text_issues.problem: Terminological anachronism.
history_text_issues.correction: He was elected king of West Francia (rex Francorum). “France” as the name of the kingdom is later.

history_text_issues.claim: The history jumps from the Burgundian kingdom to the duchy.
history_text_issues.problem: A significant omission, especially for a Portuguese audience.
history_text_issues.correction: Missing are the Kingdom of Burgundy (888) and of Arles (933), absorbed by the Empire in 1032, and the County of Burgundy (Franche-Comté). Also missing is the Capetian duchy (1032–1361), whose house produced Count Henry of Burgundy, father of Afonso Henriques and founder of the first Portuguese dynasty.

history_text_issues.claim: Monastic culture supposedly flourished under Burgundian patronage.
history_text_issues.problem: Partly wrong attribution.
history_text_issues.correction: Cluny was founded (910) by William I, Duke of Aquitaine, albeit on Burgundian territory. Cîteaux (1098) was founded by Robert of Molesme, with the support of Duke Odo I.

history_text_issues.claim: Burgundy was supposedly a crossroads between France, Spain, Italy and Germany.
history_text_issues.problem: Spain does not border Burgundy.
history_text_issues.correction: The Saône–Rhône axis linked France, the Empire and Italy (through the Alpine passes of Savoy).

history_text_issues.claim: Philip the Bold supposedly acquired “influence” in Flanders through marriage.
history_text_issues.problem: It understates what was obtained.
history_text_issues.correction: He married Margaret of Male (1369) and, on his father-in-law's death in 1384, the couple inherited Flanders, Artois, the Franche-Comté, Nevers and Rethel. Flanders remained a fief of the French Crown and the Franche-Comté a fief of the Empire.

history_text_issues.claim: John the Fearless was supposedly assassinated “immediately” after taking Paris.
history_text_issues.problem: Wrong chronology and omission of the cause.
history_text_issues.correction: The Burgundians took Paris in May 1418, and John was killed on the bridge at Montereau on 10 September 1419, during a meeting with the Dauphin Charles, 15 months later. The text omits that the civil war began with the assassination of Louis of Orléans (1407), ordered by John himself.

history_text_issues.claim: Philip the Good's alliance with the English was supposedly “previously unthinkable”.
history_text_issues.problem: Exaggeration.
history_text_issues.correction: John the Fearless had already negotiated with Henry V (Calais, 1416). The alliance was formalised in the Treaty of Troyes (1420).

history_text_issues.claim: Philip supposedly captured Joan of Arc and sold her to the English in 1430.
history_text_issues.problem: Simplified attribution.
history_text_issues.correction: Joan was captured at Compiègne (23 May 1430) by men of John of Luxembourg (the Bastard of Wandonne), Philip's vassal and ally, and it was John of Luxembourg who sold her to the English for 10,000 livres. Philip was the overlord, was at the siege and visited her, but he was neither the captor nor the seller.

history_text_issues.claim: The Burgundian army supposedly had great success thanks to cutting-edge technology and mostly professional forces.
history_text_issues.problem: Exaggeration.
history_text_issues.correction: The standing army only existed from 1471. Before that, the dukes relied on feudal levies, militias and mercenaries. The record is mixed: Montlhéry (1465) was indecisive, Neuss (1474–75) failed, and then came the disasters of Grandson, Morat and Nancy.

history_text_issues.claim: Military power supposedly bred in Charles the Bold a “delusion” of kingship.
history_text_issues.problem: Disparaging framing.
history_text_issues.correction: The crown was seriously negotiated with Emperor Frederick III at Trier (September to November 1473) and came close to being granted. In context, it was a rational dynastic project.

history_text_issues.claim: A failed invasion of the Swiss Confederacy supposedly culminated in his death.
history_text_issues.problem: Geographical and sequential simplification.
history_text_issues.correction: The 1476 campaign targeted Swiss (chiefly Bernese) positions in Savoyard Vaud, with the defeats at Grandson and Morat. Charles died later, at Nancy (5 January 1477), against René II of Lorraine and his Swiss mercenaries.

history_text_issues.claim: Maximilian supposedly married “Philip's daughter Mary”.
history_text_issues.problem: Factual error.
history_text_issues.correction: Mary of Burgundy (1457–1482) was the daughter of Charles the Bold and Isabella of Bourbon, and the granddaughter of Philip the Good.

history_text_issues.claim: General omissions in the text.
history_text_issues.problem: Central figures and facts are missing.
history_text_issues.correction: Missing is Isabella of Portugal, daughter of John I, wife of Philip the Good, mother of Charles the Bold and an active diplomat: the Golden Fleece was founded during the celebrations of her wedding in Bruges (1430). Also missing are Nicopolis (1396), Flemish painting (Van Eyck was Philip's valet de chambre) and the Feast of the Pheasant (1454).

missing_features: The Order of the Golden Fleece (1430) and court culture (pas d'armes, the Feast of the Pheasant, 1454).
The English mercenary archers and the pikemen, whom Charles tried to organise on the Swiss model.
The urban crossbowmen's and archers' guilds (schutterijen) of the Low Countries.
The textile and financial economy (Flemish drapery, Bruges and Antwerp, the Hansa, Italian banks) expressed as trade.
State administration: the Chambres des comptes in Dijon and Lille, the Parlement of Mechelen (1473), the States General of the Low Countries (1464).
The arts: Flemish painting, Arras and Tournai tapestries, music of the Franco-Flemish school.
Crusading ambitions: Nicopolis (1396), the fleet of the 1440s, the Vow of the Pheasant.
The dynastic link to Portugal: Henry of Burgundy, Isabella of Portugal, and the half-Portuguese Charles the Bold.

proposals.title: Replace Flemish Revolution with “Schutterij” (crossbowmen's guilds)
proposals.description: Give Arbalester to the tech tree. The UT allows Arbalesters and Flemish Militia to be trained at Town Centers, at -30% cost.
proposals.historical_basis: The crossbowmen's guilds (Sint-Joris) and archers' guilds of the Flemish and Brabantine cities supplied armed contingents to urban and ducal armies.

proposals.title: UT “Charles's Ordinances” (the lance of 1471–73)
proposals.description: Each Castle spawns a “lance”: Coustillier, Knight, Mounted Crossbowman, Hand Cannoneer and Pikeman. It reuses the unit-spawning mechanism of the Sicilians' First Crusade.
proposals.historical_basis: The ordinances of Abbeville (1471), Bohain (1472) and Saint-Maximin de Trier (1473), which fixed the mixed composition of the Burgundian lance.

proposals.title: UT “English Archers”
proposals.description: Allows Longbowmen to be trained at the Archery Range.
proposals.historical_basis: Charles the Bold recruited English archers, the elite of his infantry (Vaughan), present at Neuss and Morat, following the alliance with Edward IV (marriage to Margaret of York, 1468).

proposals.title: UT or bonus “Order of the Golden Fleece”
proposals.description: Knight-line and Coustilliers +15% HP, and Relics generate +X% gold. Replaces the relic team bonus with something more coherent.
proposals.historical_basis: The Order of the Golden Fleece, founded by Philip the Good in Bruges (1430) as an instrument of cohesion for the nobility of his territories.

proposals.title: Bonus “Bruges Bourse”
proposals.description: Replace “Stable technologies -50%” with: Market fee -X%, Trade Carts and Trade Cogs +15% gold.
proposals.historical_basis: Bruges and later Antwerp as European entrepôts (Ter Beurze, Hansa, Medici).

proposals.title: Give Siege Engineers and UT “Great Bombards”
proposals.description: Add Siege Engineers to the tech tree. The UT gives Bombard Cannons +1 range and +25% damage against buildings.
proposals.historical_basis: The great ducal bombards (Mons Meg) and the artillery park studied by Smith and DeVries.

proposals.title: Team Bonus “Gravelines Mercantile Truces”
proposals.description: As a discussion exercise linked to Portugal: Trade Carts and Trade Cogs trading with allies yield +10% gold, and tributes between allies pay no fee.
proposals.historical_basis: Isabella of Portugal led the Anglo-Burgundian conferences at Gravelines (1439), which restored trade between England and Flanders, and negotiated the release of Charles of Orléans (1440) (Monique Sommé).

contested: Whether the Burgundian State was a viable “quasi-kingdom” or an ephemeral dynastic construct (Vaughan and Schnerb vs. Blockmans and Prevenier); Huizinga's “Autumn of the Middle Ages” thesis is also debated.
The exact composition of the 1471–73 lance: whether crossbowmen, couleuvriniers and pikemen were members of the lance or separate companies.
The extent of a Burgundian “military revolution” in the 15th century.
The number of artillery pieces lost at Grandson (the popular figures of c. 400 are not well confirmed).
The degree of Philip the Good's responsibility for the handing over of Joan of Arc.
Whether John's epithet “sans Peur” comes from Nicopolis (1396) or from Othée (1408).
The origin and dating of the Dulle Griet.
