groups.cross_civ_notes:
1) Britons and Saxons. With The Viking Sagas (update 185872), England has two civs, and the two history texts narrate the same period and the same battle (Stamford Bridge and Hastings, 1066). The logical division would be Saxons = 450–1066 and Britons renamed “English” = 1066–1500. A whole layer is missing, the Normans: Anglo-Norman England and the duchy of Normandy itself. The Sicilians cover only the Normans of Italy.

2) The Britons/Celts inversion. The real Britons (Welsh, Cornish, Bretons) are inside the “Celts”, while the English use the name “Britons”. Edward I's army relied in part on Welsh soldiers, many of them archers (Falkirk, 1298), but the Celts do not even have Arbalester. The Bretons, who were relevant in the Hundred Years' War (du Guesclin), do not exist in the game.

3) Huscarls. The Huskarl is still the Goths' UU, but huscarls are an 11th-century Anglo-Scandinavian reality (the guards of Cnut and of Harold). In the current game, the bodyguard tradition appears in the Saxons' Hearth Troop and in the regional unit Varangian Guard (Byzantines, Danes, Saxons, Varangians, Vikings); the Danes' UU is the Jomsviking.

4) Regional units of The Viking Sagas pack. Mounted Crossbowman, Heavy Mounted Crossbowman and Cranequins were distributed in a not very historical way: the Saxons (before 1066) and the Celts have the heavy version, and the Saxons, Britons and Franks have Cranequins. The Burgundians, whose ordonnances included crossbowmen, have neither the heavy version, nor Cranequins, nor Arbalester. The Carrack is inverted too: the Britons do not have it, but the Saxons and Celts do.

5) Gunpowder. The Saxons, consistently, have no gunpowder. The Britons and Celts also lack Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon (they have only Cannon Galleon), which is unhistorical for the 15th century (Henry V at Harfleur; Mons Meg and the death of James II at Roxburgh, 1460). The Franks and Burgundians have it, and rightly so.

6) Franks, Burgundians and Teutons. The 15th-century Burgundians are a branch of the French Valois. The Burgundians' Coustillier and the Franks' UT Ordonnance Companies come from the same institution (the ordonnance lance, French in 1445 and Burgundian in 1471). The first Burgundians were conquered by the Franks (534). The Carolingian heritage is shared with the Teutons (East Francia), and the Burgundian heritage passes to the Habsburgs and to Spain (Cross of Burgundy).

7) Franks and Saxons. The continental Saxons were subjugated by Charlemagne (772–804), and the name “Saxons” could legitimately designate them. The central figure of the Carolingian Renaissance was an Anglo-Saxon, Alcuin of York, and the Anglo-Saxon missionaries (Willibrord, Boniface) worked under Frankish protection.

8) Paladin. The name comes from Charlemagne's paladins: consistent for the Franks, less so for other civs.

9) Links to Portugal, useful for the user. The first Portuguese dynasty is Burgundian (Count Henry of Burgundy, father of Afonso Henriques). Isabella of Portugal was Duchess of Burgundy, and the Order of the Golden Fleece was founded at her wedding (1430). Charles the Bold was half Portuguese. The Celts' text also simplifies pre-Roman Iberia, which included the Lusitanians, whose Celtic affiliation is debated.

10) Auld Alliance and Mons Meg. Scotland (Celts) and France (Franks) were allied from 1295, and Burgundy gave artillery to Scotland. These are diplomatic links that the design ignores.

11) Common pattern. All five civs receive the generic late-medieval tree (Halberdier, Champion, Galleon), which is an engine convention. But where the game makes active choices (bonuses, UTs, regional units), the weakest choices are those that import stereotypes: Celts with blue paint and siege engines, French unable to use the crossbow, and Saxons with castles and arrows. Conversely, the most recent elements (Saxons, Burgundians) show that the DE designers did more research than in 1999.

Method note: the web search for this review reached the search limit; some details (the exact proportions of the English army at Agincourt, the number of English archers in the service of Charles the Bold, the first attestation of the epithet “Martellus”) were therefore phrased more cautiously rather than confirmed.

verification_log.change: Agincourt: the ratio of c. 5 archers per man-at-arms was attributed to Anne Curry; corrected to Sumption, Barker and Rogers, with Curry's higher estimate (c. 9,000) given separately and the topic added to contested.
Harfleur: removed the bombard name “London”, which could not be confirmed; kept “Messenger” and “King's Daughter”, with the mention of c. 12 great bombards.

Carrack: the Grace Dieu (1418) was not a carrack in the strict sense; rewritten to refer to the carracks captured at the battle of the Seine (1416) and to the Grace Dieu as a great ship designed to rival them.
Danegeld: the claim that the text mixes periods was qualified, because the Chronicle already records in 865 a promise of money from the men of Kent in exchange for peace; severity reduced to minor.

Alfred “the only one called the Great”: “This is false” became “debatable”, because Cnut was not English and Alfred is the only native king with the epithet; the late dating of the epithet was kept (13th century, popularised in the 16th).
Hundred Years' War: “inverts cause and consequence” became “simplification”, because Edward III asserted his claim as early as 1337; severity reduced to minor.

Added flaws in the text that had been left out: Scotland in 800 was not all “Celtic” (Lothian was Northumbrian), Harald “harðráði” is mistranslated, Fulford is omitted and the conquest is shortened to “two years” (resistance lasted until 1070–71).
Yeomen: dates of the Assize of Arms corrected (1181, renewed in 1242 and 1252); the link to the Yeomen Warders is now marked as speculation. “Great Custom” became the “Ancient Custom” of 1275.
Mounted Crossbowman: added that there were English crossbowmen in garrisons and armies, to avoid suggesting they were entirely absent.
Furor Celtica reclassified from stretched to anachronistic: the name is a commonplace from Antiquity (Polybius, Lucan) and the effect on siege engines has no basis whatsoever.

Lumberjacks: removed the claim that medieval Ireland was already heavily deforested (Irish woodlands remained important until the 16th–17th centuries); added that the Celts do not even have Two-Man Saw.
Paladin: Gerald of Wales says that the Irish rode without saddle or spurs; the reference to stirrups was removed.
Mons Meg: the date of the gift to James II became “between 1454 and 1457”, because the sources differ.
Braveheart: removed the categorical claim that the epithet is associated with Bruce; it now says that it has no medieval basis for Wallace and is sometimes associated with Bruce's heart.
Added the “Hammer of the Scots” error: the inscription “Scotorum Malleus” on Edward I's tomb dates from the 16th century (Abbot Feckenham).
“Current form in the 11th century” qualified: true for the mainland core (Lothian, Strathclyde), false for the islands and Berwick. “Northern Europe” reduced to minor.
Clontarf: removed the claim that the Dublin Norse were “mostly Norwegian” (a debated question, Downham); added to contested.

Infantry speed: added that Scottish raids depended on moving on horseback (Jean le Bel, 1327). Verdict corrected from “three bonuses and a UT” for siege to two bonuses (one of them a team bonus) and a UT. Carlisle 1315: added the ineffective catapult, in addition to the siege tower that got bogged down.

Galloglass proposal: the 1259 date was made more precise as the dowry of 160 Hebridean warriors received by Áed Ó Conchobair. Schiltron proposal corrected, because Falkirk was a defeat for the schiltrons.
1055 episode: “contrary to custom” comes from John of Worcester; the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says only that the English fled because they were on horseback. Attribution corrected.
Orderic Vitalis: his comment explains the weak English resistance after 1066, not the defeat at Hastings; context corrected.
Team bonus: added that “trinoda necessitas” is a mistaken modern reading; “select fyrd” is now marked as a contested model (Hollister vs. Abels), and the proposal was renamed “Fyrd”.
Hengist and Horsa: severity reduced to minor, because the sources themselves use “Saxones” generically. Added Cerdic's Brittonic name.
Longships: added that the Chronicle says Alfred's ships followed neither the Danish nor the Frisian model. Burhs: added the later stone facing of some of them, which makes the game text less wrong.
Shield Wall: removed the term “scildweall”, whose attestation could not be confirmed; kept the “bordweall” of Brunanburh.
Removed the spurious error “the empire coalesced into two parts”: after Meerssen (870) and Ribemont (880), the division into West and East Francia is an acceptable summary.
“Martellus” epithet: removed the unconfirmed claim that it appears in 9th-century sources; changed to “later Carolingian chronicles”.

Ordonnance Companies: explanation rewritten, because the mounted archers of the companies used the bow or the crossbow, which makes the link to the Mounted Crossbowmen defensible; removed the idea that the effect was “the opposite” of the institution.
Hugh Capet: qualified (part of the Robertian power had dispersed to Blois and Anjou). Added the exaggeration of Clovis as lord of “much of western Europe”.

Francs-Archers proposal: basis corrected according to the ordinance of 28 April 1448 (one archer per parish or per group of 50 to 80 hearths, exempt from the taille). Bureau UT: Formigny replaced by the reconquest of Normandy, because the role of the Bureaus at Formigny is less direct.
Tech tree: added that the Franks have Heavy Mounted Crossbowman and Cranequins but not Arbalester; Bloodlines qualified.
Dulle Griet: no longer presented as a ducal bombard, because it was used in 1452 by rebel Ghent against Oudenaarde, that is, against the duke; it became an ironic caveat.
Inheritance of 1384: removed the expression “in full sovereignty”, because Flanders was a French fief and the Franche-Comté an imperial fief.
English archers: removed the figure “thousands”, which could not be confirmed; changed to “significant contingents” (Vaughan).

Severity reduced in three cases: Mary as Philip's daughter (from major to moderate, an isolated genealogical error), the capture of Joan of Arc (from moderate to minor, a simplified attribution) and the “invasion of Switzerland” (from moderate to minor, because the 1476 campaign did in fact target Bernese positions).
Gundobad as a “devout Christian”: reduced to minor and qualified (it is not false; he was a Homoian, but close to Avitus of Vienne).

The weak proposal “Isabella's Court” was replaced by the team bonus “Gravelines Mercantile Truces”, based on the documented role of Isabella of Portugal in the 1439 conferences. Added Cranequins to the list of missing items.

Cross-civ notes: corrected note 3 (the Danes' UU is the Jomsviking, not a huscarl; the Varangian Guard is a regional unit shared by five civs), confirmed the update number (185872) in the repository and added the method note on the search limit.

civs.represents: The Christian kingdoms of the Iberian Peninsula (Asturias/León, Castile, Crown of Aragon/Catalonia, Navarre) and, above all, the composite monarchy of the Catholic Monarchs and Charles V. In practice, the game's design portrays the imperial Castile/Spain of the Granada War, the Italian Wars and the conquest of the Americas.
civs.period: c. 718 (Covadonga) – 1556 (abdication of Charles V); the design concentrates on c. 1480–1550.
civs.verdict: The Spanish design portrays the Spain of 1480–1550 (gunpowder, conquistadors, missionaries, Inquisition) and almost ignores the eight medieval Iberian centuries that AoE2's time frame should cover. There are good abstractions: cheap metalworking (Biscayan iron, Toledo steel), firearms for the end of the period, and trade. But both unique units post-date 1519 and are poorly characterised (Cortés's horsemen fought with the lance, the friars went on foot), Inquisition inverts the real function of the institution, the gold-per-technology bonus has no basis, and the absence of Crossbowman/Arbalester (only the Spanish and Bulgarians, out of 56 civs, lack it) contradicts one of the best-documented military hallmarks of Christian Iberia. Missing are the light cavalry riding a la jineta, the almogavars, the military orders, and Catalan-Aragonese and Castilian naval power. The history text has chronological inaccuracies ('within 50 years', 'unification' in 1469) and rests on a framework of continuous 'Reconquista' that is now much debated.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Spanish” is an anachronistic label for most of the Middle Ages. 'Hispania/España' was a geographical term, and the political entities were Asturias-León, Castile, Navarre, Aragon, the Catalan counties and Portugal. A 'Spanish' monarchy exists only as a dynastic union from 1479 onwards, and institutional unification begins only with the Nueva Planta decrees (1707–1716), which even so left out Navarre and the Basque provinces. The design, built on Conquistador, Missionary, Inquisition, Supremacy and Cannon Galleon, lies almost entirely after 1492, outside the ~500–1500 frame. The label also conflates 'Spain' with Castile: the Crown of Aragon, with its Mediterranean empire, barely appears, and Navarre and the Basques do not appear at all. There is also overlap with other civs: the text talks about al-Andalus, but in the game that world belongs to the Berbers and Saracens; the Visigoths are diluted into the Goths; Iberian a la jineta cavalry exists only as the Berbers' Genitour.

elements.explanation: Gunpowder is defensible for the end of the period. Castilian artillery was decisive in the Granada War (1482–1492), with the artillery train organised by Francisco Ramírez de Madrid, and Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba won at Cerignola (1503) with entrenched arquebusiers. The religious component is also real: Reconquista as crusade, military orders, Catholic Monarchs. But the label describes the Spain of 1480–1550 and not medieval Iberia, whose military hallmark was cavalry (heavy, and light 'a la jineta') supported by crossbowmen.
It can be linked to Castile as a 'land of castles' and to the repoblación with fortified frontier towns, but there is nothing specifically Hispanic about building speed. It is mainly balance.

elements.element: Receive +20 gold for each technology researched
elements.explanation: It has no identifiable historical anchor. If the inspiration is American silver (Potosí 1545, Zacatecas 1546), it is anachronistic (much later than 1500) and had nothing to do with research; read as 'royal patronage', it is generic and applicable to any monarchy. It is a balance bonus.

A reasonable abstraction. Biscayan iron (Basque ferrerías) was exported in bulk to England and Flanders, and Toledo blades were famous, especially in the 15th–16th centuries. Abundant, cheap metalworking is a real trait.

Arquebusiers in Spanish service distinguished themselves in the Italian Wars (Cerignola 1503, Bicocca 1522, Pavia 1525), and the tercios (1534–1536) codified the combination of pike and arquebus. But almost all of this is after 1500. The Peninsula has some of the earliest European references to gunpowder, above all on the Nasrid side (Huéscar 1324, Algeciras 1342–1344), but in the 15th century the centres of innovation in portable firearms were Italy, Burgundy, Bohemia and the German world.

elements.element: Cannon Galleons fire more accurately at moving targets
elements.explanation: The galleon is a 16th-century ship (developed mainly from the 1530s–1540s onwards), and Spanish naval artillery had no reputation for accuracy: in 1588 the Armada showed a lower rate of fire than the English, with heterogeneous guns and poorly suited carriages (Martin and Parker). In the medieval period, Iberian naval power meant the Catalan-Aragonese galleys of Roger of Lauria and the Castilian galleys (Ambrosio Bocanegra's victory over the English fleet at La Rochelle, 1372).

The figure is real and emblematic, but there are two problems. First, it belongs to 1519–1550, outside the medieval frame (although The Conquerors expansion extended the game to those decades). Second, the conquistador horsemen fought with lance and sword, and firearms were few and carried by infantry: according to Bernal Díaz, Cortés's expedition (1519) had 16 horses, 13 arquebusiers and 32 crossbowmen. The mounted arquebusier did exist, but it appears in the Italian Wars (1520s–1540s) and is not the characteristic type of the American conquistador.

Missionaries in the Americas were mostly mendicants (Franciscans, Dominicans, later Jesuits). The Franciscan Rule of 1223 forbids riding on horseback except in case of necessity or illness, and the Franciscan 'Twelve Apostles' of 1524 walked from Veracruz to Mexico City. Mounted missionaries appear later on the northern frontiers of New Spain (the Jesuit Eusebio Kino, 1680s–1700s), already outside the period. In medieval Iberia there were mounted religious: the brethren of the military orders (Calatrava 1158, Santiago 1170), a much more faithful basis for a 'mounted monk'.

The institution is real (bull of Sixtus IV in 1478, first auto-da-fé in Seville in 1481), but it converted no one. It had jurisdiction only over the baptised: conversos accused of Judaising and, later, Moriscos and Protestants. Forced conversions came from royal decisions, such as the expulsion of the Jews in 1492 and the conversions of Mudéjars in Granada, Castile, Valencia and Aragon between 1499 and 1526. The 'convert faster' mechanic inverts the function: the Inquisition watched over those already converted.

It is a generic name with no historical referent, created for gameplay reasons. Ironically, there is a real basis that could support the effect: the fueros of the Castilian frontier towns (Sepúlveda 1076, Cuenca c. 1190) obliged the householders to serve in the municipal militias, and the 'caballería villana' gave status to commoners who kept a horse. The game does not make this connection.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Trade Units generate +25% gold
elements.explanation: Castile had an export economy based on merino wool (Mesta 1273, Consulado de Burgos 1494, the fairs of Medina del Campo), and the Crown of Aragon a Mediterranean commercial empire (Barcelona, Llibre del Consolat de Mar). The bonus is generic, but defensible.

tree_issues.problem: The Spanish and the Bulgarians are the only 2 civs, out of 56, without Crossbowman. Yet the crossbow was a central weapon in Christian Iberia: crossbowmen of the Crown of Aragon (praised by Muntaner), crossbowmen of the Castilian municipal militias and, in the 15th century, the 'ballesteros de nómina' registered by the Crown of Castile. On Cortés's expedition there were more crossbowmen (32) than arquebusiers (13). Having Mounted Crossbowman and Heavy Mounted Crossbowman softens the problem (mounted crossbowmen did exist), but does not solve it.

tree_issues.item: Siege Engineers, Treadmill Crane, Heated Shot (absent)
tree_issues.problem: The Granada War was won largely through artillery sieges (Ronda 1485, Málaga 1487, Baza 1489), and the engineer Pedro Navarro was a pioneer of gunpowder mines (Castel Nuovo, Naples, 1503). Lacking the siege engineering technology is a historical contradiction, even if it is understandable for balance reasons.

This absence is correct: Iberian light cavalry (jinetes) fought with lance and javelins (azagayas), not with the bow. The problem lies elsewhere: a la jineta cavalry exists in the game only as the Berbers' Genitour.
Consistent: Castilian and Aragonese heavy cavalry is well served (the Paladin exists in only 10 of the 56 civs), and the Hussar can be read as a generic stand-in for the frontier jinete.

A minor absence, arguable both ways. The Castilian economy was heavily pastoral (Mesta, transhumance of merino sheep), but the huertas of Valencia and Murcia inherited a sophisticated Andalusi irrigated agriculture.

history_text_issues.claim: The Visigoths supposedly came “from the southwestern plains of modern Russia”, displaced by the Huns.
history_text_issues.problem: Geographical and chronological inaccuracy. In 376 the Tervingi, the core of the future Visigoths, lived north of the lower Danube (present-day Romania and Moldova, with the Chernyakhov culture extending into Ukraine). They went through Adrianople (378), the sack of Rome (410) and the kingdom of Toulouse (418), and only after Vouillé (507) did they centre themselves on Hispania.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that the Visigoths entered the Empire across the Danube in 376, first founded a kingdom in Gaul (Toulouse) and only after 507 made Toledo their centre.

history_text_issues.claim: Hispania was supposedly 'discarded' by the Empire and occupied by the Visigoths.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the invasion of 409 by Vandals, Suebi and Alans, and the fact that the Visigoths entered Hispania as foederati in Roman service (campaigns of 416–418 against the Vandals and Alans). The Suebian kingdom of Gallaecia (capital at Braga) lasted until 585.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention the entry of 409, the Visigoths' initial role as allies of Rome, and the Suebian kingdom.

history_text_issues.claim: The Visigoths “became Christian” and occupied the centre of the peninsula for centuries.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits that they had been Arian Christians since the 4th century (Ulfilas) and that the conversion to Nicene Catholicism, under Reccared (587) and the Third Council of Toledo (589), was decisive in fusing the Gothic and Hispano-Roman elites. It also understates their territorial dominance: they absorbed the Suebian kingdom (585) and expelled the Byzantines from Spania around 625.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention Arianism, the conversion of 587/589 and the rule of practically the whole peninsula from Toledo.

history_text_issues.claim: A Visigothic lord supposedly asked the Muslims of North Africa for help against the king, opening the door to the invasion.
history_text_issues.problem: What is a late tradition is presented as fact. The Count Julian version only appears in 9th-century Arabic sources (Ibn Abd al-Hakam) and was later romanticised (La Cava); other Arabic sources speak of the sons of Wittiza. The Mozarabic Chronicle of 754, the closest source, does not mention Julian and points instead to a succession crisis (Roderic against the faction of Wittiza/Achila II, who minted coins). The game's vague wording is compatible with this civil war.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the 'invitation' as tradition; the secure context is a Visigothic civil war exploited by Tariq ibn Ziyad and Musa ibn Nusayr.

history_text_issues.claim: “Within 50 years” the Muslims supposedly took most of the peninsula.
history_text_issues.problem: It is not literally false, but it is misleading. The conquest was lightning-fast: Guadalete and Toledo (711), Mérida (713), Zaragoza (714). By around 716–718 almost the whole peninsula had been subdued, and Narbonne fell c. 719–720.
history_text_issues.correction: In less than a decade.

history_text_issues.claim: Córdoba supposedly had “a population of over 500,000”.
history_text_issues.problem: A figure at the upper end of the estimates, presented as fact. Modern proposals vary widely (from about 100,000 to about 450,000, and the Arabic chronicles give even larger numbers), and many fall well below half a million.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that caliphal Córdoba was among the largest cities in Europe, with widely varying estimates (from about 100,000 to over 400,000 inhabitants).

history_text_issues.claim: Al-Andalus supposedly prospered “in relative peace”.
history_text_issues.problem: An exaggeration. There was the muwallad revolt of Umar ibn Hafsun and his sons (880–928), constant wars with the northern kingdoms, and the fitna (1009–1031), which destroyed Madinat al-Zahra and fragmented the caliphate into taifas.
history_text_issues.correction: Real prosperity, especially in the 10th century, but with strong internal conflicts.

history_text_issues.claim: The marriage of 1469 supposedly united “the two competing Christian kingdoms”.
history_text_issues.problem: It was a personal dynastic union: Castile and Aragon kept their own laws, Cortes, coinage and customs until the Nueva Planta decrees (1707–1716). In 1469 neither bride nor groom reigned in Castile or in Aragon (Ferdinand had already been king of Sicily since 1468). Isabella only came to the throne in 1474 and had to win a war of succession (1475–1479); Ferdinand became king of Aragon in 1479.
history_text_issues.correction: Speak of a dynastic union of the crowns (effective from 1479), not of a unification of the kingdoms.

history_text_issues.claim: The reconquista “dragged on for eight centuries”.
history_text_issues.problem: It presents as a continuous project what was a discontinuous process. There were long periods of stable frontier, alliances between Christians and Muslims (El Cid served the taifa kings of Zaragoza between 1081 and 1086), payment of parias, and wars between Christian kingdoms. The idea of a continuous 'Reconquista' has ideological roots as early as the Prophetic Chronicle (883) and was reinforced by 19th-century nationalism; its usefulness as a category is debated.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe an intermittent Christian expansion, with phases (the 11th–13th centuries being decisive) and varied motivations, and note that the term is debated.

history_text_issues.claim: Medieval Spain as a synthesis of “Latin, Jewish, Christian, Arab, and Muslim” influences, with intolerance mentioned only in vague terms.
history_text_issues.problem: It mixes ethno-linguistic and religious categories and omits the concrete landmarks of intolerance: the massacres of 1391, the Inquisition (1478), the expulsion of the Jews (Alhambra Decree, 1492) and the forced conversion of the Mudéjars (1499–1526). In a text that ends in 1492, omitting the expulsion carries weight.
history_text_issues.correction: Explicitly mention 1391, 1478 and 1492.

history_text_issues.claim: Columbus supposedly discovered for Europeans “the great continents of the New World”.
history_text_issues.problem: In 1492 Columbus reached the Antilles (Bahamas, Cuba, Hispaniola). He only touched the mainland in 1498 (Paria) and died convinced that he was close to Asia. The Norse had already been at L'Anse aux Meadows around the year 1000.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that he reached the Caribbean in 1492, opening permanent contact between Europe and the Americas.

history_text_issues.claim: The medieval history of 'Spain' reduced to three chapters: Visigoths, al-Andalus and Reconquista.
history_text_issues.problem: A Castile-centred view. It ignores the Crown of Aragon and its Mediterranean empire (Sicily 1282, Sardinia from 1323, Naples 1442), the almogavars and the Catalan Company in the East, Navarre and the Basques.
history_text_issues.correction: Add a paragraph on the Crown of Aragon and the Mediterranean.

missing_features: Light cavalry 'a la jineta' (jinetes): short stirrups, lance and javelins (azagayas), tornafuye tactics; hired throughout Europe as 'genetours'.
Almogavars: Catalan-Aragonese light infantry with azconas (javelins) and short sword; the Catalan Company in the East (1303–1311) and the victory at Halmyros (1311).
Military orders (Calatrava 1158, Santiago 1170, Alcántara, Montesa 1317): knight-brethren who were lords of the frontier.
Naval power of the Crown of Aragon: Roger of Lauria (Malta 1283, Gulf of Naples 1284, Formigues 1285); the galleys of Barcelona; Llibre del Consolat de Mar.
Castilian galley navy, often commanded by Genoese (Egidio Bocanegra, 1340s; victory at La Rochelle, 1372; Pero Niño's raids in the Channel, c. 1405).
Foot crossbowmen, far more central than the game suggests.
Municipal militias and 'caballería villana' provided for in the frontier fueros.
Mesta (1273) and the export of merino wool, the basis of the Castilian economy.
Toledo School of Translators (12th–13th centuries), which transmitted Arabic and Greek learning to Latin Europe.
Rodeleros (sword-and-buckler infantry) of Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba.
Repoblación (cartas pueblas, presuras) as internal colonisation of the frontier.

proposals.title: Restore Crossbowman and Arbalester
proposals.description: Give back the full line of foot crossbowmen and, optionally, add a Castle Age unique tech, 'Ballesteros de Nómina': Crossbowman-line +1 attack and 10% faster reload.
proposals.historical_basis: Crossbowmen of the Crown of Aragon and of Castile (13th–15th centuries), municipal militias, corps of crossbowmen registered by the Crown in the 15th century, their presence in the Granada War and in the expeditions to the Americas (32 crossbowmen against 13 arquebusiers with Cortés, according to Bernal Díaz).

proposals.title: Almogàver (new unique unit)
proposals.description: Light, fast and cheap infantry (food and wood). Uses the existing charge attack mechanic (Xianbei Raider, Bolas Rider) to throw an azcona before melee, and has a bonus against cavalry.
proposals.historical_basis: Chronicles of Ramon Muntaner and Bernat Desclot. The almogavars fought French and Angevin cavalry successfully in Sicily and Calabria (1282–1302); the Catalan Company destroyed the cavalry of the Duchy of Athens at Halmyros (1311).

proposals.title: Jinete instead of Conquistador (or Conquistador only in the Imperial Age)
proposals.description: Castle Age light cavalry, very fast, with a melee attack and short-range javelin throwing, and a bonus against horse archers and Monks. The Conquistador can remain as an Imperial Age upgrade, with a lance and a secondary firearm.
proposals.historical_basis: Riding 'a la jineta', of Zenata origin, adopted by the Christian kingdoms. The jinetes were decisive in the Granada War and were exported as 'genetours' to England, France and Italy.

proposals.title: Órdenes Militares (replaces Inquisition)
proposals.description: Knight-line +20 HP and +50% resistance to conversion; the Missionary heals 25% faster. Alternative: the Missionary is replaced by a mounted 'Freire' with a weak attack and the ability to heal.
proposals.historical_basis: Orders of Calatrava (1158), Santiago (1170), Alcántara and Montesa (1317): monk-knights who garrisoned frontier castles and lordships.

proposals.title: Milicias Concejiles (replaces Supremacy)
proposals.description: Same effect on villagers, and the Town Center fires +3 arrows when garrisoned with villagers.
proposals.historical_basis: Fueros of Sepúlveda (1076) and of Cuenca (c. 1190): the householders of frontier towns were obliged to serve in the host, and the 'caballeros villanos' had privileges for keeping a horse.

proposals.title: Consolat de Mar (new team bonus)
proposals.description: The team's Trade Cogs +25% gold and +10% speed, instead of the generic bonus to all trade units.
proposals.historical_basis: Llibre del Consolat de Mar (Barcelona/Valencia, 14th century, printed in 1484), the most influential maritime law code in the Mediterranean, and the Catalan trading network.

proposals.title: Mesta (economic bonus)
proposals.description: Shepherds work +20% faster and herd animals give +25% food, in place of the gold-per-technology bonus.
proposals.historical_basis: Honrado Concejo de la Mesta (1273) and the merino wool trade, a pillar of Castilian finances.

contested: The concept of 'Reconquista' as a continuous project: a historiographical construct (García Sanjuán, Ríos Saloma) or a still-useful category (García Fitz, O'Callaghan).
The 'convivencia': Américo Castro versus Sánchez-Albornoz; Menocal (2002) versus Fernández-Morera (2016); Maya Soifer's revision (2009).
Population of Córdoba in the 10th century: estimates between about 100,000 and over 400,000.
Causes of 711: the tradition of Count Julian or of the sons of Wittiza versus a Visigothic civil war.
Iberian priority in the use of gunpowder (Huéscar 1324, Algeciras 1342–1344): the reading of the Nasrid and Castilian sources is disputed.
Weight of artillery in the fall of Granada (Cook 1993) relative to the Nasrid civil war and economic exhaustion.
Number of victims and character of the Inquisition, and the 'Leyenda Negra' (Kamen; Contreras and Henningsen).
The Spanish role in the 'military revolution' (Roberts, Parker).
key_sources: Mozarabic Chronicle of 754
Ibn Abd al-Hakam, Futuh Misr (9th century)
Chronicle of Alfonso III and Prophetic Chronicle (c. 883)
Ramon Muntaner, Crònica (c. 1325–1328)

civs.represents: The Kingdom of Portugal (County of Portugal from 868, kingdom from 1139/1143). The game's design centres on the maritime expansion of the Aviz dynasty: trading posts (feitorias), caravels and naval artillery.
civs.period: 868 (presura of Portucale) – 1580 (Iberian Union); design concentrated on c. 1415–1550.
civs.verdict: The Portuguese have a recognisable and well-founded maritime identity (Caravel, Feitoria, sturdier ships, naval artillery), but almost all of it belongs to the 15th–16th centuries. The two core economic bonuses (foragers that produce wood, -20% gold on all units) have no historical basis, the Organ Gun is not specifically Portuguese, and Circumnavigation celebrates an expedition in the service of Castile (Magellan/Elcano, 1519–1522). The three centuries of the medieval kingdom are absent: the Reconquista, the besteiros do conto, the ginetes, Aljubarrota, the English alliance. The history text contains errors (the collapse of the Caliphate placed in the 1140s, the copper and tin mines), ignores the Suebian kingdom of Braga, repeats a hagiographic view of Prince Henry the Navigator and omits the slave trade.
civs.naming_scope_issues: The endonym is appropriate and the political entity is coherent from 1139/1143 onwards (before that, it was the County of Portugal, dependent on León). The problem is one of period: the design represents the Portugal of the Discoveries (1415–1550) and even uses a feat from 1519–1522 (Circumnavigation), while the medieval Portugal of 1139–1415 (the Reconquista, the crisis of 1383–85, Aljubarrota) has no mechanical expression. The history text duplicates the outline of the Spanish text (Visigoths, Islam, Reconquista) and ignores the Suebian kingdom (409–585, capital at Braga), the most direct political antecedent of Portuguese territory.

elements.explanation: 'Naval' is faithful for the 15th–16th centuries: the Portuguese pioneered heavy shipborne artillery in the Indian Ocean (the bombardment of Calicut in 1502, Diu 1509). Before 1400 the Portuguese navy was modest and was organised with Genoese help (Manuel Pessanha, 1317). 'Gunpowder' on land is less distinctive than in other European kingdoms.

elements.element: Foragers generate wood in addition to food
elements.explanation: No identifiable historical link; at most, a vague allusion to forest products such as cork. It is pure game balance.

Medieval Portugal was a small kingdom (around 1 to 1.5 million inhabitants) and poor in coined metal. Gold from Mina (trade from 1471, fortress in 1482) increased revenue, but that would translate into income, not cheaper units. It is a balance bonus inherited from old versions.

Feitorias were the central institution of the Portuguese commercial empire: Flanders (Bruges, later Antwerp), Arguin (1440s), São Jorge da Mina (1482), Calicut and Cochin (1500–1503). Generating resources passively is a good abstraction of a network of trading posts. Two caveats: it is a 15th–16th-century institution, and many African feitorias traded in enslaved people.
An acceptable abstraction of the large, sturdy naus (carracks) of the Carreira da Índia and of Atlantic seafaring experience. The scaling by age is purely mechanical.

Ribauldequins ('organs') were a pan-European weapon: attributed to the army of Edward III of England from 1339, used in Flanders (Beverhoutsveld, 1382), by Burgundy and by the Italian states, and drawn by Leonardo. There is no evidence of a Portuguese specialisation. Portugal's strength lay in naval artillery and fortress artillery.

The lateen caravel was perfected in Portugal over the course of the 15th century and used on the Guinea voyages and by Bartolomeu Dias (1487–1488). It also served as an armed patrol ship in the Strait of Gibraltar and off the Moroccan coast. Caveat: it was above all an exploration ship, light and with little artillery; large-scale naval warfare was waged with naus and, later, galleons. The armed 'caravela redonda' is the closest combat version.

Ferdinand Magellan was Portuguese, but the 1519–1522 expedition was Castilian, was completed by Elcano, and Portugal tried to intercept it (the ship Trinidad was captured in the Moluccas). It also post-dates 1500. The Portuguese feats that would justify an 'explored map' are different ones: the Cape route (Dias 1488, Gama 1498), astronomical navigation (Regimento do Astrolábio) and cartography (the Cantino planisphere, 1502).

The arquebus was a pan-European weapon of German and Burgundian origin (Hakenbüchse, 15th century). The Portuguese role was mainly one of diffusion: they introduced it to Japan (Tanegashima, 1543) and used arquebusiers in Morocco and India. Nothing supports the specific effect of accuracy against moving targets.

It seems to allude to Portuguese nautical science, which did exist (the tables of Abraham Zacuto, printed in Leiria in 1496; later Pedro Nunes). But the famous 'School of Sagres' is a myth, and speeding up all technologies is generic.

tree_issues.problem: The ginetes, light cavalry riding à la gineta, were an important arm in Portugal: frontier warfare in Morocco (Ceuta 1415, Asilah and Tangier 1471), the raids and mounted forays of the Reconquista, the non-noble knights (cavaleiros-vilãos). It is a historically significant absence (the Portuguese stop at Light Cavalry).

Well founded. The besteiros do conto, municipal militias with fixed quotas per municipality (13th–15th centuries), and the mounted crossbowmen (besteiros de cavalo) were central to the Portuguese army, for example at Aljubarrota (1385). They even deserve a bonus of their own.

tree_issues.item: Cannon Galleon, Elite Cannon Galleon and Bombard Tower (present)
tree_issues.problem: Consistent with the pioneering use of naval and fortress artillery (Calicut 1502, Diu 1509, the fortresses of Goa and Hormuz), albeit already in the 16th century.

The Carrack now exists as a generic ship (48 of the 56 civs) and as a melee-attack ship (boarding). The Portuguese nau of the Carreira da Índia, which combined heavy artillery and boarding, receives no dedicated treatment, despite being one of the ships most closely identified with Portugal.

A debatable absence: Portugal had a dense network of frontier castles, remodelled by King Denis (late 13th–early 14th century) with keeps and machicolations. A minor absence, but hardly consistent with that tradition.
An acceptable absence: Portuguese gold came mainly from trade (Mina, the 'Gold Coast'); alluvial gold extraction (Adiça, on the Tagus) was small-scale. The Feitoria is the right representation.

Acceptable and of no special significance (only 10 of the 56 civs have the Paladin). In the great battles of the 14th century (Atoleiros 1384, Aljubarrota 1385) the Portuguese men-at-arms fought dismounted, in the English manner.

history_text_issues.claim: Portuguese medieval history supposedly begins with the expansion of the Visigothic kingdom.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the Suebian kingdom (409–585), with its capital at Braga, which dominated Gallaecia and a large part of present-day Portuguese territory for more than a century and a half. The Suebian king Rechiar (c. 448) was the first Catholic Germanic king, and St Martin of Dumio/Braga (6th century) was a central figure. It is the most direct antecedent of Portuguese territory.
history_text_issues.correction: Add the Suebian kingdom of Braga before its absorption by the Visigoths (585).

history_text_issues.claim: Pelagius was “a Visigoth nobleman” and the first to re-establish a Christian stronghold (c. 722).
history_text_issues.problem: Pelagius's Gothic origin comes from the Chronicle of Alfonso III (c. 883), a late and legitimist source. Some historians see him as a local Asturian chieftain. The date (718 or 722) and the scale of Covadonga are uncertain.
history_text_issues.correction: Flag the uncertainty over his origin and the date.

history_text_issues.claim: The Portuguese language supposedly revealed a difference from León, and the sense of a unique identity supposedly fuelled the desire for independence.
history_text_issues.problem: Anachronistic proto-nationalism. In the 12th century Galician-Portuguese was common to Galicia and northern Portugal; the separation of Galician came later (14th century). Independence resulted from a feudal and dynastic conflict: the county was granted to Henry of Burgundy and Teresa (1096), Afonso Henriques confronted his mother and the Galician Traba faction at São Mamede (1128), there was the Treaty of Zamora (1143) and papal recognition through the bull Manifestis Probatum (1179).
history_text_issues.correction: Explain independence as a political and dynastic process, with 'national' identity consolidating afterwards.

history_text_issues.claim: Afonso Henriques supposedly took advantage of “the collapse of the Umayyad Caliphate”.
history_text_issues.problem: The Caliphate of Córdoba disappeared in 1031. What Afonso Henriques exploited in the 1140s was the crisis of Almoravid rule and the second taifa kingdoms, before the Almohad consolidation.
history_text_issues.correction: Replace with 'the disintegration of Almoravid power'.

history_text_issues.claim: The kingdom supposedly possessed “one of the richest sources of copper and tin in Medieval Europe”.
history_text_issues.problem: An unsupported claim for the Middle Ages. The Iberian Pyrite Belt (Aljustrel, São Domingos) and the tin of the north-west were exploited mainly in Antiquity and from the 19th century onwards; today Neves-Corvo is a major copper and tin mine, which may explain the confusion. In the 15th–16th centuries Portugal imported enormous quantities of copper from Central Europe (the Fugger, via Antwerp) for the African trade, including manillas.
history_text_issues.correction: Remove the claim, or state that Portugal was above all a major importer and redistributor of Central European copper.

history_text_issues.claim: With the incorporation of the Algarve, wine and salt supposedly began to be exported to England and Flanders.
history_text_issues.problem: Imprecise causality and attribution. Exported salt came mainly from Setúbal, Aveiro and the Tagus estuary (the Algarve had smaller saltworks, such as Castro Marim); the Algarve exported mainly dried fruit (figs, raisins, almonds) and fish; the wine came from other regions.
history_text_issues.correction: Correct the producing regions and detach the trade with the north from the conquest of the Algarve.

history_text_issues.claim: Prince Henry the Navigator supposedly oversaw the development of the caravel and was the main initiator of the Age of Discovery.
history_text_issues.problem: Outdated historiography. The 'School of Sagres' is a myth, and the caravel evolved from coastal and fishing craft. The epithet 'Navigator' was never used in his lifetime: it dates from the 19th century and was popularised in English by R. H. Major (1868). Henry's motivations were crusading, seigneurial and commercial (revenues of the Order of Christ, monopolies, the slave trade), and the expansion had other drivers, such as Ceuta (1415), the Crown and merchants.
history_text_issues.correction: Present him as an important patron, but not as the inventor of the caravel nor as the sole initiator (Peter Russell, 2000).

history_text_issues.claim: The trade network supposedly ushered in a 'golden age' financed by trade.
history_text_issues.problem: A serious omission: Portugal began the European Atlantic trade in enslaved people (first captives in 1441, the Lagos auction in 1444, described by Zurara; Arguin; Mina). The Feitoria, the civ's unique building, was precisely the institution of that trade.
history_text_issues.correction: Explicitly mention the Portuguese role in the trade in enslaved people.

history_text_issues.claim: The Portuguese army of the 15th–16th centuries was supposedly “one of the most technologically advanced armies in the world”.
history_text_issues.problem: An exaggeration. The Portuguese advantage was naval (shipborne artillery) and in overseas fortification; the land armies were small, and the defeat at Alcácer Quibir (1578) shows the limits.
history_text_issues.correction: Restrict the claim to the navy and naval artillery.

history_text_issues.claim: The text jumps from 1250 to the maritime expansion.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the crisis of 1383–1385, Atoleiros and Aljubarrota (1385), the rise of the Aviz dynasty and the English alliance (1373; Treaty of Windsor, 1386), founding moments of late-medieval Portugal.
history_text_issues.correction: Add a paragraph on 1383–1386.

history_text_issues.claim: Afonso IV and Prince Henry the Navigator as major investors in the navy.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits that it was King Denis who founded the royal navy, by hiring the Genoese Manuel Pessanha as admiral (1317). The 1341 expedition to the Canary Islands, in the reign of Afonso IV, was commanded by Italians (Nicoloso da Recco and Angiolino del Tegghia).
history_text_issues.correction: Mention King Denis and the Genoese origin of the admiralty.

missing_features: Besteiros do conto and besteiros de cavalo (municipal crossbowman militia).
The defensive tactics of Atoleiros (1384) and Aljubarrota (1385): dismounted men-at-arms, wings of crossbowmen and English archers, wolf pits and abatis (Nuno Álvares Pereira).
The Anglo-Portuguese Alliance (1373; Treaty of Windsor, 1386).
Military orders (the Templars, then the Order of Christ in 1319; Aviz; Santiago) as drivers of the Reconquista and of expansion.
Ginetes and frontier warfare in Morocco.
Astronomical navigation and the 'volta do mar'.
The nau (carrack) of the Carreira da Índia and the Portuguese galleon as distinct ships (the game's Carrack is generic).
Overseas fortresses (Elmina, Mazagan, Goa, Hormuz, Malacca).
Fishing and salt: sardines, Newfoundland cod (from c. 1500), the saltworks of Setúbal and Aveiro.
The Law of Sesmarias (1375), an agrarian policy to force land into cultivation.
The Suebian kingdom of Braga (409–585) as the early-medieval root of the territory.

proposals.title: Volta do Mar (replaces Circumnavigation)
proposals.description: Ships +10% speed, and reveals all water tiles and coastline on the map (not the whole map).
proposals.historical_basis: The technique of returning from Guinea via the open sea (by way of the Azores), mastered by Portuguese pilots in the 15th century, and astronomical navigation (Regimento do Astrolábio, c. 1509), which made the voyages of Dias and Gama possible.

proposals.title: Aljubarrota (new Castle Age UT)
proposals.description: Infantry +1/+1 armour, and Arbalester and Halberdier +2 attack against cavalry.
proposals.historical_basis: Atoleiros (1384) and Aljubarrota (1385): Nuno Álvares Pereira defeated the Castilian cavalry with dismounted infantry, crossbowmen and field obstacles.

proposals.title: Besteiro do Conto (replaces Organ Gun)
proposals.description: Cheap foot crossbowman (food and wood), trainable at the Castle and the Town Center, with high attack and a slow rate of fire.
proposals.historical_basis: The besteiros do conto, raised by the municipalities in fixed numbers ('conto') between the 13th and 15th centuries, were the backbone of the Portuguese infantry.

proposals.title: Fishing and Sesmarias (replaces forager wood)
proposals.description: Fishing Ships +15% work rate and Fish Traps -33% wood. Alternative: Farms -25% wood, reflecting the Law of Sesmarias.
proposals.historical_basis: The weight of fishing and salt in the Portuguese economy (exports of salt and fish to northern Europe) and the Law of Sesmarias of Ferdinand I (1375).

proposals.title: Give Hussar (ginetes)
proposals.description: Add the Hussar to the tech tree and, optionally, Light Cavalry -15% cost.
proposals.historical_basis: The Portuguese ginetes in the Moroccan strongholds and in frontier warfare in the Peninsula (14th–16th centuries).

proposals.title: Nau da Índia (naval UT)
proposals.description: Carrack +20% HP and gains a short-range secondary ranged attack (cannon), while keeping its melee boarding attack.
proposals.historical_basis: The naus of the Carreira da Índia (from 1497–1498), large high-sided ships that combined artillery and boarding, the basis of Portuguese dominance in the Indian Ocean (Diu, 1509).

proposals.title: Treaty of Windsor (new team bonus)
proposals.description: Team Archery Ranges work +15% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: The Anglo-Portuguese Alliance (1373/1386), with English archers at Aljubarrota and the expedition of John of Gaunt (1386).

contested: The role of Prince Henry the Navigator and the 'School of Sagres' (Peter Russell versus nationalist historiography).
Origins of independence: proto-national identity or feudal-dynastic conflict (Herculano, Mattoso).
The Battle of Ourique (1139) and the 'miracle', a founding myth constructed later.
Technical origin of the caravel (Portuguese innovation or Mediterranean and Arab heritage).
Pelagius: Visigothic noble or local Asturian chieftain.
Reasons for Portuguese success in the Indian Ocean: technical superiority or exploitation of local rivalries (Subrahmanyam).
The extent of the 'Portuguese Renaissance'.

civs.represents: The city-states and maritime republics of central and northern Italy (Venice, Genoa, Pisa, Amalfi, Milan, Florence) and the Papal States, from the communal movement to the Renaissance. The design favours Venice and Genoa (sea, trade, crossbowmen) and Florence and Milan (universities, gunpowder, mercenaries).
civs.period: c. 1000 (communes and maritime republics) – 1559 (Peace of Cateau-Cambrésis); peak represented c. 1250–1500.
civs.verdict: The Italians are one of the best-grounded designs in this group. The Genoese Crossbowman, the Dock and University bonuses, the naval emphasis and Silk Road reflect real traits of the maritime republics and of Italy's universities. The weak point is the Condottiero: the name designated the hired captain, the classic companies of the 14th–15th centuries were mostly heavy cavalry, and the 'anti-gunpowder' infantry role is invented (light infantry companies such as the Bande Nere only appear in the 16th century). Missing are banking and finance (the most influential Italian innovation of the period), communal infantry (Halberdier absent) and military engineering (Siege Engineers absent). Pirotechnia is a 1540 treatise applied to an effect that has nothing to do with it. The history text has several errors of chronology and terminology.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Italians” is an umbrella label for dozens of entities with no common state before 1861: maritime republics, communes, lordships, the Papal States, the Kingdom of Naples. The text treats 'the Italians' as a continuous people since 572, a teleological reading. The design mainly represents the period 1250–1530 and reaches into the Italian Wars (1494–1559), partly outside the timeframe. There are overlaps: southern Italy also appears in the Sicilians and the Byzantines; the Ostrogoths in the Goths; the Lombards have no civ of their own; and Venice has Byzantine roots.

elements.explanation: The 'Naval' is faithful (Venice, Genoa, Pisa). The 'Archer' is justified by the Genoese and communal crossbowmen. But the label overlooks heavy cavalry, the core of Italian armies in the 14th–15th centuries, and the commercial and financial dimension.

elements.element: Advancing to the next Age costs -15%
elements.explanation: A vague abstraction of Italian precocity (commercial revolution, communes, Renaissance). There is no specific historical mechanism, but the 'advanced society' trait is real.

elements.element: Foot Archers and Condottieri +1 melee/+1 pierce armor
elements.explanation: Well founded for the crossbowmen: the pavise (a large shield whose name probably comes from Pavia) and the pavesari protected them. Milan's armour industry (the Missaglia family in the 15th century, the Negroli in the 16th) was the best in Europe. Applying it to the Condottiero inherits the unit's weaknesses.

Both halves rest on facts. The Venetian Arsenal (founded in the early 12th century, enlarged in the 14th–15th centuries) mass-produced galleys. Italian universities are among the oldest in Europe (Bologna, conventional date 1088; Padua 1222; Naples 1224), and there is a tradition of engineering (Brunelleschi, Taccola, Francesco di Giorgio Martini, 'alla moderna' fortification).

The Florentine document of 11 February 1326 is, together with the English manuscript of Walter de Milemete from the same year, one of the two oldest European references to metal cannon. Brescia and Milan were arms-manufacturing centres, and Italian gun-founders were among the best. Reducing the cost is an acceptable abstraction, although in the 15th century Burgundy, France and the German world were as advanced as Italy in artillery, or more so.
The maritime republics were mercantile and military powers, not great fishing powers (unlike the Basques, the Portuguese, the Hansa or the Dutch). A weak link to the naval theme.

Genoese crossbowmen were the most sought-after mercenary missile troops in Europe: they served France (Crécy, 1346), Castile, Byzantium and the Italian states. The 'exceptionally strong against cavalry' bonus is an abstraction. Protected by pavises, they held up well against cavalry, but at Crécy, according to the chronicle tradition, they fought without their pavises (left in the baggage) and were routed.

The name is real, but it is applied in a forced way. The condottiero was the captain hired under a 'condotta', and the companies of the 14th–15th centuries were mostly heavy cavalry organised in 'lance' of three men (man-at-arms, squire, page); the equestrian statues of Gattamelata (Donatello) and Colleoni (Verrocchio) depict horsemen. Hired infantry (provvisionati) grew in the 15th century, and in the 16th century there were fast companies of infantry and light cavalry, such as Giovanni de' Medici's Bande Nere, but they were themselves arquebus troops. A soldier called a 'condottiero' with an 'anti-gunpowder' role has no basis.

Venice and Genoa controlled the western termini of Euro-Asian trade: Caffa, Tana and Pera on the Black Sea, Alexandria and Acre in the Levant, and Marco Polo as its emblem. Caveat: 'Silk Road' is a modern term (Richthofen, 1877), and Italian trade with Asia was mainly in spices via the Levant.

Vannoccio Biringuccio published De la pirotechnia in Venice in 1540. It is the first comprehensive printed treatise on metallurgy, cannon founding and gunpowder making. It falls outside the timeframe and deals with artillery founding, not with the accuracy of hand cannoneers.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Condottiero available at the Barracks in Imperial Age
elements.explanation: Hiring Italian mercenaries for allies is coherent: condottieri such as Gian Giacomo Trivulzio or Prospero Colonna served France and Spain in the Italian Wars. But it inherits the problem of the unit type.

tree_issues.problem: Communal infantry with polearms was decisive in medieval Italy: the Milanese around the Carroccio withstood Barbarossa's cavalry at Legnano (1176), and in 1506 Machiavelli organised a Florentine militia of pikemen. It is a historically relevant absence (43 of the 56 civs have Halberdier).

This runs against one of the most solid Italian traditions: the military engineering of Taccola, Francesco di Giorgio Martini and Leonardo, and the Italian engineers hired all over Europe. It is inconsistent with the civ's own University bonus.

Heavy cavalry was the core of Italian armies in the 14th–15th centuries, with the best plate armour in Europe (Milan). But only 10 of the 56 civs have Paladin, and the Italians have Cavalier; the absence is not a specific claim by the game. The real problem is that there is no expression at all of Italian heavy cavalry.
Plausible: the stradioti, Albanian and Greek light cavalry in Venetian service from the 1470s.
Plausible: the 'balestrieri a cavallo' were a regular component of the armies of Milan and Venice in the 15th century.
Consistent with the early adoption of gunpowder (Florence, 1326) and with the importance of Italian gun-founders.

history_text_issues.claim: The Italians have supposedly inhabited the peninsula continuously “since roughly 572 AD”.
history_text_issues.problem: An arbitrary date (the Lombards' capture of Pavia after a three-year siege). Italian ethnogenesis was gradual, and Latin populations had inhabited the peninsula long before.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe the slow formation of regional identities out of the Romano-Italic populations and the Lombard, Byzantine and other contributions.

history_text_issues.claim: In 476, Rome supposedly fell “to the Germanic tribes under the rule of Odoacer”.
history_text_issues.problem: Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus in Ravenna, the capital, and did not conquer Rome. He was an officer of the Roman army in Italy, acclaimed king by the federate troops (Heruli, Sciri, Rugii), and he kept the Senate and the administration.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that Odoacer, commander of the federate troops in Italy, deposed the last Western emperor in Ravenna.

history_text_issues.claim: In 493 the Byzantines supposedly persuaded Theodoric to conquer Italy.
history_text_issues.problem: Zeno sent Theodoric in 488. The invasion began in 489 and ended in 493, with the capture of Ravenna and the murder of Odoacer.
history_text_issues.correction: Correct the dates to 488–493.

history_text_issues.claim: Byzantine rule was supposedly “mostly displaced by 572”.
history_text_issues.problem: The Lombards invaded in 568, but for centuries Byzantium kept the Exarchate of Ravenna (until 751), Rome, Naples, Venice, Apulia, Calabria and Sicily (Bari until 1071).
history_text_issues.correction: Speak of an Italy divided between Lombards and Byzantines for centuries.

history_text_issues.claim: The fall of “Charlemagne's Holy Roman Empire” supposedly gave rise to Milan, Genoa, Florence and Venice.
history_text_issues.problem: Anachronism and wrong causality. The designation 'Sacrum Imperium' appears in 1157 and 'Sacrum Romanum Imperium' in 1254. The communes emerge in the 11th–12th centuries, and Venice never belonged to the Carolingian kingdom: it evolved out of Byzantine rule (recognised in the Pax Nicephori, 812).
history_text_issues.correction: Speak of the Carolingian Empire and of the communal movement of the 11th–12th centuries.

history_text_issues.claim: After 962, Italy supposedly became involved in the affairs of the “German city-states”.
history_text_issues.problem: These were not German city-states but the German kingdom and its duchies. The Regnum Italiae became tied to the German imperial crown.
history_text_issues.correction: Replace with 'German kingdom/Empire'.

history_text_issues.claim: Southern Italy supposedly remained under the Lombards and Byzantines until the 11th century.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the Emirate of Sicily (831/902–1091) and the Emirate of Bari (847–871).
history_text_issues.correction: Include the Islamic presence in the South.

history_text_issues.claim: Condottieri whose loyalty went to the highest bidder, and wars that maintained the status quo.
history_text_issues.problem: It reproduces Machiavelli's polemic. Michael Mallett and others have shown that many condottieri had long-term contracts (Venice created near-permanent forces in the 15th century) and that there were bloody battles (Caravaggio 1448, Fornovo 1495).
history_text_issues.correction: Present Machiavelli's view as a contemporary critique, not as fact.

history_text_issues.claim: The Italian Wars placed as being “of the 16th century”.
history_text_issues.problem: They began in 1494, with the invasion of Charles VIII, and lasted until 1559.

history_text_issues.claim: Leonardo da Vinci presented as a Florentine figure who pushed technology to its limit.
history_text_issues.problem: Leonardo was born in Vinci and spent much of his career in Milan, in the service of Ludovico Sforza (1482–1499), and later in France. His military and mechanical designs almost all remained on paper; they had no practical impact on the technology of the time.
history_text_issues.correction: Place him between Florence, Milan and France, and distinguish his drawings from the inventions actually put to use.

history_text_issues.claim: The Italians supposedly 'finally' unified in 1861 under Victor Emmanuel II and Garibaldi.
history_text_issues.problem: The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861, but Venice was only annexed in 1866 and Rome in 1870. The text omits Cavour, and the 'finally' is teleological.
history_text_issues.correction: Refer to the process of 1859–1870.

missing_features: Banking and finance: bills of exchange, double-entry bookkeeping (Pacioli, 1494), the Bardi and Peruzzi, the Medici, the Banco di San Giorgio (1407), the florin (1252) and the Venetian ducat (1284).
The Venetian Arsenal, with standardised galley production.
The galley (the war 'galea sottile' and the merchant 'galea grossa') as the dominant ship of the Mediterranean.
Heavy men-at-arms ('lance') and Milanese armour.
Communal infantry and the Carroccio (Legnano, 1176; Cortenuova, 1237).
Pavesari, the pavise-bearers who protected the crossbowmen.
Military engineering and 'alla moderna' fortification (angle bastion, Sangallo, Francesco di Giorgio, late 15th century).
Overseas colonies and trading posts (Caffa, Tana, Pera, Chios, Crete, Negroponte), earlier than the Portuguese ones.
Permanent diplomacy (resident ambassadors, 15th century).
Stradioti (Balkan light cavalry in Venetian service).

proposals.title: Condottiero as mercenary heavy cavalry
proposals.description: Turn the Condottiero into Stable/Castle heavy cavalry, paid almost entirely in gold (no food), strong against infantry and gunpowder, and available to allies as it is today.
proposals.historical_basis: Condottieri companies were organised in 'lance' of heavy cavalry (Mallett 1974). Hawkwood, Sforza, Braccio da Montone, Gattamelata and Colleoni were cavalry captains.

proposals.title: Pirotechnia aligned with the treatise
proposals.description: Bombard Cannon and Cannon Galleon -20% cost and +15% production speed, instead of the effect on hand cannoneers.
proposals.historical_basis: De la pirotechnia (Biringuccio, 1540) deals with cannon founding, metallurgy and gunpowder. Italian gun-founders were at the forefront of bronze artillery.

proposals.title: Banking (replaces Fishing Ships -15%)
proposals.description: Tributes pay no fee and the Market has better buying and selling rates, for example a maximum commission of 15%.
proposals.historical_basis: Bills of exchange, double-entry bookkeeping and great banks (Bardi, Peruzzi, Medici); Genoa's Banco di San Giorgio (1407).

proposals.title: Arsenale (new UT)
proposals.description: Galley-line ships and Fire Ships are produced +33% faster, and Docks cost -25% wood.
proposals.historical_basis: The Venetian Arsenal (early 12th century, enlarged in the 14th–15th centuries) produced galleys on an assembly line; Dante describes it in the Inferno (canto XXI).

proposals.title: Carroccio and Halberdier
proposals.description: Grant Halberdier and add the Carroccio: a slow, non-combatant cart that gives +1/+1 armour and +10% attack to nearby infantry, using the same aura mechanism as the Centurion.
proposals.historical_basis: The Milanese Carroccio (c. 1037–1039, Archbishop Aribert of Intimiano) was the rallying point of the communal infantry; Legnano (1176) against Frederick Barbarossa.

proposals.title: Trace italienne and Siege Engineers
proposals.description: Castles, Towers and Walls +25% HP and +2 armour against siege; restore Siege Engineers to the tech tree.
proposals.historical_basis: The development of the angle bastion in Italy in the late 15th century (Francesco di Giorgio Martini, the Sangallo family), copied all over Europe, and the tradition of Italian military engineers (Taccola, Leonardo).

contested: Effectiveness and loyalty of the condottieri: Machiavelli versus Mallett, Caferro and Covini.
'Bloodless battles' (Anghiari 1440, Molinella 1467): reality or rhetoric.
The concept of the 'Renaissance' (Burckhardt, 1860) versus medieval continuity (Haskins, 1927).
Origins of the communes: rupture or continuity (Wickham, 2015).
The 1088 date for the University of Bologna is conventional, fixed in the 19th century (1888 commemoration).
The first European reference to cannon: Florence and Milemete (1326) versus contested earlier references.
Causes of the Genoese defeat at Crécy (missing pavises, wet bowstrings, French order of battle).

civs.represents: The Norman Kingdom of Sicily (Hauteville/Altavilla dynasty), including the Norman conquest of Apulia and Calabria and, by extension, the Italo-Normans of the First Crusade (Bohemond of Taranto, Tancred, Principality of Antioch).
civs.period: c. 1030 (Aversa) – 1194 (end of the Hauteville dynasty); possibly up to 1266 (Hohenstaufen).
civs.verdict: The Sicilians are, in practice, the 'Italo-Normans', and the design reasonably captures their character as castle-building conquerors. The Donjon, fast fortifications and Town Centers, naval transports and Sicily's agricultural wealth are good abstractions, and First Crusade refers to a real feat of the Italo-Normans of Apulia (Bohemond, Tancred), though not of the Sicilian state. But what makes Norman Sicily historically unique has almost no mechanics: a trilingual state that integrated Muslims, Greeks and Latins into the army, the navy and the administration (there are no Saracen archers, no naval bonus and no dīwān). Hauberk is generic European equipment. The history text ends with serious errors: it reverses the trajectory of tolerance and invents a 'rapid' decline under spheres of influence that include Byzantium.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Sicilians” suggests the island's inhabitants (Greeks, Arabs and Berbers, Latins, Lombards, Jews), but the design represents the Norman conquering elite and includes mainland Italy and even the Principality of Antioch (Bohemond, Tancred). The effective period is narrow, c. 1040–1194. Left out are Islamic Sicily (827–1091, which in the game falls to the Saracens and Berbers), Hohenstaufen Sicily (Frederick II) and Aragonese Sicily after the Vespers (1282). 'Donjon' and 'Serjeant' are French and Anglo-Norman terms, not Sicilian ones. The Normans in general are diluted into the Franks.

elements.explanation: The Normans of Italy won mainly with cavalry (Civitate 1053, Cerami 1063, Dyrrhachium 1081), supported by locally recruited infantry (Lombards, Greeks, Muslims). The label is acceptable, but it omits the most distinctive elements: Saracen archers and the navy.
An abstraction of the Norman fortification programme (Melfi, Adrano, Paternò, Caccamo), used to control newly conquered territories.

Sicily was a major wheat exporter from Antiquity onwards (the 'granary of Rome') and remained one in the Norman and Swabian periods. The Islamic period brought irrigation (the qanats of Palermo), citrus fruit, sugar cane, cotton and the mulberry tree. The basis is solid, although the mechanism is abstract and the scale of the 'Arab agricultural revolution' (Watson) is debated.
It has no historical referent; it is pure balancing to withstand counter-units.

The Normans built keeps in Italy (Adrano and Paternò, attributed to Roger I), and the text rightly highlights them. But 'donjon' is a French term (in Italy: mastio or torre), and having it in the Dark Age is anachronistic, because Norman stone keeps date from the 11th–12th centuries.

elements.element: Fortifications built +50% faster; Town Centers built +100% faster
elements.explanation: A good abstraction of rapid expansion through castles and of the consolidation of conquests. The Normans quickly raised earth-and-timber fortifications, as they also did in England.

The 'sergents' (servientes) were non-noble fighters, mounted or on foot, present in Norman and crusader armies and documented in the Kingdom of Sicily (the Catalogus Baronum, c. 1150–1168, counts milites and servientes). The term is a generic one from the Anglo-Norman and French world, and the ability to build Donjons is an abstraction.

The association with the Italo-Normans is legitimate: Bohemond of Taranto (son of Robert Guiscard, and therefore a Hauteville) and his nephew Tancred led one of the main contingents and founded the Principality of Antioch (1098). But the Sicilian state did not take part: according to Malaterra, when Bohemond's men took the cross at the siege of Amalfi (1096), Count Roger I saw his army depleted and returned to Sicily; Ibn al-Athir relates (a late anecdote) that Roger turned down a Frankish proposal to attack Ifriqiya. The mechanic (Town Centers that spawn Serjeants) reverses the real effect: the crusade drained warriors away from southern Italy.
The hauberk, the long mail shirt, was standard equipment for all Western cavalry in the 11th–13th centuries (see the Bayeux Tapestry), not something specific to Sicily.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Transport Ships +5 line of sight and cost -50%
elements.explanation: The crossing of the Strait of Messina (1061), the transport of cavalry to Epirus (1081) and Roger II's expeditions to Ifriqiya (Mahdia, 1148) show a real amphibious capability, including the transport of horses by sea.

tree_issues.problem: This contradicts the text itself, which presents them as 'impressive builders': the cathedrals of Cefalù (1131) and Monreale (1174), the Palatine Chapel (consecrated in 1140), La Zisa and La Cuba. The Donjon replaces the towers, but the building technologies are missing.

Muslim archers were an important part of the armies of Roger I (Calabria; the siege of Capua in 1098) and of Frederick II (the Lucera colony, from the 1220s to 1300). They were mainly infantry, so the bigger gap is the absence of any bonus for Saracen archers, rather than the lack of the Cavalry Archer.

Neutral, but it wastes a real trait: in 1098 Pope Urban II granted Roger I the apostolic legation (the origin of the 'Monarchia Sicula'), and the ruler controlled the Church of the kingdom. This would be a good basis for a Monastery bonus.

tree_issues.item: No Bombard Cannon or Hand Cannoneer
tree_issues.problem: Correct for a period that ends in the 12th–13th centuries.

history_text_issues.claim: Italy and Sicily supposedly fell “successively to the Vandals and then the Ostrogoths”.
history_text_issues.problem: The Vandals attacked Sicily (from 440 onwards) and sacked Rome (455), but never ruled Italy. Sicily was under Vandal control between c. 468 and 476 and was ceded to Odoacer in exchange for tribute; the Ostrogoths only arrive after 489–493.
history_text_issues.correction: Distinguish Vandal rule over Sicily from the Italy of Odoacer and, later, of the Ostrogoths.

history_text_issues.claim: Islamic rule supposedly brought a “stable, peaceful administration”.
history_text_issues.problem: The Kalbid emirate was prosperous, but in the 11th century the island was fragmented among rival qaids (Ibn al-Thumna, Ibn al-Hawwas). It was precisely Ibn al-Thumna who called in Roger in 1061, and the text omits that invitation.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention the Islamic civil war that opened the door to the Normans.

history_text_issues.claim: Tancred was supposedly a noble warrior who sought to prevent the massacre of civilians in Jerusalem.
history_text_issues.problem: This image comes mainly from the Gesta Tancredi of Ralph of Caen, a panegyric. In 1099 Tancred's banner over the al-Aqsa Mosque did not prevent the massacre of those who had taken refuge there (Gesta Francorum, Ibn al-Athir), and Tancred himself stripped the Dome of the Rock (Templum Domini) of its silver, an episode reported by Ralph of Caen and Albert of Aachen.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the reputation as a construction of the panegyric source, together with the facts that contradict it.

history_text_issues.claim: The narrative of the First Crusade (Bohemond, Tancred) is presented as part of 'Sicilian' history.
history_text_issues.problem: It conflates distinct entities. Bohemond was a Norman from Apulia, on tense terms with his uncle Roger I and his half-brother Roger Borsa, and he founded a separate principality at Antioch. The County of Sicily stayed out of the crusade.
history_text_issues.correction: Clearly separate the County/Kingdom of Sicily from the crusader principalities.

history_text_issues.claim: The Italo-Normans mainly resembled their “Viking and Frankish forebears”.
history_text_issues.problem: A romantic trope. The 11th-century Normans were fully French-speaking and Christian. Their success was due to cavalry, papal alliances (Melfi, 1059), mercenary service and the use of local troops, not to a 'Viking' heritage.
history_text_issues.correction: Emphasise the Franco-Norman matrix and the policy of alliances.

history_text_issues.claim: An “increasingly tolerant” treatment of local populations and religious groups.
history_text_issues.problem: The trajectory is reversed. The pragmatic tolerance of Roger I and Roger II gave way to violence: attacks on the Muslims of Palermo (1161), flight to the interior, the revolt of 1189–1190, deportation to Lucera by Frederick II (1220s–1240s) and the destruction of Lucera in 1300, with its inhabitants sold as slaves. Ibn Jubayr (1184–1185) already describes the anxiety of the Sicilian Muslims.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe an initial pragmatic coexistence followed by increasing Latinisation and persecution.

history_text_issues.claim: Roger II's less competent successors supposedly let the kingdom fall into German, Frankish, Spanish and Byzantine spheres, with rapid decline and absorption.
history_text_issues.problem: Several errors. William II (1166–1189) had a prosperous reign (Monreale). The passage to the Hohenstaufen (1194) was dynastic, through the marriage of Constance, daughter of Roger II, to Henry VI. Byzantium never recovered Sicily (the 1155–1156 campaign failed at Brindisi). And the kingdom survived: Frederick II (1198–1250), the Angevins (1266), the Aragonese after the Vespers (1282), and the kingdoms of Sicily and Naples down to the Two Sicilies (1816–1861).
history_text_issues.correction: Describe the succession of dynasties without speaking of collapse; the kingdom endured for centuries.

history_text_issues.claim: The conquest is presented as the work of Norman 'speed' and cunning.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits that the conquest of Sicily took 30 years (1061–1091) and depended on local troops and fleets. It also omits the Arabic and Greek administration (dīwān), the admirals Christodoulos and George of Antioch, the 'Kingdom of Africa' (1146–1160) and al-Idrisi (Tabula Rogeriana, 1154).
history_text_issues.correction: Add the duration of the conquest and the multicultural administrative and naval apparatus.

missing_features: Muslim archers and troops in the royal army (Roger I; Frederick II's Lucera colony).

A powerful navy: George of Antioch, 'ammiratus ammiratorum' (one of the routes by which the word admiral came about), the conquest of Mahdia, Tripoli and the 'Kingdom of Africa' (1146–1160), raids against Byzantium (1147).
Trilingual administration (Latin, Greek, Arabic): the dīwān and the chanceries.
Silk and tiraz of Palermo (Greek artisans brought from Thebes and Corinth in 1147), sugar and cotton.
Science and cartography: al-Idrisi and the Tabula Rogeriana (1154).
The Assizes of Ariano (conventional date 1140), an early legal codification.
The apostolic legation (1098) and royal control of the Church.
The Norman heavy cavalry charge (Civitate 1053, Cerami 1063).

proposals.title: Saraceni di Lucera (new UT)
proposals.description: Archer-line and Crossbowman-line +1 attack and +1 range, also trainable at the Donjon; give Thumb Ring.
proposals.historical_basis: Muslim archers in the service of Roger I and, above all, of Frederick II (the Lucera colony, c. 1224–1300), used as a loyal guard.

proposals.title: Amiratus (new naval UT)
proposals.description: Galley-line and Fire Ships +10% HP and +1 attack; Docks work +20% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: The admirals George of Antioch and, later, Margaritus of Brindisi; the conquest of Mahdia (1148) and of the coast of Ifriqiya; the fleet that attacked Corinth and Thebes (1147).

proposals.title: Tabula Rogeriana or Dīwān (replaces First Crusade)
proposals.description: Option A, Tabula Rogeriana: reveals the map and +2 line of sight for all units. Option B, Dīwān: Market technologies -50% and trade +15% gold. If First Crusade is kept, reverse the mechanic to something like 'Castle units +conversion and +speed, but the Town Center loses production for a while'.
proposals.historical_basis: Al-Idrisi composed the Kitab Rujar and the silver planisphere for Roger II (1154). The Arabic-Greek dīwān managed the royal finances (Jeremy Johns, 2002).

proposals.title: Rename the civ 'Normans' or 'Italo-Normans'
proposals.description: Bring the name into line with the actual content of the design, or keep 'Sicilians' and add non-Norman elements (Saracen troops, a Greek and Arab navy).
proposals.historical_basis: The design (Serjeant, Donjon, Hauberk, First Crusade) is Norman, not Sicilian in the broad sense.

proposals.title: Give back Architecture, Treadmill Crane and Fortified Wall
proposals.description: Restore the building technologies that give coherence to the 'builders' identity.
proposals.historical_basis: Cefalù, Monreale, the Palatine Chapel, the palaces of Palermo and Norman castles.

proposals.title: Norman charge (replaces -40% bonus damage)
proposals.description: Knight-line with a charge attack (the Coustillier mechanic) from the Castle Age.
proposals.historical_basis: The couched-lance charge was decisive at Civitate (1053), Cerami (1063) and Dyrrhachium (1081), according to William of Apulia, Malaterra and Anna Komnene.

contested: The real degree of tolerance or 'convivencia' in Norman Sicily (Metcalfe, Johns, Birk).
'Viking' heritage versus Franco-Norman identity.
The reputation of William I, 'the Bad', which comes mainly from the hostile Hugo Falcandus.
Bohemond's motivations (Malaterra: ambition for Byzantine lands; Gesta Francorum: piety).
D. C. Douglas's 'Norman achievement' versus more recent readings.
The extent of the 'Arab agricultural revolution' (Andrew Watson) in Sicily.
The birth dates and epithets of the Hautevilles.
