civs.represents: The Western Roman Empire in Late Antiquity, from Theodosius I to Odoacer: field army (comitatenses), artillery, state fabricae and the late Roman navy. The iconography (centurion, legionary), however, evokes the Principate (1st–2nd centuries).
civs.period: AD 395–476/480, with extensions to c. 500; almost entirely before AoE2's ~500–1500 frame.
civs.verdict: The Romans capture several real features of the late Roman army. The infantry is well protected thanks to the state fabricae, with mail and scale armour and, correctly, without Plate Mail. There is cheap and abundant torsion artillery (Vegetius), horse archers (equites sagittarii) and the name Comitatenses. The main problems are the Centurion (the name and iconography of the classical infantry centurion applied to a heavy cavalry unit, although the successor rank, centenarius, also existed in late mounted units), the Dromon (a 6th-century ship) and the lack of the Treadmill Crane, a Roman invention described by Vitruvius. The biggest absence is the foederati system, which defined the 5th century militarily. The history text is competent, but it follows the 'decline' narrative and Luttwak's 'defence in depth', both contested, omits Aetius and the Catalaunian Plains and gets the chronology of the loss of Africa wrong.
civs.naming_scope_issues: The game calls the West of 395–476 'Romans' and the Eastern Romans, who called themselves Rhomaioi until 1453, 'Byzantines'. The term 'Byzantine' was popularised by Hieronymus Wolf (1557), so the game splits a people with the same identity into two civs. The period falls almost entirely before the year 500, and the civ comes from the Return of Rome content (2023). The figures of the centurion and the legionary point to the army of the Principate, not that of the 5th century. The same events (Attila, the sack of 410, Odoacer) appear in the texts of the Huns, Goths and Italians.

elements.explanation: The late Roman field army combined infantry legions and auxilia palatina with cavalry vexillationes, including cataphracts and horse archers, whose importance grew in the 4th–5th centuries.

elements.element: Villagers gather, build, and repair +5% faster
elements.explanation: A generic reading of Roman organisational and engineering capacity (roads, aqueducts, fabricae, annona). The link to the 5th century is weak, but it is acceptable as an abstraction.

elements.element: Infantry armor upgrade effects are doubled
elements.explanation: Late Roman infantry continued to use mail (lorica hamata), scale (squamata) and ridge helmets, produced in state fabricae (the Notitia Dignitatum lists about 35). There is debate: Vegetius (I.20) complains that the infantry had abandoned cuirasses and helmets, but many historians read this as rhetoric. Consistent with the absence of Plate Mail Armor.

Vegetius (II.25) assigns each legion 55 carroballistae and 10 onagri, and Ammianus Marcellinus describes scorpions and ballistae in sieges (Amida, 359). Light torsion artillery was ubiquitous and standardised.

elements.element: Galley-line and Dromons +1 melee/+1 pierce armor
elements.explanation: The 5th-century western navy was weak: Majorian's fleet was destroyed by the Vandals near Cartagena (460), and the great expedition of 468, mainly eastern, was wrecked by fireships at Cape Bon. The Dromon is a 6th-century ship (Cassiodorus c. 526, Procopius 533), already from the Ostrogothic and Byzantine period.

The centurion of the Principate was an infantry officer who commanded a century on foot. Vegetius (II.8 and II.13) says that in his time centurions were called centenarii, and the rank of centenarius also existed in late Roman cavalry units, in the hierarchy running from the circitor and the biarchus to the ducenarius and the primicerius. A mounted officer of that rank is therefore defensible for the 5th century; what is stretched is using the name and image of the classical infantry centurion. The aura that speeds up infantry is a good abstraction of leadership.

Legions still existed in the 5th century (legiones comitatenses and palatinae, of about 1,000 men). But the late legionary fought with spear, spatha, plumbatae and oval shield, in a close shield formation (Ammianus describes it at Strasbourg, 357; the term 'fulcum' only appears in the Strategikon, c. 600), and not with the classical Principate image of gladius and pilum. As a replacement for the Two-Handed Swordsman it is reasonable.

In the Late Empire 'ballista' denoted the machine that shot bolts and 'onager' the one that threw stones (Ammianus, 23.4). Shipborne artillery is documented, such as the liburnians with towers and machines described by Vegetius (book IV). The effect (rate of fire and naval attack) is consistent.

The institution is real: the mobile field army consolidated between Diocletian and Constantine (c. 300–330), as opposed to the limitanei. Training faster is a vague abstraction; more mobility would be more faithful. The 'charge attack' can be read as the initial impact of the charge or the volley of plumbatae before contact; late infantry knew how to receive charges in a shield wall (Strasbourg, 357), but it also charged, so there is no contradiction.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Scorpions minimum range reduced
elements.explanation: The Romans had light, manoeuvrable artillery (the cart-mounted carroballista, the manuballista). Reducing the minimum range is an acceptable abstraction.

tree_issues.problem: The human-powered wheel crane (polyspastos, treadwheel) is a Roman technology, described by Vitruvius (De architectura X.2) and depicted on the Haterii relief (c. AD 100). Removing it from the Romans, of all civs, is an error.
Anachronistic for the Roman West: the dromon is attested from the early 6th century (Cassiodorus; Belisarius' fleet in 533). The typical Roman warship was the liburnian.

tree_issues.item: Cavalry Archer and Heavy Cavalry Archer (present)
tree_issues.problem: Well founded: the Notitia Dignitatum lists numerous units of equites sagittarii, and Aetius used Hunnic contingents.

A debatable absence: the Notitia lists many sagittarii units, both foot and mounted, and Vegetius (I.15) recommends training a substantial share of recruits with the bow. Having horse archers without the archery upgrades is hardly consistent.
Correct: plate armour belongs to the 14th–15th centuries. Doubling Scale Mail and Chain Mail corresponds to the lorica squamata and the hamata.
A trivial anachronism shared by many civs: woodblock printing on paper only reached Europe in the 14th–15th centuries.

tree_issues.item: No gunpowder (Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon, Cannon Galleon)
tree_issues.problem: Correct.

history_text_issues.claim: In 395 the empire was divided in two “for the last time”.
history_text_issues.problem: It was an administrative division between Arcadius and Honorius. Contemporaries still saw a single empire, with shared consulships and common legislation.
history_text_issues.correction: Speak of two imperial courts of an empire still conceived of as one.

history_text_issues.claim: In 395 Rome was supposedly already 'poorly equipped', with run-down frontiers and badly paid, understrength legions.
history_text_issues.problem: A decline narrative in the Gibbonian mould. In 394 Theodosius still won the great civil war at the Frigidus, and the Notitia (c. 395–420) lists an enormous army. The western collapse accelerates after 405–410 and above all after 439, with the loss of Africa.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the fragility as gradual and located mainly in the 5th century.

history_text_issues.claim: The new strategy was supposedly to hold the frontiers with a token force and rely on an elite mobile reserve.
history_text_issues.problem: This is Luttwak's 'defence in depth' thesis (1976), which is heavily contested (Isaac, Whittaker, Wheeler). The comitatenses were consolidated c. 300–330, not as a response in 395, and the limitanei were real garrisons, not 'token'.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the thesis as a debated interpretation and date the creation of the field army correctly.

history_text_issues.claim: The federates were supposedly “unwilling to assimilate”, of fickle loyalty and a huge financial drain.
history_text_issues.problem: A moralising reading. Goffart and Halsall show that barbarian leaders sought offices and a place in the Roman system (Alaric wanted the command of magister militum and supplies). The sack of 410 followed broken agreements and the massacre of the families of barbarian soldiers after the execution of Stilicho (408, Zosimus V.35). And many federates were loyal (the Visigoths at the Catalaunian Plains, 451).
history_text_issues.correction: Describe the federates as an integral, negotiated part of the Roman military system, with tensions on both sides.

history_text_issues.claim: The Visigoths sacked Rome in 410 and took (“seize”) a large part of Gaul.
history_text_issues.problem: The settlement in Aquitaine (418) was made by treaty with Constantius III. Large-scale expansion only came with Euric, after 466.
history_text_issues.correction: Distinguish the federate settlement of 418 from the later expansion.

history_text_issues.claim: The text jumps from Attila's peak to his death in 453; Attila supposedly came close to sacking Rome.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits Flavius Aetius, the leading western general, and the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains (451), in which a Roman-Gothic-Frankish-Alan coalition stopped Attila. In 452 Attila devastated northern Italy (Aquileia) but did not come near Rome; the meeting with Leo I took place by the Mincio.
history_text_issues.correction: Add Aetius and 451, and place the 452 campaign in northern Italy.

history_text_issues.claim: After Attila's death (453), the Vandals supposedly took the Empire's granary in North Africa.
history_text_issues.problem: A chronological error. The Vandals crossed to Africa in 429 and took Carthage in 439, fourteen years before Attila's death; the loss of Africa was one of the causes, not a consequence, of the later crisis. The text also omits the Vandal sack of Rome in 455.
history_text_issues.correction: Date the Vandal conquest of Africa (429–439) and mention the sack of 455.

history_text_issues.claim: A “Germanic chieftain, Odoacer” deposed the last Western emperor in 476, ending Roman rule.
history_text_issues.problem: Odoacer was an officer of the Roman army in Italy, of Scirian or Rugian origin. He sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople and ruled nominally under Zeno. Julius Nepos continued to be recognised as emperor until 480, Syagrius' domain in Gaul lasted until 486, and the Roman Senate and administration carried on.
history_text_issues.correction: Present 476 as a conventional date and mention 480 and the institutional continuity.

history_text_issues.claim: The migration of the Huns as a 'chain reaction' that pushed Germanic peoples and Alans.
history_text_issues.problem: This is the domino model (Heather). Halsall gives much more weight to internal Roman politics. The claim is not wrong, but it is contested.
history_text_issues.correction: Flag the debate.

missing_features: Foederati and allied contingents (Goths, Huns, Alans, Franks), the essence of the 5th-century army; Aetius and the Catalaunian Plains (451).
Limitanei and burgi (frontier towers) of the limes system.
Plumbatae or martiobarbuli, lead-weighted darts (Ioviani and Herculiani).
Bucellarii, the private retinue cavalry of generals (Stilicho, Aetius).
Cataphracts and clibanarii (fabricae clibanariae).
Annona militaris (state supply) and cursus publicus.
State arms fabricae (the Notitia lists about 35).
Engineering: treadwheel crane, concrete, roads.
Christianisation and the role of bishops as civic leaders (Leo I).
Late city walls (Aurelian; Ravenna as a capital protected by marshes).

proposals.title: Centurion becomes Tribunus, Comes or Centenarius
proposals.description: Keep the mounted unit and the aura, but rename it 'Tribunus' or 'Comes' (unit and army commanders) or, for greater accuracy of rank, 'Centenarius'. Alternative: create an infantry 'Centenarius' in the Barracks with the same aura.
proposals.historical_basis: Late Roman senior officers (tribuni, comites, duces) were mounted; the classical centurion was an infantry rank, and its late successor, the centenarius (Vegetius II.8 and II.13), existed in both the infantry and the cavalry (Speidel 2006).

proposals.title: Foederati (new UT)
proposals.description: The Castle now trains two federate units paid only in gold: Gothic infantry (Huskarl-type stats) and a Hunnic horse archer (elite Cavalry Archer type), with a population limit.
proposals.historical_basis: The treaty of 382 with the Goths; Aetius' Huns; the coalition at the Catalaunian Plains (451) with Visigoths, Franks, Burgundians and Alans.

proposals.title: Plumbatae (new UT)
proposals.description: Legionary and Militia-line gain a short-range charged ranged attack before melee (a mechanism already used by the Xianbei Raider and the Bolas Rider).
proposals.historical_basis: Vegetius (I.17) describes the martiobarbuli or plumbatae and the legions of the Ioviani and Herculiani that used them; De Rebus Bellicis also mentions them.

proposals.title: Treadmill Crane and Liburna
proposals.description: Give the Treadmill Crane and replace the Dromon with a Romans-only 'Liburna' (a galley with +1/+1 armour).
proposals.historical_basis: Vitruvius X.2 and the Haterii relief; Vegetius (book IV) on liburnians; the dromon only appears in the 6th century.

proposals.title: Limitanei (bonus)
proposals.description: Watch Towers and Palisade/Stone Walls -25% stone, and towers +2 pierce armour when garrisoned with infantry.
proposals.historical_basis: The limes system with burgi and limitanei garrisons along the Rhine and the Danube.

proposals.title: Cursus Publicus (new team bonus)
proposals.description: The team's Trade Carts and Monks +10% speed.
proposals.historical_basis: The state postal and transport service that used the Roman road network.

contested: Fall or transformation: Gibbon and Ward-Perkins/Heather versus Peter Brown, Halsall and Goffart.
'Grand strategy' and defence in depth: Luttwak versus Isaac, Whittaker and Wheeler.
Vegetius on infantry without armour (I.20): rhetoric or reality.
'Barbarisation' of the army as a cause of the collapse.
End date: 476, 480 (Julius Nepos) or 486 (Syagrius).
Attila's withdrawal in 452: Leo I (Prosper) or famine, disease and attacks by Marcian (Hydatius).
Actual strength of the late Roman army compared with the Notitia figures.
The settlement of 418: a division of land or of tax revenues (Goffart).
Exact meaning of the late ranks (centenarius, ducenarius): command of men or pay grades (Speidel).

groups.cross_civ_notes:
1) Iberia duplicated and truncated. The Spanish and Portuguese history texts open with the same outline (Visigoths, al-Andalus, Reconquista), both ignoring the Suebi and the entry of 409, and both designs jump to 1480–1550 (gunpowder, Conquistador, Missionary, Caravel, Feitoria, Circumnavigation). Medieval Christian Iberia is left with almost no mechanical representation. Cavalry riding a la jineta exists only as the Berbers' Genitour: the Zenata origin is real, but the 'genetours' that Europe knew were mostly Christian Iberian horsemen. The Visigoths are diluted into the Goths, a mass-infantry design that ignores the Kingdom of Toledo. Al-Andalus is split between Berbers and Saracens with no Andalusi civ, and the Crown of Aragon and Navarre/the Basques have no voice. There is an obvious inconsistency: the Portuguese have Arbalester while the Spanish (who, with the Bulgarians, are the only 2 of 56 civs lacking it) do not even have Crossbowman, even though both used crossbowmen in large numbers; the generic Mounted Crossbowman does little to soften this.

2) Italy fragmented across five civs. Southern Italy appears in the Italians' text, in the Sicilians (Normans), in the Byzantines (Catepanate until 1071) and, implicitly, in the Saracens (emirates of Sicily and Bari). Aragonese Sicily after the Vespers (1282) belongs to no one. The Normans have no civ of their own: they are diluted between the Franks and the Sicilians.

3) The Roman paradox. The game calls the West of 395–476 'Romans' and the Eastern Romans, who called themselves Rhomaioi until 1453, 'Byzantines' ('Byzantine' was popularised by Hieronymus Wolf in 1557). The Dromon is shared (Armenians, Byzantines, Goths, Huns, Romans) and is more Byzantine than Western Roman. The Romans, Italians and Sicilians texts repeat the 5th–6th centuries (Odoacer, Theodoric, Belisarius, Justinian), and the Goths and Huns cover the same events (410, Attila).

4) Redundant gunpowder. Spanish, Portuguese and Italians are three Mediterranean 'gunpowder' civs with almost interchangeable bonuses (fire rate, -20% gold, -20% cost). Historically, primacy in European gunpowder is disputed: the earliest references to cannon are Florentine and English (1326), Nasrid Iberia has early uses (Huéscar 1324, Algeciras 1342–1344), and in the 15th century the great centres were Italy, Burgundy, Bohemia and the German world. Christian Castile only stands out from Granada (1482–1492) and Cerignola (1503) onwards.

5) Iberian dependence on Italian nautical expertise, which the game ignores. The Portuguese royal navy was organised by the Genoese Manuel Pessanha (1317), Castile had Genoese admirals (Egidio Boccanegra, 1340s), the Portuguese expedition to the Canaries of 1341 was commanded by Italians, and Columbus was Genoese. An Italian naval team bonus (for example, faster team Docks) would be more faithful than the current one.

6) Generic Iberian ships. The Carrack is now a generic ship (48 of the 56 civs), presented as a melee boarding ship. The Portuguese nau and the Genoese and Catalan carracks, which combined artillery and boarding, get no treatment of their own; this is a missed opportunity to differentiate Portuguese, Spanish and Italians.

7) Mercenaries and heavy cavalry. Since the condottieri companies were mostly heavy cavalry, a corrected Condottiero would overlap conceptually with the Burgundians' Coustillier and the Franks' knights. One solution is to differentiate it through payment in gold and availability to allies.

8) Credit in the right place and in the wrong one. Circumnavigation (Portuguese) celebrates a Castilian expedition. First Crusade (Sicilians) is more defensible than it seems, because Bohemond and Tancred were Italo-Normans, but Roger I's Sicilian state kept its distance from the crusade. Their own achievements, such as the Portuguese 'volta do mar' and the Sicilian Tabula Rogeriana, go unused.

9) Calibration. None of the five civs is arbitrary. Italians, Sicilians and Romans (6) have well-founded cores with isolated errors; Portuguese (5) has a strong maritime identity but unfounded economic bonuses; Spanish (4) is the most displaced in time and the furthest removed from its medieval past. The group average (5.4) is slightly above the game average, which is to be expected for European civs, which the designers know better.

verification_log.change: '+20 gold per technology' bonus reclassified from 'stretched' to 'unfounded': the draft itself admitted that there was no historical anchor.

Gunpowder bonus: corrected the claim that Iberia was not an early adopter; added the verified Nasrid uses at Huéscar (1324) and Algeciras (1342–1344), and kept the caveat about the 15th-century centres of innovation. Dating of the tercios adjusted to 1534–1536.
History, 1469: corrected the claim 'neither of the couple reigned'. Ferdinand had been King of Sicily since 1468 (verified); the sentence now reads 'neither reigned in Castile or Aragon'.

History: Count Julian downgraded from 'moderate' to 'minor' (the game's vague wording is compatible with the attested Visigothic civil war); 'in 50 years' downgraded to 'minor' (misleading, but not literally false).
Added the error in the text that omits the invasion of 409 (Vandals, Suebi, Alans) and the entry of the Visigoths as federates of Rome.
Córdoba: the range of estimates is now presented as highly variable and contested, because the literature ranges from about 100,000 to much higher figures.

Missionary: added the nuance of the later mounted missionaries (Kino, late 17th century). Conquistador: added that the mounted arquebusier existed in the Italian Wars (1520s–1540s), but not as a type of the American conquistador.

Cannon Galleon: added the Castilian naval victory at La Rochelle (1372) and the technical explanation of 1588. Crossbowmen proposal: removed the unverifiable reference to crossbowmen at Las Navas (1212) and replaced the name 'Ballesteros del Rey' with 'Ballesteros de Nómina'. Removed the Santa Hermandad from the list of crossbowmen.

Naming: 'unitary state in the 18th century' corrected to 'institutional unification from the Nueva Planta onwards', which left out Navarre and the Basque provinces. Added the Castilian navy to the absences and Iberian primacy in gunpowder to the contested issues.
Added the error of omission of the Suebian kingdom of Braga (409–585), severity 'moderate', and the corresponding element in the absences and in the naming.
'Navigator' epithet: 'creation of English authors' corrected to '19th-century epithet, popularised in English by R. H. Major (1868)'. The first coinage is uncertain.

Copper and tin: added the probable explanation of the confusion (the Iberian Pyrite Belt and Neves-Corvo, mined in antiquity and in the contemporary era). Algarve: acknowledged the minor salt pans of Castro Marim and reframed as a problem of causality.

Organ Gun: dating of Edward III's ribauldequins adjusted to 1339 and the Flemish use of 1382 added. Medieval population adjusted to 1 to 1.5 million. 1341 expedition: names of the Italian commanders added.

Added tech tree issues: generic Carrack (48/56) with no Portuguese trait, Arrowslits and Hoardings missing despite King Denis's network of castles, and a note that only 10/56 civs have Paladin. Gold Shaft Mining moved from 'correct' to 'acceptable' (there was alluvial gold at Adiça). Added the 'Nau da Índia' proposal.

Condottiero reclassified from 'wrong' to 'stretched': in the 15th century hired infantry (provvisionati) grew, and in the 16th century there were fast-moving companies of infantry and light cavalry (Bande Nere). The core problem is the captain's title applied to a soldier and the invented 'anti-gunpowder' role. Verdict updated.

Paladin missing: added that only 10 of the 56 civs have it, so its absence is not a specific statement by the game. Added the absence of Siege Engineers and Siege Ram, inconsistent with the Italian tradition of military engineering.

Cannons of 1326: the Florentine document is now 'one of the two earliest references', alongside the English Milemete manuscript. Etymology of the pavise marked as probable. Added the error in the text about Leonardo (Vinci/Milan/France, projects never carried out).

First Crusade reclassified from 'stretched' to 'plausible': Bohemond (son of Guiscard, a Hauteville) and Tancred were Italo-Normans, and the civ represents the Italo-Normans. The criticism that Roger I's state kept its distance and that the mechanic inverts the effect is retained. The sentence 'the Hautevilles of Sicily did not take part' has been corrected. Verdict and cross-civ notes updated.

Tancred: the source for the looting of the Templum Domini is now Ralph of Caen and Albert of Aachen, and the source for the massacre at al-Aqsa is the Gesta Francorum and Ibn al-Athir. Roger I's withdrawal at Amalfi is attributed to Malaterra. Watson and the 'Arab agricultural revolution' were added to the contested issues.

Centurion reclassified from 'wrong' to 'stretched': verified that Vegetius (II.8, II.13) equates centuriones with centenarii, and that the rank of centenarius existed in late Roman cavalry units (circitor–biarchus–centenarius–ducenarius hierarchy). Renaming proposal adjusted and Speidel (2006) added to the sources.

Comitatenses: removed the claim that the charge attack 'contradicts' late Roman tactics; it can be read as the impact of a charge or a volley of plumbatae. Legionary: corrected the anachronism 'fulcum' (a term from the Strategikon, c. 600).
Naval bonus: corrected the expeditions against the Vandals (441 was an Eastern fleet that was recalled; 460, Majorian's fleet destroyed near Cartagena; 468 mostly Eastern).

Added the chronological error in the text that places the Vandal conquest of Africa after the death of Attila (Carthage fell in 439), the omission of the sack of 455 and the exaggeration of Attila 'nearly sacking Rome'. Added the absence of Bracer and Thumb Ring despite the numerous sagittarii units.

Fidelity scores kept (Spanish 4, Portuguese 5, Italians 6, Sicilians 6, Romans 6) after reassessing the elements; calibration note added. Cross-civ note on the generic Carrack added. Spelling standardised to pt-PT (AO90): 'tática', 'excecionalmente', 'Córdova', 'Cerignola'.

civs.represents: The kingdom of East Francia/Germany and the Holy Roman Empire (Ottonian, Salian, Staufen, Luxembourg and Habsburg dynasties), mixed with the Teutonic Order, an autonomous monastic-military state in Prussia and Livonia. In the game's imagery (campaigns, wiki) it also absorbs the crusading orders in general (Templars, Hospitallers).
civs.period: c. 919 (election of Henry I) – c. 1500 (reforms of Maximilian I, Landsknechte); Teutonic Order 1190–1525.
civs.verdict: This is a 1999 design that captures real facets: the density of castles and fortified towns, the quality of German armour, monastic and hospitaller medicine, and the religious-military character of the Order. No bonus is pure invention, but almost all are generic, and the “slow, defensive infantry” identity only really fits the end of the period. The unique unit turns an order of mounted knights into infantry, and the tech tree denies the civ the very things in which the Germans led Europe: silver mining, cranes and cathedral architecture, and Hanseatic shipping. The history text, inherited from the original version, has factual errors (the division of the empire on Charlemagne's death, “Holy Roman Emperor” in 800, Vikings in the Salian period) and an outdated narrative of “near-barbarian Germans” and of a “minor power”.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Teutons” is a learned exonym. The Teutones were a northern people (traditionally from Jutland), of disputed Germanic or Celtic affiliation, defeated by Marius at Aquae Sextiae (102 BC). In the Middle Ages, “Teutonicus” served as the Latin equivalent of theodiscus/diutisc (“deutsch”) and was used above all by Italians and by the Curia: Gregory VII addressed Henry IV as “rex Teutonicorum” precisely to deny him the Roman dimension of the title. The rulers themselves preferred “rex Romanorum”/“imperium Romanum”. The label merges three realities: the German kingdom/Empire, which was multi-ethnic (Czechs, Italians, Burgundians, Flemings), the Teutonic Order (a separate state on the Baltic, with a Prussian, Polish and German population) and, according to the wiki itself, the Templars and Hospitallers. It overlaps with the Franks (the text claims Charlemagne as the origin of Germany), Burgundians, Sicilians (Staufen Sicily), Italians, Bohemians (a member of the Empire) and Goths. The “Saxons” civ apparently denotes the Anglo-Saxons (Hearth Troop, Shield Wall), but the Ottonian dynasty was continental Saxon, which may cause confusion. Within the game's 500–1500 frame, the civ only makes sense from c. 900; before that it is Frankish territory.

elements.explanation: The term existed in the Middle Ages (“Teutonici”, Ordo domus Sanctae Mariae Theutonicorum), so it is defensible. But it is a Latin/Italian exonym and, in Portuguese and English, it mainly evokes the Teutonic Order. “Germans” or “Holy Roman Empire” would better describe the entity represented.

“Defensive” is sound: the German lands had one of the highest densities of castles in Europe (estimates speak of more than ten thousand Burgen), as well as walled towns. “Infantry” only clearly applies to the end of the period (Maximilian's Landsknechte, c. 1487, and urban militias). Between the 10th and 14th centuries, the elite arm of German armies was heavy cavalry: the Ottonian loricati at Lechfeld (955), the Staufen knights, the German companies in Italy in the 14th century. The real weight of infantry in Ottonian armies is debated (Bachrach versus Leyser).

It can be read as the Ostsiedlung (12th–14th centuries): mass agricultural colonisation east of the Elbe under the ius Teutonicum, with holdings (Hufen) exempt from dues in the first years (Freijahre), the heavy plough and three-field rotation. The bonus does not make this explicit; it is a reasonable mechanical translation of a real trait, not a direct link.

It ties in well with the so-called Burgenordnung of Henry I during the truce with the Magyars (926–933): refuge strongholds where, according to Widukind of Corvey, one in every nine agrarii milites lived permanently, a system that paved the way for the victory at Riade (933). Whether this was a systematic ordinance is debated. The later walled towns strengthen the link.

elements.element: Infantry and Mounted Units +1/+2 melee armor in Castle/Imperial Age
elements.explanation: Nuremberg, Augsburg and Landshut were major European centres of armour-making in the 15th century, with “Gothic” armour and workshops such as that of the Helmschmid family of Augsburg. Solingen and Passau were famous for their blades. The link is good for the Imperial Age and more generic for the Castle Age.

The Teutonic Order was born as a field hospital at the siege of Acre (1190), founded by merchants from Bremen and Lübeck, and only became militarised in 1198. German monastic medicine (Hildegard of Bingen) strengthens the link.

Murder Holes illustrates castle culture in a generic way. Herbal Medicine has good support in the Lorscher Arzneibuch (c. 795), in the Hortulus of Walafrid Strabo (Reichenau, 9th century) and in Hildegard's work. Even so, both techniques were common to all of Latin Europe.

The Order existed, and the resistance to conversion reflects the religious vows well. But the knight-brothers fought mainly mounted, as heavy cavalry (Durbe 1260, Grunwald 1410). They numbered a few hundred on campaign, supported by sergeants, “guest” crusaders and Prussian auxiliaries. Making them slow infantry inverts their tactical role; at most, it represents dismounted knights in sieges and garrisons.

“Ironclad” is a 19th-century term (La Gloire, 1859; Monitor and Virginia, 1862). Protecting siege engines with hides, mantlets or planks (the “cat”, Katze) was universal practice, with nothing specifically German about it. The anachronism lies in the name; the mechanic is merely generic.

elements.element: Crenellations (Castles +3 range, garrisoned Infantry fires arrows)
elements.explanation: Crenellations existed throughout Europe, in the Islamic world and in Asia. The idea of a garrison shooting from the walls is generic. Only German castle density vaguely justifies a defensive tech.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Units more resistant to conversion
elements.explanation: An acceptable abstraction of the fervour of the crusading orders and the imperial Church. It has no specific basis, but it is consistent with the Order's crusading identity.

tree_issues.problem: Crossbowmen were central to the Teutonic Order (arsenals and crossbowmen in the Prussian fortresses) and to German towns, where shooting confraternities (Schützengilden) appear from the 14th century. The gap is mitigated: the Teutons have the Crossbowman and the new Mounted Crossbowman/Heavy Mounted Crossbowman. Only the last foot upgrade is missing, which, in a game where 26 of 56 civs lack it, is a minor absence and not “one of the most unhistorical”.

Germany was the mining heartland of medieval Europe: Rammelsberg/Goslar (silver, traditionally since c. 968), Freiberg (1168), the Harz, the Erzgebirge, Schwaz in Tyrol (Fugger, late 15th century). German miners (“Saxons”) opened mining districts in Bohemia, Hungary, Serbia (Novo Brdo) and Bosnia, and Agricola codified this knowledge in De re metallica (1556).

The human-powered treadwheel crane is almost a German symbol: the medieval crane of Cologne Cathedral stood atop the south tower from the mid-15th century until 1868, and the Danzig Krantor (1442–44) was built under the Order. Speyer, Cologne, Baltic Brick Gothic and Marienburg (the largest brick castle in the world) make the lack of Architecture hard to justify.

The Hansa (c. 1250–1500) dominated Baltic and North Sea trade with its cogs and prevailed over Denmark (Peace of Stralsund, 1370). The Teutonic Order itself was the only territorial ruler that was a member of the Hansa, and it conquered Gotland in 1398. A mediocre navy contradicts this.

tree_issues.item: Paladin and Bloodlines (present) versus the infantry label
tree_issues.problem: Their presence is historically right (German heavy cavalry; the Paladin exists for only 10 of 56 civs, which underlines the point). But it shows that the “Infantry” label and the dismounted UU do not match German military reality before c. 1480.

tree_issues.item: Mounted Crossbowman and Heavy Mounted Crossbowman (present)
tree_issues.problem: Plausible: mounted crossbowmen appear in German and Order armies in the 14th–15th centuries (the Order's service records provide for mounted fighters with crossbows).

The lack of horse archers and of the Hussar is correct. That of Light Cavalry is debatable: the Order made large-scale use of native Prussian light cavalry (the so-called Turkopolen) in raids through the frontier forest (Wildnis) against Lithuania.

tree_issues.item: Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon, Bombard Tower (present)
tree_issues.problem: Correct: firearms reached the German lands early (the Faule Mette of Brunswick, 1411; the Hakenbüchse; urban arsenals), and the Order had artillery at Grunwald (1410). The legend of Berthold Schwarz as the inventor of gunpowder is mythical.

history_text_issues.claim: The origin of Germany goes back to Charlemagne's coronation as “Holy Roman Emperor” in 800.
history_text_issues.problem: Anachronistic title and a teleological reading. Charlemagne was crowned emperor “governing the Roman Empire”; “sacrum imperium” only appears in 1157 and “Sacrum Romanum Imperium” in 1254.
history_text_issues.correction: In 800 Charlemagne was crowned emperor. A distinctly “German” kingdom took shape gradually between 843 (Verdun), 911/919 and the 11th–12th centuries (Brühl, Ehlers, Reuter; chronology contested).

history_text_issues.claim: On Charlemagne's death, the empire was divided into three parts.
history_text_issues.problem: False. Charlemagne planned a three-way division in the Divisio regnorum (806), but two of his sons died before him, and in 814 the empire passed whole to Louis the Pious.
history_text_issues.correction: The three-way division (Lothair, Louis the German, Charles the Bald) came with the Treaty of Verdun, in 843, among Charlemagne's grandsons.

history_text_issues.claim: The imperial title remained in Charlemagne's family until the family died out in the 10th century.
history_text_issues.problem: Imprecise. There were non-Carolingian emperors as early as the 9th century (Guy and Lambert of Spoleto, 891–898), and the eastern Carolingian line died out in 911 with Louis the Child. Conrad I (911–918) is omitted.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention Conrad I, the transition of 911–919 and the imperial vacancy between 924 (death of Berengar I) and 962.

history_text_issues.claim: In 919, Henry of Saxony was elected “king of Germany” by the other dukes.
history_text_issues.problem: At Fritzlar he was elected only by Franks and Saxons; Swabia and Bavaria only recognised him later (919–921). “King of Germany” is an anachronistic title.
history_text_issues.correction: Henry I was elected king of the East Franks by Saxons and Franks and later imposed himself on the southern dukes.

history_text_issues.claim: The Germans were supposedly very close to a state of barbarism, having been conquered by Charlemagne a century earlier.
history_text_issues.problem: Pejorative and largely wrong. Only the Saxons were conquered as pagans (772–804); Bavaria was annexed in 788, but it had been Christian for more than a century, and the Alemanni, Thuringians and East Franks had long been integrated. It ignores the “Ottonian Renaissance” (Reichenau, Hrotsvitha of Gandersheim, the bronze doors of Bernward of Hildesheim).
history_text_issues.correction: Present the Ottonian kingdom as a Carolingian successor with first-rate ecclesiastical and artistic culture, which in the 10th century influenced Italy as much as it was influenced by it.

history_text_issues.claim: The imperial armies were supposedly made up of ecclesiastical tenants and ministeriales, serfs trained as knights.
history_text_issues.problem: Chronological conflation. The ministeriales emerge as a group mainly in the 11th–12th centuries (Salians and Staufen). In the 10th century, contingents came from bishops, abbots and noble retinues (Indiculus loricatorum, 981).
history_text_issues.correction: Distinguish the Ottonian imperial Church system (armoured horsemen supplied by bishoprics and abbeys) from the Salian-Staufen ministeriales, legally unfree knights.

history_text_issues.claim: The army defended the kingdom against Vikings and Magyars, and during the Investiture Controversy the princes were still fighting the Vikings.
history_text_issues.problem: Viking raids on East Francia peaked in the 880s (Aachen 881; Viking defeat on the Dyle, 891). By the time of the Investiture Controversy (1075–1122) the Viking age was over. The real threats were the Magyars until 955 and the Elbe Slavs (revolt of 983).
history_text_issues.correction: Replace the Vikings with the Magyars (until 955) and the Polabian Slavs; remove the Viking reference from the Salian period.

history_text_issues.claim: The Teutonic Knights were stopped by Alexander Nevsky at the Battle of Lake Peipus.
history_text_issues.problem: A half-truth, amplified by Eisenstein's film (1938). In 1242 it was the Livonian branch of the Order (the former Sword Brothers, absorbed in 1237) that fought, with troops from the bishopric of Dorpat and Danish Estonia; the Livonian Rhymed Chronicle records 20 brothers killed and 6 captured. The battle (together with Rakvere, 1268) helped fix the border with Novgorod and Pskov, but the Order kept expanding in Prussia, Pomerelia (1308–09) and Gotland (1398).
history_text_issues.correction: Say that Peipus halted the Livonian advance against Rus'; the Order's expansion was contained by Poland-Lithuania at Grunwald (1410) and, decisively, in the Thirteen Years' War (1454–66, Second Peace of Thorn).

history_text_issues.claim: In the mid-13th century the throne stood empty for 20 years.
history_text_issues.problem: During the Interregnum (1250/54–1273) there were rival elected kings: William of Holland, Richard of Cornwall and Alfonso X of Castile. By contrast, the imperial throne (coronation in Rome) remained vacant much longer, from 1250 to 1312.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe the Interregnum as a period of rival, weak kings, ended by Rudolf of Habsburg (1273), and distinguish the King of the Romans from a crowned emperor.

history_text_issues.claim: The ministeriales rebelled, seized towns and castles and declared themselves free.
history_text_issues.problem: Dramatisation. Most ministeriales gradually merged into the lower nobility (13th–14th centuries); there were isolated conflicts, not a general revolt.
history_text_issues.correction: Speak of the gradual social rise of the ministeriales into the nobility.

history_text_issues.claim: The Lombard League refused to recognise the emperor.
history_text_issues.problem: After Legnano (1176), the Peace of Constance (1183) guaranteed the cities autonomy, and they formally recognised imperial suzerainty.
history_text_issues.correction: The cities obtained self-government within the imperial framework.

history_text_issues.claim: Germany remained a minor power for centuries.
history_text_issues.problem: Wrong and teleological (the “failed nation-state” narrative). Charles IV made Prague an imperial capital and promulgated the Golden Bull (1356), the Hansa dominated northern trade, Maximilian I was one of the most powerful sovereigns in Europe, and Gutenberg's printing press (c. 1450) and German mining transformed the continent.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the Empire as a decentralised but functional political structure that was economically central (Whaley, Wilson).

missing_features: The Hansa and Baltic trade (cogs, Kontore in Bruges, London, Bergen and Novgorod)
Silver mining and metallurgy (Rammelsberg, Freiberg, Schwaz) and German mining law (Bergrecht) exported to Central Europe
The Ostsiedlung and Magdeburg law/ius Teutonicum, which founded towns and villages in Poland, Bohemia, Hungary and Lithuania
Ottonian and Staufen heavy cavalry; the ministeriales as unfree knights
The imperial Church: bishops and abbots as suppliers of armoured horsemen (Indiculus loricatorum, 981)
Landsknechte (pikes and Zweihänder, Doppelsöldner) in the late 15th century
Shooting confraternities and urban militias of the free imperial cities
Gutenberg's printing press (Mainz, c. 1450)
Brick Gothic and the great cathedrals with their cranes
Prussian light cavalry in the Order's service and the Litauerreisen with guest knights from all over Europe

proposals.title: Restore crossbow, mining, crane and shipyard upgrades
proposals.description: Give Arbalester, Gold Shaft Mining, Architecture, Treadmill Crane, Dry Dock and Shipwright. If compensation is needed, remove Siege Onager or one of the free upgrades.
proposals.historical_basis: Shooting confraternities and the Order's arsenals; the Rammelsberg, Freiberg and Schwaz mines; the Cologne Cathedral crane and the Danzig Krantor; Hanseatic fleets.

proposals.title: Teutonic Knight as cavalry and Landsknecht as infantry
proposals.description: Convert the Teutonic Knight into a Castle cavalry unit: slow, with very high melee armor and strong resistance to conversion. Create a Landsknecht at the Barracks (Imperial Age) with a bonus against the Spearman line and small area damage (the Doppelsöldner's Zweihänder).
proposals.historical_basis: The brethren of the Order fought mounted (Durbe 1260, Grunwald 1410). The Landsknechte were created by Maximilian I c. 1487 as the German answer to the Swiss pikemen, at the very end of the game's time frame.

proposals.title: Hanse (replaces Ironclad)
proposals.description: Trade Cogs and Trade Carts generate +25% gold and Docks cost -25% wood.
proposals.historical_basis: The Hanseatic League controlled trade between Novgorod, the Baltic, Bruges and London, prevailed militarily over Denmark (Stralsund, 1370) and included the Teutonic Order itself as a member.

proposals.title: Reichskirchensystem (replaces Crenellations)
proposals.description: Monasteries become able to train the Knight line; knights trained there receive additional resistance to conversion.
proposals.historical_basis: In the Indiculus loricatorum (981), Otto II requested some 2000 armoured horsemen for Italy, mostly from bishoprics and abbeys. Warrior bishops such as Christian of Mainz and Rainald of Dassel commanded imperial armies in Italy.

proposals.title: Bergrecht: Saxon miners
proposals.description: Gold Miners and Stone Miners work +15% faster. As a team bonus, allied Mining Camps work +10% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: German miners were recruited for Kutná Hora, Jihlava, Kremnica, Banská Štiavnica and Novo Brdo, taking with them the mining law of Freiberg/Iglau.

contested: When was “Germany” born: in 843 (Verdun), in 911/919 or only in the 11th–12th centuries (Brühl, Ehlers, Reuter)?
Scale and importance of the Battle on the Ice (1242): Soviet/Russian historiography versus the minimalist reading (Fennell, Christiansen, Urban) based on the Livonian Rhymed Chronicle.
Nature of the Ottonian armies: dominant heavy cavalry (Leyser) or mixed armies with infantry and good siege capability (Bernard and David Bachrach)?
Existence of a systematic “Burgenordnung” under Henry I and the meaning of agrarii milites in Widukind.
The late Empire: “fragmentation and failure” (Prussian national historiography) or a functional political system (Whaley, Wilson)?
Origin of the Teutones (Germanic or Celtic) and the relationship between teutonicus and theodiscus.

civs.represents: The Kingdom of Bohemia and the lands of its Crown (Moravia, Silesia, Lusatia), from the Přemyslids to the Luxembourgs and the Jagiellons. The design is heavily centred on the Hussites (1419–1471).
civs.period: c. 870 (Bořivoj I) – 1526 (Mohács); the core of the design covers 1419–1471.
civs.verdict: For the period it focuses on, it is one of the best-grounded designs in the game. The Hussite wagon, the early, large-scale use of firearms, the polearms against cavalry, the silver of Kutná Hora, the University of Prague and the clerical poverty of the Four Articles are all well translated. There are three weak points. First, the almost exclusive focus on the 1420s makes the chivalric Bohemia of Ottokar II and John the Blind disappear (no Bloodlines or Plate Barding). Second, the Houfnice has its role inverted. Third, a “Monk civilization” represents a movement that was largely iconoclastic and anti-monastic, although priests did play a real role in the armies. The history text is good overall, but it gets Rudolf of Habsburg, Sigismund's titles and the outcome of the Hussite Wars wrong.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Bohemians” is a good political name (Regnum Bohemiae), derived from Boiohaemum, the land of the Celtic Boii; the ethnic endonym is Češi. But medieval Bohemia was bilingual: the mining towns (Kutná Hora, Jihlava) and many royal towns had German burgher classes, and the Crown included Silesia and Lusatia. The design treats “Bohemians” as a synonym for “Czech Hussites” and forgets that the King of Bohemia was one of the prince-electors of the Empire. It overlaps with the Teutons (a member of the Empire) and, in the text, mixes up Great Moravia with the Přemyslid state, which are different entities. Within the game's framework, the civ only begins to make sense around 870–900.

elements.explanation: It is the name of the medieval kingdom and Crown, and it matches the usage of the sources (Bohemi, Boemi).

“Gunpowder” is faithful: the Hussites were among the first to use hand-held firearms en masse. “Monk” is ambivalent. Priests accompanied and led armies (Prokop the Great was a Taborite priest; Jan Želivský, a radical Prague preacher, had been a Premonstratensian canon of the monastery of Želiv). On the other hand, the Taborites destroyed many monasteries in 1419–21 and were iconoclastic and hostile to the cult of relics.

Jihlava (c. 1240) and above all Kutná Hora (from the late 13th century) were among the largest silver mines in Europe. They financed the Prague groschen (reform of Wenceslaus II, 1300) and the power of Ottokar II, the “Iron and Golden King”. There was also gold at Jílové and Kašperské Hory.
Charles University (1348) was the first in Central Europe, and Jan Hus himself was its rector (1409–10). The link to the Blacksmith is more generic (Bohemian metallurgy and armourers).
Hussite infantry used sudlice, halberds, hooks and flails from the wagons to unhorse and kill knights. As the flail was the emblematic weapon, the Spearman line is only an approximation.
A reasonable abstraction of Hussite lay religiosity: communion in both kinds (Utraquism), peasant “warriors of God”, Taborite communities.

elements.element: Chemistry and Hand Cannoneer available in Castle Age
elements.explanation: The Hussites used the píšťala (the disputed origin of the word “pistol”) en masse from 1420 (Sudoměř; Kutná Hora 1421–22). This anticipates its general spread across Europe, so the early access is justified.

It corresponds to the Hussite vozová hradba: wagons reinforced with pavises and mixed crews of crossbowmen, gunners and flailmen. The Military Ordinance of 1423 is mainly a code of discipline and marching; the composition of the crews is known from later sources and modern reconstructions (Durdík). Protecting the troops behind it captures the function well, with the caveat that the real wagon worked in a closed, static formation, not as an isolated piece.

The name is authentic (Haubitze and howitzer derive from it), but the houfnice was a short piece of medium calibre that fired stones or grapeshot at short range against masses of infantry and cavalry charges (houf means “crowd”). The game turns it into a long-range super-bombard against buildings, one that cannot fire at close range: the function is inverted.

The concept is authentic, but the Wagenburg was a static defensive formation. Giving gunpowder units +10% speed connects only indirectly to the mobility of the Hussite columns, which marched in several lines of wagons and closed up the fort quickly.
The Four Articles of Prague (1420) demanded clerical poverty and the secularisation of Church property. A clergy that costs no gold is an ingenious translation.
Prague was a major trading centre (the Týnský dvůr/Ungelt), and the Prague groschen circulated throughout Central Europe. The link is generic, but not arbitrary.

tree_issues.item: Bloodlines and Plate Barding Armor (missing); Paladin (missing)
tree_issues.problem: Přemyslid and Luxembourg Bohemia had first-rate heavy cavalry: Ottokar II won at Kressenbrunn (1260) with his armoured cavalry, and John the Blind died in the charge at Crécy (1346). The lack of Bloodlines and Plate Barding (which 37 and 36 of 56 civs have, respectively) reflects only the Hussite phase. The lack of the Paladin is normal in the game (only 10 civs have it).

tree_issues.item: Arbalester (present) and Mounted Crossbowman (present, without upgrade)
tree_issues.problem: Correct: crossbowmen were an essential part of the wagon crews and of the garrisons; there were also mounted crossbowmen.

tree_issues.item: Bombard Cannon with upgrade to Houfnice
tree_issues.problem: Heavy siege artillery (bombards) did exist, but the houfnice was the light anti-personnel piece. The upgrade chain is the wrong way round.
These absences are correct.

tree_issues.item: Carvel Hull, Dry Dock, Fast Fire Ship (missing) and Elite Cannon Galleon (present)
tree_issues.problem: The absences are consistent with a landlocked kingdom, but the presence of the Elite Cannon Galleon is ironic (it is an upgrade that many maritime civs lack).

tree_issues.item: Hoardings, Treadmill Crane and Crop Rotation (missing)
tree_issues.problem: A minor issue. Charles IV was a great builder (Karlštejn, Charles Bridge, Peter Parler's St Vitus Cathedral), and Bohemia had a developed cereal agriculture.

history_text_issues.claim: At the end of the Roman Empire, the region was inhabited by Lombards and Alemanni.
history_text_issues.problem: The Alemanni occupied south-western Germania, not Bohemia.
history_text_issues.correction: First the Marcomanni (and the Quadi in Moravia); then, in passing, Thuringians and Lombards (5th–6th centuries).

history_text_issues.claim: The first rulers of Great Moravia invited “Orthodox” missionaries from Byzantium.
history_text_issues.problem: Anachronism. Cyril and Methodius arrived in 863, before the schism of 1054. Methodius was consecrated archbishop by Pope Adrian II, and the Slavonic liturgy was approved by Rome (Industriae tuae, 880).
history_text_issues.correction: Speak of a Byzantine/Greco-Slavonic mission, recognised by Rome and later pushed aside by the Frankish clergy under Svatopluk and Bishop Wiching (expulsion of the disciples in 885–86).

history_text_issues.claim: Svatopluk extended the empire to Poland and Pannonia and died in war.
history_text_issues.problem: The extent of Great Moravia is much debated, and the sources (Annals of Fulda, Regino) do not say that Svatopluk died in battle; the later traditions (Constantine VII, Cosmas) are legendary.
history_text_issues.correction: State that the extent is uncertain and that the circumstances of Svatopluk's death (894) are unknown.

history_text_issues.claim: Boleslaus I obtained Moravia after helping Otto I crush the Magyars at Lechfeld (955).
history_text_issues.problem: According to Widukind, the Bohemian contingent (about a thousand men) guarded the baggage and was routed by the Magyars. The date of the annexation of Moravia is debated: it is only securely Bohemian from 1019/1029. The text also omits the murder of his brother, St Wenceslaus (935, or 929).
history_text_issues.correction: Present the participation at Lechfeld as modest and the annexation of Moravia as a debated process, completed in the 11th century.

history_text_issues.claim: Ottokar's peers elected Rudolf of Habsburg “Holy Roman Emperor”.
history_text_issues.problem: Rudolf was elected King of the Romans (1273) and was never crowned emperor. The victory on the Marchfeld (1278) owed much to the Hungarian-Cuman army of Ladislaus IV.
history_text_issues.correction: Rudolf was elected King of the Romans and defeated Ottokar at Dürnkrut with Hungarian and Cuman support.

history_text_issues.claim: After the fall of the Přemyslids in 1306, the throne passed to the House of Luxembourg.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the 1306–1310 interlude (Rudolf of Habsburg, son of Albert I, and Henry of Carinthia). John of Luxembourg reigned only from 1310.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention the succession dispute and the arrival of the Luxembourgs in 1310.

history_text_issues.claim: The Luxembourgs brought a “brief golden age”, with no further detail.
history_text_issues.problem: Misleading omission: it does not name Charles IV (king 1346–1378, emperor 1355), who made Prague an imperial capital, founded the university (1348) and the New Town, and promulgated the Golden Bull (1356).
history_text_issues.correction: Name Charles IV and Prague's role as the centre of the Empire.

history_text_issues.claim: In 1415, Emperor Sigismund ordered the execution of Jan Hus, which triggered the Hussite Wars.
history_text_issues.problem: Partly correct. Hus was condemned by the Council of Constance and handed over to the secular arm; Sigismund, who had given him a safe conduct, handed him over to the Elector Palatine Louis III, who had the sentence carried out on 6 July 1415. But Sigismund was at that time King of the Romans (he was only crowned emperor in 1433), and the wars only began in 1419, with the Defenestration of Prague.
history_text_issues.correction: Attribute the condemnation to the Council, with execution by Sigismund's secular authority, and date the war to 1419.

history_text_issues.claim: The Hussites prevailed against the imperial forces and won religious freedom.
history_text_issues.problem: They did indeed defeat five crusades (1420–1431, up to Domažlice), but the radicals (Taborites and Orphans) were crushed at Lipany (1434) by a league of moderate Utraquists and Catholics, and Prokop the Great died in the battle. The Compactata of Basel (1436) gave legal recognition to the Utraquist Church, a rare case in Europe, but not general religious freedom.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention Lipany and the Compactata as a limited compromise.

history_text_issues.claim: After the Hussites, Bohemia slid into the Polish, Hungarian and Austrian orbit.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits George of Poděbrady (1458–1471), the Hussite king with his project for a European peace league, and the Jagiellonian dynasty (1471–1526).
history_text_issues.correction: Mention George of Poděbrady and the Jagiellonian kings up to Mohács.

missing_features: The pavéza, the large Bohemian pavise used throughout Central Europe
Peasant flail infantry (cepníci) and sudlice
The hymn “Ktož jsú boží bojovníci” and its psychological effect (the flight of the crusaders at Domažlice, 1431, according to tradition)
Přemyslid armoured cavalry and the King of Bohemia as an imperial elector
Charles IV and Prague as capital of the Empire
Hussite offensive expeditions (spanilé jízdy, 1427–1433, as far as the Baltic)
Czech mercenaries in Hungary (Jan Jiskra and the bratříci) and on both sides of the Thirteen Years' War
The Prague groschen as a regional currency

proposals.title: Houfnice as an anti-personnel piece
proposals.description: Turn the Houfnice into a Siege Workshop piece available in the Castle Age, with short to medium range, area damage (stone grapeshot) and a bonus against infantry and cavalry, with no bonus against buildings. The Bombard Cannon remains the normal siege piece.
proposals.historical_basis: The houfnice fired stones at short range against masses of men and horses; the name comes from houf (“crowd”) and gave rise to Haubitze/howitzer.

proposals.title: Pavéza
proposals.description: Arbalesters and Hand Cannoneers gain +2 pierce armour when stationary, and an additional +1 when next to a Hussite Wagon.
proposals.historical_basis: The large Bohemian pavise protected crossbowmen and gunners between the wagons and was exported and imitated across Central Europe.

proposals.title: The Iron and Golden King
proposals.description: Restore Bloodlines and Plate Barding Armor, or create a Castle tech that gives the Knight line +20 HP, to represent pre-Hussite Bohemia.
proposals.historical_basis: Ottokar II (Kressenbrunn 1260, Marchfeld 1278) and John the Blind (Crécy 1346) commanded heavy cavalry of European standing.

proposals.title: Ktož jsú boží bojovníci
proposals.description: Enemy units within a radius of 6 of a Hussite Wagon or a Bohemian Monk suffer -15% attack, and Bohemian units within that radius gain +1 attack.
proposals.historical_basis: The Hussite war hymn was sung before battle. According to tradition, the army of the fifth crusade broke up at Domažlice (1431) on hearing the Hussites approach.

proposals.title: Cepník (flailman)
proposals.description: Cheap peasant infantry, trained at the Barracks after a Castle tech, with a bonus against cavalry and the ability to ignore part of the melee armour.
proposals.historical_basis: The reinforced threshing flail was the typical weapon of Hussite peasants, used from the wagons to bring down knights.

contested: Location and extent of Great Moravia: the consensus points to southern Moravia, against the Sirmium hypothesis (Boba, Eggers, Bowlus).
Date of the integration of Moravia into Bohemia: the 950s or 1019/1029?
Date of St Wenceslaus's death: 929 or 935?
Nature of Hussitism: religious reform (the “First Reformation” for Šmahel, Fudge and Kaminsky), social revolution (Macek, Marxist historiography) or Czech national movement (Palacký)?
Etymology of “pistol”: from Czech píšťala or from the city of Pistoia?
Žižka's participation at Grunwald (1410): a tradition without solid proof.
Authorship of the Military Ordinance of 1423 (Žižka as author or co-author).
Real weight of the hymn and of fear of the wagons in the flight at Domažlice (1431).
Original meaning of houfnice: sling/throwing engine or cannon?

civs.represents: The duchy and later Kingdom of Poland under the Piasts (c. 960–1370) and the Jagiellonians (1386–1572), with several elements of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth (1569–1795).
civs.period: c. 966 (baptism of Mieszko I) – c. 1572; key elements (Winged Hussar, serf-based folwark, szlachta privileges) pull it towards 1500–1683.
civs.verdict: A creative design with real anchors: the folwark, the szlachta privileges, Wieliczka salt abstracted as stone that generates gold, and the cavalry focus. But it is chronologically tilted towards early modern Poland of the 16th–17th centuries. The Winged Hussar is a 17th-century icon and, in the game, serves as light raiding cavalry, when it was a shock lancer. The Obuch turns a nobleman's weapon into an infantry type that never existed, and Lechitic Legacy has no basis. Villager regeneration evokes, in a forced way, the hypothesis of low Black Death mortality. The medieval knightly cavalry that won at Grunwald is missing (no Plate Barding). The history text is solid, but it repeats the myth of Casimir's quarantine and projects 16th-century religious tolerance backwards.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Poles” is an endonym (Polacy, from Polanie), although whether the Polans tribe itself existed as a political unit is debated (Urbańczyk). The main problem is chronological: the design mixes Piast Poland, Jagiellonian Poland and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth (1569–1795). Both the Winged Hussar and the serf-based folwark belong mainly to the 16th–17th centuries, outside the game's 500–1500 frame. The Winged Hussar is shared with the Lithuanians, which dilutes the identity of both civs. The “Slavs” civ (mainly the Rus') uses an umbrella label that, strictly speaking, would also cover Poles and Czechs.

elements.explanation: Correct endonym for the kingdom and its people from the 10th century onwards.
Cavalry was always the main arm: knights organised in banners (chorągwie) in the Middle Ages, light cavalry against the Tatars and, later, the hussars.

The folwark (from the German Vorwerk) was the manorial demesne worked with serf corvée labour, the engine of grain exports through Gdańsk. It is attested from the 13th–14th centuries and becomes dominant in the 15th–16th centuries (Statute of Piotrków, 1496; Statute of Toruń, 1520, with a minimum corvée of one day per week). Collecting part of the food from neighbouring farms is a good translation. The caveat is that it is mainly a post-1450 reality.

It does not correspond to any direct historical trait. The likely link is the idea of a Poland relatively spared by the Black Death, which the game's own text invokes. That hypothesis has some support (pollen data from Izdebski et al., 2022), but the “regeneration” of individuals is a very forced translation of lower regional mortality.

elements.element: Stone Miners generate gold in addition to stone
elements.explanation: A good abstraction of the rock salt of Wieliczka and Bochnia (the żupy krakowskie). The traditional estimate says that salt yielded about a third of the crown's revenues in the time of Casimir III. Added to this are the silver and lead mines of Olkusz.

elements.element: Bloodlines and Scout Cavalry-line upgrades cost -50% food
elements.explanation: Reasonably reflects horse breeding and the weight of light cavalry in the wars against the Tatars and Lithuanians.

The obuch/nadziak was a war hammer-pick effective against armour, so the “armour-tearing” mechanic has a basis. But it was the nobleman's weapon, often used on horseback and also a status symbol and a brawling weapon, mainly in the 16th–17th centuries. An “obuch” infantry type never existed.

The Polish hussars emerged c. 1500 from Serbian and Hungarian light horsemen. The wings and the long lance (kopia) became the hallmark of heavy shock cavalry in the second half of the 16th century, especially after Stephen Báthory, peaking at Kircholm (1605), Kłuszyn (1610) and Vienna (1683). The problem is twofold: it is outside the period and of the wrong type, because the game makes it the Light Cavalry upgrade, for scouting and raiding.

The privileges of Košice (1374), Nieszawa (1454) and Nihil novi (1505) traded exemptions and political power for military service. In the pospolite ruszenie, nobles served on horseback at their own expense, so knights costing less gold is a reasonable translation.
“Lechitic” denotes a linguistic branch and refers back to the legendary Lech. There is no connection whatsoever with light cavalry trample damage.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Scout Cavalry-line +1 attack vs. Ranged Soldiers
elements.explanation: A very vague link to light cavalry fighting against Tatar horse archers; it is generic.

tree_issues.problem: Polish heavy cavalry (Zawisza Czarny of Garbów, knights in Western-pattern armour) was the core at Grunwald, with about 50 Polish banners according to Długosz. In a “Cavalry civilization”, the lack of Plate Barding (which 36 of 56 civs have) is the most significant gap. The lack of the Paladin matters less, because only 10 civs have it.

Poland used firearms from the 1380s (hakownice, later rusznice). In the Thirteen Years' War it hired Czech mercenaries with firearms and Wagenburg (Świecino, 1462), and later had “Hungarian” arquebusier infantry (Stephen Báthory). With the Bombard Cannon present, the absence is hard to justify, although it is common in the game (33 of 56 civs lack it).
According to Długosz, Casimir III built or fortified dozens of castles and towns. Kraków was a member of the Hanse and a major trading centre, and Gdańsk passed to the Polish crown in 1454/1466.
Poland–Lithuania was a major exporter of timber, potash and pitch to the West via Gdańsk. The absence is ironic, though minor.
A minor point: long polearms were common in Polish and mercenary infantry of the 15th century. It is not a distinctive trait, but there is also no historical reason for its absence.
Acceptable, although Polish light cavalry (strzelcy, later “kozacy”/pancerni) used composite bows until the 17th century.

tree_issues.item: Mounted Crossbowman and Heavy Mounted Crossbowman (present)
tree_issues.problem: Plausible: there were mounted crossbowmen in Polish armies of the 14th–15th centuries.

history_text_issues.claim: Small Baltic-speaking groups “settled” in the north-east in the 6th century.
history_text_issues.problem: The Balts (Prussians, Yotvingians/Sudovians) had been indigenous to the region since long before; Tacitus's Aestii are generally identified with them.
history_text_issues.correction: The Balts already inhabited the north-east; it was the Slavs who were the newcomers.

history_text_issues.claim: In the 8th–9th centuries, the region was threatened by Avar and Moravian invaders.
history_text_issues.problem: The Avar presence in the Polish lands is poorly attested, and Moravian rule over the Vistulans (Life of Methodius) is debated.
history_text_issues.correction: Present Moravian influence over the Kraków region as possible and limited.

history_text_issues.claim: Christianisation was driven by Mieszko's wife, Dobrawa.
history_text_issues.problem: This matches Thietmar's account, but omits the political motives: alliance with Bohemia, avoiding dependence on the German mission, and a bishopric of its own (Poznań, 968).
history_text_issues.correction: Add the political dimension of the baptism of 966.

history_text_issues.claim: The period of growth continued for about a century under the successors of Bolesław the Brave.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the crisis of the 1030s: Mieszko II's loss of the crown, the pagan reaction, social revolt and the raid of Bretislaus I of Bohemia (1038–39), which sacked Gniezno.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention the crisis of 1031–1039 and the reconstruction under Casimir I the Restorer.

history_text_issues.claim: In the 11th–12th centuries, the kingdom developed a feudal structure based on serfdom, imitating its Western neighbours.
history_text_issues.problem: Anachronistic. Piast Poland operated under “ducal law” and service villages. Serfdom intensified at the end of the 15th century and in the 16th century (the “second serfdom”), precisely when it was declining in the West.
history_text_issues.correction: Distinguish the early ducal organisation from the early modern serfdom tied to the folwark and grain exports.

history_text_issues.claim: Bolesław III divided “the kingdom” among his sons in 1138.
history_text_issues.problem: Poland was then a duchy: there was no royal coronation between 1079 and 1295. The testament established the seniorate principle.
history_text_issues.correction: Speak of a duchy and of the feudal fragmentation of 1138–1320.

history_text_issues.claim: The conflict with the Teutonic Order was due in part to the Order's disapproval of Polish religious tolerance.
history_text_issues.problem: The main cause was territorial: the Order's seizure of Gdańsk Pomerania in 1308 (the Gdańsk massacre) and the disputes over Kuyavia and Dobrzyń. The ideological polemic (Włodkowic against Falkenberg, at the Council of Constance) postdates 1410.
history_text_issues.correction: Bring the dispute over Pomerania to the foreground and place the polemic on the rights of pagans in 1414–1418.

history_text_issues.claim: Poland was relatively spared by the Black Death thanks to Casimir III's quarantines.
history_text_issues.problem: Two different claims. The lower mortality is a hypothesis with some support: the pollen study by Izdebski et al. (2022) shows agricultural continuity or even expansion in Poland, unlike other regions. The royal quarantines, on the other hand, have no contemporary evidence at all, and the later waves (from the 1360s onwards) did hit Poland.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the lower mortality as a debated hypothesis, explicable by low population density and trade routes, and Casimir's quarantine as a modern legend.

history_text_issues.claim: Poland was extremely progressive on the rights of religious minorities, and reinforced tolerance gave it stability while Europe was torn apart by religious conflicts.
history_text_issues.problem: The privileges granted to the Jews (Statute of Kalisz, 1264, extended by Casimir III) are real, but “religious tolerance” as a general policy belongs mainly to the 16th century (Warsaw Confederation, 1573). The 15th century saw the Edict of Wieluń against the Hussites (1424), anti-Jewish riots in Kraków (1407) and the transfer of the Jews to Kazimierz (1495).
history_text_issues.correction: Distinguish the medieval privileges granted to the Jews from the confessional tolerance of the 16th century.

history_text_issues.claim: Jadwiga was an elite political strategist who engineered the union with Lithuania.
history_text_issues.problem: An exaggeration. Crowned in 1384 (according to tradition, as “rex”), Jadwiga was about 11 years old at the time of the Krewo agreement (1385), which was negotiated mainly by the magnates of Lesser Poland with Jogaila's envoys. She was pressured into giving up her betrothal to William of Habsburg. Her later political role is real (Red Ruthenia in 1387, her bequest for the refoundation of the University of Kraków).
history_text_issues.correction: Attribute the union to the lords of Lesser Poland and to Jogaila, and highlight Jadwiga's role after 1387.

history_text_issues.claim: Jogaila broke the power of the Order at Grunwald (1410).
history_text_issues.problem: Grunwald was a crushing military victory, but the First Peace of Thorn (1411) was territorially modest, although the indemnity (100,000 kopas of Prague groschen) ruined the Order's finances. The decisive weakening came with the Thirteen Years' War and the Second Peace of Thorn (1466), which gave Poland Royal Prussia, Gdańsk and Malbork.
history_text_issues.correction: Present Grunwald as a decisive victory on the battlefield and the start of the decline, but politically incomplete.

history_text_issues.claim: Improved agricultural techniques increased productivity, exports and the power of the nobility.
history_text_issues.problem: The boom rested on grain exports through Gdańsk based on serf corvée labour, an extensive model and not necessarily a technically better one. It benefited the nobility at the expense of the peasants and the towns, and the text omits serfdom.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention the second serfdom and the folwark export model.

missing_features: Medieval knightly cavalry in chorągwie, with heraldic clans and war cries (zawołanie)
The grody (earth-and-timber forts of caisson construction) of the 8th–11th centuries
Adoption of the Hussite tabor and Czech mercenaries in the 15th century
Gdańsk and the grain and timber trade along the Vistula
The University of Kraków (1364/1400) and Copernicus
The Statute of Kalisz (1264) and Jewish communities in the urban economy
Lekka jazda (light cavalry with bow and lance) and border defence against the Tatars
The pospolite ruszenie (general levy of the nobility)

proposals.title: Winged Hussar as a heavy lancer in the Imperial Age
proposals.description: Remove the Winged Hussar from the Light Cavalry line and restore the generic Hussar. The Winged Hussar becomes a Stable unit available only in the Imperial Age, expensive, with high first-charge damage (kopia) and medium armour.
proposals.historical_basis: The hussars of the great victories (Kircholm 1605, Kłuszyn 1610, Vienna 1683) were shock cavalry with long lances and half-armour, and they appear at the end of the game's time frame or after it.

proposals.title: Chorągiew (the banners of Grunwald)
proposals.description: Gives access to Plate Barding Armor, and the Knight line gains +1 armour when there are at least 5 knights within a radius of 4.
proposals.historical_basis: Polish cavalry fought in territorial and clan banners. At Grunwald, about 50 Polish banners formed the core of the army (Długosz).

proposals.title: Murowana Polska (replaces villager regeneration)
proposals.description: Castles and towers cost -20% stone and Town Centers are built +50% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: According to the tradition passed down by Długosz, Casimir III “found Poland made of wood and left it made of stone”, fortifying dozens of castles and towns.

proposals.title: Tabor and arquebusiers
proposals.description: Restore the Hand Cannoneer and create a technology that gives Town Centers and Castles the ability to deploy a temporary wagon formation that protects units against projectiles.
proposals.historical_basis: In the Thirteen Years' War (Świecino, 1462), Poland used Czech mercenaries with Wagenburg and firearms.

proposals.title: Pospolite ruszenie (replaces Lechitic Legacy)
proposals.description: When researched, each Town Center immediately spawns 2–3 Knights (up to 5 TCs), like the Sicilians' First Crusade.
proposals.historical_basis: The general levy of the nobility obliged the szlachta to serve on horseback in defence of the kingdom, in exchange for their privileges.

proposals.title: Rename the stone bonus to Żupy krakowskie
proposals.description: Make it explicit that the gold generated by stone miners represents the salt of Wieliczka and Bochnia, and add +10% gold on stone trades at the Market.
proposals.historical_basis: The Kraków salt works were a royal monopoly and one of the crown's main sources of revenue in the 14th–15th centuries.

contested: Origin of the Slavs in the Polish lands: allochthonous (Godłowski) or autochthonous (Kostrzewski and the Poznań school)?
Existence of the Polans as a tribe before Mieszko (Urbańczyk).
Impact of the Black Death on Poland (Guzowski; Izdebski et al. 2022, which supports a smaller impact) and Casimir's supposed quarantine, for which there is no documentary evidence.
Causes and chronology of the “second serfdom” (Małowist, Topolski, recent critiques).
Jadwiga's personal role in the Union of Krewo and the meaning of her coronation as “rex”.
Origin and function of the hussars' wings: decorative, psychological or a defence against lassos?

Thietmar of Merseburg, Chronicon
Wincenty Kadłubek, Chronica Polonorum (c. 1200)
