civs.represents: The Grand Duchy of Lithuania (c. 1236–1569). It was a pagan state until 1387 (Samogitia until 1413–17) and, from the 14th century onwards, had a mostly Ruthenian population (Orthodox Slavs). United with Poland in 1385, and institutionally in 1569.
civs.period: c. 1236 (Mindaugas) – 1569 (Union of Lublin); peak c. 1316–1430 (from Gediminas to Vytautas).
civs.verdict: It contains some of the most learned details in the game, such as the hillforts (Hill Forts) and the leičiai as a unique unit, and it gets the cavalry focus right. But the core identity is blurred: the last pagan state of Latin Europe appears as a “Monk civilization” whose main bonus depends on relics. That is justified only by Orthodox Ruthenia and by the post-1387 phase, which the civ does not represent. The food-per-Town-Center bonus has no basis, the Leitis is an extrapolation from a poorly known social group and the Winged Hussar is anachronistic. The history text has an acceptable structure, but it opens with a romantic trope and simplifies Saule, Mindaugas and Lublin.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Lithuanians” fits the dynastic core (the Gediminids) well, but the title used in the 15th–16th centuries was “Grand Duchy of Lithuania, Ruthenia and Samogitia”. After Algirdas, most of the population and the language of the chancery were Ruthenian (ancestors of Belarusians and Ukrainians), something the civ ignores and which makes it overlap with the “Slavs”. At the same time, the civ absorbs the whole pagan Baltic world (Old Prussians, Curonians, Semigallians, Yotvingians), which has no representation of its own. The Winged Hussar and the Commonwealth phase (1569–1795) pull the civ outside the game's frame.

elements.explanation: Correct for the dynasty and the ethnic core, but it hides the multi-ethnic and mostly Ruthenian character of the Grand Duchy after c. 1350.

“Cavalry” is faithful (raids, light cavalry with lances and javelins). “Monk” clashes with the pagan character of the dynasty and of the Lithuanian core until 1387. It has some basis in the Orthodox Ruthenian lands, with their monasteries (the Kyiv Pechersk Lavra came under Lithuanian suzerainty from c. 1362), and in the Catholic phase after 1387, but it is not the trait that defines the medieval state.
There is no identifiable historical basis.
An acceptable abstraction of the warfare waged by light troops in the forests and marshes of the “Wildnis” between Prussia and Lithuania.

elements.element: Each garrisoned Relic +1 attack to Knight-line and Leitis
elements.explanation: The cult of relics was Christian. In the Lithuanian core it only makes sense after 1387 (the legend of St Casimir guiding the army at Polotsk, 1518); in the Ruthenian lands it had existed all along (the Orthodox martyrs of Vilnius of 1347). For the pagan Lithuania of Gediminas, which is the centre of the civ's identity, it is an inversion.

The leičiai did exist: first written mention in 1407, as servitors of the grand duke with duties of frontier guard, military service and horse breeding (Dubonis). There is no evidence that they were elite heavy cavalry, and the armor-ignoring mechanic is invented.

Hussar cavalry in Lithuania belongs to the 16th–17th centuries (Kircholm, 1605, under the Lithuanian hetman Jan Karol Chodkiewicz): outside the period and of the wrong type (light in the game, heavy in reality).

Lithuania has hundreds of hillforts (piliakalniai), such as Kernavė, Gediminas Hill in Vilnius or Merkinė, and wooden hilltop castles were central to the defence against the Orders. The mechanic is an abstraction, but the theme is accurate.

elements.element: Tower Shields (Spearman-line and Skirmishers +2 pierce armor)
elements.explanation: The game's own text attributes pavises to the Lithuanian infantry, and large pavise-type shields circulated on the frontier between Rus', the Baltic and Poland (Masovia) from the 13th century. But the pavise is mainly associated with Italy and Bohemia, Lithuanian infantry was a secondary component (at Grunwald the main force was the cavalry), and there is no solid evidence of a specifically Lithuanian pavise.

Gediminas invited Franciscans and Dominicans (letters of 1323), but the state remained pagan. Catholic monasteries only gained weight after 1387; before that, monasteries were mostly Orthodox and Ruthenian.

tree_issues.item: Cavalry Archer and Heavy Cavalry Archer (present)
tree_issues.problem: The Lithuanians were light cavalry with lances and javelins (sulica), not mounted archers. Their presence is justified only by the Tatars settled by Vytautas (Lipka, c. 1397–98; Jalal ad-Din's contingent at Grunwald). It is tolerable, but it should be made explicit.

Lithuanian heavy cavalry belongs mainly to the 15th century, under the influence of Poland and of the Ruthenian nobility; in the 14th century it was rare. A minor issue, and a curious one given that the Poles do not have Plate Barding.
Consistent with the weak Lithuanian siege capability (failure before Marienburg in 1410).

tree_issues.item: Blast Furnace and Plate Mail Armor (absent)
tree_issues.problem: Consistent with bog iron and lighter equipment.
Plausible: the chronicles credit Vytautas with cannons and hand guns at the Vorskla (1399) and in the sieges of the 1420s.

tree_issues.item: Dry Dock, Carvel Hull, Fast Fire Ship, Elite Cannon Galleon (present)
tree_issues.problem: Excessive for a state with minimal access to the sea (the Palanga strip, secured only in 1422) and no naval tradition. A minor issue.

history_text_issues.claim: The Lithuanians are said to be “one of the oldest European civilizations”, with Baltic ancestors going back to the 3rd millennium BC.
history_text_issues.problem: A romantic-nationalist trope. Ethnic continuity since the Corded Ware culture is debated, and “civilization” is vague and value-laden here.
history_text_issues.correction: The Balts have been present in the region at least since the Iron Age; Lithuanian ethnogenesis is medieval (9th–13th centuries).

history_text_issues.claim: Pressure from Rus' and Viking raids led the chiefs to cooperate.
history_text_issues.problem: The Viking contacts (Grobiņa; Apuolė, 853) concern mainly the Curonians and predate the formation of the state by centuries. The decisive pressure (c. 1180–1240) came from the crusading orders (Sword Brothers, 1202; Teutonic Order, 1226/30) and from the Rus' principalities, alongside a raiding economy of their own.
history_text_issues.correction: Put the Baltic crusades and the rivalry with Rus' at the centre of state formation.

history_text_issues.claim: The Lithuanians, united under Mindaugas, decimated the Sword Brothers.
history_text_issues.problem: Saule (1236) was mainly a Samogitian victory (with Semigallians), and Mindaugas' participation is not attested. The survivors were absorbed into the Teutonic Order in 1237.
history_text_issues.correction: Attribute Saule to the Samogitians, probably under Vykintas.

history_text_issues.claim: Unable to win by force, Mindaugas converted in order to remove the motive for the crusade.
history_text_issues.problem: The baptism (1251) took place during a civil war against his nephews Tautvilas and Edivydas and against Vykintas, who were allied with the Livonian Order and Galicia–Volhynia. It was a manoeuvre to break up that coalition, involving the cession of parts of Samogitia. His apostasy around 1261 is debated.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the conversion as diplomacy in a civil war; the 1263 assassination by Treniota and Daumantas was a power struggle.

history_text_issues.claim: In 1253 the pope recognised Mindaugas and crowned him king.
history_text_issues.problem: The coronation (July 1253) was performed by Bishop Heidenreich of Chełmno, on the mandate of Pope Innocent IV (bull of 1251), and not by the pope. The text also links the crusade to Gregory IX, but the coronation already belongs to the following pontificate.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that Mindaugas was crowned with the authorisation of Innocent IV.

history_text_issues.claim: Gediminas founded a new capital at Vilnius.
history_text_issues.problem: Vilnius is first mentioned in Gediminas' letters (1323), but the settlement is older. The role of the leičiai in guarding the hillforts is a modern interpretation.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that Gediminas made Vilnius the capital.

history_text_issues.claim: Under Jogaila (r. 1377–1381), Christianisation and the Polish marriage Polonised Lithuanian culture.
history_text_issues.problem: Jogaila reigned in Lithuania in 1377–81 and 1382–92. The Polonisation of the elite was gradual (15th–17th centuries); the chancery used Ruthenian, and the Statutes of Lithuania (1529, 1566, 1588) were drafted in Ruthenian.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe a slow Polonisation of the nobility and the lasting weight of Ruthenian.

history_text_issues.claim: In 1380, Lithuania was trapped between Christian Europe and Orthodox Muscovy.
history_text_issues.problem: This has a basis as a choice of conversion: Jogaila considered marrying a daughter of Dmitry Donskoy, which would have meant Orthodox baptism, and Algirdas had already waged war on Moscow (1368–72). But the immediate military pressure came from the Teutonic Order, and the Grand Duchy itself had an Orthodox majority, which makes the “Christians versus pagans” opposition misleading.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the 1385 decision as a choice between the Latin option (Poland) and the Orthodox one (Moscow), under pressure from the Order, in a state that was already mostly Orthodox Christian.

history_text_issues.claim: The Lithuanians strengthened the union and created the Commonwealth in 1569, and Lithuania remained an independent state.
history_text_issues.problem: The Union of Lublin was extracted under pressure: before the signing, the Polish crown annexed Podlachia, Volhynia, Bracław and Kyiv. The Grand Duchy kept its own army, treasury, laws and offices, but it was autonomous, not independent.
history_text_issues.correction: Speak of autonomy within a commonwealth with a shared elected monarch.

missing_features: Baltic pagan religion (Perkūnas, sacred groves, the sacred fire of Vilnius) and late conversion (1387/1413–17)
The raiding economy and its mirror image: the Order's Litauerreisen with knights from all over Europe (Henry Bolingbroke in 1390; Chaucer's Knight)
Light javelin cavalry (sulica) and the feigned retreat
Lipka Tatars and the Karaites of Trakai
Orthodox Ruthenian majority, Ruthenian boyars and the Statutes of Lithuania
Brick castles (Trakai, Kaunas, Medininkai)
The forest frontier (Wildnis) as a defensive system
Battles of Blue Waters (1362) and the Vorskla (1399)

proposals.title: Krikštas: the conversion of 1387
proposals.description: Until this technology is researched (Castle Age), the civ cannot use Monastery technologies or garrison relics, but its Monks (pagan priests) heal +50% faster and units near forests receive +1 armor. After the research, the Monastery technologies and the current relic bonus are activated.
proposals.historical_basis: Lithuania was the last pagan state in Europe; the official conversion of 1387 under Jogaila was a political and cultural turning point.

proposals.title: Sulica horseman
proposals.description: Replace or complement the Leitis with a light javelin cavalry unit (a mounted skirmisher, like the Genitour): fast, strong against infantry and slow cavalry.
proposals.historical_basis: The core of Lithuanian armies consisted of light horsemen with shields and javelins (sulica), as the game's own text acknowledges.

proposals.title: Lipka Tatars
proposals.description: Cavalry Archers no longer cost gold (extra food cost instead), or each Castle spawns 5 elite Cavalry Archers, in the style of Cuman Mercenaries.
proposals.historical_basis: Vytautas settled Tatars in the Grand Duchy (c. 1397–98), and a Tatar contingent fought at Grunwald.

proposals.title: Grobis: raiding economy (replaces +100 food per TC)
proposals.description: Cavalry collects 20% of the cost of the buildings it destroys, plus +5 food for each enemy villager killed.
proposals.historical_basis: Lithuanian raids into Prussia, Livonia, Masovia and Rus' sought captives, livestock and plunder, as the Order's chronicles describe (Peter of Dusburg, Wigand of Marburg). The name avoids “Reise”, which referred to the Order's own campaigns.

proposals.title: Ruthenian boyars
proposals.description: In the Imperial Age, Castles can train the Boyar (shared with the Slavs) at a reduced cost.
proposals.historical_basis: After Algirdas, the Orthodox Ruthenian nobility supplied much of the Grand Duchy's heavy cavalry.

contested: Etymology of Lietuva from the leičiai (Dubonis, Karaliūnas) or from the hydronym Lietava; critics point to a West Baltic origin for leičiai.
Who commanded at Saule (1236): Vykintas and the Samogitians, or Mindaugas?
Mindaugas' apostasy around 1261.
The Lithuanian retreat at Grunwald: a feigned manoeuvre (a thesis supported, among others, by a document identified by Sven Ekdahl) or a real flight (Długosz)?
Nature and depth of the 1387 conversion (Rowell, Baronas).
Pace of the Polonisation of the Lithuanian nobility.
Origin and spread of the pavise in Eastern Europe (a proto-pavise on the Baltic–Ruthenian–Polish frontier?).
Existence and functions of the pagan high priest (Kriwe) described by Peter of Dusburg.

civs.represents: The Magyars of the Conquest (895–970), a nomadic confederation of horse archers, and the Kingdom of Hungary (1000–1526) of the Árpáds, the Angevins, Sigismund, Hunyadi and Matthias Corvinus.
civs.period: c. 895 (conquest of the Carpathian Basin) – 1526 (Mohács).
civs.verdict: The “steppe” layer is well captured: recurve bows, mounted archers, Parthian Tactics and the link between the hussars and 15th-century Hungary. But the civ almost ignores the five-century Christian kingdom that followed. Keep and Fortified Wall are missing for one of the most heavily castled frontier kingdoms (post-1241 castles, a line of fortresses against the Ottomans). Firearms are missing entirely for a power whose army under Matthias had one of the highest proportions of handgunners in Europe. Corvinian Army has a real basis in the recruitment of hussars by peasant plot, but the name evokes the very expensive mercenary core. The wolf bonus is pure fantasy. The history text has glaring errors: coronation “by the Pope”, “first foreign king”, bulwark against “the Russians”, “easternmost Christian kingdom”.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Magyars” is an endonym (magyar), which is a point in its favour; “Hungarians” probably derives from Onogur. But the civ covers two distinct worlds: the nomadic tribal confederation, with the Kabars and perhaps other Turkic groups, and the multi-ethnic Kingdom of Hungary (Slavs, Germans — Transylvanian Saxons and Zipsers —, Vlachs, Cumans, Jász, Székelys, Jews). It overlaps with the Huns (the medieval myth of Hunnic descent in Simon of Kéza), with the Cumans (settled in Hungary in 1239; Ladislaus IV “the Cuman”) and, through the name of the hussars, with the Poles and Lithuanians (Winged Hussar) and with the generic Hussar of 30 civs.

elements.explanation: Correct endonym, used by the people themselves since the time of the Conquest.
Mounted archers of the Conquest, knights and banderia in the kingdom, and hussars in the 15th century.

elements.element: Villagers defeat wolves with one strike
elements.explanation: Pure game flavour, with no historical basis.
The abundance of horses on the Pannonian plain and a numerous, cheap light cavalry justify it.
Weak link to the Conquest-period sabre (the so-called “Sabre of Charlemagne”, in Vienna, is probably 9th–10th-century Eastern European work). Hungarian metalworking was not exceptional.

Hussars appear in documents from southern Hungary in the first half of the 15th century (the dates of the earliest mentions, 1403 or 1432, are debated). They were light cavalry, probably of Serbian origin, organised on a large scale under Matthias Corvinus. It is late (15th century) for a Castle Age unit, and the “Strong vs. Siege Weapons” is arbitrary.

The mechanic (gold-free Huszar) has a basis: the militia portalis (Diet of Temesvár, 1397) obliged lords to arm one horseman for every 20 peasant plots, Matthias restored the system (Szeged laws, 1459) and, according to Hungarian historiography, a decree of his (usually dated to 1481) linked this recruitment to the hussars. The caveat lies in the name: the mercenary core of Matthias's army (the “Black Army”, a later name) was famously expensive, paid for with extraordinary taxes, and fell apart after 1490 for lack of pay.
Reflex composite bows with bone plates have been found in Conquest-period graves, and mounted archery tactics are described in Leo VI's Tactica and in Western sources.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Mounted Archers train +25% faster
elements.explanation: Consistent with the Magyar mounted-archery tradition and that of the Cuman, Pecheneg and Székely auxiliaries.

tree_issues.item: Keep, Fortified Wall, Architecture, Arrowslits and Bombard Tower (missing)
tree_issues.problem: After 1241, Béla IV encouraged the nobility to build stone castles, which multiplied until 1300. In the 15th century there was a belt of frontier fortresses (Belgrade/Nándorfehérvár, Jajce, Szabács) and famous sieges such as that of Belgrade (1456). These absences are unhistorical, especially that of the Keep, which 37 of 56 civs have.

According to current estimates, about one in four foot soldiers in Matthias's army had a firearm, a high proportion for the time, and Matthias had a large artillery train. Hussite tactics reached Hungary through Czech mercenaries: Jan Jiskra fought Hunyadi in the north (Lučenec, 1451), and his former soldiers (bratříci) were later incorporated into Matthias's army. Hunyadi also used the Wagenburg (Varna 1444, Kosovo 1448). This is the most serious absence in the group.

The kingdom of the “holy kings” (Stephen, Emeric, Ladislaus; Elizabeth and Margaret of Hungary), with the Archabbey of Pannonhalma (996) and the Order of St Paul the First Hermit (founded in Hungary c. 1250). A minor irony.
Matthias's army had heavy infantry (pavise-bearers, armoured foot), and the Angevin knights were of Western standard. A moderate issue.

tree_issues.item: Gold Shaft Mining (present, with no associated bonus); Stone Shaft Mining (missing)
tree_issues.problem: Angevin Hungary was Europe's great gold producer in the 14th century (Kremnica/Körmöcbánya; Hungarian florin from 1325–26). The kingdom's most distinctive economic trait is given no prominence.

tree_issues.item: Paladin, Hussar, Heavy Cavalry Archer, Parthian Tactics (present)
tree_issues.problem: Consistent with history.

history_text_issues.claim: The origin of the Magyars goes back to at least 2000 BC, as nomadic hunters between the Volga and the Urals.
history_text_issues.problem: At that time, the Proto-Ugrians were forest-steppe hunter-fishers, not nomads. Nomadic pastoralism is much later, and the location of the original homeland is debated.
history_text_issues.correction: Distinguish the Ugric hunting-and-fishing phase from the adoption of pastoral nomadism on the steppe, which came only in the 1st millennium BC or AD.

history_text_issues.claim: Around AD 500 the Magyars began to migrate to Central Europe.
history_text_issues.problem: The chronology is very uncertain. Part of the people remained in Magna Hungaria (near present-day Bashkiria), where Friar Julian found Hungarian speakers in 1235.
history_text_issues.correction: Present Levedia and Etelköz (8th–9th centuries) as attested stages and the rest as hypothesis.

history_text_issues.claim: In the 9th century, a civil war drove them from the Don to present-day Ukraine.
history_text_issues.problem: This refers, confusingly, to the revolt of the Kabars against the Khazars (De Administrando Imperio), who then joined the Magyars. The main pressure came from the Pechenegs.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention the Kabar revolt and the Pecheneg pressure.

history_text_issues.claim: The Bulgarian–Byzantine war forced the migration around 896.
history_text_issues.problem: The Magyars were allies of Byzantium against Simeon (894–896). What forced them out was the Bulgarian–Pecheneg counter-attack on Etelköz, and the Pechenegs are omitted.
history_text_issues.correction: Add the Pecheneg attack as a direct cause.

history_text_issues.claim: They conquered the “few Slavs” of the Carpathian Basin.
history_text_issues.problem: The basin had Slavs, Avar remnants, Bulgarians in the east, Moravians in the north and an organised Frankish Pannonia (Mosaburg/Zalavár). It was not a void.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe a mixed and politically fragmented population.

history_text_issues.claim: After Lechfeld (955), the Magyars began to give up raiding.
history_text_issues.problem: Raids against Byzantium continued until 970 (Arcadiopolis).
history_text_issues.correction: Raids to the west ceased after 955 and those to the south after 970.

history_text_issues.claim: The coronation of Stephen I “by the Pope” in 1000 founded the kingdom.
history_text_issues.problem: Stephen was crowned in Hungary (25 December 1000 or 1 January 1001), probably at Esztergom, by Hungarian prelates, with a crown sent by Sylvester II (Hartvic legend) and with the agreement of Otto III. The pope was not present.
history_text_issues.correction: Crowned in Hungary with a crown sent by the pope.

history_text_issues.claim: Charles Robert of Anjou was the first foreign king of Hungary.
history_text_issues.problem: False: Peter Orseolo, a Venetian, reigned in 1038–41 and 1044–46, and between 1301 and 1307 Wenceslaus (a Přemyslid) and Otto of Bavaria reigned. Charles Robert was descended from the Árpáds through the female line.
history_text_issues.correction: Present him as the first Angevin and the winner of the succession wars of 1301–1310.

history_text_issues.claim: From Stephen onwards, Hungary was supposedly the easternmost Christian kingdom.
history_text_issues.problem: A Latin-centric view: Byzantium, Bulgaria, Rus', Georgia and Armenia were Christian kingdoms further east.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that it was one of the easternmost kingdoms of Latin Christendom, alongside Poland.

history_text_issues.claim: Hungary was a Christian bulwark against the Mongols and, later, against the Russians, and against the Byzantine Empire.
history_text_issues.problem: There was no Russian threat to medieval Hungary; it was Hungary that intervened in Galicia (Rus') in the 12th–13th centuries. Calling Byzantium, a Christian empire, an enemy of the “Christian bulwark” is incoherent: the wars with Manuel I (until 1167) were rivalries between Christian states. The title antemurale Christianitatis refers to the Ottomans.
history_text_issues.correction: Remove the Russians, present Byzantium as a regional rival and emphasise the Mongols (1241, 1285) and the Ottomans.

history_text_issues.claim: In 1456, Hunyadi halted Ottoman expansion in Europe for decades.
history_text_issues.problem: The victory at Belgrade (with the crusaders of John of Capistrano) protected Hungary until 1521, but the Ottomans took Serbia in 1459 and Bosnia in 1463.
history_text_issues.correction: Speak of a halt to the offensive against Hungary, not against Europe in general.

history_text_issues.claim: The text jumps from Hunyadi to the 16th-century fall without naming Matthias Corvinus or Mohács.
history_text_issues.problem: A significant omission: Matthias (1458–1490), his mercenary army and the defeat at Mohács (1526), which the game itself alludes to in the Corvinian Army tech. The division of the kingdom is described as a division into two parts, leaving out the Principality of Transylvania.
history_text_issues.correction: Add Matthias Corvinus, Mohács (1526) and the tripartite division of the kingdom.

missing_features: The gold of Kremnica and the Hungarian florin (1325–26), the largest European gold production of the 14th century
Matthias's army: handgunners, pavise-bearers, Wagenburg and artillery
Post-1241 castles and the belt of frontier fortresses against the Ottomans
The feigned retreat and the terror of the raids (the Modena hymn: “ab Ungerorum nos defendas iaculis”)
The Székelys as frontier guards and archer vanguard; Cuman, Pecheneg and Jász auxiliaries
Exports of grey cattle and wine
The banderia and the militia portalis
The Holy Crown and the cult of the holy kings

proposals.title: Fekete sereg (Matthias's army)
proposals.description: Restore Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon. Create an Imperial Age tech in which Hand Cannoneers and the Spearman line gain +1/+1 armour and train +25% faster, but cost +15% gold, reflecting their mercenary character.
proposals.historical_basis: Matthias Corvinus's standing army combined heavy and light cavalry with pikemen, pavise-bearers and a high proportion of handgunners, and was paid for with extraordinary taxes.

proposals.title: Rename Corvinian Army to Militia Portalis
proposals.description: Keep the mechanic (the Huszar's gold is replaced by food), but with the name and rationale of hussar recruitment from peasant plots, leaving the name “Corvinian/Black Army” for the mercenary tech above.
proposals.historical_basis: The Diet of Temesvár (1397) obliged lords to equip one horseman for every 20 peasant plots; Matthias restored the system in 1459 and linked it to the hussars.

proposals.title: Végvár
proposals.description: Restore Keep and Fortified Wall. The new tech reduces the stone cost of towers and Castles by 20%, gives them +15% hit points and allows garrisoned units to be healed.
proposals.historical_basis: Stone castles multiplied after the Mongol invasion of 1241 (the causal link is debated), and in the 15th century the kingdom built a belt of frontier fortresses from Belgrade to Jajce.

proposals.title: Kremnica Florin (replaces the wolf bonus)
proposals.description: Gold Miners work +15% faster and gold mines last +20% longer.
proposals.historical_basis: Charles Robert controlled the mines of Kremnica and other mining towns as a royal monopoly, and minted the Hungarian florin from 1325–26.

proposals.title: Székely Guards
proposals.description: Towers and Castles can train cheap Cavalry Archers with +2 line of sight, and mounted archer units near their own towers gain +1 attack.
proposals.historical_basis: The Székelys (and the Pechenegs) guarded the frontiers and served as the archer vanguard in the armies of the Árpáds (for example, at the Battle of the Fischa, 1146, according to Otto of Freising).

contested: Hungarian ethnogenesis: a Finno-Ugric linguistic origin is a matter of consensus, but the original homeland, the chronology and the admixture with Turkic populations are debated (genetic studies from 2018–2020 show mixed ancestry among the conquerors).
Location and chronology of Magna Hungaria, Levedia and Etelköz.
Etymology of “huszár”: from Serbian husar/gusar (from cursarius) or from Hungarian “húsz” (twenty)? And the date of the first mention (1403 or 1432)?
Authenticity of the phrase “De sagittis Hungarorum libera nos, Domine”, which is not attested; the actual formula in the Modena hymn is different.
Causal relationship between the Mongol invasion of 1241 and the wave of stone castles (Fügedi versus Janeš).
Actual proportion of handgunners in Matthias's army and the scope of the name “Black Army” (coined after 1490).
Ethnic origin of John Hunyadi (Vlach, according to most sources, or Hungarian).

Leo VI, Tactica (c. 900)

groups.cross_civ_notes:
1) Triplicated hussars. The Magyar Huszar (Magyars), the Winged Hussar (Poles and Lithuanians) and the generic Hussar (30 of 56 civs, including Koreans, Mongols, Khmer and the Chinese Wei and Wu) all come from the same 15th-century Hungarian-Serbian light cavalry. The generic Hussar is an anachronistic European label for “advanced light cavalry”. The Winged Hussar combines anachronism (16th–17th centuries) with a type error (in the game it is light cavalry, in reality it was a heavy lancer), and sharing it between Poles and Lithuanians dilutes both civs.

2) The Teutonic Order is spread across five texts. It appears in the Teutons' unique unit and in the history texts of the Teutons, Bohemians (Ottokar II's Prussian crusade; Königsberg bears his name), Poles and Lithuanians (Grunwald told twice). But its Prussian-Livonian state, distinct from the Empire, is not represented anywhere, nor are the Baltic peoples it fought (Old Prussians, Curonians, Estonians, Livonians), who are either absorbed or absent.

3) The pavise is in the least obvious civ. Tower Shields give Lithuania a piece of equipment whose archetype is Italian and above all Bohemian (although pavise-type shields did circulate on the Baltic-Polish frontier). The Bohemians, the historical owners of the pavéza, only have it implicitly in the Hussite Wagon. Sharing this trait would make both more faithful.

4) Mining with inverted logic. The Bohemians get free mining (Kutná Hora), the Poles turn stone into gold (Wieliczka salt) and the Magyars have Gold Shaft Mining with no particular emphasis (Kremnica gold). The Teutons, on the other hand, do not even have Gold Shaft Mining, when it was German miners, under the mining law of Freiberg/Iglau, who opened Kutná Hora, Jihlava, Kremnica, Banská Štiavnica and Novo Brdo. Likewise, the Ostsiedlung and Magdeburg law (ius Teutonicum), which founded hundreds of towns in Poland, Bohemia, Hungary and even in Vilnius (1387), appear in none of the five civs.

5) Wagon and firearm tactics were regional, but only the Bohemians have them. Vytautas was already using wagons and cannons at the Vorskla (1399), before the Hussites; Hunyadi used the Wagenburg (Varna 1444, Kosovo 1448); Jan Jiskra's Czech mercenaries later passed into Matthias's army; and Poland used the Wagenburg and Czech shooters in the Thirteen Years' War (Świecino, 1462). Two problems follow from this: Magyars without any firearm and Poles without the Hand Cannoneer.

6) Three cavalry civs, only partly differentiated. Poles, Lithuanians and Magyars are all “Cavalry”. History allows them to be separated better: heavy banner knights for medieval Poland, light javelin and raiding cavalry (plus Tatar auxiliaries) for Lithuania, the horse archery of the conquest period and hussars for Hungary. The current design captures the Hungarian case well and the other two poorly. Paradox: Lithuania has Paladin and Plate Barding, while Poland, whose heavy cavalry decided Grunwald, does not have Plate Barding.

7) Overlapping umbrella labels. The “Slavs” (mostly Rus': Boyar, Druzhina, Detinets) use a name that, strictly speaking, would cover Poles and Bohemians and that coincides with the Ruthenian majority of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. The Teutons overlap with Franks, Burgundians, Sicilians (Staufen), Italians and the name “Saxons”: the Ottonian dynasty was continental Saxon, which may confuse the player, because the Saxons civ appears to represent the Anglo-Saxons. The Magyars overlap with the Huns (the medieval Hungarian myth of descent from Attila) and with the Cumans, who settled in Hungary in 1239.

8) A common chronological mismatch. Bohemians (1420s), Poles (1500–1683) and Lithuanians (Winged Hussar) pull towards the end of the 500–1500 frame, or beyond it. The Teutons are stuck with a narrative from the original version (1999) that ends at the Interregnum and ignores the 14th–15th centuries. The Magyars, by contrast, exaggerate the nomadic phase and forget the late kingdom.

9) Monks and paganism. The Lithuanians, whose dynastic core was pagan until 1387, are a “Monk civilization” with relic bonuses, which can be justified only by Orthodox Ruthenia (which the civ does not represent) and by the post-1387 phase. The Bohemians, a largely iconoclastic movement, are also “Monk”, although priests did lead armies. The Magyars, the kingdom of the “holy kings”, have neither Atonement, Redemption nor Faith. The distribution of religious techs does not follow the religious history of the region.

10) Rarity context in the game. Several “absences” should be read in light of frequency in the game: the Paladin exists for only 10 of 56 civs, the Hand Cannoneer for 23 and the Arbalester for 30. So the lack of the Paladin for Poles and Bohemians, or of the Arbalester for the Teutons, is normal in the game; the genuinely anomalous gaps are Plate Barding (Poles, Bohemians), Keep and firearms (Magyars) and Gold Shaft Mining (Teutons). The new Mounted Crossbowman (15 civs, including Teutons, Poles and Bohemians) is a historically defensible addition for Central Europe.

11) Quality of the texts. The more recent texts (Bohemians, Poles, Lithuanians) are generally better than the older ones (Teutons, Magyars). Even so, they repeat popular myths (Casimir's quarantine, “oldest civilization”) and simplifications of imperial nomenclature (“Holy Roman Emperor” applied to Charlemagne, Rudolf and Sigismund, who did not hold that title at the dates referred to).

verification_log.change: fidelity_score from 4 to 5: no element is “unfounded” or “wrong” and the bonuses are mostly plausible. The score is now in line with Poles and Magyars, which have unfounded elements, and with Lithuanians (4).
Farms cost -40% moves from “plausible” to “abstraction”: the draft itself admitted that the bonus does not express the Ostsiedlung, it only translates it mechanically.

Tree issue “Arbalester”: I checked in data.json that the Teutons have Crossbowman, Mounted Crossbowman and Heavy Mounted Crossbowman, and that the Arbalester exists for only 30 of 56 civs. The absence is no longer “among the most unhistorical”. The Schützengilden are now dated to the 14th century, not the 13th.

Tree issues: added the Mounted Crossbowman/Heavy Mounted Crossbowman item (present). Light Cavalry is no longer a “correct” absence, because of the Order's Prussian light cavalry (Turkopolen). In the Hansa item, added that the Order was a member of the Hansa and conquered Gotland (1398). Added the rarity of the Paladin (10 of 56).

History: Peipus goes down from “major” to “moderate” and is rewritten. The battle did in fact fix the Livonian-Novgorodian border (together with Rakvere, 1268); the Livonian branch had formally been part of the Order since 1237. Removed the vague claim of “another 170 years of expansion” and replaced it with examples (Pomerelia 1308–09, Gotland 1398).

History: added the Divisio regnorum of 806 to the item on the three-way division, and corrected “sons of Louis” to grandsons of Charlemagne. Nuanced the item on the “barbarians”: Bavaria was also annexed by Charlemagne (788), but it was Christian. Added to the Interregnum item that the imperial throne (coronation) was vacant from 1250 to 1312.

Corrected in naming_scope: in Latin, the rulers used “rex Romanorum”/“imperium Romanum”, not “Reich”. Marius's battle identified (Aquae Sextiae). The Saxons civ was confirmed in the data as probably Anglo-Saxon (Hearth Troop, Shield Wall). Added the existence of a systematic “Burgenordnung” as contested.

Corrected: Prokop the Great was a Taborite priest, not a “Utraquist” in the moderate sense. Added that Jan Želivský had been a Premonstratensian canon of Želiv, which nuances the “Monk” label. The epithet “of iron and gold” belongs to Ottokar II, not to the kings in general.

Hussite Wagon: removed the claim that the Military Ordinance of 1423 describes the wagon crews. It is above all a disciplinary and marching code; the composition of the crews comes from later sources and from reconstructions (Durdík).

History: the item on Sigismund and Hus goes down from “moderate” to “minor”. After the conciliar condemnation, Sigismund handed Hus over to the Elector Palatine Louis III, who had the sentence carried out (Richental), so “ordered the execution” is not entirely false. The error lies in the imperial title and in the date given for the start of the war.

History: the item “gained religious freedom” goes down from “major” to “moderate”, because the Compactata (1436) did in fact give legal recognition to the Utraquist Church. Added the omitted problem of the 1306–1310 interlude before the Luxembourgs.

Tree issues: Paladin contextualised (only 10 civs have it). Added, as per data.json, Elite Cannon Galleon present (ironic for a kingdom with no coastline), Mounted Crossbowman, and Hoardings, Treadmill Crane and Crop Rotation absent. Anthem proposal: Domažlice (1431) was the fifth crusade, not the fourth, and the episode is now presented as a tradition.

“Villagers regenerate” moves from “unfounded” to “stretched”. The probable link to the hypothesis of lower Black Death mortality, which the game text itself invokes, has some scientific support. Even so, the mechanic is a considerable stretch.

History: the Black Death item goes down from “major” to “moderate” and has been corrected. I checked that Izdebski et al. (2022) support a low impact in Poland (agricultural continuity or even expansion), whereas the draft only said “highly variable impacts”. Casimir's quarantine is still classified as a legend without evidence.

History: nuanced the Grunwald item, because the First Peace of Thorn was modest in territorial terms but the indemnity ruined the Order. Added two omitted problems: the crisis of the 1030s (Bretislaus I, pagan reaction) and the backward projection of 16th-century religious tolerance (Wieluń 1424; Kazimierz 1495). The 1520 statute was identified as that of Toruń.

Tree issues reoriented on the basis of data.json. The significant gap is Plate Barding Armor (absent), not the Paladin (only 10 of 56 civs have it). The Hand Cannoneer was contextualised (only 23 of 56 civs have it) and the absent Halberdier was added. The Chorągiew proposal now gives Plate Barding instead of Paladin.

History: the item “trapped between Christian Europe and Orthodox Muscovy” goes down from “moderate” to “minor” and has been rewritten. The draft said that Moscow was only a rival at the end of the 15th century, but Algirdas waged war on Moscow in 1368–72 and Jogaila considered marrying a daughter of Dmitry Donskoy, with Orthodox baptism.

Added an omitted problem: Mindaugas was crowned in 1253 by the Bishop of Chełmno on the mandate of Innocent IV, not by the pope. The first mention of the leičiai (1407) was confirmed, and Bracław was added to the annexations of 1569.

“Monk” label, relic bonuses and team bonus nuanced: the Grand Duchy had an Orthodox population with monasteries, such as the Kyiv Lavra under Lithuanian suzerainty from c. 1362. The “stretched” rating stands, but “inversion” applies only to the pagan core.

Tower Shields: the explanation now acknowledges that the game text itself attributes pavises to the Lithuanian infantry and that pavise-type shields existed on the Baltic-Polish frontier. The “stretched” rating stands and the origin of the pavise was added to contested. The “Reysa” proposal was renamed “Grobis”, because Reise referred to the Order's own campaigns against Lithuania.

Corvinian Army moves from “wrong” to “plausible”. I checked that the militia portalis (1397) was restored by Matthias (Szeged, 1459) and that Hungarian historiography attributes to him a decree (c. 1481) on hussars recruited according to peasant holdings. The “Huszar without gold” mechanic has a basis; the mismatch lies only in the name, which evokes the expensive mercenary core. The rename proposal was kept, with an adjusted justification.

Corrected an error in the draft: Jan Jiskra was Hunyadi's adversary (Lučenec, 1451), not his mentor. Hussite tactics were passed on through Czech mercenaries (the bratříci absorbed by Matthias), and Hunyadi used the Wagenburg at Varna and at Kosovo. The proportion of shooters is now presented as a common estimate (about 1 in every 4 infantrymen).

Magyar Huszar: the first mention of hussars changed from “1432” to “first half of the 15th century (1403 or 1432, debated)”. Added to contested the date and the fact that the name “Black Army” was coined after 1490.

History: added to the “bulwark” item the inconsistency of casting Byzantium, a Christian empire, as an enemy of a “Christian bulwark”. Severity of the omission of Matthias and Mohács kept at “moderate”, with the note that the text already alludes to Renaissance Buda and to the 16th-century partition, but forgets Transylvania.
Tree issues completed with data.json: Arrowslits and Bombard Tower (in the fortifications item) and Stone Shaft Mining are also missing. Florin dated to 1325–26.

Corrected a factual error: the generic Hussar does not exist for the Chinese (data.json). The 30 civs include Koreans, Mongols, Khmer, Wei and Wu. Added note 10 on the rarity of Paladin, Hand Cannoneer and Arbalester in the game and on the new Mounted Crossbowman. Note 5 was corrected: Vytautas at the Vorskla predates the Hussites, and Jiskra was Hunyadi's adversary. Added to note 6 the Plate Barding paradox between Lithuanians and Poles.

civs.represents: Viking Age Scandinavians in general. With Danes and Varangians in the same DLC (The Viking Sagas, present in the repository), the civ in practice comes to represent the Norwegians and the Atlantic Norse world: Iceland, the Faroes, Orkney, the Hebrides, Dublin and Greenland. The history text, however, still talks about all Scandinavians, including the Danes and the Rus'.
civs.period: c. 793–1066 (the Viking Age proper). It can be extended to c. 550–1266 if one includes the Vendel/Merovingian period and the Norwegian monarchy up to Largs (1263) and the Treaty of Perth (1266).
civs.verdict: The core of the design captures with reasonable fidelity what the sources say about the Viking Age Norse: resilient infantry, cheap warships, Longship, Berserk and naval archers (Bogsveigar). The weak points are the unfounded economic bonus (free Wheelbarrow/Hand Cart) and Chieftains, whose name has nothing to do with the anti-cavalry effect and whose function has only an indirect basis in the battles against Frankish mounted forces. The tech tree is incoherent: it gives Knight, Cavalier and Mounted Crossbowman, keeps the “pagan” Monastery until 1500 and omits central traits such as the leiðangr, the thing, the slave and silver trade and the Atlantic colonisation. The history text is the most outdated of the group: wrong etymology of “viking”, Vinland as a mere hypothesis, the siege of Paris misdated, Baldwin I as a Norman and the end of the raids in c. 1000. With Danes and Varangians in the same DLC, the name “Vikings”, which denotes an activity and not a people, has become even more ambiguous.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Viking” (Old Norse víkingr; fara í víking) denotes an activity, the seaborne expedition for plunder and trade, and not an ethnic group. Not all Scandinavians were vikings, and the term only covers c. 793–1066, so a “Vikings” civ in the Imperial Age (15th century) is contradictory. With Danes and Varangians in the same DLC, the civ is left without a clear scope. The history text still claims Lindisfarne, the Danelaw, Cnut, Kiev and the Normans, all now repeated in other civs. The most coherent choice would be “Norse” or “Norwegians” (Norway and its Atlantic colonies), in line with the other civs, which are named after peoples or kingdoms.

elements.explanation: Viking Age armies were naval forces that fought on foot, in a shield wall (skjaldborg). They used horses to get around, not to charge: the ASC records in 866 that the Great Army was provided with horses in East Anglia. A fair label.

There is no record of any Norse excellence in land transport. The Oseberg wagon (burial of 834) is a ceremonial funerary object. The Scandinavian economy was agro-pastoral and maritime. It is an economic balance bonus.

elements.element: Infantry +20% HP starting in Feudal Age
elements.explanation: It is an acceptable abstraction of the toughness and cohesion of shield-wall infantry. Note that the mail shirt (brynja) was expensive and confined to the elites, and the Gjermundbu helmet (10th century) is the only near-complete Viking helmet known. The bonus represents the shield and discipline more than the equipment.

It reflects Scandinavian clinker-built naval technology (Oseberg, Gokstad, Skuldelev, Roskilde 6 at c. 36–37 m), the abundance of timber and the leiðangr, a system in which the districts (skipreiður) were obliged to build, crew and supply ships for the king. The dating of the formal leiðangr is contested: Snorri attributes it to Haakon the Good (mid-10th century), but the laws regulating it date from the 12th–13th centuries. Even so, it is one of the best-founded bonuses in the game.

The berserkir are attested in skaldic poetry: Þorbjörn hornklofi's Haraldskvæði/Hrafnsmál (c. 900) links them to Hafrsfjord. Snorri (Ynglinga saga, ch. 6) describes warriors without mail, raging like dogs or wolves, biting their shields, whom neither fire nor iron could wound. The HP regeneration renders this invulnerability creatively. But they were an elite, or cult, minority, not troops recruitable en masse. In the sagas they are often villains, and the ecclesiastical-law section of the Icelandic Grágás (c. 1122–1133) punished berserk fury with lesser outlawry.

elements.element: Chieftains (Infantry +5 attack vs. Cavalry, +4 vs. Camel Units)
elements.explanation: The name is generic (höfðingi, goði, jarl) and has nothing to do with the effect. The anti-cavalry function has only an indirect basis: on the Continent, Norse armies frequently faced Carolingian and Breton forces with a strong mounted component, and the usual response was the shield wall with spears and the fortified camp. At the Dyle (891), according to the Annales Fuldenses, the Franks had to dismount to attack the Viking camp, a sign of their preference for mounted combat. The English cavalry charge at Stamford Bridge narrated by Snorri is probably contamination from the account of Hastings. The bonus against camels is irrelevant, and, ironically, the civ does not have Halberdier.

The name is a legitimate Old Norse compound (bogsveigir, “bow-bender”, i.e. archer). The bow was central to Scandinavian naval battles: Einarr Þambarskelfir at Svolder (c. 1000) is the most famous archer of the sagas. The Norwegian leiðangr laws (Gulaþingslög) required a bow and arrows per rowing bench, and the Konungs skuggsjá (c. 1250) deals with bows and crossbows in naval warfare. Pairing archers with Longships is well founded.
It is a neutral abstraction of maritime culture, without historical problems.

tree_issues.problem: It is anachronistic for the Viking Age. The mounted crossbow is a 13th–15th-century phenomenon in continental Europe. 13th-century Norway knew the crossbow and some hirð cavalry (the Konungs skuggsjá deals with both), but the combination was never a Norwegian trait. It results from a regional “Western Europe” block applied indiscriminately.

tree_issues.item: Absence of Redemption, Illumination, Theocracy, Sanctity and Herbal Medicine
tree_issues.problem: It represents paganism, which is acceptable in the Dark/Feudal Age, but Norway was Christianised c. 995–1030 (Olaf Tryggvason, St Olaf, Stiklestad 1030). The archdiocese of Nidaros dates from 1152/53 and the cult of St Olaf had a pan-Nordic reach. Keeping the civ “pagan” until 1500 is anachronistic.

tree_issues.item: Knight and Cavalier present; absence of Cavalry Archer, Thumb Ring, Hussar, Bloodlines, Husbandry and Plate Barding Armor
tree_issues.problem: The absence of mounted archers and of horse-breeding upgrades is consistent with a mountainous, maritime territory without a strong equestrian tradition. But the presence of Knight and Cavalier is debatable: Norway only had a small court cavalry in the 13th century, with no weight comparable to that of the continental monarchies.
Historically acceptable (the halberd belongs to the 14th–15th centuries), but inconsistent with Chieftains, which makes generic infantry the anti-cavalry answer.

Faithful. Harald Hardrada served in the Guard (c. 1034–1043) before becoming king of Norway, and other Norwegians and Icelanders did the same (Bolli Bollason, Laxdæla saga). The Longship is the symbol of Norse shipbuilding.
It is a minor gap: Norway built stone fortifications in the 13th century (Bergenhus/Håkonshallen, Tunsberghus in Tønsberg, Akershus c. 1299).

history_text_issues.claim: “The Vikings (meaning "northmen")”
history_text_issues.problem: “Víkingr” does not mean “northmen”. “Nordmanni/Northmen” is a different term, used mainly by the Frankish sources.
history_text_issues.correction: The etymology is debated: vík (bay), Víken (the Oslofjord region), víkja (to turn aside/be away) or Anglo-Saxon wīc (emporium). “Going on víking” denotes an expedition, not an ethnic group.

history_text_issues.claim: The vikings were supposedly the last of the “barbarian” tribes that the Romans called Germani.
history_text_issues.problem: It projects the Roman perspective onto the 8th century, when there was no longer a Western Roman Empire, and treats the Scandinavians as “a tribe”. As a statement restricted to Germanic-speaking peoples, it is defensible in a broad sense (Magyars and Mongols do not count here), but the framing is anachronistic.
history_text_issues.correction: The Scandinavians spoke North Germanic languages and were organised into kingdoms and chiefdoms. Tacitus knew the Suiones, but the “barbarian” label reflects the perspective of the monastic chroniclers.

history_text_issues.claim: They were called “dragon boats” because of the dragon heads on the prow and stern.
history_text_issues.problem: It is a generalisation. “Dreki” appears in poetry and the sagas (Olaf Tryggvason's Ormr inn langi), but the archaeological evidence for dragon heads is scarce and most ships did not have them. “Drakkar” is a 19th-century coinage.
history_text_issues.correction: Distinguish the literary designations (dreki, snekkja, skeið) from the archaeological typology.

history_text_issues.claim: Being pagans, they did not hesitate to kill clergy and plunder churches.
history_text_issues.problem: It reproduces the perspective of the monastic sources. Monasteries were targets because they were rich and defenceless, and Christians attacked them too: the Irish annals record armed conflicts between monasteries and attacks by Irish kings on religious houses, and Charlemagne destroyed the Saxon Irminsul in 772.
history_text_issues.correction: Contextualise the economic motivation and the bias of the sources.

history_text_issues.claim: “They discovered Iceland in 825 ... and settled there in 875.”
history_text_issues.problem: 825 is the date of Dicuil's work (De mensura orbis terrae), which mentions Irish monks in “Thule” c. 795. It is not the date of the Norse discovery.
history_text_issues.correction: Norse discovery c. 860 (Naddoddr, Garðarr Svavarsson, Flóki, according to the Landnámabók). Settlement from c. 870–874 (Ingólfr Arnarson, according to the Íslendingabók).

history_text_issues.claim: “Some people think that the Vikings reached Newfoundland”
history_text_issues.problem: It is outdated. L'Anse aux Meadows was excavated by Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad (1961–68) and has been a World Heritage Site since 1978. Dendrochronology (Kuitems et al., Nature 601, 2022) dates the felling of trees with metal tools to 1021.
history_text_issues.correction: The Norse presence in Newfoundland c. 1000–1021 is an established fact. What is debated is the location of Vinland and the extent of the voyages.

history_text_issues.claim: The vikings supposedly began attacking and colonising the eastern Baltic in the 6th–7th centuries.
history_text_issues.problem: Calling 6th–7th-century Scandinavians “vikings” is anachronistic, because this is the Vendel period.
history_text_issues.correction: There are pre-Viking Scandinavian colonies and expeditions (Grobiņa, in Latvia, c. 650–800; the Salme ship burials, in Estonia, c. 750), but not “vikings”.

history_text_issues.claim: “in 907 a force of 2000 ships and 80,000 men attacked Constantinople”
history_text_issues.problem: It is presented as fact, but Oleg's 907 campaign appears only in Nestor's Chronicle (c. 1113), without Byzantine confirmation, and the numbers (2000 ships with 40 men each) are legendary.
history_text_issues.correction: The well-attested Rus' attacks are those of 860, 941 (crushed with Greek fire) and 1043. The treaty of 911 is preserved. The 907 campaign is historiographically contested.

history_text_issues.claim: “Danes attacked and looted the famous island monastery at Lindisfarne”
history_text_issues.problem: The sources on Lindisfarne (ASC, Alcuin's letters) speak only of “heathens”. In Old English, “Dene” denoted Scandinavians in general: the ASC itself calls the attackers at Portland (c. 789) “Danes”, and some versions say they came from Hǫrðaland, in Norway.
history_text_issues.correction: State that the origin of the attackers is uncertain, probably Norwegian, and that “Danes” is here a generic usage of the English sources.

history_text_issues.claim: After 865 the Danes supposedly dominated much of England for two centuries.
history_text_issues.problem: It is an exaggeration. The Danelaw was reconquered by Wessex between 917 and 954, the year the last Scandinavian king of York, Eric (traditionally, but not unanimously, identified with Eric Bloodaxe), was expelled.
history_text_issues.correction: Danish rule over all of England is limited to 1013–14 and 1016–1042. The Danelaw survived as a legal and cultural region.

history_text_issues.claim: “In 871 another large fleet sailed up the Seine ... besieged the city for two years”
history_text_issues.problem: The date and the duration are wrong, and so is the destination of the authorised plunder.
history_text_issues.correction: The great siege of Paris took place in 885–886 (c. 11 months). Charles the Fat paid 700 pounds of silver and authorised them to plunder Burgundy, not “western France”. The first great sack of Paris was in 845 (Reginherus, 7000 pounds).

history_text_issues.claim: In 911 the Frankish king supposedly made the Viking chief of Normandy a duke.
history_text_issues.problem: By the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, Rollo received lands around Rouen. The ducal title only became fixed with Richard I and Richard II (late 10th–early 11th century).
history_text_issues.correction: Rollo was count/princeps of Rouen; the “dukes of Normandy” come later.

history_text_issues.claim: Baldwin I of Jerusalem appears among the warriors who came out of Normandy.
history_text_issues.problem: It is wrong: Baldwin I (of Boulogne), brother of Godfrey of Bouillon, belonged to the House of Boulogne and was not a Norman.
history_text_issues.correction: The Normans of the First Crusade were Bohemond of Taranto, Tancred and Robert Curthose.

history_text_issues.claim: “Viking raids stopped at the end of the tenth century.”
history_text_issues.problem: It is wrong. The “second Viking Age” begins precisely in the 980s–990s: Maldon (991), growing Danegeld (991–1012), Sweyn's conquest (1013), Cnut (1016), Stamford Bridge (1066) and the expeditions of Magnus Barefoot (1098–1103).
history_text_issues.correction: Historiographical convention places the end of the Viking Age c. 1066.

history_text_issues.claim: “the Rus became Russians”
history_text_issues.problem: It is teleological and anachronistic. The Rus' elite assimilated into the East Slavs, from whom Ukrainians, Belarusians and Russians descend.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that the Rus' merged with the East Slavs of Kievan Rus'.

missing_features: Assemblies (thing/Althing, 930) and the figure of the lögsögumaðr (lawspeaker): Norse politics was assembly-based.
The leiðangr (compulsory naval levy by districts) as the basis of Norwegian royal power.
The colonisation of the North Atlantic (Iceland, the Faroes, Greenland, Vinland) as a defining trait: exploration, settlement and pastoralism.
The slave trade (þrælar) and the bullion silver economy (hacksilver), drivers of the raids.
Fortified winter camps and longphuirt (Dublin 841, Torksey 872–873, Repton 873–874).
The trade in dried cod (stockfish) from Lofoten via Bergen and Greenland walrus ivory.
The use of skis in war (Sverris saga; the birkebeinar and the rescue of Haakon Haakonsson in 1205–1206).
Christian, monarchical Norway: St Olaf, Nidaros, the civil wars of 1130–1240 and the Atlantic “empire” of Haakon IV.

proposals.title: Rename to “Norse” (or “Norwegians”) and rewrite the text
proposals.description: Rename the civ and centre the history text on Norway and the North Atlantic: Harald Fairhair and Hafrsfjord (traditionally c. 872, now often placed in the 880s), Olaf Tryggvason, St Olaf, Harald Hardrada, Sverre, Haakon IV, Largs (1263) and the union with Denmark and Sweden at Kalmar (1397). Remove the Danelaw, Cnut and the Rus', which are left to Danes and Varangians.
proposals.historical_basis: “Víkingr” is an activity; it is the medieval kingdoms that are the political units comparable to the other civs.

proposals.title: Leiðangr (replaces Chieftains)
proposals.description: Castle Age: Warships and Transport Ships are created 50% faster and each Dock gives +5 population.
proposals.historical_basis: Gulaþingslög and Frostaþingslög (12th–13th centuries). Snorri attributes to Haakon the Good (mid-10th century) the organisation into skipreiður, which obliged each district to provide a ship, crew and provisions; the actual date of its institutionalisation is debated.

proposals.title: Stockfish (replaces free Wheelbarrow/Hand Cart)
proposals.description: From the Castle Age, Fishing Ships and Fish Traps generate gold equal to 10% of the food gathered.
proposals.historical_basis: Egils saga shows Þórólfr Kveldúlfsson exporting dried fish to England (c. 875). Bergen was the great emporium for Lofoten dried cod from the 12th century, which attracted the Hansa (Bryggen).

proposals.title: Skíðamenn (ski scouts)
proposals.description: Replaces the Scout Cavalry with a cheap, goldless and very fast infantry scout, with a speed bonus on snow terrain.
proposals.historical_basis: Sverris saga mentions ski scouts in the Norwegian civil wars, and tradition tells of the rescue of the young Haakon Haakonsson by the birkebeinar in 1205–1206. The Konungs skuggsjá and Saxo also mention Scandinavian and Sami skill with skis.

proposals.title: Conversion (Kristnitaka) as a mutually exclusive choice
proposals.description: A Castle Age tech in the Monastery that unlocks Redemption, Illumination, Theocracy and Sanctity and speeds up Monks, but prevents the creation of new Berserks (or removes their regeneration).
proposals.historical_basis: Christianisation imposed by Olaf Tryggvason and St Olaf (995–1030) and accepted by the Icelandic Althing in 999/1000 (the kristnitaka proper). The Grágás punishes berserk fury and the sagas show Christian kings persecuting berserkir. Archdiocese of Nidaros in 1152/53.

contested: Etymology of víkingr (vík, Víken, víkja or wīc).
Nature of the berserkir: Odinic cult, ritual trance or mushroom or henbane hypotheses, all speculative.
Size of Viking armies: Peter Sawyer's minimalism (hundreds) versus estimates of thousands for the Great Army (Torksey camp).
Whether Viking violence was exceptional compared with that of contemporaries (Sawyer's revisionism vs. Neil Price and others).
Historicity of Oleg's campaign against Constantinople in 907.
Date and degree of organisation of the leiðangr before the provincial laws of the 12th–13th centuries.
Date of Hafrsfjord (traditional c. 872 vs. the 880s) and the real extent of Harald Fairhair's unification.
Location and extent of Vinland, beyond L'Anse aux Meadows.
key_sources: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle
Annales Bertiniani; Annales Fuldenses
Abbo of Saint-Germain, Bella Parisiacae urbis (c. 897)
Dicuil, De mensura orbis terrae (825)
Ari Þorgilsson, Íslendingabók; Landnámabók
Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla (Ynglinga saga; Hákonar saga góða; Haralds saga harðráða)
Þorbjörn hornklofi, Haraldskvæði/Hrafnsmál
Gulaþingslög; Konungs skuggsjá (c. 1250); Grágás
Povest' vremennykh let (Nestor's Chronicle)
Neil Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020)
Peter Sawyer (ed.), The Oxford Illustrated History of the Vikings (1997)
Judith Jesch, Ships and Men in the Late Viking Age (2001)
Kuitems et al., 'Evidence for European presence in the Americas in AD 1021', Nature 601 (2022)

civs.represents: The Danish people and the kingdom of Denmark, almost exclusively in the Viking phase: Godfred and the Danevirke, the Great Heathen Army, the Danelaw, Gorm and Harald Bluetooth (Jelling), Sweyn Forkbeard and Cnut's North Sea empire, plus the legendary Jomsvikings.
civs.period: The design centres on c. 790–1042. Christian medieval Denmark (the Valdemars 1157–1241, the Kalmar Union 1397–1523) is virtually absent, despite fitting entirely within the AoE2 window.
civs.verdict: The infantry identity and the loot bonus (an abstraction of the Danegeld) are solid, and Jomsviking and Hamask draw on authentic material, though it is largely literary and legendary. The “Siege” component is the weakest: Danish armies took towns mainly by surprise, fortified camps and levied tribute, and the siege of Paris (885–886) did not take the city. Ironically, the tech tree denies Fortified Wall and Architecture to the people of the Danevirke and of Harald Bluetooth's ring fortresses. The civ freezes Denmark in 1042 and ignores the kingdom of knights, crossbowmen, Baltic crusades and the Kalmar Union. The history text is reasonable but contains errors: it makes Harthacnut Cnut's grandson and places the first major engagement in 865, when Godfred was already challenging Charlemagne in 808–810. It also attributes the founding of the Jomsvikings to Harald Bluetooth without reservation.
civs.naming_scope_issues: It is a legitimate ethnonym and endonym (Danir), attested from the 6th century in Jordanes, Procopius and Gregory of Tours. The problem is the period: the design and the text stop in 1042. There is direct overlap with Vikings (Lindisfarne, the Great Army and Cnut appear in both texts) and with Saxons (Danelaw). The Jomsvikings are associated with Wolin, in Slavic Pomerania, and not with Denmark proper.

elements.explanation: “Infantry” is faithful: the shield wall, the Great Army and Cnut's þingalið. “Siege” is weak. The Great Army took walled towns mainly by surprise (York, 866), preferred to fortify camps (Reading 870–871, Repton 873–874) and levied tribute. At Paris (885–886) it used battering rams, mantlets and fire ships, according to Abbo, but did not take the city. Danish engineering excelled in fortification, not in assault.

elements.element: Fishing Ships and Villagers drop off +5% food
elements.explanation: Herring fishing in the Øresund and the Scania Market (Skånemarkedet, 12th–15th centuries) were a major economic engine of medieval Denmark, with exports to the whole of Europe. The Villagers part is generic.

elements.element: Loot 25% of the resource cost of each destroyed building
elements.explanation: A good abstraction of the plunder economy and the Danegeld. The ASC records tributes ranging from 10,000 pounds (991) to 48,000 (1012), and Paris paid 7,000 pounds in 845. Linking wealth to the destruction of buildings is coherent.

elements.element: Barracks and Siege Workshop upgrades cost -66% gold
elements.explanation: It has no identifiable historical correlate; it is a balancing mechanism.

elements.element: Varangian Guards and Longships move +10% faster
elements.explanation: The speed of the warships is well documented (Skuldelev 2, built in Dublin c. 1042; the replica Havhingsten fra Glendalough). There were Danes in the Varangian Guard: the Knýtlinga saga recounts the reception of Eric I Ejegod in Constantinople c. 1103. The speed is an abstraction.

The Jomsvikings are known mainly from the Jómsvíkinga saga (c. 1200), a legendary source. The battle of Hjǫrungavágr (c. 986) is, however, attested in skaldic poetry close to the events, and Jomsborg is usually identified with Wolin (Adam of Bremen's “Iumne”). The torches abstract the burning of settlements and ships. Being “exceptionally strong against cavalry” is invention. The existence of an organised order is contested.

elements.element: Hamask (Infantry deal more damage as they lose HP)
elements.explanation: Hamask (Old Norse hamask, “to go into a frenzy”, related to hamr, “shape/skin”) describes the berserk fury, and more damage at lower HP is an ingenious translation. There is Danish material: Saxo Grammaticus (Gesta Danorum) is full of berserkir, and the Hrólfs saga kraka places frenzied champions at the legendary court of Lejre. But the sources are literary and late, and the theme duplicates the Vikings' Berserk.

elements.element: Northmen's Fury (Mangonel-line/Catapult Galleons +1 range; siege +40% vs buildings)
elements.explanation: The name alludes to the supposed prayer “A furore Normannorum libera nos, Domine”, which is not attested in that form; the closest is a Carolingian antiphon asking for deliverance “from the fierce Norman people”. The artillery effect rests, at most, on Paris (885–886), where Abbo describes battering rams, mantlets and fire ships, but there is no record of a Norse tradition of projectile artillery, and the siege did not take the city.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Siege Weapons +2 line of sight
elements.explanation: No historical basis; it is pure balance.

tree_issues.item: Absence of Fortified Wall (and of Architecture, Treadmill Crane and Two-Man Saw)
tree_issues.problem: It is ironic. The Danevirke has phases from c. 500, was reinforced c. 737 and by Godfred in 808 (Annales regni Francorum) and received a brick wall from Valdemar in the 1160s. There are also the Trelleborg-type ring fortresses (Trelleborg, Fyrkat, Aggersborg, Borgring, c. 975–980) and the Ravning bridge (c. 980, c. 760 m). This is first-rate military engineering.
The Denmark of the Valdemars (1157–1241) fought with armoured knights (Lyndanisse 1219, Bornhöved 1227), and the leding was reformed around heavy cavalry (herremænd).

tree_issues.item: No Arbalester, but Mounted Crossbowman, Heavy Mounted Crossbowman and Cranequins present
tree_issues.problem: It is inconsistent. The crossbow is plausible in 13th–15th-century Denmark, but the civ only has the foot Crossbowman and gets the heavy mounted variant with a cranequin (15th century). For a civ designed around the Viking Age, both are anachronistic; for late Denmark, the Arbalester is missing.

tree_issues.item: Siege Onager and Fast Fire Ship
tree_issues.problem: There is no specific basis: there is no record of Danish projectile artillery in the Viking Age, and the fire ships at Paris (885) were a one-off.

tree_issues.item: Absence of Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon and Cannon Galleon
tree_issues.problem: Consistent with the Viking Age, but not with Kalmar-era Denmark, which used gunpowder artillery in the 15th century, including aboard royal ships such as the Gribshunden.
It is a minor gap. Kalmar-era Denmark had large carvel-built ships in the 15th century, such as John I's Gribshunden (sunk in 1495).

history_text_issues.claim: The Danes are said to have inhabited Denmark “since at least 3,000 BCE”.
history_text_issues.problem: It projects a medieval ethnic group onto the Neolithic. There has been human settlement since c. 12,500 BC (Hamburg culture) and agriculture since c. 3900 BC, but the ethnonym Dani only appears in the 6th century (Jordanes, Getica, c. 551; the raid of Chlochilaich c. 515/520 in Gregory of Tours).
history_text_issues.correction: Distinguish prehistoric settlement from ethnogenesis; the Dani appear in the sources in the 6th century.

history_text_issues.claim: “Their first major military engagement outside of these raids came in 865 CE”
history_text_issues.problem: This is wrong. Godfred confronted Charlemagne (attack on the Obotrites in 808, Frisia in 810 with c. 200 ships). Dorestad was sacked repeatedly (834–837), Paris in 845, there were overwinterings on Thanet (850–851) and the battle of Aclea (851).
history_text_issues.correction: Large-scale Danish conflicts begin in the early 9th century, against the Carolingian Empire.

history_text_issues.claim: The Great Army is said to have been led by Halfdan Ragnarsson, Ivar the Boneless and Ubbe Ragnarsson.
history_text_issues.problem: Healfdene and Ivar (Inwær) appear in the ASC, and Ubba in Abbo of Fleury (Passio S. Eadmundi) and other English sources. The descent from Ragnar Loðbrók is a later tradition: Adam of Bremen (c. 1075) already calls Ivar “son of Lodbrok”, but Ragnar's historicity is highly uncertain and the details come from the 13th-century sagas.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the link to Ragnar as a tradition later than the events.

history_text_issues.claim: The territory of the Danelaw is said to have lasted until the Norman Conquest.
history_text_issues.problem: As a political entity, the Danelaw was reconquered by Wessex between 917 and 954. The text says “under various rulers”, which is technically defensible, but it suggests a political continuity that did not exist.
history_text_issues.correction: It survived as a legal and cultural region: the term “Dena lage” appears in the laws drafted by Wulfstan in the early 11th century.

history_text_issues.claim: Cnut is said to have extended Danish hegemony to Sweden.
history_text_issues.problem: Cnut only claimed “part of the Swedes” (letter of 1027: partis Suanorum), and his Swedish rule is uncertain.
history_text_issues.correction: Say Denmark, England, Norway (1028–35) and part of Sweden.

history_text_issues.claim: “Knut's son Harold Harefoot and his grandson Harthaknut”
history_text_issues.problem: This is wrong: Harthacnut was the son of Cnut and Emma of Normandy, and the half-brother of Harold Harefoot.
history_text_issues.correction: Cnut's two sons, Harold (1035/37–1040) and Harthacnut (1040–1042), reigned in England.

history_text_issues.claim: Gorm the Old is said to have raised the Jelling rune stones.
history_text_issues.problem: Gorm raised only the smaller stone, in memory of Thyra. The large stone (c. 965) was raised by Harald Bluetooth, who on it proclaims himself the Christianiser of the Danes.
history_text_issues.correction: Distinguish the two stones (DR 41 and DR 42).

history_text_issues.claim: Harald Bluetooth is said to have founded the legendary mercenary order of the Jomsvikings.
history_text_issues.problem: The text acknowledges the legendary character, but chooses a single version. The Jómsvíkinga saga attributes the founding to Pálnatóki, with lands from the Wendish king Búrisleifr. The Knýtlinga saga and Saxo link Harald to Jomsborg/Julin, and Adam of Bremen says only that he died a refugee in Iumne.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the competing versions and the largely literary character of the “order”.

history_text_issues.claim: Trade in furs and amber exchanged for luxury goods.
history_text_issues.problem: It is an omission: slaves were a central commodity (the Hedeby market; Rimbert's Vita Anskarii).
history_text_issues.correction: Include the slave trade among the economic foundations.

history_text_issues.claim: In the first half of the 9th century, “Danish Vikings” are said to have raided Ireland.
history_text_issues.problem: The raids on Ireland up to c. 850 are attributed mainly to Norwegians. The Irish annals only distinguish the Dubgaill (“dark foreigners”, often read as Danes) from 851 onwards, and that identification is debated.
history_text_issues.correction: Attribute the first raids on Ireland to Scandinavians, probably Norwegians, and flag the debate over Finngaill/Dubgaill.

missing_features: The Danevirke, the Trelleborg-type ring fortresses and the Ravning bridge: Harald Bluetooth's state engineering.
The Danegeld and the heregeld as a tribute system (the latter paid the þingalið in England).
The emporia of Hedeby/Haithabu and Ribe, coinage and the slave trade.
The Scanian herring fishery and the Øresund toll (Sound Dues, introduced by Eric of Pomerania c. 1429).
Christian Denmark: the archdiocese of Lund (1103/04), warrior bishops such as Absalon, the Baltic crusades (Arkona 1168, Estonia 1219) and the legend of the Dannebrog.
The Kalmar Union (1397–1523) under Margaret I.
The heavy cavalry and crossbowmen of 12th–14th-century Denmark.
Cnut's þingalið/húskarlar, currently assigned to the Goths in the form of the Huskarl.

proposals.title: Danevirke
proposals.description: Castle Age: Palisade and Stone Walls +40% HP and 50% faster construction. Also restore Fortified Wall to the tech tree.
proposals.historical_basis: Danevirke phases c. 500, c. 737, 808 (Godfred) and Valdemar's brick wall (1160s).

proposals.title: Trelleborg (unique building)
proposals.description: A ring fortress available in the Feudal Age, cheaper and weaker than the Castle, that trains infantry and Varangian Guards and can be garrisoned.
proposals.historical_basis: Trelleborg, Fyrkat, Aggersborg and Borgring (dendrochronologically dated to c. 975–980) were built to a royal geometric plan under Harald Bluetooth.

proposals.title: Housecarl/Þingalið (transfer the Huskarl from the Goths)
proposals.description: Give the Huskarl to the Danes (or to the Saxons/Anglo-Danes) as elite infantry with the Danish axe, keeping the Jomsviking or turning it into a technology.
proposals.historical_basis: The húskarlar of Cnut and his successors (Sven Aggesen's Lex Castrensis, 1180s), paid by the heregeld, and Harold II's housecarls at Hastings.

proposals.title: Danegeld
proposals.description: Infantry generates gold when attacking enemy buildings (like the Keshik or the Varangian Guard when fighting units), instead of the generic loot.
proposals.historical_basis: Payments recorded in the ASC between 991 and 1012 and the Paris tribute of 845.

proposals.title: Valdemarian army
proposals.description: Add Cavalier and Arbalester. Imperial Age technology “Absalon”: Warships +1 attack and Monks +2 melee armor.
proposals.historical_basis: Valdemar I and II and Archbishop Absalon, who commanded fleets against the Wends and took Arkona (1168); the conquest of Estonia (1219).

proposals.title: Øresund Toll
proposals.description: Imperial Age: each Dock generates a slow trickle of gold, increased by allied or enemy Trade Cogs passing within its range.
proposals.historical_basis: Sound Dues levied by the Danish Crown from c. 1429.

contested: Historicity of the Jomsvikings and location of Jomsborg (Wolin?).
Historicity of Ragnar Loðbrók and the parentage of the Great Army's leaders.
Scale of Danish settlement in the Danelaw (place-names and genetics: Sawyer vs. Cameron and recent studies).
Function of the Trelleborg-type fortresses (barracks, internal control or preparation for invading England).
Chronology of the Danevirke and degree of centralisation of royal power in the 10th century.
Actual extent of Cnut's rule over Sweden.
Ethnic identification of the Finngaill and Dubgaill of the Irish annals.
