civs.represents: Scandinavians, mainly from eastern Sweden and Gotland, active in Eastern Europe as merchants, warriors and founders of the Rus' elite. It also represents, and above all in the text, the Varangian Guard of Byzantium (from 988), which later recruited Norwegians, Danes, Icelanders and, after 1066, Englishmen. Vendel Legacy and Jarl also point to Sweden.
civs.period: c. 750–1050 for the Varangians in the East. 988–c. 1204 for the Guard's heyday; it is still mentioned in the 14th century (Pseudo-Kodinos). Vendel Legacy points to c. 550–790, and the cavalry Jarl evokes, at most, 13th-century Sweden.
civs.verdict: The economic layer is the most successful part. Gold obtained from hunting abstracts the trade in furs and Islamic silver, the Caravan bonus the river routes, and the Varangian Guard's gold the guardsmen's pay and plunder. But the military identity is inverted: the “Cavalry civilization” label and the mounted Jarl contradict the main contemporary source, Leo the Deacon, who shows Sviatoslav's Rus' fighting on foot and inept on horseback at Dorostolon (971). Gothikon is a misconception: it was a Byzantine court dance performed by the circus factions, not a Varangian practice. The tree gives them Hussar, Heavy Mounted Crossbowman and Fast Fire Ship, when the Rus' were victims of Greek fire. The text focuses almost solely on the Guard and omits Rus' history, which is the bulk of the Varangian presence in the East.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Varangian” is an exonym (Gr. Varangoi, Old Slavic Varyagi, Ar. Warank, Norse Væringjar) that only appears in the sources in the 11th century. The civ merges three realities: (1) the Scandinavians who founded the Rus' elite (8th–10th centuries); (2) the Varangian Guard, a multi-ethnic Byzantine unit; (3) Swedish motifs (Vendel, Jarl), without representing the medieval Swedish kingdom of Uppsala, Birka, Sigtuna, Birger Jarl and Kalmar. It overlaps with Slavs (Kievan Rus'), Byzantines (who also have the Varangian Guard) and Vikings. The Normanist question is politically sensitive.

elements.explanation: “Naval” is faithful: river fleets of monoxyla and attacks on Constantinople (860, 941, 1043) and the Caspian. “Cavalry” is contradicted by the sources. Leo the Deacon (History, books VIII–IX) shows the Rus' fighting on foot and presents their mounted sortie at Dorostolon as an unsuccessful novelty, underlining their ineptitude on horseback. The Guard in Byzantium was also axe infantry.

elements.element: Shepherding, fishing, and hunting also generate gold
elements.explanation: Hunting as a source of gold is a good abstraction of the trade in furs (beaver, black fox, marten) exchanged for silver. Ibn Khordadbeh (c. 870) and Ibn Fadlan (922) describe it, and the dirham hoards confirm it: Spillings, on Gotland, c. 870, with c. 14,300 coins. The shepherding part is contradicted by De Administrando Imperio (ch. 2), according to which the Rus' bought cattle, horses and sheep from the Pechenegs because they had none of their own.

Caravan is well founded: the route “from the Varangians to the Greeks” (Dnieper) and the Volga route were the Varangians' raison d'être in the East. Bloodlines has no basis, because horses were bought from the Pechenegs (DAI 2) and the 10th-century Rus' were not horsemen.

elements.element: Varangian Guards attack +25% faster and generate +50% gold
elements.explanation: The gold part has a solid basis. The Guard was extremely wealthy: Heimskringla (Haralds saga harðráða) mentions the right of pólútasvarf (plundering the palace on the emperor's death), which Harald is said to have exercised three times, and the fortune he sent into Yaroslav's keeping in Hólmgarðr (Novgorod). Anna Komnene and Psellos stress the ferocity of the “axe-bearing barbarians”. The faster attack, by contrast, is an abstraction with no specific source.

elements.element: Longships and Catapult Galleons attack +15% faster
elements.explanation: Longships have some foundation in the Rus' naval raids. Catapult Galleons have none: the Rus' fleets were light boats carrying infantry, with no known shipborne artillery, and they were destroyed by Greek fire in 941 and, with the help of a storm, in 1043.

“Jarl” is a Scandinavian aristocratic title (earl), not a type of troop. There is a link to the East in the sagas: Rögnvaldr Úlfsson is said to have received the jarldom of Aldeigjuborg (Staraya Ladoga) from Yaroslav c. 1019. But in Rus' the elite was the knyaz' and his druzhina, and the 10th-century Varangians fought on foot. A cavalry Jarl would make sense in 13th-century Sweden (Birger Jarl, 1248–1266, and the cavalry of the frälse), not among the Varangians of the 9th–11th centuries.

There is a real and ingenious basis. The boat graves of Vendel and Valsgärde (Uppland, from c. 550) include horses, and the helmet plates show riders with lances, sometimes over a fallen enemy, a motif inherited from the tombstones of Roman cavalrymen and also present at Sutton Hoo. This justifies the trample. But it is a pre-Viking period, and the iconography is prestige imagery, not proof of shock-cavalry tactics.

The Gothikon (“Gothic game”) described in De Ceremoniis (I.83) was an entertainment at a court Christmas banquet. It was performed by members of the Blue and Green circus factions, masked and dressed in furs as “Goths”, beating their shields with staves and singing in a corrupted Latin-Gothic. It was not a Varangian combat practice, and the work was compiled in the mid-10th century, before the Guard existed. The hypothesis that it originated in a Scandinavian Yule custom is a minority view and contested. Throwing axes have no basis either: the Danish axe was two-handed, and the typical throwing axe is the Frankish francisca.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Knight-line +1 attack vs. Infantry
elements.explanation: No basis; it reinforces a cavalry identity that the Varangians did not have.

tree_issues.item: Cavalier, Hussar, Heavy Mounted Crossbowman, Cranequins
tree_issues.problem: Anachronistic and contrary to the sources. The 10th-century Rus'/Varangians fought on foot. The Hussar is 15th-century Hungarian-Serbian, and the cranequin and the heavy mounted crossbow belong to the 15th-century West. The Rus' archery tradition came to be the steppe-type composite bow. The Cavalier would only be justified in a 13th-century “Swedish” reading.
It is ironic: there is no record of Rus' naval incendiary weapons, and the Rus' were precisely the victims of Greek fire (Igor in 941, Vladimir Yaroslavich in 1043).
No basis: there is no known Rus' or Varangian shipborne artillery.
Faithful; this is the legitimate core of the identity. The absence of Champion is acceptable, because the VG covers heavy infantry.

tree_issues.item: Absence of Keep, Arrowslits and Hoardings
tree_issues.problem: Consistent with the timber-and-earth fortifications (gorod) of the Varangian and Rus' centres (Staraya Ladoga, Gnezdovo, Kiev).

history_text_issues.claim: The name supposedly comes from várr (oath) and gangi (companion).
history_text_issues.problem: It is one of the proposed etymologies, but it is disputed. Many philologists derive væringi from vár (“oath, pledge”) + the suffix -ingi.
history_text_issues.correction: Present it as contested: “men of the oath” is generally agreed, the exact derivation is not.

history_text_issues.claim: “First established by Emperor Basil II in 988 CE”
history_text_issues.problem: It is the conventional date (the c. 6,000 warriors sent by Vladimir of Kiev, used at Chrysopolis and Abydos in 988–989), but the term “Varangian” only appears in Greek sources in the 11th century, and there were already Rus' in Byzantine service (the Crete expeditions of 911 and 949).
history_text_issues.correction: Indicate the gradual formation and the precedent of the 10th-century Rus' mercenaries.

history_text_issues.claim: Byzantium supposedly recognised the martial worth of the Varangians “immediately”.
history_text_issues.problem: After a peaceful embassy in 839 (Annales Bertiniani), the first major contact was hostile: the Rus' attack on Constantinople in 860 (homilies of Photius), repeated in 941.
history_text_issues.correction: The Rus' were first attackers and trading partners (treaties of 911 and 944) before they were guards.

history_text_issues.claim: The Guard was supposedly also “a secret police force” and had its headquarters in the Noumera prison.
history_text_issues.problem: “Secret police” is an anachronism. The Guard carried out arrests and executions on imperial orders, but the link to the Noumera as headquarters is poorly documented.
history_text_issues.correction: Refer to its roles as palace guard, making arrests and carrying out imperial orders.

history_text_issues.claim: The famous masked helmets (“iconic masked helmets”).
history_text_issues.problem: There is no evidence that the Guard wore them. Helmets with masks or spectacle guards are mostly from the Vendel period (Gjermundbu, 10th century, is an exception), and in Byzantium the equipment was largely supplied by the state.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention the two-handed axe (Anna Komnene's pelekyphoroi) and mail.

history_text_issues.claim: The Varangians outside Sweden supposedly assimilated into the Slavic culture of the Rus' states.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits that, according to Nestor's Chronicle, it was the Varangians/Rus' themselves who founded the Rurikid dynasty and the Rus' states (Rurik 862, Oleg 882). Nor does it mention Kiev, Novgorod, Sviatoslav, Ibn Fadlan or the trade with the Caliphate, which are the main part of Varangian history.
history_text_issues.correction: Include Kievan Rus' and the trade routes, noting the Normanist controversy.

history_text_issues.claim: The Varangians supposedly also used cavalry against their enemies.
history_text_issues.problem: They occasionally rode to get from place to place, but Leo the Deacon shows Rus' inexperience on horseback in 971. The text thus contradicts the civ's own label.
history_text_issues.correction: Stress that they were infantry.

missing_features: River routes and portage at the Dnieper rapids (De Administrando Imperio, ch. 9: monoxyla bought from the Slavs and dragged overland).
Trade in slaves (saqaliba) and furs for Islamic silver via Volga Bulgaria and Khazaria; Birka, Staraya Ladoga, Gnezdovo.
The collection of tribute (poliudie) by the Rus' princes from the Slavic tribes (DAI 9).
The ship funeral described by Ibn Fadlan (922).
Attacks on Constantinople (860, 941, 1043) and the Caspian (c. 913, Barda'a 943/944).
Varangian mercenaries in the service of Vladimir and Yaroslav (980–1019).
The Swedish kingdom: Uppsala, Birka, Sigtuna, the Ingvar runestones (expedition to the East c. 1036–1041), Birger Jarl and the crusades in Finland.
Dependence on horses and cattle bought from the Pechenegs.

proposals.title: Re-scoping: “Rus'/Varangians” or “Swedes”
proposals.description: Option A: a Varangian-Rus' civ (750–1050), centred on river trade, leaving later Rus' to Slavs. Option B: “Swedes” (from the Vendel period to Kalmar and Engelbrekt, 1434), which would justify the Jarl as 13th-century cavalry and Vendel Legacy, with the Guard kept as a regional unit.
proposals.historical_basis: The Annales Bertiniani (839) identify the “Rhos” as Sueones. The Alsnö stadga (c. 1280) exempted from taxes those who served the king on horseback, creating the Swedish cavalry nobility (frälse), and the Erikskrönikan (c. 1320–1335) describes that chivalric world.

proposals.title: Monoxyla/Portage
proposals.description: Longships and Transport Ships -25% wood and +15% speed; Transport Ships load and unload instantly.
proposals.historical_basis: DAI 9 describes the monoxyle boats bought every spring and the portage at the seven Dnieper rapids.

proposals.title: Pólútasvarf (replaces Gothikon)
proposals.description: When an enemy Castle, Wonder or Town Center is destroyed with Varangian Guards nearby, the player receives 200 gold.
proposals.historical_basis: Haralds saga harðráða (Heimskringla): the guards' right to plunder the palace on the emperor's death, exercised three times by Harald.

proposals.title: Gost' (merchant-warrior)
proposals.description: Replace the Jarl with an armed trading unit created at the Market: it carries gold like a Trade Cart, but has melee attack and armour to defend itself.
proposals.historical_basis: Ibn Fadlan says that every Rus' always carried an axe, a sword and a knife. According to Nestor's Chronicle (terms of 907 and treaty of 944), the Byzantines required Rus' merchants to enter the city unarmed, in groups of 50 and through a single gate, which shows that they arrived in armed fleets.

proposals.title: Clear the tree of cavalry and fire
proposals.description: Remove Hussar, Heavy Mounted Crossbowman, Cranequins, Fast Fire Ship and Catapult Galleon. Add Champion and replace Bloodlines +50% with a Market bonus (dirhams: fixed buy and sell rates).
proposals.historical_basis: Leo the Deacon, books VIII–IX; DAI 2; Scandinavian dirham hoards.

contested: Normanist vs. anti-Normanist controversy over the origin of the Rus' and of the Kievan state.
Etymology of væringi (vár + gengi or vár + -ingi).
Date and manner of the Guard's foundation (988 or formalisation in the 11th century).
Scale of the English presence in the Guard after 1066 (the narratives of a mass exodus are partly legendary).
Origin of the Gothikon (Gothic soldiers in the service of Rome/Byzantium or a Scandinavian Yule custom).
Existence and location of the “Rus' Khaganate” (839).
Birger Jarl's participation in the Battle of the Neva (1240), known only from later Russian sources.

Photius, Homilies on the Rus' attack of 860

civs.represents: Originally, all Slavs. With Bulgarians (2019), Poles and Bohemians (2021) as civs of their own, the Slavs have in practice become the East Slavs/Rus': Kievan Rus', Novgorod, Vladimir-Suzdal and Muscovy. The text, however, still lays claim to the Bulgarian Empire and Great Moravia.
civs.period: c. 500–1500: Slavic expansion (6th–7th centuries), Kievan Rus' (882–1240), the Novgorod Republic (1136–1478) and Muscovy up to Ivan III (1462–1505).
civs.verdict: Detinets is one of the most faithful techs in the game (the timber-and-earth citadels of the Rus'). The Boyar is a defensible abstraction of the mounted warrior aristocracy, and the farming and Monk bonuses have reasonable justification. Druzhina is misapplied: the druzhina was the prince's retinue, which in the 10th century fought on foot in the Scandinavian manner but became cavalry from the 11th century onwards, and not a type of infantry. The “Infantry and Siege” label ignores the fact that Rus' and Muscovite warfare relied increasingly on cavalry and the composite bow. The tech tree denies land gunpowder to a Muscovy that had firearms from 1382 and a Cannon Yard in 1479. The history text is a pan-Slavic mosaic: it calls the Bulgaria of 681 the first great Slavic state and Kievan Rus' the last, and it generalises the boyars to all Slavs.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Slavs” is a language family, not a political entity. Since Bulgarians, Poles and Bohemians, this civ is in fact “Rus'/East Slavs”, but the text still includes Bulgaria and Great Moravia, which are already covered by other civs. Serbs, Croats and the Polabian Slavs/Wends are left unrepresented. The heritage of Kievan Rus' is shared by Ukrainians, Belarusians and Russians, so the name should avoid “Russians”. “Rus'” or “Ruthenians” is suggested. Boyar, Druzhina and Detinets are Rus' terms, consistent with that reading.

elements.explanation: The infantry side has a basis in the early Slavs (Pseudo-Maurice, Strategikon XI.4: javelins, shields and ambushes in forests and marshes), in 10th-century Rus' and in the urban militias of Novgorod (Battle on the Ice, 1242). But the forces of Kiev from the 11th century onwards and those of Muscovy were dominated by the mounted druzhina and, in the 14th–15th centuries, by mass cavalry. Siege warfare has little tradition before artillery.

Procopius and the Strategikon describe the Slavs as farmers rich in livestock and grain, above all millet. The Slavic expansion was agrarian, and Rus' combined slash-and-burn agriculture (podseka) in the north with black-earth lands in the south. It is a reasonable abstraction.

Gambesons is plausible as an equivalent of the tegilyai, the padded coat common in the Muscovite army of the 15th–17th centuries. Arson is a generic tech with no specific Slavic link; the only conceivable association would be Olga's legendary revenge on Iskorosten (946, with incendiary birds, according to Nestor's Chronicle), which is a folkloric motif and not a military practice.

The Slavs learned siege techniques from the Avars and Byzantium (Thessalonica, Miracula S. Demetrii, c. 615–618; Constantinople 626), but the Rus' tradition of siege engines is modest until the artillery of the 15th century.

It is connected to the mission of Cyril and Methodius (863) and above all to the “monastic colonisation” of north-eastern Rus' (Sergius of Radonezh c. 1337/45, Kirillo-Belozersky 1397, Solovetsky 1429/1436), in which monks opened up frontiers. It is a defensible link.

The boyars were the landed aristocracy and the prince's “senior druzhina”, and they fought as armoured cavalry (mail, lamellar armour, conical helmets). Turning a social class into a unit is an abstraction, but heavy-armoured melee is defensible.

elements.element: Detinets (40% of Castle/Tower stone cost replaced by wood)
elements.explanation: Rus' citadels (detinets/kremlin) were built of timber and earth, with log cribs (gorodni). The Moscow Kremlin had oak walls in 1339 and only later white stone (1367–68) and brick (1485–95). The Novgorod detinets only gained stone walls in the 14th century. It is one of the most faithful techs in the game.

The druzhina was the prince's armed retinue, a social category and not a troop type. In the 10th century, with a strong Varangian component, it fought on foot (Sviatoslav's army at Dorostolon, according to Leo the Deacon), but from the 11th century onwards it became essentially mounted, as warrior graves with horses and stirrups show. Associating it with infantry only holds for the early phase, and the trample is a mechanical invention.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Military buildings provide +5 population
elements.explanation: No historical basis; it is pure balance.

tree_issues.item: No Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon or Bombard Tower
tree_issues.problem: An error for late Rus'. The chronicles record firearms (tyufyaki and pushki) in the defence of Moscow against Tokhtamysh in 1382, artillery at Pskov and Novgorod in the 15th century, pishchali on the Ugra (1480) and Ivan III's Pushechny Dvor (Cannon Yard) in 1479, with Aristotele Fioravanti.

This is odd, because Rus' used the steppe-type composite bow and had nomadic archer allies (the Chorni Klobuky of the Ros river, 12th century). Having Cavalry Archer and Heavy Cavalry Archer, by contrast, is a positive.
This is inconsistent. Rus' had no ocean-going war navy in the period; it had river fleets (lod'i) and the river pirates of Novgorod (ushkuiniki, 14th century).

tree_issues.item: No Architecture, Treadmill Crane, Arrowslits or Keep
tree_issues.problem: Consistent with timber fortification (Detinets). But the brick Kremlin of 1485–95, built by Italian architects, would justify some stone tech in the Imperial Age.
This is a minor gap: crossbows (samostrel) are known in Rus' from the 12th–13th centuries, but they were secondary to the bow.

history_text_issues.claim: From c. 500 the Slavs are said to have dominated the “north-east” of Europe, left vacant by the Hunnic migrations.
history_text_issues.problem: The Slavic expansion (6th–7th centuries) was mainly into central, eastern and Balkan Europe; the north-east (the Novgorod region) was only colonised in the 8th–9th centuries. The origin is debated, and Florin Curta argues that Slavic identity was “made” on the Danube frontier.
history_text_issues.correction: Place the expansion in central, eastern and south-eastern Europe and note the debate about origins.

history_text_issues.claim: “The first great Slavic state, the Bulgarian Empire, formed in 681 AD.”
history_text_issues.problem: The text itself acknowledges that Bulgaria was founded by Turkic Bulgars and only became Slavicised in the 10th century, which contradicts the label “first Slavic state”. There were earlier Slavic polities, such as Samo's kingdom (c. 623–658, Fredegar) and Carantania. Bulgaria also has its own civ (Bulgarians).
history_text_issues.correction: Present Bulgaria as a mixed state that became Slavicised and mention Samo and Carantania.

history_text_issues.claim: Great Moravia is said never to have reached a dominant position; “King Rastislav”.
history_text_issues.problem: Under Svatopluk I (870–894), Great Moravia dominated much of central Europe (Bohemia, Pannonia, the lands of the Vistulans). Rastislav was a prince (dux/kъnędzь), not a king.
history_text_issues.correction: Acknowledge the peak under Svatopluk and correct the title.

history_text_issues.claim: Kievan Rus' is described as perhaps the last great medieval Slavic state.
history_text_issues.problem: This is wrong. The Kingdom of Poland (1025), the Kingdom of Bohemia (1198), Dušan's Serbian Empire (1346), the Novgorod Republic and the Grand Principality of Moscow arose or consolidated later.
history_text_issues.correction: Remove “the last”.

history_text_issues.claim: The Scandinavians are said to have taken power by defeating the Turkic Khazars who ruled the region.
history_text_issues.problem: According to Nestor's Chronicle, Rurik was invited in (862, a contested tradition) and Oleg took Kiev from Askold and Dir (882), later freeing some tribes from the Khazar tribute. The destruction of Khazaria only came with Sviatoslav (965–969). “Kingdom” is also inappropriate: it was a grand principality.
history_text_issues.correction: Correct the sequence and note the Normanist controversy.

history_text_issues.claim: The region is said to have been near the Byzantines and the “Persians”.
history_text_issues.problem: This is vague but defensible: most of the Islamic silver in 10th-century Rus' hoards consists of Samanid dirhams (the Samanids being a Persian dynasty of Central Asia), which arrived via Volga Bulgaria and Khazaria.
history_text_issues.correction: Be specific: the Abbasid Caliphate and the Samanids, via the Volga route.

history_text_issues.claim: Under Yaroslav, the Kievan state is said to have been “the largest of its time”.
history_text_issues.problem: This is exaggerated in global terms (Song China, for example, was much larger). By area, Rus' was probably the largest European state of the 11th century.
history_text_issues.correction: Say “the largest European state by extent”.

history_text_issues.claim: Under Yaroslav there is said to have been a “high literacy rate”.
history_text_issues.problem: The birch-bark letters show urban literacy (above all in Novgorod, 11th–15th centuries), but a “high rate” cannot be quantified.
history_text_issues.correction: Speak of urban literacy attested by the birch-bark letters.

history_text_issues.claim: Legal penalties are said generally not to have included death.
history_text_issues.problem: This is a half-truth. The Russkaya Pravda favours monetary compensation (vira), but Yaroslav's version still allowed blood vengeance by the victim's kin; only his sons replaced it with fines.
history_text_issues.correction: Explain the shift from blood vengeance to monetary compensation in the second half of the 11th century.

history_text_issues.claim: Unlike in the rest of Europe, the power of Slavic kings is said to have been limited by the boyars.
history_text_issues.problem: This is a mistaken generalisation. Aristocratic limitation of monarchy was common throughout Europe (Magna Carta 1215, the Hungarian Golden Bull 1222, the Polish nobility). “Boyar” applies to Rus', Bulgaria, Serbia and Wallachia/Moldavia (the latter two not Slavic), not to Poland or Bohemia, and the Rus' princes were not “kings”.
history_text_issues.correction: Restrict the claim to Rus' and the Balkans and remove the contrast with “other parts of Europe”.

history_text_issues.claim: Late medieval absolutism is said to have brought down the boyars.
history_text_issues.problem: This is anachronistic: the Boyar Duma retained power in the 16th–17th centuries.
history_text_issues.correction: The weakening comes with Ivan IV's oprichnina (1565–72), and the title disappears under Peter I (early 18th century).

history_text_issues.claim: The text mentions the fall to the Mongols in 1240 but omits the rest of Rus' history.
history_text_issues.problem: It does not mention the baptism of Rus' (988), the rule of the Golden Horde (1240–1480), the Novgorod Republic or the rise of Moscow, which are central to the civ that effectively represents Rus'.
history_text_issues.correction: Include Vladimir and the baptism of 988, the Golden Horde, Novgorod and the rise of Moscow up to the Ugra (1480).

missing_features: Novgorod: the veche (assembly), the fur trade with the Hansa (Peterhof) and the birch-bark letters.
The composite bow and nomadic allies (Chorni Klobuky), with strong steppe influence on Rus' warfare.
The baptism of Rus' (988), the Orthodox Church, church architecture and icons (St Sophia of Kiev, Rublev).
The poliudie tribute and the princely system of collection.
River fleets (lod'i) and the ushkuiniki of Novgorod.
Muscovite artillery and the pishchal'niki (15th-century shooters).
Abatis defensive lines (zaseki) against the nomads.
The pagan Polabian Slavs (the temple of Svantevit at Arkona, Rethra) and the Wendish Crusade (1147).
Mongol suzerainty and the yarlyk of the Golden Horde.

proposals.title: Rename to “Rus'” (or “Ruthenians”) and rewrite the text
proposals.description: Centre the civ and the text on Kievan Rus', Novgorod, Vladimir-Suzdal and Muscovy, leaving Bulgaria and Great Moravia to Bulgarians and Bohemians.
proposals.historical_basis: Removes overlaps and aligns the civ with Boyar, Druzhina and Detinets, which are Rus' terms.

proposals.title: Corrected Druzhina (cavalry)
proposals.description: Move the trample to Boyars and the Knight line (“Druzhina: heavy cavalry deals trample damage” or +20% HP).
proposals.historical_basis: From the 11th century onwards the druzhina was the prince's mounted retinue (Nestor's Chronicle; warrior graves with horses at Gnezdovo and Chernigov). The 10th-century phase on foot can remain represented by the generic infantry.

proposals.title: Pushechny Dvor (Cannon Yard)
proposals.description: Imperial Age: unlocks Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon, and Bombard Cannons cost -25%.
proposals.historical_basis: Firearms in Moscow (1382), pishchali on the Ugra (1480) and the arsenal founded by Ivan III in 1479, with Aristotele Fioravanti.

proposals.title: Chorni Klobuky (Black Hoods)
proposals.description: Castle Age: Cavalry Archers -25% gold and access to Thumb Ring.
proposals.historical_basis: Turkic nomads (Berendei, Torks, Pechenegs) settled on the Ros river as Kiev's frontier guard in the 12th century (Hypatian Chronicle).

proposals.title: Monastic colonisation
proposals.description: Replaces Monks +20% speed: Monasteries accept wood and food drop-offs (they work as a Mill and Lumber Camp).
proposals.historical_basis: Trinity-St Sergius, Kirillo-Belozersky and Solovetsky as centres of agrarian colonisation of the north-east (Klyuchevsky's thesis).

proposals.title: Novgorod Veche
proposals.description: Allies' Trade Carts and Trade Cogs +10% gold.
proposals.historical_basis: Novgorod as a Hansa trading post (Peterhof) and a merchant republic governed by the veche (1136–1478).

contested: Origin and ethnogenesis of the Slavs (migration from the Prague-Korchak culture vs. Curta's “formation” on the Byzantine frontier).
Origin of the Bulgars (Turkic/Oghur dominant; Iranian hypotheses) and whether the Bulgaria of 681 was a “Slavic state”.
The Normanist question about the Scandinavian role in the formation of Rus'.
Applicability of the concept of “feudalism” to Rus' (Soviet and Western historiographical debate).
Location of Great Moravia (consensus north of the Danube; southern hypotheses of Boba and Bowlus).
Actual levels of literacy in Kievan Rus'.
Pace of the druzhina's transition from infantry to cavalry (10th–11th centuries).

civs.represents: The Goths, an East Germanic people: the 4th-century Tervingi and Greuthungi, the Visigoths (kingdom of Toulouse 418–507 and of Toledo until 711–725) and the Ostrogoths (Italy 493–553/554), with no distinction between them.
civs.period: c. 238–711, peaking between 376 and 552, largely before AoE2's 500–1500 window. The Crimean Goths (Gothia/Principality of Theodoro) survived until 1475.
civs.verdict: This is the least faithful civ in the group: a “barbarian horde” stereotype (cheap infantry, hunters, no walls, specialists in destroying buildings) that the sources contradict on almost every point. The decisive Gothic force was lance-armed cavalry (Ammianus on Adrianople; Procopius on the Ostrogoths). The Goths were notoriously bad at besieging cities (“at peace with walls”, said Fritigern). The Ostrogoths and Visigoths ruled Italy and Hispania as heirs to the Roman administration, restoring walls and cities. Huskarl is an 11th-century Norse word with no connection to the Goths, and the Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon are grossly anachronistic. There are a few isolated hits: the Dromon (Theodoric's thousand dromons) and, loosely, Anarchy, which evokes the Visigothic habit of deposing kings. The history text misdates the sack of Rome (410, not 409), repeats the Gotland myth, says the Goths were the first to sack Rome and omits Arianism and Ulfilas' Bible.
civs.naming_scope_issues: The Goths are a Late Antique people: their kingdoms disappear in 553/554 (Ostrogoths) and 711–725 (Visigoths), before or at the threshold of the 500–1500 window. The civ merges the Visigoths and Ostrogoths, whose trajectories were very different: Visigothic Hispania, Catholic from 589 and a lawmaking kingdom, and Ostrogothic Italy, Romano-Gothic and Arian. An Imperial Age with gunpowder has no Gothic counterpart, except for the Crimean Goths (Theodoro, Mangup, until 1475). “Gothic” architecture (12th–16th centuries) is a pejorative Renaissance label with no connection to the Goths. With the Romans (Return of Rome) in the game, the Goths would fit better in that context (Abritus 251, Adrianople 378, the sack of 410). There is also overlap with the Spanish/Portuguese (Visigothic heritage and Asturian Neo-Gothicism) and the Italians.

elements.explanation: Gothic armies included numerous infantry, but the decisive, elite arm was the cavalry. At Adrianople (378) it was the return of the Greuthungian and Alan cavalry of Alatheus and Saphrax, “like a thunderbolt”, that crushed the Romans (Ammianus 31.12.17). Procopius (Wars V.27.27–29) says that the Ostrogothic horsemen used only lance and sword and that the archers fought on foot, and at Taginae (552) it was a Gothic cavalry charge that broke against Narses' archers. The “cavalry victory” thesis for Adrianople is debated, but the infantry civ label reflects the horde stereotype.
No historical basis; it is pure balance.

elements.element: Hunters carry +15; hunted animals last +20% longer
elements.explanation: This is a “barbarian hunter” trope. The Cherniakhov culture (3rd–4th centuries), associated with the Goths, was sedentary and agricultural, with wheel-thrown pottery and trade with Rome, and the Visigothic and Ostrogothic kingdoms managed Roman agrarian economies.

It rests on the idea of countless masses. Modern estimates for 376 are around 15,000–20,000 warriors across the Tervingi and Greuthungi (Heather), and the figures in the sources are inflated. The Goths were a people in arms, but not “cheap” infantry.

The Goths were notoriously weak at assaulting fortifications. Fritigern declared himself “at peace with walls” when giving up the siege of Adrianople (Ammianus 31.6.4). They failed against Adrianople and Constantinople in 378, and Vitiges failed in the siege of Rome (537–538). Rome fell in 410 after prolonged blockades (the sources speak of treachery, but the mechanism is uncertain) and in 546 through the treachery of Isaurian soldiers. The devastation of the Balkans and Greece (377–382, 395–396) gives some basis for the destruction of rural buildings.
No historical basis; it reinforces the horde stereotype.

Húskarl (Old Norse, “house man”) refers to the household guards of the Scandinavian and Anglo-Danish kings of the 10th–11th centuries, such as those of Cnut and those of Harold II at Hastings. It belongs to another people and comes five hundred years after the Gothic kingdoms. Real Gothic equivalents would be the gardingi (Visigothic royal retainers), the buccellarii (private armed retinues, in the Code of Euric) or the saiones (Ostrogothic royal agents). Moreover, “anti-archer” infantry contradicts Procopius, for whom the Ostrogothic infantry consisted mainly of archers.

elements.element: Anarchy (Huskarls can be trained at Barracks)
elements.explanation: It may evoke Visigothic political instability: Fredegar (IV.82) criticises the Gothic habit of deposing kings, which historians call morbus Gothorum. There is a long series of kings who were killed (Athaulf 415, Thorismund 453, Amalaric 531, Theudis 548, Theudigisel 549, Witteric 610). The mechanical effect is arbitrary.
“Perfusion” is a term with no connection to the Goths; it is pure balance.
No historical basis.

tree_issues.item: No Stone Wall, Gate, Guard Tower, Keep or Fortified Wall
tree_issues.problem: Historical error. Theodoric restored the walls of Rome and of other cities (Cassiodorus, Variae; Anonymus Valesianus). Leovigild founded the walled city of Reccopolis (578), and Toledo, Septimania and the Pyrenees had Visigothic fortifications. The absence of walls is the stereotype of the nomadic barbarian, not the reality of kingdoms that succeeded Rome.
Grossly anachronistic: the Gothic kingdoms had disappeared by 711–725, and gunpowder reached Europe c. 1320. Only the Crimean Goths still existed in the 15th century.

This is a notable hit. Theodoric had a thousand dromons built (Cassiodorus, Variae V.16–17, c. 525–526). Totila had a fleet at Sena Gallica (551), and Isidore praises Sisebut's fleet; Wamba's naval victory appears only in the Chronicle of Alfonso III (late 9th century) and is doubtful.

tree_issues.item: No Siege Ram, Siege Engineers or Arson
tree_issues.problem: Consistent with Gothic weakness in sieges (Fritigern), but contradicts the infantry bonus against buildings.

tree_issues.item: No Plate Mail Armor (or Plate Barding Armor)
tree_issues.problem: It reinforces the idea of expendable infantry. The Gothic elite wore mail and Spangenhelm-type helmets of Roman derivation, and was not an army of poorly armed peasants.

tree_issues.item: Cavalry Archer, Heavy Cavalry Archer and Hussar
tree_issues.problem: The horse archer is defensible for the Greuthungi under Hunnic and Alan influence, but Procopius says the Ostrogothic cavalry did not use the bow. The Hussar (15th century) is anachronistic.

This is ironic: the Goths were Homoian (“Arian”) Christians, the “heretics” par excellence in the eyes of Rome until the Visigothic conversion in 589. The Monastery tree could be a pillar of the civ's identity.

history_text_issues.claim: The Goths were supposedly known to the Romans from the 1st century onwards, on the Danube frontier.
history_text_issues.problem: Tacitus (Germania 43–44, c. 98) and Ptolemy place the Gotones by the Vistula, not the Danube.
history_text_issues.correction: The Goths reached the Danube and the Black Sea in the 3rd century: the sack of Histria (238) and Abritus (251), where the emperor Decius died.

history_text_issues.claim: “The Goths originated on the island of Gotland ... to the best of our knowledge”
history_text_issues.problem: Jordanes (Getica, 551) speaks of “Scandza”, not Gotland. The link to Gotland rests on the similarity of the names and on the late Guta saga (13th century), and Jordanes' narrative itself is largely a literary construction (Christensen 2002; Goffart). Archaeology links the Goths to the Wielbark (Pomerania, 1st–3rd centuries) and Cherniakhov (3rd–4th centuries) cultures.
history_text_issues.correction: The Scandinavian origin is contested, and a Gotland origin in particular has no solid support.

history_text_issues.claim: The Visigoths and Ostrogoths had supposedly already split in the 2nd century (Visigoths in Romania, Ostrogoths on the Black Sea).
history_text_issues.problem: This is anachronistic: the Goths only reached those regions in the 3rd century. The 4th-century sources speak mostly of Tervingi and Greuthungi. The names Vesi/Austrogoti already appear in the late 4th century, but the political groups “Visigoths” and “Ostrogoths” formed after 376 (Alaric's coalition) and in the 5th century (Theodoric's Amals). “Visi” did not originally mean “western”.
history_text_issues.correction: Distinguish the Tervingi/Greuthungi (4th century) from the Visigoths/Ostrogoths (5th–6th centuries) and flag the debate about the continuity between them.

history_text_issues.claim: They defeated “a Roman army from Constantinople”.
history_text_issues.problem: This is a serious omission. At Adrianople (9 August 378) the emperor Valens died and a large part of the eastern field army was destroyed, one of the worst Roman defeats.
history_text_issues.correction: Name Adrianople and Valens, and mention the treaty of 382 (foederati).

history_text_issues.claim: “In 409 they sacked Rome under their king Alaric”
history_text_issues.problem: The date is wrong.
history_text_issues.correction: Rome was blockaded in 408 and 409, and the sack began on 24 August 410.

history_text_issues.claim: Theodoric was supposedly “king of modern Switzerland and the Balkans”.
history_text_issues.problem: The name is misspelt (“Theodric”) and the title is anachronistic: “Switzerland” makes no sense.
history_text_issues.correction: Theodoric was king of the Ostrogoths and, at the same time, a Roman magister militum and patricius in the Balkans (Moesia). He left for Italy at Zeno's request.

history_text_issues.claim: The Goths supposedly entered Italy in 488.
history_text_issues.problem: Theodoric left Moesia in the autumn of 488, but only entered Italy in 489 (battle of the Isonzo, August 489).
history_text_issues.correction: Departure in 488, entry in 489, fall of Ravenna in 493.

history_text_issues.claim: Clovis supposedly drove the Visigoths out of France at the end of the 5th century.
history_text_issues.problem: The battle of Vouillé was in 507 (early 6th century), and the Visigoths kept Septimania (Narbonne) until c. 720, thanks in part to Ostrogothic protection after 507.
history_text_issues.correction: Correct the date and the extent of the loss.

history_text_issues.claim: The Goths are supposedly remembered for having been “the first to sack Rome”.
history_text_issues.problem: This is wrong: Brennus' Gauls sacked Rome c. 390/387 BC.
history_text_issues.correction: The sack of 410 was the first in c. 800 years.

history_text_issues.claim: The Romance languages (including Romanian) supposedly owed their survival to Gothic admiration for Rome; English is supposedly a variation of German.
history_text_issues.problem: This is misleading. The Romance languages survived because of the demography of the Roman population, and Romanian Latinity owes nothing to the Goths, who left Dacia in 376. English is a West Germanic language, not “a variation of German”.
history_text_issues.correction: Rephrase: the Gothic kingdoms preserved Roman institutions (Cassiodorus, Boethius, Visigothic law), but Latinity is not owed to them.

history_text_issues.claim: The text does not mention the religion or the written culture of the Goths.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits Arianism (Homoianism), Ulfilas' Gothic Bible (4th century; Codex Argenteus, 6th century), the Visigothic conversion to Catholicism (Third Council of Toledo, 589), the councils of Toledo, the Liber Iudiciorum (654) and Isidore of Seville.
history_text_issues.correction: Include these elements, which are central to Gothic identity.

history_text_issues.claim: The Muslims supposedly destroyed the last Gothic kingdom in four years.
history_text_issues.problem: The main conquest (711–c. 716) was quick, but Septimania held out until c. 720–725. The text also omits the survival of the Crimean Goths (Theodoro until 1475) and the Neo-Gothic ideology of Asturias (Chronicle of Alfonso III).
history_text_issues.correction: Mention these continuities.

missing_features: Ostrogothic heavy lance cavalry (contus), combined with foot archers.
The wagon circle (carrago) used as a fortress at Adrianople (Ammianus 31.7.7; 31.12.11).
The status of foederati and integration into the Roman army (Gainas, Alaric as magister militum per Illyricum).
Arianism and Ulfilas' Gothic Bible.
The Roman administration preserved by Theodoric (Cassiodorus, Boethius) and the buildings of Ravenna (Mausoleum, Sant'Apollinare Nuovo).
Visigothic law (Code of Euric, Liber Iudiciorum) and the councils of Toledo.
Goldsmithing (cloisonné eagle fibulae, the Guarrazar votive crowns).
The fleets (Theodoric's dromons, Totila at Sena Gallica, Sisebut).
The late medieval continuity of the Crimean Goths (Mangup/Theodoro).

proposals.title: Gothic Lancer (replaces the Huskarl)
proposals.description: Heavy lance cavalry, strong against infantry and cavalry and weak against archers. Change the label to “Cavalry and Infantry civilization”.
proposals.historical_basis: Procopius (Wars V.27.27–29; VIII.32 on Taginae); Ammianus 31.12.17 on Adrianople.

proposals.title: Theodoric's Restoration
proposals.description: Restore Stone Walls, Gates and Towers. Castle Age: walls -33% stone and stone buildings +15% HP. Remove Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon.
proposals.historical_basis: Cassiodorus (Variae) on the restoration of walls, aqueducts and buildings; Anonymus Valesianus on the walls of Rome; the foundation of Reccopolis (578).

proposals.title: Carrago (wagon fort)
proposals.description: Unique building, built by Villagers anywhere from the Feudal Age: a cheap wooden structure that can be garrisoned with infantry and fires arrows.
proposals.historical_basis: Ammianus 31.7.7 (the Goths call their wagon circle carrago) and 31.12.11 (the wagons arranged in a circle before Adrianople).

proposals.title: Ulfilas' Bible / Third Council of Toledo
proposals.description: Two mutually exclusive technologies at the Monastery. “Homoian Church”: free Heresy and Monks +1 range. “Council of Toledo (589)”: unlocks Atonement and Redemption, with Monastery technologies -50%.
proposals.historical_basis: Ulfilas' translation of the Bible (4th century); Reccared's conversion in 589.

proposals.title: Foederati
proposals.description: Allies can train Gothic Lancers at the Castle, like the Condottiero.
proposals.historical_basis: The treaty of 382 and the foedus of 418 in Aquitaine: the Goths as a federate army of Rome.

proposals.title: A Thousand Dromons (replaces Perfusion)
proposals.description: Dromons -33% cost and 50% faster creation.
proposals.historical_basis: Cassiodorus, Variae V.16–17 (c. 525–526): Theodoric orders a thousand dromons to be built.

proposals.title: Split into Visigoths and Ostrogoths, or move to the Return of Rome context
proposals.description: Separate into two civs or reposition the Goths among the Late Antique civs, alongside the Romans, leaving the late medieval window to the Spanish and others.
proposals.historical_basis: Distinct trajectories and a chronology mostly before 500.

contested: Scandinavian origin of the Goths (Jordanes/Scandza; Wielbark culture): Heather accepts a partial migration, Kulikowski and Christensen are sceptical.
Continuity between the Tervingi/Greuthungi and the Visigoths/Ostrogoths, and the meaning of Vesi/Austrogoti.
Ethnogenesis (Vienna School: Wolfram, Pohl) vs. the critiques of Goffart and Kulikowski.
Weight of the cavalry at Adrianople (Oman's classic thesis vs. the revisionists).
Numbers of the Goths in 376 and of the Gothic armies.
Role of the Goths in the “fall” of Rome: catastrophe (Ward-Perkins) or transformation (Brown).
Reality of Gothic continuity in Asturias (Neo-Gothicism as a later ideology).
