groups.cross_civ_notes:
1) Triple Scandinavian coverage. With Danes and Varangians (DLC The Viking Sagas, present in the repository), the Vikings text duplicates the other two: Lindisfarne, the Great Army, the Danelaw and Cnut recur in Vikings and Danes, and Kiev and Constantinople recur in Vikings, Varangians and Slavs. The ideal would be a clear partition: Vikings → Norway and the North Atlantic (“Norse/Norwegians”); Danes → Denmark, including the post-Viking phase (the Valdemars, Kalmar); Varangians → Sweden and the Varangian Rus', plus the Guard; Slavs → Slavic Rus' (Kiev, Novgorod, Muscovy).

2) Regional units. The Longship is shared by Vikings, Danes, Varangians and Saxons. For the Saxons it is acceptable on account of the common clinker-built tradition (Sutton Hoo, Graveney), but not on account of Alfred's ships: the ASC (896) says expressly that they followed neither the Frisian nor the Danish model. The Varangian Guard is shared by Byzantines, Danes, Saxons, Varangians and Vikings: it is fine for the Byzantines (it was a Byzantine unit) and for the Saxons (Englishmen after 1066). In the Norse civs it only makes sense as returning veterans (Harald Hardrada, Bolli Bollason). The three Norse civs also receive the “Western” block of Mounted Crossbowman (and, for Danes and Varangians, Heavy Mounted Crossbowman and Cranequins), which is anachronistic for the Viking Age and wholly alien to the Rus', whose tradition came to be the steppe-type composite bow.

3) Badly distributed themes and names. The Goths' Huskarl is a Norse term of the 10th–11th centuries (Cnut's húskarlar) and should belong to Danes or Saxons; the Saxons now have the Hearth Troop, the Anglo-Saxon equivalent, which makes the Gothic Huskarl even more incongruous. The berserk frenzy appears twice: Berserk in the Vikings and Hamask in the Danes (which has some basis in Saxo, but duplicates the theme). The Varangians' Gothikon refers to a Byzantine court ritual of “Goths” staged by the circus factions, confusingly crossing Goths, Varangians and Byzantines. The Slavs' Druzhina was, in the 10th century, a partly Varangian retinue that fought on foot, which makes Slavs and Varangians overlap and explains, without justifying, its association with infantry.

4) Slavs as a residual umbrella. Since the Bulgarians, Poles and Bohemians were added, the Slavs text claims Bulgaria and Great Moravia, which already have their own civs, and leaves Serbs, Croats and Polabian Slavs unrepresented. In practice, Slavs = Rus', which calls for a new name.

5) Identity inversions. The Varangians are “Cavalry”, whereas Leo the Deacon shows the 10th-century Rus' as infantry inept on horseback. The Goths are “Infantry”, whereas their elite was lance-armed cavalry. The Slavs are “Infantry and Siege”, whereas the Rus' from the 11th century onwards and Muscovy relied on cavalry. The labels seem to have been chosen for roster balance, not for history.

6) Paganism and chronology. Vikings (and, in part, Varangians) keep “pagan” Monastery trees until 1500, even though Denmark (c. 965), the Rus' (988) and Norway (995–1030) were Christianised early and Sweden completed the process in the 12th century (archdiocese of Uppsala, 1164). The Goths, Arian Christians since the 4th century, do not have Heresy. The Goths exist as kingdoms only until 711–725 but have gunpowder, while the Slavs, whose Muscovy had artillery in the 15th century, only have the Cannon Galleon.

7) Links to other civs. Goths overlap with Romans (Return of Rome: Adrianople, 410), Byzantines (Belisarius and Narses), Italians (Ostrogothic Italy) and Spanish/Portuguese (Visigothic heritage and Asturian neo-Gothicism). Danes and Vikings overlap with Saxons (Danelaw, 1066) and with Sicilians (the Normans of Italy, cited in the Vikings text). Varangians overlap with Byzantines. Slavs overlap with Cumans and Tatars (steppe) and with Lithuanians (western Rus' under Lithuania). The group's pattern is one of civs designed around popular clichés (fierce Vikings, Gothic barbarians, peasant Slavs), with notable isolated successes (Detinets, Gothic Dromon, the Vikings' naval bonus, the Varangian Guard's gold, Vendel Legacy) that show that a more faithful design was perfectly possible.

verification_log.change: The session's WebSearch budget was exhausted, so no new searches could be made. The quotations from Ammianus were checked by direct WebFetch of the Latin text (The Latin Library). The rest is based on established knowledge, and claims I could not confirm (for example, Leo the Deacon's exact wording about the reins) were softened. The trees of the five civs were confirmed in the repository's data/data.json.

Chieftains went from “unfounded” to “stretched”. The claim that the Norse “rarely faced heavy cavalry” was corrected: on the Continent they frequently fought Carolingian and Breton forces with a strong mounted component, which gives an indirect basis to the anti-cavalry role, though not to the name.

In the naval bonus I added that the dating of the formal leiðangr is contested (Snorri attributes it to Haakon the Good; the laws date from the 12th–13th centuries). The point was also added to the contested list and to the Leiðangr proposal.
Berserk: the date of the Grágás was made more precise (ecclesiastical law section, c. 1122–1133) and the penalty was specified (lesser outlawry).

Tree: I added that the civ has Knight and Cavalier (the draft only praised the absence of cavalry) and that it lacks Halberdier, which is inconsistent with Chieftains. I qualified the Mounted Crossbowman point with the Konungs skuggsjá.
The “last barbarian tribe” issue was lowered from moderate to minor. The counter-example of the Magyars and Mongols was removed, because the game's claim is restricted to Germanic peoples.
Lindisfarne: I added that “Dene” was a generic usage in Old English and that the ASC itself calls the raiders at Portland, who came from Hǫrðaland, “Danes”.

The identification of Eric of York with Eric Bloodaxe was flagged as not universally accepted. Hafrsfjord now carries its disputed dating (c. 872 vs. the 880s). I specified that “kristnitaka” refers to the Icelandic conversion of 999/1000.
Hamask: I corrected the claim that the sources on berserkir were mainly Norwegian and Icelandic. Saxo Grammaticus and the Hrólfs saga kraka (court of Lejre) provide Danish material.

Northmen's Fury: I replaced “tradition of torsion artillery” with a defensible wording (there is no record of Norse missile-throwing artillery) and specified the siege means used at Paris according to Abbo.
Ragnar: the link between the leaders of the Great Army and Lodbrok is already in Adam of Bremen (c. 1075), not only in the 13th-century sagas. I also specified the sources for Ubba (Abbo of Fleury).

The Danelaw issue was lowered from moderate to minor, because the text speaks of “several rulers”, which is defensible. The Jomsvikings issue was also lowered to minor, because the text already admits their legendary character; I added Saxo's version.

I added a new issue in the text (the first raids on Ireland were mainly Norwegian; the Finngaill/Dubgaill debate), a new issue in the tree (absence of gunpowder compared with Denmark in the Kalmar period) and Borgring to the list of ring fortresses. On the “Siege” label, I noted that York was taken by surprise in 866.

The fidelity_score dropped from 5 to 4, because of the inversion of the military identity (cavalry), the wrong Gothikon and the cavalry-and-gunpowder tree, to keep the scale consistent with Danes and Slavs.
The Varangian Guard bonus went from “faithful” to “plausible”: the gold has a solid basis, but the +25% faster attack has no source.

The Leo the Deacon citation was softened to “books VIII–IX” and to Rus' ineptitude on horseback, without the unverified wording about the reins. I corrected the destination of Harald's fortune, which according to the saga was sent to Yaroslav in Hólmgarðr/Novgorod, and not to Kiev.
Jarl: I added Rögnvaldr Úlfsson, jarl of Aldeigjuborg/Ladoga according to the sagas, as a partial link to the East, keeping “stretched”.
Gost' proposal: I corrected the historical basis. The treaties do not regulate “armed merchants”; they required them to enter Constantinople unarmed, which proves that they arrived armed.

Swedes proposal: I replaced the Battle of the Neva (Birger's participation is contested) with the Alsnö stadga (c. 1280) and the Erikskrönikan as the basis for Swedish cavalry. The Neva moved to the contested list. I added the peaceful embassy of 839 to the issue of “immediate” recognition.

Druzhina went from “wrong” to “stretched”. The 10th-century druzhina (Sviatoslav at Dorostolon) fought on foot, and the draft contradicted its own analysis of the Varangians. The “Corrected Druzhina” proposal and cross-civ note 3 were adjusted.

The “Persians” issue was reframed as defensible: Samanid dirhams, from a Persian dynasty, dominate Rus' hoards. The Bulgaria issue was lowered to minor, because the text itself acknowledges the Turkic origin and the later Slavicisation.

New issues in the text: “the largest state of its time” (defensible only on a European scale) and the absence of the death penalty (Yaroslav's Pravda still allowed blood vengeance). The omissions issue was corrected, because the text mentions the fall of 1240.

The fidelity_score rose from 2 to 3: there are real successes (Dromon, Anarchy as an echo of the morbus Gothorum, Cavalry Archer defensible for the Greuthungi) that do not justify an almost-nil value on a scale where the average is 5.

I corrected the Ammianus citations, checked against the Latin text: carrago at 31.7.7 (not 31.7.5), wagons in a circle at 31.12.11, the return of the cavalry of Alatheus and Saphrax at 31.12.17, and Fritigern at 31.6.4.

The Gotland issue was lowered from major to moderate (the text has a caveat and there is the late Guta saga). In the Visigoths/Ostrogoths issue I added that the names Vesi/Austrogoti already appear in the late 4th century.

New issue in the text: Theodoric set out in 488 but entered Italy in 489. New item in the tree: absence of Plate Mail and Plate Barding Armor. Wamba's naval victory was marked as a late and doubtful tradition, and I added Sisebut (Isidore).

Anarchy: “morbus Gothorum” is now presented as a historiographical label inspired by Fredegar IV.82. The sack of 410 is no longer presented as certainly the work of treachery, because the mechanism is uncertain.

I corrected a factual error in the draft: the ASC (896) says that Alfred's ships followed neither the Frisian nor the Danish model, so it cannot serve as proof that they were “of the same type” as the Longships. The justification now rests on the common clinker-built tradition (Sutton Hoo, Graveney).

I corrected the chronology of Christianisation: Denmark c. 965, the Rus' 988 and Norway 995–1030, but Sweden only in the 12th century (Uppsala, 1164), and not “c. 960–1030” for all of them. I also specified that the Slavs have the Cannon Galleon and lack only land-based gunpowder.

civs.represents: The Eastern Roman Empire (the “Byzantines” of modern historiography), with its capital at Constantinople. The design mainly blends features of the middle Byzantine army of the 7th–11th centuries: the kataphraktoi of Nikephoros II Phokas, the Varangian Guard of Basil II, the dromons with Greek fire and the Theodosian Walls. To these it adds a few late Roman elements (camels) and Palaiologan ones (gunpowder).
civs.period: c. 527 (Justinian I) – 1453 (fall of Constantinople); the successor states lasted until 1460 (Morea) and 1461 (Trebizond). The core inspiration of the design lies in c. 670–1100.
civs.verdict: It is one of the most recognisable civilizations and, in essence, one of the best-founded in the game: sturdy walls, the Cataphract, Greek fire and the Varangian Guard (now in the Byzantine Barracks) correspond to real, well-documented traits. The problems lie in the details: the Imperial Age bonus is a pun, the name Logistica bears no relation to the effect, and the Dromon appears as an Imperial Age bombardment ship, when it was the siphon galley of the 6th–12th centuries. The tech tree denies precisely what the Eastern Romans excelled at (horse breeding, siege engineering, architecture, hospitals), and the horse-archer identity of the 6th-century army is missing. A thousand-year state is flattened into a single package, from late Roman camels to the bombards of 1453. The history text is reasonable, but it has errors and dated framings: the exonym, the “defence of Europe”, the “masses of untrained warriors”, heavy infantry described as swordsmen, and Manzikert as an immediate catastrophe.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Byzantines” is an exonym established by Western humanists (Hieronymus Wolf, Corpus Historiae Byzantinae, 1557) and popularised between the 17th and 19th centuries. They called themselves Rhomaioi (Romans) and their state Basileia tōn Rhomaiōn; their Muslim neighbours called them Rūm. The game deepens the artificial break by also having a “Romans” civ (late Empire, 4th–5th centuries), when the institutional continuity (law, coinage, army, imperial title) is complete. The 527–1453 period fits well within the game's 500–1500 frame. However, a single package covers radically different armies, in five phases: the Justinianic army of horse archers and federates (6th century); the defensive thematic army (7th–9th centuries); the offensive Macedonian army of kataphraktoi and tagmata (10th–11th centuries); the Komnenian army of mercenaries, Latin knights and pronoia (12th century); and the Palaiologan rump state (1261–1453). The name also covers Greek, Armenian, Slavic and other populations; several emperors and generals were of Armenian origin, certain or disputed, which overlaps with the Armenians civ.

elements.explanation: Defensible. The survival of Constantinople rested on the Theodosian Walls (408–413, rebuilt after the earthquake of 447) and on a doctrine that avoided risky pitched battles: Maurice's Strategikon (c. 600) and De velitatione (10th century) recommend wearing the enemy down, ambushing and negotiating. There were, however, strongly offensive phases: Justinian's reconquests and the expansion under Nikephoros II, John I Tzimiskes and Basil II (c. 960–1025). The thesis of an essentially defensive “grand strategy” (Luttwak, 2009) is debated.

The Theodosian Walls withstood the Avars and Persians (626), the Arabs (the first attack, traditionally dated to 674–678, is now debated; and the great siege of 717–718), the Bulgars (813; Symeon before the walls in 913 and 924) and the naval raids of the Rus' (860, 941). They were never breached by a land assault before 1453: in 1081 Alexios Komnenos got in through the treachery of mercenaries at the Gate of Charisius, in 1204 the crusaders attacked via the sea walls on the Golden Horn, and in 1261 Alexios Strategopoulos got in by surprise. The network of fortified kastra created in Anatolia from the 7th century onwards reinforces the idea. It is a well-chosen abstraction with a solid basis.

elements.element: Camel Riders, Skirmishers and Spearman-line cost -25%
elements.explanation: The spearmen and skirmishers have a real basis: the skutatoi were heavy infantry with the kontarion, the 10th-century menavlatoi were heavy anti-cavalry spearmen described in the Praecepta Militaria, and the psiloi and akontistai were archers and javelin-throwers. The camels are only justified in the late Roman period, with the alae dromedariorum of Egypt and the East listed in the Notitia Dignitatum (early 5th century). After the loss of those provinces (636–642) there is no record of regular Byzantine camel units; the camel appears mainly as a pack animal. At bottom, it is a balance bonus that makes the counter units (trash units) cheap.

It works well as an abstraction of the Byzantine intelligence network: spies and scouts (kataskopoi, trapezitai), the beacon chain attributed to Leo the Mathematician (reign of Theophilos, 829–842), which linked the fortress of Loulon, near the Cilician Gates, to the Great Palace, and the frontier-surveillance doctrine of De velitatione.

It is essentially a pun on “Imperial”: the Empire par excellence, the direct heir of Rome. Roman imperial legitimacy was real and central to Byzantine ideology, but it has no connection with a cheaper technological advance. In practice, it is a balance bonus for a civ built for the long game.

elements.element: Fire Ships and Dromons attack +25% faster
elements.explanation: The Fire Ships half captures the most famous Byzantine naval trait well: dromons fitted with Greek-fire siphons, decisive in 717–718 and against the fleet of Igor of Kiev in 941 (Pryor & Jeffreys, The Age of the Dromon, 2006). The Dromon half applies to a long-range bombardment ship, a role the historical dromon did not have. It is also wise not to exaggerate “naval supremacy”: the Byzantines were defeated at the Battle of the Masts (655), lost Crete to a corsair emirate (c. 824/827–961) and did not prevent the sack of Thessalonica by Leo of Tripoli (904). The superiority was real but intermittent, above all in the 8th and 10th centuries.

The Praecepta Militaria of Nikephoros II Phokas (c. 965) and the Taktika of Nikephoros Ouranos (c. 1000) describe the kataphraktoi: rider and horse were armoured in felt and iron, armed with iron maces (siderorabdia), sabres and lances, and they formed up in a blunt wedge to break the enemy centre. This matches the role in the game (“very strong against infantry”) well. Caveats: it was a small, short-lived elite corps (c. 950–1050), with horse archers within the formation itself; the name also evokes the late Roman and Sasanian cataphractarii and clibanarii.

According to Theophanes, Greek fire was brought c. 672 by Kallinikos, a refugee architect from Heliopolis in Syria (Baalbek). It is the most famous Byzantine technological trait and was decisive in 717–718 and in 941; its use in the first Arab attack (dated by Theophanes to 674–678) depends on a chronology that is now debated. Giving Fire Ships more range is reasonable, and more area of effect for Dromons is acceptable. Increasing the blast radius of Bombard Towers is anachronistic: it confuses a petroleum-based incendiary liquid, projected by siphon or in ceramic grenades, with gunpowder artillery. The last secure description of naval use is Anna Komnene's, against the Pisans (1099); the loss of the secret after the 12th century is plausible, but not proven.

The name evokes Byzantine organisational sophistication: military manuals, the baggage train (touldon), the mustering camps (aplekta) on the eastern route and the imperial stud farms. The effect, however, is trample damage, which has nothing to do with logistics; it would rather represent the shock of the kataphraktoi wedge or the axes of the Varangian Guard. Many modern handbooks state that Leo VI defined “logistics” as a branch of warfare, but that quotation has an uncertain textual basis.

Byzantium developed hospitals with salaried physicians: the Basileias of Basil of Caesarea (c. 370) and the xenon of the Pantokrator (typikon of 1136); see T. Miller, The Birth of the Hospital in the Byzantine Empire. The Strategikon (II.9) provided for medics (deputatoi) paid for each wounded man they rescued. Monasteries had charitable functions, although the healer was as much the lay physician as the monk. The link is reasonable.

elements.element: Varangian Guard (shared unit, trained at the Barracks from the Castle Age)
elements.explanation: The Varangian Guard originated in the contingent of c. 6,000 Rus' sent by Vladimir of Kiev to Basil II c. 988; its formalisation as the emperor's personal guard is sometimes dated later. After 1066, and especially in the 1070s–1080s, it recruited many Anglo-Saxons. Anna Komnene calls them the “axe-bearing barbarians” (Blöndal, The Varangians of Byzantium). Generating gold in combat is a nice abstraction of the high pay and of the right to plunder the treasury on the emperor's death (pólútasvarf, according to the saga of Haraldr Harðráði in Heimskringla). It is one of the most faithful elements of the civ, and historically it belongs more to Byzantium than to the Vikings, Danes or Saxons, who also receive it.

The name is faithful, but the role is not. In the game it is a long-range siege ship with an explosive projectile, available only in the Imperial Age and in place of the Cannon Galleon. The historical dromon was an oared galley (first with a single bank of oars, later a bireme), attested from the early 6th century: Cassiodorus records Theodoric's order to build a thousand dromones (Variae V.16–17, c. 526), and Procopius describes Belisarius' 92 dromones (533). It fought with Greek-fire siphons, archers, possibly small throwing engines, and boarding, not with long-range bombardment. In the 12th century it was replaced by Italian-type galleys. The absence of the Cannon Galleon is, on the other hand, historically correct.

tree_issues.problem: The state maintained large imperial stud farms (mitata), such as the one at Malagina, in Bithynia, and others in Phrygia and Cappadocia, which supplied the cavalry. The history text itself notes that Anatolia was the empire's source of horses. Denying Bloodlines to a civ whose UU is heavy cavalry is ahistorical.

They are mechanically compensated for by the HP bonus, but symbolically ironic for the builders of Hagia Sophia (537, Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus), of the Theodosian Walls and of hundreds of kastra and domed churches.

tree_issues.item: Siege Engineers, Heavy Scorpion, Siege Onager (missing)
tree_issues.problem: Byzantium inherited and continued Roman poliorcetics: the siege treatise of the so-called Heron of Byzantium (10th century) and the siege chapters of Leo VI's Taktika. It took fortified cities by formal siege, such as Chandax (960–961), Mopsuestia and Tarsus (965); Antioch (969), by contrast, fell to a surprise night assault with ladders. The Komnenoi used large throwing engines (for example at Zeugminon, 1165, according to Niketas Choniates). Chevedden argues for a Byzantine origin of the counterweight trebuchet, a contested thesis. Denying Siege Engineers runs counter to history.
It is the most glaring omission, given Byzantine pioneering in hospitals and the corps of military medics in the Strategikon. It becomes even more incoherent alongside the healing team bonus.

tree_issues.item: Parthian Tactics (missing) and lack of a horse-archer identity
tree_issues.problem: The civ has the Cavalry Archer, Heavy Cavalry Archer and Thumb Ring, but neither Parthian Tactics nor any bonus. In the 6th century, the armoured horse archer (hippotoxotēs) was the core of Belisarius' army; Procopius explicitly defends him in the prologue to the Wars (I.1). The Strategikon (I.2) expects Roman cavalrymen to be archers, reserving lance and shield for young foreigners who have not mastered the bow.
Anachronistic after c. 640. Only the late Roman dromedarii of Egypt and the East justify it, and those provinces were lost to the Arabs.

tree_issues.item: Bombard Cannon, Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Tower
tree_issues.problem: They are marginal. In 1453 the defenders had a few small pieces and hand guns, partly with Giustiniani's Genoese. According to Doukas, the gun-founder Orban first offered his services to Constantine XI, who could not pay him, and then went on to build Mehmed II's great cannons. Gunpowder was the weapon that destroyed Byzantium, not the one that defined it.

tree_issues.item: Dromon only in the Imperial Age
tree_issues.problem: The chronology is reversed: the dromon belongs to the 6th–12th centuries, the equivalent of the game's Feudal and Castle Ages, and no longer existed in the final phase of the empire.

tree_issues.item: Paladin, Plate Barding Armor, Hussar and Fast Fire Ship (present)
tree_issues.problem: Consistent: armoured heavy cavalry and incendiary naval warfare are genuine traits. It is one more sign that the absence of Bloodlines is a balance choice, not a historical one.

history_text_issues.claim: The Byzantines supposedly took their name from the city of Byzantium.
history_text_issues.problem: It presents the modern exonym as if it were a self-designation.
history_text_issues.correction: “Byzantine” is a convention of Western scholars, established by Hieronymus Wolf (1557). The inhabitants called themselves Rhomaioi and the state was the Roman Empire. Kaldellis (Romanland, 2019) argues for abandoning the term, and many historians today prefer “Eastern Roman Empire”.

history_text_issues.claim: At its 6th-century peak, only the Iberian Peninsula, Gaul and Britain were supposedly missing.
history_text_issues.problem: Incorrect as regards Hispania, and incomplete.
history_text_issues.correction: Justinian conquered a strip of south-eastern Iberia, the province of Spania (c. 552–624), with Cartagena and Málaga. Also missing were, for example, Raetia, much of Noricum and the lands north of the Danube.

history_text_issues.claim: The empire supposedly defended Europe against invasions from the east.
history_text_issues.problem: A Eurocentric “bulwark of Christendom” framing.
history_text_issues.correction: Byzantium defended its own interests and allied itself, when it suited it, with Persians, Arabs, Turks, Mongols and Cumans. The idea of a “shield of Western Europe” is a retrospective reading.

history_text_issues.claim: Belisarius supposedly defeated the Persians, Vandals, Ostrogoths and “Bulgars and Slavs” in the Balkans.
history_text_issues.problem: It concentrates everything on Belisarius and credits him with campaigns he did not fight.
history_text_issues.correction: Belisarius won at Dara (530) but was defeated at Callinicum (531). The Gothic War was concluded by Narses, at Taginae/Busta Gallorum (552) and Mons Lactarius (552 or 553). In the Balkans, Belisarius fought only the Kutrigurs, at Melantias (559); there is no campaign of his against the Slavs. The text also omits the Plague of Justinian (from 541 onwards), which exhausted the empire.

history_text_issues.claim: The core of the army was supposedly heavy cavalry supported by archers and by heavy infantry of “armored swordsmen”; officers supposedly received an education in history and military theory.
history_text_issues.problem: An imprecise characterisation of the infantry and an exaggeration about officer training.
history_text_issues.correction: Byzantine heavy infantry consisted mainly of spearmen with shields (skutatoi with the kontarion; menavlatoi in the 10th century), and the sword was a secondary weapon. The military manuals (Strategikon, Leo VI's Taktika, Praecepta) show a written culture of command, but there is no sign of systematic officer training.

history_text_issues.claim: The army supposedly won despite being outnumbered by “masses of untrained warriors”.
history_text_issues.problem: An Orientalist stereotype, false for the main enemies.
history_text_issues.correction: The Sasanian, Umayyad, Abbasid, Fatimid and Seljuk armies were organised, professional and often technically sophisticated. The Byzantine manuals themselves, such as the Strategikon (book XI), study the tactics of the Persians, Avars and other peoples with respect.

history_text_issues.claim: In the 8th century, the Arab attack was supposedly defeated mainly by Greek fire.
history_text_issues.problem: A simplification with significant omissions.
history_text_issues.correction: In the siege of 717–718, the harsh winter, the famine in the Arab camp, the leadership of Leo III and the intervention of the Bulgar khan Tervel, who according to Theophanes killed some 22,000 Arabs, also played a part.Greek fire had already been used in the earlier Arab attack, which Theophanes dates to 674–678 (a chronology now debated).

history_text_issues.claim: Egypt, the Middle East, North Africa and Spain supposedly remained “permanently” outside Byzantine control.
history_text_issues.problem: Incorrect on two points.
history_text_issues.correction: Byzantine Hispania had already been lost to the Visigoths (c. 624), before the Arabs. In the 10th century, Byzantium recovered Crete (961), Cyprus (965), Cilicia and Antioch (969), which it held until 1084, and parts of northern Syria.

history_text_issues.claim: The Turkish victory at Manzikert (1071) supposedly led to the devastation of Asia Minor.
history_text_issues.problem: Dated historiography that treats Manzikert as an immediate military catastrophe.
history_text_issues.correction: Losses at Manzikert were limited, and Alp Arslan released Romanos IV with a moderate treaty. The Anatolian collapse was due mainly to the civil wars that followed: the Doukas family against Romanos IV and the revolts of mercenaries such as Roussel de Bailleul, which opened the region to the Turkmens (Cheynet; Beihammer, 2017). The relative weight of Manzikert is still debated.

history_text_issues.claim: In 1204, Crusaders led by the Doge of Venice supposedly used treachery to sack Constantinople.
history_text_issues.problem: It simplifies the leadership and the causation and omits the restoration.
history_text_issues.correction: The nominal leader was Boniface of Montferrat, although Enrico Dandolo played a central role. The diversion resulted from the debts owed to Venice and the promises of Alexios IV Angelos; Queller & Madden reject the theory of a premeditated conspiracy. The text jumps from 1204 to the 14th century without mentioning the restoration of the empire in 1261 by Michael VIII Palaiologos, from Nicaea.

history_text_issues.claim: In the 14th century the Turks supposedly invaded Europe and captured Adrianople.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits that the Ottomans came in as Byzantine allies.
history_text_issues.correction: The Ottomans crossed into Europe as allies and mercenaries of John VI Kantakouzenos in the civil wars of the 1340s–1350s. They settled at Gallipoli (1354), and Adrianople fell c. 1369 (a disputed date, between 1361 and 1371).

history_text_issues.claim: The nomisma was supposedly the monetary standard of the Mediterranean for 800 years.
history_text_issues.problem: A generous rounding and an exaggerated claim of hegemony.
history_text_issues.correction: The solidus/nomisma kept its fineness from Constantine (c. 309) until the debasements of the mid-11th century, and Alexios I replaced it with the hyperpyron in 1092: some 730 years of stability and almost 800 of existence. It was the great prestige coin, but from 696/697 it competed with the Islamic dinar, and the West mainly used silver.

history_text_issues.claim: The fall of the city in 1453 supposedly put an end to the Byzantine Empire.
history_text_issues.problem: A minor omission.
history_text_issues.correction: The Greek successor states survived only a few years: the Despotate of the Morea fell in 1460 and the Empire of Trebizond in 1461.

missing_features: Armoured horse archers of the 6th century (Belisarius' hippotoxotai, according to Procopius) and the bow-and-lance cavalry of Maurice's Strategikon (c. 600).
The theme system (themata) and soldiers holding military lands (stratiotika ktemata), the basis of defence between the 7th and 10th centuries; many of these stratiotai served on horseback.

Diplomacy, subsidies, tribute and bribery as strategic weapons: Constantine VII's De Administrando Imperio, payments to Avars, Pechenegs and Cumans, dynastic marriages and the game of playing neighbours off against one another.
State silk monopoly and a regulated guild economy (Book of the Eparch, c. 900); silk also served as a diplomatic gift.
Tagmata, the professional regiments of the capital (Scholai, Exkoubitores, Vigla, Hikanatoi), and massive use of mercenaries (Franks/Latins, Pechenegs, Cumans, the Catalan Company).
Frontier warfare of ambush and shadowing (akritai, De velitatione), with populations evacuated to fortresses.
Orthodox missions and the conversion of the Slavs and the Rus' (Cyril and Methodius, 863; baptism of Vladimir, 988/989) as an instrument of power.
Imperial stud farms and real logistics (aplekta, touldon), which would give the name Logistica real meaning.
A military medical corps and hospitals (xenones).

proposals.title: Hippotoxotai (Strategikon)
proposals.description: New Castle Age UT: Cavalry Archer-line +20 HP and +1/+1 armour. Parthian Tactics is added to the tech tree. Alternatively, Cataphracts gain a short-range secondary ranged attack.
proposals.historical_basis: Procopius (Wars I.1) presents the armoured horse archer as the decisive arm of Justinian's army. Maurice's Strategikon (I.2) expects Roman cavalrymen to master the bow as well as the lance.

proposals.title: Themata (soldiers holding military lands)
proposals.description: Replaces the Imperial Age discount. Town Centers can train the Spearman-line, Skirmisher-line and Scout Cavalry-line, and Villagers gain +1/+1 armour from the Feudal Age.
proposals.historical_basis: Between the 7th and 10th centuries defence rested on provincial armies of soldiers holding military lands (stratiotika ktemata), many of them cavalrymen, mobilised locally (Haldon, Warfare, State and Society in the Byzantine World, 1999). The dating and the manner of the themes' creation, under Heraclius or Constans II, are debated.

proposals.title: De Administrando Imperio (subsidy diplomacy)
proposals.description: Imperial Age UT: tribute without a fee, Spies/Treason -75%, and enemy units attacked by allies are revealed for 10 s.
proposals.historical_basis: Constantine VII's De Administrando Imperio (c. 948–952) teaches how to buy and manipulate the Pechenegs, Rus', Magyars and Bulgars, and subsidies and bribery were constant strategic instruments. There is also administrative continuity: the scrinium barbarorum of the Notitia Dignitatum (early 5th century) and, on 9th–10th-century seals, officials “epi tōn barbarōn”. The espionage role of these offices is not proven.

proposals.title: Rename Logistica to “Praecepta Militaria”
proposals.description: Keeps trample on Cataphracts and the Varangian Guard, but with a name that describes the effect: the shock of the kataphraktoi wedge. A possible “Logistica” technology would then have a logistics effect: units slowly heal near Castles and Siege Workshops, and the food cost of military units drops by 10%.
proposals.historical_basis: In the Praecepta Militaria of Nikephoros II Phokas (c. 965) the blunt wedge formation of the kataphraktoi broke enemy lines (McGeer, Sowing the Dragon's Teeth, 1995). The aplekta and the touldon were the real logistics.

proposals.title: Tech tree fixes: stud farms, hospitals and poliorcetics
proposals.description: Add Bloodlines, Herbal Medicine, Siege Engineers and Masonry/Architecture, reducing the HP bonus if necessary. Remove the Camel Rider or limit it to the Feudal/Castle Age. Move the Dromon to the Castle Age as a short-range siphon galley, with area damage against ships. Greek Fire no longer affects Bombard Towers and instead gives incendiary damage to garrisoned Towers.
proposals.historical_basis: The Malagina stud farm; the xenon of the Pantokrator (1136) and the deputatoi of the Strategikon; the siege treatise of Heron of Byzantium and Leo VI's Taktika. Pryor & Jeffreys (The Age of the Dromon) on the chronology and function of the dromon. Greek fire launched from the walls and in ceramic grenades.

proposals.title: Imperial Sericulture
proposals.description: Market technology (Castle Age): Trade Carts and Trade Cogs generate +15% gold, and Market exchange rates become more favourable.
proposals.historical_basis: Monks smuggled silkworm eggs into Byzantium c. 552 (Procopius, Wars VIII.17). Silk production and sale were regulated by the state (Book of the Eparch), and silk was used as a diplomatic gift.

contested: Origin and dating of the theme system: under Heraclius or Constans II, and whether it resulted from a planned reform or from gradual evolution (Haldon, Treadgold, Kaegi).
Chronology of the first Arab attack on Constantinople: Theophanes' “seven-year siege” of 674–678 vs. a concentrated campaign in c. 667–669 (Jankowiak, 2013).
Whether Byzantium had an essentially defensive “grand strategy” (Luttwak, 2009) or a reactive and opportunistic policy (critiques by Haldon and Kaldellis).
Exact composition of Greek fire (crude petroleum with resins; the role of saltpetre is now little accepted) and when the secret was lost.
Date on which the Rus' contingent of 988 formally became the emperor's personal guard.
Real impact of Manzikert compared with the civil wars of 1071–1081.
Venetian premeditation of the diversion of the Fourth Crusade (conspiracy thesis vs. Queller & Madden).
Origin of the counterweight trebuchet: Byzantine (Chevedden) or Islamic/Chinese by diffusion.
Use of the term “Byzantine” and the nature of Byzantine Roman identity (Kaldellis vs. “Greek” or multi-ethnic readings).
Armenian origin of several imperial dynasties, such as those of Basil I and Heraclius.

civs.represents: Medieval Bulgaria in two phases. First, the First Bulgarian Empire (681–1018): a khanate and, from Simeon onwards, a tsardom, formed by the fusion of a Proto-Bulgarian elite of steppe origin (Bulgars speaking an Oghuric Turkic language, according to the majority view) with a Slavic majority. Then the Second Bulgarian Empire (1185–1396), of the Asen dynasty, with a significant Vlach and Cuman component.
civs.period: 681 (treaty with Constantine IV) – 1396 (fall of Vidin); Tarnovo fell in 1393.
civs.verdict: The design gets some things right: the Krepost as a mountain fortress, the aristocratic heavy cavalry and the Siege Workshop discount, which recalls Krum's siege train; the absence of gunpowder is also consistent with a state that fell in 1396. But the “swordsman infantry” identity is mainly a matter of balance, Stirrups rests on a contested national claim, and Bagains applies a Proto-Bulgarian military rank to swordsmen. The tech tree contradicts the civ's own history text by removing four core monastery technologies (Faith, Atonement, Block Printing, Sanctity) from a people whose greatest legacy was Christianisation and Slavic writing. Missing are the horse archery of the steppe, the Cuman allies of the Second Empire and the ambushes in the Balkan passes, which decided the great Bulgarian victories (811, 1190, 1205). The history text is ambitious and generally correct, but it has exaggerations with a national tone.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Bulgarians” is a legitimate ethnonym, but the civ merges three components: the Proto-Bulgarian elite, which was Turkic-speaking, bore titles such as kana, boila, bagain and tarkhan, and wrote its inscriptions in Greek; the Slavic majority; and, in the Second Empire, Vlachs and Cumans (Niketas Choniates calls the Asen brothers “Vlachs”). The text acknowledges the Slav–Bulgar fusion but ignores the Vlachs and Cumans. It does not distinguish Volga Bulgaria (a Muslim Bulgar state from 922, destroyed by the Mongols in 1236), another heir of Kubrat's Old Great Bulgaria. The Slavic names (Konnik, “horseman”; Krepost, “fortress”) are anachronistic for the Proto-Bulgarian phase; moreover, in Old Slavonic krěpostĭ seems to have meant mainly “strength, firmness”, the sense of “fortress” being essentially modern, while medieval texts prefer grad. “Empire” is accurate only from Simeon onwards (title of tsar c. 913/925, recognised by Byzantium in 927). The period 681–1396 fits the game's framework well. In the absence of Serbs and Vlachs, the civ often serves as a generic stand-in for the Slavic Balkans.

elements.explanation: Defensible as a synthesis of Slavic infantry and Proto-Bulgarian cavalry. However, historical Slavic infantry consisted mainly of spearmen, javelin-throwers and light archers, not heavy swordsmen, and the label erases the horse-archer component.

It is meant to represent numerous infantry, but the Slavic infantry of the Balkans fought with spears, javelins and bows, and the sword was mainly a weapon of the mounted aristocracy. No source associates the Bulgarians with heavy infantry swordsmen. It is mainly a balance choice; ironically, the civ does not even have the Champion.

elements.element: Blacksmith and Siege Workshop technologies cost -50% food
elements.explanation: The siege part is well founded. According to Theophanes, a baptised Arab, an expert in siege engines, whom Nikephoros I had settled in Adrianople, deserted to Krum for lack of pay and taught the Bulgarians to build machines; with them Krum took Mesembria (812), where he captured siphons and a stock of Greek fire. Serdica (809), by contrast, was taken by deception and promises after a siege, with the massacre of 6,000 soldiers. The Scriptor incertus describes the huge preparation of engines and armoured wagons to attack Constantinople in 814. The Blacksmith part is a weaker abstraction of metalworking and armour, although the Proto-Bulgarian inventory inscriptions record the distribution of mail coats and helmets.

It may allude to the great fortified centres (Pliska, Preslav, Tarnovo) or to the alleged urbanisation in the history text, but the link is weak. Pliska was mainly a vast earthen enclosure (c. 23 km²) with a stone citadel, of steppe type, rather than a dense urban network.

elements.element: Can build Krepost in Castle Age
elements.explanation: Medieval Bulgaria, especially that of the Second Empire, relied on a dense network of mountain and river fortresses: Tsarevets in Tarnovo, Baba Vida in Vidin, Asen's Fortress near Asenovgrad (strengthened by Ivan Asen II in 1231), Lovech and Ovech. A fortress smaller and cheaper than a Castle is a good abstraction.

The concept of a compact hilltop fortress fits the Second Empire well; for the First Empire, the great earth and stone walls of Pliska and Preslav and the Erkesia earthwork would be more characteristic. The name is a modern Bulgarian word (see the naming section).

The heavy cavalry of the aristocracy (boilas/bolyars) was indeed the elite core of Bulgarian armies, and “konnik” is the common Bulgarian word for horseman, a generic but acceptable name. The mechanic of continuing to fight on foot when the horse falls is a game invention: dismounting was common practice among many peoples, and no source makes it a Bulgarian speciality.

Stirrups reached Europe mainly through the Avars (late 6th century), and Maurice's Strategikon (c. 600) is the first European textual mention of them. The Proto-Bulgarians, who lived in the Avar orbit, used them, but the idea that they introduced them to Europe is popular in Bulgaria and a minority view in historiography. Moreover, the effect (33% faster attack) does not match the function of the stirrup, which is stability; and Lynn White's thesis on the stirrup and the shock charge is now largely rejected.

“Bagain” is a real title from the 9th-century Proto-Bulgarian inscriptions. According to T. Slavova (Eslavística Complutense, 2009), it designated a military rank with several hierarchical grades, whereas bagatur was an honorific title. Applying it as armour for infantry swordsmen is a forced transposition: the title belonged to the military hierarchy of the elite, which fought mainly on horseback.

There was mining and metalworking in the Balkans (for example in the Chiprovtsi region, especially from the end of the Middle Ages), but nothing that distinguishes Bulgaria from its neighbours. It is a generic abstraction of “abundant weaponry”, with little specific basis.

tree_issues.problem: The civ keeps Redemption, Illumination, Theocracy, Fervor, Devotion and Heresy, but loses four core monastery technologies. The history text itself makes the Christianisation under Boris I (864/865) and the literary schools the centre of Bulgarian identity: in 886 the disciples of Cyril and Methodius (Clement, Naum, Angelarius) were received in Preslav and Ohrid; the Patriarchate was recognised in 927 and restored in 1235; later came the Tarnovo school (Patriarch Euthymius, 14th century) and the Rila Monastery. Block Printing is the most ironic absence for the cradle of Slavic literature. Having Heresy, on the other hand, fits well with the Bogomils (10th century).

Pliska had a citadel with stone walls more than 2 m thick, and Preslav had stone walls. The First Empire built the great Erkesia earthwork in Thrace. The Krepost partly compensates, but the absence of fortified walls runs counter to the archaeology.

tree_issues.item: Cavalry Archer / Heavy Cavalry Archer / Parthian Tactics / Thumb Ring (present, but with no bonus)
tree_issues.problem: The Proto-Bulgarians were steppe horse archers, and the Second Empire won at Adrianople (1205) with Cuman archers and a feigned retreat. The potential is in the tech tree, but the design pushes the civ towards swordsmen, leaving the best-documented military trait without expression.
Ironic for a civ with free Militia-line upgrades and a heavy cavalry UU, but historically neutral: these are balance choices.

tree_issues.item: Bombard Cannon, Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Tower (absent)
tree_issues.problem: Consistent: the Second Empire fell in 1393–1396, before gunpowder carried weight in the Balkans. It is one of the most faithful points of the tech tree.
Acceptable for the First Empire. In the Second Empire the crossbow spread in the Balkans through Latin and Venetian contacts (13th–14th centuries), so the absence is debatable, but minor.

tree_issues.item: Reduced navy (no Fast Fire Ship, Heavy Demolition Ship, Dry Dock, Carvel Hull, Shipwright)
tree_issues.problem: Consistent: Bulgaria was never a great naval power. Only the Despotate of Dobruja (Dobrotitsa, 1360s–1370s) had a small fleet in the Black Sea.

history_text_issues.claim: Despite their common culture, the Slavs “did not develop any state”.
history_text_issues.problem: A false generalisation, with a national-romantic flavour, according to which statehood was brought by the Bulgars.
history_text_issues.correction: Slavic polities did exist: Samo's kingdom (c. 623–658), Carantania and, in the Balkans, the sklaviniai with their own chiefs, including the “Seven Tribes” of Moesia that Asparuh subjugated (Theophanes; Curta, 2006).

history_text_issues.claim: The Bulgars were supposedly semi-nomadic horsemen who came from Central Asia.
history_text_issues.problem: The origin is simplified and debated.
history_text_issues.correction: Asparuh's people came directly from the Pontic–Caspian steppes (Kubrat's Old Great Bulgaria, by the Sea of Azov), after Khazar pressure. The remote origin is debated: the Oghuric Turkic thesis is the majority view, and there is an Iranian/Pamiri thesis, popular in Bulgaria but a minority view.

history_text_issues.claim: Heavy cavalry was supposedly the backbone of the army throughout the Middle Ages and one of the most feared forces in Europe.
history_text_issues.problem: Hyperbole.
history_text_issues.correction: The great Bulgarian victories resulted mainly from ambushes in mountain passes (Varbitsa 811, Tryavna 1190), from light cavalry and from Cuman archers (Adrianople 1205). In the 9th–10th centuries infantry and fortifications carried great weight. “Among the most feared in Europe” has no comparative support.

history_text_issues.claim: Boris I supposedly founded the Pliska-Preslav school, which stimulated the creation of Cyrillic.
history_text_issues.problem: Omissions that distort the genesis of Slavic writing.
history_text_issues.correction: The first Slavic script, Glagolitic, was created by Constantine-Cyril and Methodius c. 862–863 for Great Moravia. Boris received their disciples in 886, and Cyrillic emerged in Preslav in the 890s, under Simeon, with disputed authorship (Clement, Naum or Constantine of Preslav). The text also ignores the Ohrid school (Clement).

history_text_issues.claim: Old Bulgarian supposedly replaced Greek as a “lingua franca”.
history_text_issues.problem: A strong exaggeration.
history_text_issues.correction: Old Church Slavonic became the liturgical and literary language of the Slavia Orthodoxa (Serbia, Rus', later Wallachia), which is a remarkable achievement. Greek, however, remained the language of prestige, diplomacy and trade in the eastern Mediterranean.

history_text_issues.claim: Simeon supposedly controlled almost the whole of the Balkans.
history_text_issues.problem: Territorial exaggeration.
history_text_issues.correction: Simeon dominated much of the Balkan interior and Serbia (924), but not Constantinople, Thessalonica, peninsular Greece, Dalmatia or Croatia; his army was defeated by the Croats c. 926.

history_text_issues.claim: Trade supposedly created levels of urbanisation among the highest in Europe.
history_text_issues.problem: A claim without comparative support.
history_text_issues.correction: Pliska and Preslav were large centres, but Bulgaria was not comparable in urbanisation to the Byzantine Empire, Italy or al-Andalus. A good economic fact to use would be the trade war of 894: Simeon invaded Byzantium when the Bulgarian market was moved from Constantinople to Thessalonica.

history_text_issues.claim: After Simeon, Bulgaria supposedly went into decline and was conquered by the Byzantines in 1018.
history_text_issues.problem: Omits essential phases.
history_text_issues.correction: Missing are the long peace of Peter I (927–969), the invasion by Sviatoslav of Kiev, the conquest of eastern Bulgaria and Preslav by John I Tzimiskes (971) and the resistance of Samuel and the Cometopuli from Ohrid (976–1014). Also missing are the defeat at Kleidion (1014) and the mass blinding of the prisoners, whose numbers are disputed.

history_text_issues.claim: Revolt of the “aristocratic brothers Asen and Peter” in 1185.
history_text_issues.problem: Omits the Vlach and Cuman component.
history_text_issues.correction: The Byzantine sources (Niketas Choniates) call the Asen brothers Vlachs, and the Second Empire depended on Cuman allies. The origin of the Asens (Bulgarian, Vlach or Cuman) is debated (Madgearu, The Asanids, 2016).

history_text_issues.claim: Absence of Kaloyan and of the Battle of Adrianople (1205).
history_text_issues.problem: Omission of the greatest military triumph of the Second Empire.
history_text_issues.correction: Kaloyan (r. 1197–1207) annihilated the army of the Latin Empire at Adrianople (14 April 1205), with Cuman cavalry and a feigned retreat, and captured Emperor Baldwin I (Villehardouin, Robert de Clari).

history_text_issues.claim: “After Ivan II” the empire was supposedly under constant threat.
history_text_issues.problem: Imprecise designation of the ruler.
history_text_issues.correction: This refers to Ivan Asen II (r. 1218–1241), victor of Klokotnitsa (1230), the standard designation in historiography.

missing_features: Horse archery in the Proto-Bulgarian steppe tradition and, in the Second Empire, Cuman allies and mercenaries (Adrianople 1205; Tryavna 1190).
Ambushes in the Balkan passes: Varbitsa (811), where Nikephoros I was killed and his skull turned into a cup by Krum, and Tryavna (1190), against Isaac II.
Earthen fortifications and large enclosures (Erkesia, the outer enclosure of Pliska) and fortified camps.
Krum's siege train and the capture of Byzantine engineers and equipment (Mesembria 812, including Greek fire siphons).
Christianisation, an autocephalous Patriarchate (927, 1235), Slavic writing and the literary schools of Preslav, Ohrid and Tarnovo.
Bogomilism (10th century), a dualist heresy with a Europe-wide impact.
Extortion of tribute from Byzantium (treaties of 681, 716 and 927) and control of Danube and Balkan trade.
Krum's law code and the centralisation of the khanate.
The Vlach component and mountain pastoralism in the Second Empire.

proposals.title: Cuman Alliance (Kaloyan)
proposals.description: Replaces Stirrups. Castle Age UT: Cavalry Archers cost -50% gold and train 25% faster, and Parthian Tactics becomes free.
proposals.historical_basis: At Adrianople (14 April 1205), Kaloyan used Cuman horse archers and a feigned retreat to destroy the Latin cavalry and capture Baldwin I (Villehardouin; Robert de Clari; Akropolites). The Cumans were structural allies of the Asens (Vásáry, Cumans and Tatars, 2005).

proposals.title: Ambush in the Passes (Varbitsa)
proposals.description: Replaces Town Centers -50% stone: stationary military units next to forests become invisible beyond 4 tiles, and the first attack of each unit from higher elevation deals +25% damage (stacking with the game's normal elevation bonus).
proposals.historical_basis: In 811 Krum trapped and annihilated the army of Nikephoros I in the Varbitsa pass, after blocking the exit with palisades (Theophanes; Scriptor incertus). In 1190 the Asens ambushed Isaac II in the Tryavna pass (Niketas Choniates).

proposals.title: Preslav Literary School
proposals.description: Restore Faith, Atonement, Block Printing and Sanctity. New Monastery technology: Monastery technologies -50% cost and Monks +1 conversion range.
proposals.historical_basis: Boris I received the disciples of Cyril and Methodius in 886. Cyrillic developed in Preslav under Simeon, the Ohrid school evangelised Macedonia, and Bulgaria was the driving force of the Slavia Orthodoxa (Obolensky, The Byzantine Commonwealth).

proposals.title: Konnik becomes “Bolyar”; Bagains moves to the cavalry
proposals.description: The UU is renamed Bolyar, the mounted aristocracy. Bagains now gives +2/+1 armour to the Knight-line and the Bolyar, instead of +5 to swordsmen. The Militia-line bonus is reduced to half-price upgrades.
proposals.historical_basis: The boilas/bolyars were the mounted military nobility, and the bagain was a hierarchical military rank in the 9th-century Proto-Bulgarian inscriptions (T. Slavova, 2009; Beševliev, Die protobulgarischen Inschriften).

proposals.title: Krum's Siege Train
proposals.description: Alternative Imperial Age UT: Siege Workshop units are built 50% faster and gain +20% HP, and Battering Rams can carry 2 more infantry units.
proposals.historical_basis: Theophanes reports that Krum took Mesembria (812) with engines built thanks to a deserting Arab engineer, capturing Greek fire siphons. The Scriptor incertus describes the vast preparation of engines and armoured wagons to attack Constantinople in 814.

proposals.title: Erkesia and the walls of Pliska
proposals.description: Add Fortified Wall. Palisade Walls with +100% HP and built 50% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: The great Erkesia earthwork in Thrace (probably later than the peace of 815/816), the outer earthen enclosure of Pliska (c. 23 km²) and the inner stone citadel. The stone walls of Preslav.

contested: Proto-Bulgarian ethnogenesis: Oghuric Turkic origin (majority view) vs. Iranian/Pamiri theses (P. Dobrev and others).
Introduction of the stirrup into Europe: attribution to the Avars (consensus) vs. to the Proto-Bulgarians (minority national thesis).
Exact meaning of the titles bagain, boila and kana subigi.
Origin of the Asen brothers: Bulgarian, Vlach or Cuman.
Authorship of Cyrillic: Clement of Ohrid, Naum or Constantine of Preslav.
Number of prisoners blinded after Kleidion (14–15,000 according to Skylitzes; for Stephenson, the legendary scale grew later).
Dating and attribution of the Madara Rider (Tervel? Krum?).
Degree of urbanisation of Pliska: a city or a large steppe-type palace-camp.
key_sources: Theophanes the Confessor, Chronographia; Nikephoros, Breviarium
Scriptor incertus de Leone Armenio (on Krum)
