civs.represents: Armenians of Greater Armenia: the Bagratid kingdom of Ani (884/885–1045), the Artsruni kingdom of Vaspurakan (908–1021/1022) and the nakharar principalities under Persian and Arab rule. The civ also represents the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia (Rubenid barony from c. 1080; kingdom 1198–1375).
civs.period: c. 451 (Avarayr) – 1375 (fall of Sis to the Mamluks); core from 885 to 1375.
civs.verdict: The civ gets some identity traits right: the first Christian state, the culture of relics, the fortified monasteries and the archery tradition. But it inverts the military priorities: medieval Armenians were famous above all for their noble cavalry (azatk, commanded by the Mamikonian sparapets), which fought with lance and bow, and the game denies them Paladin, Plate Barding, Hussar, Heavy Cavalry Archer, Parthian Tactics and Thumb Ring, giving them a poorly documented “infantry and navy” identity. It merges two very different realities into a single civ: mountainous Greater Armenia and Mediterranean, feudal, Latinised Cilicia. The history text has two serious errors: composite bows “adopted” because of the nomads, and the end of the Cilician kingdom attributed to Timur, when it was the Mamluks in 1375. Denying Architecture and Keep to the builders of Ani and of the Cilician castles is particularly unfortunate.
civs.naming_scope_issues: The endonym is Hay (pl. Hayer) and the country Hayastan; “Armenians” is a neutral and acceptable exonym. The problem is one of scope. The civ merges Greater Armenia, a mountainous plateau of kingdoms and nakharar principalities, with the Kingdom of Cilicia, which was coastal, feudalised in the Frankish manner, allied with the Crusaders and ruled by the Lusignans from 1342. Mule Carts and the mountain idea come from the former; the navy, crossbows and Latin alliances come from the latter. The text begins in 451, before the game's 500–1500 frame, and ends with an error (Timur in 1400). There is strong overlap with Byzantines (emperors and generals of Armenian origin, the Armenian themes of the 10th–11th centuries, Byzantine Cilicia and the shared Dromon), with Persians (Sasanian Armenia and the Battle of Avarayr) and with Georgians (shared buildings and disputed figures such as Gregory Pakourianos).

elements.explanation: Medieval Armenian armies rested mainly on the cavalry of the nakharar and azat: Sasanians and Byzantines recruited Armenian horsemen, and the Mamikonians were hereditary sparapets. Infantry existed, but it was not the distinctive arm. The naval character is weak: Cilicia had important ports (Ayas/Laiazzo, Korykos), but it depended on Genoese, Venetian and Cypriot ships and never had a significant war fleet.

An abstraction of transport by pack animals on a mountainous plateau and of the Armenian role in the caravan trade (Dvin, Ani, Artsn). It is generic and shared with Georgia. The most celebrated Armenian mercantile reputation (New Julfa) dates from the 17th century.
A purely mechanical reinforcement of the previous bonus, with no specific historical link beyond the mountain economy.

elements.element: Spearman- and Militia-line upgrades (except Man-at-Arms) available one age earlier
elements.explanation: No source singles out Armenian infantry as early or superior. The Armenia of Ani had urban militias and mountain infantry, and Cilicia had spearmen, but the elite force was mounted. It is mainly a game-identity choice.

elements.element: First Fortified Church receives a free Relic
elements.explanation: A good symbolic abstraction. Armenia is traditionally the first state to adopt Christianity (Tiridates III and Gregory the Illuminator; traditional date 301, more probably c. 314). It has a strong relic culture: the Holy Lance of Geghard, the relics of Etchmiadzin and the reliquary of the right hand of Gregory the Illuminator.

elements.element: Galley-line and Dromons fire an additional projectile
elements.explanation: A very weak basis: the only link is the Cilician coast. Armenian Cilicia did not stand out in naval warfare, and the dromon is a Byzantine ship that the Armenians did not use as a type of their own.

The Armenian archery tradition is extremely ancient: the legendary Hayk kills Bel with an arrow (Movsés Khorenatsi), Xenophon and Strabo mention archers from the region, and Armenian archers served in Byzantine and Muslim armies. The name is generic, since the composite bow was used by almost every people of the Near East, and the foot unit ignores the fact that many Armenian archers were mounted. The armour-ignoring mechanic has no basis, and the history text's justification is wrong (see below).

The best possible basis is the role of the clergy at Avarayr (451): the priest Ghevond (Leontius) exhorted the fighters and was later martyred in Persia together with other clerics (Yeghishe). The Armenian clergy accompanied and legitimised war, but there is no documented tradition of priest-swordsmen as regular troops. The military orders present in Cilicia (Templars, Hospitallers, Teutonic Knights) were Latin, not Armenian.

The name refers to the real Cilicia, but there was no notable “Cilician fleet” of warships. Cilicia's maritime importance was commercial: Ayas was one of the great emporia of the Mongol era, where Marco Polo landed in 1271 and whose trade Pegolotti describes. Improving galleys and demolition ships invents a naval tradition.

No medieval Armenian military term or institution by this name is known. The form recalls the Latin feretrum (a litter or reliquary carried in procession) and the English feretory, that is, Western ecclesiastical vocabulary; the exact origin of the name chosen by the developers is not documented. There is a real Armenian parallel (ajatar, “bearer of the right-hand relic”, the nickname of Catholicos Sarkis II in the 15th century), but nothing that justifies the effect (+30 HP for infantry and faster healing by Warrior Priests), which is purely mechanical.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Infantry +2 line of sight
elements.explanation: No identifiable historical link. With a great deal of goodwill it could evoke keeping watch from the heights, but that would apply to any mountain people.

elements.element: Fortified Church (unique building, shared with Georgians)
elements.explanation: Many Armenian monasteries were walled complexes that served as refuges, as centres of learning and sometimes for defence: Haghpat and Sanahin (10th century), Tatev (9th century), Noravank and Geghard (13th century). The idea is sound. But sharing it wholesale with Georgia erases real differences: distinct architectural traditions and the church schism completed c. 607–609 between Abraham I of Armenia and Kyrion I of Iberia.

elements.element: Mule Cart (unique building, shared with Georgians)
elements.explanation: A mobile drop-off point that abstracts the mountain economy based on pack animals. Mechanically original, historically generic.

tree_issues.problem: This is the main historical inversion. The Armenian nobility (azatk/nakharark) was a famous heavy cavalry, commanded by hereditary sparapets (Mamikonian). The sources (Faustus of Byzantium, Yeghishe, Ghazar Parpetsi) count armies by the number of horsemen, and Sasanians and Byzantines recruited Armenian cavalry. Cilicia adopted knightly cavalry in the Frankish manner.

tree_issues.item: Heavy Cavalry Archer, Parthian Tactics and Thumb Ring (missing)
tree_issues.problem: The Armenian noble cavalry of Late Antiquity fought in the Parthian-Sasanian style, with lance and bow, and the archery tradition is the very foundation of the UU. Being left with a Cavalry Archer without its final upgrade, without Parthian Tactics and without Thumb Ring is inconsistent with the identity the game assigns them.

Armenia was one of the great centres of medieval architecture: Zvartnots (643–652); Ani Cathedral, by Trdat (989–1001), the architect who rebuilt the dome of Hagia Sophia after the earthquake of 989; Ani, the “city of 1001 churches”. Cilicia had a dense network of castles (Sis, Vahka, Lampron, Korykos, Anazarbus), studied by Robert Edwards. Denying Keep and Architecture is ahistorical.
A small irony for a culture of building in tuff stone and of khachkars (carved stone crosses).

tree_issues.item: Fast Fire Ship and Shipwright (missing) in a “Naval” civ
tree_issues.problem: A minor internal inconsistency: the naval label rests on Galleys and Dromons, without any strong historical basis, while other pieces of the naval line are missing.
It is a Byzantine ship type; there were no Armenian dromons. Misattributed, especially when combined with Cilician Fleet.
Plausible: Cilicia adopted Latin weaponry, including the crossbow, through contact with the Crusaders, the military orders and the Lusignans.
Consistent with the strong tradition of fortress-monasteries, although the present appearance of many of these complexes is later.

history_text_issues.claim: Nomadic invasions supposedly led the Armenians to incorporate “cohorts of composite bowmen”.
history_text_issues.problem: Factual error: it presents a millennia-old tradition, the very justification for the UU itself, as an 11th-century innovation.
history_text_issues.correction: The composite bow had been used in the Near East since antiquity (Assyrians, Parthians, Sasanians). Armenia had renowned archers long before the Seljuks: the founding myth of Hayk, the noble cavalry with lance and bow of the 4th–5th centuries, Armenian archers in the service of Byzantium and the caliphates. There was no new adoption in the 11th century.

history_text_issues.claim: “The last straw for the battered kingdom was Tamerlane's invasion of 1400”.
history_text_issues.problem: Factual error: it confuses Cilicia with Greater Armenia.
history_text_issues.correction: The Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia fell to the Mamluks in 1375: Sis was taken and Leo V captured; later released, he died in Paris in 1393. Timur's campaigns (1386–1403) devastated Greater Armenia, not Cilicia, which no longer existed as a kingdom.

history_text_issues.claim: Byzantium supposedly incorporated the “leftover pieces” after the Seljuk raids.
history_text_issues.problem: Chronology largely reversed.
history_text_issues.correction: Byzantium annexed Vaspurakan (1021/1022) and Ani (1045) before the great Seljuk conquests; Alp Arslan took Ani in 1064. The first Turkish raids on Vaspurakan (c. 1016–1021) weighed on Senekerim's cession, but it was the Byzantine annexations that dismantled the Armenian defences and made the Turkish conquest easier (Aristakes Lastivertsi).

history_text_issues.claim: Ashot I supposedly allied shrewdly with the Byzantines and became the first king in four centuries.
history_text_issues.problem: Misleading framing.
history_text_issues.correction: Ashot I was recognised as “prince of princes” by the caliph (862) and crowned king c. 884–885 with a crown sent by the Abbasid caliph al-Muʿtamid; Basil I later sent another crown. His initial legitimacy came mainly from Baghdad, and Ashot balanced between the two.

history_text_issues.claim: Under Thoros II the Armeno-Cilicians supposedly prevailed against 12th-century Byzantine designs.
history_text_issues.problem: Simplification.
history_text_issues.correction: John II Komnenos conquered Cilicia in 1137 and took Leo I prisoner to Constantinople. Thoros II recovered the region and defeated Andronikos Komnenos at Mamistra (1152), but in 1158 he had to submit to Manuel I as a vassal.

history_text_issues.claim: The text does not mention the elevation of Cilicia to a kingdom.
history_text_issues.problem: Structural omission.
history_text_issues.correction: Leo I (Levon) was crowned king in Tarsus on 6 January 1198 (some authors: 1199), with a crown promised by Emperor Henry VI and the papacy and delivered by Conrad, Archbishop of Mainz. This is the founding milestone of the kingdom, later ruled by the Hetumids and by the Lusignans (1342).

history_text_issues.claim: Armenian Cilicia supposedly allied “wisely” with the Mongols.
history_text_issues.problem: Debatable value judgement.
history_text_issues.correction: Hetum I submitted to the Mongols (Smbat's mission in 1247; the king's own journey to Karakorum in 1254). The alliance brought gains, but also Mamluk retaliation: the disaster of Mari (1266), the sack of Sis and the campaigns up to 1375. Angus Stewart, among others, discusses its overall balance.

history_text_issues.claim: Avarayr (451): Vardan Mamikonian died defending the homeland.
history_text_issues.problem: Correct, but incomplete.
history_text_issues.correction: The military defeat at Avarayr led, after the revolt of Vahan Mamikonian, to the treaty of Nvarsak (484), which guaranteed religious freedom and autonomy; that is why the battle is celebrated as a moral victory. The text also omits the role of Armenians in the Byzantine elite and their cultural achievements: the alphabet of Mesrop Mashtots (c. 405), architecture and the illuminated manuscripts of Toros Roslin (13th century).

missing_features: Noble cavalry (azatk/nakharark), with lance and bow, and the hereditary office of sparapet (Mamikonian), Armenia's most characteristic military force.
Architecture and engineering: Zvartnots, Ani, Trdat and the dome of Hagia Sophia, the khachkars; Cilician castles.
The nakharar system of great semi-autonomous noble houses, the basis of political and military organisation.
Trade: Dvin and Ani as caravan cities, and the Cilician port of Ayas as a Euro-Mongol emporium (13th–14th centuries).
Written culture: the Mashtots alphabet, a rich historiography (Movsés Khorenatsi, Yeghishe, Sebeos, Matthew of Edessa) and illumination (Toros Roslin).
Military diaspora in the service of Byzantium and the Fatimids (for example Badr al-Jamali, Armenian vizier of Egypt).
Latin integration in Cilicia: marriages with Crusaders, feudal law (the Assizes of Antioch translated by Smbat), military orders and the Lusignan dynasty.
Mountain fortresses of Greater Armenia (Amberd, Bjni) and of Cilicia.

proposals.title: Sparapet (nakharar cavalry)
proposals.description: New Castle Age UT: Knight-line +2 melee armour and +20 HP. Add Plate Barding Armor, Paladin, Heavy Cavalry Archer and Thumb Ring to the tree and remove the early Spearman/Militia bonus.
proposals.historical_basis: The sparapet was the hereditary commander-in-chief (Mamikonian) of the noble cavalry; the title survived in Cilicia (Smbat Sparapet, 13th century). Armenian sources (Faustus of Byzantium, Yeghishe) count armies in horsemen, and Sasanians and Byzantines recruited Armenian heavy cavalry (Garsoïan; Hewsen).

proposals.title: Port of Ayas
proposals.description: Replaces Cilician Fleet. Trade Cogs and Trade Carts generate +20% gold, Docks are 25% cheaper, and the Galley-line loses the extra projectile from the civ bonus.
proposals.historical_basis: In the 13th–14th centuries Ayas (Laiazzo) was one of the great ports linking the Mediterranean with the Mongol route to Persia and Asia. Marco Polo landed there in 1271, and Pegolotti (Pratica della mercatura) describes its trade.

proposals.title: Trdat the Architect
proposals.description: Add Architecture, Keep and Stone Shaft Mining. Civ bonus: Fortified Churches and Castles +20% HP and built 25% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: Trdat built Ani Cathedral (989–1001) and rebuilt the dome of Hagia Sophia after the earthquake of 989. Cilicia had dozens of castles (Robert W. Edwards, The Fortifications of Armenian Cilicia, 1987).

proposals.title: Composite Bowman becomes “Aghegnavor” and gets Thumb Ring
proposals.description: Rename the UU with the Armenian term for archer (aghegnavor, from aghegn, “bow”) and add Thumb Ring to the tree. Correct the history text to present the archery tradition as ancient and not as a reaction to the Seljuks.
proposals.historical_basis: The myth of Hayk the archer (Movsés Khorenatsi); Armenian archers in the service of Byzantium and the caliphates; the composite-bow tradition in the Near East since antiquity.

proposals.title: Warrior Priest becomes the “Yerets” of Avarayr
proposals.description: Turn the unit into a support unit without strong melee combat: an aura that gives +1 attack and slow regeneration to nearby infantry and cavalry, with no conversion ability.
proposals.historical_basis: The priest Ghevond and the clergy who accompanied Vardan's army at Avarayr (451) exhorted the soldiers and were later martyred (Yeghishe, History of Vardan). This is a role of morale and legitimation, not of shock troops.

proposals.title: Latin Alliance (Cilicia)
proposals.description: Imperial Age UT: Castles can train military-order knights (Paladin equivalents with +2/+2 and conversion resistance), and Arbalesters gain +1 range.
proposals.historical_basis: Leo I gave Seleucia/Silifke to the Hospitallers (1210), and the Teutonic Knights received Amouda. The Cilician court adopted Frankish institutions and titles, and the Lusignans took the crown in 1342 (Boase, The Cilician Kingdom of Armenia, 1978).

contested: Date of Armenia's conversion: 301 (tradition) vs. c. 314 (most scholars).
Whether Mesrop Mashtots also created the Georgian and Caucasian Albanian alphabets (a claim made by Koryun, contested by Georgian historiography).
Armenian origin of Byzantine emperors such as Heraclius and Basil I.
Identity of Gregory Pakourianos: Anna Komnene gives him noble Armenian lineage, while the typikon of Petritsoni (1083) presents him as Iberian (Georgian); probably a Chalcedonian from Tao.
Date of Leo I's coronation: 1198 or 1199.
Assessment of the Armenian-Mongol alliance: sensible pragmatism or the cause of the Mamluk destruction.
Nature and degree of Armenia's autonomy under the Abbasids and the role of the Bagratids.
key_sources: Movsés Khorenatsi, History of the Armenians
Faustus of Byzantium (Buzandaran Patmutiwnk)
Yeghishe, History of Vardan and the Armenian War; Ghazar Parpetsi
Sebeos; Ghevond; Hovhannes Draskhanakerttsi
Aristakes Lastivertsi; Matthew of Edessa
Smbat Sparapet, Chronicle; Hetum of Korykos, La Flor des estoires (1307)
Nina Garsoïan, studies on Late Antique Armenia and the nakharar system
Robert H. Hewsen, Armenia: A Historical Atlas (2001)
Richard Hovannisian (ed.), The Armenian People from Ancient to Modern Times (1997)
Cyril Toumanoff, Studies in Christian Caucasian History (1963)
Robert W. Edwards, The Fortifications of Armenian Cilicia (1987)
T. S. R. Boase (ed.), The Cilician Kingdom of Armenia (1978)
Angus Stewart, The Armenian Kingdom and the Mamluks (2001)
Tim Greenwood, studies on Armenia under Arab rule

civs.represents: Kingdom of Georgia (Sakartvelo) under the Bagrationi dynasty, unified by Bagrat III (1008/1010), with the golden age of David IV the Builder (r. 1089–1125) and Queen Tamar (r. 1184–1213). It implicitly includes its predecessors Kartli (Iberia), Egrisi (Lazica), the Kingdom of Abkhazia and Tao-Klarjeti.
civs.period: c. 888 (Adarnase IV, “king of the Iberians”) / 1008 – 1490 (formal division of the kingdom into Kartli, Kakheti and Imereti); core from 1089 to 1213.
civs.verdict: One of the most coherent of the recent civs: the Monaspa (royal guard created by David IV), the Svaneti towers, the aznauri, the elevation advantage and the team bonus pun on “David the Builder” have a real basis, and the absence of Bombard Cannon and Bombard Tower is coherent. The weak points are an unfounded mechanic (mounted-unit regeneration), the generic sharing of Mule Cart and Fortified Church with the Armenians, and the total absence of the Kipchaks (Cumans) settled by David IV, without whom Didgori (1121) cannot be explained. The history text opens with a false premise: that the small kingdoms escaped foreign domination thanks to isolation. It also omits Didgori, the capture of Tbilisi (1122) and the Khwarazmian invasion, and attributes the end of the kingdom solely to the Turkomans, when it was above all a matter of dynastic fragmentation.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Georgians” is an exonym, probably derived from Persian gurj/gorj; the endonym is Kartvelebi and the country is Sakartvelo. The civ mainly represents the unified kingdom of 1008–1490, which fits the game's framework well. However, it absorbs without distinction Abkhazians, Svans, Mingrelians/Laz, Kakhetians and the ancient kingdoms of Kartli/Iberia and Egrisi/Lazica, the latter being the stage of the Lazic War (541–562) between Byzantium and Persia. It also ignores the fact that Kipchaks and Alans were a structural part of the army of David IV and Tamar. There is overlap with Armenians (Tao-Klarjeti, Pakourianos, shared buildings) and with Cumans (the Kipchaks).

elements.explanation: Appropriate. Georgian armies of the golden age were dominated by cavalry (royal guard, aznauri and Kipchaks), and the kingdom relied on mountain fortresses and towers. Even so, the period of David IV and Tamar was markedly offensive: Shirvan, Ani (1199) and support for the creation of the Empire of Trebizond (1204).
An abstraction of the mountain economy based on pack animals. Generic and shared with the Armenians.

elements.element: Units and buildings receive -15% damage when located on higher elevation
elements.explanation: A good abstraction of defence in mountainous terrain: high-altitude fortresses, the valleys of the Greater Caucasus and prolonged resistance to the Mongols and to Timur. Didgori (1121) was fought on rugged terrain chosen by David IV.

elements.element: Mounted Units regenerate 2/8/14 HP per minute in Feudal/Castle/Imperial Age
elements.explanation: No identifiable historical basis. It could evoke remount horses or mountain pastures, but nothing sets Georgia apart in this respect. It is a balance mechanic for a cavalry civ.

elements.element: Fortified Churches provide Villagers in a 9 tiles radius with +10% work rate
elements.explanation: A reasonable abstraction of the economic role of the monasteries, which were large landowners and centres of agrarian organisation and of learning: Gelati (1106), Ikalto, Shio-Mgvime and the monasteries of David Gareja.

The monaspa (literally “host of servants”, from mona, “servant”, and spa, “army”) was the mounted royal guard formed by David IV in the military reform of c. 1118; it was well armed, with lance and bow, and in the direct service of the king. The strength of c. 5,000 horsemen is commonly cited in modern historiography, but its exact documentary basis is uncertain, and its composition (young Kipchaks, royal servants or petty nobility) is debated. The mechanic of growing stronger when grouped is a reasonable abstraction of a cohesive elite unit.

The tower-houses of Svaneti (generally dated to the 9th–13th centuries, many of them later) are real and emblematic. They were towers for family defence against feuds, vendettas and raids, not state fortifications. The pass-through damage mechanic is invented, but the name is well founded.

The aznauri were the Georgian middle nobility who served on horseback with their own retinues, the basis of the feudal cavalry. Taking up less population space can abstract warriors who equipped and maintained themselves. The etymology is debated: the tradition of Leonti Mroveli links it to Azon, while linguists point to an Iranian origin (cf. Armenian azat, “free/noble”).
A pun on Aghmashenebeli (“the Builder” or “the Restorer”), the epithet of David IV, who rebuilt the kingdom after the Seljuk devastations. It is a pun, but an elegant one with a real basis.

elements.element: Fortified Church (unique building, shared with Armenians)
elements.explanation: Georgia has fortified religious complexes, but the most iconic ones (Ananuri, 17th century; Gremi, 1565) postdate the game's period. The most relevant medieval examples are walled monasteries and rock-cut monasteries such as Vardzia (begun under George III, consecrated c. 1185 under Tamar). Sharing the building wholesale with Armenia ignores the ecclesiastical schism of c. 607–609.

elements.element: Mule Cart (unique building, shared with Armenians)
elements.explanation: A mobile drop-off point that abstracts the mountain economy; generic.

tree_issues.problem: Historical irony: Colchis and Svaneti were famous for their gold. Strabo (Geography XI.2.19) describes the Svans collecting gold from rivers with sheepskins, the rationalised origin of the myth of the Golden Fleece.
Of little relevance for the crossbow, but Thumb Ring makes sense: the monaspa used the bow, and the c. 15,000 Kipchaks estimated at Didgori were steppe horse archers.
A small inconsistency given Georgia's strong monastic culture: the Gelati Academy (1106), Iviron on Mount Athos (c. 980), the Monastery of the Cross in Jerusalem and Petritsoni/Bachkovo (1083).

Minor: gunpowder only reached Georgia in the 15th–16th centuries, and the kingdom never had a significant war navy, despite the Abkhazian coast on the Black Sea. The civ has Galleon, Fast Fire Ship and Cannon Galleon (without Elite), but not Carrack, Dry Dock or Shipwright. This is a gap common to most civs.

tree_issues.item: Bombard Cannon, Bombard Tower and Paladin (missing)
tree_issues.problem: Coherent with the chronology and with an identity built on royal cavalry and the middle nobility rather than on Western-style knights.

tree_issues.item: Heavy Cavalry Archer and Parthian Tactics (present)
tree_issues.problem: Coherent and positive: this reflects the Kipchaks and the bow-armed guard, even though no bonus expresses it.

history_text_issues.claim: The small kingdoms supposedly escaped foreign domination “largely through geographical isolation”.
history_text_issues.problem: False premise.
history_text_issues.correction: Kartli was under Sasanian rule, and its monarchy was abolished by the Persians c. 580. Lazica was the stage of the Byzantine–Persian war of 541–562. Tbilisi was an Arab emirate from c. 736 to 1122, and the region suffered devastating Arab campaigns, such as that of Bugha al-Kabir in 853. Georgia was a contested crossroads, not an isolated refuge (Rapp, 2014).

history_text_issues.claim: Byzantium supposedly tried occasionally to extend its influence, without lasting gains.
history_text_issues.problem: Underestimates Byzantine influence.
history_text_issues.correction: Byzantium annexed Tao after the death of David III Kouropalates (1000). Basil II waged war on George I (Shirimni, 1021, and the campaign of 1022). Georgian rulers used Byzantine titles (kouropalates, sebastos), and Georgian ecclesiastical and artistic culture was deeply Byzantinised.

history_text_issues.claim: David IV supposedly reformed infrastructure, stabilised the kingdom and increased its military power.
history_text_issues.problem: Omits the central military facts.
history_text_issues.correction: Left out are the military reform with the settlement of tens of thousands of Kipchak families (c. 1118), the victory at Didgori (12 August 1121) over Ilghazi's coalition and the conquest of Tbilisi (1122), which ended four centuries of emirate.

history_text_issues.claim: Tamar was supposedly “on the verge of participating in future Crusades”.
history_text_issues.problem: Speculative.
history_text_issues.correction: There is no evidence of crusading plans. Tamar protected the Georgian monasteries in the Holy Land and won at Shamkor (1195) and Basiani (c. 1202/1205). She also played a decisive role in the founding of the Empire of Trebizond (1204): more relevant facts, which the text omits.

history_text_issues.problem: Life dates given without the regnal dates, and the birth date is uncertain.
history_text_issues.correction: Tamar was born c. 1160 (date debated), was co-ruler from 1178 and reigned alone from 1184 to 1213.

history_text_issues.claim: Georgian armies were supposedly “led by the Monaspa”.
history_text_issues.problem: Imprecise.
history_text_issues.correction: The monaspa was the elite royal guard. Command of the army lay with the king and the amirspasalari (commander-in-chief), and the bulk of the forces came from the aznauri, the regional levies and the Kipchaks.

history_text_issues.claim: The golden age supposedly ended abruptly with the 13th-century Mongol waves.
history_text_issues.problem: Omits the Khwarazmian invasion.
history_text_issues.correction: After a first Mongol raid (1220–1221), the decisive blow came from Jalal al-Din of Khwarazm, who defeated the Georgians at Garni (1225) and sacked Tbilisi (1226). The Mongol conquest proper took place in 1236–1240.

history_text_issues.claim: The kingdom supposedly collapsed in the 15th century in the face of Turkoman invasions.
history_text_issues.problem: Misleading causality.
history_text_issues.correction: The invasions of the Qara Qoyunlu and Aq Qoyunlu took their toll, but the kingdom split mainly through internal dynastic war (c. 1460–1490), giving rise to the kingdoms of Kartli, Kakheti and Imereti and the principality of Samtskhe. These Georgian states survived until the Russian annexations of 1801–1810.

history_text_issues.claim: Gregory Pakourianos is presented as a Georgian officer.
history_text_issues.problem: His identity is contested.
history_text_issues.correction: Anna Komnene describes him as being of noble Armenian lineage; his typikon for Petritsoni (1083) presents him as an Iberian. He was probably a Chalcedonian from Tao, a region of mixed identity. He was Domestic of the Schools of the West (1081) and died fighting the Pechenegs (1086).

missing_features: Kipchak (Cuman) and Alan (Ossetian) allies and settlers, settled by David IV c. 1118 and decisive at Didgori (1121).
Victories that define the golden age: Didgori (1121), Tbilisi (1122), Shamkor (1195), Basiani (c. 1202/1205).
External power projection: support for the founding of the Empire of Trebizond (1204) and the vassalage of Shirvan.
Culture and learning: the Gelati Academy (1106), Ioane Petritsi, Shota Rustaveli's The Knight in the Panther's Skin (c. 1200) and Georgian monasteries abroad (Iviron, Petritsoni, Jerusalem).
Gold from Svaneti and Colchis, and the trade of Tbilisi as a hub between Persia, Byzantium and the steppe.
Viticulture (wine in qvevri), an economic and cultural trait thousands of years old.
Rock-cut monasteries (Vardzia, David Gareja) and highlanders (Svans, Khevsurs, Pshavs) as warrior levies.
Royal institutions: the amirspasalari, the mandaturtukhutsesi and the council of the darbazi.

proposals.title: Kipchak settlers (c. 1118)
proposals.description: Replaces Aznauri Cavalry or the mounted-unit regeneration. Castle Age UT: Stables can train Kipchak horse archers, equivalent to the Cavalry Archer, with no gold cost and +1 range. Thumb Ring is added to the tech tree.
proposals.historical_basis: According to the Life of David, King of Kings (Kartlis Tskhovreba), David IV settled a large number of Kipchaks in Georgia (the chronicle speaks of 40,000 warriors; the real number is debated), with each family providing one soldier. Modern estimates point to c. 15,000 Kipchaks at Didgori (1121).

proposals.title: Svaneti gold
proposals.description: Add Gold Shaft Mining. Gold miners work +10% faster, and Mule Carts near gold give a further +5%.
proposals.historical_basis: Strabo (XI.2.19) describes the Svans collecting gold in rivers with sheepskins. The gold wealth of Colchis lies at the origin of the myth of the Golden Fleece.

proposals.title: Gelati Academy
proposals.description: UT or Fortified Church technology: University technologies -33% cost and +50% research speed. Add Illumination and Atonement.
proposals.historical_basis: David IV founded the monastery and academy of Gelati in 1106, associated with the teaching of Ioane Petritsi. David's chronicler presents it as a “second Jerusalem” and “another Athens”, a centre of philosophy, theology and the sciences.

proposals.title: Didgori charge
proposals.description: Replaces the mounted-unit regeneration: the Monaspa and the Knight-line gain a charge attack (+10 damage on the first hit, rechargeable), in the manner of other charge units in the game.
proposals.historical_basis: At Didgori (12 August 1121), according to Ibn al-Athir, a Kipchak detachment feigned desertion or negotiation and launched a surprise attack on the Seljuk leaders; this was followed by the attack of David IV's cavalry, which broke Ilghazi's coalition. Walter the Chancellor and Matthew of Edessa also mention a small Frankish contingent.

proposals.title: Protectorate of Trebizond
proposals.description: Market technology (Imperial Age): Trade Carts and Trade Cogs +15% gold, and allies receive +10% gold from trade with the Georgian player.
proposals.historical_basis: In 1204 Alexios and David Komnenos, relatives of Tamar, founded the Empire of Trebizond with Georgian troops, creating a network of clients on the Black Sea. Tbilisi was then a major entrepôt between Persia, the Caucasus and the Black Sea.

contested: Composition of the monaspa: Kipchaks, royal servants (in the sense of mamluks) or Georgian petty nobility; and the documentary basis for the strength of 5,000.
Number of Kipchaks settled by David IV: 40,000 warriors/families according to the standard reading of the chronicle, against considerably lower numbers proposed by some Georgian historians.
Troop numbers at Didgori: Christian sources give hundreds of thousands of Muslims, Ibn al-Athir c. 30,000; modern estimates vary widely.
Identity of Gregory Pakourianos (Georgian vs. Chalcedonian Armenian).
Date of unification: 1008 (Kartli) vs. 1010 (Kakheti-Hereti).
Dating of the Svaneti towers.
Etymology of aznauri and of “Georgia”.
Whether Mesrop Mashtots created the Georgian alphabet (Armenian thesis, rejected by Georgian historiography).
key_sources: Kartlis Tskhovreba (Georgian Chronicles), especially the Life of David, King of Kings and the Histories and Eulogies of the Sovereigns (Tamar)
Leonti Mroveli; Vakhushti Bagrationi (18th century)
Matthew of Edessa, Chronicle; Walter the Chancellor, Bella Antiochena; Ibn al-Athir, al-Kamil (Didgori)
Strabo, Geography XI.2.19 (Svaneti gold)
Anna Komnene, Alexiad (Pakourianos); typikon of Petritsoni (1083)
Cyril Toumanoff, Studies in Christian Caucasian History (1963)
W. E. D. Allen, A History of the Georgian People (1932)
Donald Rayfield, Edge of Empires: A History of Georgia (2012)
Ronald Grigor Suny, The Making of the Georgian Nation (1988; 2nd ed. 1994)
Stephen H. Rapp Jr., Studies in Medieval Georgian Historiography (2003) and The Sasanian World through Georgian Eyes (2014)
Antony Eastmond, Royal Imagery in Medieval Georgia (1998)
Alexander Mikaberidze, Historical Dictionary of Georgia

groups.cross_civ_notes:
1) Generic Caucasian package: Armenians and Georgians share the Mule Cart and the Fortified Church and were released together (The Mountain Royals, 2023). Historically, the two churches split c. 607–609, with Armenia Miaphysite and Georgia Chalcedonian. Their architecture belongs to distinct traditions, and the most iconic Georgian fortress-churches (Ananuri, Gremi) date from the 16th–17th centuries. Distinguishing the two buildings, for example as a Georgian monastery-academy and a walled Armenian complex, would make both civs more faithful.
2) The cavalry paradox: Byzantines (Cataphract), Bulgarians (Konnik) and Georgians (Monaspa) get unique heavy cavalry. The Armenians, by contrast, lack the Paladin, Plate Barding, Hussar and Heavy Cavalry Archer, although their mounted nobility is perhaps the oldest and most influential in the region: it supplied cavalry to the Sasanians and to Byzantium, and gave Byzantium emperors and generals.
3) Byzantine–Armenian overlap: several emperors were of Armenian origin, certain or disputed (Leo V, Romanos I Lekapenos, John I Tzimiskes, Basil I, Heraclius). Beware of a common misconception: the Armeniakon theme lay in north-eastern Anatolia and merely inherited the name of the old army of Armenia; the Armenian themes proper (Taron, c. 966/967; Vaspurakan, 1021/1022; Ani/Iberia, 1045) date from the late 10th and the 11th century. Cilicia was Byzantine from 965 until c. 1080 and was contested again in the 12th century. Byzantium annexed Ani in 1045, opening the way for the Seljuks. Gregory Pakourianos is claimed as both Georgian and Armenian.
4) Dromon: shared by Byzantines, Armenians, Goths, Huns and Romans. It is faithful for Byzantium and, surprisingly, has a basis for the Goths: Cassiodorus (Variae V.16–17) records Theodoric's order, c. 526, to build a thousand dromons, one of the earliest attestations of the term. It is acceptable, if late, for the Romans; stretched for the Armenians; and unfounded for the Huns, who had no navy. In every case, its role as an Imperial Age bombardment ship contradicts the history of the siphon-armed galley of the 6th–12th centuries.
5) Varangian Guard: shared by Byzantines, Vikings, Danes, Saxons and Varangians. It is a Byzantine institution (its core was sent to Basil II c. 988), so its presence in the Byzantine Barracks is the most faithful of all. For the Varangians (Rus') it is justified as the source of recruitment; for the Norse and Anglo-Saxon peoples it represents, at most, returning veterans.
6) Bulgarians and Byzantines: a centuries-long war (Krum in 811 and 813, Simeon in 917, Basil II “the Bulgar-Slayer” in 1014–1018), but also a decisive alliance. In 717–718 Khan Tervel helped save Constantinople from the Arabs, and neither of the two texts mentions it. In 812 Krum captured Greek fire siphons at Mesembria, a curious link between Greek Fire and the Bulgarian discount at the Siege Workshop.
7) The Cuman/Kipchak factor, omitted in three civs: the Cumans/Kipchaks were decisive in the Second Bulgarian Empire (Adrianople 1205; possible Cuman origin of the Asen dynasty), in the Georgia of David IV (Didgori 1121) and as mercenaries of Byzantium (under the Komnenoi and the Palaiologoi). The Cumans civ exists, but none of these designs reflects the relationship.
8) The poorly represented antagonists: the great adversary of all these civs in the 11th century is Seljuk power (sack of Ani 1064, Manzikert 1071, Didgori 1121), but the Turks civ has an Ottoman, gunpowder identity. Persians mixes the Sasanians (Avarayr 451, Lazica, abolition of the monarchy of Kartli) with later phases, and the caliphate appears diluted into Saracens.
9) Regional gaps: there are no Serbs (Empire of Stefan Dušan, 1346–1355; Kosovo 1389), Wallachians/Romanians, Croats, Albanians or Alans. Bulgarians and Slavs serve as generic stand-ins for the Balkans. Volga Bulgaria, a distinct Muslim Bulgar state, has no representation.
10) Romans vs. Byzantines: the split reinforces the outdated idea of a rupture in 476 in the East. The continuity of law, coinage, imperial title and army could be acknowledged, for example by giving the Byzantines more elements shared with the Romans, such as heavy infantry units (skutatoi).
11) Calibration (game average ≈ 5): Byzantines and Georgians (6/10) are above average, because their core elements (walls, Greek fire, Cataphract, Varangian Guard; Monaspa, Svan Towers, aznauri) have a real documentary basis. Bulgarians (4/10) fall below it: their elements are mostly plausible or stretched, none of them directly faithful, and the swordsman identity displaces the best-documented trait (horse archers, ambushes, Cuman allies). Armenians (3/10) fall further below: the “infantry and navy” identity inverts the best-documented military trait (noble cavalry with lance and bow), two elements are unfounded (Fereters, team bonus) and the history text contains two serious factual errors; the score stays close to 4 thanks to the solid basis of the relics, the fortified monasteries and the archery tradition.
12) Note on method: the tech tree details were confirmed in the repository's data/trees/*.json files. External verification remained incomplete because this session's web search limit was exhausted; some points (for example Cassiodorus, Variae V.16–17, and the etymology of krepost) rest on reference knowledge without online confirmation in this session.

verification_log.change: HP bonus: corrected the claim that the walls “were taken only in 1204 and 1453”. Added 1081 (Alexios Komnenos's entry through treachery at the Gate of Charisius) and 1261 (a surprise entry); the wording is now that they were never breached by a land assault before 1453.
The Arab siege of 674–678 is now marked as a disputed dating (Jankowiak, 2013, proposes c. 667–669), in the HP bonus, in Greek Fire, in the history text, in contested and in key_sources.

“Fire Ships and Dromons attack +25% faster” downgraded from faithful to plausible. The Dromon half applies to a non-historical role, and the “naval supremacy for centuries” was corrected with the Battle of the Masts (655), the Emirate of Crete (c. 824/827–961) and the sack of Thessalonica (904).
Dromon: the first attestation of the term is no longer attributed to Procopius; it now cites Cassiodorus (Variae V.16–17, c. 526, Theodoric's thousand dromons), keeping Procopius for 533.

Greek Fire: the sentence “the secret was lost before the 13th century” was qualified. The last secure naval description cited is Anna Komnene's (1099, against the Pisans), and the loss of the secret is left as plausible but unproven.

Parthian Tactics: corrected the claim that the Strategikon required all horsemen to carry a bow. The Strategikon (I.2) expects archers among the Roman horsemen and reserves the lance for foreigners without skill in archery. Confirmed in the data that the civ has Thumb Ring and Heavy Cavalry Archer, but not Parthian Tactics.

Siege Engineers: Antioch (969) is no longer used as an example of a formal siege, because it was taken by a night assault with ladders. Replaced by Chandax (960–961), Mopsuestia and Tarsus (965), plus Zeugminon (1165) for the Komnenoi.

History text: new issue about the heavy infantry being described as “armored swordsmen” (they were mostly spearmen, skutatoi and menavlatoi) and about the alleged formal education of officers. New issue about 1453 as the end of the empire (the Morea fell in 1460 and Trebizond in 1461).

Belisarius: added that he never campaigned against the Slavs, and Mons Lactarius dated to 552/553. Nomisma: the “exaggeration” was reworded as rounding (c. 730 years of stability and almost 800 of existence), keeping the criticism of the idea of a standard for the whole Mediterranean.

Proposal “Skrinion tōn Barbarōn” replaced by “De Administrando Imperio”. The claim that the office was attested from the 6th century was wrong: the scrinium barbarorum appears in the Notitia Dignitatum (early 5th century), officials “epi tōn barbarōn” appear on seals of the 9th–10th centuries, and the espionage function is unproven.

The Themata proposal now includes cavalry, because many thematic stratiotai served on horseback. The proposal to rename Logistica now uses “Praecepta Militaria”, without asserting an uncertain technical Greek term (“Trigōnon”).

Varangian Guard: the date c. 988 now refers to the original contingent, and its formalisation as a personal guard is marked as disputed. The word pólútasvarf is attributed to the Heimskringla. Added a positive tree_issue (Paladin, Plate Barding, Hussar, Fast Fire Ship), confirmed in the tree files.

Krum: Serdica (809) was taken by deceit and promises after a siege, with the massacre of 6,000 soldiers, and not with siege engines. The engines built with the Arab deserter (settled in Adrianople by Nikephoros I) apply to Mesembria (812).

Corrected the claim that the civ loses “almost the whole monastery”. The data show that only Faith, Atonement, Block Printing and Sanctity are missing; Redemption, Illumination, Theocracy, Fervor, Devotion and Heresy are present. Verdict and tree_issue adjusted.

New tree_issues confirmed in the data: Champion and Paladin are missing (a balance irony), and Bombard Cannon, Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Tower are missing (consistent with the fall in 1396). Added Thumb Ring to the list of horse archer items present.

Names: added that krěpostĭ, in Old Slavonic, seems to mean mainly “strength/firmness”, the sense of “fortress” being essentially modern (claim marked as probable). Bagains: the citation of Slavova (2009) was verified and made more precise (bagain is a military rank with several grades; bagatur is an honorific title).

Varbitsa proposal redesigned so as not to duplicate the elevation mechanic the game already has (invisibility near forests and a first-attack bonus). Madgearu, The Asanids, dated to 2016 (Brill). History text: added the peace of Peter I (927–969) to the omissions.

fidelity_score lowered from 4 to 3 to keep the scale consistent: it has fewer plausible elements than Bulgarians, two unfounded elements, an inverted military identity and two serious errors in the text.

New tree_issue confirmed in the data: Heavy Cavalry Archer, Parthian Tactics and Thumb Ring are missing. The Armenian noble cavalry fought with lance and bow. The standalone Thumb Ring item was absorbed, and the missing Fast Fire Ship/Shipwright in a “Naval” civ were added.

Fereters: removed the categorical claim about the English feretrar. The origin of the name is left as undocumented (probably an echo of the Latin feretrum), with the Armenian parallel ajatar (Sarkis II, 15th century). The unfounded classification stands. The naval bonus no longer says “no basis” alongside a stretched rating; it now says “very weak basis” (the Cilician coast).

Coronation of Leo I: 6 January 1198 (some authors: 1199), with a crown promised by Henry VI and the papacy and delivered by Conrad of Mainz, instead of “sent by Henry VI”, who had already died in 1197. “Leftover pieces”: added the first Turkish raids into Vaspurakan (c. 1016–1021) as a factor in the cession.

Leo V: added that he was released before he died in Paris (1393). Hetum I: Smbat's mission (1247) is now distinguished from the king's journey (1254). Pakourianos: Anna Komnene attributes noble Armenian lineage to him, confirmed. Council of Dvin reworded as the split of c. 607–609 between Abraham I and Kirion I.

Monaspa: removed the unverified claim that the numbers (5,000) come from Matthew of Edessa and the Life of David. The strength is now “current in modern historiography, with an uncertain documentary basis”, and the composition is left as disputed. The translation of monaspa was adjusted to “host of servants”.

“Didgori charge” proposal: removed the “feigned desertion of 200 horsemen”, which has no support. Replaced by Ibn al-Athir's account of a Kipchak detachment that pretended to desert or to negotiate; added the Frankish contingent (Walter the Chancellor; Matthew of Edessa). Kipchaks: the chronicle's figure (40,000) marked as disputed.

Tree_issues corrected against the data: the civ has Galleon, Fast Fire Ship, Cannon Galleon (without Elite) and Hand Cannoneer, and lacks Carrack, Dry Dock and Shipwright. New positive tree_issue: Bombard Cannon, Bombard Tower and Paladin are missing, which is consistent.

Minor refinements: Vardzia begun under George III; Shirimni in 1021, with a new campaign in 1022; Tamar's birth marked as disputed; period starting c. 888 with Adarnase IV; contested updated with Ibn al-Athir's estimates for Didgori.

Note 3 corrected: the Armeniakon theme lay in north-eastern Anatolia and is not “Armenia”; the real Armenian themes (Taron, Vaspurakan, Ani/Iberia) were added. Note 4 corrected: the Dromon has a basis for the Goths (Cassiodorus, Theodoric's thousand dromons, c. 526), and is not “anachronistic/wrong” for them. Note 9: Dušan's empire dated to 1346–1355. Note 11 recalibrated (6/6/4/3). Note 12 added on the verification left incomplete because the web search limit was exhausted.

civs.represents: The European Huns: the confederation dominated by an elite of horse archers of steppe origin that appears north of the Black Sea c. 370 (Ammianus Marcellinus), settles on the Pannonian plain (c. 400–420) and reaches its peak under Rua/Ruga (c. 420–434/435), Bleda (until c. 445) and Attila (434–453). It included many subject peoples: Goths, Gepids, Heruli, Sciri, Rugii and Alans. In practice, the game's design mixes this period with later elements (Avars, Bulgars, Göktürks, Hephthalites) and with the Christian image of the “pagan Hun”, the “scourge of God”.
civs.period: c. 370–469 (peak in 434–453, under Attila; the empire breaks up after the battle of Nedao in 454, and Dengizich dies in 469). It almost entirely predates AoE2's c. 500–1500 window. Several elements (the title “tarkan”, the trebuchets) belong to the 6th–9th centuries.
civs.verdict: In terms of fidelity, the Huns are the weakest civ in this group. The core (cheap horse archers, no houses, fast stables) is a defensible abstraction of what Ammianus Marcellinus, Priscus of Panium and Sidonius Apollinaris describe. The rest is anachronistic or wrong. The “Tarkan” is a title attested among the Göktürks, Khazars, Bulgars and Hephthalites of the 6th–9th centuries, never among Attila's Huns. The trebuchet bonus refers to a weapon that is only documented in the Mediterranean from the Avar-Slav siege of Thessalonica (586) onwards, and the counterweight model that the game shows only appears in the 12th century. “Atheism” contradicts what the sources say about Hunnic religion: soothsayers, funeral rites and Attila's “sword of Mars”. The history text repeats classic errors: the stirrups, Szeged, the empire “from the Urals to the Rhône” and Châlons as the salvation of Christendom. Several of the problematic elements would make sense if the civ represented the Avars of Pannonia (567–796).
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Huns” (Gk. Οὖννοι, Lat. Hunni) is a Graeco-Roman exonym. We do not know what they called themselves or what language they spoke: the Turkic, Yeniseian and other hypotheses are all speculative. The civ represents a period (c. 370–469) earlier than the game's c. 500–1500 window, which forced the designers to “stretch” it forward in time: the Tarkan and the trebuchet bonus come from the Avar, Bulgar and Göktürk world (6th–9th centuries). Byzantine and Latin writers used “Hun” in an archaising way for almost all later nomads: Kutrigurs and Utigurs in Procopius, Avars in the Carolingian annals, and sometimes Magyars. In Central Asia, Iran and India, the term designates distinct groups (Kidarites, Hephthalites or “White Huns”, Alchon, the Indian “Huna”), whose connection to Attila's Huns is uncertain. Two medieval traditions added to the confusion: the Hungarian one (Simon of Kéza, Gesta Hunnorum et Hungarorum, c. 1282–1285), which made the Magyars descendants of Attila, and the Bulgarian one (the Nominalia of the Bulgarian khans), whose “Avitohol” is sometimes identified with Attila. Since AoE2 has no Avar civ, the Huns serve as generic “Pannonian nomads”.

elements.explanation: The Huns were above all horse archers (Ammianus 31.2; Sidonius Apollinaris), so “Cavalry Archer civilization” would be more accurate. The label also hides the fact that Attila's armies included large contingents of subject Germanic infantry, such as Ardaric's Gepids and Valamir's Ostrogoths (Jordanes, Getica 199–200).

elements.element: Do not need houses, but start with -100 wood
elements.explanation: Ammianus (31.2.4) says that the Huns avoided buildings “like tombs” and lived on horseback and in wagons, which reasonably justifies doing without houses. But this portrait dates from the 4th century and is partly an ethnographic topos: in 449, Priscus describes Attila's residence as a permanent village, with wooden houses, a plank enclosure with towers and a stone bathhouse built for Onegesius by a captive from Sirmium. The -100 wood is pure game balance.

elements.element: Cavalry Archers cost -10/20% in Castle/Imperial Age
elements.explanation: The backbone of the Hunnic military was the horse archer, armed with an asymmetric reflex composite bow; bone stiffening laths and gold-sheathed ceremonial bows appear in graves of the Hunnic period. Making the unit cheaper, and therefore more plentiful, translates this trait directly. The mechanism (a cost discount) is naturally a game convention.

elements.element: Trebuchets fire more accurately at units and small targets
elements.explanation: The traction trebuchet is only documented in the Mediterranean world from the Avar-Slav attack on Thessalonica (586) onwards, described in the Miracles of St Demetrius; whether the Avars brought it from the steppe or the Byzantines already knew it is debated. The counterweight trebuchet, which is what the game shows, only appears in the 12th century. The Huns took cities (Naissus in 442/443, Metz in 451, Aquileia in 452), but at Naissus Priscus describes suspended rams and wheeled platforms for archers, and Jordanes (Getica 221) speaks of “machinae” and “tormenta” at Aquileia, that is, Roman-type engines, not trebuchets.

elements.element: On Nomadic maps, the first Town Center spawns a scouting Horse
elements.explanation: A minor detail that alludes to wealth in horses and to mobility. It is harmless, but generic: it would suit any steppe people.

“Tarqan/tarkhan” is a dignitary's title attested among the Göktürks (Orkhon inscriptions, 8th century), the Khazars, the Danube Bulgars (Proto-Bulgarian inscriptions of the 9th century), the late Hephthalites (Tarkhan Nizak of Badghis, early 8th century), possibly the Avars, and later the Mongols (“darqan”, a status of exemption). The etymology is disputed. It never appears among Attila's Huns, of whose language only personal names and three words survive (medos, kamos, strava), and the Hunnic origin of those words is itself debated. The role of heavy cavalry that demolishes buildings is a vague abstraction of the sacking of cities, which the Huns carried out with siege engines and subject infantry, not with horsemen charging at walls.

elements.element: Marauders (Tarkans can be trained at Stables)
elements.explanation: Training Tarkans at the stables, en masse, captures large-scale raiding warfare well, such as the Balkan campaigns of 441–442 and 447. The link is reasonable, but it inherits the problem of the Tarkan name.

elements.element: Atheism (Enemy Relics -50% resources; Wonder/Relic victory +100 years)
elements.explanation: The Huns were not atheists. Jordanes (Getica 196) describes Attila's soothsayers examining the entrails of cattle and the veins of scraped bones before the Catalaunian Plains. According to Priscus (via Jordanes, Getica 183), Attila presented a sword found by a herdsman as the “sword of Mars”, a sign of divine favour. The strava and the chants at Attila's funeral were religious rites. The Greek word “atheos” existed in Antiquity, but as a polemical accusation (pagans applied it to Christians), not as a description of foreign peoples. The effect (devaluing relics, delaying victories) seems to draw on the later Christian image of the pagan Hun who destroyed churches and of the “scourge of God”, which is hagiography, not contemporary testimony.

An acceptable abstraction of the abundance of horses and of riding from childhood. Ammianus (31.2.6) describes the Huns as “glued” to their horses, on which they ate, drank and did business, and Sidonius Apollinaris (Carmina 2) says that a Hun child can barely stand and is already riding. Even so, it is generic: it applies to any steppe people.

tree_issues.item: Trebuchet (and the accuracy bonus) / no Onager
tree_issues.problem: For the 5th century, the logical choice would be the reverse: Roman-style torsion artillery (“tormenta” at Aquileia, according to Jordanes), rams and siege towers (Naissus, according to Priscus), and not trebuchets, which only appear in the Mediterranean at the end of the 6th century.
Faithful: Priscus describes rams suspended from beams and wheeled platforms for archers at the siege of Naissus.

The heaviest shock cavalry line is the one that least represents the Huns. The elite had some armour, but its strength was the bow. The confederation's heavy lancers were mostly allied or subject Alans, of Sarmatian tradition.

The absence of the Champion fits the equestrian nature of the Huns, but the game does not represent at all the subject Germanic infantry (Gepids, Ostrogoths, Rugii), which was decisive in Attila's armies.

tree_issues.item: Navy: Galleon, Hulk/War Hulk, Dromon, Dry Dock, Carvel Hull
tree_issues.problem: The Huns had no navy: according to Priscus, they crossed rivers in dugout canoes and in their subjects' boats. The Dromon is a Byzantine warship from the 6th century onwards, and the Hulk a northern European ship type of the Late Middle Ages. It is fair to note that the Dromon deliberately replaces the Cannon Galleon (the Huns also lack the Fast Fire Ship and the Carrack), which is less anachronistic than a ship with cannons. The navy is, even so, a universal concession of the game.

tree_issues.item: No House, Guard Tower, Keep, Fortified Wall (but with Palisade, Stone Wall, Gate and Watch Tower)
tree_issues.problem: The absence of houses and advanced fortifications is consistent with the nomadic image. The Palisade Walls and the Watch Towers are even defensible (the wooden enclosure with towers at Attila's residence, according to Priscus). The Stone Walls and the stone Gates are the least justified element.
A Hungarian term, probably of Serbian origin, only documented in the 15th century: anachronistic. The problem is common to almost all civs that have this unit.
The Alans integrated into the Hunnic confederation were heavy lancers of Sarmatian tradition. The absence is defensible, but it impoverishes the real diversity of the army.

history_text_issues.claim: The Huns are said to have come from the area of Mongolia and to have begun migrating westwards in the 3rd century, probably because of climate change.
history_text_issues.problem: The origin is presented as fact, the date is too early and the climatic cause is speculative.
history_text_issues.correction: The Huns only appear in the sources north of the Black Sea c. 370 (Ammianus). The link to the Xiongnu, proposed by de Guignes in 1757, is debated. De la Vaissière argues for continuity of the name: the Sogdian Ancient Letters (c. 313) use “xwn” for the Xiongnu. The genomic study by Gnecchi-Ruscone et al. (PNAS, 2025) found DNA segments shared between some individuals of the Hunnic period in the Carpathian Basin and the late Xiongnu elite, but also a highly heterogeneous population, with no large community of eastern ancestry. The hypothesis of drought in Central Asia (dendrochronology, c. 350–370) is only a hypothesis.

history_text_issues.claim: Thanks to their military prowess and discipline, the Huns are said to have been unstoppable and to have set off a “domino effect” that eventually brought down the Western Empire in 476.
history_text_issues.problem: It simplifies an open historiographical debate and omits that the Huns were also allies of Rome.
history_text_issues.correction: Heather (2005) assigns the Huns an indirect but strong causal role: the Gothic crossing of the Danube in 376 and the crossing of the Rhine in 406. Halsall, Goffart and others give more weight to internal Roman crises. The Huns also served Rome: Uldin against Radagaisus (406) and Aetius' auxiliaries against the Burgundians (436–437). By 476, the Hunnic empire had already been gone for two decades.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that “some believe they invented the stirrup” and that they shot standing in the stirrups, forwards, sideways and backwards.
history_text_issues.problem: Factual error: the Huns did not use stirrups.
history_text_issues.correction: The Huns used a wooden-framed saddle, without stirrups. The first stirrups are Chinese: a figurine from a tomb at Changsha (302) has a single mounting stirrup, and the tomb of Feng Sufu (415) has a pair. Stirrups reached Europe with the Avars in the 6th century, and Maurice's Strategikon (c. 600) is the first European reference. The thesis that the stirrup was decisive for the lance charge comes from Lynn White (1962) and is now widely contested.

history_text_issues.claim: The Hunnic headquarters is said to have been at the “city of Szeged”, by the Tisza.
history_text_issues.problem: The location is unknown and it was not a city.
history_text_issues.correction: Priscus (449) describes a royal village with a wooden palace, reached after crossing several rivers, one of them probably the Tisza. The exact location is unknown and there are several hypotheses on the Great Hungarian Plain.

history_text_issues.claim: The Hunnic empire is said to have stretched from the Urals to the Rhône.
history_text_issues.problem: Territorial exaggeration.
history_text_issues.correction: Hunnic hegemony extended, at best, from the Pontic steppe and the Caucasus (the Akatziri were subjugated c. 448) to the middle Danube and the vicinity of the Rhine, through tributary peoples. The Huns never controlled Gaul: they fought there as auxiliaries of Aetius (430s) or during the invasion of 451.

history_text_issues.claim: The Hunnic composite bow is said to have been far superior to anything used in the West.
history_text_issues.problem: It overstates the technological gap.
history_text_issues.correction: The Romans had used composite bows with bone laths since the early Empire, especially in eastern auxiliary units (laths have been found at forts in Britain, such as Bar Hill). The Hunnic bow was larger and asymmetric, and it was imitated, but its advantage has been exaggerated by historiography.

history_text_issues.claim: The Huns are said to have been a light cavalry army, with a political structure that depended on a strong leader.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the subject infantry and the allies, and simplifies an open debate.
history_text_issues.correction: In 451, Attila's army included a great deal of Germanic infantry and Alan contingents. As for the political structure, Hyun Jin Kim (2013) argues for an organised state hierarchy, with the “logades” as the elite; Thompson, Heather and others see a more fragile confederation, dependent on plunder and tribute.

history_text_issues.claim: Attila, leader from 433, is said to have launched raids into southern Russia and Persia.
history_text_issues.problem: Confusion of chronology and of protagonists.
history_text_issues.correction: The great Hunnic raid across the Caucasus against Persia and the Roman East took place in 395–396, under Basich and Kursich, before Attila. Attila shared power with Bleda from 434/435 to c. 445. Priscus only mentions speculation about a plan by Attila against Persia.

history_text_issues.claim: In 450, Attila is said to have crossed the Rhine with perhaps 100,000 warriors and sacked most of the cities of northern France.
history_text_issues.problem: The date is wrong, the numbers have no basis and the extent of the sacking is exaggerated.
history_text_issues.correction: The invasion of Gaul took place in 451. The numbers are unknown (Jordanes goes as far as half a million, an absurd figure). Metz was sacked, Orléans was besieged and relieved, but Paris and Troyes were spared, as the legends of Saint Genevieve and Saint Lupus recall.

history_text_issues.claim: Aetius is said to have assembled a Gallo-Roman army and defeated Attila at Châlons.
history_text_issues.problem: It erases the real composition of the coalition and the uncertain outcome of the battle.
history_text_issues.correction: The coalition was dominated by the Visigoths of Theodoric I, who died in the battle, and included Sangiban's Alans, Franks, Burgundians and others (Jordanes, Getica 191). The battle of the Catalaunian Plains (or Campus Mauriacus) has an uncertain location and had a tactically indecisive outcome; Attila withdrew in good order and invaded Italy the following year.

history_text_issues.claim: The defeat at Châlons is said to have been one of the decisive battles of history, which prevented the collapse of Christianity and domination “by Asian peoples”.
history_text_issues.problem: A Eurocentric and outdated 19th-century framing.
history_text_issues.correction: This reading comes from Edward Creasy (Fifteen Decisive Battles of the World, 1851). Attila had no anti-Christian agenda whatsoever, he had Roman Christians in his service and some of his Germanic subjects were already Homoian (“Arian”) Christians. The Hunnic empire broke up a few years later in any case. Current historiography plays down the “decisive” character of the battle.

history_text_issues.claim: Attila is said to have agreed to withdraw from Italy after the meeting with Pope Leo I; refugees are said to have founded Venice.
history_text_issues.problem: It simplifies the reasons for the withdrawal; the founding of Venice is tradition (the text acknowledges this).
history_text_issues.correction: The meeting by the Mincio (452), with Leo, Avienus and Trygetius, is historical (Prosper of Aquitaine). Hydatius also attributes the withdrawal to famine, disease and attacks by troops sent by the eastern emperor Marcian. The settlement of the Venetian lagoon was gradual.

history_text_issues.claim: The Huns are said to have eventually disappeared under a wave of new invaders, such as the Avars.
history_text_issues.problem: Compressed chronology.
history_text_issues.correction: The Hunnic empire fell apart in 454 (Nedao) and Dengizich died in 469. The Avars only reached central Europe in the 560s; in between, the groups that inherited from the Huns were the Kutrigurs, Utigurs and Bulgars.

history_text_issues.claim: Paragraphs after the game text (editorial commentary from the wiki, not official text): Huns “active in the Middle Ages”, “White Huns” as a branch of the Huns, “killed by the Turks” in India in 528, massacred in 563, and the name “Hungarians” derived from the Latin word for Huns.
history_text_issues.problem: Several errors, although they are not the game's responsibility.
history_text_issues.correction: The Huns belong to Late Antiquity, not to the Middle Ages. The link between the Hephthalites and the European Huns is uncertain (it is true that they helped Kavad I regain the Persian throne in 498/499). In India, Mihirakula's Alchon Huns were defeated by Yasodharman (c. 528), not by Turks. The Hephthalites were destroyed by the Göktürk–Sasanian alliance c. 557–560. “Hungarian” comes from Onogur (via Slavic *ǫgrinъ, Lat. Ungri); the initial H- was added by association with the Huns.

missing_features: The subject Germanic and Alan infantry (Gepids, Ostrogoths, Heruli, Rugii, Alans), which made up a large part of Attila's armies.

The tribute economy: the Roman gold paid under the treaty of Margus (435 or 439, 700 pounds of gold a year) and the peace of Anatolius (443 or 447, dating disputed: 6,000 pounds in arrears and 2,100 a year). It was the engine of Hunnic power.
Service as allies and auxiliaries of Rome (Uldin in 406; Aetius in the 430s) and the role of secretaries and officials of Roman origin at Attila's court (Orestes, Constantius).
The siege engines of Naissus (442/443) and Aquileia (452): rams, wheeled towers for archers and Roman-type artillery.
The lasso used in combat, according to Ammianus 31.2.9.
The sacral dimension of power: the soothsayers, the “sword of Mars” and Attila's funeral with the strava.
Cultural markers: artificial cranial deformation, bronze cauldrons, diadems and the diplomatic banquet described by Priscus.

proposals.title: Reinterpret the civ as the Avars (or create an Avar civ)
proposals.description: Shift the civ's focus to the Avar Khaganate of Pannonia (567–796), which fits within the game's window. Keep the trebuchet accuracy bonus and a unit bearing a dignitary's title. Add heavy cavalry with stirrups and lamellar armour, with protected horses, fighting with both bow and lance. Attila's Huns would be left for scenarios or campaigns.
proposals.historical_basis: Maurice's Strategikon (c. 600) describes the Avars with stirrups, mail coats, protected horses for the chiefs and a dual weapon (bow and lance). The Miracles of St Demetrius report the use of traction trebuchets at Thessalonica (586), and the Avars besieged Constantinople in 626. W. Pohl, The Avars (2018).

proposals.title: Replace “Atheism” with “Roman Tribute”
proposals.description: Castle Age tech: the player receives a passive gold income for each enemy Town Center or Castle within X tiles of Hunnic military units, or a one-off gold payment whenever they destroy a high-value enemy building. It represents the extortion of tribute through military threat.
proposals.historical_basis: Treaty of Margus (435 or 439: the tribute doubles to 700 pounds of gold a year) and peace of Anatolius (443 or 447: 6,000 pounds in arrears and 2,100 a year). Priscus, fragments; C. Kelly, Attila the Hun (2008).

proposals.title: Replace the trebuchet bonus with “Engines of Naissus”
proposals.description: Remove the trebuchet accuracy bonus and give access to the Onager. Instead of the bonus: Battering Ram-line and Siege Tower with +20% HP and -25% cost, and Siege Towers available in the Feudal Age, with garrisoned archers shooting from the tower.
proposals.historical_basis: Priscus (fr. 6.2 Blockley) describes the siege of Naissus: wheeled platforms, protected by wickerwork and hides, from which archers swept the battlements, and rams suspended from beams that breached the wall. Jordanes (Getica 221) mentions engines and “tormenta” at the siege of Aquileia (452).

proposals.title: “Germanic Federates”
proposals.description: Barracks units cost -15% food and gold. A Castle Age tech gives access to the Champion line (or to a “Gepid Warrior” unit trained at the Castle), representing the infantry of the subject peoples.
proposals.historical_basis: Jordanes (Getica 199–200) describes Ardaric's Gepids and the Ostrogoths of Valamir, Theodemir and Vidimir in Attila's army in 451. The revolt of these subjects at Nedao (454) put an end to the Hunnic empire.

proposals.title: Rename the Tarkan to “Logas” (Logades)
proposals.description: Keep a cavalry unique unit, but call it “Logas” (plural “Logades”), Attila's trusted elite. The unit would become an elite heavy horse archer instead of an anti-building specialist.
proposals.historical_basis: Priscus uses the Greek term “logades” (“picked men”) for Attila's notables, such as Onegesius, Edeco and Orestes. Whether it was a technical title is disputed: Hyun Jin Kim (2013) interprets them as a hierarchical aristocracy, others as a simple descriptive expression.

proposals.title: Hunnic “Lasso”
proposals.description: Imperial Age tech: each Cavalry Archer's first attack against a unit slows it by 30% for 2 seconds (the game already has slowing mechanics).
proposals.historical_basis: Ammianus Marcellinus (31.2.9) reports that, while an opponent was warding off their sword blows, the Huns threw lassos of plaited strips over him to immobilise him.

proposals.title: Correct the history text
proposals.description: Remove the stirrups, Szeged as a “city” and the phrase “from the Urals to the Rhône”. Date the invasion of Gaul to 451, attribute the Persian raid to Basich and Kursich (395–396), describe Aetius' coalition with the Visigoths and abandon Creasy's framing of the “salvation of Christendom”.
proposals.historical_basis: Ammianus, Priscus, Jordanes, Hydatius and Prosper; Maenchen-Helfen (1973); Heather (2005); Kelly (2008); Kim (2013).

contested: The Xiongnu–Hun link: de la Vaissière and Kim argue for continuity (at least of name and of elite); Maenchen-Helfen and others are sceptical. The 2025 genomic work supports a partial link, at the level of some elite individuals, within a heterogeneous population.
The language of the Huns: Turkic, Yeniseian, mixed or unknown. The data are scarce (personal names and three words whose origin is also disputed).
The weight of the Huns in the fall of the West: Heather (strong indirect cause) versus Halsall and Goffart (internal Roman factors).
The arrival of the traction trebuchet in the Mediterranean: introduced by the Avars from the steppe, or already known to the Byzantines before 586.
The chronology of the treaties: Margus (435 or 439) and the peace of Anatolius (443 or 447); also the date of the siege of Naissus (442 or 443).
The location, the exact date and the “decisive” character of the Catalaunian Plains (451).
The nature of Hunnic power: a hierarchical state (Kim) or a loose confederation, dependent on plunder and tribute (Thompson, Heather).
The identification of “Avitohol”, in the Bulgarian Nominalia, with Attila.
The size of Hunnic armies, traditionally inflated by the ancient sources.
key_sources: Ammianus Marcellinus, Res Gestae, XXXI.2
Priscus of Panium, fragments (ed. and trans. R. C. Blockley, The Fragmentary Classicising Historians of the Later Roman Empire, 1983)
Jordanes, Getica (551)
Hydatius, Chronicle; Prosper of Aquitaine, Chronicle
Sidonius Apollinaris, Carmina (Panegyrics)
Maurice's Strategikon (c. 600), for the contrast with the Avars
Miracles of St Demetrius (siege of Thessalonica, 586)
O. J. Maenchen-Helfen, The World of the Huns (1973)
E. A. Thompson, A History of Attila and the Huns (1948; reissued as The Huns, 1996, with an afterword by P. Heather)
P. Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005); Empires and Barbarians (2009)
C. Kelly, Attila the Hun: Barbarian Terror and the Fall of the Roman Empire (2008)
Hyun Jin Kim, The Huns, Rome and the Birth of Europe (2013); The Huns (2016)
