W. Pohl, The Avars: A Steppe Empire in Central Europe, 567–822 (2018)

civs.represents: The Mongol Empire (Yeke Mongγol Ulus), founded by Temüjin/Chinggis Khan in 1206, and its expansion under Ögödei, Güyük and Möngke until the division of c. 1260. More loosely, it also represents the Toluid successor khanates: the Yuan in China (1271–1368) and the Ilkhanate in Persia (1256–1335). The Ulus of Jochi (“Golden Horde”) and the Timurids go to the Tatars civ, although the Mongols' history text also talks about Timur.
civs.period: 1206–1368 (peak in 1206–1294). The history text extends to Timur (1370–1405).
civs.verdict: In essence, the Mongols are among the best-grounded civs in the game. They have elite horse archers, hunting as military training (the great hunt, or nerge), hardy light cavalry thanks to remounts, and a mobile siege train served by Chinese and Muslim engineers. The flaws are mostly of omission and distribution. The kheshig, Chinggis's imperial guard, exists in the game only as the Tatars' Keshik. There is no trace at all of the yam postal relay, the decimal organisation, religious tolerance or Eurasian trade, and the tech tree ignores the gunpowder used by the Yuan. “Mangudai” has a real basis (the Manggud tribe, Chinggis's vanguard), but the popular idea of a “suicide squad” has no support in the known primary sources. The history text gets the general chronology right, but has specific errors: Ögödei “dying on campaign”, Timur “a descendant of Chinggis”, and death tolls given uncritically.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Mongol” is the endonym (Mongγol), which is positive. The problem is one of scope. The civ covers the unified empire (1206–1260) and, implicitly, the Yuan and the Ilkhanate, which were very different realities: Yuan China had a navy, paper money, gunpowder and a Chinese-style bureaucracy; the Ilkhanate converted to Islam under Ghazan, in 1295. The history text includes Timur, whom the game also assigns to the Tatars, which duplicates and confuses the two civs. The kheshig, the quintessential Mongol institution, appears in the Tatars. In Europe and in Rus', the Mongols were called “Tartars”, and in China “Dada”, which feeds the confusion with the Tatars civ.

elements.explanation: John of Plano Carpini (Ystoria Mongalorum, 1247) says that each warrior had to carry two or three bows (or at least one good one) and three large quivers. The horse archer was the foundation of the army.

Juvaini describes the great hunt (nerge/jerge), in which the army encircled the game for weeks with the discipline of a campaign, and attributes to Chinggis the idea that hunting was the proper training for commanders. Hunting was also vital to the survival of Temüjin's family after it was abandoned (Secret History). Caveat: the Mongol economic base was herding (horses, sheep, milk); hunting was a supplement and a military school. Even so, it is one of the best translations of a historical trait into a game mechanic.
An abstraction of volume of fire, of training from childhood and of saturation tactics (continuous shooting before the charge). It is not literally verifiable, but it is consistent with the sources.

elements.element: Scout Cavalry-line and Steppe Lancers +20/30% HP in Castle/Imperial Age
elements.explanation: Each warrior took several remounts (the sources speak of many; historians such as Timothy May estimate 3–5 per man), which gave the mounted forces exceptional endurance. Mongol lancers in lamellar armour were real. More HP is a reasonable translation of this endurance.

The unit itself, an elite horse archer, is faithful. The name comes from the Manggud (Mangqut), a tribe that, with the Uru'ud, formed Chinggis's vanguard against the Kereyid at Qalaqaljit Elet, in 1203 (Secret History, §170–171, with Quyildar and Jürchedei). The popular explanation as a “suicide squad” has no support in the known primary sources and appears to be a modern construction.

elements.element: Nomads (Lost Houses do not decrease population space)
elements.explanation: It alludes to the collapsible ger (yurts), carried on wagons: Rubruck tells of 22 oxen pulling a single house on one cart. But the effect (losing houses does not reduce population) is minimal and captures very little of that reality.

The Mongols had a corps of Chinese and Muslim engineers: according to Juvaini and Rashid al-Din, Möngke sent with Hülegü a thousand families of Chinese engine operators, naphtha throwers and crossbowmen. The engines were often built on site with levied materials and labour. The mobility of the siege train is real, but the name “Drill” (training) is odd.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Scout Cavalry-line +2 line of sight
elements.explanation: The Mongols relied on long-range reconnaissance, on scouts spread out in a fan, and on information from merchants and spies, as in the preparation of the 1241 campaign. It is a reasonable abstraction.

tree_issues.item: No Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon or Bombard Tower (but has Cannon Galleon)
tree_issues.problem: This is inconsistent. For the 1206–1260 core, the absence of cannon is defensible (the bombs and fire lances of Kaifeng, 1232, were Jin weapons used against the Mongols, who later adopted them). But the Yuan used early firearms: the Heilongjiang hand cannon (c. 1288) is associated with the campaign against Nayan, and the Xanadu cannon bears the date 1298. They also used ceramic bombs (tetsuhō) in Japan in 1274 and 1281, confirmed by the underwater finds at Takashima.
Carpini describes horse armour of hardened leather, in several lamellar pieces, for the heavy cavalry. Its absence contradicts the sources.
Defensible: Mongol heavy cavalry consisted of lancers in lamellar armour, closer to the Steppe Lancer than to the European knight.
The Mongols used Bactrian camels as pack animals, not as combat cavalry.

tree_issues.item: Siege Onager, Heavy Scorpion, Siege Ram, Siege Engineers
tree_issues.problem: Faithful. The Mongols employed Chinese and Persian engineers, siege crossbows and catapults at Kaifeng (1232), Baghdad (1258) and Xiangyang (1268–1273). At the last of these, the “huihui pao” counterweight trebuchets were built by the Muslim engineers Ismail and Ala al-Din.
This is odd for the empire that did most to protect Eurasian trade, with ortoq partnerships, paiza safe-conducts, Yuan paper money and the “Pax Mongolica”. The civ has no trade bonus at all.

Plausible, with irony: the Yuan fleets against Japan (1274: c. 900 ships; 1281: c. 4,400) were hastily built by Korean and Chinese shipyards. The archaeology at Takashima (Randall Sasaki) shows poorly built ships and even river vessels. “Cheap and fast” is accurate; the quality is not.
A 15th-century Hungarian term, anachronistic for the Mongols.
Consistent: pike infantry was not part of the Mongol army proper.

history_text_issues.claim: Translates “Genghis Khan” as “powerful ruler”.
history_text_issues.problem: The meaning is debated.
history_text_issues.correction: The proposals include “oceanic/universal ruler” (from Turkic tengiz, “sea”, Pelliot) and “firm/hard ruler” (Igor de Rachewiltz, from Mongolian čing). It should be presented as a hypothesis.

history_text_issues.claim: Attributes to Chinggis the ambition of ruling all the lands between the Pacific and the Atlantic.
history_text_issues.problem: Presents a disputed point as certain.
history_text_issues.correction: The ideology of universal rule by mandate of Heaven (Möngke Tengri) is explicit mainly in his successors: Güyük's letter to Innocent IV (1246) and Möngke's to Louis IX, carried by Rubruck. Whether and when Chinggis formulated it is debated; no document attributes to him a plan to reach the Atlantic.

history_text_issues.claim: Chinggis supposedly started with only about 25,000 warriors.
history_text_issues.problem: The figure has no clear source.
history_text_issues.correction: The numbers for the beginning of Temüjin's career are unknown. In 1206, the Secret History (§202) lists 95 minggan (nominal units of a thousand), which gives a theoretical order of magnitude of c. 95,000 men.

history_text_issues.claim: Chinggis supposedly took Beijing in 1215, in a campaign that may have cost 30 million Chinese lives.
history_text_issues.problem: The figure and the attribution are misleading.
history_text_issues.correction: Zhongdu (Beijing) fell in 1215 to Mongol generals (Samukha and the Khitan defector Shimo Ming'an), without Chinggis present. The figures of millions dead are inferred from the huge drop between the Jin tax registers of the early 13th century and the Mongol censuses of the 1230s. That drop reflects deaths, but also flight and the collapse of tax registration over more than twenty years of war (1211–1234), not a single campaign.

history_text_issues.claim: Bukhara (1220) was supposedly razed by fire and all its inhabitants murdered.
history_text_issues.problem: Exaggerated.
history_text_issues.correction: According to Juvaini, the fire spread mainly through the wooden houses. The citadel garrison was massacred, the population was expelled and despoiled, the artisans deported and the men forcibly conscripted (hashar) for the siege of Samarkand. Total massacres are better documented at Nishapur, Merv and Urgench (1221).

history_text_issues.claim: Ögödei supposedly advanced into Europe and destroyed Kiev in 1240.
history_text_issues.problem: Confuses who ruled with who commanded.
history_text_issues.correction: The western campaign of 1236–1242 was commanded by Batu and Subutai, with Güyük and Möngke. Ögödei stayed in Mongolia.

history_text_issues.claim: Ögödei supposedly died on campaign in 1241, forcing the whole army to withdraw.
history_text_issues.problem: Factual error about his death and simplification of a debate.
history_text_issues.correction: Ögödei died in Mongolia on 11 December 1241, after a night of drinking. The reasons for the withdrawal from Hungary in 1242 are debated: the succession (already in Carpini), Batu's own interests, logistics, or a wet climate that flooded the plain (Büntgen and Di Cosmo, 2016).

history_text_issues.claim: Says that “Europe was spared”.
history_text_issues.problem: Major omission.
history_text_issues.correction: The Golden Horde subjugated Rus' for about two centuries, attacked Poland (1259–1260, 1287–1288) and Hungary (1285–1286), and made Bulgaria a vassal.

history_text_issues.claim: Hülegü supposedly “exterminated” the Muslim “Assassins”.
history_text_issues.problem: Exaggeration.
history_text_issues.correction: Hülegü destroyed the Nizari Ismaili state in Persia (fall of Alamut, 1256) and massacred many of its members, but the Syrian fortresses held out until the Mamluk conquest and the Nizari community has survived to this day.

history_text_issues.claim: In Baghdad (1258), most of the 100,000 inhabitants were supposedly murdered.
history_text_issues.problem: The figures are uncertain.
history_text_issues.correction: Estimates range from tens of thousands to Rashid al-Din's 800,000, and the city's actual population is unknown. The Christians were spared, partly through the intercession of Doquz Khatun.

history_text_issues.claim: Ain Jalut (1260) supposedly put an end to the Mongol threat to Islam and its holy cities.
history_text_issues.problem: Problematic framing and factually incomplete.
history_text_issues.correction: At Ain Jalut, the Mamluks defeated a reduced force under Kitbuqa, after Hülegü had withdrawn the bulk of the army. The Ilkhanids invaded Syria again in 1281 (Homs), 1299–1300 (Mongol victory at Wadi al-Khazandar and temporary occupation of Damascus) and 1303 (Marj al-Saffar). Moreover, the Ilkhanate became Muslim under Ghazan (1295), and Berke of the Golden Horde, already a Muslim, allied himself with the Mamluks.

history_text_issues.claim: The empire supposedly reached the Baltic Sea and controlled parts of Vietnam, Burma and India.
history_text_issues.problem: Territorial exaggeration.
history_text_issues.correction: The Mongols never ruled the Baltic coast: Novgorod paid tribute without being conquered. Đại Việt repelled three invasions (1258, 1285 and 1287–1288, with the battle of Bạch Đằng in 1288). Pagan was invaded and northern Burma briefly had a Yuan province. In India, control was limited, intermittently, to parts of the Punjab and Sind.

history_text_issues.claim: Timur was supposedly a Turco-Mongol warrior who claimed descent from Chinggis Khan and sought to restore the Mongol Empire.
history_text_issues.problem: Factual error about Timur's legitimacy; an aim presented as certain.
history_text_issues.correction: Timur, of the Turkicised Barlas tribe, did not claim descent from Chinggis. He legitimised himself through marriage to Chinggisid princesses (hence the title güregen, “son-in-law”) and ruled through puppet khans (Suyurghatmish, Sultan Mahmud). Later Timurid genealogy (the Gur-i Amir inscription) created a mythical common ancestor (Bodonchar, son of Alan Qo'a), not direct descent. His aims are debated (Manz).

history_text_issues.claim: In 1398, Timur supposedly sacked Delhi and murdered 100,000 inhabitants.
history_text_issues.problem: Conflates two episodes.
history_text_issues.correction: The figure of 100,000 comes mainly from the execution of Indian prisoners ordered before the battle, for fear that they would join the enemy (Yazdi). The massacre of Delhi's population came afterwards, during the sack, following a revolt against the troops; its scale is unknown.

history_text_issues.claim: For lack of stable government, the empire inherited by Timur's sons supposedly fell apart quickly.
history_text_issues.problem: Simplifies the Timurid period.
history_text_issues.correction: After a few years of succession war, Shah Rukh reunified most of the empire and ruled from Herat until 1447; it was mainly the west that was lost (to the Qara Qoyunlu). The Timurids lasted until 1507, and Babur founded the Mughal Empire in 1526.

history_text_issues.claim: The Mongols supposedly followed “in the footsteps of the Huns”, their predecessors a thousand years earlier.
history_text_issues.problem: Suggests an undemonstrated continuity.
history_text_issues.correction: There is no demonstrated ethnic or political continuity between the European Huns and the Mongols. The similarity is one of way of life and tactics.

missing_features: The kheshig, Chinggis's imperial guard and training school for cadres (assigned, in the game, to the Tatars).
The yam/örtöö, the network of couriers and relay stations institutionalised by Ögödei (c. 1234–1235), and the paiza tablets.
The decimal organisation (arban, jaghun, minggan, tümen) and the tribal reorganisation of 1206.
The tactics of feigned retreat, envelopment and fan-shaped encirclement, and psychological warfare (surrender or massacre).
Trade and finance: ortoq partners, Yuan paper money (chao) and the protection of Silk Road caravans.
Religious tolerance and the tax exemptions (darqan/tarkhan) for Buddhist, Taoist, Christian and Muslim clergy; the Karakorum religious debate (1254).
The systematic deportation of artisans and engineers and the forced conscription of captives (hashar).
Steppe logistics: dried meat (borts), kumis and dried milk carried by each rider.
The naval dimension and gunpowder of the Yuan era (Japan 1274/1281; Java 1293).

proposals.title: “Kheshig” for the Mongols
proposals.description: Move the concept of the Tatars' Keshik to the Mongols (or share it). Castle Age tech: the Castle can now train an elite guard (“Kheshig”) of heavy cavalry with bow and lance. Alternative: all units trained at the Castle gain +15% HP, and the King (in regicide) gains +100% HP.
proposals.historical_basis: The Secret History (§191 and §224–234) describes the creation of the guard in 1204 (70 day guards and 80 night guards) and its expansion to 10,000 men in 1206, including the quiver-bearers (qorchi). The kheshig trained future commanders and governors.

proposals.title: “Örtöö” (yam)
proposals.description: Trade Carts +20% speed, Outposts and Watch Towers +3 line of sight, and mounted units slowly regain HP near an Outpost. Represents the network of relay stations and the flow of information.
proposals.historical_basis: Ögödei institutionalised the yam c. 1234–1235. Marco Polo describes stations every 25–30 miles with hundreds of horses, and the paiza tablets guaranteed their bearers passage and mounts.

proposals.title: “Huihui Pao” and Yuan gunpowder
proposals.description: Give the Mongols a trebuchet tech with +2 range and 50% faster construction (the concept of the current Timurid Siegecraft). Add Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Tower in the Imperial Age, without Bombard Cannon.
proposals.historical_basis: The Muslim engineers Ismail and Ala al-Din built counterweight trebuchets for Kublai at the siege of Xiangyang/Fancheng (1273). There are Yuan hand cannons (Heilongjiang, c. 1288; Xanadu, 1298) and tetsuhō bombs recovered at Takashima (invasions of 1274/1281).

proposals.title: Collapsible ger
proposals.description: Mongol Houses can be packed (like a Trebuchet) onto a slow wagon and set up elsewhere, keeping the population they provide. Replaces the Nomads tech, which would become redundant.
proposals.historical_basis: Rubruck (1253–1255) and Carpini describe felt yurts carried whole on large ox-drawn carts, and camps that moved seasonally.

proposals.title: “Noyan” and decimal organisation
proposals.description: A command unit trained at the Castle, a horseman without much attack power, with an aura similar to that of the Roman Centurion: mounted units within a 6-tile radius gain +1/+1 armour and +10% attack speed.
proposals.historical_basis: The decimal hierarchy (arban of 10, jaghun of 100, minggan of 1,000, tümen of 10,000) and the noyan appointed by Chinggis in 1206 (Secret History, §202), commanded by flag and drum signals (Carpini).

proposals.title: “Darqan” (religious tolerance)
proposals.description: Monasteries and Monks -33% cost. Each Monastery generates a small trickle of gold (+0.1 per second), representing the tax exemptions granted to the clergy in exchange for prayers for the khan.
proposals.historical_basis: Chinggis exempted the Taoist Changchun and his order (1223). The khans extended darqan/tarkhan status to the Buddhist, Christian, Muslim and Taoist clergy, and Möngke organised the Karakorum religious debate (1254, reported by Rubruck).

contested: The meaning of “Chinggis”: “oceanic/universal” or “firm/hard”.
When the ideology of universal rule arose: with Chinggis or only with his successors.
The death tolls of the conquests (northern China, Khwarazm, Baghdad): historical demography gives widely divergent estimates, and the tax registers mix deaths, flight and administrative collapse.
The reasons for the withdrawal from Hungary in 1242: succession, Batu's strategy, logistics or climate (Büntgen and Di Cosmo, 2016).
Mongol use of gunpowder in the West (for example, at Mohi, 1241): some authors assert it, but Kenneth Chase and others see no solid evidence.
What the “mangudai” were: the ethnonym Manggud is certain, but the idea of a “suicide” unit has no known primary source.
The assessment of the “Pax Mongolica”: positive readings (Weatherford, Allsen, Favereau) versus the traditional emphasis on destruction.
The real size of Mongol armies and the weight of non-Mongol contingents.
How decisive Ain Jalut was, given the Ilkhanate's later campaigns in Syria.
key_sources: The Secret History of the Mongols (trans. Igor de Rachewiltz, 2004/2006)
ʿAta-Malik Juvaini, Tarikh-i Jahangushay (trans. J. A. Boyle, The History of the World-Conqueror)

civs.represents: A composite civ that combines two powers. The first is the Ulus of Jochi (“Golden Horde”), the western wing of the Mongol Empire, Turkicised and Islamised, from c. 1242 to 1502. The second is the Timurid Empire (1370–1507), of Timur and his successors, in Central Asia and Iran. The name also refers to the original Tatar confederation of eastern Mongolia, destroyed by Chinggis in 1202, and to the European exonym “Tartars”. The game's campaign is that of Timur (Tamerlane).
civs.period: c. 1242–1502 (Golden Horde) and 1370–1507 (Timurids). Includes references to the 8th–12th centuries for the original Tatars.
civs.verdict: The Tatars are a kind of “leftovers civ” from the Mongol conquests. They combine two powers that ended up as mortal enemies: Timur began by backing Tokhtamysh in winning the throne of the Horde (1376–1378), but then devastated it in 1391 and 1395. They receive a typically Mongol institution (the kheshig) and a 20th-century myth (the silk shirts). There are things the civ gets right: herding, the thumb ring and shooting backwards, Timurid siege capability and, with reservations about the sources, the flaming camels of Delhi (1398). But the elevation bonus is unfounded, and almost everything that defined these states is missing: Islam (Berke, Özbeg, Timur's religiosity), the trade of Sarai, Caffa and Tana, the tribute system imposed on the Rus', and the architectural and scientific patronage of Samarkand. The history text is reasonable and honest about the ambiguity of the name, but it reinforces the fusion of the two realities.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Tatar” is an exonym whose meaning has varied. It first designated a confederation in eastern Mongolia that was an enemy of the Mongols and was annihilated by Chinggis in 1202. Then Europe and the Rus' applied it to the Mongols themselves; the spelling “Tartari” comes from the pun on Tartarus, already present in Matthew Paris. Later it came to designate distinct Turkic-speaking peoples: the Volga Tatars (largely heirs of the Volga Bulgars and the Kipchaks), the Crimean Tatars and the Siberian Tatars. The civ merges the Golden Horde with the Timurids, when Timur was precisely the great devastator of the Horde. It also receives the kheshig, which belongs first and foremost to the Mongols. There is overlap with the Cumans: the Golden Horde was Kipchak-speaking and Muslim sources call its territory Dasht-i Qipchaq (hence the modern name “Kipchak Khanate”). And there is overlap with the Mongols, whose history text also narrates Timur. The Crimean Khanate (1441–1783) falls almost entirely outside the game's window.

elements.explanation: Suits the Golden Horde, whose armies were essentially made up of horse archers. It is less suited to the Timurids, whose armies combined heavy cavalry, infantry, engineers and even captured elephants.
Herding (sheep, horses, cattle) was the economic base of the Horde. Rubruck (1253) and Ibn Battuta (1332–1334) describe immense herds, mutton and kumis. It is a coherent abstraction.

elements.element: Units deal +25% damage when fighting from higher elevation
elements.explanation: The advantage of fighting from above is universal. There is no specific association of the Golden Horde or the Timurids with fighting from high ground, and steppe warfare was waged mainly on the plains. It is a pure gameplay bonus.

elements.element: New Town Centers spawn 2 Sheep starting in Castle Age
elements.explanation: Represents each new camp as a pastoral node. The link is weak, but consistent with the theme.

Drawing the bow with the thumb and a ring, shooting backwards and the feigned retreat are well documented in steppe warfare and in the thumb rings found at Horde sites. Examples: Edigu lured and enveloped Vytautas's army at the Battle of the Vorskla (1399), and Timur and Tokhtamysh manoeuvred in this way at Kondurcha (1391). The name “Parthian” is classical, but the technique is the same.

The kheshig was the imperial guard of Chinggis and the great khans (Secret History, §191 and §224–234). It persisted in the successor states, such as the Yuan and the Ilkhanate, and it probably also existed in the Horde, so a heavy guard cavalry is defensible in a “successor” civ. The main problem is one of distribution: it is the Mongol institution par excellence and it is absent from the Mongols civ. The effect of generating gold in combat is pure gameplay, perhaps inspired by plunder.

Based on the episode at the Battle of Delhi (17 December 1398): Timur is said to have sent camels loaded with burning straw and wood against the sultanate's elephants. The account appears mainly in Timur's pseudo-memoirs (Malfuzat-i Timuri, from the 17th century, of very doubtful authenticity) and in later narratives; the Timurid accounts of the battle lay more stress on ditches, tethered buffaloes and iron caltrops. It is a unique, Timurid episode, not a Golden Horde one.

The idea that Mongol warriors wore silk shirts to make it easier to extract arrows does not appear in any known medieval source. The earliest identified mention is that of Michael Prawdin (Dschingis-Khan, 1934), who seems to have modelled it on the silk bulletproof vests of the early 20th century. Carpini describes lamellar armour of hardened leather and of iron. Silk was, however, a luxury good and a mark of distinction in the Horde and in the Timurid world. The effect (+1/+1 armour for light cavalry) is generic.

Timur conducted many sieges with engines, mines and towers: Urgench (destroyed in 1388), Baghdad (1401) and Smyrna (1402), taken from the Hospitallers in about two weeks. The name is correct for the Timurids, but it does not apply to the Golden Horde.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Mounted Archers +2 line of sight
elements.explanation: A generic abstraction of steppe reconnaissance. Harmless.

tree_issues.item: No Faith, Heresy, Sanctity, Redemption, Theocracy
tree_issues.problem: One of the weakest Monastery trees in the game, for Islamised states: Berke converted before coming to the throne (reigned 1257–1266), Özbeg (1313–1341) made Islam the state religion, and Timur legitimised himself as a ghazi and patron of Sufi shrines, such as the mausoleum of Ahmad Yasawi (commissioned in 1389).

The Timurids are among the greatest medieval builders: Ak-Saray in Shahrisabz, the Bibi-Khanym Mosque and the Gur-i Amir. The Horde founded cities such as Sarai and Sarai al-Jadid and revitalised others, such as Bolghar. The absence contradicts the civ's own history section.

tree_issues.item: Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Tower (no Bombard Cannon)
tree_issues.problem: Plausible for the end of the period: the Khanate of Kazan and the Great Horde used firearms in the 15th–16th centuries. But the first reliable mention of firearms in Rus' is the defence of Moscow against Tokhtamysh (1382), conducted by the Russians, and the Timurids were not noted for their use of gunpowder.
Camels were pack animals in the Horde and in the Timurid army, not combat cavalry.
Timur took Indian elephants captured at Delhi and used them at the Battle of Ankara (1402), against Bayezid I (Yazdi, Ibn Arabshah). A Timurid unit or technology could reflect this.

tree_issues.item: No Arbalester or Champion; no Chain Mail or Plate Mail Armor
tree_issues.problem: Broadly consistent, for cavalry armies. Caveat: the Russian sources on Kulikovo (1380) mention “Fryazi” (Genoese) in Mamai's army, but the presence of Genoese infantry from Caffa at the battle is disputed.
A 15th-century Hungarian term, anachronistic.

history_text_issues.claim: The term “Tatar” was supposedly first applied to a confederation in north-eastern Mongolia from the 5th century onwards.
history_text_issues.problem: Date unsupported by the sources.
history_text_issues.correction: The first secure attestation is in the Orkhon inscriptions: “Otuz Tatar” in the Kül Tegin inscription (732) and “Toquz Tatar” in that of Bilge Qaghan (735). The links to the Rouran or the Shiwei, which would push the date back, are speculative.

history_text_issues.claim: The Tatars had supposedly been in bitter war with the Mongols since the 11th century.
history_text_issues.problem: Imprecise chronology.
history_text_issues.correction: The documented conflicts date from the 12th century: the Tatars handed Ambaghai over to the Jin and poisoned Yesügei, father of Temüjin, c. 1170.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the Mongols defeated the Tatars under the rule of Chinggis Khan (r. 1206–1227).
history_text_issues.problem: The decisive defeats predate 1206.
history_text_issues.correction: The Tatars were defeated in 1196 (by Temüjin and Toghrul, allies of the Jin, on the Ulja River) and annihilated in 1202 (Dalan Nemürges). Chinggis had the men taller than the linchpin of a cart put to death (Secret History, §154).

history_text_issues.claim: After Chinggis's death, “these Tatars” supposedly founded the successor states.
history_text_issues.problem: Confuses the exonym with the founders.
history_text_issues.correction: The successor states were founded by Chinggisid princes: Jochids, Chagataids and Toluids. “Tatar” is here merely the name given by Europeans.

history_text_issues.claim: Uses the name “Golden Horde (1227–1502)”.
history_text_issues.problem: Anachronistic term presented as contemporary.
history_text_issues.correction: “Golden Horde” (Zolotaya Orda) is a 16th-century Russian term (History of Kazan, 1560s). Contemporaries spoke of the Ulus of Jochi, Ulugh Ulus or Desht-i Kipchak. The capital Sarai only appears after the campaign of 1236–1242.

history_text_issues.claim: Under Batu, the Tatars supposedly conquered Cumania, Volga Bulgaria, Kievan Rus' and “Eastern Europe”.
history_text_issues.problem: Exaggeration.
history_text_issues.correction: Cumania, Volga Bulgaria and Rus' were indeed subjugated. Poland and Hungary were devastated in 1241–1242, but not conquered; Bulgaria only became a tributary.

history_text_issues.claim: The Horde supposedly relied on light cavalry armies and hired Chinese engineers for sieges.
history_text_issues.problem: Simplification.
history_text_issues.correction: The armies also had heavy cavalry with lamellar armour. The Chinese and Muslim engineers were generally recruited by force or deported, not hired.

history_text_issues.claim: Özbeg supposedly moved the capital, Sarai, to a new site.
history_text_issues.problem: Disputed attribution.
history_text_issues.correction: The existence of two Sarais (Sarai Batu and Sarai Berke/al-Jadid) and who moved the capital (Berke, Özbeg or Jani Beg) are questions debated by archaeology and historiography.

history_text_issues.claim: The Black Death supposedly disrupted the economy and the empire supposedly fragmented into smaller khanates.
history_text_issues.problem: Omission of decisive phases.
history_text_issues.correction: Missing are the “Great Troubles” (1359–1381), the reunification under Tokhtamysh (c. 1380, with the sack of Moscow in 1382) and Timur's devastation of Sarai, Astrakhan and Tana (1395). The relative weight of the plague (emphasised by Uli Schamiloglu) and of Timur's campaigns in the Horde's decline is debated. The fragmentation into khanates (Kazan, Crimea, Astrakhan) belongs mainly to the 15th century.

history_text_issues.claim: Presents Timur as “a new Tatar warlord”.
history_text_issues.problem: Conflation of two enemy powers.
history_text_issues.correction: Timur was a Turco-Mongol Barlas of the ulus of Chagatai. Europeans called him a “Tartar”, but he was the enemy and the great devastator of the Golden Horde (Kondurcha 1391, Terek 1395). The text, like the design, merges them into a single identity.

history_text_issues.claim: Timur supposedly raised “minarets” of skulls at Delhi and Aleppo.
history_text_issues.problem: Aleppo is documented; Delhi is a poorly chosen example.
history_text_issues.correction: The towers of skulls are well documented at Isfahan (1387), Aleppo (1400) and Baghdad (1401). At Delhi, the most frequently cited episode is the execution of tens of thousands of prisoners before the battle (Yazdi) and the massacre during the sack.

history_text_issues.claim: The Timurids supposedly mastered the “Seljuk architectural style”.
history_text_issues.problem: Imprecise stylistic affiliation.
history_text_issues.correction: Timurid architecture chiefly develops the Ilkhanid Persian tradition (double domes, polychrome tilework), with Khwarazmian and Seljuk antecedents. “Timurid” or “Turco-Persian” would be more accurate terms.

history_text_issues.claim: Concludes that the era of Tatar dominance ended with Timur's death.
history_text_issues.problem: False for the following period.
history_text_issues.correction: The Great Horde lasted until 1502, and Kazan and Astrakhan until 1552/1556. The Crimean Khanate (1441–1783) remained a power and burned Moscow in 1571. The Timurid Babur founded the Mughal Empire in 1526.

missing_features: Islam as the state religion (Berke, Özbeg) and Timur's religious role: Sufi patronage and Islamic legitimation.
Trade: Sarai as an entrepôt, and the partnership and conflict with the Genoese and Venetian colonies (Caffa, Tana, Soldaia), through the northern Silk Road and the slave trade to Egypt.
The tribute system imposed on the Rus': yarlyk (patent of investiture), baskaks, darughachi and the census of 1257–1259.
Timurid patronage: the deportation of artisans to Samarkand, monumental architecture and Ulugh Beg's observatory (1420s).
The elephants captured and used by Timur (Ankara, 1402).
The Timur–Tokhtamysh rivalry, the great political axis of the late 14th century.
Coinage and monetisation: the Horde's silver dirhams (Russian “denga” comes from Turkic “tanga”).

proposals.title: Split the civ into “Golden Horde” and “Timurids”
proposals.description: Rename the Tatars to “Golden Horde” (or “Jochids”), with the focus on herding, trade, tribute and Islam. Move the Timurid elements (Flaming Camel, Timurid Siegecraft, the Tamerlane campaign) to a new “Timurids” civ, with siege, architecture and elephant bonuses.
proposals.historical_basis: The two states had different dynasties (Jochid and Barlas/Chagataid), distinct territorial bases (the Pontic–Caspian steppe versus Transoxiana and Iran) and were direct enemies (1391, 1395). B. F. Manz (1989); M. Favereau (2021).

proposals.title: “Yarlyk” (tribute)
proposals.description: Each Castle generates gold passively (+0.5 per second), with +50% if there is an enemy Town Center within 15 tiles. Represents the tribute levied through military threat and through the investiture of vassal princes.
proposals.historical_basis: The grand princes of Rus' could only reign with a yarlyk from the khan. The tribute (vykhod) was collected by baskaks and, later, by the princes of Moscow themselves (Halperin, 1985; Ostrowski, 1998).

proposals.title: “Sarai and Caffa” (trade)
proposals.description: Trade Carts and Trade Cogs generate +20% gold and the Market charges no tribute fee. An alternative (also applicable to the Mongols) would be to give access to a version of the Silk Road technology.
proposals.historical_basis: Ibn Battuta describes Sarai as one of the great cities of the world. The Genoese colony of Caffa and the Venetian and Genoese colonies of Tana linked the Horde to the Mediterranean, and the Horde's economy rested largely on long-distance trade (Favereau, 2021).

proposals.title: Restore the religious tree and add “Ghazi”
proposals.description: Give access to Faith, Sanctity and Redemption. Add a “Ghazi” technology: Monks cost -25% and mounted units get +5% attack within a radius of 5 tiles of a Monk.
proposals.historical_basis: Islamisation under Berke (r. 1257–1266) and Özbeg (1313). Timur presented his campaigns in India and against Christians (Smyrna 1402) as holy war and funded Sufi shrines (Ahmad Yasawi).

proposals.title: “Artisans of Samarkand” (Timurids)
proposals.description: Monasteries, Universities and Wonders are built 50% faster and cost -20%. Architecture becomes available.
proposals.historical_basis: Timur deported artisans from Damascus, Delhi, Shiraz and other cities to Samarkand. Ruy González de Clavijo (embassy of 1403–1406) describes the building works of Samarkand and the Ak-Saray palace at Kesh/Shahrisabz.

proposals.title: “Elephants of Delhi” (Timurids)
proposals.description: Imperial Age technology that allows Battle Elephants to be trained at the Castle.
proposals.historical_basis: After the sack of Delhi (1398), Timur took war elephants with him and used them at the Battle of Ankara (1402) against Bayezid I (Ibn Arabshah; Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi).

proposals.title: Share the Keshik with the Mongols and create the “Oğlan” (Ulan)
proposals.description: The Tatars (or the future “Golden Horde”) gain a fast light lancer called “Oğlan/Ulan”, with a bonus against cavalry archers. Remove the elevation bonus, which is unfounded.
proposals.historical_basis: “Oğlan” (youth, prince) was the title of the Chinggisid princes of the Horde (for example, Tokhtamysh Oğlan). The Lithuanian Tatars (Lipka) carried the term into Polish as “ułan”, which gave the European “uhlan”.

contested: The origin of the name “Tatar” and its possible link to the Rouran or the Shiwei.

The impact of the “Tatar yoke” on Russia: the traditional reading of destruction and backwardness versus Ostrowski (1998) and Halperin (1985), who emphasise Mongol institutional influences on Muscovy.
The identification of Sarai Batu, Sarai Berke and Sarai al-Jadid, and who moved the capital (Berke, Özbeg or Jani Beg).
The relative weight of the Black Death (Schamiloglu) and of Timur's campaigns (1391, 1395) in the Horde's decline.
The historicity of the flaming camels episode at Delhi (1398), attested mainly in late sources of doubtful authenticity.
The presence of Genoese infantry in Mamai's army at Kulikovo (1380).
Timur's aims: to restore Chinggis's empire, to build an Islamic empire of his own, or mainly to plunder (Manz).
The Horde's role (siege of Caffa, 1346) in the arrival of the Black Death in Europe, which comes from the account of Gabriele de' Mussis.
key_sources: Orkhon inscriptions (Kül Tegin, 732; Bilge Qaghan, 735)
The Secret History of the Mongols (§153–154, on the original Tatars)
Ibn Battuta, Rihla (visit to Özbeg, 1332–1334)
Al-ʿUmari, Masalik al-absar
Russian chronicles (Laurentian, Nikon, Hypatian); Zadonshchina
Ruy González de Clavijo, Embajada a Tamorlán (1403–1406)
Sharaf al-Din ʿAli Yazdi, Zafarnama; Nizam al-Din Shami, Zafarnama
Ibn ʿArabshah, ʿAja'ib al-maqdur fi nawa'ib Timur
Ibn Khaldun (meeting with Timur in Damascus, 1401)
B. F. Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989); Power, Politics and Religion in Timurid Iran (2007)
J. Marozzi, Tamerlane: Sword of Islam, Conqueror of the World (2004)
M. Favereau, The Horde: How the Mongols Changed the World (2021)
C. Halperin, Russia and the Golden Horde (1985)
D. Ostrowski, Muscovy and the Mongols (1998)
I. Vásáry, Cumans and Tatars (2005)
P. B. Golden, An Introduction to the History of the Turkic Peoples (1992)
T. Lentz and G. Lowry, Timur and the Princely Vision (1989)
U. Schamiloglu, on the Black Death in the Golden Horde

civs.represents: The Cuman-Kipchak confederation: Cumans to Latins and Byzantines, Polovtsy in the Rus' chronicles, Kun to the Hungarians, Qipchaq in Muslim sources. It dominated the Desht-i Kipchak, from the Danube to the Irtysh, from c. 1050/1060 until the Mongol conquest (1223–1241). It also represents their diaspora: the Cumans of Hungary (Kunság), of Bulgaria (the Terter dynasty and, according to some, the Asenids), of Georgia (the settlers of David IV) and of Egypt (the Bahri Mamluks).
civs.period: c. 1050–1241 on the Pontic steppe; diaspora until c. 1400 (and, in Hungary, well beyond that). Fits well within the game's window.
civs.verdict: The Cumans have a well-chosen core: fast cavalry, horse archers and no stone walls. The standout is “Cuman Mercenaries”, which faithfully reflects the Cumans' role as mercenaries and military settlers in Byzantium, Hungary, Bulgaria, Georgia and Rus'. The economic bonuses (a second Town Center in the Feudal Age, cheaper Archery Ranges and Stables) and the siege bonus (rams in the Feudal Age), on the other hand, are gameplay inventions with a weak link to history. The Cumans were not siege specialists, although the Rus' chronicles record siege engines of Konchak (1184/1185). Missing are the ancestor cult with stone statues, marriage diplomacy, the captive trade and the armoured elites with face masks. The history text is one of the best in the group, with minor errors: the “balbals” and an origin presented as certain.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Cumans” (Lat. Comani, Gr. Koumanoi) is a Western exonym. The relationship between Cumans and Kipchaks (one people, two branches of one confederation, or two associated peoples) is debated. Calling the unique unit “Kipchak” is ambiguous, because it is an ethnonym and not a type of warrior, and it blurs two overlaps. The first is with the Tatars: the Golden Horde absorbed the Kipchaks and was Turkicised by them, and Muslim sources call its territory Dasht-i Qipchaq. The second is with the Saracens' Mamluks, many of whom were of Kipchak origin, such as Baybars and Qalawun. The period fits well within the game's window, but the civ ignores the long diaspora, which is a central part of its history.

elements.explanation: The Cumans fought essentially on horseback, as archers and as lancers, and each warrior brought several remounts.

elements.element: One additional Town Center can be built in Feudal Age
elements.explanation: Perhaps it is meant to evoke a scattered confederation of autonomous clans. But a Town Center is a fixed centre, and the Cumans had very few permanent settlements: the Rus' chronicles mention the “towns” of Sharukan and Sugrov, taken in the 1111 campaign, which were probably also inhabited by non-Cuman sedentary populations. The link is weak and mainly serves gameplay.

elements.element: Mounted Units move +5/10/15% faster in Feudal/Castle/Imperial Age
elements.explanation: An abstraction of steppe mobility. Robert de Clari (ch. 65) says that each Cuman had ten or twelve horses trained to follow him and that they covered in one night and one day a distance of several days' journey; Boniak's raid on Kiev in 1096 is a good example. In the game, this bonus replaces the Husbandry tech, which the Cumans lack.

elements.element: Archery Ranges and Stables cost -75 wood
elements.explanation: A very vague link to the idea that nomads did not need expensive infrastructure. It is essentially an economy bonus for aggressive strategies.

elements.element: Siege Workshop and Battering Ram in Feudal Age; Capped Ram in Castle Age
elements.explanation: The Cumans relied on surprise raids and plunder, not on sieges. The Hypatian Chronicle records that Konchak brought against Rus' (1184/1185) a huge crossbow that 50 men could barely span and a Muslim who hurled “living fire”. This points to siege crossbows and fire, not to early rams.
The horse archer was the core of the Cuman army, so the unit is faithful in concept. Firing several arrows is an abstraction of volume of fire. The name is an ethnonym and not a type of warrior.

elements.element: Steppe Husbandry (Scout Cavalry-line, Steppe Lancers and Cavalry Archers train +100% faster)
elements.explanation: It represents the abundance of horses and the fact that every adult man was a trained horseman, which made it possible to mobilise large forces quickly.

elements.element: Cuman Mercenaries (team members train 5 free Elite Kipchaks per Castle)
elements.explanation: One of the most faithful elements in the game. The Cumans served Byzantium (Levounion, 1091, with Tugorkan and Boniak; later Nicaea and Michael VIII), Georgia (tens of thousands of families settled by David IV c. 1118–1120, decisive at Didgori, 1121), Bulgaria (the revolt of 1185; Adrianople, 1205), Hungary (Béla IV, 1239; Marchfeld, 1278) and the princes of Rus'. In Egypt, the Kipchaks reached the throne, but as slave soldiers (Mamluks), not as mercenaries.
There is no specific Cuman tradition of palisades. The more fitting historical reference would be the wagon camp (the vezhi of the Rus' chronicles) and mobile dwellings on wheels.

tree_issues.problem: It is odd that a people of horse archers lacks the final range and attack upgrade for archers. It is a balance choice that contradicts the historical identity. The lack of Husbandry is offset by the speed bonus and raises no problem.

tree_issues.item: No Stone Wall, Gate, Guard Tower, Keep, Fortified Wall
tree_issues.problem: Faithful: the Cumans did not build stone fortifications and had few fixed settlements.
Konchak's “great crossbow” (1184/1185), which required dozens of men, suggests precisely a weapon of this type. The Heavy Scorpion would be more justifiable than the early rams.

tree_issues.item: Siege Onager and rams in the Feudal Age
tree_issues.problem: Stretched: Cuman siege capability was limited and occasional.

Plausible. The Cuman elite wore mail, lamellar armour and helmets with anthropomorphic iron face masks, as the archaeology of the kurgans shows, and the game's own text speaks of heavily armoured lancers.
The Rus' chronicles record camels among the plunder taken from Polovtsian camps (for example, in 1103), but as pack animals, not as cavalry.
Of little relevance: the Cumans fought mounted. It is a minor balance issue.

history_text_issues.claim: The Cumans supposedly originated east of the Yellow River, from where they were said to have been driven out by the Khitan tribes.
history_text_issues.problem: A hypothesis is presented as fact.
history_text_issues.correction: The idea comes from al-Marwazi (c. 1120), who describes the Qun leaving the “land of Qitay” for fear of the khan of the Khitan and pushing other peoples westwards. The identification Qun = Cumans and the Yellow River detail are hypotheses. Peter Golden and others also discuss an origin in the Kimek-Kipchak milieu of the Irtysh.

history_text_issues.claim: The Cumans supposedly migrated west during the 10th century, reaching the steppes of Kazakhstan.
history_text_issues.problem: Imprecise chronology, but not clearly wrong.
history_text_issues.correction: The movement of the Qun described by al-Marwazi is often dated to the early 11th century. On the Pontic steppe, the Cumans only appear around the 1050s: the first contact with Rus' dates from 1055, the first attack from 1061 (under Iskal) and the victory over the princes of Kiev on the Alta River from 1068.

history_text_issues.claim: The Cumans and Kipchaks supposedly allied and quickly merged into a single people.
history_text_issues.problem: Simplifies a debated question.
history_text_issues.correction: It is not clear whether they were a single people, two branches (western and eastern) of the same confederation, or two peoples that became associated. The sources use the names variably depending on the language.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that mangonels and ballistae were used regularly.
history_text_issues.problem: An exaggeration.
history_text_issues.correction: The evidence is occasional, above all Konchak's siege engines (Hypatian Chronicle, 1184/1185). The sources describe an army made up essentially of raiding cavalry.

history_text_issues.claim: Elizabeth, queen of Hungary, was supposedly the daughter of the chieftain Seyhan.
history_text_issues.problem: A disputed identification.
history_text_issues.correction: The parentage of Elizabeth the Cuman is debated: many historians make her the daughter of Köten; others rely on a letter in which Béla IV calls a certain Seyhan a “kinsman”. Since “Seyhan” may be a title, it is not even certain that these are different people.

history_text_issues.claim: It calls the anthropomorphic Cuman ancestor statues “balbals”.
history_text_issues.problem: Terminological confusion.
history_text_issues.correction: In Turkology, balbals are simple stones from the Göktürk-era necropolises (6th–8th centuries) that represented slain enemies. The Cuman ancestor statues, which hold a cup, are the “kamennye baby” (kurgan stelae) of the 11th–13th centuries, which Rubruck saw beside the tombs.

history_text_issues.claim: Mongol and Tatar armies supposedly conquered the confederation in the early 13th century, with Köten's defeat at the Kalka in 1223.
history_text_issues.problem: Compresses the chronology and omits a central episode.
history_text_issues.correction: The Battle of the Kalka (1223) was part of a reconnaissance raid by Jebe and Subutai. The conquest only came with Batu's campaign (1236–1241). Missing are Köten's flight to Hungary with around 40,000 families (1239) and his murder in Pest (March 1241), which led the Cumans to devastate the country and leave for the Balkans (Roger of Torre Maggiore, Carmen miserabile).

history_text_issues.claim: The Cuman diaspora appears only as assimilation and slavery.
history_text_issues.problem: Omission of central episodes of the diaspora.
history_text_issues.correction: Missing are Georgia (David IV's marriage to Gurandukht, daughter of Atrak; military settlers; Didgori, 1121), Hungary (Kunság, Ladislaus IV “the Cuman”, Marchfeld 1278, the Cuman bishopric of Milcov in 1227–1228; the last known speaker of Cuman in Hungary died in 1770) and Adrianople (1205), where Cuman cavalry in the service of Kaloyan helped defeat and capture the Latin emperor Baldwin I.

history_text_issues.claim: Sultan “al-Sahil Ayyubi” supposedly bought many Cuman-Kipchaks, and for more than a century the Mamluk sultans were supposedly of that origin.
history_text_issues.problem: A typo in the name and a generalisation.
history_text_issues.correction: This is al-Salih Ayyub (r. 1240–1249). The Bahri sultans (1250–1382) were mostly Kipchaks, such as Baybars and Qalawun, but not all of them: Kitbugha was an Oirat Mongol. From 1382 onwards the Circassians (Burji) dominated.

missing_features: The ancestor cult and the stone stelae (“kamennye baby”) in kurgan sanctuaries.
Marriage diplomacy with Rus', Georgia, Hungary and Bulgaria, for example the daughters of Köten and of Atrak.
The trade in captives and slaves to Soldaia/Sudak and to Egypt, in which the Cumans were at once agents and victims, and which lies at the origin of the Mamluks.
The armoured elite with face masks, mail and lamellar armour.
The camps and dwellings on wagons (vezhi).
Partial Christianisation and the Codex Cumanicus (early 14th century), a monument of the Cuman language.
The long existence of the Cuman communities in Hungary (Kunság), with their own privileges until the 19th century.
The absence of centralised power: a confederation of autonomous khans (Sharukan, Boniak, Konchak, Köten).
The ritual oath with a sacrificed dog, described by Joinville in the alliance between the Cumans and the Latins of Constantinople.

proposals.title: “Konchak's Great Crossbow” and “Living Fire”
proposals.description: Remove the rams from the Feudal Age and give access to the Heavy Scorpion. Add a Castle Age tech in which Scorpions and Mangonels leave fire on the ground for a few seconds.
proposals.historical_basis: The Hypatian Chronicle (1184/1185) relates that Konchak advanced against Rus' with a crossbow so large that 50 men could barely span it, and with a Muslim who hurled “living fire”. The fire-thrower was captured by the forces of Sviatoslav III of Kiev at the battle of the Khorol River.

proposals.title: “Kurgan Sanctuary”
proposals.description: A unique building that replaces the Monastery. It does not train Monks; instead, military units within 8 tiles regenerate HP and gain +1 attack, representing the blessings of the ancestors. Relics kept in the sanctuary generate gold, as in Monasteries.
proposals.historical_basis: Rubruck describes Cuman tombs with mounds and stone statues facing east, holding a cup in their hands. S. A. Pletneva (1990) studied the kurgan-stela sanctuaries of the 11th–13th centuries, which were dedicated to the ancestor cult.

proposals.title: “Vezha” (wagon camp)
proposals.description: Replace the Palisades bonus with wagon-wall segments, built at the Town Center, which can be packed up and transported (like a Trebuchet) and reassembled elsewhere.
proposals.historical_basis: The Rus' chronicles speak of the Polovtsian vezhi (dwellings and camps on wheels) captured in the campaigns of 1103 and 1111. Robert de Clari describes the Cumans as living in felt tents, without houses.

proposals.title: Mask-wearing lancer (“Masked Lancer”)
proposals.description: A second unique unit: elite heavy cavalry armed with a lance. It has an attack bonus against horse archers and a short aura that reduces the attack of nearby enemy units by 10%, representing the intimidating effect of the mask. It is trained at the Castle.
proposals.historical_basis: The archaeology of the kurgans of the Cumans and of the Chernye Klobuky includes helmets with anthropomorphic iron face masks, as well as mail and lamellar armour. The game's own text speaks of heavily armoured lancers.

proposals.title: “Dynastic Marriages”
proposals.description: A Castle Age tech: allies get -15% cost on Stable units and can train Steppe Lancers at the Castle. The Cuman player receives, once only, gold equivalent to a “dowry” per ally.
proposals.historical_basis: Atrak gave his daughter Gurandukht to David IV of Georgia, and Köten married a daughter to Mstislav Mstislavich of Galicia, who for that reason supported him at the Kalka (1223). Elizabeth the Cuman married Stephen V of Hungary. Many princes of Rus' had Cuman mothers or wives.

proposals.title: “Captive Raids”
proposals.description: Each enemy Villager killed by Cuman mounted units yields +5 gold. It represents the raiding economy and the captive trade.
proposals.historical_basis: The Rus' chronicles record Polovtsian raids that carried off captives, and Robert de Clari says that they returned from their winter incursions with plunder and prisoners. The Crimean markets (Soldaia/Sudak) exported slaves to Egypt; the Mamluk recruitment of Kipchaks is the other side of the same trade (Ibn al-Athir; Golden).

proposals.title: Fix the tech tree: add Bracer
proposals.description: Give the Cumans Bracer, compensating by removing the Feudal Age rams or the wood discount on military buildings.
proposals.historical_basis: The Cumans were, first and foremost, horse archers: shooting backwards, the feigned retreat and the ambush are described in Byzantine, Russian and Hungarian sources.

contested: The origin of the Cumans: al-Marwazi's Qun or the Kimek-Kipchak confederation of the Irtysh. Golden changed his position over the course of his career.
The Cuman–Kipchak relationship: one people, two branches or two associated peoples.
The meaning of the ethnonyms: Polovtsy (“pale/yellowish”?), Kun and Sary; the claims about the Cumans' blond hair are disputed.
The parentage of Elizabeth the Cuman (Köten or Seyhan, which may even be a title).
The Cuman, Vlach or Bulgarian origin of the Asenid dynasty.
The real extent of Cuman siege capabilities.
The number of Cumans settled in Hungary (1239 and after 1246) and in Georgia (c. 1118–1120).
