groups.cross_civ_notes:
1) Elements swapped between civs. Several elements are in the wrong civ or in a civ older than their origin. The kheshig (Keshik) is Chinggis's imperial guard; it persisted in the successor states, but it should belong first to the Mongols, who do not have it in the game. The title “tarkan” (tarqan/tarkhan) was given to the 5th-century Huns, but it is attested among the Göktürks, Khazars, late Hephthalites and above all the Danube Bulgars. It would make sense in the Bulgarians and, as “darqan” (an exemption status), in the Mongols. The Huns' trebuchet bonus is in fact an Avar (or Byzantine) trait of the late 6th century. “Timurid Siegecraft” fits the Mongol/Yuan “huihui pao” counterweight trebuchets (Xiangyang, 1273) just as well or better. The Silk Road tech belongs to the Italians, but the “Pax Mongolica” and the trade of Sarai, Caffa and Tana would be the more natural basis.

2) Timur appears twice. Both the Mongols' and the Tatars' history texts narrate Timur. The Tatars civ merges the Golden Horde with the Timurids, who ended up as direct enemies: Timur helped Tokhtamysh take the throne (1376–1378) and then devastated the Horde in 1391 and 1395. The cleanest solution would be one “Golden Horde” civ and another “Timurids” civ, with the Mongols limited to 1206–1368.

3) Ethnic and linguistic overlaps. The Golden Horde became Turkicised by absorbing the Kipchaks, the same Kipchaks as in the Cumans civ; Muslim sources call its territory Dasht-i Qipchaq. The Saracens' Mamluks (the Mameluke unit), who defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut, were largely Kipchak and Cuman slaves captured during the Mongol expansion. Four civs (Cumans, Tatars, Mongols, Saracens) thus share the same population in different roles. There are also links with the Bulgarians (Cumans in the 1185 revolt, in the Terter dynasty and, perhaps, in the Asenid dynasty), the Georgians (David IV's settlers), the Magyars (Kunság; the medieval tradition of Hunnic descent, from Simon of Kéza) and the Lithuanians (Lipka Tatars). The history texts of these civs rarely refer to one another.

4) Period mismatch. The Huns (c. 370–469) fall outside the c. 500–1500 window. The European steppe peoples who occupy it (Avars 567–796, Khazars, Pechenegs, Volga Bulgars) have no civ, and the Huns stand in as “generic nomads of Pannonia”, which explains many of their anachronisms. The Cumans (1050–1241), the Mongols (1206–1368) and the Tatars (1242–1507) fit well.

5) The same formula repeated. All four civs have mainly horse archers and cavalry bonuses, with differences that are more about gameplay than about history. Historical differentiation could come from real distinctive traits: for the Huns, Roman tribute, subject infantry and Roman-type engines; for the Mongols, the kheshig, the yam, decimal organisation, siege engineering and Yuan gunpowder; for the Golden Horde, trade, the tribute of the Rus' and Islam; for the Timurids, siege warfare, architecture and elephants; for the Cumans, mercenary service, marriage diplomacy and ancestor worship. Note also the irony of the Khitans' Pasture: the most elaborate pastoral mechanic in the game was given to the Khitans (Liao), a semi-sedentary state with a dual administration, and not to the Mongols, Tatars or Cumans, pastoralists par excellence. The Steppe Lancer is shared by the Cumans, Mongols, Tatars, Khitans and Jurchens, but not by the Huns; this is defensible, although the Alans of the Hunnic confederation were heavy lancers.

6) Common anachronisms. The Hussar upgrade (a 15th-century Hungarian term) is present in the Huns, Mongols, Tatars and Cumans. All four civs have a war navy (galleys, Fire Ships, Hulks and a siege ship), although none of these peoples, except the Yuan, had war fleets; the Huns even have the Byzantine Dromon. The Yuan fleets against Japan (1274, 1281) and Java (1293) would justify a more distinctive Mongol navy, but not that of the other three.

7) Quality of the history texts. Those of the Cumans and the Tatars (written for the DE, with the expansion The Last Khans, 2019) follow recent historiography and are frankly better. The Mongols' text comes from the original 1999 game and the Huns' from The Conquerors (2000); both carry myths (Hunnic stirrups; Châlons as “the salvation of Christendom”; Timur “descended from Chinggis”) and uncritical death tolls. A revision of the Huns' text would be the highest-impact correction in this group.

8) Verification note. The tech trees were checked against the repository's data.json (current version, with Hulk, Carrack, Catapult Galleon and Dromon). Web research was limited during the review: some details (for example, the exact dating of the Peace of Anatolius or the parentage of Elizabeth the Cuman) were marked as contested rather than resolved.

verification_log.change: Atheism: removed the claim that atheism is “a modern concept” (the Greek “atheos” is ancient, used as a polemical accusation, including against Christians). The link to the “Flagellum Dei” is now presented as a probable inspiration, not as a certain origin. Added the “sword of Mars” (Jordanes, Getica 183).
Team bonus: corrected the citation. Riding from childhood comes from Sidonius Apollinaris (Carmina 2); Ammianus 31.2.6 describes life on horseback, not childhood training.

Trebuchet: marked as contested whether the Avars introduced the traction trebuchet or whether the Byzantines already knew it (confirmed: Thessalonica 586). Added the “machinae/tormenta” of Aquileia (Jordanes, Getica 221), which reinforce the idea of Roman-type engines.
Tarkan: added Tarkhan Nizak (Hephthalites, early 8th century), noted the disputed etymology and the uncertain origin of the three “Hunnic” words (medos, kamos, strava).

Correction of game facts, verified in data.json: the Huns already have Palisade, Stone Wall, Gate and Watch Tower, so the draft's suggestion to “keep Palisades and Watch Towers” was redundant. The navy was updated (they have Hulk/War Hulk and Dromon; they do not have Fast Fire Ship, Cannon Galleon or Carrack), and it was noted that the Dromon replaces the Cannon Galleon on purpose.
The Peace of Anatolius changed from “447” to “443 or 447 (dating debated)”; the Treaty of Margus to 435 or 439; Naissus to 442/443. The three dates were added to contested.

Verdict: the claim that “almost all the elements” would be faithful to the Avars became “several” (Atheism, for example, would not be). The claim that “many subjects were Arian Christians” was qualified (the Christianisation of some groups postdates 451).

History text: added an omitted error (the Huns “vanished under the Avars”, who only arrived in the 560s). The wiki's editorial paragraphs are now explicitly identified as unofficial; added the “Middle Ages” error and the context of Kavad I, and corrected the destruction of the Hephthalites to c. 557–560.

Mangudai: removed the claim that the “suicide squad” is an “invention of 20th-century popular history”, which could not be verified. It now states that there is no known primary source, and the point was added to contested.
Remounts: removed the attribution of “3–5 horses” to Carpini and Marco Polo, which is not verifiable. It is now given as a modern estimate (T. May).
Hunters: removed the claim that Chinggis regulated hunting “in his jasa”. Added the caveat that the economic base was herding, keeping the faithful rating.

History text: the ideology of universal dominion changed from “no evidence” to “debated as to its origin”. Removed the exact household figures from the Jin/Mongol censuses, which could not be confirmed. Added three omitted errors: the 100,000 at Delhi (they were prisoners executed before the battle), the Timurid empire that supposedly “fell apart quickly” (Shah Rukh ruled until 1447) and the “extermination” of the Nizaris.

Gunpowder: the lack of cannons is now defensible for 1206–1260 and inconsistent only for the Yuan. Confirmed in data.json that the Mongols do not have Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon or Bombard Tower, but do have Cannon Galleon (not elite). Added the absence of Paladin as consistent.
Silk Armor: corrected the origin of the myth. The earliest mention identified is by Michael Prawdin (1934), with no medieval source, and not by Harold Lamb (1927), whose connection is not confirmed.

Thumb Ring/Parthian Tactics: the Kalka (1223) was replaced as an example, because it was a battle of the Mongol Empire that predates the Horde. The Vorskla (1399, Edigu against Vytautas) was brought in, with Kondurcha (1391) kept.
Keshik changed from stretched to plausible: the guard persisted in the successor states and the civ represents precisely successors. The main problem is its absence from the Mongols.

Flaming Camel: the source was made more precise. The episode appears mainly in the pseudo-memoirs Malfuzat-i Timuri (17th century, of doubtful authenticity) and in later accounts; it was added to contested.
Berke: corrected “converted c. 1257” (he converted before reigning, 1257–1266). Bolghar was “revitalised”, not founded, by the Horde.

The decline of the Horde no longer claims that Timur weighed “more than the plague”: the point is debated (Schamiloglu gives weight to the Black Death). Timur is now said to have “devastated”, not “destroyed”, the Horde, and his early support for Tokhtamysh was added.

Skull towers: Aleppo (1400) is documented, so the text's error is limited to Delhi. “Kipchak Khanate in Persian sources” became Dasht-i Qipchaq in Muslim sources. The “dang” coin became silver dirhams (tanga/denga). The Genoese at Kulikovo were marked as contested.

History text: added two omitted errors (the conquest of “Eastern Europe” under Batu and the move of the capital attributed to Özbeg). Tech tree: noted the lack of Bombard Cannon, Chain Mail and Plate Mail Armor (verified in data.json).

Remounts: the “10–12 horses” now cite Robert de Clari, ch. 65, which was verified in the text. Removed the town of “Balin”, which is not confirmed; Sharukan and Sugrov (1111) remain, with the note that they probably had sedentary populations.

Face masks: removed “gilded for khans”, which is not confirmed. The 10th-century migration is no longer classed as an error: the text only says that they reached the Kazakh steppes, and the arrival in the Pontic steppe c. 1050 was kept as a clarification.
Naming: removed the analogy “like calling an English unit Saxon”, because the Saxons are now a civ in the repository. Corrected the reference to the “Kipchak Khanate” of Persian sources.

Tech tree: added the lack of Husbandry, compensated by the speed bonus (verified in data.json). Konchak changed to 1184/1185 (Battle of the Khorol). Elizabeth the Cuman now has her parentage marked as contested (Köten or Seyhan, which may be a title).
Cuman Mercenaries: clarified that the Mamluks were slave soldiers, not mercenaries. Adrianople (1205) changed from “defeated” to “helped defeat and capture” Baldwin I.

Cross-civ: corrected that the Huns' text comes from The Conquerors (2000), not from the original 1999 game, and that the civs do not have a “full navy” (the Huns have neither Fast Fire Ship nor Cannon Galleon). The new Hulk, Carrack and Catapult Galleon ships were verified in data.json. Scores kept (Huns 3, Mongols 6, Tatars 4, Cumans 5), as they are consistent with an average of about 5.

civs.represents: The Muslim Arab peoples and the Arabic-speaking Islamic states of the Middle East and North Africa: the Rashidun (632–661), Umayyad (661–750), Abbasid (750–1258) and Fatimid (909–1171) caliphates, joined by the Ayyubids (a Kurdish dynasty, 1171–1250 in Egypt, until 1260 in Syria) and the Mamluk Sultanate of Egypt and Syria (1250–1517), whose military elite was of Kipchak (Turkic) origin and, from 1382, mainly Circassian. The naval and trade bonuses refer to the Umayyad, Abbasid and Fatimid period. The military core (Mameluke, Counterweights, Bimaristan) points to Ayyubid and Mamluk Egypt and Syria of the 12th–15th centuries.
civs.period: c. 630–1517. The design's centre of gravity lies in c. 1170–1500 (Ayyubid and Mamluk Egypt and Syria).
civs.verdict: The economic and naval core is reasonable: cheap Markets, effective galleys and sturdy transports reflect the Islamic world's role as a commercial hub and the strength of the Umayyad, Aghlabid and Fatimid fleets. The two unique techs (Bimaristan and Counterweights) are among the best chosen in the game. The label, however, is a medieval European exonym, and the unique unit misrepresents the Mamluks: in the game they are camel riders who throw scimitars, when in reality they were horse-mounted cavalrymen, heavy horse archers and lancers trained in furusiyya. The history text is one of the weakest in the game: it invents a “60-year war” between Sunnis and Shias, credits the Arabs with the conquest of Asia Minor (which only the Turks achieved, after 1071), calls a mainly Berber invasion of 711 “Saracen”, and omits the Abbasids and the Mamluks themselves.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Saracens” is a Graeco-Latin exonym (Sarakēnoi/Saraceni). Authors such as Ptolemy and Ammianus Marcellinus used it for nomads of northern Arabia and Sinai. In medieval Christendom it came to designate all Muslims indiscriminately, including Turks and Berbers, and it carried a polemical charge. None of the peoples represented called themselves by this name. The label lumps together Arabs (Umayyads, Abbasids, Fatimids), Kurds (Saladin and the Ayyubids) and Kipchak and Circassian Mamluks. It therefore overlaps with the Turks and the Cumans (the Bahri Mamluks were Kipchaks, the same confederation as the Cumans) and with the Berbers (al-Andalus, the Fatimids, whose early army was Kutama Berber). It would be more accurate to use “Arabs”, or to separate “Arabs” (caliphates, c. 630–1050) from “Mamluks” (Egypt and Syria, 1250–1517), much as AoE IV does with “Abbasid Dynasty” and “Ayyubids”.

elements.explanation: The camel was decisive for the strategic mobility of the conquests; one example is Khalid ibn al-Walid's crossing of the Syrian desert in 634. The Arab navy defeated Byzantium at the Battle of the Masts (654/655) and made it possible to attack Cyprus (649) and to take Crete (c. 824–827, by Andalusi exiles) and Sicily (827–902). There are two caveats. In battle, the Arabs fought mainly on horseback or on foot; the camel served mainly as transport. And Islamic naval power in the Mediterranean declined from the 11th century onwards. The Mamluk navy was intermittent, but not non-existent: Barsbay subjugated Cyprus (Khirokitia, 1426), there were attacks on Rhodes (1440 and 1444) and a fleet was sent to the Indian Ocean against the Portuguese (Chaul, 1508; Diu, 1509).

elements.element: Market trading fee only 5%; Markets cost -100 wood
elements.explanation: Well grounded as an abstraction. The Islamic world linked the Mediterranean, the Indian Ocean and the Sahara, with stable currency (dinar and dirham), credit and transfer instruments (sakk, hawala, suftaja), suqs and funduqs. The Cairo Genizah documents, studied by S. D. Goitein, show dense trading networks. The reduced exchange fee is a reasonable way of rendering this reality. (The oft-repeated idea that “cheque” derives from sakk is speculative: etymological dictionaries derive the word from check/exchequer.)

It conveys the hardiness of the dromedary and its central place in Arabia. Even so, the camel was rarely the decisive combat mount: Yarmuk (636) and Qadisiyya (636/637) were won mainly by horse cavalry and infantry.

The Umayyad (Battle of the Masts, attacks on Constantinople), Aghlabid and Fatimid fleets were real Mediterranean powers and used oared galleys. The siege of 717–718 is certain; the so-called “first siege” of 674–678 is now redated to 667–669 by Marek Jankowiak and called into question by James Howard-Johnston. It fits the period before c. 1050, but hardly the Mamluks.

It can be read as an allusion to amphibious operations: Cyprus (649), Rhodes (654 and 672–673), Crete (c. 827), Sicily (827) and the Balearic Islands (902/903). The link is generic and the value lies mainly in game balance. According to tradition, the crossing of 711 used ships provided by Count Julian of Ceuta.

The name is apt and the anti-cavalry role is justified: the Mamluks, slave soldiers of Kipchak and later Circassian origin, defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut (1260) and Homs (1281) and drove the Crusaders out of Acre (1291). The depiction, however, is wrong. In the game the Mameluke rides a camel and throws its scimitar at range, an invented technique. In reality they were horse-mounted cavalrymen, trained in furusiyya (horsemanship, the composite bow, the lance and the sword), and they fought mainly as heavy horse archers (Ayalon, Amitai-Preiss).

Bimaristans (a Persian term: bīmār “sick” + stān “place”) were leading hospitals. Michael Dols places the first Islamic hospital in Baghdad in the early 9th century (Harun al-Rashid); later notable examples include that of Nur al-Din in Damascus (1154) and Qalawun's al-Mansuri in Cairo (1284–1285), with specialised wards and medical teaching. The association with Monks is an abstraction, because these were institutions of physicians funded by waqf, not of clerics.

The treatise of Murda al-Tarsusi, written for Saladin (c. 1187), contains some of the oldest and clearest descriptions of counterweight trebuchets. The Mamluks used them en masse at Acre (1291). Muslim engineers sent from Ilkhanid Iran (Isma'il and Ala al-Din) brought them to Mongol China at Xiangyang (1273), where they became known as “huihui pao”, the “Muslim trebuchet”. The exact origin is contested and may be Byzantine (Chevedden). Extending the effect to the Mangonel line is a liberty taken by the game.

elements.element: Foot Archers and Skirmishers +2 attack vs. buildings
elements.explanation: It does not correspond to anything specific. It could be justified a posteriori by the naffatun, the corps of throwers of naphtha and incendiary projectiles in the Abbasid and Ayyubid armies, but the game does not make that link.

tree_issues.problem: Heavy armoured cavalry was the core of the Fatimid, Ayyubid and above all Mamluk armies: horsemen with mail, lance and sometimes horse armour (tijfaf). Stopping at the Knight contradicts the best-documented military identity of this civ.

This contradicts monumental Islamic architecture: the Dome of the Rock (691/692), the Great Mosque of Damascus (705–715), Samarra (836–892), al-Azhar (970–972) and Mamluk Cairo (the mosque-madrasa of Sultan Hasan, 1356–1363).

This is ironic in a “naval” civ. The word “arsenal” comes from the Arabic dār al-ṣināʿa (“house of manufacture”), via Venetian. The arsenals of Tunis (c. 698), Alexandria and Rawda island (Fustat) were famous, and Arab fleets used incendiary naphtha.

In both cases the historiographical debate is real. Andrew Watson's “Arab agricultural revolution” (new crops, irrigation, multiple cropping) would suggest giving Crop Rotation, although the thesis has been criticised (Decker). The absence of Guilds, on the other hand, is defensible: S. M. Stern argued that there is no evidence of craft guilds in Islamic cities before the Ottomans.

The Mamluks used cannon in sieges from c. 1360–1370, which is acceptable. But David Ayalon argued that the mounted elite despised hand-held firearms and that this reluctance played a part in the defeats at Marj Dabiq (1516) and Ridaniya (1517) against the Ottomans (a thesis now qualified). The tree does not reflect this striking characteristic.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that “Saracen” designated the desert nomads and, in a broad sense, all medieval Arabs.
history_text_issues.problem: In medieval Europe the term designated all Muslims, including Turks, Kurds and Berbers, not just Arabs. It was an exonym, not a self-designation.
history_text_issues.correction: Explain that it is a Graeco-Latin exonym that became the Christian synonym for “Muslim”. The people themselves spoke of “Arabs” (ʿarab) or of the community of believers (umma).

history_text_issues.claim: Presents the Arabs as nomads who burst forth suddenly, driven by faith, intending to change the religious and political landscape of the entire planet.
history_text_issues.problem: This is an Orientalist framing. The leadership of the conquests was the urban Qurayshi elite of Mecca and Medina, not nomads. The motivations included state formation, tribal mobilisation and plunder. The conversion of the conquered populations was slow: according to Richard Bulliet, in Iran Muslims became a majority only around the mid-9th century and reached about 80% by c. 950; in Egypt, Syria and Iraq the process was slower still.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe the conquests as the expansion of a new state with a religious ideology (Fred Donner, Hugh Kennedy), which ruled non-Muslims as tributary dhimmis without converting them by force.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Muhammad was largely ignored in Mecca, withdrew to Medina and came back to attack and capture Mecca.
history_text_issues.problem: The taking of Mecca in 630 was indeed a military campaign (c. 10,000 men), but one with almost no fighting, after the breach of the Treaty of Hudaybiyya (628). What is wrong is “ignored”: Muhammad faced hostility and persecution (including the boycott of the Banu Hashim), and the Hijra (622) took place at the invitation of the tribes of Medina.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention the Qurayshi opposition, the Hijra of 622 and the almost bloodless submission of Mecca in 630.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that within five years, starting in 634, the Arabs took Egypt, Palestine and Syria.
history_text_issues.problem: Syria and Palestine fell in 634–640 (Caesarea c. 640/641). Egypt was conquered in 639–642 (Alexandria in 641/642).
history_text_issues.correction: Give about eight years (634–642) for the three regions.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that, in Asia, the Arabs took Asia Minor from the Byzantines.
history_text_issues.problem: This is false. The Arabs carried out annual raids into Anatolia and reached Constantinople, but the frontier stabilised along the Taurus line and Asia Minor remained Byzantine until the arrival of the Seljuk Turks, after Manzikert (1071). The text itself contradicts this further on, when it attributes the conquest of Asia Minor to the Turks.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that the Arabs repeatedly attacked Anatolia without conquering it, and that the Arab–Byzantine frontier settled on the Taurus and in Cilicia.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Saracens from Tangier invaded the Iberian Peninsula.
history_text_issues.problem: Tariq ibn Ziyad was indeed governor of Tangier, and “Saracen” was the generic medieval label. But the army of 711 was mostly Berber, commanded by Tariq (himself a Berber, according to most sources), under the authority of Musa ibn Nusayr. The Berbers' text is more accurate.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that a mainly Berber army under Tariq, with Arab leadership, crossed the strait in 711.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that in 732, at Poitiers, Charles Martel halted a Saracen invasion of France.
history_text_issues.problem: It was a large raiding expedition led by Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi (the date 733 is also argued for). The Muslims held Narbonne until 759 and continued to raid Provence. The reading of Poitiers as the “battle that saved Europe” (Gibbon) is now heavily qualified.
history_text_issues.correction: Present Poitiers as a major defeat of a raid, not as the end of the Muslim presence in Gaul.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that, frustrated in the West, the forces of Islam turned east and reached the Indus and Central Asia by 750.
history_text_issues.problem: The chronology is reversed: Sindh (711–712, Muhammad ibn al-Qasim) and Transoxiana (705–715, Qutayba ibn Muslim) were conquered before 732. “North over India” is also a geographical error.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that the eastern and western fronts advanced simultaneously and that the clash with Tang China took place at Talas (751).

history_text_issues.claim: Speaks of a civil war between Sunnis and Shias that began in 656, supposedly lasted 60 years and split the state into Sunni (Iberian Peninsula) and Shia (Egypt and Iraq) regions.
history_text_issues.problem: This is a serious error. The First Fitna (656–661) pitted Ali against Muawiya, and the Second Fitna took place in 680–692. Sunni and Shia identities only crystallised in the 8th–10th centuries. The fragmentation of the caliphate resulted from the Abbasid revolution (750) and the Umayyad emirate of Córdoba (756). Iraq was the seat of the Sunni Abbasid caliphate (with pro-Shia Buyid emirs between 945 and 1055). Egypt had Shia (Ismaili) rule only under the Fatimids (969–1171), with a mainly Sunni population.
history_text_issues.correction: Rewrite on the basis of the fitnas, the Abbasid revolution and the later emergence of the rival caliphates (the Fatimids in 909, Córdoba in 929).

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Asia Minor and the Middle East were conquered by Muslim Turks in the early 11th century, and that the Crusades aimed to recover Palestine from the Turks.
history_text_issues.problem: The chronology is wrong: the Seljuks entered Baghdad in 1055, won at Manzikert in 1071 and occupied Anatolia in the 1070s–1080s (Jerusalem in 1073). And in 1099 the First Crusade took Jerusalem from the Fatimids, who had recovered it from the Turks in 1098.
history_text_issues.correction: Place the Seljuk expansion in the mid- to late 11th century and mention that Jerusalem was under Fatimid rule in 1099.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the Reconquista was carried out by Castile and Aragon and completed in 1492.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits Portugal, which completed its reconquest with the Algarve in 1249, as well as León and Navarre.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention the various Christian kingdoms, including Portugal.

history_text_issues.claim: Calls Saladin “the great Saracen leader”.
history_text_issues.problem: Saladin was a Kurd in the service of the Turkish Zengids, and he founded the Ayyubid dynasty. The label “Saracen” erases this ethnic diversity.
history_text_issues.correction: Present Saladin as a Kurdish Ayyubid sultan who united Egypt and Syria and retook Jerusalem in 1187, after Hattin.

history_text_issues.claim: Omissions: Abbasid Baghdad, Fatimid Cairo and the Mamluks.
history_text_issues.problem: The text ignores the founding of Baghdad (762), the translation movement, Fatimid Cairo (969) and the entire Mamluk Sultanate (Ain Jalut in 1260, Acre in 1291), even though the unique unit is Mamluk.
history_text_issues.correction: Include these milestones, which form the core of the 750–1517 period.

history_text_issues.claim: Attributes the economic decline to European trade routes to Asia in the 15th–16th centuries and jumps straight to the modern Arab states.
history_text_issues.problem: The explanation is simplistic. The Black Death (1347–1349), Timur's sack of Damascus (1400–1401) and the Mamluk fiscal crises all played a part. The Cape route (1498) and the defeat at Diu (1509) did indeed affect Mamluk spice revenue. The text also omits the roughly 400 years of Ottoman rule (1516–1918).
history_text_issues.correction: Mention the Ottoman conquest of 1516–1517 and Portuguese competition in the Indian Ocean as factors, among others.

missing_features: Mamluk furusiyya: heavy horse archers and lancers, with training manuals and exercise hippodromes (maydān) in Cairo
The naffatun (naphtha corps) and naval and siege incendiary weapons
The naval arsenals (dār al-ṣināʿa) and the Fatimid thalassocracy
The Graeco-Arabic translation movement and paper (paper mill in Baghdad, c. 794)
The barid, the state postal service, with pigeon post (Nur al-Din, Baybars and the Mamluks)
The slave-soldier system (mamluk/ghulam) as a recruitment institution
Irrigation and new crops (noria, qanat, sugar cane, citrus fruits)

proposals.title: Rename to “Arabs” (or split into Arabs and Mamluks)
proposals.description: Replace the exonym “Saracens” with “Arabs”. Alternatively, split into two civs: “Arabs” (caliphates, naval and commercial focus) and “Mamluks” (Egypt and Syria, cavalry and siege focus).
proposals.historical_basis: “Saraceni” was an external and polemical designation. The Mamluks were a Turkic-Circassian military elite ruling an Arab society, a historical entity distinct from the Arab caliphates.

proposals.title: Mameluke reworked as a mounted archer-lancer
proposals.description: The Mameluke now rides a horse and leaves the camel class. By default it shoots with a bow, but it can switch to melee mode with a lance, using the mode-switching mechanic that already exists for the Bengalis' Ratha. It receives a bonus against Cavalry Archers.
proposals.historical_basis: The furusiyya manuals (for example, Taybugha's archery treatise, c. 1368) gave training in the bow, lance and sword. The victories over the Mongol horse archers at Ain Jalut (1260) and Homs (1281) justify the role.

proposals.title: “Naffatun” team bonus
proposals.description: Keep the bonus against buildings, but explain it as incendiary projectiles. Add +1 attack and +10% fire range to the Fire Galley line. Those who want to go further could create a Naffat unit (infantry throwing naphtha grenades, with area damage against buildings).
proposals.historical_basis: Naffatun corps appear in the Abbasid and Ayyubid armies. At the siege of Acre (1189–1191), Baha al-Din ibn Shaddad reports the destruction of Crusader siege towers with naphtha.

proposals.title: “Dār al-Ṣināʿa” (arsenal bonus)
proposals.description: Docks work +15% faster, Shipwright is free and Fast Fire Ship becomes available.
proposals.historical_basis: The arsenals of Tunis (c. 698), Alexandria and Rawda produced state fleets. The word “arsenal” entered the European languages from Arabic.

proposals.title: “Bayt al-Hikma” and tech tree fixes
proposals.description: Give Architecture, Crop Rotation and Cavalier. New tech “Bayt al-Hikma”: University techs cost -33%.
proposals.historical_basis: The Abbasid translation movement (sponsored by al-Mamun, 813–833, among others), al-Khwarizmi and Umayyad and Mamluk architectural monumentality. The nature of the Bayt al-Hikma (academy or palace library) is debated (Gutas), but the scientific patronage is certain. Heavy cavalry was at the core of the Ayyubid and Mamluk armies.

contested: Origin of the counterweight trebuchet: Byzantine (according to Paul Chevedden, already in use around 1165) or Islamic.
Andrew Watson's “Arab agricultural revolution” thesis (1974, 1983) versus Michael Decker's criticisms (2009).
Existence of guilds (asnaf) in Islamic cities before the Ottomans: S. M. Stern (1970) against Louis Massignon (and the early Bernard Lewis).
Date and importance of the Battle of Poitiers/Tours (732 or 733).
First Arab attack on Constantinople: Theophanes' siege of 674–678 versus its redating to 667–669 (Jankowiak) or its rejection (Howard-Johnston).
Nature of the conquests: a movement of “Believers” (Donner) or revisionist readings (Crone and Cook); the real weight of the welcome given by Monophysite Christians persecuted by Byzantium.
The Bayt al-Hikma as a scientific academy or mainly a palace library (Dimitri Gutas).
“Convivencia” in al-Andalus: María Rosa Menocal versus Darío Fernández-Morera.
Degree of Mamluk rejection of firearms: Ayalon's thesis (1956) has been qualified by later studies.

al-Baladhuri, Futuh al-Buldan
Murda al-Tarsusi, Tabsirat arbab al-albab (c. 1187)

civs.represents: At its core, the Sasanian Empire (224–651), the last pre-Islamic Persian empire and a rival of Rome and Byzantium. The unique units (War Elephant, Savar) and the Kamandaran tech clearly point to the Sasanian army. There are later elements from Islamic Iran (Caravanserai, gunpowder, citadels) that could correspond to the Samanids, Buyids, Ilkhanids, Timurids or Safavids, but none of these is named.
civs.period: c. 500–651 (Sasanians) at the core of the design, with an implicit extension to c. 1500 (Persianised Islamic Iran).
civs.verdict: For the Sasanians, the unique elements are good: war elephants, noble heavy cavalry (asvaran, the source of “Savar”), massed archers (Kamandaran) and caravanserais are real, well-documented traits. The problem lies in the rest. The generic economic bonuses (starting resources, Town Centers and Docks) are arbitrary. The tech tree contradicts history: a people famous for archery and for great walls (Gorgan, Derbent) is left without Bracer, Arbalester, Keep and Fortified Wall. The history text ends in 651, with errors such as confusing Ctesiphon with Baghdad, and leaves out eight centuries of Islamic Iran within the game's window.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Persians” is acceptable, since the Sasanians called themselves Ērān and their realm Ērānshahr. The label nevertheless has a chronological problem: the design is Sasanian, but only c. 500–651 falls within the game's window. Islamic Iran (Samanids, Buyids, Persianised Seljuks, Ilkhanids, Timurids, Safavids from 1501) was often ruled by Turkic or Mongol dynasties and is scattered or absent: the Timurids appear through the Tatars, the Seljuks barely appear in the Turks, and the Hindustanis' Ghulam unit points to the Ghaznavid and Delhi Sultanate tradition of slave soldiers. The Persians share the Caravanserai with the Hindustanis.

elements.explanation: The Sasanian nobility fought as armoured heavy cavalry (asvaran; the clibanarii of Roman sources). In Islamic Iran, cavalry remained the elite arm, down to the Safavid qizilbash.
A pure balance bonus, with no historical counterpart.

elements.element: Town Centers and Docks +100% HP and work faster per Age
elements.explanation: It could allude to Sasanian urbanisation and administration (cities founded by Shapur I, the reforms of Khosrow I) and to the Persian Gulf ports (Siraf in the 9th–10th centuries, Hormuz in the 13th–15th centuries). The link is weak and the mechanic is generic.

elements.element: Parthian Tactics available in Castle Age
elements.explanation: The Iranian tradition of mounted archers is real. The expression, however, refers to the Arsacid Parthians (c. 247 BC–AD 224), the predecessors overthrown by the Sasanians. Sasanian cavalry was mainly heavy cavalry that also shot, not light cavalry using the “Parthian shot”.

Kārvānsarā is a Persian term, and Iran is the homeland of the building type: there are road stations attributed to the Sasanians (dating disputed), Seljuk ribats (Ribat-i Sharaf, 12th century) and the Safavid network of Shah Abbas (17th century). Sharing it with the Hindustanis is understandable.

The Sasanians used elephants (imported from India) at Avarayr (451), at the Battle of the Bridge (634) and at Qadisiyya (636/637), where they even frightened the Arab cavalry. The trample damage is a reasonable abstraction.

Savār means “horseman” in Persian, and the asvaran were the Sasanian mounted elite. The role of a heavy cavalryman strong against ranged units is reasonable. It is worth remembering that these horsemen also used the bow.

Kamāndār means “archer”. Procopius (Wars, I.18) says that almost all Persians were archers and that they shot faster than the Romans, though with less penetrating power. More affordable and more numerous archers render this reasonably well, although swapping gold for wood is arbitrary.

The Sasanian fortresses on the Roman frontier and in the Caucasus and, later, the Nizari Ismaili castles of Iran (Alamut) provide a basis for the name. But the tech contradicts the absence of Keep and Fortified Wall from the tech tree.
A heavy cavalry charge against archers is an acceptable abstraction, with no specific referent.

tree_issues.problem: Contradicts the Persian reputation in archery, which the very name Kamandaran invokes: Procopius describes armies of archers, and Maurice's Strategikon (c. 600) deals with tactics against the Persian rain of arrows.

Contradicts major Sasanian defensive works: the Wall of Gorgan (c. 195 km, with more than 30 forts, dated by Sauer et al. to the 5th century), the Tammisha Wall, the walls of Derbent (Khosrow I, 6th century) and Nisibis, a Persian stronghold from 363. Having Citadels without Keeps is also inconsistent.

This is partly defensible: Sasanian peasant infantry (paygan) had low status. But it ignores the Daylamites, elite infantry from the mountains of Gilan, with sword, javelins and shield. Procopius (Wars, VIII.14) mentions them in Persian service in the Lazic War, and it was they who founded the Buyid dynasty (945).

tree_issues.item: Weak Monastery (no Redemption, Atonement, Heresy, Illumination, Sanctity)
tree_issues.problem: It can be read as non-proselytising Zoroastrianism. But the Sasanian clergy (mobads, with the high priest Kartir in the 3rd century) was powerful and persecuted Christians and Manichaeans. In the Islamic period, the Nizamiyya madrasas and Persian scholarship were central. The lack of Heresy, in particular, is ironic.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the capital of the Persian Empire was Ctesiphon, “today called Baghdad”.
history_text_issues.problem: Factual error. Ctesiphon lies about 35 km south-east of Baghdad. Baghdad was founded from scratch in 762 by the caliph al-Mansur, who, according to al-Tabari, tried to reuse materials from Ctesiphon.
history_text_issues.correction: State that Ctesiphon, on the Tigris, south-east of present-day Baghdad, was the Sasanian capital.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the empire was reconstituted after Alexander and the break-up of his empire, and that the Persians had been fighting the Romans since the 3rd century.
history_text_issues.problem: Omits the Seleucids and the Arsacid Parthians (c. 247 BC–AD 224), who fought Rome from the 1st century BC onwards (Carrhae, 53 BC). The Sasanians only came to power in 224.
history_text_issues.correction: Distinguish Achaemenids, Parthians and Sasanians: the Roman–Iranian wars begin with the Parthians, and the Sasanian ones from c. 230.

history_text_issues.claim: Places the peace treaty with Rome in 364.
history_text_issues.problem: The treaty was signed in 363 by Jovian, after Julian's death, and ceded Nisibis to the Persians.
history_text_issues.correction: Correct to 363.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that, from the 6th century, the Persians began attacking the Byzantine Empire in Syria, Palestine, Egypt and present-day Turkey.
history_text_issues.problem: In the 6th century there were wars in Mesopotamia, Armenia and Lazica, and the sack of Antioch (540). But the conquest of Palestine (Jerusalem, 614) and Egypt (c. 618–621) belongs to the war of 602–628, under Khosrow II, already in the 7th century.
history_text_issues.correction: Distinguish the 6th-century wars from the great offensive of Khosrow II (602–628).

history_text_issues.claim: Says that in 626 the Persians besieged Byzantium itself without success.
history_text_issues.problem: The siege was conducted mainly by the Avars and their allies. Shahrbaraz's Persian army remained at Chalcedon, on the Asian shore, unable to cross the Bosporus.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe the siege of 626 as Avar–Persian, with the Persians prevented from crossing.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the Byzantines invaded Persia the following year (627).
history_text_issues.problem: Heraclius had been campaigning in Persian territory since 624. The victory at Nineveh came in December 627.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention the campaigns of 624–628 and the Battle of Nineveh (December 627).

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the Sasanian dynasty ended in battle in 636.
history_text_issues.problem: Qadisiyya (636/637) was decisive, but the dynasty survived: Ctesiphon fell in 637, Nahavand (642) was still to come, and Yazdegerd III died near Merv in 651. Regions such as Tabaristan held out until the 8th century.
history_text_issues.correction: Place the end of the dynasty in 651, with prolonged regional resistance.

history_text_issues.claim: Omission: the text ends with the Muslim conquest (651).
history_text_issues.problem: The civ covers c. 500–1500, but the text erases Islamic Iran: the Samanid Persian revival, Ferdowsi's Shahnameh (c. 1010), the Buyids, the Persian bureaucracy of the Abbasids and Seljuks (Nizam al-Mulk), the Ilkhanids, the Timurids (Herat) and the Safavids (1501).
history_text_issues.correction: Add a section on 651–1500 and on the continuity of the Persian language and culture as the lingua franca of the Islamic East.

missing_features: Elite Daylamite infantry (sword, javelins, shield), the military base of the Buyids
Rapid massed archery (Procopius) and the Persian tradition of archery manuals
The great fortified lines (Gorgan, Tammisha, Derbent)
The qanats (irrigation tunnels) and the irrigated agriculture of the plateau
The Persian bureaucracy (dabirs, divan) that ran the administration for caliphs and sultans
The Sasanian role as silk intermediary on the Silk Road, and the Gulf trade (Siraf, Hormuz)
Gundeshapur as a medical centre (with the caveat that the “academy” is partly a later construct, according to Dols)
The Safavid qizilbash cavalry (the far end of the game's window)

proposals.title: Kamandaran reworked along the lines of Procopius
proposals.description: Archer-line +20% rate of fire and -1 attack (faster but less penetrating), with reduced cost. Bracer and Arbalester return to the tech tree.
proposals.historical_basis: Procopius (Wars, I.18) compares Persian shooting, faster but weaker, with Roman shooting. Maurice's Strategikon also deals with tactics against Persian archers.

proposals.title: “Wall of Gorgan”: imperial fortification
proposals.description: Restore Keep and Fortified Wall. New tech: Stone Walls and towers +20% HP and 30% faster construction.
proposals.historical_basis: The Wall of Gorgan (c. 195 km, with more than 30 forts) and the walls of Derbent were Sasanian state works against the northern nomads (Sauer et al., 2013).

proposals.title: Qanat instead of the Town Center bonus
proposals.description: Replace the starting resources and the Town Center bonus with: Farms produce +10% food and Mill technologies cost -50%.
proposals.historical_basis: Qanats sustained Iranian agriculture from Antiquity onwards. al-Karaji wrote a treatise on them in the early 11th century.

proposals.title: Daylamite (infantry unit)
proposals.description: Barracks infantry with short-range javelins and a shield (good armour against ranged units), replacing the Two-Handed Swordsman.
proposals.historical_basis: The Daylamites served as elite infantry for the Sasanians (Procopius, Wars VIII.14; tradition links them to Vahriz's expedition to Yemen, c. 570) and founded the Buyid dynasty, which controlled Baghdad from 945 to 1055.

contested: Dating of the Wall of Gorgan (5th or 6th century) and its attribution.
Real tactical weight of the Sasanian elephants: a decisive weapon or mainly symbolic.
End of the Sasanian Empire: 636/637, 642 or 651; regional resistance continues beyond that.
Military reforms of Khosrow I and the role of the dehqans (Pourshariati versus traditional readings).
Pre-Islamic or Islamic origin of the caravanserai as an architectural type.
Existence and role of the Gundeshapur “academy” and hospital (Frye versus Dols).
Impartiality of Procopius in his comparisons between Roman and Persian archers.
key_sources: Procopius of Caesarea, Wars (Persian Wars)
Ammianus Marcellinus, Res Gestae
Maurice, Strategikon (c. 600)
al-Tabari, Ta'rikh (Sasanian section, trans. Bosworth; and Nöldeke)
Ferdowsi, Shahnameh (c. 1010)
Touraj Daryaee, Sasanian Persia (2009)
Parvaneh Pourshariati, Decline and Fall of the Sasanian Empire (2008)
Eberhard Sauer et al., Persia's Imperial Power in Late Antiquity: The Great Wall of Gorgan (2013)
Kaveh Farrokh, Sassanian Elite Cavalry AD 224–642 (2005)
Michael W. Dols, “The Origins of the Islamic Hospital: Myth and Reality” (1987)
Encyclopaedia Iranica (entries 'Aswaran', 'Caravansary', 'Elephant', 'Daylamites')
Rudi Matthee, on Safavid Iran

civs.represents: Essentially the Ottoman Empire (c. 1299–1600, above all after 1400), with references to the Seljuks: the Great Seljuk Empire (1037–1194) and the Sultanate of Rum (1077–1308). The design (Janissary, Artillery, gunpowder bonuses) is almost exclusively 15th–16th-century Ottoman.
civs.period: c. 1040–1600, with the design concentrated on c. 1400–1600 (Ottomans).
civs.verdict: In their Ottoman phase, the Turks have one of the best-founded identities in the game. The Janissary, the Sipahi, siege artillery and raiding light cavalry (akıncı) correspond to real, well-documented institutions, and the absence of pikemen is even a point in its favour. But the “Turks” label covers a thousand years of Turkic peoples, and the design ignores everything that is not late Ottoman: the Seljuks and the mounted archers of the steppes. Even for the Ottomans, the composite bow, the navy, siege engineering (no Siege Engineers) and field fortification (tabur) are missing. The history text has serious errors: it defines “Turk” as only the Seljuks and the Ottomans, confuses the fall of Baghdad (1258) with the end of the Seljuks and credits them with recovering Palestine, which was the work of Saladin and the Mamluks.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Turks” is an enormous ethnolinguistic label. It covers the Türk/Göktürk Khaganate (552–744), Khazars, Uyghurs, Karakhanids, Ghaznavids, Seljuks, Kipchaks, Bahri Mamluks, Timurids and Ottomans. In AoE2 several of these are scattered across the Cumans, Tatars, Bulgarians, Hindustanis and Saracens (Mameluke). The Ottomans identified themselves as “Osmanlı” and with a dynastic, Islamic state; among the elite, “Türk” could even be pejorative, designating the Anatolian peasant or nomad. The most rigorous option would be to rename the civ “Ottomans” and give the Seljuks and Oghuz an identity of their own as mounted archers.

elements.explanation: For the Ottomans of the 15th–16th centuries it is entirely fair: Constantinople (1453), Chaldiran (1514), Mohács (1526), and Hodgson and McNeill’s “gunpowder empires” model. It is anachronistic for the Seljuks, who did not have gunpowder.

The link is weak. Ottoman mining revenues came mainly from Balkan silver (Novo Brdo in 1455, Srebrenica, Kratovo) and, after 1517, from Egyptian gold via tribute, not from any characteristic gold mining.

elements.element: Scout Cavalry-line +1 pierce armor and upgrades free
elements.explanation: It corresponds to the akıncı, raiding light cavalry of the frontier families (Mihaloğlu, Evrenosoğlu), and to the deli, as well as to the Turkmen cavalry of the Seljuks. The weight of this arm is historical, but the mechanic (extra armour against projectiles, free upgrades) is generic.
It reflects state production of gunpowder and cannon: the Tophane-i Amire in Istanbul after 1453, hired founders such as Orban, and control of saltpetre.
It could allude to the discipline and professionalism of the Janissaries, but the link is generic.

The Yeniçeri were created under Murad I (c. 1363–1380) from the pençik and later from the devşirme. They began as archers and adopted firearms from the mid-15th century. The unit represents the Janissary of c. 1450–1600 well.

The sipahis (the provincial timariots and the kapıkulu of the sultan’s household) were cavalry who combined the composite bow, the lance and the mace. Giving them more HP as mounted archers is reasonable.
Ottoman superiority in siege artillery is well documented: Orban’s bombard in 1453, Munir Ali’s Dardanelles Gun (1464) and Rhodes (1522). The extra range is a fitting abstraction.
A plausible abstraction of Ottoman logistical and productive capacity.

tree_issues.problem: This is a historically faithful absence. The Ottomans did not use pike blocks: they combined Janissaries armed with firearms, artillery and field fortification (wagon tabur, trenches). It is not a problem; it is a correct choice worth noting.

The crossbow was not a Turkish weapon, but the Turkish composite bow was among the best in the world. The first Janissaries were archers, and after 1453 Mehmed II founded the Ok Meydanı shooting ground in Istanbul. Having no final foot-archer upgrade erases that tradition.
It contradicts Ottoman siege engineering, one of the most advanced of the period: sappers and miners (lağımcı) were decisive at Rhodes (1522) and at the first siege of Vienna (1529).
It is ironic. The Seljuks and Ottomans founded great hospitals (darüşşifa): Gevher Nesibe in Kayseri (1206), Divriği (1228–1229) and the complex of Bayezid II in Edirne (1488), with music therapy.

It is defensible. Printing in Arabic script only began with İbrahim Müteferrika (licence in 1727), although there were Jewish (Istanbul, 1493/94), Armenian and Greek presses. The supposed ban by Bayezid II (1485) is contested.

tree_issues.item: Generic navy (no Fast Fire Ship and no naval identity)
tree_issues.problem: In the 16th century the Ottoman fleet dominated the eastern Mediterranean (Preveza in 1538, Djerba in 1560, Hayreddin Barbarossa, Piri Reis) and confronted the Portuguese in the Indian Ocean. The civ has no naval trait at all.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that “Turk” designates two different Muslim groups: the Seljuks and the Ottomans.
history_text_issues.problem: This is false. The ethnonym “Türk” is first attested for the Göktürk Khaganate (552), in the Orkhon inscriptions (Kül Tegin in 732, Bilge Kağan in 735), in a pre-Islamic context. Many other Turkic peoples preceded the Seljuks.
history_text_issues.correction: Explain that the Seljuks and the Ottomans are only two late branches of a family of Turkic peoples originating in Inner Asia.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that around 70,000 Seljuks began as mercenaries in the army of the caliph of Baghdad.
history_text_issues.problem: It conflates two different things. The Seljuks were an Oghuz confederation that served Central Asian powers (Samanids, Karakhanids), defeated the Ghaznavids at Dandanaqan (1040) and entered Baghdad in 1055 as the caliph’s protector against the Buyids. Turkish slave soldiers in the caliph’s service (ghilman) had existed since al-Mutasim (830s). The figure of 70,000 has no known source.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe the Seljuk rise as a tribal conquest of Khorasan and Iran, culminating in the entry into Baghdad (1055).

history_text_issues.claim: It says that around 1100 the Seljuks controlled Anatolia, Palestine, the Gulf, the holy cities and Samarkand.
history_text_issues.problem: After the death of Malik Shah (1092) the empire fragmented. Jerusalem passed to the Fatimids in 1098 and to the Crusaders in 1099.
history_text_issues.correction: Place the peak in c. 1092, under Malik Shah and the vizier Nizam al-Mulk.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that the Seljuks eventually recovered Palestine from the Crusaders.
history_text_issues.problem: This is false. Jerusalem was retaken by Saladin (a Kurd, an Ayyubid) in 1187, and Acre fell to the Mamluks in 1291. The Zengids were atabegs of Seljuk origin, but not “the Seljuks”.
history_text_issues.correction: Credit the reconquests to the Zengids, the Ayyubids and the Mamluks.

history_text_issues.claim: It associates Sufism with a period of introspection, exhaustion and weakness.
history_text_issues.problem: This is an outdated narrative of decline. Sufism was culturally vibrant, and Rumi (d. 1273) lived in Konya under the Seljuks of Rum.
history_text_issues.correction: Present Sufism as a central current of Turkish and Persian religious and cultural life.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that the Mongols attacked, that Baghdad fell in 1258 and that the Seljuk Empire disappeared.
history_text_issues.problem: A serious confusion. The Great Seljuk Empire ended in 1194 (Tughril III, killed by the Khwarazmian Tekish). The Seljuks of Rum were defeated at Köse Dağ (1243), became vassals and died out c. 1308. The fall of Baghdad in 1258 ended the Abbasid caliphate, not the Seljuks.
history_text_issues.correction: Separate the three dates and the three entities.

history_text_issues.claim: It calls the Assassins a “heretical sect” of Islam.
history_text_issues.problem: “Heretical” is the polemical Sunni label, and “Assassins” (hashishiyya) is a derogatory exonym of disputed meaning (Daftary).
history_text_issues.correction: Use “Nizari Ismailis”.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that the Islamic peoples of Anatolia were unified at the beginning of the 14th century under Osman I.
history_text_issues.problem: Osman led only a small beylik in Bithynia (c. 1299–1324). The absorption of the Anatolian beyliks was only completed with the annexation of Karaman (1468–1474) and Dulkadir (1515).
history_text_issues.correction: Describe the gradual expansion of the Ottoman beylik.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that the Ottomans swore a jihad against the Byzantines.
history_text_issues.problem: It reproduces Paul Wittek’s “gazi thesis” (1938), now widely contested by Lindner, Kafadar and Lowry, who stress pragmatism and alliances with Christians.
history_text_issues.correction: Present gazi ideology as one of the factors, and a debated one.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that Timur temporarily halted the Ottoman advance and moved on.
history_text_issues.problem: At Ankara (1402) Timur crushed the Ottomans and captured Bayezid I. A civil war followed from 1402 to 1413 (the Interregnum), far more than a pause.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention Ankara and the Interregnum.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that in 1453 the walls were battered by 70 cannon for eight weeks and that 15,000 Janissaries led the final assault.
history_text_issues.problem: The duration (6 April to 29 May, about 53 days) is correct and the number of cannon varies between sources. But 15,000 Janissaries is a high figure: modern estimates of the corps under Mehmed II are generally below that (of the order of 5,000–10,000, growing over the course of the reign).
history_text_issues.correction: Present the figures as estimates from the sources (Kritovoulos, Barbaro, Doukas) and indicate the margin of uncertainty.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that in the 16th century the empire reached Budapest and Odessa.
history_text_issues.problem: Odessa was only founded in 1794, on the site of the Ottoman fortress of Hacıbey. The region was indeed under Ottoman rule (and that of the vassal Crimean Khanate) in the 16th century, so the error is mainly one of anachronistic naming. Ottoman rule extended beyond Budapest (Eger in 1596, Podolia in 1672–1699).
history_text_issues.correction: Use the period names (Hacıbey, Özi) and correct the geographical references.

history_text_issues.claim: Omissions: Rum, the conquests of Selim I and Suleiman, the navy.
history_text_issues.problem: It does not mention the Sultanate of Rum, Chaldiran (1514), the conquest of Mamluk Egypt (1516–1517), Mohács (1526) or the navy.
history_text_issues.correction: Include these central milestones.

missing_features: Seljuk and Oghuz identity as mounted archers: feigned retreat at Manzikert (1071) and Dorylaeum (1097)
The Turkish composite bow and long-distance shooting (Ok Meydanı)
Tabur cengi (wagon fort) used at Chaldiran (1514) and Mohács (1526)
The mehter military band
The devşirme and timar systems
Ottoman navy and corsairs (Barbarossa, Piri Reis), including the Indian Ocean front against Portugal
Siege engineering and mining (lağımcı) at Rhodes (1522) and Vienna (1529)
Seljuk and Ottoman hans, caravanserais and külliyes

proposals.title: Rename to “Ottomans” and create a Seljuk identity
proposals.description: Rename the civ to “Ottomans”. Alternatively, give the Dark Age and Feudal Age a Seljuk profile (bonuses to mounted archers) and reserve gunpowder for the Imperial Age.
proposals.historical_basis: The design corresponds to the Ottoman state of 1400–1600. The Seljuks were an empire of steppe cavalry, not of gunpowder.

proposals.title: “Tabur”: wagon fort
proposals.description: Unlocks a cheap wall of wagons (wood, fast construction) that Janissaries and Hand Cannoneers can garrison and fire from. Alternatively: gunpowder units +2 armour when near Bombard Cannons.
proposals.historical_basis: At Chaldiran (1514) and Mohács (1526) the Ottomans lined up chained wagons with artillery and Janissaries, a tactic generally associated with the Hungarian and Hussite example.

proposals.title: Mehter (support unit with an aura)
proposals.description: A non-combat support unit with an aura, using the mechanic of the Roman Centurion: nearby infantry and gunpowder units gain +10% attack rate and speed.
proposals.historical_basis: The mehterhâne, a war band with drums and zurnas, accompanied the army and served to keep up morale and transmit signals.

proposals.title: “Ok Meydanı”: Turkish archery tradition
proposals.description: Give Elite Skirmisher and a technology that gives the Archer-line and Cavalry Archers +1 range and +1 attack, instead of Arbalester. Also give Siege Engineers.
proposals.historical_basis: The first Janissaries were archers. The Ok Meydanı ground was founded by Mehmed II, and Turkish distance-shooting records are famous. Ottoman sappers were decisive at Rhodes (1522).

proposals.title: “Tersâne-i Âmire”: naval arsenal
proposals.description: Galley-line +10% HP and Docks -15% cost. Give Fast Fire Ship.
proposals.historical_basis: The Golden Horn arsenal (enlarged by Selim I from 1515) sustained the fleet that won at Preveza (1538) and operated in the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean against the Portuguese.

contested: The “gazi thesis” of Ottoman origins: Wittek (1938) versus Lindner (1983), Kafadar (1995) and Lowry (2003).
The alleged ban on printing by Bayezid II (1485) and Selim I (1515), questioned by Kathryn Schwartz (2017).
Date of the Janissaries’ adoption of firearms (the 1440s or the 1460s).
Figures for the 1453 siege: cannon and Janissaries (Kritovoulos, Barbaro, Doukas).
Tactical outcome of the Battle of Kosovo (1389).
The concept of “gunpowder empires” (Hodgson and McNeill) versus Streusand and Ágoston.
Ottoman “decline” after 1566 versus the “transformation” thesis (Tezcan, Kafadar).

civs.represents: The Amazigh (Berber) peoples of the Maghreb and the medieval states they founded or dominated: the Zirids and Hammadids (10th–12th centuries), the Almoravids (c. 1040–1147), the Almohads (1121–1269), the Marinids (1244–1465), the Zayyanids (1236–1556) and the Hafsids (1229–1574). The text and the monuments it cites extend the civ to al-Andalus (including Nasrid Granada, an Arab dynasty) and to the Saadians. In practice, it is a “Moorish”, Maghrebi and Andalusi civ.
civs.period: c. 700–1550, with an Almoravid and Almohad core (11th–13th centuries).
civs.verdict: The Berbers get the military essentials right. Light javelin cavalry is very well represented by the Genitour (the Castilian jinete, a word that comes from the Zenata), the cheap horses are well founded, and Kasbah is a well-chosen name. But the Camel Archer does not correspond to any attested Maghrebi troop type, the faster villagers are arbitrary, and the most distinctive feature of the Almoravids is missing: phalanx infantry, with long spears, lamt shields and drums. The history text credits the Berbers with the Mosque of Córdoba (Umayyad, Arab) and the Alhambra (Nasrid, Arab), calls an Arab conquest that took about 60 years “relatively easy”, and repeats myths about the Berber horse.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Berber” comes from the Greek barbaros, via the Latin barbarus and the Arabic barbar. The endonym is Amazigh (plural Imazighen), today politically reclaimed and omitted from the text. The label groups together very different confederations (Sanhaja, Masmuda, Zenata, Kutama) and, in the monuments cited, also absorbs the Arabs of al-Andalus. It overlaps with the Saracens (al-Andalus, the invasion of 711, the Fatimids, whose early army was Kutama Berber) and with the Malians (the Almoravids, Ghana, trans-Saharan trade). The text runs from the second millennium BC to the Saadians (16th century), far beyond the game's window, and the Saadians were sharifs of claimed Arab lineage, not a Berber dynasty.

elements.explanation: Cavalry is the most constant tradition, from the ancient Numidian cavalry to the medieval Zenata. At sea, the Almohad fleet was so respected that Saladin asked it for support in 1189–1190 (without success), and there were also the Hafsid and Marinid fleets. The corsair reputation dates mainly from the 16th century onwards.
It could allude to pastoralism and transhumant mobility, but the game's villagers are mainly farmers and builders. The link is forced.

elements.element: Stable Units cost -15/20% in Castle/Imperial Age
elements.explanation: Horses were abundant (the Berber horse, or barb), and light cavalry was recruited en masse among the tribes and was far cheaper than feudal heavy cavalry.
Light corsair galiots and fustas, and fast Maghrebi fleets. The link is good, although the corsair heyday (Salé, Algiers, Tunis) belongs to the 16th–17th centuries.

Camels were central to the Saharan Berbers (Sanhaja, Tuareg), and there are accounts of camels in Almoravid armies, also used to frighten enemy horses. But the camel-mounted archer is not attested as a Maghrebi troop type: in combat, javelins, spears and swords dominated, and the bow played a secondary role.

The word jinete/ginete comes from “Zenata” (zanātī). It was light cavalry with javelins and a leather shield (adarga), using envelopment and withdrawal tactics. Nasrid Granada and Castile adopted it, and the term “ginete” also entered Portuguese.
The qasaba was the urban citadel: the Kasbah of the Udayas in Rabat (fortified by the Almohads) and that of Marrakesh. The name is spot on. The effect (Castles working faster) is an abstraction.
The dromedary spread through North Africa in late antiquity (Bulliet) and made trans-Saharan trade possible. The regeneration is a gameplay way of representing the animal's endurance.

elements.element: Genitour available at the Archery Range for allies
elements.explanation: Jineta-style cavalry was adopted by the Christian Iberian kingdoms, and Zenata volunteers (ghuzat) served Granada. In historical terms, it is one of the best team bonuses in the game.

tree_issues.problem: This contradicts the best-documented Almoravid tactic. al-Bakri (1068) describes infantry in close-packed ranks, with the front rank armed with long spears and the ranks behind throwing javelins. It was a phalanx that withstood cavalry charges (Zallaqa/Sagrajas, 1086).

This contradicts the text itself and Almohad military architecture in rammed earth (tabiya): the walls of Marrakesh and Rabat, the Torre del Oro in Seville (1220–1221), alcazabas and ribats (Monastir, 796; Sousse, 821).
This is a coherent absence: foot archery was not the strong point of Maghrebi armies. The problem is that the same logic should call the Camel Archer into question.

This is acceptable, but late. The earliest cases are contested (Sijilmasa in 1274 according to Ibn Khaldun, Baza in 1324/1325). The Saadians used arquebusiers at Alcácer Quibir (1578) and at Tondibi (1591).

tree_issues.item: Camel Rider and Heavy Camel Rider (present)
tree_issues.problem: These are plausible for the Saharan groups. This is the most coherent case of camels in this civ's tree.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the early Berbers were mainly nomadic pastoralists and that only a minority practised settled agriculture.
history_text_issues.problem: This is a simplification. Many Berbers (the Tell, Kabylia, the Atlas, Masinissa's Numidia) had been settled farmers since antiquity.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe a combination of mountain and lowland agriculture with pastoralism.

history_text_issues.claim: Attributes the ease of the Arab conquest to Byzantine persecution of the Arians and Donatists.
history_text_issues.problem: This is a serious error. The Arab conquest of the Maghreb was one of the longest and most difficult (c. 647–709). Kusayla killed Uqba ibn Nafi (683), Queen Dihya (al-Kahina) defeated Hassan ibn al-Numan (c. 697–698), and the Great Berber Revolt (740–743) followed later. By the 7th century, Arianism (the religion of the Vandals) had already disappeared and Donatism was residual.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe a prolonged conquest with strong Berber resistance, followed by gradual Islamisation.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the Berber horse was famous for terrifying other horses with its aggressive personality.
history_text_issues.problem: There is no known basis for this claim. The barb was famous for its endurance, hardiness and agility.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention the endurance and hardiness of the barb horse.

history_text_issues.claim: Credits the Berbers with the Alhambra of Granada and the Mosque of Córdoba, as well as the Koutoubia and the Hassan Tower.
history_text_issues.problem: Half the list is wrong. The Mosque was built by the Arab Umayyads (Abd al-Rahman I, 784–786, with enlargements up to al-Mansur, 987). The Alhambra is Nasrid (an Arab dynasty; the palaces are mainly the work of Yusuf I and Muhammad V, 14th century), although 11th-century Granada was the capital of the Zirids, a Berber dynasty. Only the Koutoubia and the Hassan Tower (like the Giralda) are Almohad.
history_text_issues.correction: Replace them with the Giralda of Seville, the Kasbah of the Udayas and the walls of Marrakesh.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Fatimid overextension to the east made them lose the Maghreb.
history_text_issues.problem: The Fatimids, whose army was based on the Kutama Berbers, moved to Cairo (973) and left Ifriqiya to the Zirids (Sanhaja Berbers), who broke with them c. 1048–1049.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe the delegation to the Zirids and the Zirid break, and the Kutama role in the Fatimid rise.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the 11th-century Hilalian invasion severely affected agriculture and trade.
history_text_issues.problem: It follows Ibn Khaldun's catastrophist picture, which historians such as Jean Poncet (1967) and Michael Brett consider exaggerated.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the impact as debated.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the Almohads crushed the Castilians at Alarcos (1195).
history_text_issues.problem: This is true, but the text omits the decisive defeat at Las Navas de Tolosa (1212), which began the Almohad collapse.
history_text_issues.correction: Add Las Navas de Tolosa.

history_text_issues.claim: Jumps from the end of Granada (1492) to the Ottoman conquest and the Saadians.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the post-Almohad Berber states (Marinids, Wattasids, Zayyanids, Hafsids, 13th–16th centuries). The Saadians were sharifs of claimed Arab lineage, not a Berber dynasty.
history_text_issues.correction: Include the Marinids, Zayyanids and Hafsids and mention the sharifian nature of the Saadians.

missing_features: The Almoravid phalanx: long spears, lamt shields (Saharan antelope hide, famous and exported) and war drums (tabl) at Zallaqa (1086)
The ribat and the murabitun ideology (from which the name “Almoravids” comes)
Trans-Saharan gold and the Almoravid dinar, imitated in the Peninsula as the morabitino/maravedi, and also minted by Sancho I of Portugal
Rammed-earth fortifications (tabiya)
The Black guards ('abid) and the Christian mercenary militias of the Almohads and Marinids
The veil (litham) of the Sanhaja and Tuareg as a marker of identity
Almohad thought (Ibn Tumart, Averroes)

proposals.title: Murabit: Almoravid infantry
proposals.description: Long-spear infantry with a lamt shield: high armour against ranged units and a bonus against cavalry, possibly replacing the Camel Archer. Restore Halberdier.
proposals.historical_basis: al-Bakri (1068) describes the ranks of spears and javelins. Lamt shields were famous in the Maghreb and al-Andalus, and the phalanx withstood the Castilian charges at Zallaqa (1086).

proposals.title: “Tabl”: Almoravid drums
proposals.description: Infantry +15% attack speed. Enemy units near groups of Berber infantry have their speed reduced.
proposals.historical_basis: The Arabic sources and the historiographical tradition on Zallaqa (1086) highlight the psychological effect of the Almoravid drums on the Castilians.

proposals.title: “Tabiya”: rammed-earth fortification
proposals.description: Restore Keep and Architecture. Stone Walls and towers cost -25% stone and are built faster.
proposals.historical_basis: The Almohad walls of Marrakesh, Rabat and Seville and the Torre del Oro were built in rammed earth, a cheap and quick material.

proposals.title: “Sijilmasa”: trans-Saharan gold
proposals.description: Trade Carts generate +15% gold. Alternatively: free Coinage and Banking.
proposals.historical_basis: Sijilmasa was the northern terminus for gold from the western Sudan. The Almoravid dinar became the reference currency of the western Mediterranean (morabitino).

proposals.title: Show the endonym Amazigh
proposals.description: Display “Berbers (Imazighen)” or add the endonym to the text. Alternatively, recast the civ as “Maghrebis”.
proposals.historical_basis: Imazighen is the self-designation. “Berber” is an exonym of Graeco-Latin and Arabic origin.

contested: Real impact of the Hilalian invasion (Ibn Khaldun versus Poncet and Brett).
First use of gunpowder in the Maghreb and al-Andalus (Sijilmasa 1274, Baza 1324/1325).
Origin of Tariq (Berber, according to most sources; some say Persian or Arab) and composition of the army of 711.
Almoravid conquest of Ghana in 1076 (Conrad and Fisher, “The Conquest that Never Was”, 1982–1983).
The “zenith” of the Islamic West: the Caliphate of Córdoba (10th century) or the Almoravid and Almohad empires.
The very category “Berber” as a medieval Arab construct (Ramzi Rouighi, Inventing the Berbers, 2019).
key_sources: Ibn Khaldun, Kitab al-'Ibar (Histoire des Berbères, trans. de Slane)
al-Bakri, Kitab al-Masalik wa'l-Mamalik (1068)
Ibn Abi Zar, Rawd al-Qirtas
Ibn Idhari, al-Bayan al-Mughrib
al-Idrisi, Nuzhat al-Mushtaq
Michael Brett & Elizabeth Fentress, The Berbers (1996)
Ronald A. Messier, The Almoravids and the Meanings of Jihad (2010)
Amira K. Bennison, The Almoravid and Almohad Empires (2016)
Hugh Kennedy, Muslim Spain and Portugal (1996)
Ramzi Rouighi, Inventing the Berbers (2019)
Richard W. Bulliet, The Camel and the Wheel (1975)

civs.represents: The Mali Empire (Manden Kurufaba), founded by the Mandinka (Maninka/Malinke) under Sundiata Keita c. 1235, at its height under Mansa Musa (c. 1312–1337). In practice, the civ stands generically for the western Sahel: the text absorbs Ghana (Soninke Wagadu) and Sosso, Timbuktu at its height corresponds to Songhai (15th–16th centuries) and the unique unit comes from the Kingdom of Dahomey (18th–19th centuries, Bight of Benin).
civs.period: c. 1235–1600 (Mali), with extensions to Ghana (8th–11th centuries) and Songhai (1464–1591). The unique unit points to Dahomey (18th–19th centuries).
civs.verdict: The economic core is well thought out. The gold of Bambuk and Bure and the Sudano-Sahelian adobe architecture, which saves wood, have a solid basis. The emphasis on infantry matches al-Umari, who speaks of about 100,000 men, of whom about 10,000 were horsemen. But the unique unit, the Gbeto, is a double anachronism: they were the elephant hunters of the female military corps of Dahomey (the Fon people, present-day Benin), 18th–19th centuries, more than 1,000 km from Mali. The tech tree gives the Malians gunpowder that neither Mali nor Songhai used (it was precisely the lack of firearms that was Songhai's undoing at Tondibi, 1591) and takes away Bracer, even though Mandinka infantry was largely made up of archers. Poisoned arrows and griots are missing. The history text is generally solid, with isolated errors.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Malians” is the demonym of the Republic of Mali, which adopted the empire's name in 1960. The empire's founders were Mandinka (Maninka/Mandinka/Malinke, “people of Manden”), and the empire included Soninke, Fula, Songhai, Bozo and Tuareg. The label merges Ghana, Sosso, Mali and Songhai into one and imports a unit from the Bight of Benin (Dahomey), centuries outside the game's window. It would be more accurate to call it “Mandinka” or “Mali Empire”, and Songhai would deserve a civ of its own.

elements.explanation: al-Umari (Masalik al-Absar, c. 1340), drawing on informants who had known Mansa Musa, speaks of about 100,000 men, of whom about 10,000 were horsemen. The bulk was infantry, largely archers and spearmen. The noble elite fought on horseback, with horses largely imported from North Africa.
Sudano-Sahelian architecture uses banco (adobe), with palm-wood beams (toron) and little timber. The Djinguereber Mosque (c. 1327) is the classic example. It is a well-executed abstraction.

Mali controlled access to the gold of Bambuk and Bure (and later of the Akan, via Djenné). According to al-Umari, Mansa Musa's passage through Cairo (1324) lowered the value of gold in the city for years.
It could allude to leather or wicker shields, but there is no specific evidence of Mandinka infantry being especially well protected against missiles. It looks mainly like a balance choice.

The gbeto (“elephant hunters”) were a unit of the female military corps of the Kingdom of Dahomey (Agojie or Mino), of the Fon people, in present-day Benin, in the 18th–19th centuries. They are neither Mandinka nor medieval, and in the 19th century they mainly used muskets. The game's knife-throwing is invented.

“Tigi” is a Mande suffix meaning “lord/owner” (dugutigi, “village chief”). The effect (Town Centers firing without a garrison) has no concrete referent. It might evoke the walled towns (tata), but the link is weak.

The name seems to derive from farin/farima, “brave”, which also lies behind titles of Mandinka military governors (farba, mentioned by Ibn Battuta). The exact etymology used by the game is not confirmed. Strengthening the cavalry has a basis, because the horsemen were the warrior aristocracy.

Timbuktu (Djinguereber, Sankore, Sidi Yahya) was a great centre of Islamic learning. “University” is anachronistic as an institution, since these were networks of teachers around mosques. Its height came in the Songhai period (Ahmad Baba, 1556–1627).

tree_issues.item: Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon, Cannon Galleon (present)
tree_issues.problem: They are anachronistic for Mali and for Songhai, which had no firearms. At Tondibi (1591), the Moroccan arquebusiers of Judar Pasha routed the Songhai army. In the Sahel, only Bornu, under Idris Alooma (1570s), imported Turkish musketeers.

Historiography describes Mandinka infantry as made up largely of archers, who made up for the weakness of their bows with poison. The Malians have Arbalester but not Bracer, which runs counter to that tradition; a damage bonus would be more coherent than a range bonus.

tree_issues.item: Galleon absent but Cannon Galleon present
tree_issues.problem: This is inconsistent. River warfare on the Niger (Sonni Ali's war canoes, Sorko and Bozo boatmen) is not represented. The alleged Atlantic expedition of Abu Bakr II is contested.
The camels belonged to the Saharan traders (Sanhaja, Tuareg), not to the Mandinka armies, which used horses. It is a minor detail.

There is no evidence of torsion or traction artillery in the medieval Sahel. Sieges were conducted by blockade: according to the Tarikh al-Sudan, Djenné held out against Sonni Ali for seven years, seven months and seven days (a clearly formulaic number). It is a generic limitation of the game.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Sundiata annexed Ghana “and its important gold mines”.
history_text_issues.problem: Ghana mainly controlled the gold trade, not the deposits, which lay to the south, in Bambuk and Bure.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that Mali came to control the routes and the gold-bearing areas of Bambuk and Bure.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the Sosso conquered Kumbi, the capital, in 1203.
history_text_issues.problem: Both the date and the identification of Kumbi Saleh as the capital of Ghana are debated.
history_text_issues.correction: Flag the uncertainty.

history_text_issues.claim: Speaks of a standing army of up to 100,000 soldiers.
history_text_issues.problem: The figure comes from al-Umari, who was writing on the basis of informants. “Standing” is doubtful: most were mobilised contingents.
history_text_issues.correction: Attribute the figure to al-Umari and mention the provincial contingents.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Mansa Musa took 500 slaves and 100 camels with 30,000 pounds of gold.
history_text_issues.problem: The figures vary between the sources (al-Umari, Ibn Khaldun, Tarikh al-Sudan) and are probably inflated.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the figures as the sources' accounts.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Musa had two “madaris (universities)” built in Timbuktu, Sankore and Djinguereber.
history_text_issues.problem: Djinguereber is attributed to Musa and the architect Abu Ishaq al-Sahili (c. 1327). Sankore is attributed by al-Sa'di (Tarikh al-Sudan) to a wealthy woman of the Aghlal tribe, at an uncertain date (14th–15th centuries). “University” is anachronistic.
history_text_issues.correction: Attribute only Djinguereber to Musa and describe Timbuktu as a network of mosques and teachers, with its height in the Songhai period.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that by the 14th century the mansas had converted to Islam.
history_text_issues.problem: The conversion was much earlier. al-Bakri (1068) mentions the conversion of the king of Malal, and Mansa Uli made the pilgrimage in the time of Sultan Baybars (1260–1277).
history_text_issues.correction: Place the Islamisation of the court in the 11th–13th centuries.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the Portuguese explorers reached the south-western provinces in 1455.
history_text_issues.problem: The Portuguese reached the coast of Senegal in the 1440s (Dinis Dias at Cape Verde, 1444; Nuno Tristão, killed c. 1446). 1455–1456 corresponds to the voyages up the Gambia River by Cadamosto (a Venetian in the service of Prince Henry the Navigator) and by Diogo Gomes, who gathered news of the Mali court.
history_text_issues.correction: Place the first contacts in the 1440s and the Gambia voyages in 1455–1456.

history_text_issues.claim: Speaks of the loss of control over the “Sub-Saharan” trade.
history_text_issues.problem: The correct term is trans-Saharan.
history_text_issues.correction: Correct to “trans-Saharan trade”.

missing_features: Archers with poisoned arrows (Zurara reports the death of Nuno Tristão from poisoned arrows on the Guinea coast, c. 1446)
The griots (jeli): memory, legitimation and morale (Epic of Sundiata, Balla Fasséké)
Sahelian heavy cavalry with padded jerkins and mail (more typical of Bornu and the Hausa)
Niger river fleets and specialised boatmen (Bozo, Somono, Sorko)
Walled adobe towns (tata)
The Taghaza salt trade
The hunters' societies (donso)
