proposals.title: Mande archer with poisoned arrows instead of the Gbeto
proposals.description: Cheap, short-range foot archer, with a damage bonus against cavalry and camels, or with damage over time if the engine allows it. Also give Bracer.
proposals.historical_basis: The historiography of Mali describes the infantry as made up largely of archers. The Portuguese chronicles (Zurara, Cadamosto) report the effectiveness of poisoned arrows on the coasts of Senegambia and Guinea.

proposals.title: Remove gunpowder
proposals.description: Remove Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon and Cannon Galleon. Compensate with an improved Farimba (Cavalier with +HP) and cheaper Fortified Walls.
proposals.historical_basis: Songhai was defeated at Tondibi (1591) precisely because it had no firearms. Mali never used them.

proposals.title: Jeli (griot) as a support unit with an aura
proposals.description: Support unit trained at the Monastery or the Castle, with an aura similar to the Centurion's: nearby units get +1 attack and +10% attack speed. Does not convert.
proposals.historical_basis: Griots accompanied kings and exhorted warriors. The Epic of Sundiata, transmitted by griots, is the main traditional source on the founding of Mali.

proposals.title: Niger war canoe
proposals.description: At the Docks, replace the Galleons with a fast, cheap war canoe that carries few units and fires arrows.
proposals.historical_basis: The Tarikh al-Sudan describes Sonni Ali's river fleet, and the Sorko boatmen had a military role.

proposals.title: Rename to “Mandinka” and create Songhai
proposals.description: Rename the civ to “Mandinka” or “Mali Empire” and create a Songhai civ that takes Timbuktu, the Niger fleet and the 1464–1591 period.
proposals.historical_basis: Mali and Songhai were distinct, successive empires, with different dynasties, ethnic groups and centres.

civs.represents: The Christian kingdom of the Ethiopian highlands (Abyssinia): Aksum (c. 1st–10th centuries), the Zagwe (c. 1137–1270, or from the 10th century according to another tradition) and above all the Solomonic dynasty (from 1270), with its military peak under Amda Seyon I (1314–1344) and Zara Yaqob (1434–1468), up to the war against the Adal Sultanate (1529–1543).
civs.period: c. 500–1543, with Aksum (until c. 940) and the Solomonic period (1270–1543) as the core periods.
civs.verdict: The archer-civ label has some support: Amda Seyon's Glorious Victories mention archers, and al-Umari includes the bow among Ethiopian weapons, although he gives the spear as the main weapon; this makes the free spearman upgrade even more defensible. The rest of the design is largely arbitrary. The resources-per-Age bonus has no basis. Torsion Engines evokes Greco-Roman artillery without any Ethiopian attestation. Royal Heirs has an evocative name (the princes imprisoned on Amba Geshen) but an unrelated effect. The Shotel Warrior is based on a real weapon, but one whose medieval antiquity is poorly documented. The tech tree gives Bombard Cannon but not Hand Cannoneer, when the great episode of firearms in Ethiopian history is the war of 1529–1543, with about 400 Portuguese musketeers (1541) against Arab and Ottoman musketeers in the service of Adal.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Ethiopia” is a Greek exonym (Aithiopia, “burnt faces”), but it was adopted by the Aksumite kings themselves from Ezana (4th century) onwards and by the Church (in Ge'ez, Ityopya), so it is acceptable. In European sources, including Portuguese ones, the kingdom was “Abyssinia” (from the Arabic Habasha), the realm of “Prester John”. The label covers a long sequence (Aksum, the Agaw Zagwe, the Amhara and Tigrayan Solomonids) and excludes the neighbouring Muslim states (Ifat, Adal, Hadiya) and peoples such as the Oromo, who have no civ. Aksum's peak (3rd–6th centuries) falls largely before the game's window.

elements.explanation: According to al-Umari (14th century, cited by Taddesse Tamrat), the Ethiopians' main weapon was the spear, but they also used the bow, as well as swords and spears; Taddesse notes that swords and daggers were rare. Amda Seyon's Glorious Victories (trans. Huntingford) mention archers, spearmen, cavalry and infantry, and Amda Seyon is said to have created a regiment of shield-bearers, probably to protect the archers. The bow has a basis, but it was not the dominant weapon.

elements.element: Receive +100 gold and +100 food when advancing to the next Age
elements.explanation: Pure game balance, with no historical referent.
It is a mechanical way of giving weight to the archers, with no specific attested trait (rate of fire, type of bow).

Better grounded than the archer label itself: al-Umari gives the spear, “similar to a long lance”, as the main weapon, and the infantry frequently faced the cavalry of the Muslim sultanates. There were, however, no European-style pike formations.

The shotel is a real Ethiopian curved sword, but the reliable examples and descriptions are mostly from the 18th–19th centuries. Taddesse Tamrat states that Amda Seyon increased the use of swords and daggers (probably obtained through Muslim merchants) and created a sword-armed regiment, but nothing indicates that these were shotels. The use “to get around shields or unhorse riders” is modern speculation.

The name evokes a real institution: to prevent wars of succession, the princes of the royal family were confined on Amba Geshen (a practice whose start date is uncertain, in place at least since the early Solomonic period) until Ahmad Grañ took the mountain in 1540. The effect (Shotel Warriors and Camel Riders take less damage from mounted units) has no connection whatsoever with that institution.

Torsion artillery (ballistae, onagers) is Greco-Roman and was in decline in late antiquity. There is no evidence of its use in Aksum or in medieval Ethiopia, where mountain warfare was waged with ambas (mountain fortresses) and blockades.

elements.element: Outposts +3 line of sight and cost no stone
elements.explanation: It could evoke lookout posts on the ambas of the highlands, but the link is tenuous.

tree_issues.item: Hand Cannoneer missing, Bombard Cannon present
tree_issues.problem: The historical situation is the reverse. Before the war, Lebna Dengel had only a handful of firearms. Adal used cannon from at least 1531 (Antukyah, according to Arab Faqih's chronicle), and in 1542 it received from the Ottoman governor of Zabid about 2,000 Arab musketeers and 900 Ottoman soldiers. Cristóvão da Gama's roughly 400 Portuguese musketeers landed in 1541 and, after Wayna Daga (1543), Ethiopia gradually adopted the musket. There are no significant Ethiopian siege cannons in the period.

tree_issues.item: Generic navy (no Carvel Hull or Fast Fire Ship)
tree_issues.problem: Aksum was a maritime power: Red Sea trade passed through Adulis, and Kaleb invaded Himyar (Yemen) by sea c. 525. Solomonic Ethiopia was an inland state and lost Massawa to the Ottomans in 1557. An Aksumite naval trait could exist in the early Ages.
This is partly consistent: the Christian highland army had cavalry, but it depended on imported horses and fought mostly on foot. It is not a problem.

tree_issues.item: Heavy Camel Rider and Royal Heirs (camel boost)
tree_issues.problem: Camels belonged to the lowlands (Afar, Somalis, Adal), not to the Christian highland army, which used horses and mules.

The absence of Block Printing is right, because the culture was a manuscript one until the 19th century. But Ethiopian monasticism (Debre Libanos, the movements of Takla Haymanot and Ewostatewos) and the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela have no expression in the design.
There is no evidence of torsion or traction artillery in medieval Ethiopia. These pieces are anachronistic for this civ.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Ethiopia was first mentioned around 1200 BC, in the Iliad.
history_text_issues.problem: The Iliad was composed c. 8th–7th centuries BC, although it depicts an earlier period. Egyptian sources mention Kush much earlier.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that the “Ethiopians” (Aithiopes) appear in the Homeric poems (8th–7th centuries BC).

history_text_issues.claim: Places Aksum at the mouth of the Red Sea.
history_text_issues.problem: Aksum lies inland, on the Tigray plateau, about 150–160 km from the port of Adulis on the Gulf of Zula, and not on the Bab el-Mandeb strait.
history_text_issues.correction: Distinguish the plateau capital (Aksum) from the port (Adulis).

history_text_issues.claim: Says that in the 4th century King Ezana conquered the neighbouring kingdom of Kush.
history_text_issues.problem: Ezana's inscription describes a campaign (c. 350) against the Noba in the region of the Nile and the Atbara. The kingdom of Meroë was by then in decline or already broken up, and lasting Aksumite rule over Kush is not attested.
history_text_issues.correction: Speak of an expedition by Ezana to the Meroë region, against the Noba, with no lasting conquest.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Aksum was surpassed only by Rome, Persia and China.
history_text_issues.problem: This is a statement by the prophet Mani (3rd century, Kephalaia) presented as a modern assessment.
history_text_issues.correction: Attribute the quotation to Mani.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Ethiopia maintained generally good relations with the Islamic powers until the 16th century.
history_text_issues.problem: This is misleading. There were recurring wars with the sultanates of Ifat and Adal: Amda Seyon (1332), Zara Yaqob (Gomit, 1445) and Lebna Dengel (1517). Relations with Mamluk Egypt were also tense.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention the centuries-long military rivalry with the sultanates of the Horn of Africa.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the history of the Zagwe remains shrouded in mystery.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the greatest legacy of the Zagwe: the monolithic churches of Lalibela (King Gebre Meskel Lalibela, c. 1181–1221).
history_text_issues.correction: Include Lalibela.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that, as in Aksum, the Ethiopian army consisted mainly of archers and infantry with spears and swords.
history_text_issues.problem: According to al-Umari, the spear was the main weapon and swords were rare until Amda Seyon expanded their use. The army also included cavalry.
history_text_issues.correction: Give the spear as the main weapon, with archers and cavalry, and swords as a minority weapon.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the shotel was used to unhorse riders or to get around shields.
history_text_issues.problem: This is popular speculation with no known medieval source. The reliable attestations of the shotel are late.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the shotel as a traditional curved sword, of uncertain use and chronology.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that a Portuguese expedition reached Ethiopia in 1490.
history_text_issues.problem: Pêro da Covilhã arrived alone, as an envoy of John II, c. 1490–1494. The first embassy proper was that of Dom Rodrigo de Lima, with Father Francisco Álvares (1520–1526).
history_text_issues.correction: Correct to Pêro da Covilhã and to the 1520 embassy.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Dawit II asked for help and that the Portuguese sent 400 musketeers who, together, repelled the invaders.
history_text_issues.problem: Dawit II (Lebna Dengel) did indeed ask for help, but he died in 1540, before the force arrived. Cristóvão da Gama was captured and executed in 1542, and the victory of Wayna Daga (1543), where Ahmad Grañ died, came under Emperor Galawdewos. Adal had Ottoman support.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention Cristóvão da Gama, Galawdewos, Wayna Daga and Ottoman support for Adal.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the Solomonic dynasty remained in power until the late 20th century.
history_text_issues.problem: During the Zemene Mesafint (1769–1855) the dynasty was nominal. Tewodros II (1855) was not Solomonic in the strict sense.
history_text_issues.correction: Qualify the continuity.

missing_features: The navy and trade of Aksum (Adulis) and Kaleb's expedition to Yemen (c. 525)
Aksumite elephants: Abraha and the “Year of the Elephant”; John Malalas (probably drawing on the account of Nonnosus) describes the king of Aksum on a platform drawn by four elephants
The ambas (mountain fortresses) and mountain warfare
The chewa regiments (military colonies with lands held in gult) of Amda Seyon and Zara Yaqob
The Church and monasticism (tabot, Lalibela, Debre Libanos)
The itinerant royal camp (ketema) and the gult system of land grants
The 1529–1543 war against Adal and the Ottomans, with the Portuguese alliance
The embassies to Europe (Council of Florence, 1441)

proposals.title: Musketeers and “Wayna Daga”
proposals.description: Give Hand Cannoneer in the Imperial Age and remove Bombard Cannon. New technology “Wayna Daga”: Hand Cannoneers -25% cost and +1 armour against ranged units.
proposals.historical_basis: Cristóvão da Gama's roughly 400 musketeers (1541) and the Ethiopian adoption of the musket after 1543 are documented by Miguel de Castanhoso (1564).

proposals.title: “Amba Geshen” instead of Royal Heirs
proposals.description: Castles +30% HP, garrisoned units heal faster and, in Regicide, the King garrisoned in a Castle cannot be targeted.
proposals.historical_basis: Amba Geshen held the royal princes until its capture by Ahmad Grañ (1540), which ensured dynastic stability. The ambas were almost impregnable natural fortresses.

proposals.title: “Chewa” instead of Torsion Engines
proposals.description: Barracks and Archery Range units trained 20% faster and +10 HP for the Spearman-line and Archer-line.
proposals.historical_basis: The chewa regiments, military colonies settled on granted lands, were the backbone of the army from Amda Seyon onwards (Taddesse Tamrat; Mordechai Abir).

proposals.title: Aksumite elephant (early-Age unit) or Adulis bonus
proposals.description: Option A: a light war elephant available in the Castle Age. Option B: a bonus whereby Trade Cogs generate +15% gold and Docks cost less in the Dark and Feudal Ages.
proposals.historical_basis: Abraha, a general of Aksumite origin in Yemen, attacked Mecca with elephants according to Islamic tradition (the “Year of the Elephant”, referred to in the Quran; date disputed). Adulis was the main Red Sea port in late antiquity.

proposals.title: Rock-hewn church (Lalibela)
proposals.description: A Monastery variant that costs no wood, has +50% HP and in which Monks heal passively.
proposals.historical_basis: The monolithic churches of Lalibela (c. 1200) and the central place of the Ethiopian Church in the life of the kingdom.

contested: Antiquity and medieval use of the shotel.
Identity of Queen Gudit/Yodit and date of the Zagwe foundation (c. 940 or 1137).
Causes of Aksum's decline: environmental (Butzer) or loss of the Red Sea trade.
Date of the “Year of the Elephant” (c. 552 or c. 570).
Extent of Ezana's campaign against Meroë and the Noba.
Historical value of the Kebra Nagast (14th century) as Solomonic legitimation.

Beginning of the princes' confinement on Amba Geshen.
