groups.cross_civ_notes:
1) Duplicated and contradictory narratives. The Saracens and Berbers texts both recount the 711 invasion and the history of al-Andalus. The first calls a mostly Berber army “Saracens of Tangier”; the second attributes to the Berbers the Mosque of Córdoba (Umayyad, Arab) and the Alhambra (Nasrid, Arab). Asia Minor is conquered twice: by the Arabs in the Saracens text (which is false) and by the Turks “at the beginning of the 11th century” (wrong date; it was after 1071). The Seljuks and the Crusades appear in the Saracens and Turks texts with crossed errors: the Turks “recover Palestine” and the Saracens make Saladin, who was a Kurd, a “Saracen”. The Fatimids appear implicitly in the Saracens text (as “Shiites of Egypt”) and in the Berbers text, without either text saying that their early army was made up of Kutama Berbers.

2) Mamluks. The Saracens' unique unit represents an elite of Kipchak origin, the same confederation as the Cumans, and later of Circassian origin. It would be more coherent in a “Mamluks” civ. The end of the Mamluks (Marj Dabiq in 1516, Ridaniya in 1517) at the hands of Ottoman gunpowder is echoed, by chance, in the Saracens versus Turks matchup in the Imperial Age.

3) Islamic Iran barely exists in the game. The Persians end in 651. The Timurids appear through the Tatars, the Seljuks barely appear in the Turks, the Hindustanis' Ghulam unit points to the slave-soldier tradition of the Ghaznavids and the Delhi Sultanate, and the Samanids, Buyids, Ilkhanids and Safavids appear nowhere at all. The Caravanserai is shared between the Persians and the Hindustanis.

4) Camels. All six civs have the Camel Rider. The only one with camel archers (Berbers) is the one with the least basis for it, and the Mameluke rides a camel when the Mamluks rode horses. For the Persians, Turks, Mandinka and highland Ethiopians, the camel was mainly used for logistics or belonged to their neighbours in the lowlands and the desert.

5) Incoherent gunpowder (checked against data/data.json). The Malians have the Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon and Cannon Galleon, which they never used: Songhai lost at Tondibi (1591) precisely because it had no firearms. The Ethiopians do not have the Hand Cannoneer (but do have the Bombard Cannon), despite the musketeers on both sides in 1541–1543. The Saracens do not reflect the Mamluk reluctance studied by Ayalon. The Persians have cannons, even though the Safavids were beaten at Chaldiran (1514) largely by Ottoman artillery and Janissaries. Only the Turks are coherent.

6) Sahel and Maghreb. The Almoravids link the Berbers and the Malians (the conquest of Ghana in 1076 is contested). The trans-Saharan trade in gold and salt and the Moroccan invasion of 1591 should be a shared theme, for example with trade bonuses. The Malians absorb Ghana, Mali, Songhai and even Dahomey (Gbeto), in a flattening typical of the game's treatment of Africa.

7) Structural absences. The Adal Sultanate and the Muslim sultanates of the Horn of Africa, the Oromo, Songhai, Kanem-Bornu and the Hausa have no civ, and the Ethiopian war of 1529–1543 (Ethiopia and Portugal against Adal and the Ottomans) is left without antagonists of its own.

8) Portuguese hooks for discussion. In almost all of these civs there are episodes involving Portugal: the conquest of Ceuta (1415) from the Marinids; the Battle of Salado (1340), in which Afonso IV of Portugal fought alongside Castile against the Marinids and Granada; Asilah and Tangier (1471) and Alcácer Quibir (1578) against the Saadians; Chaul (1508) and Diu (1509) against the Mamluk and Gujarati fleet; the Ottomans against the Portuguese in the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean (Piri Reis, Hormuz); Hormuz taken by Afonso de Albuquerque (1507/1515) and retaken by the Safavids in 1622; Pêro da Covilhã, Francisco Álvares and Cristóvão da Gama in Ethiopia; Nuno Tristão killed by poisoned arrows, the Gambia voyages (1455–1456) and John II's embassies to Mali; the Almoravid-inspired morabitino minted by Sancho I.

9) Religion. Ulama, madrasas, Zoroastrian clergy and the Ethiopian Church are all reduced to the generic Monk. The gaps in the Monastery seem arbitrary: the Persians without Redemption or Heresy, the Turks without Herbal Medicine despite their hospitals, the Ethiopians without Redemption. The exception is the absence of Block Printing for the Turks, Berbers and Ethiopians, which by chance largely coincides with history.

10) Note on method. The game facts (bonuses, units and tech tree gaps) were confirmed against data/data.json and data/locales/en/strings.json in the repository. Some finer claims (the exact start of the confinement on Amba Geshen, Bulliet's figures for Egypt and Syria, Janissary numbers in 1453) depend on secondary sources and are flagged as uncertain.

verification_log.change: I confirmed the game facts against data/data.json: the Saracens do not have Shipwright, Cavalier, Fast Fire Ship, Halberdier or Heavy Scorpion; the Ethiopians do indeed lack the Hand Cannoneer (but have Bombard Cannon, Cannon Galleon and Siege Onager); the Malians have Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon, Cannon Galleon, Siege Onager and Heavy Camel Rider, but not Galleon or Bracer. The draft's claims about the tech tree were correct, except for the omissions below.

The web search limit ran out partway through the verification. Some claims (the start date of Amba Geshen, Janissary numbers in 1453, the Mamluk fleet of 1426–1444) were kept on the basis of established knowledge or presented as uncertain, without further web confirmation.
I added a serious error that the draft did not have: the text says that the Arabs took Asia Minor from the Byzantines, which is false (Anatolia remained Byzantine until after 1071). Severity: major.

I added another omitted error: the text dates the Turkish conquest of Asia Minor and the Middle East to the “beginning of the 11th century” (it took place in 1055–1080) and says that the Crusades took Palestine from the Turks (in 1099 Jerusalem was Fatimid).
I corrected Bulliet's figures: in Iran a Muslim majority emerges by the mid-9th century and about 80% by c. 950, and not “only in the 10th century”.
I reworded the item on Mecca: the capture of 630 was indeed a military campaign, with almost no fighting; the real error is saying that Muhammad was “ignored”, when he faced persecution.

I lowered the severity of the “Saracens of Tangier” item to minor: Tariq was governor of Tangier and “Saracen” was the generic medieval label. I kept the correction about the Berber composition of the army.
I removed the claim that sakk is the root of “cheque”: etymological dictionaries derive it from check/exchequer, and the Arabic link is speculative.
I qualified the siege of Constantinople of 674–678 (redated by Jankowiak to 667–669 and denied by Howard-Johnston) and added it to the contested questions.
I corrected the claim that the Mamluks had a weak navy: it was intermittent, but it subdued Cyprus (1426), attacked Rhodes (1440 and 1444) and fought the Portuguese in the Indian Ocean (1508–1509).

In the Bimaristan item, I placed the first hospital in Baghdad at the beginning of the 9th century (Dols). I added Gutas' caveat about the Bayt al-Hikma and removed it from the list of missing features, where it appeared without that caveat.
I removed Dara from the list of Sasanian fortifications: it was a Roman fortress built in 505–507 against Persia. I replaced it with Nisibis (Persian since 363) and the Wall of Tammisha.
I flagged the “academy” and the hospital of Gundeshapur as contested (Dols, 1987, against Frye). The draft presented them as fact.
I lowered the severity of “Ctesiphon, now Baghdad” from major to moderate. It is a clear factual error, but of limited scope.
I added an omitted error: the text places the Persian attacks on Palestine and Egypt in the 6th century, whereas they belong to the war of 602–628.
I strengthened the proposal and the Daylamites item with Procopius (Wars VIII.14), who shows them in Persian service in Lazica.
I downgraded the Scout Cavalry-line bonus from faithful to plausible: the referent (akıncı, deli) is real, but the mechanic is generic.
I added the absence of Siege Engineers as a tech tree problem, despite Ottoman siege engineering (Rhodes, 1522; Vienna, 1529). I included it in the Ok Meydanı proposal.
I added a minor, contested item on the “15,000 Janissaries” of 1453, a high number compared with modern estimates of the corps.
I qualified the Odessa item: the region was under Ottoman and Crimean rule in the 16th century, so the error is mainly one of an anachronistic name.
I lowered the severity of the Berber horse myth to minor. To the Alhambra item I added that Granada was the capital of the Berber Zirids in the 11th century, to be fair to the text.
I added that the absence of the Arbalester is consistent with history, which makes the Camel Archer even less justified.
I softened the basis of the Tabl proposal: I removed the unverified claim that the drums were first heard in the Iberian Peninsula in 1086.
I specified that Arianism was the religion of the Vandals and had already disappeared by the 7th century.
I added the absence of Bracer and Arrowslits as a tech tree problem (the Malians have Arbalester but not Bracer), which runs counter to the tradition of archer infantry.

I removed the direct attribution to al-Umari of an army made up “mostly of archers”, which I could not confirm in the primary text. I now attribute it to the historiography; the figure of 100,000 men and 10,000 horsemen remains attributed to al-Umari.
Sankore is now attributed, following al-Sa'di, to a wealthy Aghlal woman, at an uncertain date (14th–15th centuries). I removed the “Tuareg” label as a settled fact.
I added an omitted minor error: the Portuguese did not arrive in 1455 but in the 1440s (Dinis Dias, Nuno Tristão). 1455–1456 are the dates of the Gambia voyages of Cadamosto and Diogo Gomes.
I flagged the siege of Djenné lasting “seven years, seven months and seven days” as formulaic.

I corrected an error in the draft: according to al-Umari (cited by Taddesse Tamrat, p. 92), the main weapon was the spear and not the bow, which was secondary, and swords were rare. I rewrote the label, the spearman bonus and the verdict accordingly.

In the Shotel item, I replaced the unsourced claim (“it is known that”) with Taddesse Tamrat's: Amda Seyon increased the use of swords and created a regiment armed with swords, with no indication that they were shotels.
Royal Heirs went from unfounded to stretched: the name refers to a real institution (Amba Geshen), even though the effect is arbitrary. I also marked the start date of the confinement as uncertain.

I corrected Adal's firearms. There is no evidence of Ottoman musketeers at Shimbra Kure (1529). Adal used cannon from 1531 (Antukyah) and received c. 2,000 Arab and 900 Ottoman musketeers from Zabid in 1542.
The description of the king of Aksum on a platform drawn by four elephants comes from John Malalas (probably drawing on Nonnosus), not from Cosmas Indicopleustes.
I raised the fidelity_score from 3 to 4. The spear and the bow are attested, the shotel is a real Ethiopian weapon and Royal Heirs has a referent. This brings it into line with the Malians (4).

I added two omitted minor errors: Ezana's “conquest of Kush” (it was a campaign against the Noba, with Meroë already in decline) and the composition of the army (the spear as the main weapon). I lowered the Pêro da Covilhã item to minor. I corrected the distance between Aksum and Adulis to c. 150–160 km.
I added the absence of Bloodlines and Plate Barding Armor as a tech tree problem, and as a partly accurate choice.

I added omitted Portuguese hooks: Ceuta (1415), Salado (1340), Asilah and Tangier (1471) and the Gambia voyages. I reworded the reference to the Ghaznavids and the Hindustanis, which is an interpretation and not a game fact. I corrected the explanation of Chaldiran: the Safavids were beaten mainly by Ottoman artillery and Janissaries.

civs.represents: The civ replaced the old “Indians” in The Dynasties of India (2022) and mainly represents the Turco-Persian and Afghan Muslim power of northern India. This covers the Ghaznavids in the Punjab, the Ghurids and, above all, the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526): the Mamluk (“Slave”), Khalji, Tughluq, Sayyid and Lodi dynasties. It also inherited traits from the Suri and Mughal periods: gunpowder, from Babur, and Sher Shah Suri's network of roads and sarais. The history text, however, begins with the Guptas and Harsha, and mixes classical Hindu dynasties with the conquering elites that define the design.
civs.period: The core runs from c. 1000 to 1526 (from the Ghaznavids to the Lodis). The text extends from c. 320 (Guptas) to after 1526 (Mughals). The gunpowder bonus and the Grand Trunk Road point to 1526–1545 (Babur and Sher Shah Suri).
civs.verdict: The Hindustanis are a transitional civ. They inherited the skeleton of the 2013 “Indians” (camels, gunpowder, Imperial Camel Rider, Shatagni) and in 2022 received a Delhi Sultanate veneer (Ghulam, Caravanserai). They get the Turkic horse archers, the sarais and the abundant manpower right. They miss the two military pillars that the historiography of the Sultanate highlights, imported warhorses and elephants (Digby, 1971), and they project Suri and Mughal traits backwards. The signature unit, the Ghulam, inverts the historical role of these slave soldiers, who were elite cavalry, not infantry. The “Sultans” tech itself, which fitted the Sultanate, was renamed in 2022 with a 19th-century British name. The history text has several factual errors and a confused framing of conquerors and conquered.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Hindustan” is a Persian exonym (Hindu + -stan) that the Turco-Persian elites used for northern India, especially the Indo-Gangetic plain, as opposed to the Deccan, Bengal or Gujarat. In that sense, the name is actually consistent with a Delhi Sultanate that saw itself as lord of “Hindustan”. There are, however, four problems. (1) As the name of a people, “Hindustanis” is ambiguous: today it mainly designates a language (Hindustani) and, in the Netherlands and Suriname, the Indo-Surinamese diaspora. (2) The text covers c. 320–1526+, goes beyond the 500–1500 window at both ends and puts the Guptas and Harsha together with the Turkic and Afghan elites that give the design its character. (3) The Ghaznavids and Ghurids were Turco-Persian and Tajik dynasties based in Afghanistan and overlap with the Persians and Turks. Timur overlaps with the Tatars, and the traits of the Mughals and Suris, who do not exist in the game, were absorbed here. (4) Bappa Rawal and Prithviraj Chauhan belong to the Gurjaras' sphere and appear in both texts. There are two coherent alternatives: embrace the ruling elite (“Delhi Sultanate” or “Indo-Turks”) or keep “Hindustanis” and rewrite the text from c. 1000 onwards.

elements.explanation: This is the 2013 “Indians” label, kept as it was. In northern India camels mainly had a logistical role (transport, Sind, the Thar Desert). The Sultanate's decisive force was its Turkic horse-archer cavalry, with horses imported from Central Asia and the Gulf, supported by war elephants (Simon Digby, “War-Horse and Elephant in the Dehli Sultanate”, 1971). Gunpowder only becomes a military hallmark in northern India with Babur at Panipat (1526). The label leaves out precisely the two arms that the Sultanate's chroniclers (Juzjani, Barani) emphasise most.

A reasonable abstraction of the enormous population and cheap labour of the Indo-Gangetic plain. Babur, in the Baburnama, stresses that Hindustan has “countless” workers and craftsmen of every trade. Dirk Kolff (1990) describes an immense peasant military labour market. The mechanic is generic, but defensible.

There is no documented tradition of camel-mounted shock cavalry in the Delhi Sultanate. The most famous episode involving camels is the reverse: according to the Timurid chronicles (the Zafarnama of Nizam al-Din Shami, 1404), Timur is said to have sent camels laden with burning straw against Mahmud Tughluq's elephants at Delhi (1398). Even Britannica presents the episode as “by one account”. Camels carrying small artillery pieces (shutarnal, zamburak) belong to the 17th–18th centuries.

The Lodis, the last dynasty of the Sultanate, made almost no use of firearms in the field and were defeated at Panipat (1526) by Babur's artillery and musketeers (Ustad Ali Quli, Mustafa Rumi). In the 15th century, Indian gunpowder was concentrated in Gujarat, in the Bahmani and Deccan Sultanates, and in Bengal (Iqtidar Alam Khan, 2004). The bonus describes the Mughals, not the Sultanate.

elements.element: Can build Caravanserai in Imperial Age
elements.explanation: Sarais and post stations existed on the Sultanate's routes: Ibn Battuta describes in detail the relay post of mounted (ulaq) and foot (dawa) couriers. The systematic network of sarais, about 1,700 according to tradition, is however the work of Sher Shah Suri (1540–45), already at the edge of the time frame. It is a Perso-Islamic institution, rightly shared with the Persians.

The ghulams (bandagan) of the Ghaznavids, the Ghurids and the Sultanate were Turkic slave soldiers trained mainly as horse-archer cavalry and as officers. Sabuktigin, founder of Ghaznavid power, and Aibak, Iltutmish and Balban, who rose to become sultans, were all military slaves. They were the mounted elite of the army, not foot spearmen. The name is faithful, but the role (infantry whose spear pierces through several ranks) inverts reality (Bosworth, 1963; Jackson, 1999; Kumar, 2007). The Sultanate did have infantry, but it was recruited mainly from Indian paiks, not from ghulams.

A legacy of the “Indians” of The Forgotten (2013), where it was a unique Stable upgrade. No Sultanate source describes an elite corps of camel cavalry. Camel corps (shutur-sawar) only appear in the late Mughal period and in 18th–19th-century Rajputana. The “Imperial” is simply the third upgrade tier.

Until 2022 this tech was called “Sultans”. The repository history shows the name change in DE Update 61321 (Dynasties of India), with the same +10% gold effect. The route is very ancient (the Uttarapatha of the Maurya period) and was rebuilt and equipped with sarais by Sher Shah Suri in the 1540s (Sadak-e-Azam). The name “Grand Trunk Road” is British, from the 19th century. The effect (more gold, cheaper market) is a good abstraction of Sher Shah's reforms: the standardised rupiya coin and the reduction of internal tolls. The name, however, is doubly out of period for the Sultanate.

Śataghnī (“hundred-killer”) is a weapon mentioned in the epics and in the Arthashastra, generally described as a log or stone studded with iron spikes and thrown from the walls, or as a throwing engine. Reading it as a cannon is a 19th–20th-century interpretation, popularised by Gustav Oppert (1880). Oppert relied on the Shukranitisara, which Lallanji Gopal (1962) showed to be a 19th-century compilation. Giving this ancient Sanskrit term to 16th-century Turco-Mughal cannoneers mixes periods and cultural worlds. The tech already existed for the 2013 “Indians”.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Scout Cavalry-line and Camel Units +2 attack vs. buildings
elements.explanation: Cavalry raids against cities and temples do indeed characterise this world, with Mahmud of Ghazni's traditional count of some 17 campaigns, including Somnath (1025–26). As an abstraction of plunder warfare it works, although the inclusion of camels is weak.

tree_issues.problem: This is the most serious gap (confirmed in the repository data: only Armored Elephant and Siege Elephant). The sultans of Delhi treated elephants as a royal monopoly (pil-khana): they obtained them by capture or as tribute in Bengal, Orissa and the Deccan and used them as a shock and prestige weapon (Digby, 1971; Barani). Mahmud of Ghazni already used Indian elephants, and the army of Mahmud Tughluq and Mallu Iqbal faced Timur in 1398 with a line of elephants.

The Sultanate's power rested on Turkic heavy cavalry mounted on imported horses. Alauddin Khalji instituted the dagh (branding of horses) and the chehra (descriptive roll of soldiers) to control it. Not having the Paladin makes sense, but the lack of any heavy shock cavalry is historically odd.
Faithful: Turkic horse archers were the decisive arm of the Ghaznavids, the Ghurids (Second Battle of Tarain, 1192) and the Sultanate. They deserved more prominence than the camels.

They are missing from one of the great building cultures of the period: Qutb Minar (c. 1199–1220), Alai Darwaza (1311), Siri (c. 1303), Tughlaqabad (1321–25) and Daulatabad, as well as the cities and canals of Firuz Shah Tughluq. It is an ironic absence for a state of fortresses.

tree_issues.item: Hand Cannoneer / Bombard Cannon with armor bonus
tree_issues.problem: It is anachronistic for the Sultanate (see the Lodis' defeat at Panipat, 1526). It would only be acceptable as a “Mughal era” in the Imperial Age.

tree_issues.item: Armored Elephant / Siege Elephant instead of rams
tree_issues.problem: A plausible abstraction, common to the four Indian civs. There are accounts of elephants being used to force gates, and the spiked gates of fortresses such as Mehrangarh or Amber, which already date from the 15th–16th centuries, are traditionally read as an anti-elephant defence.

tree_issues.item: Full camel line + Imperial Camel Rider
tree_issues.problem: It over-represents an arm that was marginal in the Sultanate, at the expense of horses and elephants.

history_text_issues.claim: The Gupta Empire is described as “short-lived”, and floods appear as a major problem.
history_text_issues.problem: The Guptas lasted c. 320–550, more than two centuries. Their decline was due mainly to the invasions of the Alchon Huns (Toramana, Mihirakula), the growing autonomy of feudatories and fiscal strains. Giving special weight to floods has no support in the historiography.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that the empire, after two centuries, fragmented between c. 480 and 550 under pressure from the Hunas and the regional powers.

history_text_issues.claim: The successors supposedly inherited a “sophisticated division of labor system”, presented as an advance.
history_text_issues.problem: The expression is vague. It may allude to the craft guilds (shreni), well attested in the Gupta period, or to the varna and jati (caste) system. In the latter case it is a euphemism that presents a social hierarchy as a technical achievement. Susan Bayly (1999) shows that caste was an evolving institution, not an inherited “technology”.
history_text_issues.correction: Name the guilds and/or caste society explicitly, without presenting the latter as technical progress.

history_text_issues.claim: “Sanskrit epics tell of” Harsha Vardhana, as if he were a semi-legendary figure.
history_text_issues.problem: Harsha (r. 606–647) is well documented: in Banabhatta's Harshacharita (a prose biography, not an epic), in Xuanzang's account and in inscriptions (Banskhera, Madhuban). The text also omits Harsha's defeat by Pulakeshin II on the Narmada, recorded in the Aihole inscription (634–35), although the date of the battle is debated.
history_text_issues.correction: Cite the Harshacharita and Xuanzang as historical sources and mention the southern limit imposed by the Chalukyas.

history_text_issues.claim: Bappa Rawal (8th century) appears as the man who stemmed the “tide” of Muslim invasions.
history_text_issues.problem: Bappa Rawal is the semi-legendary figure at the origin of Guhila power in Mewar, and his participation in the wars against the Arabs rests on late tradition. The documented victories against the Arabs of Sind (c. 730–740) appear in the inscriptions of Nagabhata I (Pratihara, Gwalior prashasti) and of Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin (Chalukya, Navsari plates, 739). The text also omits the conquest of Sind by Muhammad ibn Qasim (711–712) and merges Arabs, Turks and Afghans into a single “Muslim wave”.
history_text_issues.correction: Distinguish the Umayyad expansion into Sind (8th century) from the Ghaznavid Turkic raids (11th century) and cite the epigraphically attested victors.

history_text_issues.claim: The Ghurids' predecessors supposedly carried out only plundering campaigns.
history_text_issues.problem: The Ghaznavids annexed and ruled the Punjab for more than a century and a half (c. 1020–1186). After losing Ghazni (1163), they made Lahore their capital, which the Ghurids only took in 1186.
history_text_issues.correction: State that the Ghaznavids created a lasting dominion in the Punjab, which served as the Ghurids' springboard.

history_text_issues.claim: Aibak supposedly created “a new superpower”, the Delhi Sultanate.
history_text_issues.problem: This is the traditional convention, but it simplifies. Aibak's rule (1206–10) was brief and contested by Yildiz and Qabacha. The consolidation of the Sultanate as a state was the work of Iltutmish (1211–36), as Sunil Kumar (2007) stresses.
history_text_issues.correction: Present Aibak as the initiator and Iltutmish as the true consolidator.

history_text_issues.claim: The sultans supposedly merely perpetuated the existing systems.
history_text_issues.problem: This is a half-truth. They kept local chiefs and fiscal practices, but they introduced the iqta, Persian administration, standardised tanka/jital coinage, Alauddin's price controls and new cities.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention the combination of continuity and institutional innovation.

history_text_issues.claim: The Mongol invasions supposedly destroyed the region's infrastructure, though without lasting gains.
history_text_issues.problem: “Without lasting gains” is essentially right. But “destroyed the infrastructure” is an exaggeration, because the devastation was concentrated in the Punjab and Sind (Lahore was sacked in 1241). The text omits the main point: the Sultanate, above all under Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316), repeatedly repelled the Chagatai at Jalandhar (1298), Kili (1299), Amroha (1305) and on the Ravi (1306), and withstood the siege of Delhi in 1303. This resistance shaped Alauddin's military and market reforms.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the defence against the Mongols as one of the Sultanate's landmark successes.

history_text_issues.claim: Babur, a “Persified warlord”, supposedly saw a land that had not yet healed from the devastation.
history_text_issues.problem: Babur was a Timurid prince who wrote the Baburnama in Chagatai Turkic, although he was of Persianate culture. His complaints about Hindustan are mainly cultural: the lack of good horses, grapes, melons, baths, ice and refined company. At the same time he praises the country's wealth in gold and silver and its abundance of craftsmen. He also observes that villages are depopulated and rebuilt in an instant, which is a remark about mobility, not about ruins. Linking his impressions to the devastation is not a very faithful paraphrase.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe Babur as a Turkic-speaking Timurid prince of Persianate culture and paraphrase his impressions accurately.

history_text_issues.claim: The Mughal Empire supposedly ruled the region from 1526 without interruption.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the Suri interregnum (1540–1555): Sher Shah drove out Humayun, and it was he who rebuilt the great road and the sarais that the civ uses as a tech and a building.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention Sher Shah Suri and the Afghan interregnum.

history_text_issues.claim: Mahmud of Ghazni launched “seventeen separate campaigns”.
history_text_issues.problem: This is a traditional count by later chroniclers, popularised by colonial historiography (Elliot). Acceptable as a convention, but approximate. His motivations (plunder, legitimation before the caliphate, politics) are discussed by Romila Thapar (Somanatha, 2004).
history_text_issues.correction: Write “about seventeen” and situate Somnath (1025–26).

missing_features: War elephants as a royal monopoly and a symbol of sovereignty (pil-khana); Digby, 1971.
Turkic heavy cavalry and the trade in horses imported from Central Asia and the Gulf, the material basis of the Sultanate.
The iqta system: the assignment of tax revenues to commanders so that they could maintain horsemen.
Alauddin Khalji's reforms as described by Barani: market price controls, dagh and chehra.
Indo-Islamic architecture and monumental fortification (Qutb Minar, Siri, Tughlaqabad, Daulatabad).
The relay post of mounted (ulaq) and foot (dawa) couriers described by Ibn Battuta.
Infantry recruited from the peasant military market (paiks, Afghans, Rajputs); Kolff, 1990.
The Sufi dimension (Chishti order, Nizamuddin Auliya) as a religious facet of the Sultanate.
Siege engineering with manjaniq and maghribi in the campaigns of Ranthambore (1301) and Chittor (1303), described by Amir Khusrau.
The Suri interregnum: the standardised silver rupiya, the toll reform and Sher Shah's network of sarais (1540–45).

proposals.title: Ghulam as elite cavalry
proposals.description: Turn the Ghulam into a heavy horse archer trained at the Castle, with high armor and a secondary melee attack (lance), or into an armored mounted lancer. The infantry slot would then be filled by a “Paik” or by a generic infantry bonus.
proposals.historical_basis: The Turkic bandagan of Aibak, Iltutmish and Balban were horsemen and officers (Jackson, 1999; Kumar, 2007). The Ghaznavid ghulams formed the sultan's mounted guard (Bosworth, 1963).

proposals.title: Restore the Battle Elephant and create the “Pil-khana” tech
proposals.description: Give Battle Elephant and Elite Battle Elephant. Unique tech “Pil-khana”: elephants cost -20% gold and train 25% faster, and Castles can train Battle Elephants.
proposals.historical_basis: The sultans held a monopoly on elephants, obtained through tribute and capture (Digby, 1971). The Delhi army faced Timur with elephants in 1398.

proposals.title: “Dagh-o-Chehra” instead of Shatagni
proposals.description: Castle tech: Stable units cost -15% gold and gain +10% HP, representing the end of fraud at military musters.
proposals.historical_basis: Alauddin Khalji instituted the branding of horses (dagh) and a descriptive roll of each soldier (chehra) to ensure high-quality cavalry (Barani, Tarikh-i Firuz Shahi).

proposals.title: Restore the name “Sultans” (or “Rupiya”)
proposals.description: Keep the effect (+10% gold and cheaper market), but go back to the name “Sultans”, used until 2022. Alternatively, call it “Rupiya”, in reference to Sher Shah's silver coin.
proposals.historical_basis: The repository history shows that the tech was called “Sultans” before DE Update 61321. “Grand Trunk Road” is a 19th-century British name. Sher Shah's rupiya (1540s) and the toll reform justify a gold and trade bonus.

proposals.title: “Market Regulations” (Alauddin's price controls)
proposals.description: Buying and selling prices at the Market fluctuate 50% less, making the market a stable instrument of the war economy.
proposals.historical_basis: Barani describes the fixing of prices for grain, horses and cloth in Delhi, with state granaries and inspectors, to support a large standing army against the Mongols.

proposals.title: Restore Architecture and Keep and create the “Tughlaqabad” bonus
proposals.description: Give Architecture, Keep and Arrowslits. Bonus: Fortified Walls and Castles have +15% HP.
proposals.historical_basis: The fortress cities of Siri (Alauddin) and Tughlaqabad (Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq, 1321–25), with their massive sloping walls, are landmarks of Indian military architecture.

proposals.title: “Manjaniq” as a siege tech
proposals.description: Castle tech: Mangonel-line and Trebuchets get +1 range and extra damage against buildings. Gunpowder would be reserved for the Imperial Age, with no armor bonus.
proposals.historical_basis: Ghaznavid and Sultanate armies used throwing engines (manjaniq, maghribi) and naphtha throwers (naffatun). Amir Khusrau describes them at the sieges of Ranthambore (1301) and Chittor (1303).

proposals.title: Rewrite the text and rename
proposals.description: Keep “Hindustanis” but centre the text on c. 1000–1526 (from the Ghaznavids to the Lodis, with a Suri epilogue), or rename the civ “Delhi Sultanate”. The Guptas and Harsha would move to a general Indian framing.
proposals.historical_basis: The design (Ghulam, Caravanserai, horse archers) is that of a Turco-Afghan elite, not that of the Guptas.

contested: The thesis of a Gupta “golden age”, criticised by Romila Thapar and R. S. Sharma, and that of “Indian feudalism” (R. S. Sharma) versus B. D. Chattopadhyaya's integrative model.
The motivations of Mahmud of Ghazni (iconoclasm, plunder or political legitimation) and the exact number of his campaigns.

The designation “Slave dynasty”: historians prefer Mamluk, Shamsi or Ilbari, and the actual status of the bandagan is debated. It is also debated whether the true founder of the Sultanate is Aibak or Iltutmish.
The Sultanate as a “foreign” state or as an Indian state, a debate between nationalist, communalist and secular historiography.
The date gunpowder reached northern India: knowledge of it since Mongol contact in the 13th century (Iqtidar Alam Khan) versus effective military use only with Babur.
The identification of the śataghnī with a firearm (Oppert, 1880) and the dating of the Shukranitisara (Lallanji Gopal, 1962).
The historicity of the episode of Timur's burning camels (1398).
Bappa Rawal's historical role in the wars against the Arabs.
key_sources: Minhaj al-Siraj Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri (c. 1260)
Ziya al-Din Barani, Tarikh-i Firuz Shahi (1357)
Amir Khusrau, Khaza'in al-Futuh (c. 1311)
Ibn Battuta, Rihla (stay in Delhi, 1334–42)
Nizam al-Din Shami, Zafarnama (1404); Sharaf al-Din Ali Yazdi, Zafarnama (1424–28)
Babur, Baburnama (trans. A. S. Beveridge, 1912–22; W. Thackston, 1996)
Banabhatta, Harshacharita; Xuanzang, Da Tang Xiyu Ji
Peter Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate: A Political and Military History (1999)
Sunil Kumar, The Emergence of the Delhi Sultanate 1192–1286 (2007)
Simon Digby, War-Horse and Elephant in the Dehli Sultanate (1971)
Iqtidar Alam Khan, Gunpowder and Firearms: Warfare in Medieval India (2004)
C. E. Bosworth, The Ghaznavids (1963)
Dirk H. A. Kolff, Naukar, Rajput and Sepoy (1990)
Richard M. Eaton, India in the Persianate Age 1000–1765 (2019)
Romila Thapar, Somanatha: The Many Voices of a History (2004)
Gustav Oppert, On the Weapons, Army Organisation and Political Maxims of the Ancient Hindus (1880); Lallanji Gopal, “The Śukranīti — A Nineteenth-Century Text”, BSOAS (1962)
Git history of the aoe2techtree repository, commit 1a2a4cd (DE Update 61321): renaming of “Sultans” → “Grand Trunk Road”

civs.represents: The Gurjara-Pratiharas (c. 730–1036), the dominant power of northern India in the 9th–10th centuries, with their capital at Kannauj from Nagabhata II (c. 815) onwards. By extension, the kingdoms that historiography calls 'Rajput' in the west and centre: the Chauhans of Ajmer, the Paramaras of Malwa, the Chaulukyas/Solankis of Gujarat, the Chandelas, the Guhilas/Sisodias of Mewar. The text also includes the Soomras of Sind and the Sultanates of Gujarat and Malwa. In practice, it is a 'Rajputana + Gujarat' civ.
civs.period: c. 730–1576. The core is the Pratiharas (8th–11th centuries); the text goes up to Maharana Pratap and alludes to the agreement of 1615.
civs.verdict: The core of the identity is historically sound. The merchant Sulaiman (851) considered the cavalry of the king of 'Jurz' (Gurjara) the best in India and said that his camels and horses were numerous. The Pratiharas presented themselves as guardians against the Arabs of Sind, and the pastoralism of Rajasthan and Gujarat is real. But the design adds poorly anchored elements: the Chakram is attested c. 1516 in the 'kingdom of Delli' and is above all a later Sikh weapon, Kshatriyas is a caste label with an arbitrary effect, and the Shrivamsha rests on a single inscription. Central traits are missing, such as war elephants (confirmed: there is no Battle Elephant) and Gujarat's maritime dimension. The history text presents the late legend of the Prithviraj Raso as fact and misplaces the Arab threat.
civs.naming_scope_issues: 'Gurjara' is a disputed term: it designates a region (Gurjaratra, from which 'Gujarat' comes), a clan or an ethnic group. The imperial Pratiharas called themselves 'Pratihara' and do not call themselves 'Gurjara' in their own inscriptions (Sanjay Sharma, 2006). It is the inscriptions of rival dynasties and the Arab authors ('Jurz') that give them that name. The compound form 'Gurjara-Pratihara' appears only in the Rajor inscription (c. 960), of a feudatory, Mathanadeva. Today the name carries a strong political charge: Gurjar and Rajput communities dispute the heritage of Mihira Bhoja, with controversies such as the one over the Dadri statue in 2021. The civ works as an umbrella for the 'Rajputs', a name the team avoided, and mixes Hindu dynasties with Muslim sultanates (Gujarat, Malwa) and with the Soomras of Sind. The Chandelas and Paramaras lie in central India, not in the northwest. Prithviraj, the Ghurids and Aibak are repeated in the Hindustanis' text, and the text ends in 1615, well outside the game's time frame.

elements.explanation: The 'Cavalry' part is well founded. Sulaiman (Akhbar al-Sin wa'l-Hind, 851) states that no Indian prince had cavalry as good as the king of 'Jurz'. According to Rima Hooja (2006), the Hudud al-Alam (982) credits the rai of Kannauj with 150,000 horsemen. The 'Camel' part has some support in the same Sulaiman, who says that the Gurjara king's camels and horses were numerous, and in the geography of the Thar and Sind. There is, however, no evidence of a significant combat role for camels in the Pratihara period.
It has no identifiable historical connection. It is pure game balance.

elements.element: Can garrison livestock in Mills to passively produce food
elements.explanation: The economy of Rajasthan and Gujarat had a strong pastoral component (cattle, goats, camels), and the Gurjar/Gujjar community is traditionally associated with pastoralism. It is a good mechanical idea. Caveat: it links the Pratihara dynasty to the pastoral identity of a modern caste, a disputed link.

elements.element: Mounted Units deal +20/30/40% bonus damage in Feudal/Castle/Imperial Age
elements.explanation: An acceptable abstraction of the excellence of Pratihara and Rajput cavalry, attested by Sulaiman and, later, by the Rajput warrior ethic of the mounted charge.

The chakram is real and is attested within the game's time frame. Duarte Barbosa (c. 1516) describes in the 'kingdom of Delli' steel wheels sharpened on the outside (chacarani), carried on the left arm and thrown after being spun on the finger. It later becomes the emblematic weapon of the Sikh Akali Nihangs of the Punjab (17th–19th centuries). No source associates it with the Pratiharas or with Rajput armies. The link to the civ is weak and regionally misplaced (it would suit the Hindustanis better). The damage that passes through several units is fantasy.

Pratihara cavalry is well documented. The name comes from a single epigraphic reference: the Chatsu inscription of the Guhilas relates that the feudatory Harsha offered Bhoja horses of the 'Śrīvaṃśa' breed, capable of crossing 'seas of sand' (Hooja's paraphrase, 2006). The breed is a thin basis, and the ability to dodge projectiles is a game invention.

Sulaiman mentions numerous camels in the Gurjara kingdom, and the racing camels of the Thar are famous. But their use as military scouts in the Pratihara period is not documented. The unit projects onto the 9th century a later reality, that of Bikaner (founded in 1488) and Jaisalmer, which culminates in the Ganga Risala camel corps, as late as the 19th century.

Kshatriya is the warrior varna. Rajput lineages claimed that status through solar and lunar genealogies and the Agnikula myth. The name has a basis, but the effect (military units cost -25% food) has no connection to the concept. Moreover, it turns a caste category into a 'technology', which is debatable.

'Pratihara' means 'doorkeeper' or 'door guard'. Mihira Bhoja's Gwalior prashasti celebrates Nagabhata I for crushing the armies of a powerful 'mleccha' king (the Arabs of Sind, c. 730–740), and Sulaiman calls the Gurjara king the greatest enemy of the Arabs in India. The name is apt, but the effect (+4 melee armour for Camel Riders and Elephant Archers) is arbitrary.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Camel and Elephant Units train +25% faster
elements.explanation: It has no specific basis. It is a generic team bonus.

tree_issues.problem: Confirmed in the data: there are the Elephant Archer and the Armored Elephant, but no Battle Elephant. The Pratiharas and the Rajput kingdoms used many elephants. According to Hooja, the Hudud al-Alam credits the rai of Kannauj with 800, and the Chatsu inscription speaks of Harsha's mighty elephant force. The Persian chronicles of Tarain (1191–92) put elephants on Prithviraj's side, although Firishta's numbers are exaggerated.

Rajput cavalry was above all shock cavalry, with lance, sword and mail armour. The Shrivamsha Rider is light and the Hussar belongs to the scout line. The heavy cavalry that made this tradition famous is missing.
It is defensible: at Tarain the contrast was between Rajput shock cavalry and Turkic mounted archers. But horse archery existed in India, so the question is debatable.
It is relatively consistent with armies centred on cavalry, although there was numerous infantry and there were tribal archers (Bhils).

It is plausible on the side of the Gujarat Sultanate, which had artillery and 'Rumi' gunners: Rumi Khan commanded Bahadur Shah's artillery at the siege of Chittor (1535). Rana Sanga, on the other hand, fought at Khanwa (1527) practically without artillery.
Faithful: Chittorgarh, Kumbhalgarh, Ranthambore and Gwalior are emblematic hill forts.

tree_issues.item: Dry Dock / Fast Fire Ship / Shipwright (absent)
tree_issues.problem: It ignores the navy of the Gujarat Sultanate. Malik Ayaz, governor of Diu, and the Mamluk admiral Amir Husain defeated the Portuguese at Chaul (1508) and were defeated at Diu (1509), and there were the sieges of Diu of 1538 and 1546.

history_text_issues.claim: Prithviraj's story supposedly survives 'principally in the epic Prithviraj Raso': marriage to Sanyogita and an adviser who conspires with Jayachandra to call in Muhammad Ghori.
history_text_issues.problem: The Prithviraj Raso is a late text (the surviving versions date from the 16th century onwards), heavily interpolated and legendary. The contemporary sources are Jayanaka's Prithviraja Vijaya (c. 1191–92) and the Persian chronicles (Minhaj, Hasan Nizami). There is no contemporary evidence that Jayachandra invited Ghori; Jayachandra himself was killed by the Ghurids at Chandawar (1194). The 'traitor Jaichand' trope is a modern political myth (Cynthia Talbot, 2016).
history_text_issues.correction: Draw on the Prithviraja Vijaya and Minhaj, describe the two battles of Tarain (victory in 1191, defeat in 1192) and present the Raso as a later epic tradition.

history_text_issues.claim: In the 12th century, much of northern and northwestern India was supposedly under the 'hegemony' of Prithviraj Chauhan.
history_text_issues.problem: It is exaggerated. The Chauhan kingdom (Sapadalaksha) was centred on Ajmer and Delhi. The Gahadavalas (Kannauj and Varanasi), the Chaulukyas of Gujarat and the Chandelas remained independent and were often rivals; Prithviraj attacked the Chandelas in 1182–83. There was no hegemony over northern India.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe Prithviraj as one of several rival kings, powerful in eastern Rajasthan and Delhi.

history_text_issues.claim: The Pratihara kings supposedly faced ever larger Muslim invasions 'across the Hindu Kush'.
history_text_issues.problem: It is geographically wrong for the 8th–10th centuries. The threat the Pratiharas faced came from the Arab emirates of Sind and Multan, to the south. The Hindu Kush passes were guarded by the Shahis of Kabul and the Hindu Shahi until the early 11th century. Only the Ghaznavids (Mahmud sacked Kannauj in 1018) came by that route.
history_text_issues.correction: Distinguish the Arab frontier in Sind (8th–10th centuries) from the Ghaznavid invasion (11th century).

history_text_issues.claim: 'Various sources' supposedly describe a cavalry mounted on Shrivamsha horses of elite speed, endurance and agility.
history_text_issues.problem: There is a single epigraphic mention: the Chatsu inscription refers to 'Śrīvaṃśa' horses offered to Bhoja by a feudatory. The attributed qualities and the 'cavalry corps' are extrapolation. The excellence of Pratihara cavalry is attested by Sulaiman, not by these 'various sources'.
history_text_issues.correction: Cite Sulaiman (851) for the cavalry and the Chatsu inscription as an isolated reference to the breed.

history_text_issues.claim: The name 'Gurjara-Pratihara' supposedly comes from the region they ruled.
history_text_issues.problem: It presents as fact one of several disputed interpretations (territorial, clan or ethnic). It omits that the term appears mainly in rival sources and that the compound form appears only in the Rajor inscription.
history_text_issues.correction: Point out the uncertain origin of the term and the competing readings.

history_text_issues.claim: Mihira Bhoja supposedly expanded the kingdom 'throughout all of Gujarat and beyond'.
history_text_issues.problem: The centre of Bhoja's empire (c. 836–885) was Kannauj and the Ganges plain, from the eastern Punjab to western Bihar, Malwa and Kathiawar. The emphasis on Gujarat is misleading. The text also omits the sack of Kannauj by the Rashtrakuta Indra III (c. 916), the real beginning of the decline.
history_text_issues.correction: Place the empire at Kannauj and mention the Rashtrakuta blow before Mahmud (1018).

history_text_issues.claim: The Chandelas and Paramaras appear in the struggle for the 'northwest' alongside the Soomras of Sind.
history_text_issues.problem: The Chandelas (Bundelkhand, Khajuraho) and the Paramaras (Malwa, Dhar) were powers of central India. The Soomras were a Sind dynasty linked to Ismailism, in a different cultural world.
history_text_issues.correction: Group by region and explain the differences.

history_text_issues.claim: Gujarat and Malwa supposedly fell to the Mughals in the 16th century.
history_text_issues.problem: It is simplified. The Malwa Sultanate was conquered by Bahadur Shah's Gujarat in 1531 and only passed to the Mughals in 1561–62 (Baz Bahadur). Gujarat was annexed by Akbar in 1572–73.
history_text_issues.correction: Give the sequence of conquests.

history_text_issues.claim: Maharana Pratap supposedly fought the Mughals 'to a stalemate'.
history_text_issues.problem: Haldighati (1576) was a Mughal tactical victory. Pratap then waged a guerrilla war and recovered much of Mewar, but not Chittor, until his death in 1597. 'Stalemate' is defensible but romanticised, and the episode falls outside the game's time frame.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe Haldighati and the subsequent guerrilla war accurately and point out that it is a post-medieval epilogue.

history_text_issues.claim: Omissions regarding western India.
history_text_issues.problem: Missing are Mahmud's sack of Somnath (1025–26), in the reign of the Chaulukya Bhima I and central to Gujarat's memory, and Gujarat's naval wars with the Portuguese (Chaul 1508, Diu 1509, 1538, 1546).
history_text_issues.correction: Add Somnath and the maritime dimension of Cambay and Diu.

missing_features: War elephants (Hudud al-Alam according to Hooja; Chatsu inscription; Tarain).
Rajput hill forts and siege warfare (Ranthambore 1301; Chittor 1303, 1535, 1567–68).
Hydraulic engineering: stepwells (vav/baori) such as the Rani ki Vav at Patan (c. 1063) and Adalaj (1499), and reservoir tanks.
Temple architecture: Khajuraho (Chandelas), Modhera (Solankis), the Jain temples of Dilwara.

Maritime and mercantile Gujarat: the ports of Cambay and Diu and the Jain, Hindu and Muslim merchants whom Tomé Pires and Duarte Barbosa describe as dominant in the western Indian Ocean; Malik Ayaz's fleet.
Bhil archers and guerrilla warfare in the Aravallis (Mewar, 16th century).
The scholarly patronage of the Paramara Bhoja of Dhar (11th century), to whom technical treatises such as the Samarangana Sutradhara are attributed.
The saka/kesariya ethic (the last charge of warriors dressed in saffron), to be handled with care because it is linked to jauhar.

proposals.title: Give Battle Elephant and Elite Battle Elephant
proposals.description: Add the Battle Elephant line, possibly without Elite, to keep the focus on cavalry.
proposals.historical_basis: The Hudud al-Alam (982, cited by Hooja, 2006) credits the rai of Kannauj with 800 elephants. The Chatsu inscription and the chronicles of Tarain mention Rajput elephant forces.

proposals.title: Bhil Archer instead of Chakram Thrower
proposals.description: A fast, cheap foot archer, with +1 range and a speed or camouflage bonus near forests and hills, strong against light cavalry.
proposals.historical_basis: Bhil archers were constant allies of Mewar: according to tradition, the Bhil chief Rana Punja fought at Haldighati (1576), and a Bhil appears on the coat of arms of Mewar. Guhila tradition links the Bhils to the enthronement ritual of the Ranas.

proposals.title: 'Kesariya' as a last-resort technology
proposals.description: Units within 8 tiles of their own Castle or Town Center with less than 30% HP gain +4 attack and +20% speed (an aura mechanic, like the Centurion's).
proposals.historical_basis: In the sieges of Chittor (1303, 1535, 1567–68), the Rajput defenders sallied out in a final charge dressed in saffron (saka/kesariya). The implementation should avoid any reference to jauhar (the self-immolation of the women).

proposals.title: 'Vav' (stepwell) as an economic building or technology
proposals.description: A stone building that increases the gather rate of Farms within a radius of 6 tiles by 10% and allows a Farm to be reseeded for free once.
proposals.historical_basis: The stepwells of Gujarat and Rajasthan were central infrastructure in a semi-arid region: the Rani ki Vav at Patan (c. 1063), which tradition attributes to the Chaulukya queen Udayamati, and Adalaj (1499).

proposals.title: 'Malik Ayaz's Fleet': Gujarat's naval dimension
proposals.description: Give Dry Dock and Fast Fire Ship and a technology with +1 range for galleys and Cannon Galleons and -15% ship cost.
proposals.historical_basis: Malik Ayaz, governor of Diu, and the Mamluk admiral Amir Husain defeated Lourenço de Almeida at Chaul (1508). The ports of Cambay and Diu dominated the trade of the western Indian Ocean (Tomé Pires, Suma Oriental).

proposals.title: Frontier Guards reoriented towards defence
proposals.description: Towers and Castles get +2 armour and +2 line of sight. It represents the Pratiharas as India's 'doorkeepers'.
proposals.historical_basis: The Gwalior prashasti presents Nagabhata I as the one who held back the Arabs of Sind (c. 730–740). Sulaiman describes the Gurjara king as the greatest enemy of the Arabs.

proposals.title: Rename or reframe the civ
proposals.description: Rename it to 'Rajputs', accepting the Gurjar/Rajput overlap, or keep 'Gurjaras' with the text centred on the Pratiharas and the 'Rajput' kingdoms up to c. 1300. The Sultanates of Gujarat and Malwa would move to another civ or to a separate text.
proposals.historical_basis: The civ is in practice an umbrella for Rajput dynasties and regional sultanates, and the term 'Gurjara' is ambiguous and disputed.

contested: The origin of the Gurjaras: the colonial theory of a Central Asian or Hunnic origin (V. A. Smith, D. R. Bhandarkar) versus a local origin; the territorial reading (Gurjaratra) versus the clan or ethnic one.
The modern dispute between Gurjar and Rajput communities over the heritage of the Pratiharas and of Mihira Bhoja.
The formation of 'Rajput' identity: a process spanning the 7th–16th centuries (B. D. Chattopadhyaya, Tanuja Kothiyal) versus ancient genealogies (the Agnikula myth).
Who held back the Arabs c. 738: Nagabhata I, Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin or Bappa Rawal, the latter of uncertain historicity.
The historicity of the Prithviraj Raso and of the Sanyogita episode; the myth of the 'traitor Jaichand'.
The outcome of Haldighati and the assessment of Maharana Pratap's resistance.
How much weight the isolated reference to 'Śrīvaṃśa' horses carries, and the reliability of the Hudud al-Alam's figures, which recycle earlier sources.
key_sources: Sulaiman al-Tajir, Akhbar al-Sin wa'l-Hind (851), trans. in Elliot & Dowson, vol. I (1867)
Al-Mas'udi, Muruj al-Dhahab (c. 943)
Hudud al-Alam (982), trans. V. Minorsky (1937)
Gwalior prashasti of Mihira Bhoja; Chatsu inscription (Guhilas); Rajor inscription (c. 960)
Jayanaka, Prithviraja Vijaya (c. 1191–92)
Minhaj al-Siraj Juzjani, Tabaqat-i Nasiri; Hasan Nizami, Taj al-Ma'athir
B. N. Puri, The History of the Gurjara-Pratiharas (1957)
Dasharatha Sharma, Early Chauhan Dynasties (1959)
Rima Hooja, A History of Rajasthan (2006)
Cynthia Talbot, The Last Hindu Emperor: Prithviraj Chauhan and the Indian Past, 1200–2000 (2016)
B. D. Chattopadhyaya, The Making of Early Medieval India (1994)
Tanuja Kothiyal, Nomadic Narratives: A History of Mobility and Identity in the Great Indian Desert (2016)
Tomé Pires, Suma Oriental (1512–15); Duarte Barbosa, Livro (c. 1516)
Romila Thapar, Somanatha (2004)

civs.represents: Bengal, and also Bihar in the Pala phase. It includes Shashanka's kingdom in Gauda (c. 600–625), the Pala Empire (c. 750–1160), the Senas (c. 1070–1230) and above all the Bengal Sultanate (1352–1538, with an epilogue under the Karranis until 1576).
civs.verdict: The Bengalis are among the most coherent civs in the group. Elephants, river and naval warfare, Mahayana Buddhism, the term 'paik', the rice trade and even the weakness in cavalry correspond to real features of Bengal. The problems lie in mechanical choices disconnected from history: armour for Monks, cavalry that is effective against Skirmishers, and Paiks that speed up elephants and chariots, when paik means infantry soldier. The unique unit, the Ratha, rests on a dubious reading of the Pala inscriptions. The total absence of land-based gunpowder (confirmed in the data: no Hand Cannoneer, no Bombard Cannon, no Bombard Tower) contradicts João de Barros and Babur, who highlight Bengali artillery and firearms. The text has several exaggerations, such as the economy that 'outstripped Europe' and Devapala's disastrous expedition.
civs.naming_scope_issues: 'Bengalis' is an endonym (Bangali) and works well for the Sultanate, whose rulers styled themselves 'Shah-i-Bangalah' and unified the region under that name. For the Palas it is less accurate: their core included Bihar (Pataliputra, Monghyr) and the sources speak of Gauda and Vanga. The Bengali language and identity took shape gradually, with the Charyapada of the 10th–12th centuries. The time frame is good. There are overlaps: the race for Kannauj is shared with the Gurjaras and Dravidians, Devapala's expedition also appears in the Dravidians' text, and Bakhtiyar Khalji's conquest of Bengal touches on the Hindustanis. Neighbours such as Kamarupa and the Ahom (Assam), Arakan and Orissa are left out.

elements.explanation: Sulaiman (851) attributes to the king of 'Rahma/Ruhmi', usually identified with the Pala ruler (the dominant identification, but not a unanimous one), some 50,000 elephants. The number is exaggerated but revealing. The Monghyr copper-plate grant (Devapala) describes the fleet of boats on the Ganges beside the royal camp. Under the Sultanate, the river navy was essential in a delta (Banglapedia), and Babur faced Bengali boats on the Ghaghra (1529).

elements.element: Town Centers spawn 2 Villagers when the next Age is reached
elements.explanation: An abstraction of the population density of the fertile delta and of the rice surplus. Ibn Battuta (1346) says he had never seen a land where provisions were so cheap.

It has no basis. Bengal was notoriously weak in cavalry and depended on imported horses (Banglapedia calls it the weakest component of the army). According to Minhaj, Bakhtiyar Khalji took Nadia by surprise (c. 1204) with only 18 horsemen in the vanguard.

elements.element: Elephant Units receive -25% bonus damage and are more resistant to conversion
elements.explanation: A mechanical abstraction of a well-documented reality: the central place of elephants in Bengal, from the Palas to the Sultanate. The resistance to conversion is pure mechanics.

It is meant to evoke the strong Pala Buddhist monasticism (Nalanda, Vikramashila, Somapura). There is, however, no tradition of protected or fighting monks. The mahaviharas were sacked around 1200 (Odantapuri, c. 1197–1200; Vikramashila, c. 1203), the opposite of 'armoured monks'.
A vague link to Bengali river shipbuilding (the shipyards of Sonargaon and Chittagong). It is generic, but compatible with the naval identity.

War chariots had practically disappeared from Indian battlefields after the Gupta period. The mentions in the Pala inscriptions follow the traditional formula of the fourfold army (elephants, horses, chariots, infantry) and do not prove an active chariot corps. Xuanzang still mentions, in the 7th century, generals carried in chariots. The switch between bow and melee is a game mechanic.

'Paik' (from Sanskrit padatika, crossed with Persian payk) denotes the infantry soldier of Bengal and Orissa: archers, spearmen and later musketeers. They were the backbone of the armies of the Sultanate and of the Baro-Bhuyans, and later there was the Paika Rebellion (1817). The name is faithful, but the effect (speeding up Rathas and elephants) applies it to exactly the units the paiks were not.

The name is faithful: the Palas patronised Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism. Dharmapala founded Vikramashila and Somapura, and Atisha left for Tibet c. 1040. The effect (less population space) is an arbitrary abstraction.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Trade Units generate +10% food in addition to gold
elements.explanation: Bengal exported rice and sugar to the Maldives, Malacca and other ports (Tomé Pires; Ma Huan, 1433), and Ibn Battuta stresses the abundance of grain. It is a good rendering of a food-surplus economy tied to trade.

tree_issues.item: Hand Cannoneer / Bombard Cannon / Bombard Tower (absent)
tree_issues.problem: This is historically wrong for the late Sultanate. According to Banglapedia, João de Barros attributes Bengal's supremacy over Arakan and Tripura to the effectiveness of its artillery. Babur noted the battle order of the Bengali infantry, armed with bows and firearms, and considered Bengali artillery very effective. Turbak's expedition against the Ahom (1532) carried cannon and firearms, according to the Buranjis. The Bengalis' only gunpowder unit is the Cannon Galleon.
Faithful: Bengal was poor in horses, imported them from the north-west and was vulnerable to fast Turkic cavalry (Bakhtiyar Khalji, c. 1204).

tree_issues.item: Elite Battle Elephant + Elite Elephant Archer (present)
tree_issues.problem: Faithful: elephants were the prestige arm of the Palas and the sultans.

tree_issues.item: Full navy (Fast Fire Ship, Dry Dock, Shipwright)
tree_issues.problem: Faithful: river warfare in the delta.

The lack of Stone Shaft Mining is accidentally faithful, because the delta has no stone and Bengali architecture is built in brick and terracotta (Somapura, the Adina Mosque 1373–75, the Sixty Dome Mosque in Bagerhat). The lack of Treadmill Crane is less justifiable for builders of monumental temples and mosques.
This is debatable: the paik infantry was largely made up of archers, with bamboo bows. A minor gap.

history_text_issues.claim: Shashanka is said to have 'implemented a new calendar'.
history_text_issues.problem: The origin of the Bengali calendar (Bangabda) is disputed. The attribution to Shashanka is a modern hypothesis based on the coincidence of the year zero (593/594). Many historians link it to Akbar's fiscal reform (the fasli calendar, 1584) or to Alauddin Husain Shah.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the hypothesis as one among several.

history_text_issues.claim: The people are said to have elected Gopala 'according to legend', in a 'consensual vesting of power'.
history_text_issues.problem: The source is the Khalimpur copper-plate grant (Dharmapala): it says that the prakriti chose Gopala to put an end to matsyanyaya ('the law of the fishes', that is, anarchy). It is not a legend, but nor is it a popular election: the prakriti were probably chiefs and notables, and the formula serves as legitimation. Taranatha (1608) gives a late, legendary version.
history_text_issues.correction: Cite the inscription and explain that this was probably a choice made by the local power-holders, presented as legitimation.

history_text_issues.claim: Devapala is said to have made a 'pyrrhic' and disastrous expedition to the far south, and then to have recovered spectacularly.
history_text_issues.problem: Devapala's 'conquests' in the south come from Pala panegyrics (the Badal pillar, which credits him with humbling the 'Dravida' lords; the Monghyr grant, which speaks of campaigns as far as Setubandha). R. C. Majumdar and D. C. Sircar consider them hyperbolic. On the Pandya side, the Sinnamanur plates credit Srimara Srivallabha with a victory at Kudamukku over a coalition that included 'Magadhas'. From this one can speculate about a Pala–Pandya clash, but no source describes a disastrous expedition followed by a recovery. It is a constructed narrative, repeated in the Dravidians' text.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that the Pala inscriptions claim victories reaching into the south, probably exaggerated, and that any clash with the Pandyas is hypothetical.

history_text_issues.claim: Bengal's economy 'outstripped all of Europe at the time' (8th–12th centuries).
history_text_issues.problem: It has no quantitative basis: there are no data that would allow the output of Pala Bengal to be compared with that of Europe. The claim seems to project backwards popular, and debatable, estimates about Mughal Bengal in the 17th–18th centuries.
history_text_issues.correction: Speak of Bengal's agricultural and commercial wealth in qualitative terms, without numerical comparisons.

history_text_issues.claim: The Pala emperors commanded 'notably rathas' (war chariots).
history_text_issues.problem: The mention of chariots in the Pala inscriptions is formulaic (fourfold army). There are no accounts of Pala battles decided or marked by chariots.
history_text_issues.correction: Highlight elephants, infantry and boats as the main arms and present chariots as ceremonial or residual.

history_text_issues.claim: The Senas appear as a 'neighbouring' dynasty that took advantage of the Pala decline.
history_text_issues.problem: The Senas were of Karnata origin (southern India), probably arriving in Bengal as chiefs in the service of the Palas, and not a neighbouring kingdom. Vijayasena consolidated his power in the second half of the 11th century.
history_text_issues.correction: State the Karnata origin of the Senas and their starting point as feudatories.

history_text_issues.claim: In the early 13th century, the Delhi Sultanate is said to have advanced east and taken Bengal.
history_text_issues.problem: The conquest was the work of Bakhtiyar Khalji (c. 1204), a commander in the service of the Ghurids, before the Sultanate formally existed. Bengal was often only nominally subject to Delhi; Barani calls it 'Bulghakpur', the land of revolt. The text omits the sack of the mahaviharas, which was decisive for the end of institutional Buddhism and would give meaning to the civ's Buddhist bonuses.
history_text_issues.correction: Name Bakhtiyar Khalji, explain Bengali autonomy and mention the end of the great monasteries.

history_text_issues.claim: Jamdani is said to be 'also known as muslin after its iteration in the Middle East'.
history_text_issues.problem: This is wrong. Muslin is the general category of fine cotton fabric, and jamdani is a variety of muslin with woven motifs, which reached its peak in the Mughal period. 'Muslin' derives, according to the standard etymology, from Mosul (Iraq), a name used by Europeans; it does not come from a Middle Eastern 'version' of jamdani.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that Bengal was famous for its fine muslins, of which jamdani is the most celebrated figured variety. Sulaiman (851) already describes, in the kingdom of 'Rahma', fabrics that pass through a ring.

history_text_issues.claim: The Sultanate is said to have been absorbed by the Mughal Empire in the 16th century.
history_text_issues.problem: This is simplified. Sher Shah Suri took Gaur (1538), the Karranis followed, the Mughals only won at Rajmahal (1576), and the Baro-Bhuyans (Isa Khan, Musa Khan) held out until c. 1611.
history_text_issues.correction: Give the sequence Suri → Karrani → Mughals.

missing_features: The Sultanate's artillery and firearms (15th–16th centuries), according to João de Barros, Babur and the 1532 campaign against the Ahom.
River war flotillas as the main arm in a delta.
Paik infantry with bamboo bow, shield and later musket, the true military backbone.
Textile economy (muslins, silks), exports of rice and sugar, cowries as everyday currency (already mentioned by Sulaiman and Mas'udi).
The great mahaviharas as centres of international learning (Nalanda, Vikramashila, Somapura; Atisha and Tibet).
Brick and terracotta architecture owing to the lack of stone (Adina, Bagerhat).
Agrarian expansion in the eastern delta associated with Sufi pioneers (Eaton, 1993).

proposals.title: Give Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon in the Imperial Age
proposals.description: Add Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon, without Elite and without bonuses, to reflect the artillery of the late Sultanate.
proposals.historical_basis: João de Barros (Décadas da Ásia, cited by Banglapedia) attributes Bengali supremacy over Arakan and Tripura to artillery. Babur describes the Bengali infantry with bows and firearms (1529), and Turbak invaded the Ahom kingdom in 1532 with cannon.

proposals.title: Paiks as an infantry technology
proposals.description: Infantry and foot archers get +10% speed, +1 pierce armour and -15% gold cost.
proposals.historical_basis: Paik is the infantry soldier of Bengal and Orissa (bow, shield, spear, later musket), the backbone of the Sultanate's armies (Banglapedia; Abul Fazl; Kolff, 1990).

proposals.title: River warship instead of the Ratha
proposals.description: A unique ship from the Dock, fast, cheap and shallow-hulled, with a bonus against Transport Ships and Fishing Ships and +2 range against land units on the riverbank. Caveat: names such as 'kosa' or 'ghurab' are attested mainly in the 17th-century Mughal flotilla (nawara), so the name should be chosen with care.
proposals.historical_basis: Warfare in the delta was riverine: Bengali boats on the Ghaghra (1529, Baburnama), the Sultanate's navy (Banglapedia) and, later, the Mughal nawara of Dhaka.

proposals.title: 'Brick and Terracotta' as a construction bonus
proposals.description: Defensive buildings cost -25% stone and more wood, and Monasteries cost -20%.
proposals.historical_basis: Bengali architecture (Somapura, Adina, Sixty Dome) used brick and terracotta for lack of stone in the delta.

proposals.title: 'Mahavihara' instead of the Monks' armour
proposals.description: University and Monastery technologies cost -25% and are researched 25% faster. Replaces the Monks' armour bonus.
proposals.historical_basis: Nalanda, Vikramashila (founded by Dharmapala) and Somapura attracted students from Tibet, China and South-East Asia. Atisha took the Vikramashila tradition to Tibet c. 1040.

proposals.title: Replace 'Cavalry +2 vs Skirmishers'
proposals.description: Elephant Units cost -10% and can also be trained at the Castle. Alternative: Trade Cogs +10% gold, for the muslin trade.
proposals.historical_basis: Bengal was a breeding ground for elephants and a major exporter of textiles (Sulaiman; Ma Huan, 1433; Tomé Pires), not a land of cavalry.

contested: Whether Gopala's selection was an 'election' or a legitimation by local notables.
The origin of the Bengali calendar (Shashanka, Husain Shah or Akbar).
The real extent of Devapala's conquests and whether a Pala–Pandya clash took place (Badal pillar versus Sinnamanur plates).
The identification of Sulaiman's kingdom of 'Rahma' with the Palas (alternatives proposed by Reinaud and Lassen).
The actual military use of war chariots by the Palas.
Who destroyed Nalanda and when: Minhaj's account of Odantapuri, the testimony of Dharmasvamin (1234–36), who still found Nalanda partially active, and politicised alternative readings.
The causes of the Islamisation of Bengal: Richard Eaton's agrarian frontier thesis versus explanations based on forced conversion or migration.
Popular estimates of Bengal's weight in the world economy, especially Mughal Bengal.
The date when firearms were introduced into Bengal (before or after Portuguese contact).
key_sources: Khalimpur copper-plate grant (Dharmapala); Monghyr grant (Devapala); Badal pillar
Sandhyakar Nandi, Ramacharita (12th century)
Sulaiman al-Tajir, Akhbar al-Sin wa'l-Hind (851), in Elliot & Dowson, vol. I
Taranatha, History of Buddhism in India (1608)

Babur, Baburnama (1529 campaign)

Abul Fazl, Ain-i-Akbari
