civs.represents: An aggregate of southern India and the Deccan: the Chalukyas of Badami (543–753), the Rashtrakutas (753–982), the Pandyas (6th–10th centuries and again 13th–14th centuries), the imperial Cholas (c. 850–1279) and Vijayanagara (1336–1565, with an epilogue until 1646). The design (navy, infantry, wootz, urumi) draws mainly on the Tamil Cholas and on Kerala.
civs.verdict: The Dravidians get several structural traits right. Chola maritime power projection is real: Sri Lanka, the Maldives and the 1025 raid on Srivijaya, recorded in the Tanjore inscription. Armies relied on infantry and elephants, and the scarcity of horses forced them to import horses by sea. Wootz steel is genuinely South Indian. But the naval unit, the Thirisadai, has an unattested name, which comes from a fraudulent Wikipedia article (“Chola Navy”), and a model inspired by an Austronesian ship from Borobudur. Even the existence of a standing Chola navy is now contested (Kanisetti, 2025). The Urumi is a Keralan martial-arts weapon, marginal on the battlefield. Traits of the first rank are missing: granite architecture (no Architecture, Treadmill Crane or Stone Shaft Mining), the Elite Battle Elephant and the overseas merchant guilds. The name is a 19th-century linguistic label, and the text has several errors and hypotheses presented as facts.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Dravidian” in the modern sense of a language family was popularised by Robert Caldwell (1856), from the Sanskrit drāviḍa, which in medieval texts often designates only the Tamil country. Using a linguistic label as a civ name is anachronistic and very broad. It lumps together Tamil polities (Cholas, Pandyas, Pallavas), Kannada ones (Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Hoysalas, much of Vijayanagara), Telugu ones (Kakatiyas) and Malayali ones (Cheras, Calicut). It also carries 20th-century political connotations (the Dravidian movement, DMK). The design is Chola and Keralan, but the text begins in the Deccan (Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas), which were land powers. Left out are the Pallavas, the Hoysalas, the Kakatiyas, the Madurai Sultanate and the Deccan Sultanates. A coherent alternative: “Tamils” or “Cholas” for this civ and a future Deccan civ (“Kannadigas” or “Deccanis”).

elements.explanation: The maritime part rests on facts: the conquest of northern Sri Lanka (993–1017) and of the Maldives, and Rajendra I's raid on Srivijaya and Kadaram/Kedah (1025). The Tanjore inscription of 1030–31 says the king sent “many kalam” (ships) across the sea. Whether there was a standing navy or merchant ships were requisitioned is contested: Kulke et al. (2009) discuss the question, and Kanisetti (2025) finds no evidence of a royal navy. The infantry part is solid: Tamil armies were mainly infantry in named regiments, with elephants and imported horses (Marco Polo; Wassaf). Caveat: “naval” does not apply to the Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas, land powers of the Deccan.
An acceptable abstraction of the Tamil and Malabar coastal economy: the Paravar fishermen and the pearl fishery of the Gulf of Mannar, described by Marco Polo.

elements.element: Receive +200 wood when advancing to the next Age
elements.explanation: It has no clear link. One could invoke the Malabar teak used in shipbuilding, but the bonus does not reflect it. It is game balance.

elements.element: Skirmishers and Elephant Archers attack +25% faster
elements.explanation: There is no specific South Indian tradition of javelin troops or elephant archers superior to that of other regions. It is mechanical.
A reasonable abstraction of infantry-centred armies: the Chola regiments (Kaikkolar, Velaikkarar) and the masses of Vijayanagara infantry described by Domingos Paes and Fernão Nunes.
There is no specific basis for an advantage in siege engines.

The urumi (flexible whip-sword) is real, but it belongs to the Keralan martial tradition, kalarippayattu (Zarrilli, 1998). It is not attested as a weapon of Chola or Rashtrakuta battle units, and its antiquity is uncertain. The explosive charge and the strong bonus against buildings are fantasy.

No attestation of “Thirisadai” as a Chola ship class is known in inscriptions or texts. The name comes from the “Vessels and Weapons” section of the Wikipedia article “Chola Navy”, which invented ship classes (“Dharani”, “Loola”, “Thirisadai”) with fake or misattributed sources. The fraud was exposed in 2022 and the content was removed. Anirudh Kanisetti (Lords of Earth and Sea, 2025) treats it as a myth. The attested Tamil term for ships is kalam/marakkalam. The in-game model is based on the Borobudur ship (Java), with outriggers and Austronesian sails. Chola maritime power is real, but the unit's premise is not.

A Sanskrit veterinary medicine of elephants did exist: the Hastyayurveda attributed to Palakapya and the Matangalila, of Keralan origin (trans. Edgerton, 1931). Royal elephants had stables and specialised keepers. The tradition is pan-Indian, and the Hastyayurveda is associated with Anga, in the east, so it would serve the Bengalis equally well.

Wootz (from Kannada/Telugu ukku) was high-carbon crucible steel produced in southern India (Kodumanal, Telangana, Karnataka) and in Sri Lanka, and exported to the Middle East, where it gave rise to “Damascus” blades. Ignoring armour is an exaggerated abstraction, but the link is genuine (Srinivasan and Ranganathan, 2004).

elements.element: Team Bonus: Docks provide +5 population space
elements.explanation: A simple abstraction of the maritime orientation. It has no specific basis, but it is coherent.

tree_issues.item: Architecture, Treadmill Crane, Stone Shaft Mining (absent)
tree_issues.problem: This is the most ironic gap in the game. The Brihadeeswarar temple at Thanjavur (c. 1010), with a granite vimana about 66 m high, and Gangaikonda Cholapuram are masterpieces of stone engineering. The “Dravidian style” is one of the world's great architectural traditions, and Hampi (Vijayanagara) was a granite fortress-city.
The Kolar and Hutti gold fields (Karnataka) have been worked since antiquity.

tree_issues.item: Battle Elephant without Elite (confirmed in the data)
tree_issues.problem: The Cholas, the Pandyas and Vijayanagara maintained large elephant corps; Paes and Nunes describe those of Vijayanagara. It deserved the Elite version.

tree_issues.item: Knight, Cavalier, Bloodlines, Cavalry Archer, Hussar (absent)
tree_issues.problem: This is faithful for the Tamil kingdoms, which depended on imported horses that died quickly (Marco Polo, Wassaf). It is less faithful for 16th-century Vijayanagara, which imported thousands of horses via Goa and Bhatkal and had numerous cavalry.

tree_issues.item: Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon, Bombard Tower (present)
tree_issues.problem: This is plausible for late Vijayanagara, which used Portuguese arquebusiers (Cristóvão de Figueiredo at Raichur, 1520, according to Nunes) and artillery. The great gunpowder powers of the Deccan, however, were the Sultanates (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar).
This is debatable for the land of the bhakti movements (Alvars, Nayanars) and of temples that were centres of power, but monk mechanics are very abstract. A minor gap.
Consistent with Tamil maritime power projection, even if the existence of a standing royal navy is debated.

history_text_issues.claim: The summary of the south begins with the Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas and omits the Pallavas.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the Pallavas of Kanchipuram (c. 275–897), a major Tamil and maritime power (Mahendravarman I; Narasimhavarman I, who took Badami in 642; Mamallapuram). It also omits Pulakeshin II's victory over Harsha on the Narmada (Aihole inscription, 634–35).
history_text_issues.correction: Include the Chalukya–Pallava rivalry and the victory over Harsha.

history_text_issues.claim: The Pandyas supposedly ruled much of the Bay of Bengal coast and took part, sometimes unwillingly, in the “Kannauj Triangle”.
history_text_issues.problem: The Pandyas of Madurai ruled the far south (Gulf of Mannar, Palk Strait), with temporary advances as far as the Kaveri delta; most of the Coromandel coast was Pallava and later Chola. They were not contenders in the tripartite struggle for Kannauj, which was fought between the Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas. A possible clash with the Palas is only a hypothesis based on panegyrics (Badal, Sinnamanur).
history_text_issues.correction: Place the Pandyas in the far south and remove their participation in the struggle for Kannauj.

history_text_issues.claim: Devapala's southern campaign supposedly almost ruined the Rashtrakutas and Pandyas.
history_text_issues.problem: No source says so. The narrative rests on hyperbolic Pala panegyrics (Badal pillar, Monghyr grant) and repeats the reconstruction in the Bengalis' text. The Rashtrakutas were then at their peak (Amoghavarsha I), and the Pandyas' own Sinnamanur plates claim a victory by Srimara over a coalition that included “Magadhas”.
history_text_issues.correction: Remove the statement or present it as a claim made by the Pala inscriptions.

history_text_issues.claim: Rajendra Chola supposedly allied with Suryavarman I of the Khmer Empire to crush Srivijaya.
history_text_issues.problem: The alliance is a hypothesis based on slender evidence: the gift of a chariot from the king of “Kamboja” mentioned in a Chola inscription, and the Khmer conflict with Tambralinga. “Crush” is an exaggeration: the 1025 raid sacked ports and captured King Sangrama Vijayottungavarman, but Srivijaya continued to exist.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe the 1025 raid and present the Khmer alliance as a hypothesis.

history_text_issues.claim: The Chola fleet was supposedly one of the most powerful, “meticulously organised” and with a wide range of ship types.
history_text_issues.problem: Almost nothing is known about the Chola fleet's organisation or ship types. It is debated whether the 1025 expedition used a standing navy or requisitioned merchant ships (Kulke, Kesavapany and Sakhuja, 2009), and Kanisetti (2025) finds no evidence of a royal navy. The ship “classes” circulating online come from the same fraudulent Wikipedia article that gave rise to the Thirisadai.
history_text_issues.correction: State the Chola capacity for maritime power projection without inventing organisational details, and indicate that the nature of the fleet is debated.

history_text_issues.claim: Wootz was supposedly “a predecessor of modern steel” that spread as far as Europe.
history_text_issues.problem: Wootz is crucible steel, not the ancestor of modern industrial steel (Bessemer, Siemens-Martin). In Europe it influenced metallurgy mainly as an object of study in the 19th century (Stodart and Faraday, 1819–22). Crucible steel was also produced in Central Asia (Merv, Akhsiket).
history_text_issues.correction: Describe it as high-quality crucible steel exported to the Islamic world, where it gave rise to “Damascus” blades.

history_text_issues.claim: Vijayanagara supposedly imported gunpowder weapons from European merchants.
history_text_issues.problem: Vijayanagara's great import through the Portuguese was horses (Goa, Bhatkal). Firearms also arrived via the Deccan and from the Ottoman and Persian world, and the Portuguese served mainly as mercenaries (Raichur, 1520).
history_text_issues.correction: Highlight the horse trade and the use of foreign mercenaries and gunners.

history_text_issues.claim: Vijayanagara was supposedly defeated by the constant pressure of invasions “from the north”.
history_text_issues.problem: The fall came at the Battle of Talikota/Rakkasa-Tangadi (1565) against a coalition of the neighbouring Deccan Sultanates (Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar), followed by the sack of Hampi. These were not generic “invasions from the north”, and the Deccan Sultanates are not even mentioned.
history_text_issues.correction: Name Talikota and the Deccan Sultanates.

history_text_issues.claim: The urumis supposedly had an “uncanny” ability to get around defences.
history_text_issues.problem: This is a romanticised description of a Keralan martial-training weapon with little evidence of use in pitched battle.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the urumi as a weapon of the kalarippayattu tradition.

missing_features: Granite temple architecture and the temple as an economic and banking centre (donations and lands of the Brihadeeswarar).

Overseas Tamil merchant guilds, with inscriptions at Takua Pa (9th century), Barus/Lobu Tua in Sumatra (1088), Pagan and Quanzhou (1281): the Ainnurruvar (“Five Hundred of Ayyavole”) and the Manigramam.
Tank irrigation (eri) and dams such as the Kallanai.
Named Chola regiments, including the Velaikkarar, elite guards also attested in Sri Lanka (Polonnaruwa inscription).
Structural dependence on the import of horses by sea (Marco Polo, Wassaf; Vijayanagara via Goa).
The pearl fishery of the Gulf of Mannar.
Gold from Kolar and Hutti; diamonds from Golconda (Deccan).
The Hoysalas and the Kakatiyas; the campaigns of Malik Kafur (1310–11) and the Madurai Sultanate (1335–78), destroyed by Vijayanagara.
The nayaka system and the fortified capital of Hampi; Portuguese mercenaries and gunners (Paes, Nunes).
The Kunjali Marakkars, admirals of the Zamorin of Calicut against the Portuguese (16th century), and the maritime world of Malabar.

proposals.title: Rename Thirisadai to Kalam or Marakkalam
proposals.description: Keep the mechanics (a heavy, durable ship), but use the attested term kalam/marakkalam, correct the description and replace the Austronesian Borobudur model with an Indian Ocean-type ship with sewn planks.
proposals.historical_basis: Rajendra I's Tanjore inscription uses “kalam” for the ships sent across the sea. “Thirisadai” originates in a fraudulent Wikipedia article (exposed in 2022).

proposals.title: Velaikkarar instead of Urumi Swordsman
proposals.description: Elite infantry from the Castle with a lot of HP, which gains +3 attack and regenerates near a Castle or a hero unit (aura) and cannot be converted.
proposals.historical_basis: The Velaikkarar were elite guard regiments of the Chola kings, sworn to protect the monarch, attested in Chola inscriptions and in the Polonnaruwa inscription (Sri Lanka).

proposals.title: Restore Architecture, Treadmill Crane and Stone Shaft Mining and create “Vimana”
proposals.description: Give the three technologies and create the unique tech “Vimana”: Monasteries and Wonders are built 50% faster, and each Monastery generates a small trickle of gold (the temple as an economic centre).
proposals.historical_basis: The Brihadeeswarar (c. 1010) and Gangaikonda Cholapuram show top-tier granite engineering, and Chola temples accumulated land, gold and banking functions (Karashima; Stein).

proposals.title: Pearl fishery: gold from Fishing Ships
proposals.description: Replace the “+15 carry” with: Fishing Ships generate +0.1 gold for each unit of food gathered at sea.
proposals.historical_basis: Marco Polo describes the pearl fisheries of Ma'bar (Gulf of Mannar), a major source of revenue for the Pandyas and later for the Portuguese.

proposals.title: “Horse Trade” (horses by sea)
proposals.description: Once researched, Docks can train Light Cavalry and Knights (no Cavalier), at +20% gold cost. Represents imported cavalry.
proposals.historical_basis: Wassaf and Marco Polo describe the annual import of thousands of Arabian and Persian horses by the Pandya kings, and Vijayanagara depended on horses arriving via Goa (Paes, Nunes).

proposals.title: Elite Battle Elephant
proposals.description: Give the Elite upgrade and reduce the cost of elephants by 15% in the Imperial Age.
proposals.historical_basis: The Chola expedition to the Ganges (c. 1019–21) and the army of Vijayanagara (Paes) used large elephant corps.

proposals.title: “Ainnurruvar” team bonus
proposals.description: The team's Trade Cogs get +10% gold and +2 pierce armour.
proposals.historical_basis: The Tamil guilds of the Five Hundred of Ayyavole and the Manigramam left inscriptions ranging from Takua Pa and Sumatra (Lobu Tua, 1088) to Quanzhou (1281). Kanisetti (2025) locates the real Tamil maritime power in them.

proposals.title: Rename to “Tamils” or “Cholas” and create a Deccan civ
proposals.description: This civ would keep the Pallavas, Cholas and Pandyas. A future “Kannadigas” or “Deccanis” civ would receive the Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Hoysalas and Vijayanagara, or the Deccan Sultanates.
proposals.historical_basis: The maritime Tamil world and the land-based Deccan had very different military and cultural dynamics, and “Dravidian” is a 19th-century linguistic label.

contested: The nature of the Chola expeditions to Southeast Asia: conquest, punitive raid or defence of mercantile interests (Spencer, 1983; Kulke et al., 2009).
The existence of a standing Chola navy versus the use of requisitioned merchant ships (Nilakanta Sastri versus Kanisetti, 2025).
The existence of a Chola–Khmer alliance against Srivijaya and Tambralinga.
The structure of the Chola state: centralised (Nilakanta Sastri) or “segmentary” (Burton Stein); a debate taken up again by Karashima and Subbarayalu.
Vijayanagara as a “Hindu bulwark” (Sewell, A Forgotten Empire, 1900) or as a Persianised state integrated into the Deccan world (Phillip Wagoner, “Sultan among Hindu Kings”, 1996).
Whether the Bahmanis already used firearms in 1366, as Firishta says, or whether their arrival was later (Iqtidar Alam Khan).
Whether or not Muslim commanders in Vijayanagara's service committed treachery at Talikota.
The origin of crucible steel: solely South Indian or also Central Asian (Feuerbach, Juleff).
The antiquity and military use of the urumi.
The identity of the “Dravida” defeated by Devapala on the Badal pillar (Rashtrakutas or Pandyas).
key_sources: Aihole inscription (634–35); Tanjore inscription of Rajendra I (1030–31); Tiruvalangadu plates; Pandya Sinnamanur plates

groups.cross_civ_notes:
Group structure: in principle, the 2022 split into four civs is a major improvement over the old 'Indians' as a single umbrella. The 'tripartite struggle' for Kannauj (the game calls it the 'Kannauj Triangle'; historians say 'tripartite struggle') is well distributed: the Pratiharas in the Gurjaras, the Palas in the Bengalis, the Rashtrakutas in the Dravidians. The naming criteria, however, are inconsistent: a Persian exonym (Hindustanis), a disputed clan or regional term (Gurjaras), a regional endonym (Bengalis) and a 19th-century language family (Dravidians).

2013 legacy: the Hindustanis keep the skeleton of the 'Indians' from The Forgotten (camels, Imperial Camel Rider, Shatagni). The repository history (commit 1a2a4cd, DE Update 61321) shows that the 'Sultans' tech was renamed 'Grand Trunk Road' in 2022, which swapped a name suited to the Sultanate for a 19th-century British name.

Repetitions and conflicts between texts:
- The Hindustanis, Gurjaras and Bengalis texts open with the Gupta collapse, and the Dravidians text also mentions it.
- Devapala's 'disastrous' expedition to the south appears as fact in the Bengalis and Dravidians texts. In reality it rests only on contradictory panegyrics (the Badal pillar and the Sinnamanur plates).
- Prithviraj Chauhan, the Ghurids and Aibak appear in both the Hindustanis and the Gurjaras.
- Bappa Rawal, of Mewar, appears in the Hindustanis text, but Mewar belongs to the Gurjaras.
- The Delhi Sultanate is in the Hindustanis, but the Sultanates of Gujarat and Malwa are in the Gurjaras.

Conflations with other civs: the Ghaznavids and Ghurids, who give the Hindustanis their character, were Turco-Persian and Tajik dynasties from Afghanistan and overlap with the Persians and the Turks. Timur overlaps with the Tatars. The Mughals and the Suris do not exist in the game, but their traits (gunpowder, the great road, sarais) have leaked into the Hindustanis.

Common error pattern: the Ghulam as infantry repeats the pattern of the Saracens' Mameluke (mounted on a camel and throwing scimitars). In both cases, slave-soldier elites who were mainly Turkic horse-archer cavalry appear in a different role.

Elements that are in the wrong civ:
- The chakram is attested by Duarte Barbosa (c. 1516) in the 'kingdom of Delli' and is later mainly Sikh; it would suit the Hindustanis better than the Gurjaras.
- The Hastyayurveda (elephant medicine) is associated with Anga, in the east; it would suit the Bengalis as well as the Dravidians.
- Camels make more sense in the Gurjaras (Sulaiman describes them as numerous in the Gurjara kingdom; Thar and Sind) than in the Hindustanis.

Elephants: the distribution (checked in data.json) is almost the reverse of what the sources show. The Hindustanis have neither Battle Elephant nor Elephant Archer, despite the Sultanate's royal monopoly on elephants (Digby). The Gurjaras also lack Battle Elephant, despite the elephant strength attributed to Kannauj and the Chatsu inscription. The Dravidians have Battle Elephant but not the Elite version. Only the Bengalis have both lines complete, which is correct for them. The Armored Elephant shared by all four civs, in place of rams, is a plausible abstraction.

Cavalry: none of the four has the Knight. This is a design convention that erases the Turkic and Rajput heavy cavalry and the horse trade that shaped Indian military history between the 11th and 16th centuries (Digby; Gommans). At the same time, it reflects the equestrian weakness of Bengal and the Tamil south well.

Gunpowder: it is poorly distributed. The Hindustanis have the gunpowder bonus, although the Sultanate made almost no use of it. The Bengalis have no land gunpowder at all, even though João de Barros and Babur highlight Bengali artillery and firearms. The major Indian users of gunpowder before 1526 (Gujarat, the Bahmanis and the Deccan Sultanates, Bengal) appear only in diluted form.

Chola navy: the Thirisadai comes from a hoax Wikipedia article (exposed in 2022), and its model is an Austronesian ship from Borobudur. The very existence of a permanent royal Chola navy is now contested (Kulke et al., 2009; Kanisetti, 2025). It is a good case for debate on how online myths make their way into game design.

Absent or poorly framed polities: the Pallavas, Kakatiyas and Hoysalas; the Madurai Sultanate; the Deccan Sultanates (Talikota, 1565); Orissa (the Eastern Gangas, Konark; the Gajapatis); Kashmir (Karkota, Lalitaditya); Assam (the Ahom, who defeated Bengal in 1532–33); Sri Lanka (Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa, Parakramabahu I); Malabar (the Zamorin of Calicut, Kunjali Marakkar).

A Portuguese angle useful for debates: Duarte Barbosa, Tomé Pires, Domingos Paes, Fernão Nunes and João de Barros are first-rate primary sources on Gujarat, Bengal and Vijayanagara around 1500–1540. The battles of Chaul (1508) and Diu (1509) and the Portuguese arquebusiers at Raichur (1520) provide concrete material for proposals.

Overall fidelity (game average ≈ 5): Bengalis 6; Gurjaras and Dravidians 5; Hindustanis 4.

verification_log.change: Added that the 'Grand Trunk Road' tech was called 'Sultans' until 2022. Source: the repository's git history, commit 1a2a4cd (DE Update 61321). New proposal to restore the name.
Timur's burning-camels episode reattributed to Nizam al-Din Shami's Zafarnama (1404) and qualified as an uncertain account ('by one account', Britannica), instead of presenting it as fact from Yazdi.
Shatagni: added Oppert (1880) as the origin of the 'cannon' reading and Lallanji Gopal (1962), who showed that the Shukranitisara dates from the 19th century. Rating kept at 'stretched'.
Caravanserai: corrected the claim that Ibn Battuta describes inns. Ibn Battuta describes the relay courier post (ulaq/dawa); the network of sarais is mainly the work of Sher Shah Suri.
Represents and period: the traits of the great road and the sarais attributed to the Suris, not the Mughals.

Confirmed in data.json that there is neither Battle Elephant nor Elephant Archer, only Armored and Siege Elephant. Anti-elephant spikes dated cautiously (Mehrangarh and Amber, 15th–16th centuries) and the categorical claim about 'rams on elephants' removed.
The 'division of labor' issue downgraded from moderate to minor and reworded as ambiguous (shreni guilds or castes).
The Mongol invasions issue reworded: 'without lasting gains' is correct, 'destroyed the infrastructure' is an exaggeration; added the 1303 siege of Delhi.

New issues in the history text: Aibak presented as the founder when the consolidator was Iltutmish (Kumar, 2007); omission of the Suri interregnum (1540–55). The Babur item completed with his observation about villages that are depopulated and rebuilt.
The 'Naffatun/Manjaniq' proposal reworded as 'Manjaniq', based on Amir Khusrau. 'Dagh-o-Chehra' now replaces Shatagni instead of Grand Trunk Road.

Chakram Thrower: rating changed from 'anachronistic' to 'stretched'. Barbosa (c. 1516) attests the weapon in northern India within the game's time frame; the problem is the lack of a link to the Pratiharas and Rajputs, not the period.
Added Sulaiman (851) on the Gurjara king's numerous camels and horses, which supports the 'Camel' part of the label and is cited in the Camel Scout.

The Hudud al-Alam figures (150,000 horsemen, 800 elephants) are now attributed via Rima Hooja (2006), as it was not possible to confirm them in Minorsky's translation. Added Harsha's elephant strength in the Chatsu inscription.

Name: clarified that the Pratiharas never call themselves 'Gurjara' in their inscriptions (Sanjay Sharma, 2006) and that the compound form appears only in the Rajor inscription, issued by a feudatory.

New issues in the history text: the invasions 'across the Hindu Kush' misplace the Arab threat from Sind (moderate); Prithviraj's 'hegemony' over northern India is exaggerated (moderate); the fall of Malwa is simplified (minor).

Confirmed in data.json: there is no Battle Elephant; there are Elephant Archer, Armored Elephant, Hussar, Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon; and there is no Cavalry Archer or Pikeman. Bhil and Rana Punja marked as tradition.

Confirmed in data.json that there is no Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon or Bombard Tower. The claim about João de Barros was verified via Banglapedia ('Military'), and it was added that Babur noted Bengali infantry with bows and firearms.
Removed the unverified figure of '100–150 vessels' at the Ghaghra (1529); kept only the presence of Bengali boats.
The Devapala item reworded: it is not 'unsourced' but a speculative reconstruction from contradictory panegyrics (the Badal pillar versus the Sinnamanur plates). Flagged as contested.
The identification of 'Rahma' with the Palas marked as dominant but not unanimous. Added Sulaiman's mention of fabrics that pass through a ring.
New issue in the text: the Senas were not a 'neighbouring' kingdom but were of Karnata origin. Tech tree: added the absence of Treadmill Crane.
The river boat proposal ('Kosa') qualified: the term is attested mainly in the 17th-century Mughal nawara.
Thirisadai: confirmed that it originates in a hoax Wikipedia article (exposed in 2022). Added the Austronesian model from Borobudur and the position of Kanisetti (2025).

Added the debate on the existence of a permanent Chola navy (Kulke et al., 2009; Kanisetti, 2025) to the label, the tech tree, the text and contested. Added the term 'kalam' in the Tanjore inscription as the basis for the renaming proposal.

The issue of the Pandyas in the 'Kannauj Triangle' downgraded from moderate to minor, because a Pala–Pandya clash has a slender epigraphic basis (Badal, Sinnamanur), and reworded. The Devapala item adjusted in the same way.

Confirmed in data.json that there is Battle Elephant without Elite and that Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon and Bombard Tower are present. Added the Hoysalas, Kakatiyas, Malik Kafur and the Madurai Sultanate to the omissions, and Takua Pa to the guilds.

Cross-civ notes updated: the 2013 legacy and the renaming of 'Sultans', the Thirisadai hoax, Sulaiman on the Gurjara camels, and Bengali gunpowder confirmed by Barros and Babur. Scores kept (6/5/5/4), consistent with a game average of about 5. The web-search budget ran out before some minor details could be verified; those were left cautiously worded.

civs.represents: The Han Chinese and the empires that, one after another, were centred on China proper: Sui (581–618), Tang (618–907), Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms (907–979), Northern and Southern Song (960–1279), the Yuan phase under Mongol rule (1271–1368) and the early Ming (1368–). Since the 2025 rework (Three Kingdoms expansion), the design favours above all the Song and the early Ming: crossbows, fire lances, rockets, tower ships, walls and an examination bureaucracy.
civs.period: 581–c. 1500 (from the Sui to the early Ming), with an implicit emphasis on the Song (960–1279) and the early Ming (1368–c. 1450).
civs.verdict: The broad outlines are defensible: an enormous population, technical innovation, the crossbow, gunpowder and intensive agriculture are fair abstractions of real traits, and the 2025 rework added well-founded elements (Fire Lancer, Lou Chuan, Rocket Cart). The execution, however, contradicts the civ's own “Gunpowder” label: the civilization that invented the metal-barrelled firearm and the cannon (c. 1280–1380) has no Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon or Cannon Galleon, and the only barrelled piece it receives is the Bombard Tower. The most characteristic Chinese artillery up to 1273, the traction trebuchet (pao), was given only to the three 3rd-century kingdoms. The Chu Ko Nu and the Dragon Ship are picturesque but secondary choices compared with what China actually used: heavy crossbows in rotating volleys, bed crossbows, paddle-wheel ships and the Ming fleets. The history text has several factual errors (Zhao Kuangyin, city populations, “closing of the Silk Road”) and a Eurocentric framing of “isolation” and “conservatism”.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Chinese” is an umbrella label that covers nine centuries and at least five very different dynasties: the Tang, cosmopolitan and with an aristocracy partly of Xianbei origin; the Song, commercial and chronically short of horses; the Mongol Yuan; and the Ming. With the 2025 expansion the umbrella overlaps with three more Han civs (Shu, Wei, Wu), with two conquest dynasties that ruled northern China (Khitans/Liao, Jurchens/Jin) and with the Mongols (the history text itself counts the Yuan as “Chinese”). The transliteration is inconsistent: old Wade-Giles (“Chu Ko Nu”, “T'ang”, and “Zhao Kuang-ying”, which is not even correct Wade-Giles; that would be Chao K'uang-yin) coexists with the pinyin of the new units (Lou Chuan, Hei Guang, Tuntian). “Chu Ko Nu” (諸葛弩, Zhuge nu) carries the name of Zhuge Liang, chancellor of Shu, which creates a duplication with the Shu civ. A curiosity for a Portuguese user: “mandarin” entered the European languages through Portuguese (from Malay menteri, from Sanskrit mantrin); it is not a Chinese term. A more rigorous alternative would be to split the civ into “Tang” (cavalry, Sui–Tang) and “Song/Ming” (crossbows, gunpowder, navy), or at least to make the Song–Ming emphasis explicit.

elements.explanation: It is an acceptable umbrella in a game of “civilizations” for 581–1500, but it erases enormous differences between the Tang (a cavalry power with Turkic and Korean generals, such as Gao Xianzhi), the Song (a commercial state, without pastures and dependent on the tea-for-horses trade) and the Ming (gunpowder, Zheng He's fleets). It now also overlaps with Shu/Wei/Wu, Jurchens, Khitans and Mongols.

From the Warring States to the Song, the crossbow was the infantry weapon par excellence; the Wujing Zongyao (1044) calls it China's strong weapon, the one that neighbouring peoples feared most. Gunpowder is a Chinese invention (the first published formulas are in the Wujing Zongyao). The tech tree lives up to the label only in part: it has Fire Lancer, Rocket Cart, Bombard Tower and Chemistry, but no barrelled firearm for troops or siege (no Hand Cannoneer or Bombard Cannon).

elements.element: Start with +3 Villagers, but -50 wood and -200 food
elements.explanation: A reasonable abstraction of China's demographic weight. The Tang census of 754 records c. 53 million people, and Song records from c. 1100 suggest more than 100 million, the largest organised population of the medieval world.

It is a fair mechanical stand-in for documented technical innovation (Needham): woodblock printing (Diamond Sutra, 868), movable type (Bi Sheng, c. 1040, described by Shen Kuo), the nautical compass (Zhu Yu, 1119), gunpowder and state arsenals (Junqi jian, 1073). The risk is the stereotype of a timeless “inventive China”, but the link is legitimate.

elements.element: Town Centers +7 line of sight and provide +15 population space
elements.explanation: It can be read as the walled, densely populated district seats (xian) and as the network of signal towers (fenghuo tai). The link to line of sight is weak, but acceptable as an abstraction of administrative and demographic density.

elements.element: Fire Lancers and Fire Ships move +5/10% faster in Castle/Imperial Age
elements.explanation: The units themselves have a basis: the fire lance is Chinese, and so are fire ships. The speed bonus, however, has no historical basis: the fire lance was a short-range, single-shot weapon, used mainly in sieges and sallies (Chen Gui at De'an, 1132). It is pure game balance.

elements.element: Chu Ko Nu / Elite Chu Ko Nu
elements.explanation: The repeating crossbow (lian nu) is documented from the 4th century BC (a double-shot example in a Chu tomb at Qinjiazui, Hubei) to the Ming and Qing (Wubei Zhi, 1621), and tradition associates it with Zhuge Liang. It was, however, a weak weapon with little penetration, used in the defence of walls and houses and sometimes with poisoned bolts; it was never the core of elite armies. The decisive crossbow in China was the heavy single-shot crossbow, fired in rotating volleys (Tongdian, 801; Wujing Zongyao), or the Song “divine-arm crossbow” (shenbi gong, presented by Li Hong in 1068).

Replaces the Fast Fire Ship. Chinese ships with flamethrowers are real: the “fierce fire oil cabinet” (menghuo you gui), a double-piston naphtha pump, is described in the Wujing Zongyao, and the Wuyue fleet used “fire oil” in 919. The name, however, is misleading: the “dragon boats” (longzhou) were imperial ceremonial barges, such as those of Sui Yangdi on the Grand Canal in 605, or racing boats. The real warship types were different: louchuan, mengchong, doujian, haihu and the paddle-wheel ships (chechuan).

There is a real tradition of long walls (Northern Wei, Northern Qi, Sui) and of enormous rammed-earth city walls. But the iconic brick Great Wall is mostly late Ming (large sections c. 1550–1600, already outside the game's period). Neither the Tang nor the Song built long walls (the Northern Song preferred a line of rice paddies and ponds on the Liao frontier), and the most extensive fortified lines of the 12th century were built by the Jurchens/Jin (jiehao). Waldron argued, with great influence, that the idea of a single, continuous wall is largely a modern myth. That the UT covers Bombard Towers fits the Ming.

Rockets are Chinese, but the dating is contested. The “fire arrows” (huojian) presented in 969 and 1000 were probably incendiary arrows. True rockets are probable in the mid-13th century and clear in the Huolongjing (14th century) and in the Ming multiple launchers of the Wubei Zhi. Lou Chuans with rockets fit the Ming. The Scorpions, for their part, are very Chinese: bed crossbows (chuangzi nu) were a front-line Song weapon, and one of their bolts killed the Liao commander Xiao Talin at Chanyuan (1004). Only the link “rockets strengthen bed crossbows” mixes categories.

It corresponds to the Song “agricultural revolution”: the introduction of short-cycle Champa rice (1012), double cropping in the south, agricultural treatises (Chen Fu, 1149; Wang Zhen, 1313). The magnitude of this revolution is debated (Elvin vs. revisionist readings), but the link is solid.

The fire lance (huoqiang) appears in a Dunhuang painting from the mid-10th century and, in writing, at De'an in 1132 (Chen Gui). It was used by the Song, Jin and Yuan and is the direct ancestor of the firearm.

elements.element: Rocket Cart (regional unit, replaces the Mangonel line)
elements.explanation: Multiple rocket launchers on wheelbarrows are Ming (Wubei Zhi), so they fit the end of the period. The problem is that they replace all throwing artillery, when the typical Chinese piece, from c. the 4th century BC until 1273, was the traction trebuchet (pao), which is absent here.

Tower ships (louchuan) are documented from the Han (there was even a “General of the Tower Ships”, Yang Pu, in the campaign of 112–111 BC) to the Ming. An armament of trebuchets or rockets is plausible for the Song–Ming.

It is the only piece of barrelled artillery the Chinese receive. The Ming cast iron cannons from at least 1377 and mounted them on walls and passes; it fits the end of the period. It makes the absence of Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon even stranger.

tree_issues.problem: Serious historical error. China invented the metal-barrelled firearm: the Heilongjiang hand cannon (c. 1288), the Xanadu cannon dated 1298. The Ming shi (military treatise) assigns, in Hongwu's time, ten firearms to each company of a hundred men, and Andrade therefore estimates c. 10% gunners at the end of the 14th century. Under Yongle, in the early 15th century, a specialised firearms division (Shenjiying) was created.

tree_issues.item: Bombard Cannon and Cannon Galleon missing
tree_issues.problem: The Ming cast iron cannons (there are examples dated 1377), and Zheng He's fleets (1405–1433) carried firearms. An irony for a Portuguese reader: after the clashes at Tunmen (1521) and Xicaowan (1522), the Ming copied the Portuguese breech-loading falcons (folangji, “Franks”). The Jurchens, whose Jin dynasty fell in 1234, have Bombard Cannon; the Chinese do not. Having the Bombard Tower without the Bombard Cannon is incoherent.

tree_issues.item: Traction Trebuchet missing (only Shu/Wei/Wu have it)
tree_issues.problem: The traction trebuchet (pao) is a Chinese invention and was the dominant artillery of the Tang, Song and Jin; the Wujing Zongyao describes several variants (from one to seven arms, “whirlwind”, “crouching tiger”). The counterweight Trebuchet only reached China in 1273, with Muslim engineers in Kublai's service at the siege of Xiangyang (huihui pao); for the Chinese of the Yuan–Ming phase it is acceptable, but it should come after the pao. The absence of the Mangonel line is defensible (China did not use torsion catapults), although the medieval European “mangonel” was generally a traction trebuchet, of Chinese origin according to the dominant interpretation.
Incoherent with Song multiple-cropping agriculture and with the Song mercantile economy: craft and trade associations (hang), state paper money (jiaozi, 1024), the ports of Quanzhou and Canton.
Chinese siege engineering was among the most advanced in the world (Wujing Zongyao, 1044), and the Mongols recruited Chinese siege engineers, such as Guo Kan, for the Middle Eastern campaigns.

The most distinctive naval features are missing: watertight bulkheads, the sternpost rudder (cited in the history text itself), pedal-driven paddle-wheel ships (the victory at Caishi, 1161) and Zheng He's “treasure ships”. Instead, the civ has neither Carvel Hull nor Cannon Galleon.

tree_issues.item: Limited cavalry (no Hussar or Heavy Cavalry Archer)
tree_issues.problem: Defensible for the horse-poor Song, but it erases the Tang, whose Directorate of Herds reached c. 706,000 horses (c. 665) and whose frontier armies were cavalry armies.

history_text_issues.claim: China is said to have been reunified in 581 by the founders of the Sui dynasty.
history_text_issues.problem: It confuses founding with reunification.
history_text_issues.correction: Yang Jian founded the Sui in 581; reunification was only completed in 589, with the conquest of the Chen in the south.

history_text_issues.claim: Thanks to its “geographical isolation from the West”, China is said to have developed a unique culture.
history_text_issues.problem: A Eurocentric and outdated framing.
history_text_issues.correction: Tang and Song China was strongly connected to Central Asia, India, Persia and the Islamic world through the overland and maritime Silk Roads. Chang'an and Canton had Sogdian, Persian and Arab communities, and Buddhism came from India.

history_text_issues.claim: The mandarins are said to have been “conservative” officials recruited through examinations based on Confucius.
history_text_issues.problem: An anachronistic generalisation for the whole period.
history_text_issues.correction: Under the Tang the examination (keju) existed but produced a minority of officials, and recruitment was still largely aristocratic; only under the Song did the examination become the dominant route. The curriculum was the Confucian classics (with Zhu Xi's commentaries as the standard from 1313). “Mandarin” is a Portuguese term, and “conservative” is a value judgement.

history_text_issues.claim: Northern China, under the Five Dynasties, is said to have been “in the hands of barbarians”.
history_text_issues.problem: A pejorative term and a simplification.
history_text_issues.correction: Of the Five Dynasties of the north, three (Later Tang, Later Jin and Later Han) were founded by elites of Shatuo Turkic origin and two (Later Liang and Later Zhou) by Han. The Khitans held only the Sixteen Prefectures, ceded in 936–938.

history_text_issues.claim: A general “Zhao Kuang-ying” is said to have seized power in one of the southern states, and his descendants are said to have reunited China.
history_text_issues.problem: The name is wrong, and so is the origin.
history_text_issues.correction: Zhao Kuangyin (趙匡胤) was a general of the Later Zhou, a NORTHERN regime, and seized power in the Chenqiao mutiny (960). He then conquered the southern states (963–975), and the one who completed the unification, with Wuyue (978) and Northern Han (979), was his brother, Taizong, not his “descendants”.

history_text_issues.claim: Chang'an, Beijing and Canton are said to have each had more than 2 million inhabitants.
history_text_issues.problem: Inflated numbers and poorly chosen cities.
history_text_issues.correction: Reasonable estimates are around 1 million for Chang'an (Tang), 1 to 1.4 million for Kaifeng (Northern Song) and 1 to 1.5 million for Hangzhou (Southern Song); all these figures are contested. Beijing was not a Song city (it was a Liao secondary capital and later the Jin capital), and Canton was far below. The text omits precisely the two Song capitals.

history_text_issues.claim: The Mongols are said to have begun attacking in 1206 and to have moved the capital to Beijing only after conquering the Song.
history_text_issues.problem: Imprecise chronology.
history_text_issues.correction: 1206 is the year of Genghis Khan's enthronement. The attacks were on the Western Xia in 1205–1209, on the Jin from 1211 and on the Song from 1235. Dadu (Beijing) became the capital in 1271–1272, before the fall of the Song (1279).

history_text_issues.claim: The Mongol conquest is said to have caused around 30 million deaths.
history_text_issues.problem: A highly contested figure is presented as fact.
history_text_issues.correction: The drop in population records (Song and Jin combined, more than 100 million; Yuan census of 1290, c. 59 million) reflects real deaths, but also flight and fiscal under-registration. The exact figure is debated.

history_text_issues.claim: Under the Yuan, Chinese influence is said to have spread across Asia; Hanoi was taken three times.
history_text_issues.problem: A misleading omission.
history_text_issues.correction: Thăng Long was indeed occupied in 1258, 1285 and 1288, but Đại Việt repelled the Mongols every time (Bạch Đằng, 1288). The Yuan also failed in Japan (1274, 1281), in Java (1293) and in Champa. Moreover, the Yuan was a Mongol regime with an ethnic hierarchy that placed the Han of the former Song territory in the lowest tier (the degree to which this system was formalised is debated).

history_text_issues.claim: The Ming are said to have imposed isolation, banned travel abroad and “closed the Silk Road”.
history_text_issues.problem: A stereotype, with a glaring omission.
history_text_issues.correction: The maritime ban (haijin) existed from 1371 and was lifted in 1567. But it was the Ming who launched Zheng He's seven expeditions (1405–1433) as far as East Africa, maintained an intense tributary trade and, in the 16th century, absorbed a large share of the world's silver. The decline of the overland route had multiple causes; no “closure” was decreed.

history_text_issues.claim: The list of inventions includes the clock, steel and the abacus as Chinese inventions.
history_text_issues.problem: Some items are overstated.
history_text_issues.correction: Su Song's astronomical tower (1088) had a hydromechanical escapement, but the mechanical clock with a verge escapement is European (c. 1300). Steel was already known in other regions; what China developed early were its own processes, such as the decarburisation of cast iron. The abacus (suanpan) is only well attested in the late Song or the Yuan–Ming. The compass, paper, printing, paper money, gunpowder, cast iron and the sternpost rudder are solid attributions; the double stirrup appears in China in the 4th century, but its origin (China or the Xianbei steppe) is debated.

missing_features: Tang cavalry and its foreign generals (Turkic, Sogdian, Korean); the Tang Directorate of Herds reached c. 706,000 horses (c. 665).
Tang “mo dao” (陌刀) infantry, long two-handed blades against cavalry, such as that of Li Siye at Xiangji (757).
Rotating crossbow volleys (Tongdian, 801; Wujing Zongyao) and Song heavy crossbows (shenbi gong, 1068).
Multi-bow bed crossbows (chuangzi nu), the bolt artillery of the Song (Chanyuan, 1004).
Song state arsenals and workshops (Junqi jian, 1073), with gunpowder workshops in Kaifeng.
Paddle-wheel ships (chechuan), watertight bulkheads and Zheng He's fleets (1405–1433).
The Grand Canal (Sui, 605–611) as a logistical backbone.
The imperial examination (keju) and paper money (jiaozi, 1024).
The chronic shortage of horses under the Song and the tea-for-horses trade (Chamasi, 1074).
Porcelain and silk as drivers of maritime trade (Quanzhou, Canton).
The Tang militia system (fubing) and Wang Anshi's baojia.

proposals.title: Shenjiying (神機營) — Firearms Division
proposals.description: Give Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon (Imperial Age). New Imperial UT: Hand Cannoneers +20% rate of fire when in a group of 10 or more (volley fire by ranks) and Bombard Cannons -25% wood cost.
proposals.historical_basis: Hand cannons from c. 1288 and iron cannons dated 1377. Ten firearms for every hundred men under Hongwu (Ming shi). A firearms division created under Yongle. Andrade describes the use of firearms in successive lines against elephants by Mu Ying (1388).

proposals.title: Pao and Huihui Pao
proposals.description: Give the Chinese the Traction Trebuchet from the Castle Age and remove the counterweight Trebuchet from the base tree. An Imperial “Huihui Pao” technology unlocks the counterweight Trebuchet.
proposals.historical_basis: The traction pao was the Chinese artillery from the Warring States onwards. The counterweight was introduced by Ismail and Ala al-Din at the siege of Xiangyang (1273).

proposals.title: Divine Arm Crossbowman (Shenbi Crossbowman)
proposals.description: Turn the Chu Ko Nu into a cheap defensive unit (bonus when garrisoned in towers and walls). Create a heavy crossbow UU: +1 range, more pierce attack and a slow reload, with +15% rate of fire when 3 “ranks” of crossbowmen shoot together.
proposals.historical_basis: The shenbi gong crossbow, presented by Li Hong in 1068. The rotating-fire technique described in the Tongdian (801) and the Wujing Zongyao (1044). The Wubei Zhi (1621) shows the zhuge nu as a defensive weapon.

proposals.title: Chechuan — Paddle-Wheel Ship
proposals.description: Replace the Dragon Ship with a paddle-wheel ship that does not depend on the wind: constant speed, a bonus against ships on rivers and narrow lakes, and the launching of short-range incendiary bombs.
proposals.historical_basis: Pedal-driven ships were used from the Tang and Song onwards. At Caishi (1161), the Song fleet organised by Yu Yunwen used them, with “pili” bombs, to stop the Jin from crossing the Yangtze.

proposals.title: Champa Rice
proposals.description: Replace the missing Crop Rotation with a technology of its own at the Mill: Farms +15% food and 25% faster rebuilding.
proposals.historical_basis: The official distribution of short-cycle Champa rice by Emperor Zhenzong in 1012 and the spread of double cropping in the south.

proposals.title: Grand Canal
proposals.description: Unique building or technology: Docks and Markets linked by the canal generate +10% gold from trade, and Trade Carts and Trade Cogs become 15% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: The Sui Grand Canal (605–611) linked the Yangtze to the north and sustained the capital and the army until the Ming.

contested: The date of the invention of gunpowder (a Taoist text attributed to the 9th century, of uncertain dating) and of the first true rockets (12th–13th centuries).
The scale of the Song “medieval economic revolution” (Elvin, Hartwell) versus more moderate readings.
The number of deaths in the Mongol conquest, which depends on the reliability of the fiscal records.
Ming “isolation” and the decision to halt Zheng He's voyages (Brook and others).
The real effectiveness of the long walls and Waldron's thesis.
The “Needham question”: why there was no scientific revolution in China.
Whether the Yuan should be counted as a “Chinese” dynasty or as part of the Mongol empire.
Marco Polo's visit (questioned by Frances Wood, 1995; defended by Hans Ulrich Vogel, 2013, and by most specialists).
The origin of the double stirrup (4th-century China or the Xianbei/steppe world).

civs.represents: The kingdom of Shu Han (蜀漢, 221–263), founded by Liu Bei in Sichuan (Yi Province) and Hanzhong, with its capital at Chengdu. In practice it also represents Liu Bei's faction from 184 onwards. It was a Han state with non-Han subjects and allies: the peoples of Nanzhong (Yunnan and Guizhou) and the Qiang and Di of the north-west.
civs.period: c. 184–263 AD (Liu Bei's faction from the Yellow Turban Rebellion onwards; kingdom 221–263). It lies some 250 years before the nominal start of AoE2.
civs.verdict: Shu has elements directly grounded in the sources. Zhuge Liang's improvement of the repeating crossbow (Bolt Magazine) is recorded by Chen Shou himself and detailed by Pei Songzhi. Liu Bei's elite guard (the “White Feathers”) is attested in a letter by Zhuge Liang. The War Chariot has an indirect but real link to the Bazhentu: in 279 a Jin general built chariots “according to the diagram” of Zhuge Liang. The rest mixes the Romance of the Three Kingdoms (14th century) with game mechanics: the bonus of lumberjacks who produce food is stretched and the team bonus is generic. Missing are the traits that really defined Shu: brocade, the salt and gas wells of Sichuan, mountain logistics, the Nanzhong campaign and the Northern Expeditions. On top of this, it is a 3rd-century state in a medieval frame, treated as a “civilization” when it was one of three factions of the same people.
civs.naming_scope_issues: The state called itself Han (漢) and claimed continuity with the Han dynasty. “Shu” is the geographical name used by Wei and Jin historiography (Chen Shou's “Shu shu”) and harks back to the ancient Bronze Age kingdom of Shu (Sanxingdui). The period (221–263) falls outside the c. 500–1500 frame, like the Romans of Return of Rome. It is a state, not a people: its ethnicity is the same as that of Wei, Wu and the Chinese civ. Splitting the 3rd-century Han into three “civilizations”, while whole peoples of the frame are missing (Tibetans, Tanguts, Uyghurs), is disproportionate. Part of the imagery (the Oath of the Peach Garden, Zhuge Liang as the strategist of Chibi) comes from the Romance, not from the Sanguozhi.

elements.explanation: It corresponds to a real political entity, but a 3rd-century one, outside the game's frame. The name is the one its rivals gave it, not its official designation (Han).

Zhuge Liang's crossbows and the Northern Expeditions (228–234), full of sieges (Chencang, 228–229, with ladders, rams, towers and tunnels against Hao Zhao), provide a basis. Note, however, that the Expeditions failed in their sieges.

elements.element: Lumberjacks generate food in addition to wood
elements.explanation: It perhaps evokes the fertility of Sichuan, the “Land of Abundance” irrigated by the Dujiangyan system, and the region's forests. But there is no historical link between woodcutting and food production; it is a game mechanic with a very tenuous justification.

elements.element: Archery Unit technologies at the Archery Range and Blacksmith cost -25%
elements.explanation: The production and improvement of crossbows is a documented trait of Zhuge Liang's Shu (the “yuanrong” crossbow).

elements.element: Siege Weapons and Siege Warships move +10/15% faster
elements.explanation: An acceptable abstraction of the mountain logistics innovations: the “wooden oxen” (231) and the “gliding horses” (234), recorded in the Sanguozhi, and the plank roads (zhandao) through the Qinling Mountains.

elements.element: White Feather Guard / Elite White Feather Guard
elements.explanation: A real unit. In a letter to his brother Zhuge Jin, preserved in the Zhuge Liang ji and the Taiping Yulan (ch. 341), Zhuge Liang says that the troops commanded by Chen Dao were the “baimao” (白眊, also written 白毦, “white feathers”) of the late emperor's guard, the best troops of the west. Chen Dao later commanded the garrison of Yong'an. There is no indication that they were anti-cavalry infantry or that they slowed enemies down; that mechanic is invented.

By the 3rd century the war chariot had been obsolete as a shock weapon for centuries, but chariots used as mobile fortifications with archers and crossbowmen are documented: Wei Qing's “wugang” (119 BC) and, above all, the “side-box chariots” that the Jin general Ma Long built in 279 “according to the Bazhentu” of Zhuge Liang, advancing while shooting (Jin shu, biography of Ma Long). There is therefore a textual link to Zhuge Liang, but no record of their use by Shu, and the barrage mode is an invention.

The healing aura is an abstraction of Liu Bei's reputation for benevolence (ren) and of his ability to keep his followers (the crowds that followed him at Changban, 208). Historically he was a competent and resilient commander, but not an exceptional warrior. Heroes that can be trained in normal play are an exception to AoE2's usual design.

Chen Shou records that Zhuge Liang “composed the diagram of the Eight Formations” (八陣圖), but does not give their names. The traditional list (heaven, earth, wind, cloud, dragon, tiger, bird, “coiled serpent”, 蛇蟠) only appears in later texts. The idea of spearmen who strengthen each other in close formation is a reasonable abstraction.

Chen Shou himself writes that Zhuge Liang “improved the repeating crossbow”. Pei Songzhi, citing the Wei shi chunqiu, adds that it was called “yuanrong” and shot ten iron bolts of 8 cun at once. It is the best-founded element of the civ.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Foot Archers +2 line of sight
elements.explanation: It has no specific basis whatsoever; it is game balance.

elements.element: Hei Guang Cavalry / Lou Chuan / Traction Trebuchet (shared by the Three Kingdoms)
elements.explanation: The Traction Trebuchet is plausible for the 3rd century, and so is the Lou Chuan, because Shu operated fleets on the Yangtze (Yiling campaign, 221–222). The Hei Guang heavy cavalry, on the other hand, fits poorly with Shu, a state poor in pastures and horses. “Hei Guang” armour is attested in a memorial by Cao Zhi, that is, in a Wei context.

tree_issues.item: Blast Furnace and Iron Casting missing
tree_issues.problem: Han China had had blast furnaces and cast iron for centuries, with a state iron monopoly since c. 117 BC. Shu had its own officials for salt and iron (Zhang Yi was put in charge of making implements and weapons), and the tradition recorded in the Pu Yuan biezhuan credits the smith Pu Yuan with 3,000 blades forged for Zhuge Liang at Xiegu. This absence has no historical justification.
Strange in an “Archer and Siege” civ associated with Zhuge Liang: the Han used large crossbows (the “Great Yellow”, dahuang) and wall crossbows.
Sichuan was a pioneer in deep drilling: brine wells and natural-gas “fire wells” at Linqiong, used to boil the brine (Huayang Guozhi). Salt was an important source of state revenue.

In 3rd-century Sichuan there are images of the Buddha on “money trees” and in tombs (for example Mahao, Leshan), but integrated into local cults, with no organised monastic Buddhism. The relevant organised religion was Daoist: the Celestial Masters or “Five Pecks of Rice”, whose theocratic state under Zhang Lu in Hanzhong surrendered to Cao Cao in 215. A Daoist reskin would be more faithful.

tree_issues.item: Cavalry Archer and Heavy Cavalry Archer present
tree_issues.problem: Shu has the full line of mounted archers, whereas Wei lacks the generic Cavalry Archer (it has the Xianbei Raider), even though historically it had the Wuhuan cavalry of the north at its disposal. It can only be justified by the Qiang and Di allies of Ma Chao and Jiang Wei.

tree_issues.item: Absence of gunpowder, the counterweight Trebuchet and Block Printing
tree_issues.problem: A positive point: these absences are correct for the 3rd century.

history_text_issues.claim: Liu Bei is presented as a distant relative of Emperor Jing of Han.
history_text_issues.problem: It presents as fact a claim that cannot be verified.
history_text_issues.correction: The Sanguozhi gives him as a descendant of Liu Sheng, King Jing of Zhongshan (a son of Emperor Jing), through Liu Zhen, a marquis in 117 BC, but does not list the intermediate generations. The Dianlüe, cited by Pei Songzhi, links him to another branch (the marquises of Linyi). Liu Sheng had more than 120 sons, so the link cannot be verified.

history_text_issues.claim: The “Oath of the Peach Garden” with Guan Yu and Zhang Fei.
history_text_issues.problem: It is legendary; it comes from the 14th-century Romance.
history_text_issues.correction: The Sanguozhi says only that the three slept in the same bed and had an affection “like brothers”. The text calls it “legendary”, but places it within a factual narrative.

history_text_issues.claim: Liu Bei is said to have been appointed deputy magistrate in Pingyuan for his deeds against the Yellow Turbans.
history_text_issues.problem: The post and the place are wrong.
history_text_issues.correction: For his deeds against the Yellow Turbans, Liu Bei was appointed commandant (wei) of Anxi county. Pingyuan (as acting magistrate and then chancellor) came later, under Gongsun Zan.

history_text_issues.claim: In 200 Cao Cao is said to have attacked Liu Bei, forcing him to turn to Liu Biao.
history_text_issues.problem: Chronological compression.
history_text_issues.correction: In 200 Liu Bei first fled to Yuan Shao and fought in Runan; only in 201 did he take refuge with Liu Biao. The list of lords he served also leaves out Cao Cao and Yuan Shao.

history_text_issues.claim: Zhuge Liang is said to have invented a multi-bolt crossbow and written the Bazhentu, a text on chariots, crossbows, cavalry and infantry.
history_text_issues.problem: Inventing is not improving, and the Bazhentu was not a surviving treatise.
history_text_issues.correction: Repeating crossbows are older (4th century BC); Chen Shou says that Zhuge Liang improved them and that he “composed the diagram of the Eight Formations”. No treatise survives. The link to chariots is not absurd: the Jin shu says that Ma Long (279) built chariots “according to the Bazhentu”.

history_text_issues.claim: Chibi is said to have been won mainly through the strategy of Zhuge Liang and Zhou Yu.
history_text_issues.problem: This is the Romance's version.
history_text_issues.correction: According to the Sanguozhi, the command lay with Zhou Yu and Cheng Pu, and the fireship attack was proposed by Huang Gai; the Shu shu adds that an epidemic decimated the northern army. Zhuge Liang's role was diplomatic: convincing Sun Quan.

history_text_issues.claim: Liu Bei, protected by the White Feather Guard, is said to have fought Wu in 221 and been defeated.
history_text_issues.problem: There are no sources on the guard in that battle, and the chronology is incomplete.
history_text_issues.correction: The campaign lasted from 221 to 222 and ended in the decisive defeat at Xiaoting/Yiling (222), inflicted by Lu Xun with fire. No source places the “baimao” there protecting Liu Bei; Zhuge Liang's letter mentions them later, in the garrison of Baidi/Yong'an.

history_text_issues.claim: Zhuge Liang is said to have stayed on as regent; then Jiang Wan until 246, the year in which Liu Shan took full control.
history_text_issues.problem: A simplification, but grounded in the sources.
history_text_issues.correction: In 223 Liu Bei entrusted the heir to Zhuge Liang, with Li Yan as his deputy. Jiang Wan was never formally regent, but the Weilüe (cited by Pei Songzhi) does indeed say that, once Jiang Wan had died (246), Liu Shan began to direct state affairs personally. Fei Yi continued to lead the government until he was assassinated in 253, and the later reign was marked by the eunuch Huang Hao.

history_text_issues.claim: The text goes straight from the regency to the surrender of 263.
history_text_issues.problem: A central omission.
history_text_issues.correction: Left out are the Nanzhong campaign (225, against Yong Kai and Meng Huo), Zhuge Liang's Northern Expeditions (228–234) and Jiang Wei's campaigns (247–262). It is these that give meaning to the “Archer and Siege” label.

missing_features: Shu brocade (蜀錦) as the main source of external revenue; Zhuge Liang is said to have stated that the state depended on brocade to finance the war.
The brine and natural-gas wells of Sichuan.
The Dujiangyan irrigation system, with official guards for its maintenance.
Mountain logistics: wooden oxen and gliding horses, plank roads (zhandao).
The “Flying Army” (飛軍): more than ten thousand Qing Qiang families from Nanzhong transferred to Shu and organised into five divisions (Huayang Guozhi).
Non-Han allies: the Qiang and Di via Ma Chao and Jiang Wei.
Liu Ba's “worth a hundred” (zhibai) coin (214) as a wartime fiscal policy.
The ideology of Han legitimacy, the driving force behind all of its foreign policy.

proposals.title: Shu Brocade (蜀錦)
proposals.description: Replace the lumberjack bonus with: Trade Carts and Trade Cogs generate +15% gold, and the Market sells wood and food at a reduced fee.
proposals.historical_basis: Chengdu brocade, produced under official supervision (the “city of the brocade official”, jinguan cheng), was Shu's main export to Wu and Wei and financed its campaigns.

proposals.title: Fire Wells (火井)
proposals.description: Castle Age UT: Mining Camps next to stone generate a slow trickle of gold, and Stone Miners work 15% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: The Huayang Guozhi (mid-4th century) describes the natural-gas wells of Linqiong used to evaporate brine. Salt was an important source of tax revenue.

proposals.title: Wooden Ox (木牛流馬)
proposals.description: Replace the War Chariot with (or add) a logistics unit: a mobile resource depot that slowly heals nearby units and gives +10% speed to Siege Weapons around it.
proposals.historical_basis: Used in the Northern Expeditions of 231 (wooden oxen) and 234 (gliding horses) to supply the army in mountainous terrain (Sanguozhi, biography of Zhuge Liang).

proposals.title: Flying Army of Nanzhong (飛軍)
proposals.description: Light mountain infantry with hand crossbows: extra speed in forests and on hills and a bonus against archers. It can take over the role of the non-hero unique unit.
proposals.historical_basis: After 225, Zhuge Liang transferred more than ten thousand Qing Qiang families from Nanzhong and organised them into five divisions called “Feijun” (Huayang Guozhi); Wang Ping commanded “the five divisions” (Sanguozhi), probably these ones.

proposals.title: Pu Yuan's Steel
proposals.description: Give Iron Casting and Blast Furnace (the latter renamed), and Scorpions under the name “Great Yellow Crossbow”.
proposals.historical_basis: The Han iron and steel industry, the administration of iron in Shu and the Pu Yuan tradition at Xiegu.

contested: The legitimacy of Shu Han as against Wei: Chen Shou treated Wei as legitimate, whereas Xi Zuochi (4th century) and Zhu Xi (12th century) championed Shu.
Zhuge Liang's military ability: Chen Shou wrote that tactical adaptation was not his strong point.
The episode of “borrowing Jing Province”, narrated mainly by Wu sources.
The authenticity of the “second memorial on setting out” (Hou Chushi biao).
The actual design of the wooden ox (a wheelbarrow or a more complex machine).
Liu Bei's imperial ancestry.
Whether the Bazhentu was a written text or merely a scheme of formations.
key_sources: Chen Shou, Sanguozhi (Shu shu), c. 280–290
Pei Songzhi, annotations to the Sanguozhi (429), including the Wei shi chunqiu and the Weilüe
Fang Xuanling et al., Jin shu (648), biography of Ma Long
Chang Qu, Huayang Guozhi (mid-4th century)
Taiping Yulan (983) and Zhuge Liang ji, for Zhuge Liang's letters
Sima Guang, Zizhi Tongjian (1084)
Rafe de Crespigny, A Biographical Dictionary of Later Han to the Three Kingdoms (2007)
Rafe de Crespigny, Fire over Luoyang (2016)
Mark Edward Lewis, China between Empires (2009)
Luo Guanzhong, Romance of the Three Kingdoms (14th century), as the source of the legends

civs.represents: The state of Cao Wei (曹魏, 220–266) in northern China and the regime of its de facto founder, Cao Cao, who controlled the Han court from 196. Its capitals were Xu(chang), Ye and Luoyang. It includes incorporated non-Han auxiliary troops: Wuhuan, Southern Xiongnu and, occasionally, Xianbei groups.
civs.verdict: Wei is the best-founded of the three kingdoms. Three elements have direct support in the sources: the elite “Tiger and Leopard” cavalry (Hu Bao Qi), the military-agricultural colonies (Tuntian) and the Hei Guang and Ming Guang armours, mentioned in a memorial by Cao Zhi. The traction trebuchets at Guandu (200) also fit. The biggest problem lies in the “Xianbei Raider” and the text that justifies it: at White Wolf Mountain (207) Cao Cao defeated the Wuhuan, not the Xianbei, although Xianbei horsemen occasionally served Wei. The team bonus is generic, and the tech tree ignores real Wei strengths, such as its crossbowmen, the fortifications of Hefei and siege by flooding. The underlying problem remains: a 3rd-century state in a medieval frame.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Wei” is ambiguous. There was the Wei of the Warring States, Cao Wei (220–266), the Northern Wei of the Tuoba Xianbei (386–535) and the Western and Eastern Wei (535–557). Northern Wei falls WITHIN the AoE2 frame and was a Xianbei state, which would justify a “Xianbei Raider” far better than Cao Wei does. The period (189–266) is outside the frame. It is a state, not a people: the same Han ethnicity as Shu, Wu and Chinese. Cao Cao's image owes much to the Romance, which paints him as a villain.

elements.explanation: A real political entity, but from the 3rd century and outside the frame. It can be confused with the Xianbei Northern Wei (386–535).

The north had access to horses and to frontier cavalry. After 207 Cao Cao incorporated the Wuhuan cavalry, and the Sanguozhi says that the Wuhuan of the three commanderies became “the famous cavalry of the empire”. But the bulk of the Wei army was infantry and crossbowmen, and its strength lay above all in numbers and logistics.

elements.element: Receive one free Villager for each economic upgrade researched
elements.explanation: Wei was by far the most populous kingdom: c. 660,000 households and 4.4 million people registered c. 263, against c. 940,000 people in Shu. Cao Cao settled refugees and reorganised production. The link “economic technology gives population” is an acceptable abstraction.

elements.element: Hei Guang Cavalry and Xianbei Raider +20/30% HP
elements.explanation: In the memorial in which he returns suits of armour, Cao Zhi mentions having received from Cao Cao a “black light” (heiguang) armour and a “bright light” (mingguang) one. The names are attested in a Wei context, but they were rare and prestigious pieces, not mass-issue equipment.

elements.element: Traction Trebuchets and Lou Chuans cost -25%
elements.explanation: The trebuchets are faithful: at Guandu (200), Cao Cao built “stone-throwing carts”, which Yuan Shao's men called “thunder carts” (霹靂車), to use against the enemy towers. The Lou Chuans are more stretched: the Wei navy was defeated at Chibi and Cao Pi's river expeditions (222–225) failed, despite the naval training lake at Ye (208).

The “Tiger and Leopard” (虎豹騎) were the elite cavalry commanded by Cao Chun. According to the Wei shu quoted by Pei Songzhi, they were “the bravest in the empire”, some of them recruited from among commanders of a hundred men; after Cao Chun's death (210) Cao Cao refused to name a successor to him, and later Cao Xiu and Cao Zhen commanded them. They were at the siege of Nanpi (205), and Cao Chun's horsemen captured Tadun in 207 and pursued Liu Bei at Changban (208). The game's name cuts off the “Leopard”. The mechanic of growing stronger with victories is an abstraction of veteran status.

The game's justification is wrong: at White Wolf Mountain (207) Cao Cao defeated Tadun's WUHUAN and incorporated their cavalry. Kebineng's Xianbei were generally adversaries (they allied with Zhuge Liang in 231, and Kebineng was assassinated by a Wei agent in 235). There are, however, cases of Xianbei service: in 211 Kebineng led more than 3,000 horsemen to help Cao Cao's officer Yan Rou against Tian Yin's revolt, and Budugen's group submitted. Nomadic horse archers in Wei service are plausible, but they should be called “Wuhuan”. The charged attack is an invention.
The attack-speed aura abstracts his leadership. Cao Cao personally commanded decisive campaigns and wrote the oldest surviving commentary on Sunzi's Art of War. He is a fair choice for a hero.

The agricultural colonies were created in 196 at Xu, on the proposal of Zao Zhi and Han Hao. There were civil and military tuntian, such as those of Deng Ai in Huainan in the 240s, in which the soldiers produced their own grain. “Soldiers produce food” is a direct mechanical translation.

It is attested in Wei by Cao Zhi's memorial. As widespread equipment, however, mingguang armour is characteristic of the Northern dynasties and the Tang. As an upgrade for the whole mounted army it is slightly anachronistic.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Cavalry +2 attack vs. Siege Weapons
elements.explanation: It has no specific basis.
The “thunder cart” of Guandu is the best 3rd-century example. The absence of the counterweight Trebuchet also makes sense, since it would only reach China in 1273.

tree_issues.problem: The crossbow was the central weapon of Han and Wei infantry. Ma Jun, a Wei engineer, boasted that he could make Zhuge Liang's repeating crossbow five times more effective (Fu Xuan, quoted by Pei Songzhi).
Fortified defence was a Wei strength: Zhang Liao at Hefei (215), Hao Zhao with little more than 1,000 men at Chencang (228–229) and the “New City” of Hefei built by Man Chong (c. 233).
Cao Cao took Xiapi (198) and Ye (204) by flooding them, and there was tunnel and trench warfare at Guandu. Siege engineering is exactly what Wei had.
Anachronistic: woodblock printing only appears around the 7th–8th centuries.

tree_issues.item: Absence of gunpowder and of the counterweight Trebuchet
tree_issues.problem: A positive point: correct for the 3rd century.

history_text_issues.claim: In 196 Cao Cao supposedly captured the emperor and named himself “Prime Minister of the Han”.
history_text_issues.problem: Wrong chronology of titles.
history_text_issues.correction: In 196 he received Emperor Xian at Xu and became Minister of Works (sikong). Only in 208 did he restore and take up the office of Chancellor (chengxiang), and he became Duke of Wei in 213.

history_text_issues.claim: The “raiders of the Xianbei tribe” were supposedly conquered at White Wolf Mountain (207).
history_text_issues.problem: It confuses the peoples.
history_text_issues.correction: In 207 Cao Cao defeated the Wuhuan (Tadun was killed) and incorporated their cavalry. Kebineng's Xianbei were a different confederation, generally hostile to Wei, although they occasionally collaborated with it (against Tian Yin, 211).

history_text_issues.claim: The Tiger Cavalry was supposedly heavy cavalry that served as Cao Cao's personal guard.
history_text_issues.problem: A half-truth.
history_text_issues.correction: The Hu Bao Qi was above all a field shock force, although it also had guard duties (Cao Xiu “commanded the Tiger and Leopard in the palace guard”). The closest personal guard was that of Xu Chu, the “tiger warriors” (虎士). The sources do not describe it as “heavy”.

history_text_issues.claim: The campaign against Tao Qian supposedly caused “thousands” of civilian deaths.
history_text_issues.problem: It understates what the sources say.
history_text_issues.correction: The Hou Hanshu speaks of “several hundred thousand” dead and of bodies blocking the Si River (193–194). The figure is probably exaggerated, but the sources describe a large-scale massacre.

history_text_issues.claim: Liu Bei supposedly fought Dong Zhuo alongside Yuan Shao, Sun Jian and Cao Cao.
history_text_issues.problem: A single-source claim, presented as fact.
history_text_issues.correction: The Sanguozhi does not place Liu Bei in the coalition. Only the Yingxiong ji, quoted by Pei Songzhi, says that he raised troops “to take part in the campaign against Dong Zhuo”; the scene of the three alongside the coalition lords comes mostly from the Romance.

history_text_issues.claim: In 249 Sima Yi supposedly captured Cao Fang and assassinated Cao Shuang.
history_text_issues.problem: Simplification.
history_text_issues.correction: In the Incident at the Gaoping Tombs (249), Sima Yi seized Luoyang while Cao Fang and Cao Shuang were visiting imperial tombs. Cao Shuang surrendered and was executed days later along with his clan, on a charge of treason.

history_text_issues.claim: The text omits Wei's external campaigns.
history_text_issues.problem: Omission.
history_text_issues.correction: Left out are the conquest of Liaodong (238), the campaign against Goguryeo (244), the embassy of Queen Himiko of Wa (239) and, above all, the conquest of Shu by Deng Ai and Zhong Hui (263).

missing_features: The “Qingzhou Army” (青州兵): in 192, Cao Cao accepted the surrender of more than 300,000 Yellow Turbans from Qingzhou and formed the core of his army from the best of them.
The Wuhuan cavalry incorporated after 207.
The system of hereditary military households (shijia) and of family hostages.
The Nine-Rank System (jiupin zhongzheng, 220) for recruiting officials.
Ma Jun's engineering: the south-pointing chariot, chain pumps, improvements to the crossbow and the stone-thrower.
The fortifications of Hefei and Chencang.
Jian'an literature and the Bronze Sparrow Terrace (mentioned in the text, with no reflection in the game).
The contacts with Wa (Japan) and Goguryeo.

proposals.title: Wuhuan Cavalry (烏桓突騎)
proposals.description: Rename the Xianbei Raider to “Wuhuan Cavalry” and correct the history text. Alternatively, move the Xianbei concept to a future Tuoba/Northern Wei civ (386–535), which falls within the frame.
proposals.historical_basis: Sanguozhi: victory over Tadun at White Wolf Mountain (207) and integration of the Wuhuan cavalry, which became “the famous cavalry of the empire”.

proposals.title: Qingzhou Army (青州兵)
proposals.description: UT: enemy infantry units defeated near a Wei Castle have a 10% chance of switching to the Wei side; Militia-line and Spearman-line cost -15% food.
proposals.historical_basis: In 192 Cao Cao accepted the surrender of more than 300,000 soldiers and more than a million people of the Qingzhou Yellow Turbans and chose the best of them for the “Qingzhou Army” (Sanguozhi, Wu di ji).

proposals.title: New City of Hefei
proposals.description: Replace the team bonus with a UT or give Architecture and Arrowslits: Castles and Towers +2 range while garrisoned, and Walls built 50% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: Zhang Liao's defence of Hefei (215) and Man Chong's new fortress (c. 233), which withstood Wu's offensives.

proposals.title: Ma Jun's Workshop
proposals.description: Give Arbalester and Siege Engineers. Remove Block Printing and replace it with the “Nine-Rank System” (Monks and University research 15% faster).
proposals.historical_basis: Ma Jun (3rd century), Wei engineer; Chen Qun's jiupin zhongzheng system (220); printing did not exist in the 3rd century.

contested: Cao Cao's reputation: a villain in the Romance, a skilful statesman in the view of Guo Moruo (1959) and of de Crespigny.
The causes of the defeat at Chibi: fire, according to the Wu sources, or epidemic, according to Cao Cao.
The scale of the Xu massacres (193–194).
Wei's legitimacy versus Shu (Chen Shou vs. Xi Zuochi and Zhu Xi).
The real burden of the tuntian on the peasants (a 60/40 or 50/50 split).
Liu Bei's presence in the coalition against Dong Zhuo.
key_sources: Chen Shou, Sanguozhi (Wei shu, including the chapter on the Wuhuan and Xianbei)
Pei Songzhi, annotations (429), including fragments of the Wei lüe and the Wei shu
Fan Ye, Hou Hanshu (5th century)
Cao Zhi, memorial on the armour presented by the late emperor
Fang Xuanling et al., Jin shu (648)
Rafe de Crespigny, Imperial Warlord: A Biography of Cao Cao 155–220 AD (2010)
Albert E. Dien, “A Study of Early Chinese Armor”, Artibus Asiae 43 (1981)
Albert Dien and Keith Knapp (eds.), Cambridge History of China vol. 2: The Six Dynasties (2019)
Mark Edward Lewis, China between Empires (2009)

civs.represents: The state of Sun Wu or Eastern Wu (東吳; king in 221–222, emperor in 229, until 280), centred on the lower and middle Yangtze (Jiangdong/Jiangnan), with capitals at Jianye (Nanjing) and Wuchang. It includes the rise of the Sun house from Sun Jian (c. 184) and Sun Ce (195–200), and an empire with non-Han populations, such as the Shanyue of the mountains.
civs.verdict: The core identity is well captured: a river and naval power, hardy infantry and fire attacks (Chibi, 208; Yiling, 222). Red Cliffs Tactics and the “Infantry and Naval” label are faithful, and the Jian Swordsman has a documented episode behind it (Ding Feng at Dongxing, 252), which the history text itself recounts correctly. The rest is weak. The infantry regeneration, the team bonus and the food bonus have no basis, and the Sitting Tiger is a trebuchet described only in 1044, eight centuries later. The tech tree gives Wu a robust cavalry with bonuses, when the shortage of horses was a structural problem for Wu. Missing are the Shanyue, the hereditary command of troops and the maritime expeditions.
