civs.naming_scope_issues: “Wu” designates several states: the Wu of the Spring and Autumn period, Eastern Wu (222–280), the Wu of Yang Xingmi (902–937) and Wuyue (907–978). The last two fall WITHIN the AoE2 frame, and Wuyue was precisely a naval power that used “fire oil” (919). The Eastern Wu period (3rd century) is outside the frame. It is a state, not a people: the same Han ethnicity as Shu, Wei and Chinese. Several episodes in the history text openly come from the Romance.

elements.explanation: A real political entity, but from the 3rd century and outside the frame. The name is shared by later states that would fit the game better (Wuyue, 907–978).
Wu dominated the middle and lower Yangtze (Chibi, 208; Ruxu, 213 and 217; Dongxing, 252), and its army rested on infantry and navy, with little cavalry.

elements.element: Military production buildings and Docks provide +55 food when built
elements.explanation: It may evoke Wu's military colonies and the rice wealth of Jiangnan, but the link to building barracks and docks is arbitrary.
There is no historical basis; it is a balance mechanic.

elements.element: Jian Swordsmen and Hei Guang Cavalry +2 attack in Imperial Age
elements.explanation: For the swordsmen one could invoke the Wu-Yue sword tradition (the sword of Goujian) and the famous swords attributed to Sun Quan (a late tradition). For the heavy cavalry, nothing: Wu had chronic difficulty obtaining horses and even sent maritime missions to Liaodong to buy them (232–233).

Wu had shipyards at Jian'an (Fujian), with a dedicated official for shipbuilding. It built large multi-masted ships and organised expeditions to Yizhou (230, perhaps Taiwan), to Liaodong (232–233) and to Funan (the embassy of Zhu Ying and Kang Tai, variously dated between 220 and 250).

Fire attack is Wu's military signature: at Chibi (208), Huang Gai's fire ships; at Yiling (222), Lu Xun had each soldier carry a bundle of thatch to set the Shu camps alight. Incendiary archers are an acceptable abstraction, but the multiple shot is invented.

The mechanic of shedding armour to gain speed has a direct basis: at Dongxing (252), Ding Feng had his soldiers take off their cuirasses, keeping their helmets, and carry only short weapons; the Wei laughed, did not prepare and were routed (Sanguozhi, biography of Ding Feng). The name “jian” is slightly anachronistic: in the 3rd century the dominant military blade was already the ring-pommel sabre (huandao), and the straight sword was mainly an officers' weapon.

Founder of the Sun house, known for his daring and speed; it was his army, and not Guan Yu as in the Romance, that killed Hua Xiong at Yangren (191). He died in 191 or 192 (the sources differ), long before Wu existed. Sun Quan, the true founder of the state, or strategists such as Zhou Yu and Lu Xun would be more representative choices.
It corresponds directly to Huang Gai's fire-ship attack at Chibi (208), the battle that defined the tripartite division.

It corresponds to the hudun pao (虎蹲砲, “crouching tiger”), a triangular-frame traction trebuchet described in the Wujing Zongyao (1044); under the Ming the name passed to a small cannon. There is no record of it in the 3rd century, nor any association with Wu. Nor is there any record of trebuchets mounted on Wu tower ships.
It has no historical basis.

elements.element: Robust cavalry (Hei Guang, Hussar, Cavalry Archer, Bloodlines)
elements.explanation: Wu was the kingdom with the least access to horses. Its cavalry was small, and the efforts to buy horses from Gongsun Yuan ended with the execution of the envoys in 233.

tree_issues.item: Cavalry with attack bonus and Hussar
tree_issues.problem: It inverts reality: the shortage of horses was a structural limit for Wu. The tech tree should be weak at the Stable.

tree_issues.item: Fortified Wall, Arrowslits and Hoardings missing
tree_issues.problem: Wu built decisive river fortifications: the Ruxu dock-fort (濡須塢, 212–213, at Lü Meng's suggestion), which stopped Cao Cao in 213 and 217, and the Stone City (Shitoucheng) of Jianye (212).

tree_issues.item: Fast Fire Ship present and Cannon Galleon missing
tree_issues.problem: Positive point: the fire ships are faithful, and it is correct that there is no gunpowder artillery.
Positive point: correct for the 3rd century.
Here they are acceptable: the monk of Sogdian origin Kang Senghui arrived in Jianye in 247 and founded the Jianchu Temple, the first in the south.

history_text_issues.claim: “Historians tend to believe” that Sun Jian found the Imperial Seal in a well and escaped with it, despite Yuan Shao's attempts to take it from him.
history_text_issues.problem: It presents a dubious story as consensus and swaps the protagonists.
history_text_issues.correction: The find comes from Wei Zhao's Wu shu, quoted by Pei Songzhi, who called it into question. The source that speaks of an attempt to seize the seal (Shanyang gong zaiji) points to Yuan Shu, not Yuan Shao; the confrontation with Yuan Shao comes from the Romance. It is, at the very least, contested.

history_text_issues.claim: Sun Jian was supposedly “chosen” to lead the main offensive and, already on his way home, supposedly fell under the influence of Yuan Shu.
history_text_issues.problem: Inverted chronology.
history_text_issues.correction: Sun Jian was already a subordinate of Yuan Shu during the campaign against Dong Zhuo (190–191); it was Yuan Shu who appointed him inspector of Yu and supplied him. He advanced on Yuan Shu's behalf, not by the coalition's choice.

history_text_issues.claim: The text describes the exchange of the seal for troops in 195, citing the Romance.
history_text_issues.problem: The Romance is cited within a historical text.
history_text_issues.correction: The Sanguozhi records only that Sun Ce received from Yuan Shu c. 1,000 soldiers from his father's former army. The rest is novelistic material and should be kept out of a History section.

history_text_issues.claim: There was supposedly a rebellion “led by Xu Gong and White Tiger Yan”.
history_text_issues.problem: It merges distinct episodes.
history_text_issues.correction: Yan Baihu was defeated by Sun Ce c. 196 and took refuge with Xu Gong, administrator of Wu, who was conspiring with Cao Cao. Sun Ce had Xu Gong killed, and Xu Gong's retainers avenged him by wounding Sun Ce during a hunt (200).

history_text_issues.claim: Zhou Yu and Zhuge Liang are presented as the “two strategists” who destroyed Cao Cao's fleet.
history_text_issues.problem: Novelistic inflation of Zhuge Liang.
history_text_issues.correction: The command belonged to Zhou Yu and Cheng Pu, and the fire plan was Huang Gai's. Zhuge Liang was Liu Bei's diplomatic envoy.

history_text_issues.claim: Sun Quan supposedly recovered Jing province in 222.
history_text_issues.problem: Wrong date and wrong event.
history_text_issues.correction: Lü Meng took Jing at the end of 219, and Guan Yu was executed at the beginning of 220. In 222 Lu Xun defeated Liu Bei's counter-offensive at Xiaoting/Yiling, a defensive victory the text does not even mention.

history_text_issues.claim: The acceptance of the title of King of Wu granted by Cao Pi (221) was supposedly intended to punish Liu Bei.
history_text_issues.problem: Misleading interpretation.
history_text_issues.correction: Sun Quan nominally submitted to Wei to avoid a war on two fronts while he faced Liu Bei's invasion. He broke with Wei as soon as the danger had passed.

history_text_issues.claim: Wu's history is presented without its internal and maritime campaigns.
history_text_issues.problem: Major omissions.
history_text_issues.correction: Missing are the campaigns against the Shanyue (for example Zhuge Ke, 234–237, who obtained c. 40,000 soldiers), Sun Quan's defeat at Hefei (215), the victory at Shiting (228) and the expeditions to Yizhou and Funan.

missing_features: The Shanyue (山越), mountain peoples of the south-east, subjugated in successive campaigns and recruited en masse into the army.
The hereditary command of troops (shixi lingbing): generals passed their units on to their sons.
The Ruxu dock-fort and the defensive line along the Yangtze.
Maritime expeditions: Yizhou (230), Liaodong (232–233), Funan.
The shortage of horses and the trade to obtain them.
Elite units such as the “Jiefan” (解煩).
The agricultural colonisation of Jiangnan and Yue celadon ceramics.
Gan Ning's night raid with c. 100 men against Cao Cao's camp at Ruxu (the Romance turns them into 100 horsemen).

proposals.title: Shanyue Levies (山越)
proposals.description: Castle Age UT: Militia-line and Spearman-line no longer cost gold and train 20% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: The campaigns of He Qi, Lu Xun and Zhuge Ke (up to 234–237) subjugated the Shanyue and turned tens of thousands of them into soldiers (Sanguozhi, Wu shu).

proposals.title: Ruxu Dock-Fort (濡須塢)
proposals.description: Replace the Sitting Tiger: Docks gain an arrow attack and +50% HP, and Towers near the coast are built 50% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: The dock-fort built at Lü Meng's suggestion (212–213) repelled Cao Cao's offensives of 213 and 217.

proposals.title: Horse Shortage / Liaodong Trade
proposals.description: Remove Hussar and the +2 bonus for the Hei Guang Cavalry; Stable units +15% cost. A UT “Liaodong Trade” cancels that extra cost and gives cavalry +10% speed.
proposals.historical_basis: Wu's maritime missions to Liaodong to buy horses (232–233) and the execution of the envoys by Gongsun Yuan (233).

proposals.title: Hereditary Command (世襲領兵)
proposals.description: Replace the infantry regeneration: veteran infantry units (with 3 or more kills) give +10% attack to infantry units created in the same building.
proposals.historical_basis: In Wu, a general's soldiers passed to his son, which created cohesive units loyal to families such as the Lü, Zhou and Lu.

proposals.title: Yizhou Expedition
proposals.description: Imperial UT: Transport Ships and Trade Cogs +2 line of sight and +15% speed, and each returning Trade Cog also brings back food.
proposals.historical_basis: The maritime expedition of Wei Wen and Zhuge Zhi (230), which brought back thousands of captives from Yizhou, and the embassy to Funan (Zhu Ying and Kang Tai).

proposals.title: Hero Lu Xun or Sun Quan
proposals.description: Replace Sun Jian with Lu Xun (aura: nearby units deal fire damage to buildings) or with Sun Quan.
proposals.historical_basis: Lu Xun defeated Liu Bei with fire at Yiling (222). Sun Jian died in 191 or 192, before the state existed.

contested: The Imperial Seal episode (accepted by the Wu shu, questioned by Pei Songzhi).
The exact location of Chibi and the relative weight of fire and epidemic in Cao Cao's defeat.
Zhuge Liang's role at Chibi.
Sun Jian's descent from Sunzi (the Sanguozhi says only “probably”).
The narrative of “borrowing Jing” and the legitimacy of the 219 occupation.
The date of Sun Jian's death (191 or 192).
The identification of Yizhou with Taiwan and the dating of the embassy to Funan.
The succession crisis of the “Two Palaces” (241–250) and the decline of Wu.
key_sources: Chen Shou, Sanguozhi (Wu shu)
Pei Songzhi, annotations (429), with fragments of Wei Zhao's Wu shu and of the Jiang biao zhuan
Sima Guang, Zizhi Tongjian
Fragments of Kang Tai, Wu shi waiguo zhuan (3rd century)
Rafe de Crespigny, Generals of the South: The Foundation and Early History of the Three Kingdoms State of Wu (1990)
Rafe de Crespigny, A Biographical Dictionary of Later Han to the Three Kingdoms (2007)
Albert Dien and Keith Knapp (eds.), Cambridge History of China vol. 2 (2019)

civs.represents: The Jurchens (Nüzhen, 女真) of the forests and rivers of Manchuria, above all the Wanyan clan and the Jin dynasty (金, 1115–1234). The Jin overthrew the Liao (1125) and conquered the north of Song China (1127), ruling a multi-ethnic empire of Jurchens, Han, Khitans and Bohai. The Ming-era Jurchens and the Manchus/Qing are out of scope.
civs.period: c. 1114–1234 (Aguda's revolt and the Jin dynasty), with antecedents in the 11th century under Liao suzerainty.
civs.verdict: One of the best-executed civs in the group, and within the time frame. The Iron Pagoda, the iron bombs (Thunderclap Bombs), the fire lances and the combination of cavalry and gunpowder match documented facts of Jin–Song–Mongol warfare. The hunting bonus also has a basis. The problems are ones of period: Bombard Cannon, the counterweight Trebuchet and Rocket Cart postdate the fall of the Jin in 1234, and the traction trebuchet, which the Jin did in fact use, is missing. The history text has date errors (Aguda's death, the fall of the Jin) and contradicts itself by calling a forest people a “steppe tribe”. The central Jurchen institution, the meng'an mouke, is missing.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Jurchens” is a good choice: it is the name of the people, not of the dynasty, and it is within the time frame. The name reaches us through Chinese and Khitan transcriptions (Nüzhen, Jurchen); the self-designation would have been something like *jušen. The civ, however, portrays the Jin state, whose population was mostly Han: c. 50 million subjects at the end of the 12th century, of whom the meng'an mouke households numbered c. 6 million (slaves included, 1183). There is a name clash with the Jin dynasty of the Sima (266–420), cited in the Wei text, and with Nurhaci's Later Jin (1616). The Jurchen–Manchu continuity is real but falls outside the time frame. The history text describes them as a “steppe tribe”, which is wrong.

elements.explanation: It is a real people, with a dominant state in the period 1115–1234 and fully within the game's time frame.
The early army was mainly cavalry, and the Jin were among the first to use gunpowder in a war where both sides used it: iron bombs at Qizhou (1221) and fire lances at Kaifeng (1232) and Guide (1233).

elements.element: Meat of hunted and livestock animals doesn't decay
elements.explanation: A fair abstraction of the hunting and fishing economy (the great collective hunts served as military training) and of pig-rearing, which Chinese sources point to as a trait of the Jurchens' ancestors. The agriculture and villages of the (sedentary) “cooked Jurchens” are missing, but the text partly acknowledges this.

elements.element: Mounted Units and Fire Lancers attack +25% faster
elements.explanation: For the cavalry it is an acceptable abstraction of their reputation for shock (the saying attributed to the Liao: “if the Jurchens reach ten thousand, no one can resist them”). For the Fire Lancers it is stretched: they were single-shot weapons.

elements.element: Siege Engineers available in Castle Age
elements.explanation: The Jin adopted Liao and Song siege technology very quickly. In the Jingkang incident (1127) they carried off artisans, machines, instruments and books from Kaifeng.

elements.element: Siege and Fortification upgrades cost -75% wood and research +100% faster
elements.explanation: The Jin built the most extensive fortified lines of the 12th century, the jiehao ditches and walls (mostly in the second half of the 12th century), against the Mongols and Tatars, and defended Kaifeng tenaciously in 1232–1233.
There is no identifiable historical basis; it is balancing to compensate for explosive units.

Song sources on the battles of Shunchang and Yancheng (1140) describe the guard of Wuzhu (Wanyan Zongbi) as double-armoured cavalry, called “iron pagoda” (tie futu). The name is Song, not Jurchen. The idea of horses chained together in threes was criticised as fanciful by the Qianlong Emperor and by Deng Guangming, but Jin heavy cavalry is quite real.

The Jin used gunpowder bombs thrown by hand and by trebuchet. Zhao Yurong describes iron bombs at the siege of Qizhou (1221), and the Jin shi describes the “heaven-shaking thunder” bomb at Kaifeng (1232). The term “Grenadier” is a 17th-century European one; a name such as “bomb thrower” would be more accurate.

There is no specific episode of walls “regenerating”. The term “bastion” points to 16th-century European bastioned fortification. The rapid repair of walls at Kaifeng (1232) or the jiehao lines would be better bases.

Corresponds to the iron-cased bombs (zhentianlei) used by the Jin at Qizhou (1221) and Kaifeng (1232). The Jin shi says the blast could be heard a hundred li away and that they pierced iron armour. Nuance: “thunderclap” (pili) better describes the older Song bomb, which had a soft casing.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Gunpowder Units +2 line of sight
elements.explanation: It has no specific basis.
Jin “flying fire lances” (feihuoqiang) are documented at Kaifeng (1232) and at Guide (1233), where Pucha Guannu routed a Mongol camp with c. 450 fire lancers.

elements.element: Steppe Lancer (shared with Mongols, Cumans, Tatars, Khitans)
elements.explanation: Jin cavalry used lances, but the Jurchens were not a steppe people. The unit reinforces the same misconception as the history text.

The Jin fell in 1234; the earliest securely dated metal-barrelled firearms are from c. 1288–1298 (Yuan), and a possible earlier Tangut piece is of disputed date. It is paradoxical that the Jurchens have cannons and the Chinese (Ming) do not.
Multiple rocket launchers mounted on carts are Ming (or the Korean hwacha of 1451). The existence of true rockets in the Jin period is contested.

tree_issues.item: Trebuchet (counterweight) present and Traction Trebuchet absent
tree_issues.problem: The Jin made massive use of traction trebuchets, in the sieges of Kaifeng (1126–1127) and in the defence of 1232, where they hurled the iron bombs. The counterweight only arrived in 1273, after the fall of the Jin.
Anachronistic by at least half a century.

tree_issues.item: Rocket Cart present, Mangonel and Onager absent
tree_issues.problem: The multiple rocket is later; the real Jin artillery was the traction pao.

tree_issues.item: Lou Chuan boosted by Thunderclap Bombs
tree_issues.problem: Possible but ironic: Wanyan Liang's great Jin fleet was destroyed in 1161 at Tangdao (by Li Bao, with incendiary arrows) and at Caishi (with paddle-wheel ships and bombs). The navy was a weak point of the Jin.

tree_issues.item: Long Swordsman, Two-Handed Swordsman and Champion absent
tree_issues.problem: After the conquest, the Jin army used a great deal of conscripted Han infantry (qianjun) and Khitan and Bohai contingents. The image of an army that was “almost all cavalry” only holds for c. 1114–1130.
A positive point: the Zhaocheng Tripitaka was printed in Jin territory (c. 1149–1173).

history_text_issues.claim: The Jurchens supposedly rose to power under Wanyan Aguda in 1115.
history_text_issues.problem: Imprecise date.
history_text_issues.correction: The revolt began in 1114 (the victory at Ningjiang over the Liao); the Jin dynasty was proclaimed at the start of 1115.

history_text_issues.claim: Jurchen tombs supposedly contained far more hunting and fishing implements than agricultural ones.
history_text_issues.problem: Vague and partial archaeological generalisation.
history_text_issues.correction: This may hold for pre-dynastic sites, but the “cooked Jurchens” were sedentary farmers, and Jin-period sites in Manchuria have yielded many iron agricultural implements.

history_text_issues.claim: Wanyan Aguda supposedly died “in the same year” as the destruction of the Khitans (1125).
history_text_issues.problem: Wrong date.
history_text_issues.correction: Aguda died in 1123. His brother Wuqimai (Wanyan Sheng, Emperor Taizong) succeeded him and completed the destruction of the Liao in 1125, with the capture of Emperor Tianzuo.

history_text_issues.claim: Their “origin as a northern steppe tribe” supposedly explains their superior horses.
history_text_issues.problem: Wrong, and contradicts the first paragraph, which speaks of the forests.
history_text_issues.correction: The Jurchens were a people of the forests and river valleys of Manchuria: hunters, fishermen, pig and horse breeders, and farmers. The steppe peoples of the time were the Khitans, the Tatars and the Mongols.

history_text_issues.claim: Jurchen cavalry supposedly gave the Jin control of “southern China up to the Huai River”.
history_text_issues.problem: Geographical confusion.
history_text_issues.correction: The Jin conquered NORTHERN China up to the Huai, a border fixed by the Treaty of Shaoxing (1141–1142). There was a raid south of the Yangtze (1129–1130), but it was halted at Huangtiandang by Han Shizhong.

history_text_issues.claim: At Kaifeng (1126–1127) the Jurchens supposedly won with bombs, fire lances and fire arrows.
history_text_issues.problem: Partly anachronistic.
history_text_issues.correction: The use of incendiary arrows and gunpowder bombs by both sides in 1126–1127 is plausible, with Jin weapons made by captured artisans. But the first fire lance documented in writing is Song, at De'an (1132, Chen Gui), and there is no solid evidence of Jin fire lances at Kaifeng in 1127.

history_text_issues.claim: The Jurchens supposedly developed the “thunderclap bomb”, used against the Mongols at Kaifeng (1232).
history_text_issues.problem: Imprecise name and chronology.
history_text_issues.correction: The Jin bomb of 1232 was the iron-cased “heaven-shaking thunder” (zhentianlei); the “thunderclap bomb” (pili) was the older Song bomb, made of paper and bamboo. Jin iron bombs already appear at Qizhou (1221).

history_text_issues.claim: The Jin supposedly ruled “unchallenged for almost 80 years” until the arrival of the Mongols.
history_text_issues.problem: False.
history_text_issues.correction: There were the Song counter-offensives of Yue Fei (1140) and of 1163, and the Kaixi war (1206–1208). Wanyan Liang's invasion failed in 1161 and ended with his assassination. There was the great Khitan revolt (1161–1162), palace coups (Hailing killed Xizong in 1150) and constant wars with the Tatars and Mongols.

history_text_issues.claim: The Mongols supposedly attacked the Jin in 1209.
history_text_issues.problem: Wrong date.
history_text_issues.correction: In 1209 the Mongols attacked the Western Xia (Tanguts). The war against the Jin began in 1211 (Yehuling).

history_text_issues.claim: The destruction of Zhongdu (1215) supposedly forced the Jin to flee to Kaifeng.
history_text_issues.problem: Order reversed.
history_text_issues.correction: Emperor Xuanzong moved the court to Kaifeng in 1214, and Zhongdu fell in 1215, already abandoned by the court.

history_text_issues.claim: The Mongols and the Song supposedly overthrew the Jin in 1235.
history_text_issues.problem: Wrong date.
history_text_issues.correction: The Jin fell on 9 February 1234 with the fall of Caizhou, the suicide of Emperor Aizong and the death of Mozhu.

history_text_issues.claim: The Jurchens supposedly found allies in the Song before “betraying” them.
history_text_issues.problem: One-sided framing.
history_text_issues.correction: In the “Alliance Conducted at Sea” (1120) the Song also failed: they could not take Yanjing on their own and took in the defector Zhang Jue (1123). Responsibility for the breakdown is debated.

missing_features: The meng'an mouke system (猛安謀克): socio-military units of 300 families (mouke) and 1,000 (meng'an), organised by Aguda in 1114. It is the basis of the whole Jurchen organisation.
The “flank horses” (guaizi ma), light cavalry wings that accompanied the Iron Pagoda (contested interpretation).
The Jingkang incident (1127): the capture of the emperors Huizong and Qinzong and of thousands of artisans.
The jiehao fortified lines.
The Jurchen scripts (large, 1119; small, 1138) and the examinations in the Jurchen language (1173).
The tribute of gyrfalcons (haidongqing) and pearls demanded by the Liao, one of the causes of the revolt.
The multi-ethnic army: conscripted Han, Khitans, Bohai, Xi.
Jin paper money (jiaochao, c. 1154).

proposals.title: Meng'an Mouke (猛安謀克)
proposals.description: Every 10 Houses produce a free Cavalry Archer, and Villagers have +2 attack and +1/+1 armour from the Feudal Age.
proposals.historical_basis: Organisation of 1114 in which every household supplied warriors and each unit of 300 families was at once social and military (Jin shi, Bing zhi).

proposals.title: Traction Pao and Zhentianlei
proposals.description: Replace Bombard Cannon and the counterweight Trebuchet with Traction Trebuchet. The UT Thunderclap Bombs makes Traction Trebuchets hurl iron bombs (area damage against units and buildings). Remove the Rocket Cart.
proposals.historical_basis: The sieges of Qizhou (1221) and Kaifeng (1232), in which the Jin hurled iron bombs with traction trebuchets. The counterweight only arrived in 1273.

proposals.title: Artisans of Jingkang
proposals.description: UT: when Jurchen units destroy an enemy University, Siege Workshop or Castle, they receive 200 gold and siege technologies become 20% cheaper.
proposals.historical_basis: In 1127 the Jin carried off artisans, machines, books and instruments from Kaifeng, and through them assimilated Song technology.

proposals.title: Jiehao Walls
proposals.description: Rename Fortified Bastions to “Jiehao Walls”: Walls and Gates cost -50% stone and regenerate HP.
proposals.historical_basis: Lines of ditches and walls built by the Jin in Inner Mongolia and Manchuria, mostly in the second half of the 12th century.

proposals.title: Gyrfalcons of the Eastern Sea (海東青)
proposals.description: Scout Cavalry line +4 line of sight, and hunted meat is gathered 15% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: Falconry and hunting as cultural pillars; the gyrfalcons demanded as tribute by the Liao were one of the causes of the 1114 revolt.

proposals.title: Rename Grenadier
proposals.description: Rename “Grenadier” to “Huopao Thrower” (thrower of fire bombs), avoiding the 17th-century European term.
proposals.historical_basis: Terminology from Song and Jin sources (huopao, zhentianlei).

contested: The “chained horses” of the Iron Pagoda and the meaning of guaizi ma (Song accounts vs. Qianlong and Deng Guangming).
The scale of Yue Fei's victories in 1140, possibly inflated by Song historiography.
The “sinicisation” of the Jin (Ho Ping-ti vs. Rawski; Tao Jing-shen; Hok-lam Chan).
Use of gunpowder weapons by the Jin as early as 1126–1127.
Existence of true rockets in 1232.
Responsibility for the breakdown of the Alliance Conducted at Sea.
key_sources: Toghto et al., Jin shi (1344)
Xu Mengxin, Sanchao beimeng huibian (1194)
Song shi (1345)
Zhao Yurong, Xinsi Qi Qi lu (account of the siege of Qizhou, 1221)
Yue Ke, Jin Tuo cuibian (13th century)
Jing-shen Tao, The Jurchen in Twelfth-Century China (1976)
Herbert Franke, “The Chin Dynasty”, Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)
Hoyt Tillman and Stephen West (eds.), China under Jurchen Rule (1995)
Hok-lam Chan, Legitimation in Imperial China: Discussions under the Jurchen-Chin Dynasty (1984)
Tonio Andrade, The Gunpowder Age (2016)
Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China vol. 5 part 7 (1986)

civs.represents: The Khitans (Qidan, 契丹), a Para-Mongolic-speaking people of the Xar Moron valley (eastern Inner Mongolia), and the Liao empire (遼, 907/916–1125) that they founded. It was multi-ethnic (Khitans, Xi, Bohai, Han) and had a dual administration. The text also evokes the Kara-Khitai / Western Liao (1124/1132–1218) of Central Asia.
civs.period: c. 907–1125 (Liao), extended by the Kara-Khitai until 1218.
civs.verdict: The basic traits are right: pastoralism (Pasture) and heavily armoured horse archers (an early Heavy Cavalry Archer), as the Liao shi describes. From there the design moves away from the sources. The civ is labelled 'Infantry' and has a generic infantry unique unit ('Liao Dao'), when Liao armies were overwhelmingly cavalry. The Mounted Trebuchet has no Khitan record; the documented parallel is Tangut. There are clear anachronisms (Rocket Cart, counterweight Trebuchet, Cannon Galleon) and a Fire Lancer with no evidence of Liao use. Missing are Bloodlines, for one of the great horse-breeding peoples, Block Printing, for a people who printed a Tripitaka, and Architecture, for a people who built the Yingxian pagoda. The history text credits Abaoji with taking Beijing, which only happened in 936–938.
civs.naming_scope_issues: 'Khitans' is a good name: a real people, within the frame, and the origin of 'Cathay', of Old Portuguese 'Catai/Cataio' and of Russian 'Kitai'. The dynastic designation varied: 'Liao' from 947, 'Great Khitan' between 983 and 1066, then Liao again. The text merges the Liao empire with the Kara-Khitai, a distinct state in Central Asia with Muslim subjects, which defeated the Seljuks at Qatwan (1141) and echoed in the legend of Prester John. The civ ignores the agricultural, Han half of the empire: the Southern Region and the Sixteen Prefectures, which included Beijing. There is thematic overlap with Mongols, Tatars and Cumans (Steppe Lancer, pastoralism).

elements.explanation: A real people, central to the history of East Asia from 907 to 1218 and within the game's frame.

Liao armies were overwhelmingly cavalry: ordo guards, tribal armies and vassal contingents. Infantry came mainly from the Han and Bohai militias of the capitals and prefectures. The emphasis on 'Infantry' has no support in the history text itself.

The Khitan economy was pastoral (horses, cattle, sheep, camels), and the Liao had enormous state herds. But the empire had an agricultural half: the Southern Region and the towns of Han and Bohai captives settled as farmers in the north. Replacing Farms entirely erases that duality, which is the most famous institutional trait of the Liao.

elements.element: Melee attack upgrade effects are doubled
elements.explanation: There is no identifiable historical basis.

elements.element: Skirmishers, Spearman- and Scout Cavalry-line train and upgrade +15% faster
elements.explanation: Fast scouting cavalry is plausible for the Khitans. The link to skirmishers and foot spearmen has no basis.

elements.element: Heavy Cavalry Archer upgrade available in Castle Age and costs -50%
elements.explanation: The Liao shi (military treatise) describes the regular soldier: three horses, a forager and a camp guard, nine pieces of iron armour, leather or iron barding for the horse, four bows and 400 arrows, long and short spears, a mace (guduo) and an axe. That is the definition of a heavy horse archer.

The name simply means 'Liao blade' and does not correspond to any documented elite unit. Infantry was secondary in the Liao army. The real elite was the cavalry of the 'Pishi Army' (皮室軍), the guard created by Abaoji and expanded by Taizong.

There is no record of mounted trebuchets among the Khitans. The clear reference is Tangut: the Song shi (monograph on the Xia) mentions a corps of c. 200 Western Xia artillerymen, called 'poxi' (潑喜), who mounted small 'whirlwind' trebuchets on camel saddles and hurled fist-sized stones. The Liao used trebuchets and camels, but the combination is borrowed from the Tanguts, who do not exist in the game. The lingering fire on the ground has no basis either.

Lamellar armour was universal across Eurasia (Liao, Song, Tibet, Byzantium) and appears in Liao tombs. But reflecting damage back is pure game fantasy, and applying it to infantry and skirmishers inverts reality: Khitan armour was mainly a cavalry matter.

The ordo (斡魯朵) were imperial camps and households, with attached families and a cavalry guard; each emperor created his own. The regeneration can abstract the documented logistical support (each soldier with three horses, a forager and a camp guard). It is an acceptable abstraction, although the text exaggerates in saying that the main armies were 'ordo'.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Infantry +2 attack vs. Ranged Soldiers
elements.explanation: It has no specific basis.
Seasonal pastoralism and the great herds are well documented, and the imperial court moved with the seasons (nabo). It is the civ's most faithful mechanic.

The fire lance already existed by the mid-10th century (Dunhuang painting), that is, in the Liao period, but there is no evidence at all of its use by the Khitans; the first combat use documented in writing is Song (1132), after the fall of the Liao. Evidence of military use of gunpowder by the Liao is scarce, and the Song went so far as to ban the sale of saltpetre and sulphur to foreigners in the 11th century.
Multiple rocket launchers are Ming (or the Korean hwacha of 1451), centuries after the fall of the Liao in 1125.
The Liao had neither a significant navy nor gunpowder artillery. The game already limits the Khitan navy (no Galleon), but giving it the cannon ship, which not even the Chinese have, is doubly wrong.
Bactrian camels were part of the Khitan herds and appear in Liao tomb murals pulling carts. Their use as anti-cavalry cavalry is an abstraction.

tree_issues.problem: Wrong: the Khitans were horse breeders par excellence, and the Liao state herds numbered, according to the Liao shi, in the hundreds of thousands or more than a million head.

Wrong: the Liao printed the Khitan Tripitaka (c. 1031–1068), fragments of which were found in 1974 inside the Yingxian pagoda. Shen Kuo also records that Liao law punished with death anyone who took books to Song China.
Ironic, since the history text praises the Yingxian pagoda (1056), and Liao architecture includes the Guanyin Pavilion of Dule Temple (984). The Liao had five walled capitals.
Anachronistic: it only reached China in 1273. The Traction Trebuchet, which the Liao did use, is missing.

tree_issues.item: Rocket Cart and Cannon Galleon present; Fire Lancer without evidence
tree_issues.problem: Anachronistic for a state that fell in 1125; the Fire Lancer is, at the very least, undocumented for the Liao.

tree_issues.item: Farm, Heavy Plow, Horse Collar and Crop Rotation missing
tree_issues.problem: Consistent with the Pastures mechanic, but it erases the agricultural Southern Region and the colonies of captive farmers, which were essential to the Liao economy.

history_text_issues.claim: Abaoji supposedly took advantage of the Tang decline to seize territories to the south, 'including present-day Beijing'.
history_text_issues.problem: Factual error.
history_text_issues.correction: Abaoji besieged Youzhou (Beijing) in 917 without success. The Sixteen Prefectures, including Beijing, were promised in 936 and handed over in 938 by Shi Jingtang (Later Jin) to Abaoji's son, Yelü Deguang (Taizong). In 907, when Abaoji became khagan, the Tang fell that very same year.

history_text_issues.claim: Abaoji supposedly created a dual government with 'two capitals' to control the southern Chinese territories and the Khitan lands.
history_text_issues.problem: Inaccurate attribution and framing.
history_text_issues.correction: Abaoji did already create separate bodies for his Han subjects, with advisers such as Han Yanhui, but the formal dual system (Northern and Southern administrations) was consolidated under Taizong, after 938–947. Under Abaoji there were Huangdu/Shangjing (918) and the capital of the vassal kingdom of Dongdan (926, formerly Bohai), which had nothing to do with Chinese territory. The Liao eventually had FIVE capitals: Shangjing, Dongjing, Nanjing/Beijing (938), Zhongjing (1007) and Xijing (1044).

history_text_issues.claim: The main armies were supposedly made up of ordo cavalry, each soldier with a forager and an orderly.
history_text_issues.problem: Exaggeration and inaccurate attribution.
history_text_issues.correction: The Liao shi distinguishes the imperial guard, the ordo cavalry, the tribal armies, the militias of the capitals and prefectures, and the troops of the vassal states. The forager and the camp guard were assigned to every regular soldier, not only to the ordo.

history_text_issues.claim: The Liao supposedly adopted gunpowder from the Chinese progressively.
history_text_issues.problem: A claim with little documentary support.
history_text_issues.correction: There is little evidence of military use of gunpowder by the Liao, and the Song tried to prevent the sale of saltpetre and sulphur to foreigners. The claim should be presented as uncertain.

history_text_issues.claim: The Khitans supposedly created a script based on Chinese characters.
history_text_issues.problem: Simplification.
history_text_issues.correction: There were two scripts: the large script (920), of Chinese inspiration, and the small script (c. 925, attributed to Yelü Diela), partly phonetic and influenced by Uyghur. They remain largely undeciphered (Kane).

history_text_issues.claim: The Yingxian pagoda is supposedly the oldest and tallest multi-storey wooden structure in the world.
history_text_issues.problem: The 'oldest' part is wrong.
history_text_issues.correction: At c. 67 m, the Yingxian pagoda (1056) is the tallest surviving ancient wooden pagoda and the oldest entirely wooden one in China. The five-storey pagoda of Hōryū-ji, in Japan (late 7th century), is older.

history_text_issues.claim: Empress Yingtian supposedly ruled as regent for two decades.
history_text_issues.problem: Inaccurate.
history_text_issues.correction: The Liao shi confirms that she cut off her hand (926) and records the quoted words. But she then imposed the succession of Deguang (927), an adult emperor, and wielded great influence as empress dowager, without being formal regent. In 947 she was defeated and confined by her grandson Shizong.

history_text_issues.claim: The Khitans supposedly forced the Chinese to sue for peace in 1004.
history_text_issues.problem: Simplification.
history_text_issues.correction: The Treaty of Chanyuan was concluded in January 1005, after a Liao invasion that stalled before Chanyuan (where the commander Xiao Talin was killed by a bolt from a bed crossbow). It was a negotiated compromise: the Song paid silver and silk, and the two courts treated each other as equals.

history_text_issues.claim: The Kara-Khitai supposedly lasted from 1120 to 1218.
history_text_issues.problem: Wrong start date.
history_text_issues.correction: Yelü Dashi set off westwards in 1124 and proclaimed himself gurkhan c. 1131–1132. The state was usurped by Küchlüg in 1211 and conquered by the Mongols in 1218.

missing_features: The nabo (捺鉢): the mobile imperial court that moved between seasonal camps (swan hunting with gyrfalcons in spring, deer hunting in autumn).
The dual administration (tribal law for Khitans, Chinese law for Han) and the towns of captive farmers.
The Pishi Army (皮室軍), the elite cavalry guard.
The 'forager' system (da cao gu, 打草穀), which lived off plunder on campaign.
The Treaty of Chanyuan (1005): an annual Song tribute of 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk, increased in 1042.
The conquest of the kingdom of Bohai (926) and the wars with Goryeo (993–1019, including the Liao defeat at Gwiju, 1019).
Camel-drawn carts and pastoral logistics.
Liao Buddhism: printing and architecture.
The legacy of the name 'Cathay'.

proposals.title: Da Cao Gu (打草穀) — Foragers
proposals.description: Khitan mounted units gain 5 food for every 10 damage dealt to enemy buildings and 10 gold for every enemy Villager killed.
proposals.historical_basis: The Liao shi describes the foragers who accompanied each regular soldier and lived off organised plunder in enemy territory.

proposals.title: Ordo — mobile building
proposals.description: Replace the Ordo Cavalry unique tech with an 'Ordo' unique building: it trains cavalry and Villagers, serves as a food and gold drop-off point, can 'pack up' and move like a Trebuchet, and heals nearby cavalry.
proposals.historical_basis: The ordo and the nabo: the court and the imperial guards moved between seasonal camps; the centre of power was mobile.

proposals.title: Southern Chancellery
proposals.description: Castle Age unique tech: unlocks Farms and Heavy Plow while keeping Pastures, and converted or captured Villagers work Farms 15% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: The Liao dual administration (pastoral Northern Region and agricultural Southern Region) and towns populated by captive farmers.

proposals.title: Chanyuan Tribute
proposals.description: Imperial Age unique tech: +12 gold and +8 food per minute, and the Market sells at a reduced fee.
proposals.historical_basis: Treaty of Chanyuan (1005): annual Song payments in silver and silk that sustained peace and the Liao economy for 120 years.

proposals.title: Pishi Guard (皮室軍)
proposals.description: Replace the Liao Dao with armoured elite cavalry carrying bow and lance, which gains armour when near a Castle or Ordo. The Mounted Trebuchet would move to a future Tangut (Western Xia) civ.
proposals.historical_basis: A guard created by Abaoji and expanded by Taizong (Liao shi). The Tangut 'poxi' corps of camel-mounted trebuchets (Song shi).

proposals.title: Tech tree corrections
proposals.description: Give Bloodlines, Block Printing and Architecture. Remove Cannon Galleon, Rocket Cart, Fire Lancer and the counterweight Trebuchet. Add Traction Trebuchet.
proposals.historical_basis: Liao state herds, the Khitan Tripitaka, the Yingxian pagoda and the chronology of gunpowder weapons and of the counterweight (1273).

contested: Founding date of the Liao: 907 (Abaoji as khagan) or 916 (as emperor).
The nature of the Liao state: 'conquest dynasty' (Wittfogel and Feng) vs. sinicisation vs. 'permeable frontier' (Standen).
Military use of gunpowder by the Liao.
Origin and decipherment of the Khitan small script.
Authenticity of the Qidan guozhi.
Dates of the Kara-Khitai (1124/1131/1132).
The extent of Yingtian's 'regency'.
The real size of the state herds recorded in the Liao shi.
key_sources: Toghto et al., Liao shi (1344)
Qidan guozhi (attributed to Ye Longli, 12th–13th century; authenticity debated)
Accounts by Song envoys, and Shen Kuo, Mengxi bitan (c. 1088)
Song shi, monograph on the Xia (for the Tangut 'poxi' corps)
Karl Wittfogel and Feng Chia-sheng, History of Chinese Society: Liao (907–1125) (1949)
Denis Twitchett and Klaus-Peter Tietze, 'The Liao', Cambridge History of China vol. 6 (1994)
Naomi Standen, Unbounded Loyalty: Frontier Crossings in Liao China (2007)
Michal Biran, The Empire of the Qara Khitai in Eurasian History (2005)
Nancy Steinhardt, Liao Architecture (1997)
Daniel Kane, The Kitan Language and Script (2009)

groups.cross_civ_notes:
1) Disproportionate fragmentation of the Han. There are now four civs from the same Han people: Chinese (581–1500) and Shu, Wei and Wu (184–280). Three of them represent factions in a civil war of c. 60 years, outside the c. 500–1500 frame, and are treated as 'civilizations'. At the same time, peoples central to the frame are still missing: the Tibetan Empire (618–842, the great rival of the Tang), the Tanguts / Western Xia (1038–1227), the Uyghurs, the Göktürks, Bohai and Nanzhao/Dali. If China were to be differentiated by states, the Tang, the Song and the Ming, or the Xianbei Northern Wei (386–535), would make more sense than the Three Kingdoms. The presence of trainable heroes (Liu Bei, Cao Cao, Sun Jian) and of episodes from the Romance of the Three Kingdoms (14th century) in the history texts moves these civs away from the historical standard of the rest of the game. To be fair, the core elements of all three (Zhuge Liang's crossbow, 'White Feathers', Hu Bao Qi, Tuntian, Hei Guang/Ming Guang, Red Cliffs, the Ding Feng episode) come from the historical sources and not from the Romance.

2) Duplications and internal conflicts. The Chinese Chu Ko Nu is the 'crossbow of Zhuge Liang', chancellor of Shu, and duplicates the Shu UT Bolt Magazine, which is the historically grounded version. The Lou Chuan is shared by the Chinese, the Jurchens and the three kingdoms (consistent), but not by the Khitans (also consistent: the Liao had almost no navy, and the game does not even give them the Galleon). The Khitans, however, have the Cannon Galleon, which not even the Chinese have. The Hei Guang Cavalry is shared by the three kingdoms, but its documentary basis (Cao Zhi's memorial) is specifically Wei; for Wu, which was poor in horses, it makes no sense. Wei's 'Xianbei Raider' is conflated with the Wuhuan and with the Northern Wei, which was a Xianbei state. The Steppe Lancer is given to the Jurchens, who were not a steppe people.

3) Weapon chronology mixed up. This is the most serious cross-cutting problem in the group.
- The Traction Trebuchet (pao), the typical Chinese artillery from c. the 4th century BC until 1273, exists only for the three 3rd-century kingdoms. The Chinese, Jurchens and Khitans, who used it en masse (Wujing Zongyao, sieges of Kaifeng in 1126–1127 and 1232), do not have it.
- The counterweight Trebuchet, which only reached China in 1273 with Muslim engineers in the service of Kublai, is available to the Jurchens (a dynasty that fell in 1234) and to the Khitans (the Liao fell in 1125).
- The Bombard Cannon (barrelled guns are securely dated only from c. 1288) exists for the Jurchens, but not for the Chinese/Ming, who were casting iron cannon from 1377 onwards; the Chinese only have the Bombard Tower.
- The Rocket Cart is Ming and is given to the Khitans and Jurchens; the Khitan Fire Lancer is not anachronistic in the strict sense (the weapon existed c. 950), but there is no evidence of Liao use.
- Wu's Sitting Tiger is a device described in 1044.
A simple rule would make the whole group more coherent: Traction Trebuchet for everyone up to the Castle Age; counterweight only for the Chinese (Yuan–Ming) and Mongols; barrelled firearms only for the Chinese, later.

4) Jurchens and Khitans. They are well chosen as peoples and fall within the frame, and the pair reflects the real succession (the Jin destroyed the Liao in 1125). But the labels are partly swapped. The Khitans were the steppe, heavy-cavalry people, and they are given 'Infantry'. The Jurchens were a people of the Manchurian forests, and their text calls them a 'steppe tribe'. Both share the Steppe Lancer with the Mongols, Cumans and Tatars. The Khitan Mounted Trebuchet seems to come from the Tangut corps of camel-mounted trebuchets ('poxi'), which underlines the lack of a Tangut civ. The texts of the Chinese, Jurchens and Khitans contradict each other or get several dates wrong (Mongol attacks in 1206/1209 instead of 1211 against the Jin, fall of the Jin in 1234 and not 1235, Kara-Khitai from 1124/1132 and not 1120). The Yuan appear in the Chinese civ's text as 'Chinese', overlapping with the Mongols.

5) Portuguese connections. 'Mandarin' entered the European languages through Portuguese, and 'Catai' (Cathay; from the name of the Khitans, via Persian and Turkic) was the form used by the Portuguese before 'China' became established. The Ming copied the Portuguese breech-loading falcons (folangji) after the clashes of Tunmen and Xicaowan (1521–1522). In the AoE2 tech tree, however, the Chinese still lack any barrelled firearm for troops or siege (only the Bombard Tower).

6) Note on method. The game data (bonuses, units, absences) were confirmed against the repository file. Some of the primary-source checks (Sanguozhi, Jin shu) were done directly in the texts; some secondary dates and figures (for example the estimate of c. 10% Ming gunners, or the dating of the embassy to Funan) rest on the cited bibliography and should be read as estimates.

verification_log.change: The session's web search limit ran out right at the start; the checks were done by reading primary sources directly (Sanguozhi chs. 9, 30, 32, 33, 35, 55; Jin shu ch. 57) and reference pages, and some secondary claims were given more cautious wording instead of being confirmed.

Added that the Chinese have the Bombard Tower (confirmed in the repository data); corrected the rating, the verdict and the cross-civ note, which said the civ had 'no metal-barrelled firearm at all'. Added the Bombard Tower element (plausible).

Rocketry: rewrote the comment on Scorpions. Bed crossbows are very Chinese (Xiao Talin was killed at Chanyuan, 1004); only the rockets/crossbows link mixes categories. Bed crossbows added to the omissions.

Hand Cannoneer: the 'c. 10% gunners' are now supported by the Ming shi (ten firearms for every hundred men under Hongwu) and presented as Andrade's estimate. The Shenjiying proposal was corrected: Andrade describes Mu Ying (1388) with gunners in three lines, not explicit 'volleys'.

Corrected the phrase 'Jurchens, extinct in 1234': it was the Jin dynasty that fell, not the people. The idea of 'more than a dozen types' of trebuchet in the Wujing Zongyao became 'several variants'. The claim that the European mangonel derived from the Chinese trebuchet became 'the dominant interpretation'.

New history text error (minor): the examination and the 'conservative mandarins' applied to the whole period, when under the Tang recruitment was still largely aristocratic. Added Marco Polo and the origin of the stirrup to the contested section. Added the nuance about the formalisation of the Yuan four-class system.

Added the tree_issues 'limited cavalry' (no Hussar or Heavy Cavalry Archer) and Bombard Tower without Bombard Cannon. The Sixteen Prefectures became 'ceded in 936–938'. Corrected the Wade-Giles transliteration of Zhao Kuangyin.

Bolt Magazine: confirmed in Chen Shou's text ('improved the repeating crossbow') and in the Wei shi chunqiu cited by Pei Songzhi (yuanrong, ten bolts of 8 cun). The explanation now also cites Chen Shou.

War Chariot goes from 'stretched' to 'plausible'. The Jin shu states explicitly that Ma Long built his carts 'according to the Bazhentu' of Zhuge Liang (279), which gives the unit a direct textual link to Zhuge Liang. Removed the claim that chariots were anachronistic in the 3rd century.

White Feather Guard: the source is a letter from Zhuge Liang to his brother Zhuge Jin (Zhuge Liang ji; Taiping Yulan 341). Recorded the spelling 白眊 (baimao), a variant of 白毦. Corrected the claim that Chen Dao only appears later: the letter refers to the Baidi/Yong'an garrison.

Corrected the draft's claim that the 'Sanguozhi admits the genealogy was remote'. The Sanguozhi gives the lineage via Liu Zhen without the intermediate generations, and the Dianlüe points to another branch (Linyi).

Issue 'Liu Shan took over in 246': the Weilüe (cited by Pei Songzhi in ch. 33) does in fact say that Liu Shan began to govern in person after the death of Jiang Wan. The game text has a basis; the entry was downgraded to a minor nuance.

Bazhentu: severity reduced from moderate to minor, because the text says 'credited with' and the link to chariots is supported by the Jin shu. New minor error: in 200 Liu Bei first fled to Yuan Shao and only reached Liu Biao in 201.

Coiled Serpent Array: removed the unverified claims about the Wujing Zongyao and about Jiang Wei. Monastery: added the Buddha images in the Sichuan tombs (Mahao) as a nuance. Salt as a 'fiscal base' became an 'important source of revenue'. Feijun: Wang Ping became 'probably' the commander.
fidelity_score raised from 4 to 5, for consistency with Wu (5): Bolt Magazine, White Feather Guard and War Chariot have more documentary support than the draft acknowledged.

Xianbei Raider goes from 'wrong' to 'stretched'. The Sanguozhi (ch. 30) records that in 211 Kebineng led more than 3,000 horsemen to help Yan Rou, an officer of Cao Cao, against Tian Yin; there was therefore occasional Xianbei service. The history text error remains 'major' (White Wolf Mountain was fought against the Wuhuan).

Tiger Cavalry: confirmed the Wei shu cited by Pei Songzhi (the 'bravest in the empire', recruited from among commanders of a hundred; Cao Cao refused to appoint a successor to Cao Chun). Cao Xiu 'commanded the Tigers and Leopards in the palace guard', so the history text's 'personal guard' is a half-truth; the issue was reworded. Added that Cao Chun's horsemen captured Tadun (207).
Qingzhou army with exact figures (more than 300,000 soldiers and more than a million people surrendered, 192). The entry on Liu Bei against Dong Zhuo was refined using the text of the Yingxiong ji.

Jian Swordsman: confirmed the episode of Ding Feng at Dongxing (ch. 55). The soldiers took off their armour, kept their helmets and carried short weapons, and the Wei troops laughed at them. The verdict now acknowledges that the history text reports this episode correctly.
Gan Ning's raid: the Jiang biao zhuan speaks of 'more than a hundred men', not horsemen; the '100 horsemen' come from the Romance. Corrected in the omissions.

Imperial Seal issue: the text attributes the attempt to seize the seal to Yuan Shao, but the historical source (Shanyang gong zaiji) points to Yuan Shu; the confrontation with Yuan Shao comes from the Romance. Added.

Sun Jian died in 191 or 192 (sources differ). The embassy to Funan now has a contested dating. 'Complete cavalry' became 'robust cavalry', because Wu does not have the Heavy Cavalry Archer. The Shanyue Levies proposal was simplified and the hero proposal became 'Lu Xun or Sun Quan', for consistency with the description.

Population of the Jin state corrected to c. 50 million (an estimate of c. 53 million at the end of the 12th century), with the meng'an mouke households totalling c. 6 million, slaves included (1183). Date of the fall made precise (9 February 1234). Period extended to 1114.

New Steppe Lancer element (stretched). Three new history text errors (minor): the revolt in 1114 and not 1115; the name 'thunderclap' vs. zhentianlei, with iron bombs already in 1221; an archaeological generalisation about the tombs. Bombard Cannon: mentioned the possible earlier Tangut piece, whose dating is disputed.

The 'Fire Lancer and Rocket Cart' element was split in two. The Fire Lancer becomes 'stretched': the weapon existed c. 950, already in the Liao period, but there is no evidence of Khitan use. The Rocket Cart remains 'anachronistic'.

Mounted Trebuchet keeps 'wrong', but with a fairer explanation: the documented parallel is Tangut (Song shi), and the Liao did have trebuchets and camels. Cannon Galleon: noted that the game already takes the Galleon away from the Khitans.

'Dual government/two capitals': the draft simply said this was wrong. Reworded, because Abaoji already had institutions for his Han subjects, and the 'two capitals' may correspond to Shangjing and the capital of Dongdan, neither of which governed Chinese territory. New minor error: Chanyuan (January 1005) was a negotiated compromise, not a simple Song capitulation.

Corrected the origin of 'Catai' (Cathay): it comes from the name of the Khitans, and not 'from Portuguese'. Also corrected cross-civ note 5. Specified that the forager and the camp guard were assigned to every regular soldier, not only to the ordo.

Scores recalibrated: Chinese 5, Shu 5 (up from 4), Wei 6, Wu 5, Jurchens 6, Khitans 4. They sit around the average of 5, with Wei and Jurchens above it because of the number of elements with direct support in the sources.

civs.represents: Japan from the Yamato/ritsuryō state (6th–8th centuries), through the Heian court and the Kamakura (1185–1333) and Muromachi (1336–1573) shogunates, to the unification under Oda Nobunaga and Toyotomi Hideyoshi (1568–1598). The history text stops in 1333, but the design (sword-armed Samurai on foot, Hand Cannoneer, castles with “yazama” arrow slits) mainly represents the Sengoku period (1467–1600).
civs.period: c. 538 (introduction of Buddhism) – 1600 (Sekigahara); design centred on c. 1460–1600
civs.verdict: The design captures the popular image of Sengoku Japan well (samurai, firearms after 1543, castles), and some details are right: it has the Hand Cannoneer and lacks the Bombard Cannon, and the Cavalry Archer bonus acknowledges the mounted-archer tradition. The economic bonuses are arbitrary, and the infantry's “attack speed” is at best an abstraction of the 16th-century fame of the Japanese sword, because for most of the period the dominant weapon was the bow. Kataparuto has no basis: there is no Japanese tradition of trebuchets and the name is a modern loanword from English. The history text (from 1999) is the worst in the group: it repeats the myth of an isolated Japan that “took little from outside”, commits anachronisms (Fujiwara in 645, a “ceremonial” court in the 5th century) and projects the bushidō of the Edo period onto the Middle Ages. A faithful civ would bring together the mounted archer of Heian–Kamakura, the ashigaru and teppō of the Sengoku, the warrior monks (sōhei) and the silver economy.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Japanese” is acceptable: the endonym Nihon/Nippon appears in the late 7th century, and before that the sources speak of Wa (a Chinese exonym) and Yamato. The main problem is the mismatch in time: the history text covers Asuka–Kamakura (538–1333), but almost all of the design (sword-armed Samurai on foot, Hand Cannoneer, Yasama, emphasis on infantry) corresponds to the Sengoku, already at the edge of or outside AoE2's 500–1500 frame. The Emishi/Ainu of the north are not represented, nor is the kingdom of Ryūkyū (unified in 1429), which appears only as a “frontier”.

elements.explanation: Valid for the Sengoku, with mass armies of ashigaru armed with long spears (nagae-yari) and arquebuses (teppō), and for the samurai who, from the 14th century, increasingly fought on foot. But during Heian and Kamakura (c. 900–1333) the elite warrior (bushi) was first and foremost a mounted archer: his ideal was kyūba no michi, the “way of the bow and horse”. The label erases some 400 years of mounted warfare.

elements.element: Mills, Lumber- and Mining Camps cost -50%
elements.explanation: There is no identifiable historical link. It is a balance bonus for the opening of the game. Invoking timber architecture or mining does not justify these buildings costing less.

It can be read as an abstraction of the reputation of the Japanese sword, which is real but late: in the 15th–16th centuries Japan exported tens of thousands of swords to Ming China through the official trade, and Qi Jiguang, after fighting the wakō, included in his military manual a Japanese sword manual (Kage-ryū school) captured in 1561. But for most of the period the decisive weapon was the bow: the 14th-century service reports (gunchūjō) studied by Thomas Conlan show that most wounds were caused by arrows, and in the Sengoku it was above all the spear (yari) and the arquebus that counted. The idea of the katana as the main battlefield weapon is a modern myth.

elements.element: Cavalry Archers +2 attack vs. Ranged Soldiers
elements.explanation: It rightly acknowledges the tradition of the mounted samurai archer: yabusame and the ō-yoroi armour, designed for horse archers. The specific target of the bonus (“against ranged units”) is arbitrary. The Japanese bow (yumi, long and asymmetrical) is also very different from the steppe composite bow that the generic unit represents.

Fish was the main source of animal protein, especially after the Buddhist restrictions on eating meat (e.g. Tenmu's decree of 675) and thanks to intensive coastal fishing. The abstraction is reasonable, but the +100% HP is pure mechanics.

The name is unavoidable, but “samurai” (from saburau, “to serve”) originally designated armed retainers and later a social status, not a type of troop. A samurai on foot with a long sword (uchigatana/nodachi) is defensible for the 14th–16th centuries, but not for Heian–Kamakura, when he was a mounted archer. The “strong against unique units” trait is purely a game feature.

矢狭間 (yazama/yasama) is an authentic term: the arrow slits for archers in the walls and towers (yagura) of castles, alongside the teppōzama for firearms. The effect, more arrows fired by towers, is consistent. However, it is conceptually the same as Arrowslits, which the Japanese also have, and it corresponds mainly to the castles of the late 16th century (Azuchi, 1576), not to the earlier mountain forts of timber and earth (yamajiro).

“Kataparuto” is the katakana transliteration of the English “catapult”, a modern-era loanword, so the name itself is anachronistic. There is no Japanese tradition of trebuchets: according to the Nihon Shoki, Goguryeo presented the court of Suiko, in 618, with stone-throwing engines captured from the Sui, and the ritsuryō armies had the ōyumi (弩, probably a siege crossbow, with no recorded use after the 12th century), but nothing points to any significant use of trebuchets. Japanese siege warfare relied on starvation, fire and mines (e.g. Takeda Shingen's miners) and, from the last quarter of the 16th century, on cannon of European origin: the “kunikuzushi” of Ōtomo Sōrin (c. 1576) and the English and Dutch pieces used by Tokugawa Ieyasu at Ōsaka (1614–15).
It is generic. It could be linked to the pirate fleets (wakō) or to the navies of clans such as the Murakami (suigun), but there is nothing specifically Japanese about the effect.

tree_issues.item: Hand Cannoneer present / Bombard Cannon absent
tree_issues.problem: This gets it right: the arquebus reached Tanegashima in 1543 (or 1542) with the Portuguese and was quickly copied (Tanegashima, Sakai, Kunitomo, Negoro), while heavy artillery was scarce until c. 1600. It is worth saying so, because it is one of the most faithful points of the tree.
It is consistent: the ritsuryō armies of the 7th–12th centuries used the ōyumi, probably a siege crossbow capable of shooting several arrows.

tree_issues.item: Cannon Galleon and Elite Cannon Galleon present
tree_issues.problem: It is exaggerated. The Japanese fleets of the Imjin War (1592–98) had little naval artillery, and this was their great weakness against the Korean panokseon. The large ships that Kuki Yoshitaka built for Oda Nobunaga (1578), armed with cannon and described in a contemporary diary (Tamon'in nikki) as “iron ships”, were an exception, and the real extent of their armouring is debated.
It is a conceptual duplication: Yasama literally means “arrow slits”. One of the two should go, or Yasama should be replaced by something specifically Japanese, such as the “ishigaki” stone walls.

Between Kamakura and Muromachi, western Japan made double cropping of rice and barley or wheat (nimōsaku) widespread, one of the main agricultural advances of the period. In 1420 the Korean envoy Song Hŭi-gyŏng described as many as three harvests a year in the Amagasaki area. Its absence contradicts this fact.
Japan preserves some of the oldest wooden buildings in the world (Hōryū-ji, late 7th century) and built the colossal Daibutsuden of Tōdai-ji. Denying Architecture is historically odd.
It is faithful: horse barding (uma-yoroi) was rare and mostly ceremonial (Edo period).

tree_issues.item: Cavalry Archer, Heavy Cavalry Archer, Thumb Ring, Parthian Tactics
tree_issues.problem: It is faithful in spirit, because mounted archery was central. The Japanese technique is indeed a thumb draw, but made with the yugake glove rather than a ring. The name “Parthian Tactics” is Eurocentric.

history_text_issues.claim: Japan, isolated by geography and later “by choice”, supposedly developed a culture that took little from outside.
history_text_issues.problem: It is an Orientalist myth. Ancient and medieval Japanese culture is inseparable from transfers from the continent. The “isolation by choice” (sakoku, c. 1639–1853) falls outside the period and was never total.
history_text_issues.correction: From the continent came Chinese writing, Buddhism (via Baekje, 538/552), the ritsuryō code (Taihō, 701) modelled on the Tang, the grid-plan capitals (Heijō-kyō, 710, imitating Chang'an), the embassies to China (kentōshi, 630–894) and the Korean and Chinese artisans (toraijin). Even under the sakoku there was trade through Dejima, Tsushima, Satsuma/Ryūkyū and Matsumae (Ronald Toby).

history_text_issues.claim: Japan as a “land of mystery at the edge of civilization”.
history_text_issues.problem: It is a Eurocentric framing: “civilization” is implicitly centred on Europe or China.
history_text_issues.correction: Describe Japan as an integral part of the Sino-Korean cultural sphere of East Asia, with continuous diplomatic, commercial and military relations with Baekje, Silla, Tang, Song and Ming.

history_text_issues.claim: By around the 5th century, the Yamato court supposedly already had a largely ceremonial role, with real power in the hands of the clans (uji).
history_text_issues.problem: It is anachronistic: it projects onto the 5th century the pattern of a ceremonial sovereign with power “behind the throne”, typical of Heian and later periods.
history_text_issues.correction: The 5th century is the era of the great kofun tombs (Daisen) and of the “five kings of Wa” who sent missions to the Liu Song dynasty (421–478); the Inariyama sword (471) calls Wakatakeru (Yūryaku) “great king”. The clan system (uji-kabane) took shape at that time, but under a strong kingship; the struggles between clans (Mononobe, Soga) for control of the court belong mainly to the 6th century.

history_text_issues.claim: In 645 power supposedly passed from the Soga clan to the Fujiwara clan, which imposed the Taika Reform.
history_text_issues.problem: It is anachronistic. In 645 (the Isshi incident), Prince Naka no Ōe and Nakatomi no Kamatari killed Soga no Iruka. The surname Fujiwara was only granted to Kamatari in 669, and Fujiwara hegemony (the sekkan regencies) dates from the 9th–11th centuries.
history_text_issues.correction: In 645 power passed to Prince Naka no Ōe (the future Emperor Tenji) and his allies. The Taika edicts date from 646, and their real scope is debated, because the ritsuryō state only took concrete form under Tenmu and Jitō and with the Taihō code (701).

history_text_issues.claim: The Soga clan “produced” Prince Shōtoku, the first great statesman.
history_text_issues.problem: It is a simplification. Shōtoku was an imperial prince whose mother and grandmother were Soga, and the historicity of several of his deeds (e.g. the “Seventeen-Article Constitution”) is contested.
history_text_issues.correction: Present Shōtoku (574–622) as a prince regent linked to the Soga, with the caveat that his image was largely constructed by the Nihon Shoki (720) and by the later cult (Ōyama Seiichi).

history_text_issues.claim: The samurai supposedly arose from the breakdown of central authority, as in feudal Europe.
history_text_issues.problem: It is an outdated thesis. Karl Friday showed that the provincial warriors were recruited and commissioned by the Heian court itself as instruments of the state. The “feudal” parallel is now strongly contested.
history_text_issues.correction: The bushi arose from the privatisation of the military function by the state itself (commissions to provincial warriors), in a gradual process over the 9th–12th centuries, and not from a simple collapse of authority.

history_text_issues.claim: The samurai obeyed without question, was ready to die and went into battle “seeking death”.
history_text_issues.problem: It is anachronistic. This is the idealised bushidō of the Edo period (Yamaga Sokō; Hagakure, 1716), popularised by Nitobe Inazō (1899/1900) and by Meiji nationalism. Medieval warriors had a contractual relationship of reward and service (go'on/hōkō) and frequently changed sides.
history_text_issues.correction: Explain that medieval loyalty was negotiated and rewarded: the gunchūjō were requests for reward for service. Betrayals were decisive, from the Nanbokuchō wars to Sekigahara (Kobayakawa, 1600). The idealised code is a later construction (Oleg Benesch, 2014).

history_text_issues.claim: The Kamakura period was supposedly named after a “region” dominated by a new clan; military government supposedly replaced the nobility.
history_text_issues.problem: There are two inaccuracies. Kamakura is a town in Sagami province, the seat of Minamoto no Yoritomo's bakufu. The Kyoto court retained real power in parallel, at least until the Jōkyū War (1221).
history_text_issues.correction: Kamakura was the seat of the first shogunate (1185/1192–1333). After 1203, effective power passed to the Hōjō regents (shikken), and the two centres (court and bakufu) coexisted.

history_text_issues.claim: The Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281 were repelled, and a “fortuitous storm” caused heavy losses to the second fleet.
history_text_issues.problem: It is essentially correct (the typhoon of 1281 is well documented), but the wording hands the victory to chance and mentions neither the defence nor the composition of the fleets.
history_text_issues.correction: In 1281 the coastal defence, backed by the Hakata wall (genkō bōrui, 1276), prevented a landing for weeks before the typhoon. The fleets were largely Korean (Goryeo) and Chinese (former Southern Song). A decisive storm in 1274 as well, which the text does not claim but which the “kamikaze” tradition spreads, is doubtful (Arakawa Hidetoshi; Thomas Conlan, 2001).

history_text_issues.claim: The text ends with the Kamakura period.
history_text_issues.problem: It is a structural omission. Precisely the period that the design represents is missing: Muromachi, the Ōnin War (1467–77), the Sengoku, the arrival of the Portuguese (1543), Nobunaga, Hideyoshi and the invasions of Korea (1592–98).
history_text_issues.correction: Add a paragraph on the Sengoku era: the ashigaru, the teppō, stone castles, the Ikkō-ikki leagues and unification.

missing_features: The mounted samurai archer in ō-yoroi armour as the military core from c. 900 to 1350
The ashigaru (low-status infantry) with long spears and arquebuses, and the tactical revolution of the Sengoku
The warrior monks (sōhei) of Enryaku-ji and Kōfuku-ji, and the Ikkō-ikki leagues (siege of Ishiyama Hongan-ji, 1570–80)
Wakō piracy and the clan navies (Murakami suigun)

Silver mining (Iwami Ginzan, 1526, and the haifuki cupellation technique introduced from Korea in 1533), which made Japan one of the world's largest silver exporters between the late 16th century and the 17th century
The Nanban trade with the Portuguese and the Jesuits (Francis Xavier, 1549), including the Christian daimyō
The naginata as a characteristic polearm
Swords as a major export product to Ming China
The evolution of castles: from timber mountain forts to castles with ishigaki stone walls

proposals.title: Mounted Samurai (Kyūba) as a second unique unit
proposals.description: Add, in the Castle Age, a heavy mounted archer (high melee armour, lower speed than the Cavalry Archer) trained at the Castle. The foot Samurai would then mainly represent the Muromachi–Sengoku phase.
proposals.historical_basis: Genpei War (1180–85) as narrated in the Heike monogatari; the Mongol invasion scrolls (Mōko shūrai ekotoba, c. 1293); Karl Friday, Hired Swords (1992) and Samurai, Warfare and the State (2004).

proposals.title: Replace Kataparuto with “Tanegashima”
proposals.description: Imperial Age tech: Hand Cannoneers train +25% faster and cost -20% gold, and Archery Ranges can train Hand Cannoneers.
proposals.historical_basis: Arrival of the Portuguese at Tanegashima in 1543 according to the Teppōki (1606), or 1542 according to António Galvão; copying by Yaita Kinbei and mass production in Sakai, Kunitomo and Negoro; use at Nagashino (1575), whose exact importance is debated. Fernão Mendes Pinto claims to have been among the first Portuguese there, which is doubtful.

proposals.title: Ashigaru
proposals.description: Replace the infantry attack bonus: Spearman-line costs -25% and, from the Castle Age, has +1 melee range (long spears).
proposals.historical_basis: Rise of the ashigaru in the Ōnin War (1467–77), criticised by Ichijō Kaneyoshi; the 4.5–6.5 m spears of the Sengoku armies (Oda, Takeda, Uesugi).

proposals.title: Sōhei (warrior monks)
proposals.description: The Monastery trains an infantry unit with a naginata, resistant to conversion, which does not convert but heals nearby units.
proposals.historical_basis: Monastic armies of Enryaku-ji and Kōfuku-ji (10th–16th centuries); the Ikkō-ikki leagues; Nobunaga's siege of Ishiyama Hongan-ji (1570–80).

proposals.title: Iwami silver instead of cheap buildings
proposals.description: Replace “Mills, Lumber and Mining Camps -50%” with: gold miners +15% from the Castle Age, and free Gold Shaft Mining.
proposals.historical_basis: Discovery of Iwami Ginzan (1526) and introduction of haifuki cupellation from Korea (1533); Japanese silver fed the trade with China via the Portuguese.

proposals.title: Kangō bōeki (tally trade)
proposals.description: Allied Trade Cogs and Trade Carts generate +10% gold.
proposals.historical_basis: Official Ashikaga–Ming tally trade (kangō), 1404–1547, with massive exports of swords, copper and sulphur, and the merchant networks of Hakata and Sakai.

contested: Three-rank rotating volley fire at Nagashino (1575): the Shinchō kōki does not clearly describe it, and historians such as Fujimoto Masayuki dispute it.
The exact date of the arrival of firearms at Tanegashima (1543 in the Teppōki, 1542 in António Galvão) and the presence of Fernão Mendes Pinto.
Bushidō as a medieval code or as a tradition invented in the Edo and Meiji periods (Oleg Benesch).
The existence of a decisive typhoon in 1274 (“kamikaze”).
The applicability of the concept of “feudalism” to Japan (Asakawa Kan'ichi versus Jeffrey Mass and Karl Friday).
The historicity of Prince Shōtoku's deeds and the real scope of the Taika Reform.
The degree of iron armouring of Kuki Yoshitaka's ships (1578).
key_sources: Nihon Shoki (720)
Heike monogatari (13th–14th centuries)
Azuma kagami (c. 1300)
Mōko shūrai ekotoba (c. 1293)
Ōta Gyūichi, Shinchō kōki (c. 1600)
Teppōki (1606)
António Galvão, Tratado dos Descobrimentos (1563)
Luís Fróis, Historia de Japam (c. 1590)
Qi Jiguang, Jixiao xinshu (1584 ed.)
Karl F. Friday, Hired Swords (1992); Samurai, Warfare and the State in Early Medieval Japan (2004)
Thomas D. Conlan, State of War (2003); In Little Need of Divine Intervention (2001)
Oleg Benesch, Inventing the Way of the Samurai (2014)
Ronald P. Toby, State and Diplomacy in Early Modern Japan (1984)
Mary Elizabeth Berry, Hideyoshi (1982)

civs.represents: The states of the Korean peninsula: the Three Kingdoms (Goguryeo, Baekje, Silla), Unified Silla (668–935) and Balhae to the north (698–926), Goryeo (918–1392) and early Joseon (1392–1598). The unique units and techs (Turtle Ship, Rocket Cart/hwacha, singijeon, eupseong) are concentrated on Joseon and above all on the Imjin War (1592–98).
civs.period: c. 500 – 1598; design centred on 1400–1598
civs.verdict: This is one of the most coherent civs in the group. The “defensive and naval” identity does indeed match the Korean strategy of mountain fortresses and a decisive navy, and the Turtle Ship, the Rocket Cart (hwacha) and Shinkichon (singijeon) have a solid basis, even if they are concentrated in the 15th century and the 1590s. The War Wagon has no clear Korean prototype, and the absence of Mangonel/Onager and of Heavy Scorpion contradicts the tradition of catapults and heavy crossbows of Silla and Goryeo. The history text (from 2000, from The Conquerors expansion) contains concrete errors (a military regime of “sixty years”, a border “with China” in 993, woodblock printing “invented” in 1234, “first cannon-bearing armored ships”) and serious omissions (Balhae, hangul, the Ming intervention). What is missing above all is a representation of Goguryeo and Goryeo, which dominate the 500–1400 period.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Koreans” is an exonym derived from Goryeo (Koryŏ); the medieval endonyms vary (Goguryeo, Silla, Goryeo, Joseon). There is no serious conflation with other civs, but there is a temporal imbalance: the design over-represents the 1590s, outside the 500–1500 frame, and under-represents Goguryeo and Goryeo. The inclusion of Jurchens and Khitans in the game makes the gap more visible: Goryeo fought the Liao (993–1019) and the Jurchen (1107–09), and none of this comes through. Goguryeo and Balhae are also claimed by official Chinese historiography (the “Northeast Project”), which makes their representation politically sensitive.

elements.explanation: It matches the documented Korean strategy of withdrawing to mountain fortresses (sanseong) and “emptying the fields”: against the Sui (Salsu, 612) and the Tang (Ansi, 645), in the wars against the Khitan (993–1019, with fortress defences such as Heunghwajin before Gang Gam-chan's field victory at Gwiju, 1019) and against the Mongols (Gwiju, 1231; Cheoin, 1232), with the court taking refuge on Ganghwa (1232–70). It is also faithful on the naval side: Jang Bogo (Cheonghaejin, 828), Choe Mu-seon's naval cannon against the wakō (Jinpo, 1380) and Yi Sun-sin (1592–98).
It is a reasonable abstraction of the tradition of stone fortification: Goguryeo fortresses, the walls of Hanyang (1396) and the 15th-century town walls (eupseong).

elements.element: Ranged Soldiers and Infantry cost -50% wood
elements.explanation: The part concerning ranged soldiers reflects the primacy of the bow in Korean military culture: the gakgung composite bow, Joseon's military examinations (mugwa) centred on archery, and the Goguryeo murals. The discount for infantry has no specific basis.

elements.element: Archer armor and tower upgrades free
elements.explanation: It is a reasonable rendering of the “archers in fortifications” combination, central to Korean defence. The link is generic, but coherent.
Korea had a strong shipbuilding capacity. On Mongol orders, Goryeo built around 900 ships in a few months for the invasion of Japan in 1274 (Goryeosa), and Joseon developed the panokseon (1555).

There is no known Korean prototype of an “archer cart” used as a mounted archer. The hwacha were rocket-launching or gun-barrel carts, already represented by the Rocket Cart. Byeon I-jung's armoured cart with firearms (1592) used gun barrels, not bows, and is late. The tradition of war carts in formation is more Chinese (Qi Jiguang) or Hussite.

The geobukseon (guseon) is mentioned in 1413 in the Annals of Taejong and was used by Yi Sun-sin from 1592 (Sacheon, Dangpo, Hansan), armed with cheonja and jija cannon. There are two caveats: there were very few of them (probably 3 to 5), the panokseon being the backbone of the fleet, and the iron armour is not documented in the Korean sources of 1592, which describe a spiked covering.

邑城 (eupseong) refers to town/city walls, built en masse in the 15th century, above all on the south coast, against the wakō. The name is authentic, but the effect (+2 range for watch towers) is unrelated: the term calls for a bonus to walls and gates.

It corresponds to the singijeon (神機箭), rocket arrows derived from Goryeo's juhwa, renamed and standardised in 1448 and fired in volleys of up to 100 by the hwacha improved by Munjong (1451). The romanisation is odd: in Revised Romanization it is “Singijeon” and in McCune-Reischauer “Sin'gijŏn”. Extending the effect to the Turtle Ship has no basis, because the ships fired large arrows (daejanggunjeon) from cannon, not singijeon.
It has no identifiable historical link.

tree_issues.item: Rocket Cart and Heavy Rocket Cart present
tree_issues.problem: This is correct: the hwacha is well documented (1409; 1451) and was used at Haengju (1593), although its exact contribution to that victory is debated.

This is inconsistent. Goguryeo captured stone-throwing engines from the Sui and gave some to Japan in 618 (Nihon Shoki), and at the siege of Gwiju (1231) both sides used catapults (pocha), according to the Goryeosa. The Rocket Cart only exists from c. 1400, so the Korea of 500–1400 is left without throwing artillery.

It runs counter to the reputation of Silla's heavy crossbows.
