According to the Samguk Sagi (year 669), the Tang emperor Gaozong summoned the artisan Gu Jinchon, whose crossbows were said to reach 1,000 paces; in China, the ones he made only reached 30 and then 60 paces, and he blamed the wood, while it was suspected that he was hiding the secret. The Koreans have Scorpion, but not Heavy Scorpion.

tree_issues.item: Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon, Bombard Tower, Fire Lancer
tree_issues.problem: This is faithful for late Goryeo and Joseon: Choe Mu-seon's Office of Firearms (Hwatong Dogam) was created in 1377, followed by the Joseon chongtong and the seungja chongtong of the late 16th century.
It contradicts Goguryeo's armoured cavalry: the murals of Anak Tomb No. 3 (357) and of other tombs show fully armoured horses (gaema).

tree_issues.item: Cavalry Archer, Heavy Cavalry Archer, Hussar, Cavalier
tree_issues.problem: This is faithful: cavalry, including horse archers, was essential on the northern frontiers against the Khitan and Jurchen, from Goguryeo to Joseon.

history_text_issues.claim: After the coup of 1170, the military regime supposedly lasted “sixty years”.
history_text_issues.problem: The duration is wrong (it perhaps confuses the military regime with the dictatorship of the Choe family).
history_text_issues.correction: Goryeo's military regime lasted about a century (1170–1270), including the Choe family dictatorship (1196–1258), and ended with the rapprochement with the Mongols.

history_text_issues.claim: In 993 Goryeo supposedly recovered territory up to the Amnok River, on the “border with China”.
history_text_issues.problem: The border was with the Khitan Liao Empire, not with Song China, and the gain resulted from negotiation after a Khitan invasion.
history_text_issues.correction: In 993, after the first Khitan invasion, the diplomat Seo Hui negotiated with the general Xiao Sunning the cession to Goryeo of the region east of the lower Amnok (the “six garrisons”), in exchange for breaking off relations with the Song. This is all the more relevant now that the Khitans exist as a civ.

history_text_issues.claim: The unification by Silla and then by Goryeo is presented as the unification of all Korea.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits Balhae (698–926), the successor state of Goguryeo in the north, which coexisted with Unified Silla (the “Northern and Southern States” period).
history_text_issues.correction: Mention Balhae and the integration of its elites into Goryeo after 926.

history_text_issues.claim: It says Korea became a centre of learning thanks to the invention of movable type and woodblock printing “around 1234”.
history_text_issues.problem: It confuses several things. Woodblock printing is much older, movable type was invented in China, and the text places the fact in the context of Joseon, whereas 1234 belongs to the Goryeo period.
history_text_issues.correction: Korean woodblock printing goes back at least to the Mugujeonggwang Dharani Sutra (c. 751) and the two Tripitaka Koreana (1011–87; 1237–51). Movable type was invented by Bi Sheng (China, c. 1040, in ceramic). The Korean contribution is metal movable type: Sangjeong gogeum yemun, c. 1234, lost and known only from a text by Yi Gyu-bo, and Jikji, 1377, the oldest extant book printed with metal type.

history_text_issues.claim: On Joseon, the text speaks of agrarian reform, bureaucracy and Confucianism, but does not mention the alphabet.
history_text_issues.problem: This is a serious omission: hangul (Hunminjeongeum, 1443/1446, King Sejong) is Joseon's greatest cultural achievement.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention hangul and the scientific flowering under Sejong (rain gauges, water clocks, astronomy).

history_text_issues.claim: The Japanese supposedly withdrew mainly because their fleets could not maintain the supply lines.
history_text_issues.problem: This is a partial explanation. It omits the massive intervention of Ming China (recapture of Pyongyang, 1593), the volunteer armies (uibyeong) and the soldier-monks, and the fact that the final withdrawal (1598) followed Hideyoshi's death.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the war as a trilateral Joseon–Ming–Japan conflict (Kenneth Swope), in which Yi Sun-sin's naval blockade was a decisive factor, but not the only one.

history_text_issues.claim: The turtle ships were supposedly “the first cannon-bearing armored ships in history”.
history_text_issues.problem: This is debatable. Ships with cannon existed earlier (Goryeo at Jinpo, 1380; Europe; Ming China). Kuki Yoshitaka's ships for Oda Nobunaga (1578), described as “iron ships”, predate them, and the geobukseon's iron armour does not appear in the Korean sources of 1592.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that the geobukseon was a covered ship, with a spiked covering, heavily armed with cannon and very effective. Whether or not it had iron plates is debated.

history_text_issues.claim: It says the Japanese “had no answer” to the turtle ships.
history_text_issues.problem: This is exaggerated. At Chilcheollyang (1597), the Korean fleet under Won Gyun was destroyed, including the turtle ships, and the Japanese adapted by avoiding battle and fortifying harbours (wajō).
history_text_issues.correction: Mention Chilcheollyang and Yi Sun-sin's recovery at Myeongnyang (1597) with only 13 ships.

missing_features: Goguryeo's armoured cavalry (gaema musa) and the wars against the Sui and Tang (Salsu, 612; Ansi, 645)
The strategy of mountain fortresses (sanseong) and of evacuating the countryside
Silla's heavy crossbows (the Gu Jinchon episode, 669)
The pyeonjeon, a short arrow shot with a guide tube (tongah), a ranged weapon much feared by the Jurchen and the Japanese
The panokseon as Joseon's true ship of the line
The soldier-monks: Kim Yun-hu killed the Mongol general Saritai at Cheoin (1232), and Hyujeong and Yujeong commanded monk armies in 1592–93
The volunteer armies (uibyeong) of the Imjin War
Goryeo's wars against the Khitan (993–1019) and Jurchen (1107–09)
Hangul, metal-type printing and celadon ceramics as economic and cultural pillars
Jang Bogo's maritime trade (9th century)

proposals.title: Gaema Musa (Goguryeo armoured horseman)
proposals.description: Replace the War Wagon with heavy cavalry in full barding: an armoured lancer with high armour against projectiles, slow and expensive, available in the Castle Age.
proposals.historical_basis: Murals of Anak Tomb No. 3 (357) and other Goguryeo tombs; campaigns of Gwanggaeto (stele of 414); wars against the Sui and Tang.

proposals.title: Pyeonjeon
proposals.description: Archers, Cavalry Archers and Archery Range units gain +1 range and +1 pierce attack (short arrows shot with a guide tube).
proposals.historical_basis: Use of the tongah and pyeonjeon documented in Joseon military sources; range and speed greater than those of ordinary arrows, much feared by the Jurchen and the Japanese.

proposals.title: Restore pre-gunpowder artillery and Silla's crossbows
proposals.description: Give Mangonel and Onager (traction catapults), and Heavy Scorpion or a UT “Cheonbo-no” (“thousand-pace crossbow”): Scorpions +2 range.
proposals.historical_basis: Samguk Sagi, Silla annals, year 669 (Gu Jinchon); use of catapults at the siege of Gwiju (1231) according to the Goryeosa.

proposals.title: Panokseon
proposals.description: Replace the War Galley/Galleon line with a two-deck ship with high HP, short-range cannon and a bonus against boarding ships. The Turtle Ship would remain as an expensive, limited elite unit.
proposals.historical_basis: Panokseon developed in 1555; the basis of Yi Sun-sin's victories in 1592–98 (Nanjung Ilgi; Jingbirok).

proposals.title: Sanseong (mountain fortresses)
proposals.description: Castles, Towers and Walls built on high ground gain +20% HP. Villagers can garrison Castles, which then fire additional arrows.
proposals.historical_basis: Defence of Ansi (645) against Tang Taizong; defence of Gwiju and Cheoin against the Mongols (1231–32).

proposals.title: Soldier-monks (Seungbyeong)
proposals.description: Allies' Monks can switch to a combat mode with a melee attack.
proposals.historical_basis: Kim Yun-hu at Cheoin (1232); the monk armies of Hyujeong (Seosan Daesa) and Yujeong (Samyeong) in 1592–93.

proposals.title: Rename Shinkichon to Singijeon
proposals.description: Use the standard romanisation (Revised Romanization) and limit the effect to Rocket Carts.
proposals.historical_basis: Term 神機箭; specifications in Gukjo oryeui seorye (1474).

contested: Whether the geobukseon had iron plates and whether it can be considered “the first ironclad”.
The historical affiliation of Goguryeo and Balhae (Korean historiography versus the Chinese “Northeast Project”).
The nature of Silla's hwarang: a military elite or an aristocratic and religious fraternity.
The actual effectiveness of the hwacha at Haengju (1593) and the numbers of combatants.
The dating and authenticity of the 1234 metal-type printing, known only from a text by Yi Gyu-bo.

civs.represents: The Việt (Kinh) of the Red River delta and their state, called Đại Cồ Việt (968) and later Đại Việt (1054): the Ngô, Đinh, Early Lê, Lý (1009–1225), Trần (1225–1400) and Hồ (1400–07) dynasties, the Ming occupation (1407–27) and the Later Lê (1428–1788). The focus is on resistance against the Song, the Mongols and the Ming, and on the southward expansion against Champa.
civs.verdict: The civ captures some real traits: mass mobilisation and rotating militias (Conscription), the importance of missile troops and Hồ Quý Ly's paper money. The history text, written in 2016, is reasonably up to date, though it contains date errors (111 BC; 938 versus 1054). But the civ ignores the two things that made Đại Việt most feared: riverine and naval warfare (Bạch Đằng) and firearms. Paradoxically, it has no Hand Cannoneer, even though the game's own text says it was already using gunpowder in 1390, and even though it was one of the region's earliest gunpowder powers. The Sanskrit name “Chatras” belongs to the Indianised world (Champa/Khmer), not to Sinicised Đại Việt, and the Imperial Skirmisher has no basis. It is more a civ of “generic Southeast Asian archers” than the Confucian, anti-Mongol Đại Việt.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Vietnamese” is a modern name: Việt Nam was adopted only in 1804. In the Middle Ages the state was called Đại Cồ Việt/Đại Việt, and the Chinese used “Annam” or “Jiaozhi”. The civ represents only the Việt (Kinh). Champa, the Austronesian, Hindu and later partly Muslim kingdom of the centre and south of present-day Vietnam, has no civ of its own, but some of its traits are “lent” to the Vietnamese: the Sanskrit name Chatras and, in part, the emphasis on elephants. Without Champa, half of Đại Việt's military history (the “march to the south”, Nam tiến) is left without an opponent.

elements.explanation: Đại Việt's shooting tradition was above all one of the crossbow (nỏ): the legend of the magic crossbow of An Dương Vương and Cao Lỗ at Cổ Loa, the bronze crossbow triggers and the thousands of arrowheads found at Cổ Loa, Chinese references to the crossbowmen of Jiaozhi, and its use against the Song (1075–77) and the Mongols. The label is defensible, but it should emphasise the crossbow rather than the bow.

elements.element: Enemy Town Centers revealed at start
elements.explanation: It can be read as an allusion to superior intelligence and command of the terrain in the Trần guerrilla war. The link is weak, and the bonus reveals the enemy's territory, not one's own.

elements.element: Economic upgrades cost no wood, research +100% faster
elements.explanation: There is no identifiable connection. A possible abstraction would be the Lý/Lê administration or the dike system, but the effect is generic and serves game balance.
It may reflect the resilience of light infantry and the use of wicker shields, but it is arbitrary.

It connects to the system of rotating peasant-soldiers (“ngụ binh ư nông”) and to the mass mobilisation against the Mongols (the Diên Hồng conference, 1284), which the game's own text mentions when it talks about the rotation of troops in peacetime.

Wicker/rattan shields and protective gear were common in Southeast Asia and southern China (the Ming “tengpai” rattan-shield soldiers), which justifies the high pierce armour. But the characteristic missile weapon of the Việt was the crossbow, and “rattan armour” is more associated with the peoples of south-western China.
No known Vietnamese troop type corresponds to an “imperial” javelin skirmisher. It is a generic variant created for game balance.

“Chattra” (Sanskrit: royal parasol) is a term from the Indianised world (Champa, Khmer, Burma), alien to Sinicised Đại Việt, whose court language was Classical Chinese. The Vietnamese did use war elephants (the Hồ against the Ming at Đa Bang, 1407; Lê Lợi's insurrection in the 1420s), so the effect is acceptable, but the name belongs to the Cham.

Hồ Quý Ly, then regent of the Trần dynasty, issued paper money (Thông bảo hội sao) in 1396. It was a real experiment, but short-lived, unpopular and coercive. The effect (lumberjacks generate gold) is arbitrary, and paper money is a Chinese invention (jiaozi, Song, c. 1024).

elements.element: Imperial Skirmisher upgrade for allies (team bonus)
elements.explanation: It has no historical basis, because it derives from a unit that also has no basis.

tree_issues.problem: This is a fundamental error and an internal contradiction, because the game's own text says that by 1390 the Vietnamese were already using gunpowder. In that year the king of Champa, Chế Bồng Nga, was killed by fire from Vietnamese guns. Hồ Nguyên Trừng, captured in 1407, directed the manufacture of firearms for the Ming, and Ming sources praise the “Jiaozhi” guns. The Lê used firearms against Champa (1471) and Lan Xang (1479–80) (Sun Laichen, 2003). The Fire Lancer only partly makes up for this.

tree_issues.item: No naval bonus and no Fast Fire Ship
tree_issues.problem: Đại Việt owes its most celebrated victories to riverine warfare: Bạch Đằng in 938 and 1288, with stakes driven into the riverbed (tradition attributes the same tactic to Lê Hoàn in 981). The tech tree and the bonuses ignore this.

tree_issues.item: Cavalry Archer and Heavy Cavalry Archer
tree_issues.problem: This is stretched: there is no Vietnamese tradition of mounted archers, and cavalry was scarce in the delta. (The Vietnamese do not have Parthian Tactics.)

tree_issues.item: Battle Elephant and Elite Battle Elephant
tree_issues.problem: This is plausible: elephants are attested in the Hồ and Lê armies, although they were less central than in Champa or Angkor.

tree_issues.item: Bombard Cannon present without Hand Cannoneer
tree_issues.problem: The combination inverts the regional diffusion: hand-held firearms and light pieces of Ming origin arrived before any heavy artillery.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that “In the first century BC” the Han dynasty invaded the Red River delta to protect commercial interests.
history_text_issues.problem: The date is wrong, the motivation is simplified, and there are omissions: Âu Lạc and Zhao Tuo's kingdom of Nanyue (Nam Việt), which had absorbed it.
history_text_issues.correction: The Han conquest of Nanyue took place in 111 BC (2nd century BC), taking advantage of a political crisis in Nanyue, as part of Han Wudi's expansion. It would also be worth mentioning the revolt of the Trưng sisters (AD 40–43), the most famous uprising against the Han.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that Ngô Quyền, in 938, repelled “the last Chinese invasion” and proclaimed himself king of Đại Việt.
history_text_issues.problem: There are two errors. It was not the last invasion: it was followed by the Song in 981 and 1075–77, the Mongols in 1258, 1285 and 1287–88, and the Ming in 1406–07. The name Đại Việt was adopted only in 1054.
history_text_issues.correction: Bạch Đằng (938) defeated the Southern Han, and Ngô Quyền proclaimed himself king in 939. The state was called Đại Cồ Việt from 968 (Đinh Bộ Lĩnh) and Đại Việt from 1054 (Lý Thánh Tông).

history_text_issues.claim: The legendary date of 2879 BC is associated with Hùng Vương.
history_text_issues.problem: In the tradition (Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư, 1479), 2879 BC is the date attributed to Kinh Dương Vương and the Hồng Bàng dynasty; the Hùng kings come later. The text correctly identifies the episode as legend.
history_text_issues.correction: Attribute the date to Kinh Dương Vương and note that the tradition of the Hùng kings was largely elaborated between the 14th and 15th centuries (Liam Kelley).

history_text_issues.claim: It says that the Trần introduced paper money.
history_text_issues.problem: Technically it falls within the Trần period (1396), but it omits who did it and how it ended.
history_text_issues.correction: It was Hồ Quý Ly, a regent who later usurped the throne, who issued it in 1396. The measure was coercive and failed.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that, under the Lý, all nobles and bureaucrats were educated in Confucianism and recruited by examination.
history_text_issues.problem: This is anachronistic: it projects the reality of the 15th century onto the Lý.
history_text_issues.correction: The Temple of Literature (Văn Miếu) dates from 1070, the first examination was held in 1075 and the Imperial Academy (Quốc Tử Giám) was founded in 1076, but the Lý elite was Buddhist and aristocratic. Recruitment by examination only became dominant under the Lê, in the 15th century.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that the Lê converted the state to Confucianism “as the main religion”.
history_text_issues.problem: This is an inappropriate framing: Neo-Confucianism was a state ideology, not a religion one converts to.
history_text_issues.correction: Speak of the adoption of Neo-Confucianism as the official ideology (the Hồng Đức code), with Buddhism and local cults persisting.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that, in 1471, Lê Thánh Tông defeated “the Champa Kingdom”.
history_text_issues.problem: This is exaggerated and leaves things out. Champa survived as a rump state (Panduranga) until 1832, and the text omits that Champa, under Chế Bồng Nga, sacked Thăng Long in 1371 and defeated and killed the emperor Trần Duệ Tông in 1377.
history_text_issues.correction: Lê Thánh Tông conquered Vijaya, the political centre of Champa. The Việt–Cham rivalry was evenly balanced for centuries.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that the Lê dynasty held the throne for much of the pre-modern period and was the longest-lasting.
history_text_issues.problem: This is nominally true but misleading, because it omits the Mạc usurpation and the loss of real power.
history_text_issues.correction: The Mạc reigned in Thăng Long in 1527–1592. After the restoration, the Lê emperors were figureheads under the Trịnh lords (north) and the Nguyễn lords (south).

missing_features: Riverine and naval warfare, with the tactic of stakes in the Bạch Đằng River (938, 1288)
The crossbow as the national weapon, including the legend of Cao Lỗ's multiple-shot crossbow
The scorched-earth and evacuation strategy (“vườn không nhà trống”) against the Mongols
Đại Việt's own firearms and their influence on the Ming
The Red River dike system (the Trần general dikes, 1248) as the basis of agriculture
The Confucian examination state (Văn Miếu, 1070; Quốc Tử Giám, 1076) and the Hồng Đức code
The “march to the south” (Nam tiến) against Champa
The “Sát Thát” (“kill the Tatars”) tattoos of Trần soldiers as a symbol of mobilisation

proposals.title: Bạch Đằng (river stakes)
proposals.description: Allows cheap “stakes” to be built in shallow water near the shore: they deal continuous damage to enemy ships and prevent them from moving. Alternatively, enemy ships within 6 tiles of a Vietnamese Dock get -30% speed.
proposals.historical_basis: Battles of Bạch Đằng: in 938 against the Southern Han and in 1288, when Trần Hưng Đạo destroyed Omar's Yuan fleet with stakes exposed at low tide (Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư); stakes found archaeologically in the estuary.

proposals.title: Hand Cannoneer and “Hỏa khí” (Đại Việt firearms)
proposals.description: Give the Hand Cannoneer and an Imperial UT: Hand Cannoneers +1 range and +15% accuracy, and Fire Lancers train +25% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: Death of Chế Bồng Nga by firearm (1390); Hồ Nguyên Trừng in Ming service; Lê Thánh Tông's campaigns (1471, 1479–80); Sun Laichen, “Military Technology Transfers from Ming China...” (JSEAS, 2003).

proposals.title: Rattan Archer becomes a crossbowman (Nỏ Thủ) with “Nỏ Liên Châu”
proposals.description: Rename the unit as a crossbowman with a wicker shield. Add a UT that lets it fire 2 bolts per shot with -1 range.
proposals.historical_basis: The crossbow tradition in Âu Lạc and Đại Việt (Cổ Loa finds); the legend of Cao Lỗ and An Dương Vương's multiple-shot crossbow (legendary); Chinese accounts of the crossbowmen of Jiaozhi.

proposals.title: Vườn không nhà trống (empty land)
proposals.description: Enemy units inside Vietnamese territory (the radius of Town Centers and Castles) lose 1 HP every 3 s and do not regenerate. Vietnamese Villagers garrison buildings instantly.
proposals.historical_basis: The evacuation of Thăng Long and the depriving of the Yuan armies of provisions in 1258, 1285 and 1287–88; Trần Hưng Đạo's proclamation (Hịch tướng sĩ, 1284).

proposals.title: Replace Chatras with “Tượng binh” and give the Sanskrit name back to Champa
proposals.description: Keep the effect on Battle Elephants under a Sino-Vietnamese name (tượng binh: elephant troops) and reserve “Chatras” for a possible Champa civ.
proposals.historical_basis: Elephants in the Hồ and Lê armies; the term chattra belongs to the Indianised kingship of Champa and Angkor.

proposals.title: Red River dikes
proposals.description: Replace the economic tech bonus with: Farms +15% food, and Horse Collar and Heavy Plow free.
proposals.historical_basis: Systematic dike building under the Trần (1248) and state maintenance of the hydraulic network as the basis of the delta's population density.

contested: The historicity of the Hùng kings and of Văn Lang (the Đông Sơn archaeological culture versus a tradition elaborated in the 14th–15th centuries; Liam Kelley).
The origin of Vietnamese firearms (Chinese transfer versus local innovation) and the reverse influence on the Ming.
The nationalist narrative of “continuous resistance” to China, criticised by Keith W. Taylor for erasing regional diversity and periods of integration.
The nature of Champa: a unified kingdom or a federation of principalities (Po Dharma, Michael Vickery).
The use of stakes at the battle of Bạch Đằng in 981 (tradition) and the attribution of the archaeological stakes to 938 or to 1288.
key_sources: Ngô Sĩ Liên et al., Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư (1479)
Lê Tắc, An Nam chí lược (c. 1335)
Trần Hưng Đạo, Hịch tướng sĩ (1284)
Yuan shi; Ming shilu
Keith W. Taylor, The Birth of Vietnam (1983); A History of the Vietnamese (2013)
John K. Whitmore, Vietnam, Hồ Quý Ly, and the Ming (1985)
Sun Laichen, “Military Technology Transfers from Ming China and the Emergence of Northern Mainland Southeast Asia (c. 1390–1527)”, Journal of Southeast Asian Studies 34 (2003)
Liam C. Kelley, Beyond the Bronze Pillars (2005)
Momoki Shiro, studies on Lý–Trần Đại Việt

civs.represents: The Khmer Empire of Angkor (Kambuja), from Jayavarman II (traditionally 802) to the move of the capital southwards in the 15th century, with antecedents in Funan and Chenla. The high points are Suryavarman II (1113–c. 1150, Angkor Wat) and Jayavarman VII (1181–c. 1218, Bayon and Angkor Thom).
civs.period: 802 – c. 1431 (with antecedents from c. 550)
civs.verdict: The military core is among the best-founded in the game: the Ballista Elephant corresponds directly to the heavy double-bow crossbows mounted on elephants in the reliefs of the Bayon and Banteay Chhmar (late 12th–early 13th century), although the effect of Double Crossbows (an “additional projectile”) misreads the double bow. By contrast, the economic bonuses (advancing without buildings, garrisoning houses) are mechanics with no basis, and what really defined Angkor (water management, temple-mountains, the road network and Jayavarman VII's hospitals) is practically absent. The tech tree has anachronisms: Hand Cannoneer, Cavalry Archer and Parthian Tactics. The history text is good, but it presents contested theses as facts (the devarāja as “god-king”, the “hydraulic city”, the fall in 1431) and does not even name Jayavarman VII.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Khmer” is the correct endonym; the state was called Kambujadeśa. The period fits the AoE2 frame well (802–1431). There are two caveats. The Khmer identity of Funan is debated. And post-Angkor Cambodia (Longvek, 16th century), which had firearms and Portuguese and Spanish adventurers, is a different reality, and that is where the Hand Cannoneer belongs. The great rivals (Champa and Siam/Ayutthaya) do not exist as civs, although the text names them as the main enemies.

elements.explanation: The “Elephant” part is faithful: the reliefs of Angkor Wat show Suryavarman II and his generals on elephants, and those of the Bayon show war elephants. The “Siege” part is weaker: it rests on the heavy crossbows mounted on elephants and carts, but there is little evidence of elaborate siege warfare.

elements.element: No buildings required to advance to the next Age
elements.explanation: It is a pure mechanic. Any allusion to the mobility of the Khmer capitals would be far-fetched.

elements.element: Farmers don't require Mills or Town Centers to drop off food
elements.explanation: It vaguely evokes the scattered rice fields around Angkor's dams and reservoirs, but the mechanic (not needing drop-off points) does not reflect any identifiable trait.
It has no basis. According to Zhou Daguan, ordinary houses were made of wood and thatch, and had no defensive function.
It is a generic abstraction of skill with elephants. Nothing contradicts it, but nothing specifically supports it either.

The reliefs of the Bayon and Banteay Chhmar (reign of Jayavarman VII, 1181–c. 1218) show heavy double-bow crossbows mounted on elephants and also on wheeled carts. In some scenes the crews appear to wear the characteristic headdress of the Cham, which leads some authors to link them to Cham contingents in the service of Jayavarman VII. A Chinese origin (the Song multiple-bow bed crossbows) is a plausible hypothesis, but undocumented. The actual frequency of these weapons is unknown, and the ability to “destroy trees” is a game invention.
There is no solid evidence of blades attached to the tusks in the reliefs of Angkor. The practice is attested mainly in the Indian subcontinent and in later periods.

The name corresponds to the double-bow crossbows of the Khmer reliefs, which are related to the Song multiple-bow bed crossbows. But the second bow served mainly to give more power to a single large bolt, which is what the reliefs show; the effect (“fires an additional projectile”) misreads the weapon, although some Chinese bed crossbows could launch sheaves of arrows.
It is consistent with the heavy-crossbow tradition, but generic.

tree_issues.item: Cavalry Archer, Heavy Cavalry Archer, Parthian Tactics
tree_issues.problem: There is no basis: there is no evidence of Khmer mounted archers, and cavalry was marginal (small horses and riders with lances in the reliefs). Ironically, the only reference to mounted shooting in the Khmer–Cham wars comes from the opposing side: according to the Song shi, in 1171 a man from Fujian who had been swept to Champa advised the Cham king to adopt mounted archery against the Khmer elephants, and Champa bought dozens of horses.

It is anachronistic for Angkor, which declined before firearms spread in the region. Khmer firearms belong to the Longvek era (16th century), with adventurers such as Diogo Veloso and Blas Ruiz (1590s).

tree_issues.item: Champion and Plate Mail Armor absent
tree_issues.problem: It is faithful: Khmer infantry fought bare-chested or with light protection, with shield and spear (reliefs; Zhou Daguan).

tree_issues.item: Treadmill Crane absent and no building bonus
tree_issues.problem: The absence of the crane is defensible, because ramps, ropes and elephants were used. But the colossal building capacity (Angkor Wat, the barays, more than a thousand temples) has no mechanical expression at all.

tree_issues.item: Cannon Galleon and Elite Cannon Galleon
tree_issues.problem: It is anachronistic. By contrast, riverine naval warfare on the Tonle Sap, depicted in the Bayon reliefs, has no bonus.

history_text_issues.claim: Dates for Funan (68–550) and Chenla (550–802) presented as firm.
history_text_issues.problem: The dates are conventional and fragile: the Chinese sources on Funan only begin in the 3rd century (the mission of Kang Tai and Zhu Ying). The language and ethnicity of Funan are debated.
history_text_issues.correction: Give approximate dates and state the uncertainty about the Khmer identity of Funan (Michael Vickery).

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Jayavarman II crowned himself “God King (Deva Raja)” in 802, legitimising the kings as manifestations of Shiva or Vishnu.
history_text_issues.problem: It is a contested thesis presented as fact. The source is the Sdok Kak Thom inscription (1052), 250 years later. Kulke and Jacques argue that devarāja designated a protective deity of the kingdom (“king of the gods”), not the deified king. The date of 802 and the reign itself are debated.
history_text_issues.correction: Present the devarāja cult as being of debated interpretation and the date of 802 as traditional. Vickery and Jacques propose c. 770–834; Cœdès proposed 802–850.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the great irrigation systems ordered by the kings were essential for rice cultivation.
history_text_issues.problem: It is a contested thesis presented as fact: Groslier's “hydraulic city” has been criticised by van Liere and Acker. LiDAR (Evans, Fletcher) revealed a complex network, but the agricultural role of the barays remains debated.
history_text_issues.correction: Say that Angkor managed water on a large scale and that the relative weight of its irrigation, flood-control and symbolic functions is debated.

history_text_issues.claim: Presents the Siamese as the main enemies throughout the 9th–14th centuries.
history_text_issues.problem: It is partly anachronistic: the Tai/Siamese states (Sukhothai, c. 1240; Ayutthaya, 1351) only become serious rivals from the 13th century onwards.
history_text_issues.correction: For the 9th–12th centuries, the great adversaries were Champa and Đại Việt (campaigns of Suryavarman II, 1128–c. 1150); the Siamese come to the fore in the 14th–15th centuries.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the Cham attacked Angkor in 1177 and 1178.
history_text_issues.problem: The chronology is imprecise, and the main protagonist is missing.
history_text_issues.correction: Yaśodharapura was sacked in 1177. Jayavarman VII drove out the Cham (naval battle on the Tonle Sap, c. 1178–81), reigned from 1181 and subjugated Champa (a Khmer province in 1203–1220). He built the Bayon and Angkor Thom and promoted Mahāyāna Buddhism as the royal religion. The text does not even name him.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that rice cultivation declined because of a cooling of the climate.
history_text_issues.problem: It is imprecise. The best-documented climatic factor is monsoon variability.
history_text_issues.correction: Tree rings show prolonged droughts in the 14th–15th centuries, alternating with violent monsoons that damaged the hydraulic network (Buckley et al., PNAS, 2010).

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Ponhea Yat abandoned Angkor in 1431, marking the end of the empire.
history_text_issues.problem: It is a traditional date, taken from late chronicles, presented as certain. The decline was gradual, and Angkor was not completely abandoned.
history_text_issues.correction: The capital moved south (to the Phnom Penh region), partly for commercial reasons (Vickery). Angkor Wat continued to be used, and Ang Chan added reliefs to it in the mid-16th century.

missing_features: The barays and water management (the West Baray measures c. 8 × 2.1 km, 11th century)
The economy of the temple-mountains and of the labour attached to them
The road network with rest houses (121 “houses with fire”, Preah Khan inscription, 1191) and Jayavarman VII's hospitals (102 according to the Ta Prohm stele, 1186)
Naval warfare on the Tonle Sap against the Cham
The shift from Hinduism to Mahāyāna Buddhism (Jayavarman VII) and later to Theravāda
Markets run by women (Zhou Daguan)
Foreign contingents in the army, such as the “Syam Kuk” in Suryavarman II's procession at Angkor Wat
Massed infantry of spearmen with shields, the real core of the armies

proposals.title: Baray (reservoir)
proposals.description: A unique building, large and expensive in stone. Farms within a 10-tile radius produce +20% food and do not run out. It would replace “Farmers don't require Mills”.
proposals.historical_basis: East and West Barays (11th–12th centuries); work by Groslier, Fletcher and Evans (Greater Angkor Project), with the caveat that the agricultural function is debated.

proposals.title: Ārogyaśālā (Jayavarman VII's hospitals)
proposals.description: Units regenerate 20 HP/min within the radius of Monasteries and Town Centers. Herbal Medicine becomes free.
proposals.historical_basis: The hospital edict (inscriptions in dozens of hospital chapels) and the Ta Prohm stele (1186), with 102 hospitals.

proposals.title: Clean anachronisms out of the tech tree
proposals.description: Remove Cavalry Archer, Heavy Cavalry Archer, Parthian Tactics and Hand Cannoneer. In compensation, give Elephant Archer (shooters on elephants) and a cheaper infantry of spearmen with shields.
proposals.historical_basis: Reliefs of Angkor Wat, Bayon and Banteay Chhmar; Michel Jacq-Hergoualc'h, The Armies of Angkor (2007).

proposals.title: Temple-mountain
proposals.description: Replace “No buildings required to advance” with: Wonders and Monasteries are built +50% faster and cost -25% stone.
proposals.historical_basis: The construction of Angkor Wat (c. 1113–1150) and the Bayon; more than a thousand temples in the Angkor region.

proposals.title: Tonle Sap Fleet
proposals.description: Galley-line and Transport Ships +15% speed and +10% HP, and units disembark with +2 attack for 20 s.
proposals.historical_basis: Naval reliefs of the Bayon and Banteay Chhmar (war against Champa, c. 1177–81).

contested: The meaning of the devarāja cult: god-king or deity of the kingdom (Cœdès versus Kulke and Jacques).
The “hydraulic city” thesis and the function of the barays (Groslier versus van Liere and Acker; reinterpretation through LiDAR).
The “fall” of Angkor in 1431 versus a gradual decline and a commercial shift southwards.
The origin of the double-bow crossbows on elephants (Chinese via Champa? Cham contingents?).
The role of the conversion to Theravāda in the loss of royal legitimacy.
The dates of Jayavarman II and the ethnic identity of Funan.
key_sources: Zhou Daguan, Zhenla fengtu ji (The Customs of Cambodia, 1296–97)
Song shi, ch. 489 (Champa, 1171)
Inscriptions of Sdok Kak Thom (K.235, 1052), Ta Prohm (K.273, 1186) and Preah Khan (K.908, 1191)
Reliefs of Angkor Wat, Bayon and Banteay Chhmar
George Cœdès, Les États hindouisés d'Indochine et d'Indonésie (1964)
Michael Vickery, Society, Economics and Politics in Pre-Angkor Cambodia (1998)
Hermann Kulke, The Devarāja Cult (1978)
Michel Jacq-Hergoualc'h, The Armies of Angkor (2007)
Roland Fletcher, Damian Evans et al. (Greater Angkor Project, LiDAR)

civs.represents: The Bamar-dominated kingdoms of the Irrawaddy basin: the Pagan Empire (1044–1287/97) and the First Toungoo Empire (1510–1599), with antecedents in the Pyu and Mon city-states. It anachronistically includes elements of Manipur (Meitei), a neighbouring kingdom whose cavalry served the Burmese kings systematically only in the 18th–19th centuries.
civs.period: c. 1044 – 1599 (core periods: Pagan 1044–1287 and Toungoo 1510–1599)
civs.verdict: The civ has good religious touches: the cheaper Monastery and the visible relics faithfully allude to the relic policies of Anawrahta and Bayinnaung. The elephants are also coherent. But the unique unit and one of the unique techs (Arambai, Manipur Cavalry) belong to another people, the Meitei of Manipur, and above all to another era, that of the 18th–19th-century 'Kathè' cavalry. Worse still, the tech tree denies them the Hand Cannoneer, even though the game's own text stresses the Toungoo Empire's extensive use of firearms and of Portuguese gunners. The rest (infantry attack bonus, free Lumber Camp) is game balance. The history text is decent, but it confuses stupas with temples and closes the story in 1599, ignoring the rapid Toungoo restoration.
civs.naming_scope_issues: 'Burmese' is an exonym of European origin (Bamar/Myanmar). The civ merges distinct realities: the Bamar of Pagan and Toungoo, the Pyu, the Mon of Thaton and Hanthawaddy (1287–1539, a rival kingdom with its own golden age), the Arakanese of Mrauk-U, the Shan and also the Meitei of Manipur, today in India, from whom the Arambai and the Manipur Cavalry come. The Toungoo Empire, which the text values most, falls almost entirely after 1500.

elements.explanation: The game's text rightly states that the bulk of the armies was infantry, and there was cavalry (Shan contingents and Pagan cavalry). But the prestige arm was the elephants, which the label does not mention.
It may evoke the teak forests, but large-scale logging belongs mostly to the 18th–19th centuries. The link is weak.
It has no specific historical connection; it serves game balance.

Elephants were the elite of the Pagan and Toungoo armies; Bayinnaung fought the 'war of the white elephants' with Ayutthaya (1563–64). The armour is an abstraction. The bonus exactly repeats the effect of the Howdah UT.

Pagan is one of the largest religious complexes in the world, with thousands of stupas and temples (11th–13th centuries), sustained by donations to the sangha. Michael Aung-Thwin argues that these donations eventually drained the crown's resources, a debated thesis.

Arambai is the dart of the Meitei horsemen of Manipur. Manipuri cavalry in Burmese service ('Kathè', Cassay Horse) dates from the conquests of Alaungpaya and Hsinbyushin (from 1758 onwards). Bayinnaung subjugated Manipur in 1560, but there is no clear evidence of arambai units in the Toungoo army. It is therefore also an attribution to another people.
For the same reasons: Manipur cavalry as a corps of the Burmese army belongs to the 18th–19th centuries, and in the first half of the 18th century Manipur even devastated Upper Burma.

The game's text mentions platforms on elephants from which several archers shot, which is plausible. But 'howdah' is an Indo-Persian term (from the Arabic hawdaj), the platform was not really armour, and the effect repeats the civ bonus.

elements.element: Relics visible on the map (team bonus)
elements.explanation: The search for relics was royal policy. According to the chronicles, Anawrahta obtained a replica of the Buddha's Tooth Relic from Sri Lanka for the Shwezigon. In 1560–61 Bayinnaung tried to ransom the tooth captured in Jaffna by the Portuguese, which ended up destroyed in Goa (1561) by decision of the ecclesiastical authorities and of the viceroy Constantino de Bragança, and he received another 'tooth' from Kotte in 1576.

tree_issues.problem: This is a fundamental error, and it contradicts the game's own text. The Toungoo Empire made massive use of Portuguese musketeers and gunners: at the siege of Martaban (1541) and with Diogo Soares de Melo in the service of Tabinshwehti. As early as the 15th century, Ava was already using firearms of Ming origin (Sun Laichen; Lieberman). The Burmese have the Bombard Cannon, which makes the absence even more incoherent.

tree_issues.item: Cavalry Archer, Heavy Cavalry Archer, Parthian Tactics
tree_issues.problem: It is stretched: there is little evidence of Burmese mounted archers.

tree_issues.item: Arbalester, Thumb Ring, Leather and Ring Archer Armor missing
tree_issues.problem: There is no clear historical reason for the weakness of the archers: Burmese armies used bows and crossbows regularly. It is mainly a matter of balance.

tree_issues.item: No river bonus and no Fast Fire Ship
tree_issues.problem: Campaigns on the Irrawaddy depended on large fleets of oared war boats, and the Mon and Arakanese kingdoms were coastal powers. None of this appears.

history_text_issues.claim: Calls the stupas 'tall cylindrical temples'.
history_text_issues.problem: This is a conceptual error: a stupa (zedi) is a solid reliquary monument, not a temple. Pagan distinguishes stupas from hollow temples (gu).
history_text_issues.correction: The cylindrical Pyu stupas of Sri Ksetra (Bawbawgyi, Payagyi) were precursors of the Pagan stupas, such as the Shwezigon. The temples of Pagan are a different type.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Anawrahta conquered most of Upper and Lower Burma.
history_text_issues.problem: This is the traditional version of the late chronicles (including the conquest of Thaton in 1057 and the 'transmission' of Theravāda by the Mon), which the text does not discuss; Pagan's control over Lower Burma under Anawrahta is contested.
history_text_issues.correction: Mention that Michael Aung-Thwin (The Mists of Rāmañña, 2005) considers the centrality of Thaton a later historiographical myth, while others maintain the traditional reading on the basis of later inscriptions.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the Pagan army was defeated by the Mongols in 1285.
history_text_issues.problem: The chronology is simplified and the causes are incomplete.
history_text_issues.correction: There was the Battle of Ngasaunggyan (1277, described by Marco Polo) and invasions in 1283–85 and 1287. King Narathihapate fled (becoming known as 'Tayokpyemin', 'the king who fled from the Chinese') and was assassinated in 1287. The collapse was also due to internal fragmentation; whether the Mongols took Pagan itself is contested.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that in the 14th century four states filled the vacuum left by Pagan.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the Forty Years' War between Ava and Hanthawaddy (1385–1424) and the golden age of the Mon kingdom (Razadarit, Shin Sawbu, Dhammazedi). The narrative remains centred on the Bamar.
history_text_issues.correction: Give Hanthawaddy, the maritime and commercial power of Lower Burma, its due place.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that in 1599 the capital was besieged and burned, marking the end of the 'second Burmese Empire'.
history_text_issues.problem: This is misleading. Pegu was taken and destroyed by forces from Arakan and Toungoo, with mercenaries such as the Portuguese Filipe de Brito e Nicote, but the state was quickly restored.
history_text_issues.correction: Nyaungyan and Anaukpetlun rebuilt the state (Restored Toungoo, 1599–1752). In 1613 Anaukpetlun retook Syriam and executed Filipe de Brito.

missing_features: The firearms and Portuguese mercenaries of the Toungoo Empire
The irrigation of Kyaukse and Minbu, the 'granary' that sustained Pagan
The economy of temple-building and donations to the sangha
The system of service to the crown (ahmudan) and the rotating levies of the vassal states
White-elephant politics (war with Ayutthaya, 1563–64)
The river fleets of the Irrawaddy
The Mon kingdom of Hanthawaddy and the maritime trade of Pegu and Martaban
Religious ties with Sri Lanka (missions, relics, reforms of the sangha)

proposals.title: Bayingyi (Portuguese gunners)
proposals.description: Give the Hand Cannoneer to the tech tree. Imperial UT: Castles can train mercenary musketeers (gold-only cost, fast training), and Bombard Cannons and Hand Cannoneers gain +15% accuracy.
proposals.historical_basis: Portuguese in the service of Tabinshwehti and Bayinnaung (siege of Martaban, 1541; Diogo Soares de Melo); communities of gunners of Portuguese descent (bayingyi, from the Persian farangi) settled by Anaukpetlun after 1613; Fernão Mendes Pinto, Peregrinação; Victor Lieberman, Burmese Administrative Cycles (1984).

proposals.title: White Elephant (Hsinbyu)
proposals.description: Replace the Arambai with an elite elephant, limited to 1 per Castle, that gives +2 attack and +1 armour to nearby units. If it dies, nearby units lose morale (-1 attack for 30 s).
proposals.historical_basis: War of the white elephants with Ayutthaya (1563–64); Bayinnaung, the 'Lord of Many White Elephants' (Hsinbyumyashin), in the chronicle Hanthawaddy Hsinbyumyashin Ayedawbon.

proposals.title: Kyaukse (irrigation)
proposals.description: Replace 'Infantry +1/+2/+3 attack' with: Farms +15% food and free Farm rebuilding from the Castle Age.
proposals.historical_basis: Dams and canals of Kyaukse and Minbu, attributed by the chronicles to Anawrahta; Michael Aung-Thwin, Irrigation in the Heartland of Burma (1990).

proposals.title: Ahmudan (service to the crown)
proposals.description: Replace the Manipur Cavalry: Infantry and Battle Elephants trained at Castles cost -25% gold, and Villagers within a Castle's radius work +10% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: System of hereditary service groups (ahmudan) and vassal levies under the Toungoo (Lieberman).

proposals.title: Return the Arambai to the Meitei
proposals.description: Remove the Arambai and Manipur Cavalry from the Burmese civ and reserve them for a future Meitei/Manipuri civ, or for a late Imperial tech called 'Kathè Horse'.
proposals.historical_basis: Manipuri cavalry (Cassay Horse) in Burmese service belongs to the Konbaung era (from 1758 onwards).

contested: The role of the Mon and of Thaton in the formation of Pagan (G. H. Luce versus Michael Aung-Thwin).
The weight of the Mongol invasions versus the internal crisis in the fall of Pagan, and whether the Mongols reached the capital.
The myth of the 'Three Shan Brothers' and the nature of the Myinsaing/Ava period (Aung-Thwin).
The causes of the Toungoo collapse in 1599: overextension and depopulation through levies, or climatic factors (the game's text asserts the cooling as fact).
The thesis that religious donations drained Pagan's fiscal base (Aung-Thwin).
key_sources: Hmannan Yazawin (Glass Palace Chronicle, 1832)
U Kala, Maha Yazawin (c. 1724)
Myazedi inscription (1112–13) and other Pagan inscriptions
Fernão Mendes Pinto, Peregrinação (1614)
Diogo do Couto, Décadas da Ásia
G. H. Luce, Old Burma–Early Pagan (1969–70)
Michael Aung-Thwin, Pagan: The Origins of Modern Burma (1985); The Mists of Rāmañña (2005)
Victor Lieberman, Burmese Administrative Cycles (1984); Strange Parallels, vol. 1 (2003)
Than Tun, studies on Pagan
Sun Laichen, 'Military Technology Transfers from Ming China...' (2003)

civs.represents: An umbrella civ for the Malay-Indonesian world (Nusantara): Srivijaya (7th–13th centuries, Sumatra), the Javanese kingdoms (Sailendra/Mataram, Singhasari and Majapahit, 1293–c. 1527) and the Malacca Sultanate (c. 1400–1511). In practice it merges Malays and Javanese, two distinct peoples and political traditions.
civs.period: c. 671 – 1511 (from Srivijaya to the fall of Malacca)
civs.verdict: The naval label, Thalassocracy and Forced Levy reflect well the nature of the Malay thalassocracies and the manpower-centred warfare described by Anthony Reid. But the civ is an amalgam: the history text devotes a third of its length to Majapahit, a Javanese rather than Malay empire, and the unique unit (Karambit Warrior) turns a small Minangkabau utility knife into a mass troop type with no record whatsoever. The most characteristic elements are missing: the enormous Javanese jong, the Orang Laut, the light artillery (lela/rentaka) that the Portuguese found at Malacca in 1511, entrepôt trade and Islam. The text ends with a Eurocentric framing (European dominance of trade after 1511) that current historiography rejects.
civs.naming_scope_issues: This is the civ's most serious problem. 'Malay' (Melayu) originally designated the kingdom of Jambi, in Sumatra, and only later the cultural identity centred on Malacca. Majapahit and the builders of Borobudur were Javanese, with their own language, script and political tradition. The text also includes the Philippines, Timor and Borneo in the 'archipelago', extending the label to dozens of Austronesian peoples. The Islam of Malacca and Pasai, decisive from the 15th century onwards, is not reflected in the mechanics at all.

elements.explanation: Srivijaya and Malacca were thalassocracies that controlled the Strait of Malacca and the Sunda Strait, relying on the Orang Laut. The Javanese built large junks (jong).

elements.element: Advancing to the next Age is +66% faster
elements.explanation: It has no historical basis. An allusion to the rapid rise of port cities would be stretched.
Malay infantry was typically light, with a shield (perisai), spear and kris, and mail coats (baju rantai) only for elites. Free armour contradicts the historical profile.

Malacca fielded war elephants against the Portuguese in 1511 (Comentários of Afonso de Albuquerque), and the sultanates of Sumatra (later Aceh) used them. But Java had almost no war elephants, and the cost reduction is an invention.
Fixed fish traps (kelong, sero, bagan) and fish as a dietary staple are genuine features of Malay coastal societies.

The karambit, traditionally associated with the Minangkabau region (West Sumatra), is a small curved knife used in farming and for close-range defence. There is no record of military corps armed with it. Malay battle weapons were the spear, the kris, the shield and the blowpipe. The 'half population' is pure mechanics, although it evokes mass warfare by levies.
The concept, an academic term of Greek origin, applies well to Srivijaya and Malacca. Docks turned into fortified harbours with light artillery are an acceptable abstraction.

Warfare in Southeast Asia aimed above all at capturing and mobilising people: the common people (rakyat) were called up, and dependants and debt slaves (hamba) and corvée labour supplied troops (Anthony Reid). Swapping gold for food conveys levy infantry well.
Malay ports were defended with palisades and light pieces (lela, rentaka), and Malacca had four harbour masters (syahbandar), according to Tomé Pires. It is a reasonable abstraction.
It may evoke maritime intelligence networks and the Orang Laut as lookouts over the straits; it is generic.

tree_issues.problem: It is debatable. According to João de Barros, Albuquerque captured at Malacca, in 1511, about 3,000 of a total of 8,000 artillery pieces; other accounts speak of 2,000 bronze ones, and the figures are uncertain and probably inflated. Portuguese sources also mention firearms coming from Java. Light artillery (lela, rentaka) was ubiquitous. The Malay have Bombard Cannon, which makes the absence of hand-held firearms hardly consistent.
It is unfounded: the Malay world has no tradition of mounted archers.
It is stretched: cavalry was marginal in Malay warfare.
It is stretched: the bow and the crossbow carried little weight. The characteristic missile weapons were the blowpipe (sumpit), darts and throwing spears (lembing) and, later, firearms.
It is plausible for Malacca, which was defended by wooden palisades. But the Majapahit capital (Trowulan) had brick walls, another sign of the Malay/Javanese fusion.

tree_issues.item: Champion, Hussar, Heavy Cavalry Archer and heavy barding missing
tree_issues.problem: It is faithful to the profile of light-infantry and naval forces.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the islanders developed sophisticated navigation and shipbuilding 'beginning in 50,000 BC'.
history_text_issues.problem: It conflates two phenomena: the first crossing to Sahul (Australia/New Guinea), more than 50,000 years ago, by non-Austronesian populations, and the Austronesian expansion.
history_text_issues.correction: The linguistic ancestors of the Malays arrived with the Austronesian expansion (c. 3000–1500 BC, from Taiwan), which brought outrigger canoes and ocean navigation (Peter Bellwood).

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Srivijayan naval expeditions sailed up the Mekong until the rise of the Khmer halted them.
history_text_issues.problem: It rests on weak sources: an Arabic tale (Abu Zayd al-Sirafi, c. 916) about the maharaja of Zabaj who beheaded a Khmer king, and the ambiguous reference to 'Java' in the Sdok Kak Thom inscription.
history_text_issues.correction: Present it as a tradition of uncertain interpretation; it is not established that 'Java/Zabaj' is Srivijaya, nor that there was any dominion on the Mekong.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Srivijaya's vassals in Java built Borobudur and Sewu.
history_text_issues.problem: It is speculative. The relationship between the Sailendra of Central Java and Srivijaya is one of the most debated questions in the region's historiography.
history_text_issues.correction: Borobudur (c. 780–830) was built under the Sailendra dynasty. Whether the Sailendra were vassals, overlords or kin of the house of Srivijaya is not established.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Majapahit stretched from the Malay Peninsula to New Guinea.
history_text_issues.problem: It is based on the list of tributaries in a court poem, the Nagarakretagama (1365), which is above all a claim to prestige.
history_text_issues.correction: Majapahit directly controlled East Java and parts of Bali and Madura. Over the rest it exercised, at most, a nominal or commercial suzerainty.

history_text_issues.claim: Presents Gajah Mada (1313–1364) as prime minister to 'two emperors'.
history_text_issues.problem: His date of birth is unknown, and one of the two sovereigns was a queen.
history_text_issues.correction: Gajah Mada (d. 1364) was mahapatih under Queen Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi and King Hayam Wuruk; his Palapa oath is traditionally dated to 1336.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that puppet theatre and orchestras were developed under Majapahit.
history_text_issues.problem: It is misleading as to their origin.
history_text_issues.correction: Wayang performances are mentioned in Javanese inscriptions of the 9th–10th centuries (e.g. in the reign of Balitung, c. 907), and musical ensembles appear in the Borobudur reliefs. Majapahit developed these arts, but did not create them.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Parameswara converted to Islam at the end of his reign, founding the Sultanate (1414–1511).
history_text_issues.problem: It is contested. The Sejarah Melayu, Tomé Pires and the Ming sources disagree on the founding, on Parameswara's career and on who converted.
history_text_issues.correction: The conversion may have been his successor's (Megat Iskandar Shah). The title of sultan only becomes fixed with Muzaffar Shah (c. 1445). The founding date of Malacca (c. 1400) is approximate.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that, despite early contacts, Muslim communities were limited before Malacca.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the region's first sultanate.
history_text_issues.correction: Samudera-Pasai, in northern Sumatra, was already a sultanate by the end of the 13th century (gravestone of Sultan Malik al-Saleh, d. 1297), and was visited by Ibn Battuta in 1345–46.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the Portuguese conquest of 1511 marked the end of the Sultanate and that, from then on, Europeans would dominate the archipelago's trade.
history_text_issues.problem: It is Eurocentric and factually exaggerated.
history_text_issues.correction: The dynasty continued in Johor and Perak. Aceh, Johor, Banten, Makassar, Chinese junks and Gujarati merchants continued to dominate much of the trade, and European hegemony only arrived with the Dutch VOC in the 17th century (Anthony Reid).

missing_features: The Javanese jong, enormous junks described by Tomé Pires and Gaspar Correia (Pati Unus's fleet against Malacca, 1513)
The Orang Laut ('sea people'), the naval mainstay and guard of Srivijaya and Malacca
Light bronze artillery (lela, rentaka, cetbang) and the firearms of Java
Entrepôt trade and Malacca's syahbandar system, with merchants from dozens of nations
Islam as a factor of political and commercial unity from the 15th century onwards
The kris as a weapon and status object, and amok as a military phenomenon described by the Portuguese
Warfare centred on capturing populations rather than territory
The distinction between an agrarian, brick-built Java (Majapahit) and the maritime Malay world

proposals.title: Split 'Malay' and 'Javanese'
proposals.description: Keep 'Malay' for Srivijaya, Melayu and Malacca (naval, commercial, Islamic from the 15th century) and create a 'Javanese' civ for Mataram, Singhasari and Majapahit (agrarian, monumental, with cetbang and jong).
proposals.historical_basis: Linguistic, epigraphic and political differences between Sumatra/Malacca and Java; O. W. Wolters; Leonard Andaya, Leaves of the Same Tree (2008).

proposals.title: Jong
proposals.description: A very tough unique ship (high HP, high pierce armour), slow, with a large transport capacity (20 units) and shooters on board. Trained at the Harbor in the Castle Age.
proposals.historical_basis: Portuguese descriptions of Javanese junks of several hundred tons (Tomé Pires, Suma Oriental; Gaspar Correia, Lendas da Índia); studies by Pierre-Yves Manguin.

proposals.title: Lela and Rentaka
proposals.description: The Galley line, Harbors and Towers fire an extra grapeshot projectile (short range, light area damage), and Bombard Towers cost -25%.
proposals.historical_basis: Artillery captured at Malacca in 1511 (João de Barros, Décadas; Comentários of Albuquerque); light Malay-Javanese bronze pieces.

proposals.title: Orang Laut instead of Karambit Warrior
proposals.description: Amphibious infantry trained at the Harbor: half population, fast, can embark and disembark without a Transport, and has a bonus against transport and trade ships.
proposals.historical_basis: The Orang Laut as the naval force of Srivijaya and Malacca (O. W. Wolters, The Fall of Srivijaya in Malay History, 1970; Leonard Andaya).

proposals.title: Syahbandar (entrepôt)
proposals.description: Replace 'Advancing to the next Age +66% faster' with: Trade Cogs generate +20% gold, and Market rates are 10% better.
proposals.historical_basis: Malacca's four syahbandar and its multinational merchant community (Tomé Pires; Ma Huan, Yingya shenglan).

proposals.title: Tech tree consistent with Malay warfare
proposals.description: Remove Cavalry Archer, Arbalester and Thumb Ring. Add a blowpipe skirmisher (poison: damage over time) and give Hand Cannoneer from the Imperial Age.
proposals.historical_basis: Use of the blowpipe (sumpit) in the peninsula and in Borneo; Javanese and Malay firearms in the early 16th century.

contested: The nature and location of Srivijaya: Palembang, Jambi or Chaiya; a centralised empire or a network of kedatuan (Hermann Kulke).
The relationship between the Sailendra and Srivijaya.
The real extent of Majapahit according to the Nagarakretagama.
The founding date of Malacca and who converted to Islam (Parameswara or his successor).
The dating of the Majapahit cetbang to the 14th century, argued by some authors on the basis of late sources.
The figures for artillery captured at Malacca in 1511.
key_sources: Yijing, travel accounts (671–695)
Kedukan Bukit (682) and Kota Kapur (686) inscriptions
Mpu Prapanca, Nagarakretagama (1365)
Pararaton (15th–16th centuries)
Sejarah Melayu (Malay Annals)
Hikayat Raja Pasai
Ma Huan, Yingya shenglan (1433)
Tomé Pires, Suma Oriental (c. 1512–15)

groups.cross_civ_notes:
1) A common enemy that the game ignores: all six civs faced the Mongols/Yuan or had direct contact with them. This was the case for Goryeo (1231–59), Đại Việt (1258, 1285, 1287–88), Japan (1274, 1281), Pagan (1277–87) and Java (1292–93); Angkor received a Yuan embassy in 1296, which gave rise to Zhou Daguan's account. It would be an axis of identity far more historically grounded than several current bonuses: for example, Vietnamese guerrilla warfare and stakes, the Hakata wall and Korean resistance from Ganghwa.

2) Generic elephants with swapped names. Khmer, Burmese, Malay and Vietnamese share the same Battle Elephant (with Bengalis and Dravidians), and the techs use terms from other cultures: “Chatras” (Sanskrit, specific to Champa and Angkor) was given to the sinicised Đại Việt, and “Howdah” (Indo-Persian) to the Burmese. In the Burmese civ, Howdah exactly repeats the civ bonus (+1/+1 armour). What is missing is a differentiation between the Angkorian elephant (crossbow platform), the Burmese one (white elephant, royal symbol), the Malay one (Malacca, Sumatra) and the Vietnamese one (less central).

3) Firearms are inverted relative to history. Sun Laichen's research shows that firearms of Ming origin were decisive for Đại Việt and for Upper Burma between c. 1390 and 1527. Next came Portuguese guns in Japan (1543), in Toungoo Burma and in Longvek Cambodia. In the game, however, the Khmer (whose apogee predates gunpowder) have Hand Cannoneer (but not Bombard Cannon), while the Vietnamese and the Burmese, the region's true gunpowder powers, and the Malay have Bombard Cannon but not Hand Cannoneer, which also inverts the order of diffusion (light firearms before heavy artillery). In the Vietnamese and Burmese cases, the game's own texts speak of gunpowder or of Portuguese firearms and gunners.

4) Horse archers where they never existed. Khmer and Burmese have Cavalry Archer, Heavy Cavalry Archer and Parthian Tactics; the Vietnamese have Cavalry Archer and Heavy Cavalry Archer (without Parthian Tactics); the Malay have Cavalry Archer. None of these societies has a corresponding tradition (the only reference to mounted archery in the Khmer–Cham wars, in the Song shi, is on the Cham side, in 1171). For the Japanese and the Koreans, by contrast, mounted archery is central and well represented.

5) Duplications and names. The Japanese Yasama literally means “arrow slits” and coexists with Arrowslits. The Korean Eupseong means “town wall” but applies to towers. Kataparuto is transliterated English. Shinkichon uses a non-standard romanisation (Singijeon). Double Crossbows interprets the double bow as a double shot. In all civs, the Monastery techs have Christian names (Heresy, Atonement, Redemption, Theocracy), which is especially incongruous for Buddhist, Hindu and Muslim societies.

6) Overlaps with other civs. The Rocket Cart (Chinese, Koreans, Jurchens, Khitans) is faithful in the Korean case (hwacha). The Fire Lancer is shared by Chinese, Jurchens, Khitans, Koreans and Vietnamese. Paper Money belongs to the Vietnamese, although paper money is a Chinese invention (jiaozi, c. 1024) that the game's Chinese do not have as a tech. The Koreans fought the Khitans (993–1019) and the Jurchens (1107–09), now present in the game, without this being reflected (and the Korean text calls the Liao “China”). The Chinese Three Kingdoms civs (Wu, Wei, Shu, 3rd century) fall outside the time frame and shift the focus away from medieval East Asia.

7) Structural absences. Siam (Sukhothai/Ayutthaya) is cited in the Khmer and Burmese texts as the main adversary and does not exist. Champa is the centuries-old rival of Đại Việt and of Angkor, and its traits are scattered across the Vietnamese (Chatras) and the Khmer (crossbows possibly operated by Cham). Also missing are the Mon (Hanthawaddy), the Javanese (merged into the Malay), Ryūkyū and the Meitei, whose Arambai and Manipur Cavalry were assigned to the Burmese. The Malay is the most problematic umbrella civ in the group.

8) Unexplored Portuguese connections (relevant to a Portuguese user). Tanegashima (1542/43) and the Nanban trade; the conquest of Malacca (1511) and the Malay artillery captured there; the mercenaries of Tabinshwehti and Bayinnaung, and Filipe de Brito at Syriam (1599–1613); the destruction in Goa (1561) of the Buddha's tooth that Bayinnaung tried to ransom; Diogo Veloso in Cambodia (1590s). Sources such as Tomé Pires, Fernão Mendes Pinto (with caution), Luís Fróis, António Galvão and João de Barros are essential for four of these six civs.

9) Uneven quality of the history texts. Those of the Japanese (1999, The Age of Kings) and the Koreans (2000, The Conquerors) contain Orientalist tropes (Japan “isolated” and on the “margins of civilisation”, medieval bushidō) and factual errors (Fujiwara in 645, a Korean military regime of “sixty years”). Those of the Vietnamese, Khmer, Burmese and Malay (2016, Rise of the Rajas) are considerably more up to date, but present contested theses as facts: devarāja, the “hydraulic city”, the fall of Angkor in 1431, the extent of Majapahit and Anawrahta's dominion over Lower Burma.

10) Relative ranking (on a scale where the average AoE2 civ ≈ 5): Koreans and Khmer (6) are the best grounded in their military core; Japanese and Vietnamese (5) sit at the average; Burmese and Malay (4) suffer from features that belong to other peoples (Manipur, Java) and from central omissions (firearms, jong and Orang Laut).

verification_log.change: “Infantry attacks +33% faster” moved from stretched to abstraction: the fame of the Japanese sword has a documented basis in the 15th–16th centuries (massive export of swords to the Ming; a Kage-ryū manual captured in 1561 and included by Qi Jiguang in his own manual), although the bow dominated most of the period (Conlan).

Kataparuto moved from wrong to unfounded: the problem is the lack of basis and the anachronistic name, not an explicit factual premise. I added the ōyumi (ritsuryō siege crossbow, with no recorded use after the 12th century) and the gift of stone-throwers captured from the Sui by Goguryeo in 618 (Nihon Shoki); I specified that the Ōsaka cannons were used by Tokugawa Ieyasu.
New error in the history text: the “largely ceremonial” Yamato court in the 5th century is anachronistic (the period of the “five kings of Wa”, the Inariyama sword of 471).

The criticism about the Mongol invasions was lowered to minor and rephrased: the text does not claim a storm in 1274 and the 1281 typhoon is well documented; the flaw is one of omission (Hakata wall, composition of the fleets).

Tech tree: I added Heavy Scorpion as consistent (ōyumi); I specified that the armour plating of Kuki Yoshitaka's ships (1578) is attested in only one diary and is debated; I added the testimony of Song Hŭi-gyŏng (1420) on multiple harvests; I nuanced Thumb Ring (the Japanese draw is a thumb draw, with a glove).

Tanegashima: the date 1543 (Teppōki) is disputed, with 1542 (António Galvão) as the rival date, and the presence of Fernão Mendes Pinto is doubtful; this moved to contested and into the basis of the proposal.
Label: Gwiju (1019) was a pitched-battle victory by Gang Gam-chan, not a fortress defence; I reworded the list of examples (Heunghwajin, 1010).

Gu Jinchon (669): I corrected the wording “refused to reproduce”; according to the Samguk Sagi, the crossbows made in China reached only 30 and 60 paces, he blamed the wood, and he was suspected of hiding the secret.
Mangonel/Onager absent: I added the gift of Sui stone-throwers by Goguryeo to Japan in 618 and the Goryeosa reference for Gwiju (1231).
New error in the history text: the Amnok frontier in 993 was with the Liao (Khitan), not with China, and it was obtained through negotiation (Seo Hui).
Movable type: I added that the text places 1234 in the context of Joseon, when it belongs to Goryeo, and that the 1234 printing is known only from a text by Yi Gyu-bo.
I corrected the date of the Korean history text: the Koreans were introduced in The Conquerors (2000), not in 1999 (also in the cross-civ notes).

Hand Cannoneer absent: I added that the game's own text asserts the use of gunpowder in 1390, which makes the absence an internal contradiction; new entry on Bombard Cannon being present without Hand Cannoneer.
Bạch Đằng: the stakes are documented for 938 and 1288; for 981 they are only tradition. Corrected in the tech tree, in the missing features and in contested.

The criticism about paper money was rephrased: 1396 falls within the Trần period, and the problem is the omission of the agent (Hồ Quý Ly); the criticism about the Lê dynasty being the longest was lowered to minor (it is nominally true).
To the “first century BC” error I added the simplification of the motive (“trade interests”): the conquest of 111 BC took advantage of a crisis in Nanyue in the context of Han Wudi's expansion.

Proposal “Thần Cơ” renamed to “Hỏa khí” (a safe generic term), because I could not confirm “thần cơ” as a Vietnamese designation; the Cao Lỗ legend is now marked as legendary and I added the archaeological finds from Cổ Loa. I checked the years 1257/1284/1287 in the text: they correspond to the start of the campaigns in the lunar calendar, so I did not treat them as an error.

Ballista Elephant: I removed the false claim that a Song official taught the Cham to use siege crossbows in 1171–72. The Song shi (ch. 489) says that a man from Fujian taught the Cham king mounted archery (騎射) and that Champa bought dozens of horses. The Chinese origin of the double-bow crossbows is now a hypothesis; the link to Cham contingents remains as the interpretation of some authors.
Double Crossbows moved from faithful to plausible: the double bow in the reliefs gives power to a single large bolt, and the “additional projectile” effect misreads the weapon.
The label “Siege and Elephant” moved from faithful to plausible, because the siege component has little basis; Tusk Swords was rewritten without the first person.

New error in the history text: the Siamese only become main adversaries from the 13th century onwards. Jayavarman VII “promoted” Mahāyāna Buddhism rather than “converted the state”. I added the Song shi evidence (1171) to the criticism of the Cavalry Archer.

The criticism about Thaton was rephrased and lowered to minor: the text does not mention Thaton; what it asserts is Anawrahta's dominion over Lower Burma, which is contested (Aung-Thwin) rather than an established error.

Proposal “Feringhi” renamed to “Bayingyi”, the Burmese term (from the Persian farangi) for the communities of gunners of Portuguese descent (settled by Anaukpetlun after 1613). I corrected the chronicle's title to Hanthawaddy Hsinbyumyashin Ayedawbon.

Arambai: “there is no record” became “there is no clear evidence”. I toned down the attribution of the destruction of the Buddha's tooth in Goa (ecclesiastical authorities and viceroy). The 1599 climatic cooling and Aung-Thwin's fiscal thesis moved to contested.

Malacca's artillery: the figure of c. 3,000 cannons is attributed to João de Barros (3,000 out of 8,000), with other accounts of 2,000 bronze pieces; I marked the numbers as uncertain and added them to contested. I noted that the Malay have Bombard Cannon without Hand Cannoneer.

New errors in the history text: Srivijaya's expeditions to the Mekong rest on an Arab tale (Abu Zayd) and on an ambiguous reference to “Java”; Gajah Mada's birth is unknown and he served a queen and a king, not “two emperors”. Wayang was changed to “9th–10th centuries”.
Proposal “Lela and Cetbang” renamed to “Lela and Rentaka”, because the 14th-century dating of the cetbang is contested; I softened “kerah” to “corvée” in Forced Levy.

I checked the game facts in data.json: Vietnamese without Parthian Tactics; Malay with Cavalry Archer only; Khmer with Hand Cannoneer but without Bombard Cannon; Vietnamese, Burmese and Malay with Bombard Cannon but without Hand Cannoneer; Fire Lancer for Chinese, Jurchens, Khitans, Koreans and Vietnamese. I corrected notes 3, 4 and 6 accordingly.

I kept the scores (Koreans 6, Khmer 6, Japanese 5, Vietnamese 5, Burmese 4, Malay 4). The downgrade of Double Crossbows and of the Khmer label was offset by the solidity of the Ballista Elephant, and the upgrade of the Japanese bonus does not change the average.

civs.represents: The Mexica (Tenochca) of Tenochtitlan and, by extension, the Triple Alliance (Excan Tlahtoloyan: Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan) that dominated much of central Mesoamerica; implicitly, also the Nahua peoples of the Valley of Mexico.
civs.period: c. 1325 (traditional founding of Tenochtitlan) – 1521 (fall of Tenochtitlan); imperial peak 1428–1519.
civs.verdict: The military core is reasonable. An infantry civilization with no cavalry, with the elite orders (jaguar and eagle), the spear-thrower (atlatl), the villager carry bonus (tlamemeh) and the faster-training bonus (universal military education), rests on defensible abstractions. What is missing, however, is the economy that sustained the empire: chinampas, tribute, markets and pochteca. The starting gold is only loosely linked to tribute in gold, and the more lucrative Relics have no basis. The tech tree inherits serious anachronisms (Trebuchet, Siege Ram, European ships, Plate Mail, Horse Collar) and denies Architecture and Masonry to one of the great pre-modern builders, while granting Fortified Wall. The history text, inherited from 1999, is the worst part: it portrays a society “in decline” that “invented little”, attributes smallpox to earlier “traders” and reduces imperial politics to the search for victims.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Aztecs” is a scholarly term, derived from Aztlan, popularised by Clavijero (18th century) and by Humboldt and Prescott (19th century). The people called themselves Mexica or Tenochca, and the “empire” was the Triple Alliance, with the Acolhua of Texcoco and the Tepanecs of Tlacopan. The period covered (c. 1325–1521, an empire only from 1428) occupies only the last century of the game's 500–1500 frame, so the earlier central Mexican powers (Teotihuacan until c. 550–650, the Toltecs of Tula c. 900–1150) are left unrepresented or are implicitly absorbed by the Aztecs and the Mayans. “Garland Wars” is an unusual translation of xōchiyāōyōtl, whose usual form is “flower war”. The role of Texcoco and that of the Spaniards' Tlaxcaltec allies are also lost.

elements.explanation: The infantry is faithful: Mesoamerica had no horses or draught animals, and all armies were infantry. The Monk is defensible given the weight of the priesthood (tlamacazqueh), the temples and the ritual calendar. Priests also accompanied campaigns, at the head of which went the bearers of the divine images (teomamaqueh), and could capture prisoners (Hassig). However, the mechanic of “converting” enemies has no Mexica parallel.

The link is weak. Gold was not currency in Mesoamerica: exchange was carried out with cacao beans, cotton cloaks (quachtli) and, in the south and west, copper axes. The metal was a luxury good, often worked by Mixtec goldsmiths. It is true that imperial tribute included gold (gold dust in feather quills, discs and jewels, according to the Codex Mendoza), and Axayácatl's treasure impressed the Spaniards, but that does not justify a starting bonus for a Dark Age village: it is mostly balance.

It is a good abstraction of the economy of human porters (tlamemeh), who carried loads of c. 20–25 kg in daily stages in a world with neither wheeled transport nor pack animals (Hassig, Trade, Tribute, and Transportation, 1985). The tribute and the supply of Tenochtitlan depended on them and on canoes.

It corresponds to rapid mobilisation based on universal military training. Boys went through the telpochcalli (commoners) or the calmecac (nobles), and contingents were raised by calpolli and by city within a few days (Hassig, Aztec Warfare, 1988).

elements.element: Monks gain +5 HP for each researched Monastery technology
elements.explanation: The link is weak, though not arbitrary: Mexica priests practised fasting and self-sacrifice and went to war. The progression “more monastery technologies, more HP” is purely mechanical, so it does not amount to an abstraction of a real trait.

The ocelomeh (jaguar warriors) were one of the two elite military orders, alongside the cuāuhmeh (eagles). Entry depended mainly on capturing several prisoners (the Codex Mendoza illustrates the progression up to four captives) and on noble birth; there were also higher grades, such as the otontin and the cuachicqueh. The damage bonus after victories evokes this promotion through captures well, although the merit lay in capturing, not killing. They fought with the macuahuitl and wore tlahuiztli suits, and the anti-infantry role is consistent in a world without cavalry.

elements.element: Eagle Scout / Eagle Warrior / Elite Eagle Warrior (regional unit shared with Mayans)
elements.explanation: The cuāuhtli order is real and had the same status as the jaguar order. Turning it into the cheap, fast scouting unit, available from the Feudal Age (and as the starting scout in the Dark Age), inverts the social pyramid. The bulk of the army consisted of commoners (macehualtin) with shield and club, and scouts and spies formed a separate category (quimichtin, “mice”, according to Sahagún).

The spear-thrower (ahtlatl) with darts (tlacochtli) was a real and feared weapon, and some conquistador accounts credit the darts with the ability to pierce armour. It is, however, a much older pan-Mesoamerican weapon (already present at Teotihuacan), and the Mayans have another UT based on it (Hul'che). Among the Mexica it was mainly an elite weapon used at the opening of combat (Hassig).

The xōchiyāōyōtl did exist, mainly against Tlaxcala, Huexotzinco and Cholula. The bonus can be read as combat experience accumulated in those clashes, but the declared aim was to capture, not to kill, and Hassig interprets it as a strategy of attrition and a show of force. A generic +4 attack for all infantry captures neither reading well.
Relics are a Christian concept. The Mexica equivalents, the sacred bundles (tlaquimilolli) carried by the teomamaqueh, did not generate wealth. It has no historical basis.

tree_issues.item: Architecture, Masonry and Keep (missing), with Fortified Wall and Guard Tower present
tree_issues.problem: The absence is hard to defend and the combination is incoherent. The Mexica and their allies built the Templo Mayor, causeways across the lake with removable bridges, the Chapultepec aqueduct and the dike of Nezahualcóyotl (c. 1449, c. 16 km), as well as fortified frontier garrisons such as Oztuma, facing the Purépecha.

tree_issues.item: Trebuchet, Siege Onager, Siege Ram, Scorpion
tree_issues.problem: They are anachronistic. Mesoamerica knew neither torsion nor counterweight engines; cities were taken by assault, by burning the main temple and by sieges that starved them out. The only trebuchet used at Tenochtitlan was built by the Spaniards in 1521, and it failed (Bernal Díaz; Cortés, third letter).

tree_issues.item: Navy (War Galley, Fast Fire Ship, Carrack, Hulk-line, Catapult Galleon, Demolition Ship)
tree_issues.problem: It is anachronistic. The real naval force was thousands of canoes (acalli) on Lake Texcoco, which forced Cortés to build 13 brigantines in 1521. A war-canoe unit is missing.

tree_issues.item: Blacksmith: Iron Casting, Blast Furnace, Chain/Plate Mail Armor
tree_issues.problem: There was no iron: metals (copper, gold, silver) were mainly ornamental and blades were made of obsidian. On the other hand, access to Gambesons is faithful: the quilted-cotton ichcahuipilli was adopted by the Spaniards themselves.
They are anachronistic: there were neither draught animals nor ploughs. Agriculture used the digging stick (huictli; “coa” in colonial Spanish, a word of Taíno origin) and chinampas.
