The wheel had no use in transport (it appears only on figurines), and trade was carried out by pochteca, porters and canoes. Relics are a Christian concept.
It is faithful to pre-Hispanic reality.

history_text_issues.claim: States that Aztec culture invented little and passed on no significant technology, religion or political theory.
history_text_issues.problem: It is a Eurocentric and factually false judgement. The first half of the sentence (the inheritance from earlier cultures) is true; the conclusion is not.
history_text_issues.correction: Examples to the contrary: chinampas on an urban scale, the dike of Nezahualcóyotl, the tribute system (Codex Mendoza), the Tlatelolco market (Cortés spoke of more than 60,000 people a day), Nahuatl poetry and the pharmacopoeia (Codex de la Cruz-Badiano, 1552). Nahuatl was a lingua franca in colonial Mexico, and words such as chocolate, tomato and avocado come from it. Mexica institutions were put to use by the Spanish administration.

history_text_issues.claim: Presents the Aztecs, in retrospect, as a “society in decline”.
history_text_issues.problem: It is false.
history_text_issues.correction: The empire was expanding until 1519: Ahuitzotl (1486–1502) reached Soconusco, and Moctezuma II was still campaigning. There is no evidence of internal decline before the Spanish arrival.

history_text_issues.claim: Says they were already devastated by European diseases transmitted by earlier “traders”.
history_text_issues.problem: The vector is wrong: there were no European traders in Mexico before 1519. The epidemic does indeed predate the final fall (1521), but not the arrival of Cortés.
history_text_issues.correction: Smallpox arrived with the expedition of Pánfilo de Narváez (April 1520). It reached Tenochtitlan between September and December 1520, after the Noche Triste, and killed, among others, the tlatoani Cuitláhuac. It weakened the city before the siege of 1521.

history_text_issues.claim: Explains the loose control over satellite cities as a way of provoking revolts and obtaining sacrificial victims.
history_text_issues.problem: The observation (indirect control) is correct; the explanation is outdated.
history_text_issues.correction: Current historiography (Hassig 1988; Berdan, Smith et al., Aztec Imperial Strategies, 1996) describes a low-cost “hegemonic” empire: indirect rule, retention of local elites and collection of tribute. Rebellions were punished, not sought.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that sacrifices of several thousand people in a single day “were not unusual”.
history_text_issues.problem: It is an exaggeration based on figures from later chroniclers.
history_text_issues.correction: Mass sacrifices were exceptional, linked for example to the reconsecration of the Templo Mayor in 1487. Figures such as Durán's 80,400 are considered greatly inflated. Archaeology (Huey Tzompantli, INAH excavations since 2015) confirms large-scale sacrifice, but accumulated over decades.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that victims were often beheaded or flayed.
history_text_issues.problem: It generalises specific rites.
history_text_issues.correction: Flaying belonged mainly to the feast of Tlacaxipehualiztli (Xipe Totec); the most common form was heart extraction, and each feast of the calendar had its own rite.

history_text_issues.claim: Says they fought with wooden clubs to stun and only fitted them with obsidian when fighting to kill.
history_text_issues.problem: It has no support in the sources.
history_text_issues.correction: Wooden clubs without blades did exist (such as the cuauhololli), but no source describes removing or fitting the obsidian on the macuahuitl according to the aim. Capture resulted from wounding and overpowering the opponent.

history_text_issues.claim: Presents the flower wars as mere contests of bravery to capture victims.
history_text_issues.problem: It is a partial reading of a contested subject.
history_text_issues.correction: Durán and Tezozómoc give the ritual explanation, associated with Tlacaelel after the famine of 1450–54. Hassig (1988) and Isaac (1983) argue for strategic aims: attrition and the gradual encirclement of Tlaxcala.

history_text_issues.claim: Says they fell to a small Spanish army with steel, firearms and horses, and that Aztec cruelty made the Spanish alliances easier.
history_text_issues.problem: It reproduces the myth of conquest by a few and moralises the explanation.
history_text_issues.correction: The siege of 1521 involved around a thousand Spaniards and tens of thousands of indigenous allies, mainly Tlaxcaltecs, driven by old rivalries and by the burden of tribute (Restall, Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest, 2003; Townsend, Fifth Sun, 2019). The brigantines and the epidemic were decisive.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that by the end of the 15th century they controlled all of central Mexico.
history_text_issues.problem: It is an exaggeration.
history_text_issues.correction: Tlaxcala, Metztitlan, Yopitzinco and the Purépecha (Tarascan) kingdom, which defeated Axayácatl c. 1478–79, remained independent.

history_text_issues.claim: Describes them as probably a northern tribe that occupied a small town on the lake shore.
history_text_issues.problem: It is imprecise.
history_text_issues.correction: According to tradition, the Mexica migrated from Aztlan and founded Tenochtitlan c. 1325 on an islet in Lake Texcoco. They were tributaries and mercenaries of the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco, whom they defeated in 1428.

missing_features: Chinampa agriculture (raised fields in Xochimilco and Chalco), which fed a city of c. 150,000–250,000 inhabitants.
The imperial tribute system (calpixqueh, Codex Mendoza) and the model of a hegemonic empire with indirect rule.
Pochteca merchants, who were also spies and forerunners of conquest; the Tlatelolco market; cacao and cloaks (quachtli) as media of exchange.
Warfare centred on capturing prisoners, with promotion through captures and tlahuiztli suits as insignia of rank.
War canoes (acalli) and the lake capital with causeways and removable bridges.
The Triple Alliance as a coalition, including Nezahualcóyotl's Texcoco and its hydraulic engineering.
Shields (chimalli), obsidian macuahuitl and cotton armour as standard equipment.

proposals.title: Chinampas
proposals.description: Farms built within 3 tiles of water cost -25% wood and yield +15% food, or instead regenerate automatically at no cost.
proposals.historical_basis: The chinampas of Xochimilco and Chalco produced several harvests a year and were the demographic basis of Tenochtitlan (Parsons; M. E. Smith, The Aztecs).

proposals.title: Tequitl (imperial tribute)
proposals.description: Replaces Garland Wars. Each Castle and each Town Center generates a passive income of food and gold (e.g. +0.3/s of each), and the Tribute fee at the Market drops to 0%.
proposals.historical_basis: The Codex Mendoza lists 38 tributary provinces that paid maize, cloaks, cacao, feathers, gold and armour, collected by calpixqueh.

proposals.title: Acalli (war canoe)
proposals.description: Replaces the Galley line: a cheap, fast canoe that fires darts and transports 5 units. Remove Carrack, Hulk-line, Fire Ship and Demolition Ship.
proposals.historical_basis: Thousands of canoes defended Tenochtitlan in 1521, and Cortés had to build brigantines to control the lake (Cartas de relación, third letter).

proposals.title: Xōchiyāōyōtl reinterpreted: capture and promotion
proposals.description: Infantry that defeats military units generates +5 gold per captive, and each Militia-line unit with 4 victories gains +2 attack and +1 armour (promotion). The effect replaces the generic +4 attack.
proposals.historical_basis: Promotion by number of captives is illustrated in the plates of warrior grades in the Codex Mendoza (Hassig 1988).

proposals.title: Coherent Mesoamerican tech tree
proposals.description: Give Masonry, Architecture and Keep. Remove Trebuchet, the Onager-line and Siege Ram, compensating with Petard and anti-building infantry. Rename Iron Casting/Blast Furnace to “Obsidian Blades” and Plate Mail to “Ichcahuipilli”, and Horse Collar/Heavy Plow to chinampa variants.
proposals.historical_basis: Monumental and hydraulic engineering is documented (Templo Mayor, dike of Nezahualcóyotl); there was neither iron metallurgy nor siege engines.

proposals.title: Rename to “Aztecs (Mexica)”
proposals.description: Use “Mexica” or “Aztecs (Mexica)” in the texts.
proposals.historical_basis: It is the autonym used in Nahua and colonial sources (Sahagún, Chimalpahin).

contested: Scale of human sacrifice: Durán's figures (80,400 in 1487) versus much lower modern estimates. Harner's “protein” hypothesis (1977) is now rejected.
Nature of the flower wars: ritual (Durán, Tezozómoc) or a strategy of attrition (Hassig 1988; Isaac 1983).
Hegemonic or territorial empire, and the degree of provincial control (Berdan & Smith 1996).
Population of Tenochtitlan (150,000–250,000) and of central Mexico in 1519, ranging from the high figures of Borah & Cook to much smaller estimates.
The myth that Moctezuma took Cortés for Quetzalcóatl, probably constructed after the conquest (Townsend 2003; Restall 2018).
Historicity of the migration from Aztlan and the exact date of the founding of Tenochtitlan (1325 or 1345).
key_sources: Bernardino de Sahagún, Historia general de las cosas de Nueva España / Florentine Codex (c. 1577)
Diego Durán, Historia de las Indias de Nueva España (1581)
Codex Mendoza (c. 1541)
Hernán Cortés, Cartas de relación (1519–1526)
Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España
Ross Hassig, Trade, Tribute, and Transportation (1985); Aztec Warfare: Imperial Expansion and Political Control (1988)
Frances Berdan, Michael E. Smith et al., Aztec Imperial Strategies (1996)
Michael E. Smith, The Aztecs (3rd ed., 2012)
Matthew Restall, Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest (2003); When Montezuma Met Cortés (2018)
Camilla Townsend, Fifth Sun: A New History of the Aztecs (2019)
Leonardo López Luján / Proyecto Templo Mayor (INAH)

civs.represents: The Maya peoples of the lowlands and highlands of eastern Mesoamerica: Yucatán, Petén, Chiapas, Tabasco, Belize, Guatemala, western Honduras and western El Salvador. The history text focuses on the Classic (the “superstates” of Tikal and Calakmul). The military elements (bow, holkan, hul'che), by contrast, come from the Yucatec Postclassic: Chichén Itzá, Mayapán and the 16th-century chiefdoms.
civs.period: c. 250–1697 AD: Late Classic c. 600–900; Postclassic c. 900–1524 in Yucatán, and until 1697 among the Itza of Nojpetén.
civs.verdict: The “archer” identity only fits the Postclassic (the Yucatán of Landa and of Champotón), not the Classic that the text itself extols, when warfare was waged with spear, spear-thrower, axe and shield. Since the Postclassic takes up more than half of the game's time frame, the choice is defensible, but the result mixes periods. The UTs (Hul'che, Holcans) and the walls bonus have a real basis, and “resources last longer” can be read as management of the forest landscape. The remaining bonuses are balance bonuses, and the Plumed Archer is generic. Left out are writing, the calendar, divine kingship, city-state politics and maritime canoe trade. The history text is badly out of date: “empty ceremonial centres”, “simple” religion, collapse attributed to earthquakes.
civs.naming_scope_issues: In Maya studies, “Maya” is used as the name of the people and as the adjective, and “Mayan” only for the languages; “Mayans” is a popular form. More importantly, the Maya never formed a single state. They were dozens of rival city-states (Tikal, Calakmul, Caracol, Copán, Palenque…) and, in the Postclassic, Yucatec chiefdoms and K'iche' and Kaqchikel kingdoms, with some 30 languages. The game mixes the Classic (text) with the Postclassic (Yucatec units and terms). The period fits well within the 500–1500 frame. The former UT “El Dorado”, a Muisca myth, illustrates the early confusion between Amerindian cultures; it was renamed Holcans with the same effect, but the internal name “Mayan El Dorado” still persists in the repository's data/data.json.

elements.explanation: It depends on the period. In the Classic, the iconography shows spears, spear-throwers, axes and flexible shields, and the bow seems to have become widespread only in the Postclassic (the date of its adoption is debated). For late Yucatán, however, the label has a basis: at Champotón (1517) the Maya used bows, slings and darts (Bernal Díaz), and Landa describes bows and arrows with flint points used with great skill.
It is a balance bonus. It could allude to the high population densities revealed by LiDAR (PACUNAM 2018), but there is no direct connection.

It can be read as sophisticated landscape management: forest gardens, terraces, raised fields, the reservoirs of Tikal and chultuns. It is ironic that the popular narrative attributes the collapse to environmental overexploitation, a contested theme.

elements.element: Foot Archers cost -10/20/30% in Feudal/Castle/Imperial Age
elements.explanation: The link is weak: only in the Postclassic does the bow seem to have been the standard weapon of commoner levies. For the Classic it has no basis.
Feather headdresses were elite insignia throughout Mesoamerica, but no corps of “plumed archers” is documented. The high speed is invented, and the unit is generic.

elements.element: Eagle Scout / Eagle Warrior (regional unit shared with Aztecs)
elements.explanation: The eagle order is Nahua. Among the Maya, eagles and jaguars appear at Chichén Itzá (Platform of the Eagles and Jaguars, Postclassic, of central Mexican influence). Applied to the whole Maya world, it is a transposition.

Hul'che is the Yucatec term for the dart-thrower. The atlatl is well documented in Maya art; Tikal Stela 31, for example, shows Teotihuacan-style warriors carrying one. The “extra projectile” is an abstraction.

The holkan were the warriors of Postclassic Yucatán, partly paid during campaigns, commanded by the nakom (Landa). The term is well chosen; applying it to Eagle Warriors, a Nahua concept, creates a hybrid. It is a renaming of the former UT “El Dorado” (same effect), which was a Muisca myth.
Maya fortifications are documented: the ditch and rampart of Becan (Late Preclassic/Early Classic), the improvised walls of Dos Pilas (760s), the walls of Mayapán (c. 9 km), Tulum and Ek' Balam.

tree_issues.problem: The Mayans have the Militia-line, but not Gambesons. The Maya of Yucatán used quilted cotton armour, described at Champotón (1517) and by Landa, and adopted by the Spaniards.

tree_issues.item: Trebuchet, Siege Ram, Onager, Heavy Scorpion
tree_issues.problem: They are anachronistic: there were no siege engines in the Maya area.

tree_issues.item: Galleon, War Galley, Hulk-line, Carrack, Heavy Demolition Ship
tree_issues.problem: They are anachronistic. The large trading and war canoe is missing: in 1502, near Guanaja, Columbus encountered a canoe “as long as a galley”, with c. 25 paddlers and a cargo of cacao, copper, textiles and obsidian swords (account of Ferdinand Columbus).

tree_issues.item: Blacksmith: Iron Casting, Blast Furnace, Plate Mail
tree_issues.problem: The Maya made almost no use of metal until the Postclassic, and then mostly in imported objects (copper bells and axes). Weapons were of flint and obsidian.

They are consistent with the monumental architecture: Temple IV at Tikal is c. 65 m tall, and La Danta, at El Mirador, is one of the largest pre-modern structures by volume (although it is Preclassic, earlier than the game's time frame).

tree_issues.item: Horse Collar, Heavy Plow, Trade Cart
tree_issues.problem: They are anachronistic: there were no draught animals, no plough and no wheeled transport. The sacbeob were travelled on foot and loads were carried on people's backs.

history_text_issues.claim: Says they lived on land of marginal agricultural value.
history_text_issues.problem: It is misleading.
history_text_issues.correction: The lowlands supported dense populations, several million in the Late Classic according to the PACUNAM LiDAR survey (Canuto et al. 2018), thanks to terraces, raised fields, forest gardens and reservoirs.

history_text_issues.claim: Says Maya religion was “relatively simple”.
history_text_issues.problem: It is false and Eurocentric.
history_text_issues.correction: The Maya had a complex cosmology: a vast pantheon, myths recorded in the K'iche' Popol Vuh, ancestor worship, divine kingship (k'uhul ajaw), interlocking calendars (tzolk'in, haab', Long Count) and ritual self-sacrifice.

history_text_issues.claim: Says the architecture was less developed than that of other contemporary regions.
history_text_issues.problem: It is a Eurocentric and debatable judgement.
history_text_issues.correction: Despite the false vault, the Maya built structures of enormous volume, sacbeob of up to c. 100 km (Cobá–Yaxuná), hydraulic systems and planned cities.

history_text_issues.claim: Says the writing is only now being deciphered.
history_text_issues.problem: It was already out of date in 1999.
history_text_issues.correction: Thanks to Knorozov's phonetic approach (1952), Proskouriakoff's historical reading (1960) and the work of Schele, Stuart, Martin and Grube, the great majority of the texts can be read today.

history_text_issues.claim: Says three Maya books survive.
history_text_issues.problem: It is out of date.
history_text_issues.correction: Four codices survive: Dresden, Madrid, Paris and the Maya Codex of Mexico (formerly the Grolier Codex), whose authenticity, disputed in 1999, was confirmed by INAH in 2018. The famous case of destruction is the auto-da-fé at Maní, ordered by Diego de Landa in 1562.

history_text_issues.claim: Says they lived in small villages and only gathered in the centres for ceremonies.
history_text_issues.problem: It revives the “empty ceremonial centres” model (J. E. S. Thompson), now abandoned.
history_text_issues.correction: Tikal, Calakmul and Caracol were true cities, with tens of thousands of inhabitants and dense peripheries.

history_text_issues.claim: Says noble warriors and priests controlled society.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the central institution of the Classic.
history_text_issues.correction: Power was concentrated in divine kings (k'uhul ajaw) and their courts; priests gain more weight in the Postclassic.

history_text_issues.claim: Attributes the 10th-century decline perhaps to an earthquake or a volcanic eruption.
history_text_issues.problem: This explanation has no support in current research.
history_text_issues.correction: The Classic collapse in the southern lowlands (c. 750–950) is attributed to a combination of endemic warfare, severe droughts (Hodell et al. 1995; Kennett et al. 2012), demographic pressure and a crisis of divine kingship; the weight of each factor is debated. Meanwhile, the north (Chichén Itzá, Uxmal, the Puuc region) flourished.

history_text_issues.claim: Says warriors from central Mexico later invaded Maya territory.
history_text_issues.problem: It revives the “Toltec invasion” model of Chichén Itzá, now contested.
history_text_issues.correction: Today scholars mostly speak of interaction and of a shared international style between Tula and Chichén Itzá. There was, however, a documented Teotihuacan intervention at Tikal in 378 (Siyaj K'ak').

history_text_issues.claim: Says about two million people of Maya descent live in Yucatán today.
history_text_issues.problem: It underestimates the number and restricts it geographically.
history_text_issues.correction: The Maya peoples today number well over 6 million people in Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and Honduras, with some 30 living languages.

history_text_issues.claim: Places the Maya in Yucatán, Honduras and Guatemala.
history_text_issues.problem: It is incomplete.
history_text_issues.correction: They also occupied Chiapas, Tabasco, Belize and western El Salvador.

missing_features: City-state politics and hegemonies, such as the rivalry between Tikal and Kaanul/Calakmul (Tikal's victory in 695).
Divine kingship (k'uhul ajaw) and warfare to capture and display captives (Bonampak murals, c. 790).
Writing, calendar and astronomy, such as the Venus tables of the Dresden Codex.
Maritime canoe trade around Yucatán (Cozumel, Xicalango, Chontal/Putún merchants) and the trade in salt, cacao and obsidian.
Sacbeob (causeways) and water management (chultuns, reservoirs).
Flint-tipped spears, the spear-thrower and cotton armour.
Prolonged resistance: Nojpetén, the Itza capital, only fell in 1697.

proposals.title: Period-based identity
proposals.description: Change the label to “Infantry and Archer”. In the Feudal and Castle Ages, the discounts apply to the Spearman-line and Skirmishers (Classic spear and spear-thrower); in the Imperial Age they pass to Foot Archers (Postclassic bow).
proposals.historical_basis: Classic iconography (stelae, Bonampak) is dominated by spears and spear-throwers, and the bow only becomes dominant in the Postclassic (Landa; Bernal Díaz at Champotón).

proposals.title: Sacbe
proposals.description: Trade Carts and Villagers +15% speed; infantry and Monks +10% speed within the radius of their own Town Centers and Monasteries.
proposals.historical_basis: The network of sacbeob, such as the Cobá–Yaxuná causeway (c. 100 km), and the internal causeways of the cities.

proposals.title: Trade canoe
proposals.description: The Trade Cog is replaced by a cheaper large trade canoe, with +20% gold per trip, and Docks cost -25% wood. Remove Galleon and the Hulk-line.
proposals.historical_basis: The Guanaja canoe (1502, account of Ferdinand Columbus), possibly belonging to Chontal/Putún merchants, and the ports of Xicalango and Cozumel.

proposals.title: Royal captives (baak)
proposals.description: Infantry that defeat military units generate “captives” which, garrisoned in a Castle or Monastery, produce gold like a Relic, up to a maximum of 5.
proposals.historical_basis: Titles such as “lord of X captives” and the display of prisoners were central to royal legitimation (Martin & Grube).

proposals.title: Quilted cotton
proposals.description: Give Gambesons and extend it to Eagle Warriors and the Spearman-line.
proposals.historical_basis: Bernal Díaz at Champotón (1517) and Landa describe Maya cotton armour.

proposals.title: Scribes and astronomers (aj tz'ib)
proposals.description: University and Monastery technologies researched 33% faster.
proposals.historical_basis: The body of scribes and calendrical and astronomical knowledge (Dresden Codex).

contested: Causes of the Classic collapse: drought, warfare, environmental degradation or political collapse (Demarest; Kennett et al. 2012; Diamond's ecological thesis, 2005, is contested).
Degree of hegemony of the Tikal and Calakmul “superstates” (Martin & Grube) versus autonomous cities.
“Star wars” timed by the Venus cycle (Schele & Freidel) and Aldana's critiques.
Relationship between Tula and Chichén Itzá: Toltec invasion or interaction.
Date of adoption of the bow and arrow in the Maya area.
Size of the Late Classic population in the light of LiDAR.
key_sources: Diego de Landa, Relación de las cosas de Yucatán (c. 1566)
Popol Vuh (Ximénez manuscript, c. 1701)
Dresden Codex
Bernal Díaz del Castillo, Historia verdadera (Champotón, 1517)
Simon Martin & Nikolai Grube, Chronicle of the Maya Kings and Queens (2000/2008)
Simon Martin, Ancient Maya Politics (2020)
Michael D. Coe, Breaking the Maya Code (1992)
Arthur Demarest, Ancient Maya (2004)
Kennett et al., Science 338 (2012)
Canuto et al., Science 361 (2018), PACUNAM LiDAR
Grant D. Jones, The Conquest of the Last Maya Kingdom (1998)
Matthew Restall, Maya Conquistador (1998)

civs.represents: The Tawantinsuyu (“the four parts together”), the state ruled by the Inca lineage of Cusco that dominated the Andes from southern Colombia to the Maule River. It also includes the pre-imperial Kingdom of Cusco and the Vilcabamba stronghold.
civs.period: c. 1200 (Kingdom of Cusco) – 1533 (death of Atahualpa); imperial expansion c. 1400/1438–1532; Vilcabamba until 1572.
civs.verdict: This is the best-grounded civ in the group. The bonuses cleverly translate state logistics (qullqa), rotational labour (mit'a), stonemasonry and the infantry character. Slinger, Champi and Andean Sling are faithful, and Fabric Shields evokes the military and political value of textiles. The weak points are the truncated name of the Kamayuk, the lack of Architecture for the masters of stonemasonry and the absence of the roads, the chaski and the khipu, which were the empire's signature. The tech tree has the usual anachronisms (Trebuchet, galleons). The history text is reasonable, but uses Rowe's chronology without caveats and makes unfounded judgements about Topa Inca and the “Pax Incaica”.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Inca” (Inka) designated the sovereign and the ruling lineage, not the whole population. The state was called Tawantinsuyu and included dozens of peoples (Chimú, Cañari, Chanka, Wanka, Aymara lordships…). The imperial period (c. 1400/1438–1533) fits within the game's frame. The earlier Andean powers, however — Wari and Tiwanaku (c. 500–1000) and Chimor (c. 900–1470) — do not exist in the game and end up implicitly absorbed into the Incas. The regional package uses Quechua terms (champi, warak'a) that are correct only here.

elements.explanation: Andean armies were exclusively infantry: slingers, spearmen, macemen and archers from the eastern lowlands (Antisuyu).

elements.element: Houses and Settlements provide +5 population space
elements.explanation: It has no clear link. It could evoke the decimal census and the state management of the population, the residential compounds (kancha) or the tampu network, but it is mainly an economic mechanic.

It refers to Inca stonemasonry (Sacsayhuamán, Qurikancha, Ollantaytambo). Note: that stonemasonry was costly in labour (mit'a), not cheap; it would be more faithful to give stone buildings more HP or armour.

elements.element: Military Units cost -15/20/25/30% food in Dark/Feudal/Castle/Imperial Age
elements.explanation: It is an excellent abstraction of the network of state storehouses (qullqa) that fed armies on the march. Cotapachi had c. 2,400 storehouses and Huánuco Pampa c. 500, and ch'arki and chuño kept for years (Murra; D'Altroy).

elements.element: Villagers affected by Infantry Blacksmith upgrades starting in Castle Age
elements.explanation: It represents the military mit'a well: the adult peasant (hatun runa) also served as a soldier in rotating shifts.

A long-shafted spearman is plausible in the Inca army, and the Spaniards encountered long lances. But kamayuq means “specialist” or “person in charge”, as in khipukamayuq; the warrior was the awqa kamayuq, the name Guaman Poma gives to the age class of men aged 25 to 50. The name is truncated.
The sling (warak'a) was the main Andean missile weapon, preferred to the bow in the highlands. Spanish accounts of the conquest stress that the stones could seriously wound men and horses.
Champi is the Quechua term for the star-headed war mace, of stone or bronze, an emblematic weapon of the Inca infantry.

In the game, it replaces the Mill, Lumber Camp and Mining Camp as a universal drop-off point and provides population. It can evoke the administrative centres and the tampu (e.g. Huánuco Pampa), but it is a mechanic shared with very different peoples.
It is based on the Andean sling; the lack of a minimum range is a reasonable abstraction of the weapon's versatility.

Andean shields were made of wood or cane, sometimes covered with leather or cloth, and officers wore quilted cotton tunics. Fine textiles (qumpi) were the state's most politically valuable good. The English name is generic.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Start with a free Llama
elements.explanation: Llamas were the only large pack animal in the Americas (dogs only pulled travois in North America) and sustained military logistics. In the game they are merely food livestock, which wastes their real role.

tree_issues.problem: It contradicts their fame as masters of earthquake-resistant stonemasonry: Masonry and Keep are present, and Architecture should be too.

tree_issues.item: Trebuchet, Siege Ram, Onager, Heavy Scorpion
tree_issues.problem: They are anachronistic. Fortresses (pukara) were taken by assault, siege and fire; at the siege of Cusco (1536), the Incas used slings to hurl red-hot stones at the thatched roofs.
They are anachronistic. The actual naval technology was balsa rafts with cotton sails, such as the Tumbes raft intercepted by Bartolomé Ruiz c. 1526.

tree_issues.item: Blacksmith: Iron Casting, Blast Furnace, Plate Mail
tree_issues.problem: There was no iron, but the Incas spread a standardised tin bronze (Lechtman). The problem is mainly one of nomenclature.
There were no draught animals. The chaki taklla (foot plough) and agricultural terraces (andenes) were used.
Gambesons does not apply (the Incas have no Militia-line). Andean quilted tunics are represented only indirectly in Fabric Shields.

tree_issues.item: No Militia-line, with the Champi line
tree_issues.problem: It is consistent with Andean reality.

history_text_issues.claim: Presents 1438 as a firm date for the Chanka war and the founding of the empire, and 1410 for the start of Viracocha's reign.
history_text_issues.problem: This is Rowe's chronology (1945), based on Cabello Valboa (1586), which is now contested.
history_text_issues.correction: Radiocarbon dates (Ogburn 2012; Marsh et al. 2017) indicate Inca expansion before c. 1400. The Chanka war has a strong element of Pachacuti's dynastic propaganda, as shown by the myth of the pururauca stones and the figure of the discredited heir Inca Urqu.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Topa Inca was trained for war, neglecting imperial administration.
history_text_issues.problem: This is a judgement with no basis in the sources.
history_text_issues.correction: The chronicles credit Topa Inca (Tupac Inca Yupanqui) with much of the administrative consolidation: the decimal census, mitmaqkuna, roads and provincial centres.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the empire rested on enormous reserves of gold and silver, making it perhaps the richest civilization in the world.
history_text_issues.problem: It is anachronistic, because it projects a monetary economy.
history_text_issues.correction: The Tawantinsuyu did not use money; gold and silver were sacred and prestige goods. The state's wealth was labour (mit'a), storehouses and textiles. Potosí was only discovered in 1545.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Huayna Capac maintained a long “Pax Incaica”.
history_text_issues.problem: This is inaccurate.
history_text_issues.correction: The reign was marked by long campaigns in the north (Cañari, Caranqui, Pastos), including the Yahuarcocha massacre.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Huayna Capac died of smallpox in 1527 and that European diseases killed most of the inhabitants.
history_text_issues.problem: The date and the cause are debated, and the mortality is placed too early.
history_text_issues.correction: Huayna Capac died c. 1524–1528, probably of smallpox or another epidemic. The Andean demographic collapse unfolded over decades, above all after 1533.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the empire ended in 1533, when Atahualpa was captured and executed.
history_text_issues.problem: It merges two different dates.
history_text_issues.correction: Atahualpa was captured at Cajamarca on 16 November 1532 and executed in 1533 (26 July according to Porras Barrenechea; the traditional date is 29 August).

history_text_issues.claim: Presents “Ama suwa, ama llulla, ama qella” as the three basic rules of Inca society.
history_text_issues.problem: The formula is recorded only in colonial sources, and its status as an “Inca law” is debated.
history_text_issues.correction: It should be presented as a traditional maxim known through colonial sources.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that Chimor possibly had the best-armed troops in the New World and that it fell because the water supply to Chan Chan was cut off.
history_text_issues.problem: The first claim has no basis; the second is a chronicle tradition.
history_text_issues.correction: The conquest of Chimor (c. 1470) is well attested. The cutting of the canals appears in some chronicles and is plausible, but uncertain.

history_text_issues.claim: Moves from the capture of Atahualpa to Vilcabamba without mentioning the resistance.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the great rebellion of Manco Inca (1536–37) and the siege of Cusco.
history_text_issues.correction: It was the greatest Inca military effort against the Spaniards and shows tactical adaptation: incendiary slings, bolas against horses and the flooding of the plain at Ollantaytambo.

history_text_issues.claim: Presents the trade of the northern provinces with Mesoamerica as “recent research”.
history_text_issues.problem: This is imprecise.
history_text_issues.correction: Maritime contacts between Ecuador and western Mexico (metallurgy, Spondylus shells) are ancient and predate the Incas (Hosler); their continuity in the Inca period is uncertain.

missing_features: Qhapaq Ñan (c. 30,000–40,000 km of roads), suspension bridges (Q'eswachaka) and tampu.
Chaski (relay runners) and khipu (accounting and possibly narrative records).
Mitmaqkuna: the relocation of colonists as an instrument of control.
Terraces (andenes), chuño and ch'arki, and economic “verticality” (Murra).
Sun worship (Inti, Qurikancha), the cult of the royal mummies (mallki) and huacas.
Standardised tin bronze and integrated Chimú goldsmithing.
Fortresses (Sacsayhuamán, frontier pukara) and bolas (liwi, ayllu) used against cavalry in 1536.
Aqllakuna and state textile production.

proposals.title: Qhapaq Ñan and Chaski
proposals.description: All units and Trade Carts gain +10% speed; Outposts are built instantly and give +3 line of sight; Spies/Treason costs -50%.
proposals.historical_basis: The network of roads and relay runners described by Cieza de León and studied by Hyslop (The Inka Road System, 1984).

proposals.title: Khipukamayuq
proposals.description: Economic technologies (Settlement, Market, University) cost -15% and are researched 25% faster; the Market fee drops to 20%.
proposals.historical_basis: Accounting management by khipu and the decimal census (Urton; Cieza; Guaman Poma).

proposals.title: Incendiary Slings
proposals.description: Slingers gain +4 attack against buildings and deal continuous fire damage.
proposals.historical_basis: At the siege of Cusco (1536), red-hot stones wrapped in cotton set the roofs on fire (Pedro Pizarro; Titu Cusi Yupanqui).

proposals.title: Liwi (bolas)
proposals.description: Slingers slow the cavalry they hit by 25% for 3 s.
proposals.historical_basis: The use of bolas against Spanish horses in Manco Inca's rebellion (Hemming, The Conquest of the Incas).

proposals.title: Andean tech tree
proposals.description: Give Architecture. Replace Galleon, Carrack and Hulk-line with a transport and trade “Balsa”. Rename Heavy Plow to “Chaki Taklla” and Iron Casting/Blast Furnace to “Tin Bronze”.
proposals.historical_basis: The Tumbes raft (c. 1526), the Andean foot plough and bronze metallurgy (Lechtman).

proposals.title: Kamayuk → Awqa Kamayuq
proposals.description: Use the full form of the name.
proposals.historical_basis: Guaman Poma, Nueva corónica, on the age classes.

contested: Chronology: 1438 (Rowe/Cabello Valboa) or earlier radiocarbon dates (Ogburn; Marsh et al.).
Historicity of the Chanka war and of Pachacuti's role as sole reformer.
Dual government (Zuidema, Duviols) or a monarchy with linear succession.
Nature of the state: “socialist empire” (Baudin, 1928, discredited) or reciprocity and redistribution (Murra).
Khipu as writing or merely numerical records (Urton, Hyland).
Cause and date of Huayna Capac's death, and the exact date of Atahualpa's execution.
Topa Inca's voyage into the Pacific (Sarmiento de Gamboa).
key_sources: Juan de Betanzos, Suma y narración de los Incas (1551)
Pedro Cieza de León, Crónica del Perú (1553)
Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa, Historia de los Incas (1572)
Pedro Pizarro, Relación del descubrimiento y conquista del Perú (1571)
Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala, Nueva corónica y buen gobierno (c. 1615)
Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales (1609)
Bernabé Cobo, Historia del Nuevo Mundo (1653)
John V. Murra, The Economic Organization of the Inka State (1956/1980)
John Hyslop, The Inka Road System (1984)
Terence N. D'Altroy, The Incas (2002/2014)
Brian Bauer; R. Alan Covey, Inca Apocalypse (2020)
John Hemming, The Conquest of the Incas (1970)
Gary Urton, on khipu

civs.represents: The Muisca of the Altiplano Cundiboyacense, in Colombia, speakers of Muysccubun (Chibchan family). They were organised into chiefdoms and confederations: the zipazgo of Bacatá, the zacazgo of Hunza, the sacred chiefdom of Iraca (Sugamuxi) and Tundama.
civs.period: Muisca Period c. 800–1537 (Early 800–1200, Late 1200–1537), with antecedents in the Herrera Period; conquest by Jiménez de Quesada between 1537 and 1540.
civs.verdict: The design captures two real dimensions well: trade and religion (jeques, Temple of the Sun, offerings). The Guecha Warrior is a good homage to the güechas. But the “Archer” label is stretched, because the chroniclers highlight macanas, spears, darts and slings, and associate the bow mainly with the Panches. The Temple Guard has no basis, and the UT Huaracas uses a Quechua term for a Chibchan people. Missing are the salt of Zipaquirá and Nemocón and the emeralds, the true economic base, and the team bonus on gold forgets that the Muisca imported almost all the gold they used. A full ocean-going navy and stone castles for a highland people who built in wood and bahareque are incoherent.
civs.naming_scope_issues: Muisca (muysca, “people”) is the appropriate ethnonym; “Chibcha” designates the language family and was used imprecisely in the 19th century. The period (c. 800–1537) fits the 500–1500 frame very well and is the best-fitting case in the group. The problems lie in the Quechua terms (Huaracas, Champi) applied to a Chibchan people and in a history text dominated by the Spanish myth of El Dorado and by the conquest. Contrary to what the design suggests, the Muisca were not a unified kingdom.

elements.explanation: The Monk is plausible: the jeques (chyquy) trained for years in seclusion, there was the Temple of the Sun at Sugamuxi, and offerings were made in sacred lakes. The Archer is stretched: the most frequently mentioned weapons are palm-wood macanas, spears, darts and slings, with long shields. Bows and arrows, including poisoned ones, are associated mainly with the Panches, neighbours and enemies of the Muisca, and some syntheses state that the archers in Muisca service were Panche captives.

elements.element: Advancing to the next Age costs -50% gold
elements.explanation: It has no identifiable historical link: Muisca gold went mainly to offerings and insignia, not to “progress”.

elements.element: Settlements cost -33% and heal nearby units
elements.explanation: It is purely mechanical.

elements.element: Champi Warriors and Archery Range Units +1/2/3 melee armor
elements.explanation: The chroniclers describe long shields and several layers of cotton mantles, which protected even against Panche arrows, and the Muisca were great weavers. It makes sense as infantry protection; limiting the effect to melee armour and to these groups is a balance choice.
It evokes the prestige and discipline of the jeques: prolonged fasts and the ritual use of hayo (coca) and tobacco.

It is a good abstraction: the Spanish described the Muisca as less warlike than their neighbours and much given to trade. There were periodic markets (Turmequé, Sorocotá) and exchange of salt, mantles, emeralds and gold with the Panches, Muzos, Guanes and lowland peoples.

The güechas were elite frontier warriors, above all against the Panches. They wore gold or tumbaga adornments (nose ornaments, pectorals, earrings), and the number of earrings reportedly indicated the enemies defeated. Darts and long shields justify the skirmisher role. The regeneration when another guecha dies alludes to the mummies of warriors carried on men’s backs into combat.

No military corps of “temple guards” is known. There were shrines (Sugamuxi, Guatavita) with priests and attendants, but the unit described in the game (shock infantry that attacks ever faster, strong against buildings and mounted units) does not correspond to anything documented, and the anti-cavalry role makes no sense for a people who first saw horses in 1537.
Slings are attested among the Muisca. But champi is a Quechua term for the Andean mace; the Muisca equivalent was the palm-wood macana.

It is a regional mechanic (a universal drop-off site that replaces the Mill, Lumber Camp and Mining Camp). The Muisca lived in dispersed settlement and in villages with the caciques’ palisade enclosures.
Chewing hayo (coca) increased physical endurance and was common practice, so the speed is an acceptable abstraction. The generic name wastes the native term.
The Muisca use of slings is attested, but huaraca (warak'a) is a Quechua word. The name attributes Inca vocabulary to the Muisca.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Natural gold sources last +15% longer
elements.explanation: Muisca territory had little gold; they obtained it through trade with the Magdalena lowlands, in exchange for salt, mantles and emeralds. It can be read as an abstraction of tumbaga, an alloy that made scarce gold go further, but the link is not evident.

tree_issues.item: Galleon, War Galley, Hulk-line, Fire Ship, Carrack, Heavy Demolition Ship, Dry Dock
tree_issues.problem: It is absurd for an inland highland people, at c. 2,600 m. Muisca navigation amounted to reed rafts on the lakes (Guatavita, Tota, Fúquene), as suggested by the Muisca Raft found in Pasca in 1969.

tree_issues.item: Castle, Keep, Masonry, Stone Walls, Siege Onager, Trebuchet
tree_issues.problem: They are anachronistic. They built in wood, bahareque and thatch, and the defences were the caciques’ palisade enclosures.
It is consistent with building in perishable materials, but contradicts the presence of Masonry and Keep.

tree_issues.item: Blacksmith: Iron Casting, Plate Mail (no Blast Furnace)
tree_issues.problem: There was no iron. Metalworking (lost-wax casting in tumbaga) was ritual and ornamental.

tree_issues.item: Weight given to the Archery Range
tree_issues.problem: It undervalues darts and slings, which were the dominant projectile weapons.

tree_issues.item: Horse Collar, Heavy Plow, Trade Cart
tree_issues.problem: They are anachronistic: there were no draught animals and no wheeled transport.

history_text_issues.claim: It describes the Muisca as an “indigenous tribe”.
history_text_issues.problem: It is reductive.
history_text_issues.correction: They were complex chiefdom societies, with hierarchies, tribute and matrilineal succession: the son of the cacique’s sister inherited.

history_text_issues.claim: It presents without context the ritual of covering the future chief in gold and taking him to the middle of Lake Guatavita.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the late nature of the source.
history_text_issues.correction: The description comes from Juan Rodríguez Freyle (El Carnero, 1636–38), a century after the conquest. It referred to the cacique of Guatavita and had probably already fallen out of use before 1537, when the zipa had subjugated Guatavita. The Muisca Raft is the main material evidence.

history_text_issues.claim: It places the earliest evidence of this civilisation at c. 600 AD.
history_text_issues.problem: It is imprecise.
history_text_issues.correction: The archaeological Muisca Period begins c. 800 AD. Before it comes the Herrera Period, whose cultural continuity with the Muisca is debated.

history_text_issues.claim: It divides the Muisca into two large territories, Hunza (zaque) and Muyquytá (zipa).
history_text_issues.problem: It is a simplification.
history_text_issues.correction: There were also Iraca (Sugamuxi), the religious centre, Tundama (Duitama) and autonomous chiefdoms. The very idea of a “Muisca Confederation” is questioned by some authors (Langebaek).

history_text_issues.claim: It dates the Battle of Chocontá, in which both rulers died, to 1490.
history_text_issues.problem: The date and the details depend on 17th-century chroniclers (Simón, Piedrahita).
history_text_issues.correction: It should be presented as chronicle tradition, not as a precisely dated fact.

history_text_issues.claim: It gives about 500,000 Muisca at the arrival of the Spanish.
history_text_issues.problem: It is only one estimate among many.
history_text_issues.correction: Estimates range from c. 300,000 to more than a million.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that Quemuenchatocha died that same year (1537).
history_text_issues.problem: The date is wrong.
history_text_issues.correction: He was found and imprisoned in Hunza on 20 August 1537 and died in 1538, in Ramiriquí.

history_text_issues.claim: It concludes that the Spanish searched in vain for the lost city of El Dorado.
history_text_issues.problem: It is misleading.
history_text_issues.correction: Quesada and his men looted significant quantities of gold and emeralds. The El Dorado myth later shifted to other regions (Manoa, Paititi).

history_text_issues.claim: The narrative of the conquest centres on the zaque Quemuenchatocha.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits central facts.
history_text_issues.correction: Missing are the burning of the Temple of the Sun at Sugamuxi by Spanish soldiers (1537), the death of the zipa Tisquesusa (1537) and that of his successor Sagipa under torture (1539).

missing_features: Salt production at Zipaquirá, Nemocón and Tausa, by evaporating brine in ceramic vessels; it was the main trade good.
Emeralds from Somondoco/Chivor.
Cotton mantles as a valuable good, tribute and quasi-currency.
Offerings of tunjos in sacred lakes, and lost-wax tumbaga metalworking.
Matrilineal succession and the political-religious role of Iraca.
Frontier wars with the Panches, and warrior mummies carried into combat.
Darts, macanas and long shields as the main weapons.

proposals.title: Zipaquirá Salt
proposals.description: Stone miners work 20% faster, and stone can be sold at the Market for a favourable gold price (representing salt). Trade Carts yield +15% gold.
proposals.historical_basis: The salt works were the axis of the Muisca exchange economy (Cardale de Schrimpff, 1981; Groot, 2008).

proposals.title: Güecha Darts
proposals.description: Replaces Huaracas: Guecha Warriors and Skirmishers gain +1 range and +1 attack.
proposals.historical_basis: The game’s own text and the chroniclers (Simón, Piedrahita) highlight darts as a common weapon of the güechas.

proposals.title: Mummy Bearers
proposals.description: Support unit trained at the Monastery: a warrior who carries an ancestor’s mummy on his back and gives +1 attack and +1 armour to nearby Guecha Warriors.
proposals.historical_basis: The chroniclers mention mummies of famous warriors carried on men’s backs into battle (Pedro Simón; Piedrahita).

proposals.title: Remove the ocean-going navy and stonework
proposals.description: Keep only the Fishing Ship, Transport and a reed raft; remove Galleon, Hulk-line, Fire Ship, Masonry and Castle, and replace the Keep with a “cacique’s palisade”.
proposals.historical_basis: The Muisca were an inland highland people, with no seafaring and no defensive stonework.

proposals.title: Mantles and Markets
proposals.description: Replaces Herbalism or complements the market bonuses: Tribute and Market with a 10% fee, and houses generate a small gold income.
proposals.historical_basis: Cotton mantles worked as a unit of value and of tribute, and there were periodic markets.

proposals.title: Rename Champi and Huaracas
proposals.description: Use “Macana Warrior” instead of Champi, and a generic term (“Muisca Slings”) or a verified native term instead of Huaracas.
proposals.historical_basis: Champi and huaraca are Quechua words, foreign to Muysccubun.

contested: Whether the Muisca formed a “confederation” or a network of chiefdoms (Langebaek; Gamboa).
Demography before the conquest.
Existence and chronology of the El Dorado ritual (Freyle).
Reliability of the Muisca calendar reconstructed by José Domingo Duquesne in the 18th century.
Degree of bellicosity (traders or warriors), scale of warfare and actual use of the bow.
Extent of human sacrifice (moxa).
key_sources: Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada (attrib.), Epítome de la conquista del Nuevo Reino de Granada (c. 1548–50)
Juan de Castellanos, Elegías de varones ilustres de Indias (1589)
Fray Pedro Simón, Noticias historiales (1626)
Juan Rodríguez Freyle, El Carnero (1636–38)
Lucas Fernández de Piedrahita, Historia general de las conquistas del Nuevo Reino de Granada (1688)
Carl Henrik Langebaek, Los muiscas (2019)
Jorge Augusto Gamboa Mendoza, El cacicazgo muisca en los años posteriores a la Conquista (2010)
Marianne Cardale de Schrimpff, Las salinas de Zipaquirá (1981)
Ana María Groot, Sal y poder en el altiplano de Bogotá (2008)
Museo del Oro (Banco de la República), Balsa Muisca

civs.represents: The Mapuche of south-central Chile, called Reche in 16th-century sources, between the Itata/Biobío and Toltén rivers, and from the 17th–19th centuries also on the Argentine pampas. The design centres on the Arauco War (c. 1550–1656) and on 17th–18th-century institutions (butalmapu, malón).
civs.period: Antecedents: the Pitrén (1st millennium AD) and El Vergel (c. 1100–1450) complexes; frontier with the Inca c. 1470–1530; Arauco War 1541/1550–1656; frontier and parliaments until the Occupation of Araucanía (1861–1883).
civs.verdict: The design is rich in authentic vocabulary (kona, malón, butalmapu, weupife) and captures two central truths: the rapid and brilliant adoption of the horse after 1550, and the anti-cavalry response with long lances, bolas and lassos. It also captures an economy of gathering and raiding. The problem is structural: almost everything that defines this civ happens after 1541, outside the 500–1500 frame. The pre-Hispanic Mapuche world — horticulture, chilihueque, the kuel mounds, the Maule frontier with the Inca — is absent. The team bonus and the effect of Malon are arbitrary, the tech tree gives Architecture and Bombard Tower to a people without stonework, and the history text has errors: “largest native people of South America”, “hunter-gatherers”, “cacique”, cavalry at Tucapel.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Mapuche” (“people of the land”) is the current ethnonym, but it only became widespread in the 18th century. 16th-century sources speak of “reche”, and the Spanish of “araucanos”, an exonym popularised by Ercilla's La Araucana (1569). It is also an umbrella term that groups together the Picunche, Reche/Mapuche, Huilliche and Pehuenche and, later, the “Araucanised” groups of the pampas. Above all, the design (cavalry, mounted bolas, malón, butalmapu) belongs to the 16th–19th centuries, outside the game's frame; the history text itself begins in 1541. “Cacique”, used in the text, is a Taíno word.

elements.explanation: Mapuche cavalry is real and remarkable, but only from the 1550s–1560s onwards, with horses that were first captured and then bred; before 1541 there were no horses. The “Counter-Units” part is faithful: the Mapuche formed bodies of long colihue lances and used bolas and lassos to bring down the Spanish cavalry.
The economy was mixed, with a strong gathering component (araucaria pine nuts, especially among the Pehuenche, and shellfish on the coast) alongside horticulture.

elements.element: Settlements can train Spearman-line and Skirmishers
elements.explanation: It renders decentralised mobilisation well: each lof or rewe supplied warriors (weichafe), with no permanent barracks.
It reflects the hardened-leather cuirasses and helmets adopted in warfare, and the physical endurance praised by the chroniclers and by Ercilla.

elements.element: Mounted Units generate +3 gold when defeating military units
elements.explanation: It represents the raiding economy: cattle, horses, iron and captives taken in raids were wealth and prestige.

elements.element: Enemy Castles are revealed on the map
elements.explanation: The Mapuche knew the Spanish forts well (Lautaro had served the Spanish). After Curalaba (1598) they destroyed the “seven cities” south of the Biobío.
Kona denotes the young warrior or mocetón in the service of a lonko. As an elite horseman it is consistent with the phase after c. 1560.

The Mapuche used bolas and lassos against the Spanish horses; the chronicles of Tucapel (1553) describe them being used on foot. Mounted use is more characteristic of the peoples of the pampas and Patagonia and of the “Araucanisation” of the pampas in the 17th–19th centuries.
Malón (a mounted raid for plunder) is a faithful term, but belongs mainly to the 17th–19th centuries on the pampas. The pass-through projectile damage effect has nothing to do with the concept.

The futalmapu (“great lands”) were the regional alliances (coast, plain, foothills, cordillera) that negotiated with the Spanish Crown at the parliaments, mainly in the 17th–18th centuries; some authors (Boccara) see them partly as a product of the colonial relationship itself. A discount shared with the team evokes the idea of alliance well.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Spearman-line and Skirmishers +2 line of sight
elements.explanation: It has no specific historical basis.
Slings appear in Mapuche warfare, but champi is a Quechua term; Mapuche clubs were made of wood, and the stone axe (toki) was the symbol of the war leader.
It is consistent with dispersed settlement in lof and rukas, without towns.

tree_issues.problem: The Bombard Tower has a tenuous but real link: at the pucará of Quiapo (1558), according to Rosales, the Mapuche used arquebuses captured from the Spanish; it was an unsuccessful exception. Architecture and Masonry, on the other hand, make no sense for a people who built in wood and earth.

This is consistent with the absence of horses before 1550, but inconsistent with the massed cavalry of the 17th–18th centuries; the Kona comes from the Castle and the Bolas Rider from the Archery Range.

tree_issues.item: No Keep, Guard Tower or Fortified Wall
tree_issues.problem: This is faithful: the defences were pucarás of earth and palisade, ditches and staked pits. The Castle and Stone Walls, however, are anachronistic.

tree_issues.item: Galleon, Carrack, Carvel Hull, Siphons, Hulk-line
tree_issues.problem: They are anachronistic. There were dugout canoes (wampu) and, further south (Chiloé, the Huilliche and the Chono), sewn-plank dalcas.

tree_issues.item: Trebuchet, Capped Ram, Onager, Heavy Scorpion
tree_issues.problem: They are anachronistic.

tree_issues.item: Blacksmith: Iron Casting, Blast Furnace, Plate Mail
tree_issues.problem: There was no iron before contact. From the 16th century the Mapuche obtained it through capture and trade and worked it; silversmithing came later (18th–19th centuries).

history_text_issues.claim: It says that the Mapuche are today the largest native group in South America.
history_text_issues.problem: This is false.
history_text_issues.correction: The Quechua (c. 8–10 million) and the Aymara (c. 2 million) are more numerous. The Mapuche are the largest indigenous people of Chile, with c. 1.75 million in the 2017 census.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that before contact they were hunter-gatherers with basic agricultural practices.
history_text_issues.problem: This is misleading.
history_text_issues.correction: They were sedentary or semi-sedentary horticulturalists (potato, maize, quinoa, beans, madi), raised camelids (chilihueque) and practised gathering. In the Purén-Lumaco valley there are raised fields and ceremonial mounds (kuel) studied by Dillehay.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that they were organised under the authority of the cacique.
history_text_issues.problem: Both the term and the model are wrong.
history_text_issues.correction: “Cacique” is a Taíno word brought by the Spanish. The Mapuche had lonko (head of a lof), ulmen (wealthy notables) and toqui (war leader elected only in wartime), with no permanent central authority.

history_text_issues.claim: It places the archaeological evidence of Mapuche civilisation in the 5th century BC.
history_text_issues.problem: This is doubtful, and Mapuche ethnogenesis is contested.
history_text_issues.correction: The Período Alfarero Temprano begins in the centuries before the Common Era, but the recognised direct antecedents are the Pitrén (1st millennium AD) and El Vergel (c. 1100–1450) complexes, and continuity with the historical Mapuche is debated.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that Lautaro learned from the Spanish how to use cavalry and gunpowder.
history_text_issues.problem: This is exaggerated: gunpowder was not the key.
history_text_issues.correction: Lautaro, a former yanacona and Valdivia's groom, knew horsemanship and Spanish tactics. His innovations were tactical: successive waves, use of terrain, ditches and palisades, attacks in the hottest hours of the day. The use of arquebuses only appears later, at Quiapo (1558).

history_text_issues.claim: It says that Lautaro realised that the Spanish were not gods.
history_text_issues.problem: It repeats the myth of the “conquistador-god” (Restall).
history_text_issues.correction: There is no evidence that the Mapuche took the Spanish for gods.

history_text_issues.claim: It says that the Mapuche used cavalry for the first time at Tucapel (1553).
history_text_issues.problem: The chronicles do not support this.
history_text_issues.correction: Tucapel (25 December 1553) was won by squadrons on foot attacking in successive waves, using lances, clubs, bolas and lassos to bring down the Spanish horsemen. Mapuche cavalry developed over the following years and decades.

history_text_issues.claim: It presents the Konas as elite young warriors educated by the weupife.
history_text_issues.problem: It exaggerates their status.
history_text_issues.correction: Kona mainly denoted the young warrior or dependant of a lonko, not a formal elite; the weupife was the orator and keeper of oral memory.

history_text_issues.claim: It describes the Arauco War as a 300-year struggle that began in 1541.
history_text_issues.problem: The periodisation is contested.
history_text_issues.correction: Open war runs from c. 1550 to 1656. It was followed by frontier, trade and parliaments (Quilín, 1641) until the Occupation of Araucanía (1861–1883).

history_text_issues.claim: The narrative begins with Valdivia in 1540.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the Inca frontier on the Maule (c. 1470–1530), the only Mapuche military episode within the game's frame, albeit one of debated historicity.
history_text_issues.correction: According to Garcilaso and other chroniclers, the Inca troops were halted by the Promaucae and the Reche near the Maule River.

missing_features: Decentralised organisation (lof, rewe, ayllarewe), which prevented a conquest by “decapitation”, unlike what happened to the Inca and the Mexica.
The toqui elected for war (and the stone axe, toki, as insignia), assemblies (koyagtun) and parliaments with the Crown (Quilín, 1641).
Lautaro's tactics: successive waves, staked ditches, ambushes in swamps and forests.
Machi (shamans, often women) and the ngillatun ceremony.
Chilihueque (domesticated camelid) and pre-Hispanic horticulture.
The frontier with the Inca on the Maule; the victory of Curalaba (1598) and the destruction of the seven cities.
Frontier trade in ponchos and cattle, and the exchange of captives.

proposals.title: Lautaro's Squadrons
proposals.description: Infantry out of combat regenerates 20 HP/min, and the Spearman-line gets +1 armour against cavalry.
proposals.historical_basis: At Tucapel (1553), fresh squadrons relieved one another until the Spanish horsemen were exhausted (Vivar; Góngora Marmolejo).

proposals.title: Pucará
proposals.description: Cheap defensive building of earth and palisade that replaces the Castle until the Imperial Age and trains Kona and Spearman-line. It allows the construction of trap pits that slow down enemy cavalry.
proposals.historical_basis: Lautaro's pucarás (Peteroa, 1556–57) and the pucará of Quiapo (1558), and the staked pits described by the chroniclers.

proposals.title: Horse Capture
proposals.description: Each enemy mounted unit killed gives +20 food and reduces the cost of subsequent Kona by 5%, down to -30%. The Kona becomes available only in the Castle Age.
proposals.historical_basis: The Mapuche obtained their first horses through capture and quickly built up herds of their own.

proposals.title: Chilihueque
proposals.description: Replaces the +2 line of sight: each ally starts with 2 chilihueques (herdable, like the Inca llama).
proposals.historical_basis: Camelid herding (hueque) is documented among the pre-Hispanic and colonial Mapuche.

proposals.title: Headless Lof
proposals.description: When a Mapuche Settlement or Town Center is destroyed, it spawns 3 Spearmen; Settlements cost -25%.
proposals.historical_basis: The absence of a central authority meant they had to be defeated one community at a time (Bengoa; Boccara).

proposals.title: Koyagtun/Parliament
proposals.description: Replaces or complements Butalmapu: Tribute rate at 0%, and allies receive +10% gold from Relics and the Market.
proposals.historical_basis: The Spanish–Mapuche parliaments, such as that of Quilín (1641), recognised the Biobío frontier.

contested: Ethnogenesis and ethnonym: a transition from “reche” to “mapuche” (Boccara) or long continuity (Bengoa, Dillehay).
The actual extent of Inca rule south of the Maipo and the historicity of the Battle of the Maule.
Periodisation and duration of the Arauco War.
The figure of Lautaro between history and epic (Ercilla).
Origin and nature of the butalmapu (a native institution or a product of the colonial relationship).
Pre-Hispanic demography of Araucanía.
key_sources: Gerónimo de Vivar, Crónica y relación copiosa y verdadera de los reinos de Chile (1558)
Alonso de Ercilla, La Araucana (1569–1589)
Alonso de Góngora Marmolejo, Historia de todas las cosas que han acaecido en el reino de Chile (1575)
Pedro Mariño de Lobera, Crónica del Reino de Chile (c. 1595)
Diego de Rosales, Historia general del Reino de Chile (c. 1674)
Francisco Núñez de Pineda y Bascuñán, Cautiverio feliz (1673)
José Bengoa, Historia del pueblo mapuche (1985); Historia de los antiguos mapuches del sur (2003)
Guillaume Boccara, Guerre et ethnogenèse mapuche dans le Chili colonial (1998)
Tom D. Dillehay, Monuments, Empires, and Resistance (2007)
Leonardo León Solís, studies on malones and the frontier

civs.represents: The Tupi-Guarani-speaking peoples of the 16th-century Brazilian coast, above all the Tupinambá (including the “Tamoio” of Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo), Tupiniquim, Temiminó, Potiguara and Caeté. They are known chiefly through Staden, Thevet, Léry, Anchieta and Soares de Sousa.
civs.period: Tupi-Guarani expansion to the coast during the 1st millennium AD and the early 2nd (dates debated); written documentation c. 1500–1600, centred on Guanabara Bay between 1555 and 1567.
civs.verdict: The core is right: archers with large hardwood bows, the ibirapema club and palisaded villages; Blackwood Archers and Ibirapema Warrior are good ideas. But almost all the bonuses are balance bonuses. The Caciques UT uses a Taíno word and an unrelated effect, and Curare is an Amazonian and Guianese poison not documented among the coastal Tupi. The regional package imposes the Andean mace (champi) and poorly attested slings on them, and the tech tree gives them Castle, Keep and Heated Shot. The two best-documented features of Tupinambá warfare are missing: fleets of war canoes and capture warfare tied to ritual execution. And everything known from written sources dates from 1550–1570, outside the game's time frame.
civs.naming_scope_issues: “Tupi” designates a language stock and works as an umbrella term; for the group described, “Tupinambá” or “coastal Tupi” would be more accurate. The Guarani, of the same family, are left out. The civ is built almost entirely from sources of 1550–1570 (Staden, Léry, Anchieta) and from the Luso-French war over Guanabara, outside the 500–1500 frame, while the pre-colonial expansion known from archaeology is ignored. Non-Tupi terms (cacique, curare, champi) add to the confusion. There is also thematic overlap with the Portuguese civ, which in the game represents the colonising side.

elements.explanation: The bow and the club were the central weapons according to Staden, Léry and Thevet, and war was waged on foot and by canoe.
It is a balance bonus with no historical basis.
The villages (taba), with their large communal houses (oca), were surrounded by palisades, sometimes double ones, clearly visible in Staden's woodcuts.

elements.element: Fallen units return 15% of their cost
elements.explanation: It has no clear connection. If it is meant to allude to anthropophagy, it inverts it: the Tupinambá ate captive enemies, not their own dead.

elements.element: Archery Range and Barracks upgrades cost -50% food
elements.explanation: It has no direct basis. It could be reinterpreted as manioc “war flour” (farinha de guerra), the ration of expeditions.

The chroniclers describe bows larger than European ones, made of hard, dark woods (airi palm, pau-d'arco). Training in pairs at half population is an acceptable abstraction of the large masses of archers.

The ibirapema, a decorated wooden club (the term partly overlaps with tacape), is the most iconic object of Tupinambá culture. It was used in the ritual execution of captives and also in combat. The frontal area attack is an acceptable abstraction.

“Cacique” is a Taíno (Arawakan) word from the Antilles, spread by the Spanish and later also used in Brazil. The Tupi called their chiefs morubixaba, and the Portuguese chroniclers called them “principais” (“principal men”). The idea of leadership is legitimate, but the effect (Champi Warriors and Slingers attack faster) falls on units that are not even Tupi.

Curare is prepared by peoples of Amazonia and the Guianas, and the word itself comes from Cariban languages. The sources on the coastal Tupi describe points of taquara cane, bone, shark teeth and stingray spines, not plant poisons. Fortifications dealing poison damage are pure invention.

elements.element: Team Bonus: Towers and Castles provide +10 population space
elements.explanation: It has no basis: the Tupi built neither towers nor castles.

Champi is the Andean mace with a stone or bronze head, and the Tupi had no metal before contact; their club was made of wood (tacape/ibirapema). Nor is the sling a characteristic Tupinambá weapon in the 16th-century sources.
It corresponds to villages relocated every few years, with slash-and-burn (coivara) plots nearby.

tree_issues.item: Navy (War Galley, Galleon, Fast Fire Ship, Hulk-line, Catapult Galleon; no Carrack)
tree_issues.problem: It is anachronistic. The real Tupi naval force is missing: bark or dugout canoes (igara, ubá) carrying dozens of warriors, used in coastal raids and in the “Battle of the Canoes” (1566).

tree_issues.item: Castle, Keep, Guard Tower, Heated Shot, Stone Walls
tree_issues.problem: They are anachronistic. Defences were palisades and stakes.
They are anachronistic. Attacks on villages were made with fire arrows against the thatched roofs, as the text itself notes.
It is faithful to Tupi reality (although it contradicts the presence of Keep).
It is consistent with shifting slash-and-burn (coivara) agriculture.

tree_issues.item: Blacksmith: Iron Casting, Plate Mail (no Blast Furnace)
tree_issues.problem: There was no metal before contact. After 1500, iron tools arrived through barter, in exchange for brazilwood.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the tribes formed two large groups after contact with the French and Portuguese: the Temiminó and the Tamoio.
history_text_issues.problem: It is misleading.
history_text_issues.correction: These were groups and rivalries that predated contact; the “Tamoio Confederation” (c. 1554–1567) was an alliance against the Portuguese. The coast had many other groups (Potiguara, Caeté, Tupiniquim, Tupinambá of Bahia), and this dichotomy holds only for Guanabara and São Vicente.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the Temiminó included the Maracajá tribe.
history_text_issues.problem: It confuses the group's identity.
history_text_issues.correction: “Maracajá” (“wildcats”) was the name the Tupinambá gave to the Temiminó themselves, not a subdivision of them.

history_text_issues.claim: Presents Hans Staden as a “German explorer” held hostage by Cunhambebe from 1552 to 1555.
history_text_issues.problem: His profession is wrong, and the chronology and Cunhambebe's role are debatable.
history_text_issues.correction: Staden was a mercenary gunner in Portuguese service at the fort of Bertioga. He was captured by Tupinambá and taken to the village of Ubatuba, and was rescued by a French ship, reaching Honfleur in February 1555. Many specialists read his book as indicating capture in 1554 and a captivity of about nine months, although some overviews give 1552–1555. Cunhambebe (Staden's “Konyan Bebe”) was the great Tupinambá chief whose favour he won, not his direct captor.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the Portuguese settlers remarked that two or more of their men would struggle against a single Tupi warrior.
history_text_issues.problem: There is no identifiable source.
history_text_issues.correction: It should be removed or attributed to a specific source.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that they made poisoned arrows with stingray spines.
history_text_issues.problem: It conflates things.
history_text_issues.correction: Stingray spines were barbed points whose venom is incidental; they are not poisoned arrows in the curare sense.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that they practised slash-and-burn agriculture and grew maize, beans and squash.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits the staple crop.
history_text_issues.correction: The Tupinambá diet was based on manioc (flours, including “war flour”, and cauim); maize was secondary (Soares de Sousa; Léry).

history_text_issues.claim: Says only that the ibirapema was used in “ritual killings of enemies”.
history_text_issues.problem: It is a euphemism that leaves out the essential point.
history_text_issues.correction: Ritual execution followed by anthropophagy was the central institution of Tupinambá warfare and society, tied to revenge, prestige and the renaming of the killer (Fernandes; Viveiros de Castro; Fausto).

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the Tupi were not very well known for their art.
history_text_issues.problem: It is a disparaging judgement.
history_text_issues.correction: Tupinambá featherwork (mantles of scarlet ibis feathers, ornaments) is among the most remarkable in the world. A Tupinambá mantle was returned to Brazil by the National Museum of Denmark in 2024.

history_text_issues.claim: Places the Franco-Portuguese struggle for Guanabara in the late 16th century.
history_text_issues.problem: The dating is wrong.
history_text_issues.correction: France Antarctique lasted from 1555 to 1560, and the French and the Tamoio were only expelled in 1567: the middle of the century.

history_text_issues.claim: Says that the Portuguese founded Rio de Janeiro after the battle of 1567.
history_text_issues.problem: The order of events is reversed.
history_text_issues.correction: Estácio de Sá founded the city on 1 March 1565. The victory of Uruçumirim (20 January 1567), where Estácio was mortally wounded, led to the city being moved to Morro do Castelo.

history_text_issues.claim: The text begins only at contact with Europeans.
history_text_issues.problem: It omits all the history before contact.
history_text_issues.correction: The archaeology of the Tupiguarani tradition shows the Tupi expansion from southern Amazonia and the occupation of the coast, pushing out “Tapuia” (Macro-Jê) groups, centuries before 1500.

missing_features: War canoes (igara) and coastal fleets.
Capture warfare and ritual execution with anthropophagy, tied to revenge and the renaming of warriors.
Manioc, war flour and slash-and-burn (coivara) agriculture.
Shamans (pajés) and caraíbas (prophets), and the migrations in search of the “Land without Evil” (a contested topic).
Featherwork (scarlet ibis mantles), maracá and cauim.
Palisaded villages that relocated periodically.
Alliances with the French and Portuguese, and the brazilwood barter trade (after 1500).
Tupi as a lingua franca, the língua geral (Anchieta's grammar, 1595).

proposals.title: Igara (war canoe)
proposals.description: Replaces the Galley line: a fast, cheap canoe that fires arrows and carries 8 units. Remove Galleon, Hulk-line and Fire Ship.
proposals.historical_basis: Canoe expeditions described by Staden and Anchieta, and the Battle of the Canoes on Guanabara Bay (1566).

proposals.title: Capture warfare and renaming
proposals.description: Replaces “Fallen units return 15%”: Ibirapema Warriors gain +1 permanent attack for each enemy infantry unit killed (up to +5), and each kill yields +5 food.
proposals.historical_basis: The ritual executioner took new names and gained prestige (Florestan Fernandes; Viveiros de Castro).

proposals.title: Fire arrows
proposals.description: Replaces Curare: Foot Archers gain +3 attack against buildings and deal continuous fire damage.
proposals.historical_basis: The game's own text and the chroniclers mention arrows tipped with burning waxed cotton, used against villages and sugar mills.

proposals.title: War flour
proposals.description: Reworks the food discount: military units cost -15% food and slowly regenerate HP out of combat.
proposals.historical_basis: Toasted manioc flour was the long-keeping ration of war expeditions (Soares de Sousa; Léry).

proposals.title: Caciques → Morubixaba
proposals.description: Rename the UT and change its effect: units near an Elite Ibirapema Warrior gain +1 attack (leadership).
proposals.historical_basis: Morubixaba was the Tupi term for chief; cacique is a Taíno word.

proposals.title: Champi → Tacape Warrior
proposals.description: For the Tupi, rename the Champi line as Tacape Warrior, with a wooden club, and remove the Slinger.
proposals.historical_basis: The tacape was the Tupi war club; there was no metal and no documented use of slings.

contested: The reality and meaning of anthropophagy: Arens's denial (1979) is rejected by most scholars; interpretations by Fernandes, Viveiros de Castro and Fausto.
Migrations to the “Land without Evil”: a pre-colonial phenomenon (H. Clastres) or a reaction to colonialism (Pompa; Noelli).
Chronology and routes of the Tupi-Guarani expansion (Brochado vs Noelli).
Reliability and rhetorical shaping of Staden's and Léry's accounts (Whitehead), including the chronology of Staden's captivity.
The identity of Cunhambebe, with a father and son of the same name according to Thevet.
key_sources: Hans Staden, Warhaftige Historia (Marburg, 1557); ed. Whitehead & Harbsmeier (2008)
Jean de Léry, Histoire d'un voyage faict en la terre du Brésil (1578)
André Thevet, Les Singularitez de la France Antarctique (1557)
Gabriel Soares de Sousa, Tratado descritivo do Brasil em 1587
José de Anchieta, letters; Arte de grammatica da lingoa mais usada na costa do Brasil (1595)
Florestan Fernandes, A organização social dos Tupinambá (1949); A função social da guerra na sociedade Tupinambá (1952)
Alfred Métraux, La religion des Tupinamba (1928)
Eduardo Viveiros de Castro, From the Enemy's Point of View (1992); A inconstância da alma selvagem (2002)
Carlos Fausto, “Fragmentos de história e cultura tupinambá” (1992)
John Hemming, Red Gold (1978)
Francisco S. Noelli, on the archaeology of the Tupiguarani expansion

groups.cross_civ_notes:
1) Anachronisms common to all six civs (verified in data/data.json). None of these peoples knew torsion or counterweight engines, the plough, draught animals (the llama was only a pack animal), the wheel for transport, iron, gunpowder or high-sided ships. Even so, all of them have Trebuchet, Mangonel/Onager, Capped Ram, War Galley, Fire Ship, Hulk/War Hulk, Catapult Galleon and Demolition Ship, Horse Collar, Heavy Plow, Iron Casting, Plate Mail, Chemistry and Trade Cart; all except the Aztecs have Galleon, and all except the Tupi have Carrack. The abstraction is understandable for balance, but a renamed “American variant” of the techs would solve much of the problem without touching the numbers: obsidian in Mesoamerica, tin bronze in the Andes, quilted cotton, canoes and rafts in place of galleons, chinampa and chaki taklla instead of Heavy Plow. Monastery and Relics impose a Christian model on religions of priests, shamans and sacred bundles. There are also internal inconsistencies: the Aztecs have Fortified Wall but neither Masonry nor Keep; the Muisca and the Tupi have Keep, and the Mapuche have Architecture and Bombard Tower, despite building in wood and earth.

2) Duplications and transpositions in Mesoamerica. Aztecs and Mayans share the Eagle line, a Nahua military order applied to the whole Maya world and turned into a cheap unit when it was an elite. Both also have a UT based on the same spear-thrower (Atlatl / Hul'che, which means “atlatl” in Yucatec), both applied to Skirmishers. Among these six civs, only the Aztecs have Gambesons; the Mayans have the Militia-line but do not get it, although quilted cotton is well documented in Yucatán, and the four South American civs have no Militia-line, so the tech does not apply to them. The former Mayan UT “El Dorado” was a Muisca myth and was renamed Holcans with the same effect, but the internal name “Mayan El Dorado” still persists in data/data.json.

3) Homogenisation of the “South American package” (The Last Chieftains). Settlement (a universal drop-off building that replaces Mill, Lumber Camp and Mining Camp), Champi Scout/Warrior and Slinger are shared by Incas, Muisca, Mapuche and Tupi, and rest on Quechua vocabulary (champi = Andean mace; warak'a/huaraca = sling). The Settlement is an acceptable abstraction of dispersed settlement, but the rest lumps together four radically different societies: a centralised empire (Inca), highland chiefdoms and confederations (Muisca), decentralised lineage societies (Mapuche) and semi-itinerant villagers of the Atlantic coast (Tupi). Only for the Incas is the package entirely faithful. For the Tupi, with no metal and no documented slings, it is wrong. For the Muisca and Mapuche it is stretched, and the Muisca UT “Huaracas” even uses the Quechua word. The Taíno term “cacique” appears as a Tupi UT and in the Mapuche text. The bolas attributed to the Mapuche were also used by the Incas against Spanish cavalry; among the Mapuche they are attested on foot as early as Tucapel (1553), and mounted use is more typical of the Pampas.

4) Time frame. Aztecs, Incas, Mayans and Muisca fit reasonably well within the 500–1500 frame, although the Aztecs and Incas only represent the last century and the Mayans mix the Classic (text) with the Postclassic (units).
