Mapuche and Tupi are built almost entirely from events of 1541–1600 (Arauco War, Guanabara), because the written record begins with the Europeans; archaeology would make it possible to give them pre-1500 content (Pitrén/El Vergel and the Inca frontier on the Maule; the Tupi-Guarani expansion). The texts of the three most recent DLCs focus heavily on the conquest and the myth of El Dorado.

5) Regional gaps. Left without representation are American powers that would fit the 500–1500 frame better than the Mapuche and Tupi and that today end up absorbed into the existing civs. They are: Tiwanaku and Wari (c. 500–1000), Chimor (c. 900–1470, conquered by the Incas), the Purépecha or Tarascans (copper and bronze metalworkers who defeated the Mexica c. 1478–79), the Mixtecs and Zapotecs, the Tlaxcalans (decisive in 1521), the Mississippians of Cahokia (c. 1050–1350) and the Taíno.

6) Calibration. The proposed fidelity ranking is Incas (6) > Aztecs ≈ Mapuche (5) > Mayans ≈ Muisca ≈ Tupi (4), on a scale where the average AoE2 civ scores c. 5. The Incas stand out for bonuses that abstract real institutions well; the Mapuche have authentic vocabulary but displaced in time; the Mayans, Muisca and Tupi combine one or two accurate elements with balance bonuses and borrowings from other cultures. The oldest history texts (Aztecs and Mayans, from 1999) are the most outdated and Eurocentric; the most recent ones (Muisca, Mapuche, Tupi) are more respectful, but contain errors of dates and terminology.

verification_log.change: Each civ's tech tree was checked directly in data/data.json. The WebSearch quota ran out right at the start; as a result, fact-checking relied on directly consulting a few pages (Wikipedia on Staden, Quemuenchatocha, Quiapo, Tucapel, the Inca army and Muisca warfare) and on the author's own knowledge. Claims that could not be confirmed were softened or marked as contested rather than asserted.
“Start with +50 gold” moved from unfounded to stretched: imperial tribute included gold (Codex Mendoza), although the link to a starting bonus is weak.
“Monks +5 HP” moved from abstraction to stretched, because the draft itself admitted that the link was weak and the progression purely mechanical.

Smallpox item: the charge of “wrong chronology” was withdrawn. The epidemic (September to December 1520) does indeed predate the fall in 1521; the error lies in the vector (earlier “merchants”). Severity lowered from major to moderate.

Item on clubs without obsidian: changed from “myth” to “unsupported by the sources”, with a mention of the cuauhololli, and severity lowered to minor. The severity of the satellite-cities item was lowered to moderate (the observation is correct, the explanation is not). Added the item on widespread flaying and decapitation (minor).

Softened the claim that atlatl darts pierced armour, without attributing it to a specific chronicler. “Coa” corrected to huictli (coa is a Taíno-Spanish term). Refinements to the Jaguar Warrior (otontin/cuachicqueh grades) and to the verified naval list (Fast Fire Ship, Catapult Galleon, Demolition Ship; no Galleon). Flagged the inconsistency of Fortified Wall without Masonry or Keep.

“Archer civilization” moved from stretched to plausible: Landa and Bernal Díaz document archers in the Postclassic, which covers more than half of the game's time frame, although the label does not fit the Classic. “Foot Archers cost -10/20/30%” moved from unfounded to stretched. The verdict and the first proposal were rewritten (identity by period instead of “Infantry and Monk”).

Holcans described as a renaming of El Dorado with the same effect, not as a replacement. The three-codices item was lowered to minor, because the authenticity of the Grolier was only confirmed in 2018. Added the item on the omission of divine kingship (minor). Noted that La Danta is Preclassic.

Corrected “the only American pack animal” in the Llama bonus: it was the only large one, since dogs pulled travois in North America. The “Gambesons (missing)” item was replaced: the Incas have no Militia-line, so the tech does not apply.

Unverifiable claims softened. The Pedro Pizarro quotation about stones that broke swords became “Spanish accounts”. The meaning of champi became a mace with a stone or bronze head, dropping the confident equation with “bronze”. In Fabric Shields, the shields became “covered with leather or cloth”. Added the alternative date of Atahualpa's execution (29 August) and Ollantaytambo as the site of the flooding.
Corrected a tech tree error: the Muisca do NOT have Blast Furnace, and the draft listed it. Flagged that they have Masonry and Keep, which contradicts the absence of Architecture and Fortified Wall.
Removed the claim that the game gives the Temple Guard tumbaga weapons: it does not appear in the repository. The explanation was rewritten based on the unit's actual description.

Archer label: removed the unverified claim “Piedrahita mentions bows”; it now says that bows are associated mainly with the Panches (and with Panche captives). In the Guecha item, “adornments for each enemy” became “the number of earrings would indicate enemies defeated”. Corrected the description of the armour bonus, which also covers Champi Warriors and not only ranged units. The proposal “Tiradera” became “Güecha Darts”.

Added an error in the history text: Quemuenchatocha did not die in 1537; he was captured on 20 August 1537 and died in 1538, in Ramiriquí. The mummies proposal was corrected: they were carried on the backs of warriors, not by priests.

Corrected the tech tree: the Mapuche do not have Siege Ram (only Capped Ram) and do have Siphons, Architecture and Masonry. Flagged the inconsistency of Architecture and Masonry. In the Quiapo episode, the “artillery” was removed; only the arquebuses reported by Rosales remain.

Tucapel: confirmed that the chronicles describe squadrons on foot in waves, with bolas and lassos, and not Mapuche cavalry. This was worked into the Bolas Rider item and the label. The “sea-lion-hide cuirass” was softened to hardened leather. The 5th-century BC item was lowered to minor, with a mention of the Período Alfarero Temprano. Added the item on the status of the Konas and the dispute over the origin of the butalmapu.

Corrected a tech tree error: the Tupi do NOT have Blast Furnace, and the draft listed it. Naval list verified (Fast Fire Ship, Catapult Galleon; no Carrack). Flagged the contradiction between Keep and the absence of Masonry.

Caciques moved from wrong to stretched: the term is Taíno, but it became widespread as a designation for an Indigenous chief, in Brazil too; the main problem is the effect, which has nothing to do with it. Champi/Slinger stays wrong, with the champi described as a stone or bronze mace.

Staden item rewritten. His profession (gunner, not explorer) is confirmed. The chronology, 1552–1555 versus 1554 with nine months of captivity, is presented as disputed, because the English Wikipedia gives 1552–1555. Cunhambebe appears as the chief whose favour he won, not as his direct captor.
Added a previously missed error in the history text: the list of crops ignores manioc, the Tupinambá staple food (moderate).
The fidelity score rose from 3 to 4. The bow, the ibirapema and palisaded villages are faithful or plausible, which puts the Tupi on a level with the Muisca on the recalibrated scale (average ≈ 5).

Cross-civ notes revised. The list of common anachronisms was checked in data.json (Capped Ram instead of generic “rams”, Catapult Galleon, Galleon except for the Aztecs, Carrack except for the Tupi). Corrected the claim “only the Aztecs have Gambesons”: it is true among the six, but it failed to explain that the South American civs have no Militia-line. Added the role of the Settlement and the internal inconsistencies regarding masonry.

themes.title: The AoE2 game model: the systemic abstractions that distort history
themes.summary:
I analysed the repository's data/data.json (56 civs; 486 distinct items), the bonus texts, the tech trees, the item descriptions, the history texts and the parallel modes the repository also contains (chronicles/ and ror/). The main conclusion stands: AoE2 rests on a Latin-European model of c. 1000–1500 (Castle, Monastery, University, Knight/Cavalier/Paladin, Guilds, Coinage, Banking, Galleon, Carrack). That model is applied to 56 civs from five continents, whose texts range from AD 184 (Three Kingdoms) to the late 16th century (some reach 1683).

The numbers confirm the uniformity, but above all they show that the tech tree does not follow historical proximity:
- 63 items are common to all 56 civs and 102 exist in at least 50.
- On average, about 67% of each civ's tech tree (between 63% and 73%) is made up of items that at least 50 civs also have.
- The similarity (Jaccard) between Shu (3rd century) and Spanish (16th century) is 0.725, i.e. equal to the average of all pairs (0.727). Shu is more similar to the Britons (0.769) than to Wu (0.76) or Wei (0.737), its neighbours and rivals. Japanese and Britons (0.837) are more similar to each other than Vikings and Danes (0.758).

In practice, each civ is the common tech tree with pieces removed, plus a thin layer of bonuses and unique units. The pieces removed are chosen mainly for game balance, not for historical reasons.

There are reasonable abstractions and some ingenious ones: the Villager as generic labour, gold as abstract wealth, Relics that generate gold, Huns without Houses, Khitans with Pasture, the Three Kingdoms' Traction Trebuchet, the South American Settlements, the Three Kingdoms without gunpowder and the Mapuche as a mounted civ without a Stable.

But there are serious systematic distortions:
- **Religion:** the Monk/Monastery system, with Christian vocabulary, is applied to Muslims, shamanists, Mesoamericans and Andeans.
- **Ages:** the Dark/Feudal/Castle/Imperial sequence is Eurocentric and even inverts Chinese history.
- **Out-of-period siege:** counterweight Trebuchet, Petard and Galleon exist in Late Antique civs and in civs of the Americas.
- **Americas:** they receive iron, chain mail and plate armour (all six civs), blast furnace, horse collar, wheelbarrow and crossbow.
- **Gunpowder:** its diffusion is inconsistent. Chinese without Hand Cannoneer; Goths with full gunpowder, but Romans and Huns with none; Khitans (Liao, until 1125) with Rocket Cart.
- **Economy:** Market/Coinage/Banking/Guilds are imposed on the Incas, while the Aztecs, who had professional merchants, do not have Guilds.
- **Stateless and nomadic societies:** they receive Castles and Wonders.
- **Slavery:** forced labour and military slavery disappear.

The repository itself has precedents for correcting this:
- the 'antiquity' era, with Archaic/Civic/Classical ages;
- the Chronicles mode: Temple with Priestess, Syncretism and Haruspicy; Fort; Academy; Palintonon instead of Trebuchet; an ancient fleet with Trireme and Incendiary Raft; and Oligarchy/Democracy/Tyranny at the Town Center;
- the Return of Rome tech tree (ror/), with Stone/Tool/Bronze/Iron ages;
- Traction Trebuchet, Fortified Church, Krepost and Settlement.

The proposals can therefore be tested as a data mod and visualised with aoe2techtree itself.

findings.title: A 'universal' tech tree on a Latin-European template: each civ is the common tree with pieces removed, and the similarity does not follow history
findings.detail:
**How the model works**
In data/data.json, each civ is just a list of IDs drawn from a single global set (486 distinct items). The differences are made in three ways: by removing items, by adding 1 to 3 unique units and 2 unique techs, and by adding 4 or 5 bonuses. The common vocabulary is that of Latin Europe in 1000–1500:
- Knight/Cavalier/Paladin (the 'paladins' are Charlemagne's twelve peers in the Chanson de Roland);
- Man-at-Arms and Arbalester;
- Guilds, Coinage and Banking;
- University and Castle;
- Carrack, Galleon and the Hanseatic Trade Cog.

Assessment: **abstraction**. It is a conscious and defensible choice for the sake of readability and competitive balance.

**The problem: similarity between trees does not reflect historical closeness**
If the tree encoded history, neighbouring and contemporary civs would be much more alike than civs separated by continents and centuries. That is not what happens (see examples). Methodological caveat: the Jaccard index drops when a civ has many unique items, so these figures indicate a trend, not an exact measure.

**The choice of what is removed**
The criterion is balance, not history. Several omissions contradict well-documented facts; in those cases the assessment is **unfounded**. Some are compensated by bonuses: the Byzantines lack Masonry and Architecture, but their buildings get +10/20/30/40% HP, which is an acceptable abstraction. Others are not compensated by anything.

**A fair case, but incomplete**
The Thumb Ring roughly follows the real divide between the European 'Mediterranean draw' and the 'thumb draw' of the steppe and Asia. It is missing for the Britons, Franks, Teutons, Celts, Goths and Vikings, and present for the Mongols, Huns, Magyars, Turks and Koreans (**plausible**).

There are, however, two flaws:
- **Jurchens without Thumb Ring:** the thumb draw is emblematic of Manchu archery, the heir of Jurchen archery (**unfounded**).
- **Incas, Mayans and Muisca with Thumb Ring:** there is no attestation whatsoever of thumb rings in the Americas (**unfounded**).
examples: 63 items are common to all 56 civs and 102 to ≥50; on average ~67% (min. 63%, max. 73%) of each civ's tree consists of items that ≥50 civs also have (calculated from data/data.json)
Jaccard: Shu–Spanish = 0.725, equal to the mean of all 1540 pairs (0.727); Shu–Wei = 0.737 and Shu–Wu = 0.76, but the civ most similar to Shu is Britons (0.769)
Jaccard: Japanese–Britons = 0.837, higher than Vikings–Danes (0.758) and Romans–Byzantines (0.73); Franks–Burgundians = 0.81

Romans without Treadmill Crane (Teutons too, despite the famous treadwheel crane of Cologne Cathedral), although the Roman treadwheel crane appears in Vitruvius (De architectura X) and on the Haterii relief (c. 100–120 AD) — unfounded
Saxons are the only civ without Clinker Construction ('Ships move +10% faster'), yet they have Longship; the Sutton Hoo ship (c. 620) is the classic example of clinker planking — unfounded
Shu is the only civ without Iron Casting (and it also lacks Blast Furnace), even though Sichuan was a Han iron-working centre (the Zhuo family of Linqiong, Shiji 129) — unfounded
Chinese without Guilds, despite the merchant guilds (hang) of Song China — unfounded

Byzantines without Masonry, Architecture and Herbal Medicine (Hagia Sophia, the Theodosian Walls, xenones), compensated by the building HP bonus and the team bonus 'Monks heal +100% faster' (acceptable abstraction)

findings.title: A single Monk/Monastery system, with Christian vocabulary, for all religions
findings.detail:
**What the data show**
The Monk (id 125) exists in all 56 civs and the Monastery in 54. The two exceptions, which have the Fortified Church instead, are two Christian civs: Armenians and Georgians. The techs have Christian-Latin theological names (Atonement, Redemption, Heresy, Sanctity, Theocracy, Faith, Devotion, Illumination), although their effects are purely mechanical. Theocracy, for example, merely makes only one Monk rest after a group conversion.

The game's history texts speak of Buddhism, Hinduism, Islam, Zoroastrianism (Armenians), Confucianism, Daoism (Wu), shamanism (Cumans, Khitans), animism (Malians) and paganism. Mechanically, it all comes down to a 'monk'.

**Assessment by religious tradition**
- **Christians — faithful.** The healing Monk corresponds well to monastic infirmaries.
- **Buddhists — plausible.** The sangha is monastic: Burmese, Khmer, Japanese, Koreans, Khitans; the Bengalis even have the Mahayana tech.
- **Hindus — abstraction.** Mathas and sannyasins do exist.
- **Muslims — stretched.** The Quran (57:27) presents monasticism as a human innovation, and the hadith 'la rahbaniyya fi al-islam' is widely cited, although its authenticity is disputed. The right figures would be the ulama, the imams and the Sufi sheikhs in the khanqahs. The Saracens' Bimaristan tech shows that it is possible to get this right.
- **Contexts without monasticism — wrong.** The Mapuche had the machi (today mostly women, although colonial sources also mention male machi); the Tupi had pajés and karaí; the Mongols, Cumans and Huns had shamans (kam/böö).

**Three Kingdoms: a more nuanced case than it seems**
Buddhism already existed in late Han China: Ze Rong built a large Buddhist temple in Xuzhou in the 190s. The Monk is therefore plausible there too. But the most prominent organised religion of the period was Daoist, which makes 'Theocracy' a literally faithful name for the Five Pecks of Rice.

**An irony: the Muisca**
They are the most 'monastic' Amerindian case. The xeques were trained in seclusion in a 'cuca' for about 4 to 7 years ([arXiv 0812.0574](https://arxiv.org/pdf/0812.0574)).

**A purely visual change**
[Update 141935](https://www.ageofempires.com/news/age-of-empires-ii-definitive-edition-update-141935/) (10 April 2025) added:
- 6 regional Monk visuals;
- 3 new Monastery visuals (Byzantines, Ethiopians and 'shamanistic' civs);
- a 'Pagan Priest', but only in the Scenario Editor.

The developers therefore acknowledge shamanism and paganism at the visual level. The name, the techs and the mechanics remain the same.
examples: Heresy (32/56: 'Units converted by an enemy Monk die') for the Tupi, Mapuche, Huns, Mongols, Cumans, Aztecs and Incas — the concept of codified orthodoxy applied to religions that had none

Redemption (31/56) for the Aztecs, Incas, Muisca and Tupi (the Mapuche do not have it); Atonement (39/56) for the Aztecs, Mayans, Mapuche, Muisca, Huns, Mongols and Cumans (the Incas and Tupi do not have it)
Huns: UT Atheism — wrong; Jordanes (Getica 195–196) reports that Attila consulted haruspices before the Catalaunian Plains (451), and Priscus tells of the cult of the 'sword of Mars'

Lithuanians, 'Cavalry and Monk civilization', with each Relic giving +1 attack to the Knight-line and the Leitis — Lithuania was the last pagan state in Europe (baptism of 1387; Samogitia in 1413), and the game's own text speaks of the crusades against the 'pagan Lithuanians' — stretched

Shu/Wei/Wu with Monastery and Theocracy: there is Buddhism in the 190s (Ze Rong's temple), but the prominent movement was Daoist (the Yellow Turbans, 184; Zhang Lu's theocracy in Hanzhong, c. 191–215)

findings.title: Battlefield conversion ('wololo') and Relics: a mechanic with no literal basis, but with usable cores
findings.detail:
**Converting soldiers**
Converting enemy soldiers at a distance, in the middle of battle, has no basis in any religion (**unfounded** as a literal mechanic). In fairness, the mechanic can also be read as a 'change of allegiance': desertions, bribes and units that switched sides were very real (**abstraction**). The problem is giving it a religious form.

The real religious core was something else:
- the conversion of rulers, from the top down, in a process lasting generations: Clovis c. 496/508, Mieszko in 966, Vladimir in 988, Stephen of Hungary c. 1000. The year 988 is also when the Varangians text places the creation of the Varangian Guard, linked to the agreement between Basil II and Vladimir.
- it was often the conquerors who adopted the religion of the conquered: the Ilkhan Ghazan converted to Islam in 1295, and Özbeg, in the Golden Horde, c. 1313. The Yuan protected Tibetan Buddhism, the religion of a subject people.

**Aztecs and Incas: capturing instead of converting**
For these two civs, the historically correct model is not conversion but capture:
- the Mexica kept the images of the gods of defeated peoples in the Coateocalli of Tenochtitlan (according to Diego Durán);
- the Incas took the huacas of the provinces to Cusco as 'hostages'.

**Relics that generate gold**
They work surprisingly well as an abstraction:
- **Christianity — faithful:** the pilgrimage economy (Santiago, Canterbury) and the theft of relics studied by Patrick Geary (Furta Sacra, 1978);
- **Buddhism — faithful:** śarīra relics, the Buddha's Tooth in Kandy, the Shwedagon;
- **Andes — plausible:** the royal mummies (mallquis) retained land and servants through the panaqa;
- **Islam and Hinduism — abstraction:** the cult of bodily relics is marginal or contested, but shrine economies were enormous. In Islam, the ziyara to Sufi tombs and the Shia shrines (Karbala, Mashhad); the relics of the Prophet taken to Istanbul after 1517. In Hinduism, pilgrimage to the tirthas and temple economies.
examples: Monk: 'Converts enemy units to your civilization.' (56/56)
Monastery: 'Garrison relics to generate gold.' — identical in the 54 civs that have it

Aztecs: UT Garland Wars ('Infantry +4 attack') — the purpose of the flower wars is contested (capturing prisoners for sacrifice, according to the colonial sources; a strategic war of attrition, according to Ross Hassig), but a capture mechanic would be more faithful than conversion
Mongols with the 'converting' Monk, when the empire is known for its religious tolerance (Möngke's debate in Karakorum, 1254, reported by William of Rubruck)
Aztecs: team bonus 'Relics generate +33% gold' — the Mexica cult of captured images has a real parallel

findings.title: Dark/Feudal/Castle/Imperial: a Western European periodisation (already contested there) imposed on everyone
findings.detail:
**Already contested within Europe itself**
- 'Dark Ages' comes from the humanist tradition begun by Petrarch and is now avoided by medievalists.
- The concept of feudalism was challenged by Elizabeth A. R. Brown ('The Tyranny of a Construct', 1974) and by Susan Reynolds (Fiefs and Vassals, 1994).
- The castle as a private fortified residence is a phenomenon of the 10th to 15th centuries.

**Outside Europe it is even worse**
- **China — the ladder is inverted.** Fengjian is the Zhou system of the 1st millennium BC, and China has been imperial since 221 BC. The Three Kingdoms are the fragmentation of an empire, yet in the game they 'rise' to the Imperial Age.
- **India — contested.** R. S. Sharma's 'Indian feudalism' (1965) was challenged by Harbans Mukhia (1981).
- **Japan — debated.** The comparison with European feudalism is a classic one, but disputed.
- **The Americas — inapplicable.** The Tupi and Mapuche, stateless societies, reach the 'Imperial Age'.

**Assessment**
**Abstraction**: the ages are game pacing. But they have Eurocentric names and a stadial logic (Turgot and Smith, Morgan) in which everyone climbs the same ladder. In fairness, AoE2 puts all civs on the same ladder and has never put Amerindians in a 'Stone Age'.

**The repository proves that changing this is trivial**
- data.json already has an 'antiquity' era (Archaic/Civic/Classical/Imperial), and techtree.js already picks age names and images according to the civ's era (AGE_IMAGES).
- The Return of Rome tree (the ror/ folder) uses the AoE1 ages: Stone, Tool, Bronze and Iron.
- Even so, the 56 main civs (including Romans, Huns, Goths and Shu/Wei/Wu) have era='base'.
examples: data/data.json → age_names: 'antiquity' = Archaic/Civic/Classical/Imperial; 'base' = Dark/Feudal/Castle/Imperial; the 56 main civs have era='base'
chronicles/data/data.json: Achaemenids, Athenians, Macedonians, Puru, Spartans and Thracians have era='antiquity'; ror/data/data.json uses Stone/Tool/Bronze/Iron Age
Shu/Wei/Wu (texts covering 184–280 AD) start in a 'Dark Age' and end in an 'Imperial Age' — the reverse of the Han → fragmentation trajectory
Tupi and Mapuche (stateless; the butalmapu, the name of a Mapuche UT, were territorial confederations for war) reach the 'Imperial Age'

The Castle Age requires two of Archery Range/Stable/Blacksmith/Market; the Imperial Age requires a Castle/Krepost or two of University/Siege Workshop/Monastery — 'progress' is defined by Latin-European institutions (only the Khmer are exempt from the requirements)

findings.title: A 'medieval' game spanning 1400 years: each civ is a trans-historical package
findings.detail:
**The game's real time span**
- **Start:** the Three Kingdoms (the Shu text begins in 184 AD) and Late Antiquity — Romans (395–476), Huns, Goths (376–711) and Persians, whose text is entirely Sasanian and ends in 651.
- **End:** the 16th century — Conquistador, Caravel, Feitoria, Turtle Ship (Japanese invasion of 1592), Tupi (1552–1567), Mapuche (from 1541) and Incas (up to 1572).
- **Beyond:** some texts go even further (Turks up to 1683).

The clash between the eras of different civs is an acceptable 'what if?' in an RTS.

**The systemic problem: within each civ**
Because they all receive the same 16th-century endgame, each civ accumulates elements from incompatible eras in the same tree. Assessment: **anachronistic** (within the civ itself). The inconsistency is visible between civs of the same era: Romans and Huns have no gunpowder at all, but the Goths have Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon (see the section on gunpowder).

**The history texts also reveal this problem**
The Persians text is Sasanian, but the tree combines War Elephant, Savar, Caravanserai and gunpowder. The same text also has errors of its own: it identifies Ctesiphon with Baghdad and ends the dynasty in 636, when Yazdegerd III did not die until 651.

**A bias in the recent Amerindian civs**
The recent Amerindian civs are defined by the moment of contact and conquest. They are known mainly from European sources, such as Hans Staden (1557), whom the Tupi text itself cites. The texts are honest about this, but this dependence shapes what is chosen for representation.
examples: Persians: Sasanian text (364–651) and War Elephant (faithful for the Sasanians), but also Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon (Safavid era) — anachronistic
Goths (kingdoms extinct by 711) with Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon, Galleon and Carrack; Romans (395–476) and Huns without any gunpowder unit
Romans (395–476) with Galleon; Wei (3rd century) with Block Printing — Chinese woodblock printing dates from the 7th–8th centuries (Diamond Sutra, 868)
Wu: the hero Sun Jian died in 191, more than 30 years before Sun Quan became King of Wu (222) and emperor (229)
Turks: the text runs from 1055 to 1683 — Seljuks and Ottomans in a single civ

findings.title: The spread of gunpowder follows balance, not history
findings.detail:
**How gunpowder enters the game**
It is a late technology that depends on 'Chemistry' at the University (56/56). There are 23 civs with Hand Cannoneer, 25 with Bombard Cannon, 35 with Cannon Galleon and 18 with Bombard Tower.

**What it gets right — faithful**
- **Koreans:** Choe Mu-seon's gunpowder production (1377) and the hwacha.
- **Jurchens:** no Hand Cannoneer, but Fire Lancer, Rocket Cart, Grenadier and Bombard Cannon; the Jin used zhen tian lei bombs and fire lances at Kaifeng (1232–33).
- **Turks.**
- **Bohemians:** Hussite píšťala and houfnice.
- **Japanese:** they have Hand Cannoneer but not Bombard Cannon — the tanegashima arrived with the Portuguese in 1543.
- **Vietnamese:** Fire Lancer; the Ming copied Vietnamese firearms after 1407.
- **Three Kingdoms and Nordic civs:** no gunpowder at all, which is correct (but see the Petard in the next section).

**Errors and inconsistencies**
There are **unfounded** omissions, anachronisms and some poorly chosen examples:
- **Ethiopians:** they lack Hand Cannoneer and have only Bombard Cannon. The musketeers of 1541 were Cristóvão da Gama's Portuguese, and on the Adal side they were Ottomans; the game's emphasis is inverted.
- **Poles and Lithuanians:** at Grunwald (1410), the bombards belonged to the Teutonic Order, not to the Polish-Lithuanian side. These civs' gunpowder is better justified by the 15th century (for example, the Thirteen Years' War, 1454–66): **plausible**.

**The name of the tech**
'Chemistry' is anachronistic. Gunpowder was born of Daoist alchemy: the Zhenyuan miaodao yaolüe (9th century) already warns against mixtures of saltpetre, sulphur, realgar and honey. 'Alchemy' would be a more accurate name.
examples: Chinese (formulas in the Wujing Zongyao, 1044; the Heilongjiang hand cannon, c. 1288) without Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon or Cannon Galleon — only Bombard Tower, Fire Lancer and Rocket Cart (partial compensation, plausible)

Mongols without gunpowder on land, despite the ceramic bombs from the Takashima shipwreck (1281) and the Yuan firearms used against Nayan (1287), but with Cannon Galleon, just like the Britons: gunpowder only at sea
Britons without Hand Cannoneer or Bombard Cannon, despite English artillery in the Hundred Years' War (Harfleur, 1415) — unfounded

Khitans (Liao, 907–1125) with Rocket Cart — anachronistic (true rockets date from the 13th century); Fire Lancer — stretched (the fire lance appears in a Dunhuang painting from the mid-10th century, but the first recorded military use is from 1132, at De'an)
Malians with Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon: Mali did not adopt firearms; Songhai fell to Moroccan arquebusiers at Tondibi (1591) — wrong

Gurjaras (text centred on the Gurjara-Pratiharas, 8th–11th centuries) with Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon — anachronistic; the date when gunpowder reached India is contested (13th–15th centuries), but the Pratihara period is certainly earlier
Dravidians: the text itself says that Vijayanagara imported firearms from European merchants — plausible, but only for the final phase

Mapuche with Bombard Tower, but without Guard Tower or Keep — stretched: at Quiapo (1558) there was, for the first time, a Mapuche squadron with captured arquebuses (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Quiapo); the use of artillery is mentioned only by Rosales (17th century) and is uncertain

findings.title: Sieges and explosives: counterweight Trebuchet and Petard for (almost) everyone
findings.detail:
**The Trebuchet**
The game's Trebuchet ('Must be packed to move') is the counterweight trebuchet. This weapon appears in the last third of the 12th century: probable Byzantine use c. 1165 (Paul Chevedden's reading, contested) and al-Tarsusi's treatise for Saladin, c. 1187. It only reaches China in 1273, at Xiangyang, with Muslim engineers in Kublai's service.

It is in 53 of the 56 civs. Only Shu, Wei and Wu get the human-powered Traction Trebuchet in its place, which is correct for the 3rd century (**faithful**). This proves that the substitution is feasible. The traction trebuchet reached the Mediterranean at the end of the 6th century, through the Avars (siege of Thessalonica, c. 586 or 597; the date is disputed). Chronicles mode goes further and replaces the Trebuchet with the torsion-powered Palintonon for the Greeks.

A fair case: the Saracens' UT Counterweights is **faithful**, because the Islamic world pioneered the counterweight.

**The explosives**
The Petard (56/56, 'armed with explosives') is a 16th-century device: Henry of Navarre used it at Cahors in 1580, and it is Hamlet's 'petard'. The Demolition Raft/Ship (50/56) are also explosive. Both are available to peoples who never had gunpowder. Only the four Nordic civs (plus Portuguese and Koreans) lack the Demolition Ship.

**A correction regarding Wu**
The UT Red Cliffs Tactics gives fire precisely to Demolition Ships. Huang Gai's fire ships at Chibi (208) were sacrificial vessels, loaded with reeds and oil and sent burning against the enemy fleet. Mechanically they are closer to the Demolition Ship (an expendable unit) than to the game's Fire Ship, which projects fire continuously in the manner of the Byzantine siphon (7th century). Only the 'explosive' part is anachronistic: the developers' choice is a plausible **abstraction**.

**The Americas**
There was no mechanical artillery of any kind (torsion, tension or counterweight), nor any wheeled vehicles.

**A fair case: the Huns**
Having Battering Ram and Siege Tower is **faithful**: Priscus describes wheeled platforms and rams at the siege of Naissus (442).
examples: Huns with the bonus 'Trebuchets fire more accurately at units and small targets' — 5th century vs. 12th century (anachronistic)
Romans, Goths, Saxons, Vikings and Danes (texts up to c. 1066) and Varangians (text centred on 988–1066) with counterweight Trebuchet — anachronistic
Aztecs, Mayans, Incas, Muisca, Mapuche and Tupi with Trebuchet, Mangonel, Scorpion, Battering Ram, Siege Tower and Petard — wrong
Ethiopians: UT Torsion Engines — no torsion artillery is known in the Solomonic kingdom; the name evokes Graeco-Roman artillery (unfounded)
Petard ('Demolition Siege Weapon armed with explosives') for Shu, Wei, Wu, Huns, Goths and Romans — anachronistic
Positive: the four Indian civs replace the Battering Ram with Armored/Siege Elephant — a regional substitution

findings.title: The Americas with Eurasian metallurgy, agriculture, wheels and crossbows
findings.detail:
**What was rightly removed or replaced**
The American civs show the limits of this model of removing pieces. The team did well to:
- remove the Stable, Scout Cavalry, the barding armors, Husbandry and Bloodlines from the six American civs, because there were no horses before 1492;
- give the Aztecs Gambesons (the ichcahuipilli, quilted cotton armour that the Spaniards themselves adopted);
- give Eagle Scout to the Mesoamericans and, to the four South Americans, Champi Warrior (scouting and raiding infantry, instead of the Militia and the Scout) and Slinger.

**The Mapuche: a well-thought-out exception**
They have no Stable, but they are a 'Cavalry' civ, with the Kona (trained at the Castle) and the Bolas Rider (at the Archery Range). This reflects the rapid adoption of the horse: the game's own text and the historiography credit Lautaro (1553) with the first Mapuche cavalry corps (**plausible**, although the use of bolas on horseback is more typical of the pampas and of later periods).

**What stayed and should not have**
The full Eurasian package was kept: iron, chain mail and plate armour (in all six civs), blast furnace (in four), horse collar, heavy plough, wheelbarrow and crossbow. None of this existed in the Americas:
- **Andes:** metallurgy was in gold, silver, copper and bronze (the bronze star-headed maces, champi).
- **Mesoamerica:** weapons were made of obsidian (the macuahuitl), and metallurgy was late and mostly ornamental. The exception is the Purépecha, with copper tools and weapons, who are not in the game.
- **Traction:** there were no draught animals; the Andean chakitaqlla was a foot plough.
- **Wheel:** it appears only on Veracruz figurines.
- **Crossbow:** it was unknown.

**Assessment**
**Wrong** if read literally. **Abstraction** if read as 'better weapons and tools', but in that case the names should change, as has already been done with the Settlement and the Champi.
examples: Iron Casting in Aztecs, Mayans, Incas, Muisca, Mapuche and Tupi — but not in Shu, the only civ that lacks it
Chain Mail Armor and Plate Mail Armor in the six American civs; Blast Furnace in Aztecs, Mayans, Incas and Mapuche (Muisca and Tupi do not have it)
Horse Collar and Heavy Plow (55/56; only the Khitans lack them) in the six American civs, without draught animals; Wheelbarrow and Hand Cart (56/56) without wheeled transport
Crossbowman (54/56) in the six American civs; Arbalester in all of them except Mapuche
Wheelbarrow for Shu is plausible: there are wheelbarrows on Han reliefs; their identification with Zhuge Liang's 'wooden ox' is contested
Positive: Incas with Fabric Shields (textile armour) — faithful

findings.title: Economy: gold as universal currency, Market, Coinage and Banking for everyone — and Guilds for the Incas but not for the Aztecs
findings.detail:
**The game's model**
- Four resources, with gold as the universal currency.
- A Market that buys and sells resources, with 'trading fee and tribute tax at 30%'.
- Trade Carts between markets.
- Coinage and Banking (56/56), whose only effect is to lower the tax on tribute between players.

As an abstraction of 'wealth', gold is defensible.

**Three problems**
1. **Medieval Europe.** It lived mainly on a silver standard (the Carolingian denier). Gold coinage became widespread in the Latin West with the genovino and the florin, in 1252. There were earlier exceptions: the Sicilian tarì, the Castilian morabetino (c. 1172) and the augustalis of Frederick II (1231). Gold is more faithful for Byzantium (nomisma), for the Islamic world (dinar) and for Mali.
2. **Incas.** They had no currency and no merchant class comparable to the pochteca. The economy rested on the mit'a, the state storehouses (qollqa) and redistribution, with 'vertical control' of ecological tiers (John Murra, 1972). Local exchange existed (qhatu), and María Rostworowski argued for the existence of coastal merchants at Chincha, so the extent of Andean trade is **contested**. Even so, Market + Coinage + Banking + Guilds is **wrong**.
3. **Aztecs — the opposite case, faithful.** They had professional merchants (pochteca) and the great market of Tlatelolco: Cortés, in the Second Letter (1520), speaks of more than 60,000 people a day. They used cacao and quachtli cloaks as currency. Yet it is from the Aztecs that the game removes Guilds, while the Incas have it and the Muisca get it free.

**Tribute**
In real history, tribute was central:
- the Huns and the Peace of Anatolius (447): 6,000 pounds of gold in arrears plus 2,100 a year, according to Priscus;
- the Codex Mendoza of the Aztecs;
- the Golden Horde and the Chinese tributary system.

In the game, tribute is merely a transfer between allies, with the rate reduced by techs called 'Coinage' and 'Banking'.
examples: Coinage ('Tributes to other players cost only 20%') and Banking ('Tributes ... are free') — 56/56, also for the Incas, Tupi, Mapuche and Huns
Guilds (39/56): Incas yes, Aztecs no — the reverse of what is known about the pochteca merchants; the Chinese do not have it either, despite the Song guilds
Market — 'Used to buy and sell resources' — also for the Incas, Tupi and Mapuche

Muisca: free Caravan and Guilds is plausible (salt from Zipaquirá/Nemocón, emeralds, cloaks); the team bonus 'Natural gold sources last +15% longer' is stretched, because much of the Muisca gold came through trade
Aztecs: 'Start with +50 gold' — cacao and quachtli as currency (faithful as an abstraction)
Trade Cart (id 128) identical in all 56 civs; in Mesoamerica transport was done by porters (tlamemes), in the Andes by llama caravans

findings.title: An economy without a state, without taxes and without forced labour: the sanitising of the Villager
findings.detail:
**What the Villager does — and what is missing**
The Villager (56/56) gathers resources, builds castles, mines gold and repairs ships. There are no taxes, lords, serfs, corvée or slavery. It is an understandable omission in a game with a low age rating. There is even one case where the Villager gets it right: the Inca mit'a, rotating labour owed to the state.

**What the silence hides**
- **Slave soldiers.** Several unique units were, historically, military slaves, without anything in the game saying so:
  - Mameluke (Saracens);
  - Ghulam (Hindustanis): the first dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1290) is known precisely as the 'Mamluk' or 'Slave dynasty';
  - Janissary (Turks): recruited through the devşirme from the late 14th century.
- **Economies based on the capture of people:**
  - the Viking slave markets (Dublin);
  - the Crimean Tatar raids;
  - the Tupi captives destined for ritual cannibalism (described by Staden, whom the game's own text cites);
  - the prisoners of the Aztec flower wars.

**The most sensitive case for a Portuguese player: the Feitoria**
In the game, it passively generates wood, food, gold and stone. Historically:
- **Arguim** (feitoria c. 1445, fort shortly afterwards) traded in gold, slaves and gum arabic.
- **São Jorge da Mina** (1482) was above all a gold feitoria. At first, the Portuguese even sold enslaved people brought from Benin to the Akan merchants, in exchange for gold.
- **Lagos:** the 1444 auction of captives was narrated by Zurara.
- **India:** feitorias also existed in India (Cochin, 1500), geared towards spices.

**Assessment**
**Abstraction**: a deliberate omission, but with a sanitising effect.
examples: Villager: 'Gathers resources. Builds and repairs buildings.' — the only economic agent in all 56 civs
Mameluke, Ghulam and Janissary as UUs, with no reference to their servile status
Feitoria (Portuguese): 'Passively generates wood, food, gold and stone resources.'
Aztecs: Garland Wars; Tupi: Ibirapema Warrior (the game's own text says the ibirapema was used in the ritual killing of enemies)

findings.title: Castles for nomads and stateless societies
findings.detail:
**Why every civ has a Castle**
The Castle exists in all 56 civs because it is a structural piece of the model. It is where the UU is trained, the Trebuchet is built and the UTs are researched, and it is also one of the gateways to the Imperial Age. This forces nomadic and stateless peoples to build stone fortresses.

**Assessment by civ**
- **Mongols, Tatars and Khitans — plausible.** Karakorum was walled in 1235 and Dadu founded in 1267; there were Sarai, the five Liao capitals and Timurid Samarkand.
- **Huns — stretched.** Priscus describes Attila's residence as a wooden enclosure with towers; the only stone building was a bathhouse built by a captive from Sirmium.
- **Tupi — wrong.** The villages had double palisades (described by Staden): the Palisade Wall is faithful, the Castle and the Keep are not.
- **Mapuche — wrong.** They built earth-and-timber pucarás, for example at Quiapo (1558).
- **Incas — faithful.** Sacsayhuamán and the pukaras.

**What is right**
These are good abstractions of nomadism and of non-stone defences:
- the Cumans (and the Goths) have no Stone Wall or Gate;
- the Huns do not need Houses and have no Guard Tower or Keep;
- the Khitans have Pasture instead of Farm;
- the Mongols have the Nomads tech.

There are also already alternative fortifications to the Castle: Krepost (Bulgarians), Donjon (Sicilians) and Fortified Church (Armenians, Georgians).
examples: Castle (56/56): 'Used to train and upgrade your Unique Unit, build Trebuchets'
Tupi with Castle and Keep, and the team bonus 'Towers and Castles provide +10 population space'
Mapuche: bonus 'Enemy Castles are revealed on the map'; no Guard Tower or Keep, but with Bombard Tower
Cumans without Stone Wall, Gate, Guard Tower or Keep — but with Castle
Khitans: UT Ordo Cavalry — the ordo was the mobile camp-court of the Liao emperor, a natural candidate to replace the Castle

findings.title: A European navy (from galley to galleon) for everyone, including landlocked civs
examples: Muisca (Altiplano Cundiboyacense, no coastline) with Galley, Galleon, Hulk and Carrack — wrong

Huns, Cumans and Bohemians (landlocked Bohemia) with Galleon; Huns also with Dromon — unfounded (the Huns had no navy); Romans (395–476) with Dromon — slightly anachronistic (the dromon is attested from the 6th century)

Incas with Galleon and Carrack; the Andes had sailing balsa rafts, such as the one intercepted by Bartolomé Ruiz in 1526 off the coast of present-day Ecuador (probably belonging to coastal merchants, not necessarily Inca ones)
Tupi: the history text itself mentions the Battle of the Canoes (1566) — the war canoe would be the right unit
Mongols with Galleon is plausible: Yuan fleets against Japan (1274, 1281) and Java (1293), built by Korean and Song shipyards

findings.title: Wonder and University as universal institutions
examples: Wonder: 'A Wonder of the World that demonstrates the superiority of your civilization.'
Huns: Atheism — 'Wonder and Relic victory takes +100 years'
Malians: team bonus 'Universities work +80% faster' — plausible (Sankore), but it is the same University that the Tupi have
chronicles/data/trees/ATHENIANS.json: Academy, Temple and Fort instead of University, Monastery and Castle

findings.title: What is a 'civilization'? An inconsistent unit of analysis, full of exonyms
examples: Shu/Wei/Wu with the heroes Liu Bei, Cao Cao and Sun Jian; the Shu text includes the Oath of the Peach Garden (it calls it legendary), which comes from the Romance of the Three Kingdoms (14th century) and not from Chen Shou's history
Dravidians (language family): the text lumps together Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Pandyas, Cholas and Vijayanagara — Tamil-, Kannada- and Telugu-speaking dynasties, over a thousand years
Saracens = Arabs (text) + Mameluke (UU) under an exonym
Romans (395–476) and Byzantines as separate civs enshrine the Western historiographical division

findings.title: In fairness: the repository itself shows that the model already knows how to differentiate
findings.detail:
**The model is already diversifying**
The repository documents this in several ways:
- **Unique buildings that replace the generic ones:** Settlement, Pasture, Folwark, Mule Cart, Fortified Church, Krepost, Donjon, Harbor, Caravanserai and Feitoria.
- **Regional unit lines:** Fire Lancer, Rocket Cart, Lou Chuan, Steppe Lancer, Camel Rider, the elephants (Battle, Armored and Siege; the latter two replace the Battering Ram in the Indian civs), Slinger, Champi and Eagle.
- **Period substitution:** the Traction Trebuchet for the 3rd century.
- **Correct removals:** no Stable in the Americas, no gunpowder in the Three Kingdoms and the Norse civs.
- **Nomadic economic rules.**

**Chronicles mode**
It shows that the team knows how to re-theme entire institutions:
- a Temple with a Priestess and its own techs;
- Fort instead of Castle (with the torsion Palintonon instead of the Trebuchet) and Academy instead of University;
- an ancient navy (Lembos, Monoreme, Bireme, Trireme, Incendiary Raft);
- Oligarchy/Democracy/Tyranny;
- Archaic, Civic and Classical ages.

The ror/ folder adds the AoE1 ages.

**Conclusion**
The criticism is not that the model is incapable of adapting. It is that these adaptations came late, asymmetrically and often as 'bonuses' rather than as identity. The recent regionalisation is mainly visual: 6 regional Monks, 3 new Monasteries and new Castles in update 141935, and the regional Trade Cart icons in commit 55ec6a2. In data.json, the unit remains the same.
examples: Chronicles Temple: Priestess, Sacrificial Dedication, Syncretism, Hemlock, Amulet Protection, Exorcism, Purification, Haruspicy, Mystery Cults
Settlement (4/56: Incas, Mapuche, Muisca, Tupi) replaces Mill, Lumber Camp and Mining Camp; Champi Warrior and Slinger in the same 4 civs
Traction Trebuchet (3/56: Shu, Wei, Wu) instead of the counterweight Trebuchet; Palintonon in the Chronicles Fort
Cumans without Stone Wall; Huns without House; Khitans with Pasture; Khmer without building requirements to advance in age; Mapuche with mounted units but no Stable

debate_questions: If the 'generic' tech tree had been designed starting from Song China (c. 1100) rather than Capetian France, what would be common to all civs? For example: paper money, the compass, imperial examinations, the crossbow from the start, gunpowder in mid-game. How would the balance change?

Shu is more similar to the Britons than to Wu or Wei, and the Japanese are more similar to the Britons than the Vikings are to the Danes. Should the tech tree reflect historical and cultural kinship, or would that make the game predictable?

Should each civ correspond to a fixed historical window or to a thousand-year 'civilisational trajectory'? For example: Persians = Sasanians (224–651), without gunpowder, or split them into Sasanians and Safavids. What are the gains and the costs for the game?

Is conversion an acceptable metaphor for religious power, or for desertion and bribery? What mechanic would better represent Mongol tolerance, the Aztec and Inca hostage gods, or conquerors who convert to the religion of the conquered (Ghazan, 1295)?

Where is the line between abstraction and error? Is Incas with Market as serious as Incas with Arbalester? And the Aztecs without Guilds? What criteria should be used: existence, period, region or name?

Should balance take precedence over history? Are Romans without Treadmill Crane, Saxons without Clinker Construction, Britons without gunpowder on land or Chinese without Hand Cannoneer acceptable if a bonus compensates? Are there omissions that 'lie' more than others?

What names, neutral or regional, would you give the four ages? Does changing only the names (as already happens in the 'antiquity' era and in Return of Rome) solve anything, or is the real problem the logic that everyone climbs the same ladder?

How do you represent a stateless society (Tupi, Mapuche) in a game whose victory conditions are Wonders, Relics and destroying Castles? What alternative victory condition would be faithful to these societies?
How do you model a non-monetary economy (mit'a, qollqa and Inca redistribution) without breaking the Market and trade mechanics? Is it worth doing?

Should slavery, including the military slavery of Mamelukes, Ghulams and Janissaries, have some representation, even if only in the descriptions? How do other games (Crusader Kings, Total War, AoE III) deal with this?

A question for a Portuguese player: what would a historically honest Feitoria look like (gold from Mina, captives sold to the Akan, spices in India, dependence on African and Asian networks)? Is it acceptable in a game, or is the current sanitisation the lesser evil?
Does it make sense to include Romans, Huns, Goths and the Three Kingdoms in a 'medieval' game, or should they go into a separate mode, like Chronicles and Return of Rome?
If landlocked civs lost their navy, they would be weak on water maps. Is it acceptable for a civ's strength to depend on the map, as it did in history?
proposals: Run an automatic anachronism audit on the repository itself. (1) Create an 'item → first attestation (date, region)' table: for example, counterweight Trebuchet c. 1165–1187, Petard c. 1580, Galleon 16th century, Block Printing 7th–8th centuries, hand cannon c. 1288, rocket 13th century. (2) Define a historical window per civ, based on the years cited in the history texts. (3) Run a Python script over data/data.json that flags each item outside the window, adding the similarity matrix (Jaccard) to show where the tech tree contradicts historical proximity.

Use the 'era' field, which already exists in data.json and in techtree.js, to give age names by cultural group (or neutral names). Start by moving Romans, Huns, Goths, Shu, Wei and Wu to an 'antiquity'-type era, following the model of Chronicles and Return of Rome (ror/).

Re-theme the Monastery by religious tradition, following the Temple/Priestess model of Chronicles. For example: Madrasa/Khanqah with ulama or Sufis (Islam); Vihara with sangha (Buddhism); Matha (Hinduism); Ovoo with a shaman (steppe, making use of the 'Pagan Priest' that already exists in the Scenario Editor); Teocalli with tlamacazqui (Mesoamerica); Huaca/Acllawasi (Andes); pajé (Tupi); machi (Mapuche). Give the techs names specific to each tradition.

Create alternative religious mechanics: for Aztecs and Incas, capture the enemy Relic or idol (Coateocalli, huacas taken to Cusco) instead of converting; for Mongols, a 'tolerance' that allows training priests from captured Monasteries; for Huns, replace Atheism with something like 'Haruspices'.

Make period substitutions following the Traction Trebuchet model. For Romans, Goths and Huns (4th–5th centuries), torsion artillery (onager/ballista; precedent: the Chronicles Palintonon). For civs of the 6th–12th centuries (Saxons, Vikings, Danes, Sasanian Persians), the Traction Trebuchet. Remove Petard and Demolition Ship from civs without gunpowder, or rename them as mining and fireships (as Red Cliffs Tactics already suggests). In the Americas, replace artillery with assault units (escalade troops, incendiaries, sappers).

Rename the Blacksmith and economy techs by region, without touching the numbers: Iron Casting → Bronze Casting (Andes) or Obsidian Knapping (Mesoamerica); Chain/Plate Mail → Ichcahuipilli/Quilted Cotton; Horse Collar/Heavy Plow → Chinampas, Andenes, Waru Waru; Wheelbarrow/Hand Cart → Tlamemes or Llama Caravans; Crossbowman/Arbalester → 'Veteran/Elite Archer' in civs without the crossbow; Chemistry → Alchemy.

Adapt the economy: for the Incas, replace the Market with a Qollqa (state storehouse), without buying and selling and with income through the mit'a; give Guilds back to the Aztecs (pochteca) and give it to the Chinese (Song guilds); give Coinage and Banking neutral names (Tribute Collection, Treasury); also regionalise the name of the Trade Cart (Porters, Llama Caravan, Camel Caravan).

Create alternative fortifications to the Castle, as the Krepost and the Donjon already are: a mobile Orda/Ordo that can be dismantled, for the steppe civs (the word gave rise to 'horde', and the Khitans already have Ordo Cavalry); a Taba with a caiçara for the Tupi; a Pucará for the Mapuche and Incas.

Give inland civs, or civs without an oceanic tradition, a river and coastal fleet (Tupi and Aztec war canoes, Andean balsa rafts), without Galleon or Carrack. Remove the Dromon from the Huns. Rename the Hulk and replace the Catapult Galleon with a Chronicles-style 'Catapult Ship', giving it to those who historically mounted artillery on ships.

Split the civs that combine incompatible periods: Persians → Sasanians, since the text ends in 651 (with War Elephant and without gunpowder); Turks → Seljuks and Ottomans. Alternatively, at least add period indications to the descriptions (and correct the Persians text: Ctesiphon is not Baghdad).

Make the texts more honest: mention the servile status of the Mameluke, Ghulam and Janissary and the role of the feitorias in the Atlantic slave trade; revise the phrase 'the superiority of your civilization' in the Wonder description.

Fix, where balance allows, omissions that contradict history: Treadmill Crane for Romans and Teutons, Clinker Construction for Saxons, Iron Casting for Shu, Thumb Ring for Jurchens, Hand Cannoneer for Chinese, Mongols and Ethiopians (perhaps late or more expensive); remove the Rocket Cart from the Khitans and gunpowder from the Goths and Gurjaras.
Prototype all of this as a 'historical mode' (an AoE2 DE data mod) and visualise it locally with aoe2techtree itself, editing data/data.json and data/trees/*.json.

Replaced with stronger data: 0.725 is the average of all pairs (0.727); the civ most similar to Shu is Britons (0.769), above Wu (0.76) and Wei (0.737); Japanese–Britons = 0.837 > Vikings–Danes = 0.758; Romans–Byzantines = 0.73. Added the caveat about the sensitivity of Jaccard to unique items.

themes.title: Names, terminology and descriptions: where AoE2 gets it right and where it fails
themes.summary: I analysed all the unit, tech and building names in the repository's derived files (current state: 56 civs, including The Viking Sagas and the Mapuche, Muisca and Tupi civs) and cross-checked them against the history texts. I confirmed in the data which civ has what, which led me to correct several details in the draft. The problems are of three kinds. (1) The generic names (Man-at-Arms, Two-Handed Swordsman, Halberdier, Arbalester, Hussar, Paladin, Galleon, Conscription, Chemistry, Monk, Atonement) almost all come from 14th- to 16th-century Western Europe and are applied to every civ. As an abstraction of “technological level” this is acceptable. It becomes wrong when it gives the Aztecs, Incas and Tupi crossbows, trebuchets, horse collars, wheelbarrows, coinage and printing, or gives Hussars to Wei and Wu, 3rd-century Chinese kingdoms. (2) The unique names are very uneven. Many are exemplary: Holcans (which replaced El Dorado), Hul'che, Kamandaran, Bagains, Hamask, Hearth Troop, Tuntian, Ming Guang, Traction Trebuchet, Thunderclap Bombs, Detinets, Svan Towers, Burgundian Vineyards and Paper Money. Others are wrong. There are words from another language: Champi and Huaracas in Quechua for peoples who were not Inca, Caciques in Taíno for the Tupi, Huskarl in Norse for the Goths, Fereters in ecclesiastical Latin for the Armenians. There are translation or transcription errors: Garland Wars, Yasama, Kataparuto, Kamayuk, Shinkichon, and the incorrect Latin of Furor Celtica. There are attributions to the wrong people or to frauds: Gbeto, Thirisadai, Chakram, Woad Raider. There are empty names: Atheism, Anarchy, Perfusion, Supremacy. And there are ironies: Circumnavigation for the Portuguese, Flemish Revolution for the Burgundians, Chu Ko Nu ('Zhuge Liang's crossbow') for the Chinese and not for the Shu. (3) The history texts themselves contain verifiable errors: Stonehenge attributed to the Celts, Ælle 'of Essex', Alfred 'unifying' England in 886, Harthacnut as Cnut's 'grandson', the sack of Rome in 409. Almost all of this can be corrected without touching game balance, because it is only a matter of names and text.

findings.title: The generic lines use late European vocabulary and apply it to every civ
findings.detail: The names of the generic lines are the most visible layer of the game, and almost all of them come from 14th- to 16th-century Western Europe. In the 14th and 15th centuries, Man-at-Arms (homme d'armes) meant a fully armoured combatant, usually mounted, who dismounted at Crécy or Agincourt; he was not a 'Feudal Age' swordsman. Long Swordsman and Two-Handed Swordsman refer to the longsword (13th to 16th centuries) and to the two-handed sword of the 16th-century Doppelsöldner and Landsknechte. Pikeman evokes the Scottish schiltrons, the Flemings at Courtrai (1302) and the Swiss; Halberdier evokes the Swiss at Morgarten (1315). Knight → Cavalier → Paladin is a ladder of synonyms: cavalier, chevalier and caballero all mean 'knight'. Paladin comes from the Latin palatinus, by way of the twelve peers of Charlemagne in the Chanson de Roland (c. 1100). Crossbowman → Arbalester is another ladder of synonyms: arbalester (from the French arbalétrier, from the Latin arcuballista) simply means 'crossbowman'. In a shared unit list, this is a defensible abstraction. It becomes anachronistic or wrong when the name contradicts the civ's culture: an obsidian macuahuitl is not a two-handed sword, and one of Attila's Huns is not a Carolingian peer. There is an irony here: the term palatini designated elite units of the late Roman field army (Notitia Dignitatum, c. 400), and so, of the civs that have it, the Byzantines are the one for which Paladin is the least out-of-place name. The data show that these names reach dozens of civs outside Europe.
examples: Two-Handed Swordsman for Aztecs and Mayans, and Champion for the Aztecs (the Mayans do not have Champion): wrong. Proposal: Maquahuitl Warrior or Tequihua
Halberdier for Incas, Mayans and Mapuche: wrong
Paladin for Huns: anachronistic. For Cumans and Magyars: culturally out of place. For Byzantines: plausible through the root palatinus
Arbalester for Aztecs, Incas, Mayans, Muisca and Tupi: wrong
Crossbowman → Arbalester and Knight → Cavalier: redundant abstraction (they are synonyms)
Man-at-Arms as Feudal Age infantry: anachronistic (the term is from the 14th and 15th centuries and mainly designates a mounted combatant)

findings.title: Universal Hussar, redundant Magyar Huszar and a Winged Hussar with its role reversed
findings.detail: The data confirm the Hussar in 30 civs, including Wei and Wu (3rd century), Khitans, Jurchens, Khmer, Burmese, Koreans, Goths, Huns, Saxons and Varangians. The Shu do not have it. The word huszár appears in Hungary in the 15th century and probably comes from the Serbian gusar ('brigand, pirate'), which in turn comes from the medieval Latin cursarius (the 'corsair'). Organised hussar cavalry is associated with the army of Matthias Corvinus, which the game honours well with Corvinian Army. The game also creates a redundancy: the Magyars have the generic Hussar and the unique Magyar Huszar, that is, the same word in English and in Hungarian. The Winged Hussar (Poles and Lithuanians, who do not have the Hussar) inverts the original. The first Polish hussars of the early 16th century (Orsha, 1514) were indeed light cavalry of the Serbian type. But the winged husaria, which the name and the wings evoke, is the heavy shock cavalry armed with the lance (kopia) that took shape from the reign of Stephen Báthory (1576 to 1586) onwards and won at Kłuszyn (1610) and Vienna (1683). In the game it is a light scout that replaces the Hussar: anachronistic (16th and 17th centuries) and wrong as to its function.
examples: Hussar for Wei and Wu: anachronistic by more than a millennium
Hussar for Khmer, Burmese, Jurchens, Khitans and Koreans: culturally out of place
Generic Hussar plus Magyar Huszar for the Magyars: linguistic redundancy
Winged Hussar as a replacement for the Hussar: wrong as to its role (the winged husaria was heavy cavalry)

Regional alternatives for the top of the line: Akıncı (Turks), Jinete (Spanish), Stradiot (Italians); for civs whose top unit is the Light Cavalry: Hobelar (Britons), Turcopole (Sicilians). The Berbers do not need 'Jinete': they already have the Genitour, which is the same word

findings.title: Pre-Columbian civs with names of technologies that did not exist in the Americas
findings.detail: The six American civs inherit names of technologies that did not exist on the continent before 1492. According to the data, they all have Crossbowman and Trebuchet. They also have Horse Collar and Heavy Plow (55 of 56 civs; only the Khitans lack them), Wheelbarrow and Hand Cart (56 of 56) and Coinage and Banking (56 of 56). Aztecs, Incas, Mayans and Muisca have Block Printing, the Aztecs have Gambesons and the siege ship is called the Catapult Galleon. In the Americas there were no crossbows, no trebuchets, no draught animals, no drawn ploughs, no practical use of the wheel and no printing. Llamas carried loads, but they did not pull. The Incas had no writing in the conventional sense and used khipu; whether khipu also encoded narratives is an open question (Gary Urton). Nor was there money in the strict sense: the Mexica used cacao and cotton mantles (quachtli), and the economy of the Inca state rested on rotational labour (mit'a). The game is inconsistent with itself. It already removes Bloodlines, Husbandry and the three horse armours (Scale, Chain and Plate Barding Armor) from these civs, but keeps Horse Collar, which also presupposes horses. Mechanically this makes sense, because it is an economic technology, but the name could change. The game has already shown that it knows how to localise: Settlement instead of Mill, Lumber Camp and Mining Camp for Incas, Mapuche, Muisca and Tupi; no Stable; Champi instead of Eagle; Holcans instead of El Dorado. Another internal inconsistency: the Tupi have the Slinger and the Caciques technology strengthens it, but their own history text says that their two main weapons were the bow and the ibirapema.
examples: Horse Collar and Heavy Plow (Aztecs, Incas, Mayans, Mapuche, Muisca, Tupi): wrong. Alternatives: Chinampas (Aztecs), Andenes and Chakitaqlla, the foot plough (Incas), raised fields (Mayans)
Wheelbarrow and Hand Cart: wrong. Alternatives: Tlamemeh, the Mexica porters (Aztecs); llama caravans (Incas)
Coinage and Banking: wrong. Alternatives: Quachtli and cacao (Aztecs), Mit'a (Incas)
Block Printing for Incas: wrong (alternative: Khipu). For Aztecs: wrong (alternative: Amoxtli, the painted codices). For Mayans: wrong (alternative: Hu'un, the bark-paper book)
Gambesons for Aztecs: the effect is right, the name is not. Alternative: Ichcahuipilli (quilted cotton armour)
Catapult Galleon for the six civs: wrong. Alternative: war canoe (acalli in Nahuatl, ygara in Tupi)
Slinger and Caciques for the Tupi: inconsistent with their own history text

findings.title: The religious vocabulary is Christian and Latin for every religion
findings.detail: The whole Monastery tree uses Christian-Latin vocabulary: Monk, Monastery, Relic, Devotion, Faith, Fervor, Sanctity, Illumination, Atonement, Redemption, Heresy, Theocracy. For the Buddhist civs (Burmese, Khmer, Japanese, and the Bengalis with Mahayana) 'monk' works. For the Muslim civs (Saracens, Turks, Berbers, Malians, Islamic Persians, Hindustanis) it is conceptually wrong: Islam has no monasticism and no sacramental clergy, and the closest figures are the ulama, the Sufis, the khanqah, the ribat and the madrasa. The ribat is especially suitable for the Berbers, because the Almoravids (al-Murabitun) take their name from it. In Hindu societies (Gurjaras, Dravidians), the religious figure is the Brahmin or the ascetic. For the Aztecs it is the tlamacazqui (priest) in the teocalli; for the Incas, the willaq umu; for the Mapuche, the machi (often a woman); for the Tupi, the pajé or the karaíba; for the Muisca, the chyquy (the 'jeque' of the Spaniards). Atonement and Redemption are terms from the Christian theology of salvation. Relics could be localised in a remarkable way: the Inca royal mummies (mallki) were venerated and carried in procession, and the Muisca's own history text describes mummies of Guecha warriors carried into battle. To be fair, the Definitive Edition already uses regional appearances for the Monk, and there are real localisations: the Fortified Church of the Armenians and Georgians, the Missionary of the Spanish and the Warrior Priest of the Armenians. The problem lies only in the names. Mechanically it is an acceptable abstraction; as terminology it is wrong for about half the civs.
examples: Monk and Monastery for Saracens, Turks, Berbers and Malians: wrong (alternatives: Faqih or Sufi; Khanqah or Ribat)
Monk for Aztecs: wrong (alternative: Tlamacazqui; Monastery → Teocalli)
Monk for Mapuche: wrong (alternative: Machi)
Relic for Incas: plausible as a mechanic, but it could be called Mallki (ancestral mummy)
Atonement and Redemption for Bengalis, Burmese and Malians: stretched (Christian theology). The Khmer only have Redemption
Fortified Church (Armenians and Georgians): a good example of localisation

findings.title: Siege and navy: inverted chronology and misunderstood ship types
findings.detail: The Mangonel → Onager sequence inverts the chronology. The onager is the late Roman torsion catapult described by Ammianus Marcellinus (4th century). 'Mangonel', by contrast, often designated the traction trebuchet in medieval sources; this is the reading of Paul Chevedden and Peter Purton, now fairly widely accepted. The older version thus appears as an 'upgrade' of the more recent one. Hulk, War Hulk and Carrack form the melee combat line. Hulk takes its name from the holc, a large cargo ship also used by the Hanseatic League, and the Carrack was a high-sided ship for cargo and war. Its high castles were indeed used for boarding fights, so Carrack is the least bad of the three names. Galleon and Cannon Galleon (16th century), Petard (Cahors, 1580), Demolition Ship (the Antwerp 'hellburners', 1585) and Heated Shot (associated with Stephen Báthory, 1579) are post-medieval. Catapult Galleon combines two incompatible things and is given to Vikings, Danes, Saxons, Varangians and Cumans, as well as to the six American civs. Giving the Dromon to the Huns, who had no navy, is wrong. For the Goths it is plausible: Totila built a fleet, which was defeated by the Byzantines at Sena Gallica (551). Clinker Construction → Carvel Hull is the technical sequence of Northern Europe, and it is applied to junks and canoes. Wu, Wei, Shu, Jurchens and Mapuche have both; the Tupi and the Chinese only have Clinker. Ironically, the Saxons are the only civ without Clinker Construction (and they do not have Carvel Hull either), even though the Sutton Hoo ship (c. 625) is the classic example of a clinker-built hull.
examples: Mangonel → Onager: inverted chronology
Hulk and War Hulk as melee combat ships: wrong (the holc was a cargo ship)
Galleon, Petard and Heated Shot: anachronistic (16th century)
Catapult Galleon for Vikings, Danes and Saxons: anachronistic
Dromon for the Huns: wrong. For the Goths: plausible
Clinker and Carvel for Wu, Jurchens and Mapuche: stretched (a European sequence)
Saxons without Clinker Construction: an ironic error (Sutton Hoo)

findings.title: Modern concepts used as technology names
findings.detail: Several technologies are named after institutions, sciences or expressions created long after the Middle Ages. Conscription refers to modern compulsory recruitment (the Jourdan-Delbrel law, 1798); the medieval equivalents are the fyrd, the arrière-ban, the Assize of Arms (1181) or the levy. Chemistry only exists as a discipline from the 17th century; at the time the word was alchemy, and the real technical step was granulated gunpowder (corned powder, c. 1420). Even so, as a prerequisite for gunpowder the name is an understandable abstraction. 'Ballistics' is an 18th-century term. Logistica (Byzantines) is pseudo-Latin: the word 'logistics' comes from the French logistique, from logis ('billeting'), and was popularised by Jomini in the 19th century. Medical Corps (Dravidians) is 19th-century army language. Ironclad (Teutons) is the armoured warship of 1859. Grand Trunk Road is the name given by the British in the 19th century: Sher Shah Suri called it Sadak-e-Azam, and Antiquity knew it as Uttarapatha. Silk Road (Italians) is the term Seidenstraße, coined by Richthofen in 1877. Fortified Bastions (Jurchens) uses the bastion of the 15th- and 16th-century trace italienne. Grenadier (Jurchens) comes from the 17th-century French companies, although the weapon, iron bombs thrown by hand and by trebuchet, is faithful to the Jin. Thalassocracy is acceptable: it is a Greek word that historians apply to the maritime empire of Srivijaya. All these cases have medieval equivalents with names of their own.
examples: Conscription: anachronistic (alternatives: Levy, Fyrd, Arrière-ban)
Chemistry: anachronistic, but an understandable abstraction (alternatives: Saltpetre Works, Corned Powder)
Logistica (Byzantines): anachronistic (a 19th-century term)
Medical Corps (Dravidians): anachronistic (alternative: Hastyayurveda, the treatise on elephant medicine attributed to Palakapya)
Grand Trunk Road (Hindustanis): anachronistic (alternatives: Sadak-e-Azam, Uttarapatha)
Silk Road (Italians): anachronistic (alternatives: Mude, the Venetian galley convoys, or Commenda)
Fortified Bastions and Grenadier (Jurchens): anachronistic and European (alternatives: Mamian 馬面, the projecting towers of Chinese walls; Zhentianlei Bomber)
Ironclad (Teutons): anachronistic (alternatives: Mantlets or Sow)

findings.title: Generic technologies whose names do not describe the effect
findings.detail: Several generic names refer to real objects or practices, but the in-game effect has no relation to them. Bracer is the guard that protects the archer's forearm, and it gives +1 attack and +1 range. Thumb Ring is the thumb-draw technique of the steppes and Asia, but it goes to Italians, Mayans, Incas, Muisca and Malians and also improves crossbows, while the Britons do not have it. Squires were the mounted attendants of knights, and here they make infantry faster. Theocracy is a political regime, and it serves to make only one monk rest after a conversion. Parthian Tactics, the 'Parthian shot' fired in retreat, gives armour and a bonus against spearmen. Hoardings, the wooden galleries at the top of walls (11th to 13th centuries), give +1000 HP to castles. Block Printing gives conversion range: the idea (spreading religious texts) is reasonable, but woodblock printing is mainly East Asian (the Diamond Sutra, from 868); in Europe it only appears around 1400. There are also good examples. Murder Holes removes the minimum range of fortifications; it would be even more accurate to call it Machicolations, because 'murder holes' were in the ceilings of gate passages. Arrowslits, Fletching, Bodkin Arrow, Gillnets, Treadmill Crane, Two-Man Saw and Herbal Medicine also work. In most cases it is an abstraction; the useful criterion is that the name should describe the object or practice that produces the effect.
examples: Bracer (+attack and +range): stretched
Thumb Ring for Italians, Mayans, Incas and Muisca (and applied to crossbows): culturally out of place
Squires (infantry speed): stretched
Theocracy (monk rest): stretched
Hoardings (+1000 castle HP): abstraction
Block Printing: abstraction, better suited to Chinese, Koreans and Japanese than to the European civs
Murder Holes, Arrowslits and Fletching: plausible or faithful

findings.title: Unique technologies with empty names or names unrelated to the effect
findings.detail: Atheism (Huns) is the most serious case. Atheism is a concept of the early modern period, and Jordanes (Getica) reports that Attila consulted haruspices before the Catalaunian Plains. The effect (enemy relics yield less, and relic and Wonder victories take longer) is meant to evoke the pagan 'scourge' of Christian shrines, and there are better names for that. Anarchy and Perfusion (Goths) have no Gothic referent at all; 'perfusion' is a medical term. Supremacy (Spanish) is an empty name. Chieftains (Vikings) does not explain an attack bonus against cavalry and camels. Logistica (Byzantines) suggests supply, but gives Cataphracts and Varangian Guards trample damage. The right source would be the cataphract formation of the Praecepta Militaria of Nikephoros II Phokas (c. 965). Paiks (Bengalis) means 'foot soldiers' (from the Sanskrit padātika), but it makes elephants and Rathas attack faster. Royal Heirs (Ethiopians) alludes to a real fact (the princes were confined on the mountain of Amba Geshen until 1540), but the effect (less damage taken from mounted units) has nothing to do with it. Druzhina (Slavs) is a fairer case than it seems: the retinue of the Rus' prince often fought on foot in the 10th and 11th centuries (Leo the Deacon describes Sviatoslav's men this way at Dorostolon, 971) and only later became mainly mounted. Linking the name to infantry is defensible; it is the trample that is invented. All the other cases are unfounded or stretched and have documented alternatives.
examples: Atheism (Huns): wrong (alternatives: Flagellum Dei, a later legendary epithet, or a name linked to Hunnic religion)
Anarchy (Huskarls at the Barracks): unfounded (alternative: Foederati)
Perfusion (faster Barracks): unfounded (alternative: Thiufadi, from thiufa, a unit of a thousand men in the Visigothic laws)
Supremacy (stronger Villagers): unfounded (alternative: Santa Hermandad, the Castilian popular militia of 1476)
Logistica: stretched and anachronistic (alternative: Praecepta Militaria or Trigonon, the wedge)
Paiks applied to elephants: wrong (it should affect infantry; alternative: Hastyadhyaksha, the superintendent of elephants in the Arthashastra)
Druzhina applied to infantry: plausible (the trample is the invented part)

findings.title: Words from another language or another people
findings.detail: Several 'authentic' names are in the wrong language. Champi is the Quechua term for the Incas' star-shaped bronze mace, and it is also applied to Mapuche, Muisca and Tupi, who spoke Mapudungun, Muysccubun and Old Tupi (the data confirm Champi Warrior, Champi Scout and Champi Runner in all four civs). Huaracas (Muisca) is the Quechua waraka, 'sling'. Caciques (Tupi) is a Taíno (Arawakan) word from the Caribbean that the Spaniards spread; in Old Tupi the chief was the morubixaba, and that is what the sources call Cunhambebe. The Mapuche history text also uses 'cacique', when the proper term is lonko. Curare (Tupi) is a word of Carib origin, from the Guianas (dictionaries give the Macushi wurari), and it designates a poison used mainly for hunting, typical of Amazonia and the Guianas. Its use by the coastal Tupinambá is poorly documented, and the Tupi's own history text speaks of arrows tipped with stingray spines, not curare. Huskarl (Goths) is the Old Norse húskarl of the 10th and 11th centuries, about five centuries after the Goths. Chatras (Vietnamese) is the Sanskrit chattra, the royal parasol, more typical of Champa and the Khmer world than of Đại Việt. Arambai and Manipur Cavalry (Burmese) belong to Manipur and only entered the Burmese army, for the most part, in the 18th century, after the campaigns of Alaungpaya. Wagenburg Tactics is the German term for the Czech vozová hradba. Keshik was the guard of Genghis Khan: it is more Mongol than 'Tatar', although the institution passed to the successor khanates.
examples: Champi Warrior for Mapuche, Muisca and Tupi: wrong (alternatives: Weichafe for the Mapuche, Tacape Warrior for the Tupi, a neutral name for the Muisca)
Huaracas (Muisca): wrong (it is Quechua)
Caciques (Tupi): wrong (alternative: Morubixaba)
Curare (Tupi): stretched (a Carib word, and it contradicts the history text)
Huskarl (Goths): anachronistic and in the wrong language (alternatives: Gardingus or Buccellarius, Visigothic terms)
Chatras (Vietnamese): culturally out of place (alternative: Tượng binh, the elephant corps)
Wagenburg Tactics (Bohemians): plausible, but better in Czech: Vozová hradba

findings.title: Translation, transcription and romanisation errors
findings.detail: Garland Wars mistranslates xochiyaoyotl: in academic English the term is 'Flower Wars', and their function (taking captives, according to tradition, or a war of political attrition, according to Ross Hassig) is still debated. Yasama comes from 矢狭間, which is read 'yazama' (an arrow loophole), with voicing at the junction of the words, as in teppō-zama. The idea is right, the transcription is not, and loopholes of this kind are associated mainly with the castles of the 16th and 17th centuries. Kataparuto is カタパルト, the modern katakana loanword from the English word 'catapult', with no medieval standing whatsoever. Kanji dictionaries give ishihajiki as the Japanese reading of 礟 (a stone-throwing engine); the medieval attestation still needs to be confirmed. Note also that throwing artillery saw only marginal use in medieval Japan, so the problem is not just the name. Shinkichon is an irregular spelling of 신기전 (神機箭), the rocket-arrow launched by the hwacha: in Revised Romanization it is written Singijeon. Kamayuk is a truncation: kamayuq means 'specialist' or 'person in charge' (as in khipukamayuq), and the term for a warrior in Guaman Poma is awqa kamayuq. Chu Ko Nu uses Wade-Giles romanisation (in pinyin it would be Zhuge nu), while Lou Chuan, Hei Guang, Tuntian and Liao Dao use pinyin. Shatagni (Hindustanis) is śataghnī, the 'hundred-killer' of the epics and the Arthashastra, whose nature is debated (spiked log, mace or engine). Reading a 'cannon' into it is a modern interpretation, and here it gives range to Hand Cannoneers.
examples: Garland Wars: mistranslation (should be Flower Wars or Xochiyaoyotl)
Yasama: wrong transcription (should be Yazama)
Kataparuto: anachronistic (modern loanword from English; alternative still to be confirmed: Ishihajiki)
Shinkichon: irregular romanisation (should be Singijeon)
Kamayuk: misused word (should be Awqa Kamayuq)
Chu Ko Nu and Lou Chuan: inconsistent romanizations
Shatagni as a firearm upgrade: stretched

findings.title: Unique units and techs attributed to the wrong people or period, or based on myths
findings.detail: The Gbeto (Malians) comes from the elephant hunters of the Fon kingdom of Dahomey (17th to 19th centuries, present-day Benin), who according to tradition were the origin of the Mino women warriors, the 'Amazons'. It has no connection with medieval Mali. The Thirisadai (Dravidians) is an unattested ship class.
