The name apparently came from a Wikipedia article on the Chola navy with fraudulent sources, and Anirudh Kanisetti (Lords of Earth and Sea, 2025) treats it as a hoax. This information reaches us through accounts of the book, and the author himself doubts that a permanent Chola royal navy existed, which other authors dispute. The attested Tamil terms for ships are marakkalam and kalam. The Chakram Thrower (Gurjaras) brings a throwing weapon associated mainly with the Akali Sikhs of the 17th to 19th centuries, whereas the Gurjara-Pratiharas belong to the 8th to 11th centuries. The Woad Raider is based on the 'vitrum' that Caesar attributes to the Britons of the 1st century BC, a term whose interpretation is contested. The game's Celts are medieval Scots, Irish and Welsh, which would justify Gallowglass or Kern. Torsion Engines (Ethiopians) refers to Greco-Roman torsion artillery, unattested in medieval Ethiopia. The Mangudai as 'suicide troops' has no primary source. The name probably derives from the Manghud (Mangqut) tribe, which the Secret History places in the vanguard of Genghis against the Kereyid (1203); this is a hypothesis, not an established fact. Tarkan is a Turkic title (tarqan) attested among the Göktürks, Avars, Khazars and Bulgars from the 6th to 8th centuries onwards, not among Attila's Huns. Priscus speaks of the logades, the 'chosen ones'.
examples: Gbeto (Malians): wrong (the people are the Fon of Dahomey; medieval alternatives: Tontajon, the 'people of the quiver' of the Sunjata tradition, or Sofa)
Thirisadai: unfounded (attested alternatives: Marakkalam or Kalam)
Chakram Thrower (Gurjaras): anachronistic (contested)
Woad Raider: anachronistic by about a thousand years (alternatives: Gallowglass, Kern)
Torsion Engines (Ethiopians): unfounded
Mangudai: contested (the myth of the 'suicide troops')
Tarkan (Huns): anachronistic (alternative: Logades)

findings.title: Titles turned into troop types, and descriptions that invert the historical role
findings.detail: The units' help texts are purely mechanical, but they sometimes contradict the historical function. The Centurion is described as 'Heavy Cavalry', when the centurion was an infantry officer. To be fair, the effect (it speeds up nearby Militia-line units) captures the command function well, and the only problem is that it is mounted. In the late Roman army the corresponding rank was called centenarius, and the heavy cavalry were the equites cataphractarii and the clibanarii. Jarl is an aristocratic title, not a troop type; the history text itself says that the Varangians preferred to fight on foot, although they also used cavalry. The Samurai is infantry, but until the 14th century the samurai was above all a mounted archer (kyūba no michi, 'the way of horse and bow'). The Teutonic Knight fights on foot, whereas the Order's knight brothers fought mounted. The Mameluke attacks with a thrown blade, but Mamluk furusiyya rested on the mounted bow and the lance. The Karambit Warrior (Malay) is named after a small curved Minangkabau knife. The Plumed Archer is the Mayans' signature unit, but the bow only spread in the Maya area in the Postclassic (a debated point). Composite Bowman (Armenians) distinguishes nothing, because the composite bow was common across the whole of Eurasia. Kipchak (Cumans) is the people's own ethnonym (Cumans is the Western exonym), like calling an English unit 'Englishman'. Jian Swordsman (Wu) is also debatable: by the end of the Han dynasty the ring-pommel sabre (huanshou dao) had generally replaced the jian as the soldier's cutting weapon. The War Chariot (Shu) is described as a rapid-fire weapon, that is, a crossbow cart; the war chariot as a shock weapon was already obsolete in the Han period.
examples: Mounted Centurion: wrong (alternatives: Comes, Equites Cataphractarii)
Jarl as cavalry: wrong (alternatives: Druzhinnik or Hirðmaðr)
Samurai as infantry: reductive abstraction
Teutonic Knight on foot: stretched
Mameluke with a thrown blade: unfounded
Karambit Warrior: stretched (alternative: Hulubalang)
Composite Bowman: generic name used as a unique one
Jian Swordsman (Wu): stretched; War Chariot (Shu): misleading name (crossbow cart)

findings.title: Ironic attributions: the name celebrates the rival or someone else's achievement
findings.detail: Circumnavigation (Portuguese) honours the 1519–1522 voyage, which was an expedition of the Crown of Castile. Ferdinand Magellan was Portuguese, but he sailed in the service of Spain, and the voyage was completed by the Basque Elcano. The Portuguese have better achievements of their own: the volta do mar, the Carreira da Índia, the cartaz system. Flemish Militia and Flemish Revolution (Burgundians) celebrate the Flemish militias. The dukes did at times raise them (for example, at the siege of Calais in 1436), but they were above all adversaries: the Bruges revolt (1436–1438) and the Ghent War (1449–1453), crushed at Gavere. The 'revolution' would be against the player themselves. First Crusade (Sicilians) is plausible through the Hautevilles, but indirect: Roger I of Sicily declined to take part; the one who went was Bohemond of Taranto, from Apulia, and the Kingdom of Sicily only came into being in 1130. The Varangian Guard was a Byzantine corps in Constantinople, but Danes, Vikings, Varangians and Saxons also train it in their own lands. In the case of the Saxons there is a historically accurate irony: after 1066 many exiled Anglo-Saxons joined the Guard, as the Varangians' own history text mentions. But this happens only after the end of the Saxon England that the game represents. Mounted Crossbowman is given to Saxons, Danes, Vikings and Varangians, and Cranequins to Saxons, Danes and Varangians (the Vikings do not have it). The crossbow was rare in Viking Age Scandinavia, the cranequin dates from the 14th and 15th centuries, and at Hastings the crossbowmen were on the Norman side, not the Saxon one.
examples: Circumnavigation (Portuguese): ironic and stretched (alternatives: Volta do Mar, Carreira da Índia)
Flemish Revolution and Flemish Militia (Burgundians): plausible, but ironic
First Crusade (Sicilians): plausible, but indirect
Varangian Guard trained by Danes and Vikings: stretched; by Saxons: ironic, but with a post-1066 basis
Cranequins and Heavy Mounted Crossbowman for Saxons and Danes: anachronistic

findings.title: Chinese and North Asian civs: faithful names mixed with anachronisms
findings.detail: The Shu, Wei and Wu civs have some of the most faithful names in the game. Tuntian refers to Cao Cao's military-agricultural colonies (196), and the effect (soldiers produce food) is accurate. Ming Guang and Hei Guang are the armours cited in Cao Zhi's memorial. White Feather Guard is the 白毦兵 of Liu Bei's guard, commanded by Chen Dao. Tiger Cavalry is Cao Cao's 虎豹騎. Bolt Magazine refers to the repeating crossbow that Zhuge Liang perfected. The Traction Trebuchet is very faithful for Wei: Cao Cao used missile-throwing 'thunder carts' (霹靂車) at Guandu (200). Lou Chuan and Red Cliffs Tactics are also accurate. There are, however, anachronisms. Sitting Tiger is the 虎蹲砲, a traction trebuchet described in the Wujing Zongyao (1044), eight centuries after Wu; the machine is old, the name is Song. Wei and Wu get Hussar (the Shu do not), all three get Galleon, and Wu and Shu get Arbalester. Sun Jian, the Wu hero, died in 191, before the state of Wu existed (222–229); he was the father of the founders, which makes the choice plausible but not exact. There is also an irony: Chu Ko Nu means 'Zhuge's crossbow', that is, the crossbow of Zhuge Liang, the Shu chancellor, yet it is the unit of the Chinese and not of the Shu. Xianbei Raider (Wei) is debatable: Kebineng's Xianbei supported Zhuge Liang in 231, and Cao Cao's famous 'barbarian' cavalry was the Wuhuan, recruited after White Wolf Mountain (207). 'Wei' plus 'Xianbei' also evokes the Northern Wei (Tuoba, 386–535), which is a different state. The Khitans (Liao, 907–1125) have Fire Lancer and Rocket Cart. The fire lance appears in a Dunhuang painting from the mid-10th century, but its first documented use in battle dates from 1132; multiple rocket launchers are Korean, from the 15th century (hwacha). The Iron Pagoda (鐵浮屠) is faithful to the Song sources. The story of the chained horses, linked to the Guaizi Ma and often confused with the Iron Pagoda, has been contested since the Qing dynasty, and the Qianlong Emperor already doubted it.
examples: Tuntian, Ming Guang Armor, White Feather Guard and Traction Trebuchet (Wei): faithful
Sitting Tiger (Wu): anachronistic name (Song dynasty), plausible machine
Hussar (Wei and Wu) and Galleon (all three): anachronistic
Chu Ko Nu for the Chinese and not for the Shu: ironic
Xianbei Raider: stretched (alternative: Wuhuan Cavalry)
Rocket Cart for the Khitans: anachronistic
Iron Pagoda: faithful in name, contested as to the chained horses

findings.title: Civ and age names: exonyms and modern constructs
findings.detail: Several civ names are exonyms or modern categories. Saracens is the Greco-Latin term that Christians used generically for Muslims, and it was never a self-designation. Teutons is the name of a tribe defeated by Marius in 102 BC. Medieval Latin already used teutonicus for the Germans from the 10th century onwards (hence the Ordo Teutonicus), so the name is a learned exonym, not a pure anachronism. Celts is a label applied to the Irish, Scots and Welsh from Edward Lhuyd (1707) onwards, and above all in the 18th and 19th centuries; its validity is contested (Simon James, The Atlantic Celts, 1999). Vikings denotes an activity, not an ethnicity, and it now coexists with the Danes as a separate civ. Tatars is the European exonym (Tartari) used here for the Timurids and for the Golden Horde; the original Tatar were a Mongolic tribe destroyed by Genghis in 1202. Dravidians is a language family systematized by Robert Caldwell in 1856. The ages themselves are Eurocentric. 'Dark Age' is a label of Renaissance origin (Petrarch) that historians have abandoned. 'Feudal' is a 17th- and 18th-century term, and the very concept of feudalism is contested (Elizabeth Brown, 1974; Susan Reynolds, Fiefs and Vassals, 1994). Even so, it is applied to the Incas, Tupi and Mongols, and the Tupi go through a 'Castle Age'. As a game abstraction it is acceptable; as terminology it is debatable. The change from 'Indians' to 'Hindustanis' (2023) shows that such renamings are possible.
examples: Saracens: exonym (alternative: Arabs)
Teutons: plausible as a medieval Latin exonym (alternatives: Germans or Holy Roman Empire)
Celts: modern and contested construct (alternative: Gaels)
Vikings alongside the Danes: ambiguous (alternatives: Norse or Norwegians)
Dark Age and Feudal Age: Eurocentric abstraction

findings.title: Factual errors in the history texts themselves
findings.detail: The history texts (paraphrased here) contain several verifiable errors, some inherited from the original 1999 game. Saxons: Ælle appears as king of Essex, when he was king of the South Saxons (Sussex), the first in Bede's list of kings who held imperium (the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle calls them bretwalda). Middlesex appears among the great kingdoms, but it was never an independent kingdom. Hengist and Horsa are, in the tradition of Bede and of Kent, leaders associated with the Jutes. The text says that Alfred unified the country in 886, but in that year Alfred took London and was recognized by the English outside Danish rule; the unification is Æthelstan's (927). It also says that the Saxons adopted the shield wall from the Vikings, when it was a much older Germanic tactic. Danes: Harthacnut appears as Cnut's grandson, when he was his son. Celts: the text credits the Celts with building Stonehenge 5,000 years ago, but the monument is Neolithic and long predates any Celtic people. Goths: Alaric's sack of Rome is dated 409, when it was in 410 (the Romans text gives the correct date, which also makes the error an internal inconsistency); the origin in Gotland is an old and contested reading of Jordanes. Huns: the text allows that the Huns may have invented the stirrup, but there is no evidence that they used it (it reaches Europe with the Avars, in the 6th century), and the 'capital' at Szeged is speculative. Mapuche: the text uses 'cacique' (a Taíno word) instead of lonko, and describes the Mapuche as hunter-gatherers with 'basic' agriculture, which underestimates their sedentary agriculture (a debatable point). Tupi: the text speaks of arrows poisoned with stingray spines, but the game's tech is called Curare, which is an internal inconsistency. On the positive side, the etymology of 'Varangian' (from vár, 'oath', and gengi, 'companion') follows the most widely accepted analysis, although some prefer vár plus the suffix -ingi. And the Varangian Guard generating gold is a clever allusion to pólútasvarf, the right to plunder the imperial treasury that the saga of Harald Hardrada ascribes to it.
examples: Saxons: Ælle 'of Essex' is wrong (he was of Sussex); Middlesex as a kingdom is wrong
Saxons: Alfred did not unify England in 886 (Æthelstan did, in 927); the shield wall was not copied from the Vikings
Danes: Harthacnut was Cnut's son, not his grandson
Celts: the Celts did not build Stonehenge
Goths: the sack of Rome was in 410, not 409 (inconsistent with the Romans text)
Huns: the 'invention of the stirrup' is unfounded
Mapuche: 'cacique' instead of lonko; Tupi: Curare versus the text's own stingray spines
Varangians: the etymology of væringi is correct (with the caveat of the debate over the suffix)

findings.title: Unique names that are learned, apocryphal or in bad Latin
findings.detail: There is a group of names that sound authentic but come from outside the civ's culture or from literary topoi. Fereters (Armenians) is a Latin-English ecclesiastical term: the fereter (from Latin feretrum, from Greek pheretron) is the portable reliquary carried in procession. The idea (priests accompanying the army) has an Armenian basis, because the priest Ghevond was at Avarayr (451), but the word is not Armenian. Furor Celtica (Celts) is bad Latin: furor is masculine, and the correct form would be 'furor Celticus'. Moreover, it evokes the Roman topos of the fury of the ancient Gauls, and it gives siege weapons extra hit points, which has nothing to do with the name. Northmen's Fury (Danes) alludes to the famous prayer 'A furore Normannorum libera nos', which does not appear in this form in the known manuscripts; the Danes did use siege engines at Paris (885–886), so the effect is plausible. Gothikon (Varangians) is a ceremonial performance at the Byzantine court described in the De Ceremoniis (10th century): members of the Hippodrome factions, dressed in furs, chanted a song with Latin and Germanic words. There is no documented link to the Varangians or to thrown axes. Cilician Fleet (Armenians) is stretched: the maritime trade of Cilician Armenia, at Ayas (Laiazzo), was carried on mainly by the Genoese and Venetians. Stirrups (Bulgarians) gives the Bulgarians a technology that reached Europe with the Avars and was already common by the 8th century. Silk Armor (Tatars) rests on the popular idea that silk shirts helped to extract arrows, which has no clear medieval source. Lechitic Legacy (Poles) is better than it looks: Vincent Kadłubek (c. 1200) already called the Poles 'Lechitae'. Wootz Steel (Dravidians) refers to a real South Indian steel, but 'wootz' is an 18th-century English corruption of the word ukku.
examples: Fereters (Armenians): wrong language (alternative: Vardanank, the war of Vardan in 451)
Furor Celtica (Celts): bad Latin and anachronistic (at the very least: Furor Celticus)
Northmen's Fury (Danes): plausible, but based on an apocryphal phrase
Gothikon (Varangians): stretched
Cilician Fleet (Armenians): stretched
Stirrups (Bulgarians): stretched
Silk Armor (Tatars): contested
Lechitic Legacy (Poles): plausible as a name; Wootz Steel: faithful in substance, colonial in name

findings.title: Well-chosen names that show the way forward
findings.detail: A significant share of the unique names is historically well founded and should serve as a model. Holcans replaced El Dorado (in the repository the internal name is still 'Mayan El Dorado'): holkan is the Yucatec Maya term for warriors, recorded by Landa, and El Dorado was a Spanish myth linked to the Muisca. Hul'che is the atlatl in Yucatec Maya, and Atlatl is the Nahuatl word. Kamandaran is the Persian kamāndārān, 'archers'. Bagains is a Proto-Bulgarian military rank attested in 9th-century inscriptions. Hamask is the Norse verb for a berserkr's 'flying into a rage'. Bogsveigar means 'bow-benders'. Hearth Troop translates the heorðwerod of the poem The Battle of Maldon. Genitour comes from the Berber Zenata, via the Spanish jinete. Thunderclap Bombs refers to the zhentianlei bombs that the Jin used in the defence of Kaifeng (1232). Double Crossbows and Ballista Elephant correspond to the elephant-mounted double-bow crossbows of the Bayon reliefs. Coustillier, Serjeant and Donjon, Detinets, Krepost, Folwark, Feitoria, Svan Towers, Monaspa, Aznauri, Leitis, Eupseong, Ordo Cavalry, Ghulam, Sipahi and Janissary are also good. Some names also have an effect that fits. Paper Money refers to the banknotes of Hồ Quý Ly (1396). Burgundian Vineyards refers to the decree of Philip the Bold against Gamay (1395). Szlachta Privileges gives cheaper knights, like the tax privileges of the nobility (Košice, 1374). Cuman Mercenaries recalls the Kipchaks settled by David IV of Georgia (c. 1118). Warwolf refers to the siege of Stirling (1304), and Houfnice to the Czech artillery piece that gave rise to the words 'howitzer' and 'obus'. Frontier Guards is a subtle allusion: pratihara means 'doorkeeper', and the Pratiharas claimed descent from Lakshmana, Rama's doorkeeper. Farimba evokes the farin (or farba), the governor and commander of the Mali Empire, and Tigui the Mandinka suffix tigi ('owner, master', as in dugutigi, village chief), although on its own it is truncated. On the American side, Ibirapema, Guecha, Kona, Malon and Butalmapu are correct. The link between name and effect is not always strong, but the names themselves are correct.
examples: Holcans (Mayans): faithful, and corrects the old El Dorado
Hul'che Javelineers and Atlatl: faithful
Kamandaran and Bagains: linguistically faithful
Hamask, Bogsveigar and Hearth Troop: faithful
Tuntian, Thunderclap Bombs, Detinets and Svan Towers: faithful
Paper Money, Burgundian Vineyards and Szlachta Privileges: faithful, with a coherent effect
Ibirapema, Guecha and Kona: faithful

debate_questions: Should the generic names (Militia-line, Knight-line, Hussar) be localised by region, as already happens with the Monk and building graphics, or should they stay universal so as not to confuse competitive play? Where does the balance lie between readability and historical truth?
Is an anachronistic name worse than an anachronistic mechanic? For Wu, is it better to rename the Hussar or to remove the unit from the tech tree?
A civ such as the Franks runs from Clovis to Joan of Arc. Which period should dictate the terminology: that of its founding, that of its peak, or the one best known to the public?
Should exonyms such as Saracens, Teutons, Celts, Vikings and Tatars be replaced? What criterion should be used: self-designation, academic convention or public recognition?
How should 'Monk' and 'Relic' be named for Muslim, Hindu, Mesoamerican and Andean civs without breaking the conversion mechanic? Is the Inca mallki a good 'relic'? And the ribat for the Berbers?
For peoples with few written sources (Tupi, Mapuche, Muisca), is a neutral English name preferable, or a term borrowed from a neighbouring language (Quechua, Taíno, Carib)? Which is more honest?

When a name is based on a documented fraud (Thirisadai) or on a myth (suicidal Mangudai, the chained horses of the Iron Pagoda), should Forgotten Empires change it even if players are already used to it?

Should the history texts from the 1999 game (Celts and Stonehenge, Huns and the stirrup, Goths and the sack of 409) be rewritten from scratch, as has already been done for some civs, or corrected point by point?

Exercise: choose a civ and rewrite its two Unique Techs so that the name is something documented and the effect reflects what that thing actually did. For example, the Santa Hermandad for the Spanish or the Praecepta Militaria for the Byzantines.
Portuguese exercise: what name would you give 'Circumnavigation' for the Portuguese (Volta do Mar, Carreira da Índia, Cartazes, Padrões), and what mechanical effect would correspond to each?
If the ages are Dark, Feudal, Castle and Imperial, what alternative names would work for all civs without Eurocentrism? Should the Tupi even have a 'Castle Age'?
proposals: Create a 'regional glossary' of alternative names for the generic lines, without changing stats. For Mesoamerica: Maquahuitl Warrior or Tequihua instead of Two-Handed Swordsman. For the Andes: Awqa Kamayuq. For the Islamic world: Faqih or Sufi instead of Monk, and Khanqah or Ribat instead of Monastery. For the Aztecs: Teocalli. The repository already has per-language strings (data/locales/*/strings.json), so a fork can test a per-civ 'historical name' layer.

For the American civs, replace the European economic names: Horse Collar and Heavy Plow with Chinampas (Aztecs), Andenes and Chakitaqlla (Incas) and raised fields (Mayans). Wheelbarrow and Hand Cart with Tlamemeh and llama caravans. Coinage with Quachtli and cacao. Block Printing with Amoxtli (Aztecs), Hu'un (Mayans) or Khipu (Incas). Gambesons with Ichcahuipilli. Catapult Galleon with a war canoe (acalli, ygara).

Correct the transcriptions, translations and Latin errors: Garland Wars → Flower Wars (Xochiyaoyotl); Yasama → Yazama; Shinkichon → Singijeon; Kamayuk → Awqa Kamayuq; Kataparuto → a pre-modern Japanese term (Ishihajiki, to be confirmed); Furor Celtica → Furor Celticus (or another name); standardise the Chinese romanisation in pinyin (Chu Ko Nu → Zhuge Nu).

Correct the words in the wrong language: Champi only for the Incas (Weichafe for the Mapuche, Tacape Warrior for the Tupi); Caciques → Morubixaba; Huaracas → a neutral name or one in Muysccubun; Huskarl → Gardingus or Buccellarius; Chatras → Tượng binh; Curare → a tech consistent with the text (stingray-spine arrows); Fereters → Vardanank.

Replace the attributions to other peoples and the frauds: Gbeto → Tontajon or Sofa; Thirisadai → Marakkalam; Woad Raider → Gallowglass or Kern; Tarkan → Logades; Centurion (mounted) → Comes or Equites Cataphractarii; Jarl → Druzhinnik or Hirðmaðr; Torsion Engines → a documented Ethiopian technique; Karambit Warrior → Hulubalang.

Give meaning to the empty techs: Atheism → a name linked to Hunnic religion (Attila's haruspices) or Flagellum Dei; Anarchy → Foederati; Perfusion → Thiufadi; Supremacy → Santa Hermandad; Logistica → Praecepta Militaria; Paiks → an effect on infantry, or the name Hastyadhyaksha; Medical Corps → Hastyayurveda; Grand Trunk Road → Sadak-e-Azam; Silk Road → Mude; Circumnavigation → Volta do Mar.

Correct the technological sequences: Mangonel (traction) → Onager (torsion) should be reversed, or the Onager should be reserved for the Romans, whose era it belongs to; rename the Hulk line (for example, Boarding Galley or War Cog); keep Clinker for the northern civs and create Asian alternatives (the watertight bulkheads of junks); give Clinker to the Saxons.

Localise the top of the light cavalry line instead of the universal Hussar: Akıncı (Turks), Jinete (Spanish), Stradiot (Italians), Wuhuan Cavalry (Wei); and, where the top is Light Cavalry, Hobelar (Britons) and Turcopole (Sicilians). Restore the Winged Hussar as heavy shock cavalry, its historical role. For the Shu and Chinese, consider giving the Chu Ko Nu or the name 'Zhuge' to the Shu.

In a fork of aoe2techtree, add to each unit and tech a 'historical note' field, with the rating (faithful, plausible, abstraction, stretched, anachronistic, wrong, unfounded) and a source. The site would then show the degree of fidelity of each name, which would serve as a public basis for these debates.

Revise the history texts with targeted corrections: Ælle of Sussex; Middlesex was not a kingdom; unification by Æthelstan (927) and not by Alfred (886); the shield wall did not come from the Vikings; Harthacnut son of Cnut; remove Stonehenge from the Celts' text; sack of Rome in 410; remove the stirrup from the Huns' text; lonko instead of cacique; consistency between the Tupi text and the Curare tech.
verification_log: I confirmed in the data (civ_trees.md, all_items.md) that the Mayans do not have the Champion, only the Two-Handed Swordsman. I corrected the example 'Two-Handed Swordsman and Champion for Aztecs and Mayans'.

I confirmed that the Shu do not have the Hussar (the list of 30 civs includes Wei and Wu, not Shu). I corrected 'the three civs also get Hussar and Galleon' to 'Wei and Wu get Hussar; all three get Galleon'.

The Tupi have Clinker Construction but not Carvel Hull. Wu, Jurchens and Mapuche have both. I corrected the example 'Clinker and Carvel for Wu, Jurchens, Mapuche and Tupi'. I added that the Saxons do not have Carvel Hull either.
Cranequins exists for the Britons, Danes, Franks, Saxons, Sicilians and Varangians, not for the Vikings. I corrected the sentence that gave the Vikings Cranequins.
The Khmer do not have Atonement (only Redemption). I changed the example to Bengalis, Burmese and Malians, which have both.
The Varangian Guard is also trained by the Saxons. I added the historical nuance of the Anglo-Saxon exiles after 1066, which the Varangians' own text mentions.
Catapult Galleon exists in 11 civs, including Vikings, Danes, Saxons, Varangians and Cumans. I added this to the naval section.

I removed 'Jinete for the Berbers' from the alternatives to the Hussar: the Berbers already have the Genitour, which is the same word. I noted that the Britons and Sicilians do not have the Hussar, so the Hobelar and Turcopole proposals are for a line whose top is Light Cavalry.

I added the internal inconsistency of the American civs: the game already removes Bloodlines, Husbandry and the horse armour upgrades (confirmed for the six civs), but keeps Horse Collar. I also added Slinger and Caciques for the Tupi, against the history text, which only mentions the bow and the ibirapema.

Hoardings (+1000 HP), Bracer (+1 attack and +1 range), Thumb Ring, Squires, Theocracy, Parthian Tactics, Atheism, Logistica, Paiks, Royal Heirs and the remaining effects were confirmed in the game descriptions. I adjusted the text for Bracer and Chieftains (also +4 against camels).
I confirmed in the repository that Holcans has the internal name 'Mayan El Dorado' (data/data.json).

Druzhina: I softened the criticism. The Rus' retinue often fought on foot in the 10th and 11th centuries (Leo the Deacon, Dorostolon 971), so the link to infantry is plausible; it is the trampling that is invented.
Teutons: I removed the 'anachronistic' rating, because medieval Latin used teutonicus for the Germans from the 10th century onwards. It becomes a plausible learned exonym.

Paladin: I added the root palatinus and the late Roman palatini, which makes the name less out of place for the Byzantines. I also added that Crossbowman → Arbalester is a ladder of synonyms, just like Knight → Cavalier.
Winged Hussar: I added that the first Polish hussars (Orsha, 1514) were light; the heavy winged husaria took shape from Báthory onwards.

Thirisadai: according to reports (on the official AoE forum) of Kanisetti's book (2025), the book treats the ship as a fraud. I noted that the information is indirect and that the existence of a Chola royal navy is debated (Open Magazine disputes Kanisetti).
Curare: I confirmed that the etymology is Carib (wurari, Macushi; Etymonline, Wiktionary) and not Tupi. I found no confirmation of curare use by the Tupinambá and marked it as poorly documented.
Yazama: I confirmed that 矢狭間 is read 'yazama'. Kataparuto: kanji dictionaries give 'ishihajiki' as a reading of 礟; the medieval attestation remains 'to be confirmed'.

Sitting Tiger: I confirmed that the 虎蹲砲 is a traction trebuchet from the Wujing Zongyao (1044) and that the name was later reused for a Ming cannon. I added Cao Cao's 'thunder carts' (霹靂車) at Guandu (200) as a faithful example.
Iron Pagoda: the sources confirm Qianlong's doubt about the chained horses (associated with the Guaizi Ma and often confused with the Iron Pagoda). I made the wording more precise.
Etymology of væringi: vár plus gengi is the most widely accepted analysis (supported by Old English wærgenga), but there is the alternative vár plus -ingi. I added the caveat.
Fereters: I confirmed that fereter is the portable reliquary (Latin feretrum, Middle English fertre). I added it as a wrong-language name for the Armenians.
Gothikon: I confirmed that the 'Gothic games' in the De Ceremoniis were performed by the Hippodrome factions dressed in skins, with no documented link to the Varangians.
Farimba and Tigui: I confirmed farin and farba as titles of governor and commander in Mali, and tigi as 'owner, master' (dugutigi). I added them to the plausible names.

History texts: I confirmed them in the files and added newly found errors. Danes: Harthacnut as 'grandson'. Saxons: Alfred and 886, and the shield wall 'adopted' from the Vikings. Celts: Stonehenge. Goths: sack of Rome in 409 (the Romans' text says 410). Huns: the stirrup. I raised the severity of this section to 'moderate'.
Ælle: Bede does not use the term bretwalda (it comes from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle). I corrected the wording. Hengist and Horsa become 'associated with the Jutes of Kent'.

I added names not analysed in the draft: Furor Celtica (incorrect Latin: furor is masculine), Northmen's Fury (apocryphal prayer), Cilician Fleet, Stirrups, Silk Armor, Lechitic Legacy (Kadłubek uses Lechitae), Wootz (corruption of ukku), Jian Swordsman (the dao replaced the jian at the end of the Han), War Chariot (it is a crossbow cart), Sun Jian (died in 191, before Wu existed) and the irony of the Chu Ko Nu ('Zhuge's crossbow') belonging to the Chinese and not to the Shu.
Fire Lancer for the Khitans: I added the mid-10th-century Dunhuang painting as the earliest depiction, which softens the anachronism; the first documented use in battle is still from 1132.

I did not verify on the web (the search limit ran out): the exact absence of the phrase 'A furore Normannorum' from the manuscripts, the etymology of Shrivamsha and the use of slings by the Tupinambá. The first two were worded cautiously; Shrivamsha was not included.

themes.title: What is a “civilization”? Representation, granularity and names of the 56 AoE2 DE civs

findings.title: Regional imbalance: 22 European civs, 2 from sub-Saharan Africa and none from Oceania
examples: Europe (22): Britons, Celts, Saxons, Franks, Burgundians, Spanish, Portuguese, Italians, Sicilians, Romans, Teutons, Bohemians, Poles, Lithuanians, Magyars, Vikings, Danes, Varangians, Slavs, Goths, Byzantines, Bulgarians
Africa (3/56): Berbers, Malians, Ethiopians, all from the African Kingdoms expansion (2015); no African civ among the 29 that followed
Commit 3bb43b1 “Add The Viking Sagas” (11 September 2026): Saxons, Danes, Varangians
British Isles: 3 civs; Scandinavia: 3; present-day China: 6 (Chinese, Shu, Wei, Wu, Jurchens, Khitans); Oceania: 0; America north of Mexico: 0

findings.title: There is no coherent definition of “civilisation”: peoples, states, dynasties, regions, language families, institutions and even activities
findings.detail:
The 56 civs use at least seven different units of analysis:
- Ethnonyms: Magyars, Danes, Saxons.
- States or regimes: Shu, Wei and Wu are three regimes of the same Han population. Byzantines is a state.
- Dynasties: Gurjaras comes from the Gurjara-Pratihara.
- Regions or kingdoms: Bengalis; Sicilians, from the Regnum Siciliae.
- Empires used as a regional label: Malians, whose text also covers Ghana.
- Language families or scholarly constructs: Celts (Edward Lhuyd, 1707), Slavs, Tupi (the game's own text admits it is an umbrella term) and Dravidians. The Sanskrit Drāviḍa already existed in the Middle Ages, mainly for the Tamil country, but the sense of a language family and an ethnic group comes from Robert Caldwell (1856).
- Institutions: Varangians, the name given to Scandinavians in the East and associated with the Byzantine imperial guard.
- An activity: Vikings, from Old Norse víkingr, one who sets out on víking, a raiding expedition.

This is not pedantry. The unit chosen decides what counts as a “missing” civ. If Shu, Wei and Wu are worth three slots, then Song and Ming, Umayyads and Abbasids, or Castile and Aragon should count too. If “Slavs” is a civ, Bohemians, Poles and Bulgarians overlap with it. Some degree of abstraction is inevitable and often legitimate (Malians, Bengalis, Byzantines). The problem is the inconsistent application, which systematically favours the regions that already have the most slots.
examples: States/regimes: Shu, Wei, Wu (AD 220–280), three regimes of the same population
Language family: Dravidians (Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Pandyas, Cholas, Vijayanagara); modern sense from Caldwell, 1856
Activity: Vikings (víkingr = one who goes on víking, a raiding expedition)
Institution: Varangians / Varangian Guard (guard of the Byzantine emperor)
Kingdom: Sicilians, who in the game are the Italo-Normans (Serjeant, First Crusade, Hauberk, Donjon); the text itself uses “Italo-Normans”

findings.title: China over-fragmented and in the wrong period: three slots for about 60 years of the 3rd century, only one for a thousand years of medieval China
findings.detail:
“Chinese” covers the Sui, Tang, Song, Yuan and Ming in a single civ. The text runs from 581 to the Ming dynasty, and the civ has Great Wall, Rocketry, Fire Lancer and Rocket Cart. Shu, Wei and Wu take up three slots for AD 220–280, or from 184 in the Shu and Wei texts, which begin with the Yellow Turban Rebellion.

The heroes Liu Bei, Cao Cao and Sun Jian are historical figures documented in Chen Shou's Sanguozhi (late 3rd century). Their popular fame comes from the Romance of the Three Kingdoms (14th century). Sun Jian died in 191 or 192, before Wu was a kingdom (222) or an empire (229). But the text presents him as the father of the founder, just as Cao Cao died (220) before Cao Pi proclaimed the Wei empire. As founding figures, they are acceptable.

To be fair, the units are well grounded. Cao Cao's Tiger and Leopard Cavalry (虎豹骑) existed, and the “hei guang” and “ming guang” cuirasses are mentioned in a memorial by Cao Zhi. Traction Trebuchet and Hei Guang Cavalry are exclusive to the three; the Lou Chuan is also shared with Chinese and Jurchens. This shows that they are variants of a single military culture. The problem is not quality, it is granularity and period.

The Chu Ko Nu (zhuge nu) of the Chinese is not an error. The repeating crossbow is well documented in Ming China (Wubei Zhi, 1621). The attribution to Zhuge Liang is traditional, and there are already repeating crossbows in a Chu tomb of the 4th century BC. The Shu tradition is represented by the Bolt Magazine tech. It corresponds to Zhuge Liang's “yuanrong”, which according to the Weishi Chunqiu shot ten bolts at once. It is a brand duplication, not a false attribution.

Meanwhile, powers that were peers of Tang and Song China are missing:
- the Tibetan Empire (618–842), which occupied Chang'an in 763;
- the Tanguts of Western Xia (1038–1227);
- the Uyghurs: the Khanate (744–840) helped the Tang recover Chang'an and Luoyang in 757, and was followed by the kingdom of Qocho.

Assessment: Shu, Wei and Wu as main civs are anachronistic in a medieval roster. They would fit in a Late Antiquity roster, as the repository already does with the Chronicles civs.
examples: Shu.md and Wei.md begin with the Yellow Turban Rebellion of AD 184
Traction Trebuchet and Hei Guang Cavalry: only Shu, Wei, Wu; Lou Chuan: Chinese, Jurchens, Shu, Wei, Wu
Chu Ko Nu (Chinese, the zhuge nu of the Ming era) and Bolt Magazine (Shu, Zhuge Liang's yuanrong): both defensible
Tibetans, Tanguts and Uyghurs absent, with at least 6 civs in the territory of present-day China

findings.title: Norse triplication: Vikings, Danes and Varangians, plus Saxons with Longship and Varangian Guard
examples: Longship: Danes, Saxons, Varangians, Vikings (4/56); for the Saxons, supported by the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (896)
Varangian Guard / Elite Varangian Guard: Byzantines, Danes, Saxons, Varangians, Vikings (5/56)
Danes: “Varangian Guards and Longships move +10% faster”; Varangians: “Varangian Guards attack +25% faster”
Lindisfarne narrated in 3 texts, 1066 in 4 (Vikings, Saxons, Britons, Varangians)

findings.title: British Isles: “Britons” are the English, “Saxons” is an imperfect name for England before 1066, and “Celts” is an 18th-century umbrella
examples: Britons: Longbowman, Yeomen, Warwolf, in other words Plantagenet England, not the Britons (with the caveat of the Welsh bow)
Saxons (Hearth Troop = heorðwerod, Shield Wall) and Britons: two civs for the same England
Celts.md: Celts in “northern Europe” and builders of Stonehenge
Woad Raider (Celts): body paint described by Caesar for the Britanni of the 1st century BC
In pt-BR the civ is called “Bretões”, a word that in Portuguese also designates the inhabitants of French Brittany

findings.title: “Slavs” overlaps with three civs and plays as Rus', while Rus' is split between Slavs and Varangians
findings.detail:
The units and techs of the Slavs civ point mainly to Rus'. Only the Detinets is unambiguously Russian: it is the citadel of the cities of Rus', such as Novgorod. Boyar and Druzhina are broader terms. There were boyars (bolyar) in Bulgaria, Rus', Wallachia and Serbia. The druzhina (drużyna, družina) was the armed retinue of Slavic princes in general; Ibrahim ibn Yaqub describes the 3,000 men of Mieszko I of Poland.

The history text is pan-Slavic: the First Bulgarian Empire (681), Great Moravia (833) and Kievan Rus' (882, Yaroslav). After Bulgarians (2019) and Bohemians and Poles (2021), “Slavs” came to overlap with three civs and ceased to be a necessary abstraction. Serbs and Croats still have no civ.

The Varangians civ represents the eastern Scandinavians, mainly Swedes, on the river routes and in the Byzantine Guard. Its text ends with the assimilation of the Varangians into Slavic culture. The Slavs' text, for its part, says that Kievan Rus' was “led by Scandinavians”. The game thus adopts the moderate “Normanist” reading, which is the current academic consensus: according to Franklin & Shepard (The Emergence of Rus 750–1200, 1996), an elite of Scandinavian origin became Slavicised around the 11th century. But the debate remains politically charged, especially in Russian and Ukrainian historiography.

Natural proposal: rename “Slavs” to “Rus'” and treat the Varangians as a component or variant of that civ.
examples: Slavs: Detinets (Russian citadel); Boyar and Druzhina are pan-Slavic terms, also Bulgarian and Polish
Slavs.md: Bulgaria (681), Great Moravia (833) and Kievan Rus' (882), overlapping with Bulgarians, Bohemians and Varangians
Varangians.md ends with the assimilation of the Varangians into Slavic culture
Serbs (Nemanjićs, 1166–1371) and Croats without a civ of their own

findings.title: Compressed Middle East: controversial “Saracens”, Persians between Sasanian and Islamic Iran, Ottoman Turks, and no Seljuks, Mamluks or Al-Andalus
findings.detail:
“Saracens” is a Greek and Latin exonym. Sarakenoi first designated nomadic groups of north-western Arabia and later, in the West, all Muslims; the game's own text admits this broadening. Jerome and Isidore of Seville spread a Christian etymology that linked it to Sarah. Assessment: a controversial exonym, although it is a “voice of the period” of the Crusades.

The Mameluke is a subtle case. The Mamluks were soldiers of slave origin, mostly Kipchak Turks and, after 1382, Circassians, and not Arabs. But the institution (ghulam, mamluk) served Arab and Islamic states from the Abbasids (al-Mu'tasim, 830s) and the Ayyubids onwards. It is as defensible for the Saracens as the Janissaries are for the Turks, recruited by devşirme among Balkan Christians. The real problem is that the Mamluk Sultanate (1250–1517, Ain Jalut 1260) has no civ and its military identity is absorbed by the Saracens. Assessment: plausible as an abstraction.

The Persians mix two Irans:
- the Sasanian one: the text ends with the Islamic conquest; the War Elephant; the Savar, from Persian savār, “horseman” (cf. the Sasanian asvārān);
- the Islamic one: the Caravanserai.
The text says that Ctesiphon is Baghdad today, which is false: they are distinct cities and Baghdad was founded in 762. It also says that the Sasanian dynasty ended in a battle in 636. Qadisiyyah was decisive, but Yazdegerd III only died in 651. The Samanids, Buyids and Ilkhanate do not appear.

The Turks play as Ottomans: Janissary, Artillery, Sipahi, gunpowder. The text has three errors:
- it says that “Turk” designates only the Seljuks and Ottomans, forgetting the Göktürks (552), who gave the name;
- it claims that the Seljuk Empire disappeared with the fall of Baghdad in 1258, when the Great Seljuk Empire fell in 1194 and the Sultanate of Rum lasted until c. 1308;
- it credits the Seljuks with the recovery of Palestine, the work of the Kurd Saladin, an Ayyubid.
The Seljuks (Manzikert, 1071) have no civ of their own.

The Saracens' text claims that the Arabs took Asia Minor from the Byzantines. They never conquered it: they raided it and besieged Constantinople. The Berbers' text attributes to them the Alhambra (Nasrid) and the Mosque of Córdoba (Umayyad), works of two Arab dynasties. The Koutoubia and the Hassan Tower, which are Almohad, are genuinely Berber. Result: Al-Andalus is split between Saracens and Berbers without being either of them.
examples: Saracens: Mameluke, an Islamic institution of soldiers of slave origin (Turks and Circassians), analogous to the Turks' Janissaries
Persians.md: “Ctesiphon, called Baghdad today”; dynasty “ended” in 636
Turks.md: Seljuks narrated (end placed in 1258), but Ottoman gameplay (Janissary, gunpowder)
Berbers.md attributes the Alhambra and the Mosque of Córdoba to them
Absent: Seljuks, Mamluks/Ayyubids, Khwarazmians, Andalusis

findings.title: Sub-Saharan Africa: two civs, one of them with a unit from another country and another century
examples: Gbeto (Malians): a unit from Dahomey (17th–19th centuries), not from Mali (13th–15th centuries)
Malians.md covers Ghana and Mali in a single civ; Songhai only as a rival
Nubia/Makuria: archers whom the Arabs called “archers of the eyes”; Baqt of 652
Kanem-Bornu, Songhai, Kilwa, Adal, Benin and Kongo: all with written sources (several of them Portuguese) and a distinct military tradition

findings.title: Steppe and Central Asia: “Tatars” merges the Golden Horde with Timur, the Huns have unfounded elements, and the Göktürks, Uyghurs, Khazars and Avars are missing
findings.detail:
“Tatar” already appears in the Orkhon inscriptions (8th century) as the name of tribal groups. In the 12th century it designated a confederation hostile to Genghis Khan, who destroyed it in 1202. Later, Rus' and the Europeans applied the name to all the peoples under Mongol rule. The Latin form “Tartari” was associated with infernal Tartarus (Matthew Paris, 1240s), which is where the Portuguese “Tártaros” comes from. The game's text honestly acknowledges this shift in meaning.

The civ mixes the Golden Horde with the Timurids. Timurid Siegecraft and the Flaming Camel are linked to the legend of the camels set on fire against the elephants of Delhi in 1398. Timur was a Barlas Turco-Mongol and an enemy of the Horde: he defeated Toqtamish at the Kondurcha (1391) and on the Terek (1395). The text calls him a “Tatar warlord”, following outside European usage. The Keshik (keshig, the imperial guard created by Genghis) belongs to the Tatars and not to the Mongols. This is defensible, because the successor khanates kept the keshig, but it is odd.

The Huns have three problems:
- the Atheism tech (“Enemy Relics generate -50% resources”) applies a modern concept to a people with their own religious practices. Assessment: unfounded;
- they have Dromon and Galleon, without any known naval tradition;
- the text takes as certain the origin “from around Mongolia”, but the Xiongnu–Huns link is contested (in favour: de la Vaissière and Kim Hyun Jin; sceptical: Maenchen-Helfen).
The text also says that some credit the Huns with inventing the stirrup. This is wrong: the rigid stirrup only reached Europe with the Avars (6th–7th centuries).

The Göktürks (552–744, the first “Türk”), the Uyghurs (744–840), the Khazars (c. 650–969) and the Avars (c. 567–c. 800) are missing.
examples: Tatars: Timurid Siegecraft + Flaming Camel (Timurids) + Keshik (Genghis's guard) + a text centred on the Golden Horde
Huns: Atheism, without historical basis; Dromon and Galleon available
Huns.md: Mongolian origin taken as certain; stirrup attributed to the Huns
Göktürks, Uyghurs, Khazars and Avars absent

findings.title: South Asia: the 2022 split was an advance, but the four labels follow four different logics
findings.detail:
The replacement of “Indians” (2013) by Hindustanis, Gurjaras, Bengalis and Dravidians was a real advance. It came with Dynasties of India, in April 2022 (commit 1a2a4cd). The texts are interlinked, for example in the “Kannauj Triangle” between the Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas, which appears in the texts of the Bengalis, Gurjaras and Dravidians. But the names follow different logics:
- Bengalis: a region. This is reasonable.
- Gurjaras: a dynasty, the Gurjara-Pratihara, used as a label for the whole north-west. The text covers the Chandelas, Paramaras, Solankis, Chauhans, the sultanates of Gujarat and Malwa, and Mewar up to Maharana Pratap. The label is politically sensitive: there are current disputes between Gurjar and Rajput communities over the legacy of Mihira Bhoja (contested).
- Dravidians: the Sanskrit Drāviḍa existed in the Middle Ages. Kumārila Bhaṭṭa (7th century) speaks of “Āndhra-Drāviḍa” languages, and the Brahmin category Pañca-Drāviḍa even included Gujarat and Maharashtra. But the term mainly designated the Tamil country. The sense of a language family and an ethnic group comes from Caldwell (1856). The civ brings together Tamils (Cholas, Pandyas), Kannadigas (Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas) and Vijayanagara.
- Hindustanis: an Indo-Persian term for the northern plain, used for example in the Baburnama. The text is explicit about the Delhi Sultanate, but the name hides the fact that the gameplay is Indo-Islamic: Ghulam, Caravanserai, Grand Trunk Road. The road is Sher Shah Suri's (1540s); the name is British.

Assessment: plausible overall, with uneven abstractions. The Sinhalese are missing: Polonnaruwa and Parakramabahu I (1153–1186), who even launched an expedition against Burma c. 1164–1165.
examples: Commit 1a2a4cd (28 April 2022): string 10290 “Indians” → “Hindustanis”
Hindustanis: Ghulam, Imperial Camel Rider, Shatagni, Grand Trunk Road, in other words the Delhi Sultanate and the Suri period
Dravidians: a medieval Sanskrit term reinterpreted as a linguistic category in 1856
Gurjaras.md covers the Pratiharas, Chandelas, Paramaras, Solankis, Chauhans and Mewar

findings.title: Southeast Asia: “Malay” absorbs Java, the Burmese use units from Manipur, and Champa is missing
findings.detail:
“Malay” covers three states: Srivijaya (Malay, Sumatra; inscriptions in Old Malay from 683 onwards), Majapahit (Javanese) and Malacca (Malay). The text itself speaks of a “truly Javanese” culture in Majapahit. The Javanese, with their own language, court and military tradition, are thus subsumed under a neighbouring label.

The Burmese have the Arambai as their unique unit and Manipur Cavalry as a tech. Both come from the kingdom of Manipur (Meitei); the arambai is a Manipuri throwing dart. The text covers Pagan (1044–1297) and Toungoo (up to 1599). Bayinnaung subjugated Manipur in 1560. But Manipuri cavalry in Burmese service, the “Cassay Horse”, is documented mainly under the Konbaung dynasty, after the conquests of 1758. Rating: stretched. It is weak for Pagan and somewhat more defensible for Toungoo.

The Vietnamese have the tech Chatras, from Sanskrit chattra (royal parasol), a term of Indic tradition. Vietnamese kings also used ceremonial parasols (lọng), so the problem is mainly the Indic name in a state shaped on the Chinese model. Rating: stretched. Paper Money, on the other hand, is faithful: Hồ Quý Ly issued paper money in 1396.

Missing:
- Champa: a power between c. 192 and 1471 (fall of Vijaya), with Panduranga autonomous until 1832; it sacked Angkor in 1177;
- the Siamese: Sukhothai (c. 1238) and Ayutthaya (1351), a direct rival of the Toungoo, as the Burmese text itself acknowledges;
- the Sinhalese.
All of them have sources and a distinct military tradition, such as elephant warfare or the Cham fleets.
examples: Malay.md: Srivijaya, Majapahit (Javanese) and Malacca in a single civ
Burmese: Arambai and Manipur Cavalry, both from Manipur; the “Cassay Horse” belongs to the Konbaung period (post-1758)
Vietnamese: Chatras (Indic term, stretched) vs Paper Money (Hồ Quý Ly, 1396, faithful)
Champa and Siam absent, despite having been regional powers

findings.title: Americas: name improvements in 2025, but “Aztecs” is an 18th–19th-century label, Mapuche and Tupi are contact-period civs, and all of North America is missing
findings.detail:
It is fair to start with the positive. Update 141935 (commit a7b7c41, April 2025) changed “Mayans” to “Maya” and “Incas” to “Inca”. The Last Chieftains (2026) added non-imperial peoples (Muisca, Mapuche, Tupi), and the Tupi text honestly acknowledges that the name is an umbrella term.

The problems:
- “Aztecs” was popularised by Clavijero (1780–1781), Humboldt and Prescott (1843). They called themselves Mexica, and the empire was the Triple Alliance (Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, Tlacopan).
- “Inca” was the title of the ruler and the elite. The state was called Tawantinsuyu.
- “Maya” lumps together the Classic (250–900) and the Postclassic (Mayapán, K'iche', Itzá until 1697).
- Mapuche and Tupi are defined by contact with Europeans. The game's Mapuche are those of the Arauco War (from 1541): cavalry (Kona, Bolas Rider) and even Bombard Tower. Before 1492 there were no horses in the Americas. The Tupi are those of Guanabara Bay, between 1555 and 1567.

To be fair, there is a pre-Hispanic dimension of the Mapuche that could be used: the resistance to Inca expansion on the Maule River, of contested date and scale.

The texts also contain two errors:
- the Mapuche text says they are “the largest native group in South America”. It probably confuses this with “the largest in Chile”: the Quechua peoples number several million;
- the Tupi text says Hans Staden was held captive from 1552 to 1555. He was held captive for about nine months, in 1554.

Missing:
- the Purépecha, who defeated the Mexica army c. 1478–1479 and worked copper and bronze;
- the Chimú (Chan Chan, conquered by the Incas c. 1470);
- the Mixtecs;
- all of America north of Mexico: the Mississippians had Cahokia (peak c. 1050–1200) and faced De Soto at Mabila (1540).
examples: Commit a7b7c41 (19 April 2025): “Maya” and “Inca” as display names (strings 10286, 10291)
Mapuche: Kona and Bolas Rider (cavalry) + Bombard Tower, i.e. the Arauco War, 16th–17th centuries
Tupi.md: centred on 1554–1567 (Staden, Araribóia, founding of Rio)
Purépecha, Chimú and Mississippians absent; 0 civs north of Mexico

findings.title: A “medieval game” that runs from the late 2nd century to the 17th century
examples: chronicles/data/data.json: Achaemenids, Athenians, Macedonians, Puru, Spartans, Thracians → era “antiquity”; the 56 main civs → era “base”
Goths: Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon available; Huns: no gunpowder unit
Galleon available to Huns, Romans, Goths, Shu, Wei, Wu (only Aztecs, Khitans and Malians lack it)
Portuguese: Circumnavigation (Magellan–Elcano expedition, in the service of Castile)
Poles/Lithuanians: Winged Hussar, a 16th–17th-century unit

findings.title: Names: distinguishing conventional exonyms (acceptable) from misleading ones, controversial ones and retroactive nationalisms
findings.detail:
Not all exonyms are equal. I propose a scale.

Conventional and defensible:
- Byzantines: a term introduced by Hieronymus Wolf (1557) and popularised in the 17th–19th centuries. They called themselves Rhomaioi. Anthony Kaldellis (Romanland, 2019) contests it, but it remains the academic convention.
- Berbers: probably from Greek and Latin barbarus, via Arabic; the etymology is debated. The endonym is Imazighen.
- Teutons: from medieval Latin teutonicus (9th–10th centuries), also used by the Teutonic Order. Rating: plausible.
- Franks: Muslims and Byzantines called the crusaders “Franks” (al-Ifranj), so there is a legitimate “voice of the period” here. But the civ combines the Merovingian throwing axe (5th–7th centuries) with the Compagnies d'ordonnance of 1445.

National and retroactive (acceptable abstractions, but worth flagging):
- Spanish: covers Castile, León, Aragon and Navarre before there was a unified “Spain” (1479/1516). In gameplay it is Habsburg Spain.
- Italians: covers Venice, Genoa, Florence and Milan.

Misleading or ambiguous:
- Britons for the English.
- Sicilians for the Italo-Normans. It is plausible as the name of the kingdom, but it suggests the island's Greek-Arab-Latin population rather than the Norman elite.
- Romans and Byzantines in the same roster. “Romans” designates the Roman West of 395–476, alongside “Byzantines” for the only people who called themselves Romans for a further thousand years. It is a naming paradox.

Controversial:
- Saracens;
- Tatars/Tartars, linked to the infernal Tartarus.

Name of an activity:
- Vikings.

The change of “Mayans” and “Incas” in 2025 shows that the team is willing to revise names. What is missing is an explicit criterion.
examples: Byzantines (Wolf, 1557) and Romans in the same roster: two “Romans”, and the one that called itself Roman is the one that does not bear that name
Franks: Throwing Axeman (Merovingian francisca) + Ordonnance Companies (1445)
Spanish and Italians: names of modern nation-states for medieval pluralities
Berbers vs Imazighen; Aztecs vs Mexica; Inca vs Tawantinsuyu

findings.title: Unique units “borrowed” from another people or another century: poorly defined boundaries between civs create leaks
findings.detail:
When the boundary between civs is poorly defined, emblematic units end up in the wrong civ. The clearest cases:
- Huskarl (Goths): from Old Norse húskarl, the armed retinue of the 10th–11th centuries in Scandinavia and in Cnut's England. It has nothing to do with the Goths of the 4th–6th centuries, especially now that there are Danes (Jomsviking) and Saxons, whose Hearth Troop renders Old English heorðwerod, the equivalent of the housecarl. Rating: anachronistic.
- Rocket Cart (Khitans; also Jurchens): cart-mounted rocket launchers belong to the Ming and Joseon period (hwacha, 1451; Wubei Zhi, 1621). Rating: anachronistic.
- Fire Lancer (Khitans): the Liao fell in 1125, and the first textually recorded use of the fire lance is the siege of De'an (1132). But a Dunhuang painting from c. 950 (dating debated) already shows the device, and the Western Liao lasted until 1218. Rating: stretched, not strictly anachronistic.
- Mounted Trebuchet (Khitans): the clearest source for camel-mounted catapults is the History of Song (Song Shi, scroll 486). It describes 200 Western Xia artillerymen called poxi (潑喜), with “whirlwind” catapults on camel saddles. I found no equivalent source for the Liao, so the concept seems to be borrowed from the Tanguts (to be confirmed).
- Gbeto (Malians, Dahomey), Woad Raider (Celts, Antiquity) and Arambai and Manipur Cavalry (Burmese, Manipur; stretched).

Cases that at first sight look like leaks but are defensible:
- Chu Ko Nu for the Chinese: the zhuge nu is documented in the Ming period;
- Mameluke for the Saracens: it is an Islamic institution, just like the Janissary for the Turks;
- Longship for the Saxons: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, 896.

Each case on its own is a unit problem. Taken together, they show that the roster has no rule on whom each military identity belongs to.
examples: Huskarl (Goths) vs Hearth Troop (Saxons) and Jomsviking (Danes)
Song Shi, scroll 486: “有砲手二百人號潑喜…旋風砲於橐駝鞍” (Western Xia, not Liao)
Rocket Cart: Chinese, Jurchens, Khitans, Koreans; anachronistic for Khitans and Jurchens
Gbeto (Dahomey) in the Malians; Arambai (Manipur) in the Burmese

findings.title: The older history texts (1999–2015) convey Eurocentric judgements that shape how peoples are represented
examples: Aztecs.md: a culture that invented little and passed on nothing; diseases “brought by traders” before the conquest
Mayans.md: “simple” religion, three codices (four since 2018), collapse caused by earthquakes or volcanoes
Vikings.md: “Viking” = “men of the north”; raids over by the end of the 10th century
Contrast: Khitans.md, Muisca.md and Tupi.md, more balanced and with identified sources

findings.title: Assessment of the missing peoples: strong, medium and weak cases
examples: Strong: Makuria, Seljuks, Mamluks, Tibetans, Tanguts, Kanem-Bornu, Songhai, Purépecha, Serbs, Siam, Champa
Medium: Timurids, Al-Andalus, Aragon, Swiss, Wallachia, Uyghurs, Khazars, Göktürks, Avars, Khwarazmians, Kilwa, Benin, Kongo, Chimú, Mississippians, Polynesians
Weak/variants: Venice/Genoa, Teutonic Order, Prussians, Navarre, Albanians, Delhi Sultanate, Great Zimbabwe
Out of period: Mughals (1526), Safavids (1501)

findings.title: The translation layer aggravates some naming problems for people who play in Portuguese
findings.detail:
The repository includes the pt-BR localisation (data/locales/br/strings.json). It is the only one in Portuguese, and so it is the one a Portuguese player sees. Several names add to the confusion:
- “Bretões” for Britons (string 10271): in Portuguese, “bretões” are also the inhabitants of French Brittany, who were in fact a Brittonic people. The translation reinforces the original error. “Ingleses” would be the correct name for the civ's content.
- “Tártaros”: the form linked to the infernal Tartarus of 13th-century Latin propaganda.
- “Sarracenos”.
- “Chibchas” for Muisca: not strictly an error, because the English text itself gives “Chibcha” as a synonym. But Chibcha is mainly the name of the language and of the language family. English has already adopted the endonym “Muisca”, and in pt-PT it would be “Muíscas”.
- “Quitais” for Khitans: it is worth noting that this people is the origin of “Catai” (Cathay), the medieval European name for China, also used by the Portuguese.
- “Os gurjares”: it is the only civ name with an article, a translation inconsistency.
- “Varangianos”: an anglicism; Portuguese uses “varegues”.

These are not serious errors. But they show that the review of names should be carried out in every language, and not only in English.
examples: 10271 “Britons” → pt-BR “Bretões” (ambiguity with Brittany/Armorica)
10303 Tatars → “Tártaros”; 10279 Saracens → “Sarracenos”
10327 Muisca → “Chibchas” (pt-BR) vs “Muisca” (en)
10312 Gurjaras → “Os gurjares”; 10331 Varangians → “Varangianos”; 10323 Khitans → “Quitais” (origin of “Catai”)

findings.title: What has already been done well: proof that revision is possible
examples: Commit 1a2a4cd (2022): “Indians” → Hindustanis, plus Gurjaras, Bengalis and Dravidians
Commit a7b7c41 (2025): “Maya”, “Inca”
Commit b34082d (2026): Chronicles civs moved to a separate page
Tuntian (Wei), Paper Money (Vietnamese), Wagenburg Tactics (Bohemians): techs with a solid documentary basis

debate_questions: What should a “civilization” be in AoE2: a people, a state, a dynasty, a region or a cultural sphere? Choose a criterion and reclassify the 56. How many survive without a change of name or scope?

If you had 56 slots, what criterion would you use to distribute them by macro-region: population around 1200, number of states, available sources or player interest? Make the distribution with each criterion and compare the results.
After Danes and Varangians, what does the “Vikings” civ still represent? Should it become “Norse” or “Norwegians”, merge with the Danes or disappear?
How would you name “Romans” and “Byzantines” in the same game without confusing the player and without erasing the fact that the Byzantines called themselves Rhomaioi?
Should the Rus' be a Slavic civ, a Scandinavian civ or a civ with variants? Do the current texts (Slavs: Rus' “led by Scandinavians”) take sides in the Normanist controversy? Should they?
Is “Celts” as defensible as “Malay” or “Tupi”, which are also acknowledged umbrella terms? Where is the boundary between an acceptable abstraction and an anachronism?

Should period exonyms (Saracens, Tatars, Franks) be kept as the “voice of the period” or give way to scholarly terms? Is there a moral difference between a conventional exonym (Byzantine, Aztec) and a contentious one (Saracen)?
Can a civ be defined by contact with Europeans, like the mounted Mapuche or the Tupi of 1567? Where should the time limit be: 1492, 1521/1533 or 1600?
Do the Three Kingdoms justify three slots in a medieval game? If you had to swap, would you prefer Wu or Tibetans? Wei or Tanguts? Shu or Uyghurs?

When is it acceptable for a unique unit to come from another people or another century (Huskarl for the Goths, Gbeto for the Malians, Arambai for the Burmese)? And when is a “foreign” institution legitimate, like the Mameluke for the Saracens or the Janissary for the Turks? Does calling it a “mercenary” solve the problem?
If you could add only three civs, which would you choose and why? Weigh the geographical gap, historical weight, quality of sources and gameplay potential.

Should Al-Andalus have its own civ, given that the Berbers and Saracens claim its monuments? And is medieval Portugal (Afonso Henriques, Aljubarrota) well served by a civ centred on the trading posts and caravels of the 15th–16th centuries?
Should the history texts flag when a point is contested (the Xiongnu origin of the Huns, Normanism, Aztec sacrifice numbers, “flower wars”)? Or should a game give a single version?
Does a system of dynastic variants, like the one in AoE4 since 2023 (Ayyubids, Order of the Dragon, Zhu Xi's Legacy…), solve the granularity problem or merely hide it?
proposals: An explicit roster principle. A civ is a political-cultural sphere with about two centuries of continuity within c. 500–1500 (with tolerance up to c. 1550), with a distinctive military tradition documented in written or archaeological sources. All current and future civs should be assessed against these criteria, and that assessment should be published.

Use the “era” field that the repository already has. Its value is currently “antiquity” for the Chronicles and “base” for the 56 civs. I propose marking Romans, Shu, Wei and Wu (and possibly Huns and Goths) as “late-antiquity”, and Mapuche and Tupi as “contact-era”. They could move to a separate page, as was already done with the Chronicles (commit b34082d), or at least be flagged in the aoe2techtree.net interface.
verification_log: Repo data verified with fc/q.py against data/data.json: Galleon is missing only for Aztecs, Khitans and Malians, so Huns, Romans, Goths, Shu, Wei and Wu have it. Goths have Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon. Huns, Romans, Shu, Wei and Wu have no gunpowder units (added the Huns-vs-Goths contrast). Dromon: Armenians, Byzantines, Goths, Huns, Romans. Longship: 4 civs. Varangian Guard: 5. Fire Lancer: 5. Rocket Cart: Chinese, Jurchens, Khitans, Koreans. Mapuche have Bombard Tower. All era=base and meta={} for the 56; Chronicles era=antiquity.
Corrected: Lou Chuan is not exclusive to Shu/Wei/Wu; Chinese and Jurchens also have it. Only Traction Trebuchet and Hei Guang Cavalry are exclusive to the three.
Corrected string ID: Britons is 10271, not 10273 (10273 is Goths). Added pt-BR inconsistencies found in strings.json: 10312 “Os gurjares” (with article) and 10331 “Varangianos”.

Commits verified: 3bb43b1 (2026-09-11), 1a2a4cd (2022-04-28, Indians→Hindustanis), a7b7c41 (2025-04-19, Mayans→Maya, Incas→Inca), b34082d (2026-04-28). Removed groups.json as a cited repository source; it is a scratchpad helper, not part of the repo.

Count of 29 civs added after African Kingdoms, 0 African and 10 European, re-derived expansion by expansion; correct. Population figures hedged as orders of magnitude. “Dozens of states” softened to “many states”. Could not re-verify the McEvedy & Jones figures because the web-search budget ran out.

Slavs: the in-game text covers Kievan Rus' (882, Yaroslav) as well as Bulgaria and Great Moravia; the draft had omitted this. The text itself takes the Normanist line (“led by Scandinavians”). Boyar and Druzhina are pan-Slavic/Bulgarian terms (Mieszko I's druzhina in Ibrahim ibn Yaqub); only Detinets is clearly Rus'. Severity lowered to moderate.

Three Kingdoms: the heroes are historical figures documented in Chen Shou's Sanguozhi, not inventions of the 14th-c. Romance. Sun Jian died in 191 or 192. The parallel with Cao Cao dying before the Wei empire was added.

Chu Ko Nu no longer counted as a misattribution. The zhuge nu is attested in the Ming (Wubei Zhi, 1621); repeating crossbows predate Zhuge Liang; Shu's Bolt Magazine matches the ten-bolt yuanrong in the Weishi Chunqiu. Removed from the summary's leak list.

Fire Lancer for Khitans downgraded from anachronistic to stretched: there is a Dunhuang depiction c. 950 (dating debated), the first textual use is De'an 1132, and the Western Liao lasted to 1218. Rocket Cart (Ming/Joseon) added as the clear anachronism for Khitans and Jurchens.
Song Shi 486 quote checked on Wikisource: “有砲手二百人號潑喜，陟立旋風砲於橐駝鞍”. It concerns the Tangut Xia, which supports the borrowing hypothesis; I found no Liao source for camel trebuchets.

Varangian Guard: Norse of all origins served (Harald Hardrada 1034–1042, Bolli Bollason), so the problem is turning a court institution into a generic barracks unit, not the ethnic link. Saxons' Longship is defensible from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 896 (Alfred's langscipu).

Episode-overlap counts made precise from the history files: Lindisfarne in 3 texts (Vikings, Danes, Saxons), 1066 in 4 (Vikings, Saxons, Britons, Varangians), the 865 army in 3, Cnut in 3. The Vikings text's attribution of Lindisfarne to “Danes” now notes the generic OE usage “Dene”.

Vikings text errors added: it says “Viking” means “northmen”; the siege it dates to 871 lasted “two years” and is the 885–886 siege; it says they were allowed to loot “western France”, when it was Burgundy.

Mameluke softened to plausible. The mamluk/ghulam institution served Arab-Islamic states from the Abbasid 830s, analogous to the devşirme Janissaries for the Turks; the real gap is the Mamluk Sultanate having no civ.

Added verified history-text errors: Persians (Sasanian dynasty “ended in battle in 636”; Yazdegerd III died in 651); Turks (Seljuks credited with retaking Palestine, which was Saladin, an Ayyubid); Saracens (Arabs “took Asia Minor”); Huns (stirrup invention); Saxons (shield wall “adopted” from Vikings); Tupi (Staden captive “1552–1555”, actually about Jan–Oct 1554, confirmed via Deutsche Biographie and Wikipedia); Celts placed in “Northern Europe”.

Malians: the text covers Ghana and Mali, with Songhai only as a rival or successor, not as a covered polity. Added al-Umari's c. 10,000 cavalry, and Benin and Kongo as Portuguese-sourced omissions. The Adal war is linked to Cristóvão da Gama (1541–1543).

Burmese: the text covers both Pagan (1044–1297) and Taungu (to 1599). Bayinnaung subdued Manipur in 1560 and the Cassay Horse is Konbaung (post-1758), so the rating changes from anachronistic to stretched. Chatras nuanced: Vietnamese courts used parasols (lọng), so the issue is the Indic name. Paper Money noted as faithful (Hồ Quý Ly, 1396). Champa dates corrected to c. 192–1471, with Panduranga to 1832.

Hindustanis: the text is explicit about the Delhi Sultanate; only the name hides the Indo-Islamic content. Dravidians: Sanskrit Drāviḍa is medieval (Kumārila Bhaṭṭa; Pañca-Drāviḍa), so the term is not purely a 19th-century invention; Caldwell gave it the linguistic sense.

Britons: added the Welsh longbow nuance (Gerald of Wales) and noted that the Britons text itself narrates the Anglo-Saxon replacement. Saxons naming issue added (Angles, Englisc/Angelcynn, collision with continental Saxons and Ottonians). Celts debate balanced with Cunliffe and Koch; vitrum/woad marked as contested.
Tatars: the name is attested in the 8th-c. Orkhon inscriptions; the game text acknowledges the shift in meaning, which is fair to note. Added the Kondurcha battle of 1391.

Mapuche “largest native group” flagged as probably a garbling of “largest in Chile” (Quechua peoples number several million). Pre-Hispanic resistance to the Inca at the Maule added and marked contested. Muisca “Chibchas” reclassified as a dated synonym, since the English text itself gives Chibcha, not an error.

Exonyms: Wolf introduced “Byzantine” in 1557, but it was popularised in the 17th–19th c. The Berber etymology is marked as debated. “Spanish” and “Italians” added as retroactive national umbrella names. “Sicilians” softened from misleading to plausible but ambiguous (named after the Regnum Siciliae).

Proposals revised to match the corrections: Chu Ko Nu stays with Chinese; Rocket Cart is the item to remove; Teutons rename dropped; the pt translation list is extended; quota totals re-checked (56; Europe 16–18 ≈ 30%).
Spot-checked game-text quotes against the history files (Celts/Stonehenge, Aztecs, Mayans, Persians/Ctesiphon, Mapuche); game-text quotations kept short per issue, with the rest paraphrased.

themes.title: Cross-cutting audit of the tech tree: who has what they never had, and who lacks what they were famous for (verified version)
themes.summary: Audit carried out on the data in the aoe2techtree repository (data/data.json, as of the commit “Add The Viking Sagas”, later than DE Update 177723, with 56 civilizations). Every inclusion and every absence cited below was confirmed directly in the file. The generic AoE2 tree is, at bottom, a model of late-medieval Western Europe: Militia→Champion, Spearman→Halberdier, Archer→Arbalester, Scout→Hussar, Knight→Paladin, Chemistry→gunpowder, Hulk→Carrack→Galleon, and even the Petard, a 16th-century device, for every civ. This model is applied to peoples ranging from the 3rd century (Shu, Wei, Wu) and the 5th century (Western Romans) to the 16th century (Turks, Portuguese, Mapuche, Mughals). The distribution of the generic branches follows mainly game balance and each civ's “identity”, not chronology. Four kinds of error follow from this. First, anachronistic inclusions: gunpowder for the Goths, Malians, Khmer and Jurchens (Bombard Cannon); Paladin for the Huns and Celts; Galleon for the Huns and Romans. Second, glaring absences: the Chinese without Hand Cannoneer or Bombard Cannon; the Vietnamese and Burmese without Hand Cannoneer, against the game's own history text; the Spanish without foot crossbowmen; the Khitans without generic heavy cavalry, also against the game's text. Third, invented identities: the Cumans as a siege civ; for the Celts, that identity finds only partial support in 15th-century Scottish artillery. Fourth, the “Old World package” given to the American civs. One has to be fair. The Definitive Edition has been correcting the model with well-founded replacement units, such as the Three Kingdoms' Traction Trebuchet, the Indian siege elephants, the Varangian Guard, the Korean Rocket Cart, the Champi, Mapuche cavalry available only through the Castle, and the absence of the Stable in the Americas. Some frequent accusations also do not survive verification. The Gurjaras have grounds for gunpowder in the late phase their text covers (the Gujarat Sultanate, Mewar). The Gurjaras' lack of Battle Elephant is consistent with the Arabic sources, which highlight horses and camels. The lack of Ethiopian elephants is defensible. Wu's Fast Fire Ships have a direct basis in the Battle of Red Cliffs. The most promising path to “historical correctness” is to generalise the replacement mechanism, not to remove pieces wholesale. There follow 19 findings, ordered from most to least glaring.

findings.title: 1. Gunpowder handed to civs that never had it in their period
findings.detail:
In the file, the Hand Cannoneer exists in 23 civs, the Bombard Cannon in 25, the Cannon Galleon in 35 (Elite in 20) and the Bombard Tower in 18. The list does not follow the real spread of firearms. The fire lance appears in China in 1132. The earliest datable metal barrels are from c. 1288 (Heilongjiang) and 1298 (the Xanadu gun). The Islamic world and Europe follow in the 14th century, Southeast Asia in the 15th and 16th centuries, and the Sahel only in 1591.

The most serious cases:
- GOTHS: they have Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon, but the game's own history text ends in 711. The Ostrogothic kingdom fell in 552–553 and the Visigothic one in 711. The only “Gothic” survival into the gunpowder era was the principality of Theodoro (“Gothia”) in Crimea, with a Greek-Byzantine elite, conquered by the Ottomans in 1475. Rating: anachronistic.
- JURCHENS: they have Bombard Cannon, but the Jin dynasty ended in 1234, before the earliest datable metal barrels. The Wuwei bronze cannon, sometimes dated to c. 1214–1227, is contested. The Jin fire lances and “thunder” bombs are real (see point 11); the bombard cannon is not. Rating: anachronistic.
- MALIANS: they have Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon and Cannon Galleon, but not Galleon. The game's text runs to 1600, and even so there is no evidence of firearms in the Mali Empire. The first gunpowder force in the Niger bend was that of Judar Pasha's Moroccan arquebusiers at Tondibi (1591). The musketeers of Idris Alooma (1570s) were from Bornu. Rating: unfounded.
- KHMER: they have Hand Cannoneer, Cannon Galleon and Elite Cannon Galleon. The Angkor reliefs show elephant-mounted ballistae, not firearms. Firearms only spread in the post-Angkor period (Longvek, 16th century), with Iberian adventurers such as Diogo Veloso and Blas Ruiz in the 1590s. Rating: anachronistic.
- ARMENIANS: they have Bombard Tower, but the Armenian kingdom of Cilicia fell in 1375. Rating: stretched.
- GEORGIANS: they have Hand Cannoneer, but the game's text centres the golden age on David IV and Tamar (12th and 13th centuries) and ends with the 15th-century collapse. Rating: stretched.
- PERSIANS: they have Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon and Elite Cannon Galleon. The game's history text covers only the Sasanians, up to 651, but the civ also represents the Safavids (the Ismail campaign). For the Safavids, land firearms are plausible, because they adopted them after Chaldiran (1514). The Elite Cannon Galleon is unfounded: the Safavids had no ocean-going navy and needed the English East India Company's ships to take Hormuz from the Portuguese in 1622.
- ETHIOPIANS: they have Bombard Cannon and Cannon Galleon. The cannon is plausible as a late phase: in the war against Adal there were Ottoman arquebusiers on one side and Cristóvão da Gama's Portuguese (1541) on the other. The Cannon Galleon is unfounded, because Ethiopia lost Massawa to the Ottomans in 1557.

Revised downwards — GURJARAS: the game's text is not limited to the Pratiharas. It continues to the sultanates of Gujarat and Malwa and to Maharana Pratap's Mewar in the 16th century. The Gujarat Sultanate had notable artillery (Rumi Khan at the siege of Chittor, 1535; Ottoman alliance at Diu, 1538). Gunpowder is therefore plausible in the late phase, even though the civ's identity (Shrivamsha, camels) is that of the 9th and 10th centuries.

To be fair, the Turks, Spanish, Portuguese and Italians are well founded, as are the Bohemians (the Hussite píšťala), the Burgundians (Charles the Bold's artillery train, lost at Grandson, 1476), the Hindustanis (Panipat, 1526), the Japanese (tanegashima, 1543; Nagashino, 1575) and the Koreans.
examples: Goths: Hand Cannoneer + Bombard Cannon (the game's text ends in 711)
Jurchens: Bombard Cannon (Jin extinct in 1234)
Malians: Hand Cannoneer + Bombard Cannon + Cannon Galleon, without Galleon (Tondibi, 1591)
Khmer: Hand Cannoneer + Cannon Galleon + Elite Cannon Galleon
Armenians: Bombard Tower (Cilicia fell in 1375)
Georgians: Hand Cannoneer
Persians: Elite Cannon Galleon (Safavids without a navy; Hormuz, 1622)
Ethiopians: Cannon Galleon (Massawa, 1557)
Revised: Gurjaras with Hand Cannoneer/Bombard Cannon = plausible (Gujarat, Rumi Khan, 1535)

findings.title: 2. Gunpowder denied to those who invented it or adopted it early
findings.detail:
This is the reverse of the previous point.
- CHINESE: the civ is described as an “Archer and Gunpowder civilization”, but it has no Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon or Cannon Galleon (it has Bombard Tower, Fire Lancer and Rocket Cart). The real chronology: fire lance at De'an (1132, Chen Gui); Heilongjiang hand cannon (c. 1288); Xanadu gun, with an inscribed date (1298); Battle of Lake Poyang (1363); Ming firearms divisions (Shenjiying, Yongle reign). The Fire Lancer and the Rocket Cart partly make up for it (abstraction), but the lack of the hand cannon itself is unfounded.
- VIETNAMESE: they have no Hand Cannoneer (they have Bombard Cannon and Fire Lancer), even though the game's own history text says that by 1390 they had already adopted Chinese gunpowder. The Vietnamese annals attribute the death of King Chế Bồng Nga of Champa (1390) to fire from Vietnamese guns. After the Ming conquest of 1407, Hồ Nguyên Trừng was taken to China to make firearms. The direction of the technology transfer is debated (Sun Laichen, 2003).
- BURMESE: they have no Hand Cannoneer (they have Bombard Cannon and Elite Cannon Galleon), even though the game's text highlights the extensive use of firearms and the hiring of Portuguese gunners by the Toungoo.
- MAGYARS: they have no land gunpowder (only Cannon Galleon). The game's text reaches Hunyadi at Belgrade (1456), and the UT Corvinian Army is named after the Black Army of Matthias Corvinus (1458–1490). In that army, according to a much-repeated figure of unclear origin, one in four foot soldiers had an arquebus. The UT, however, only swaps the Magyar Huszar's gold cost for food: the game takes only the light cavalry from the Black Army. It is a partial selection, not an internal contradiction. Rating: stretched.
- CELTS: they have no Bombard Cannon (they have Cannon Galleon). James II of Scotland was an artillery enthusiast: he used it against the Douglases (Threave, 1455), received Mons Meg in 1457 (cast at Mons in 1449) and died at Roxburgh (1460) when one of his cannons burst. Irony: it is the strongest argument for the Celts' siege identity (point 6), and it is precisely the piece they lack.
- BRITONS: they have neither Hand Cannoneer nor Bombard Cannon, despite Henry V's siege train at Harfleur (1415). The scale of cannon use at Crécy (1346) is contested.
- SLAVS: the game's text ends with the fall of Kiev (1240) and the power of the boyars, so the absence is defensible within that scope. If the civ also represents Muscovy, it is missing the guns of Moscow's defence against Tokhtamysh (1382), the Pushechny Dvor (1479) and the streltsy (1550). Contested, because it depends on the civ's scope.
