- POLES: they have no Hand Cannoneer, but they do have Bombard Cannon. A minor absence.
- MONGOLS/Yuan: the use of hand cannons against Nayan (1287–1288) is contested as “Mongol”.

Overall rating: unfounded (identity and balance) for the Chinese, Vietnamese and Burmese; stretched for the Magyars, Celts and Britons; contested for the Slavs and Mongols.
examples: Chinese: no Hand Cannoneer, Bombard Cannon or Cannon Galleon (with Bombard Tower, Fire Lancer and Rocket Cart)
Vietnamese: no Hand Cannoneer, even though the game's text says they adopted gunpowder in 1390
Burmese: no Hand Cannoneer, even though the game's text mentions firearms and Portuguese gunners
Magyars: no land gunpowder; the UT Corvinian Army affects only the Magyar Huszar
Celts: no Bombard Cannon (Mons Meg; Roxburgh, 1460)
Britons: neither Hand Cannoneer nor Bombard Cannon (Harfleur, 1415)
Slavs: no land gunpowder (contested: the text ends in 1240)

findings.title: 3. The “Old World package” given to the American civs
findings.detail:
The designers got the essentials right: none of the six American civs has a Stable, Knight or Scout Cavalry, and the Xolotl Warrior (a post-conquest Aztec horseman) appears in no tree. There is one subtle thing they got right that the previous draft ignored: the Mapuche have cavalry (Kona and Bolas Rider, “Cavalry and Counter-Units civilization”), but only via the Castle. This is faithful, because the Mapuche adopted the horse quickly in the second half of the 16th century (Curalaba, 1598). The game's text attributes to Lautaro, with reservations (“legend says”), learning cavalry and gunpowder from Valdivia.

The rest of the European model was applied almost unfiltered:
- Crossbows (Arbalester for the Aztecs, Incas, Mayans, Muisca and Tupi), when the crossbow was unknown in the pre-Columbian Americas.
- Carrack and Galleon, when what existed were canoes and sailing balsa rafts.
- Trebuchet for all six civs; Onager; Siege Onager for the Aztecs and Muisca; Heavy Scorpion for the Incas, Mayans, Muisca, Mapuche and Tupi; Siege Ram for the Aztecs, Incas, Mayans and Tupi. All this without torsion or traction artillery, without the functional wheel and without draught animals.
- The Mapuche have Bombard Tower. It is stretched and not entirely unfounded: Lautaro captured Villagra's artillery at Marihueñu (1554), but there is no sign of systematic Mapuche use of cannons.
- In the economy: Horse Collar and Heavy Plow without horses or the plough (the Andes had the chakitaqlla, a foot plough); Blast Furnace (Aztecs, Incas, Mayans, Mapuche) without iron metallurgy (there was copper, bronze and silver metallurgy, with huayrachina furnaces); Block Printing for the Aztecs, Incas, Mayans and Muisca (the Incas had no writing and used quipus, and the Maya and Mexica codices were painted, not printed); Thumb Ring for the Incas, Mayans and Muisca.
- Internal inconsistency: the Incas, Mayans, Muisca, Mapuche and Tupi have Galleon, but the Aztecs do not; the Tupi do not have Carrack.

Eagle line: the Eagle Warrior is now only in the Aztecs and the Mayans. The Incas lost it in favour of the Champi, which is an improvement. For the Aztecs it is faithful (the cuāuhtli warrior society). For the Mayans it is plausible (the Platform of the Eagles and Jaguars at Chichén Itzá, of central Mexican influence).

Other things done right: Gambesons for the Aztecs (the quilted cotton ichcahuipilli, which the Spanish adopted), Kamayuk and Slinger.

Rating: unfounded. It is understandable as a “need for counter-units”, but it is the game's largest block of non-history.
examples: Arbalester: Aztecs, Incas, Mayans, Muisca, Tupi
Carrack: Aztecs, Incas, Mayans, Muisca, Mapuche (while Britons and Danes do not have it)
Galleon: Incas, Mayans, Muisca, Mapuche, Tupi (but not Aztecs)
Trebuchet: all six; Siege Onager: Aztecs, Muisca; Heavy Scorpion: Incas, Mayans, Muisca, Mapuche, Tupi
Bombard Tower: Mapuche (stretched: Marihueñu, 1554)
Horse Collar and Heavy Plow: all six; Blast Furnace: Aztecs, Incas, Mayans, Mapuche; Block Printing: Aztecs, Incas, Mayans, Muisca
Got right: Stable absent in all six; Mapuche with Kona and Bolas Rider only at the Castle
Eagle Warrior: only Aztecs and Mayans (Incas switched to Champi)

findings.title: 4. Horse archers: primary sources contradicted
findings.detail:
GOTHS: the Cavalry Archer and the Heavy Cavalry Archer directly contradict Procopius (Wars V.27). Belisarius explains the victory over the Goths by saying that the Romans and their Hun allies were mounted archers, and that no Goth practised that art: Gothic cavalry used lance and sword, and Gothic archers fought on foot. Rating: wrong.

Also without basis: the KHMER with Heavy Cavalry Archer and Parthian Tactics; the BURMESE with Heavy Cavalry Archer and Parthian Tactics (their Manipur cavalry threw javelins, which the Arambai represents well); the MALIANS with Heavy Cavalry Archer (Sahel cavalry used lance and javelin, and archers fought on foot); the MALAY with Cavalry Archer; the VIETNAMESE and the ETHIOPIANS with Heavy Cavalry Archer. Rating: unfounded.

As for absences, the JURCHENS have neither Thumb Ring nor Parthian Tactics, even though the game's own text says they fought mainly as mounted archers. The Manchu thumb ring (banzhi), heir to Jurchen archery, is one of the most iconic objects of Asian archery. Rating: stretched.

Three Kingdoms (corrected): WEI has no generic Cavalry Archer, but it has the Xianbei Raider as a UU, plus Thumb Ring and Parthian Tactics. The Wuhuan cavalry, incorporated by Cao Cao in 207 and which the Sanguozhi calls “the most famous in the empire”, is therefore represented by substitution (abstraction). Stranger is that WU, the horse-poor southern kingdom, has Cavalry Archer, and that mountainous SHU has Heavy Cavalry Archer: stretched.

Well founded: Romans with Heavy Cavalry Archer (equites sagittarii in the Notitia Dignitatum), Byzantines (Strategikon), Huns, Mongols, Bulgarians, Magyars (Recurve Bow), Japanese (kyūba no michi), Koreans, Georgians (the Kipchaks settled by David IV in 1118), Lithuanians (Tatar auxiliaries) and Persians with early Parthian Tactics (the Parthians were Iranian).
examples: Goths: Cavalry Archer + Heavy Cavalry Archer (against Procopius, Wars V.27)
Khmer and Burmese: Heavy Cavalry Archer + Parthian Tactics
Malians, Vietnamese, Ethiopians: Heavy Cavalry Archer; Malay: Cavalry Archer
Jurchens: no Thumb Ring and no Parthian Tactics (the game's text describes them as mounted archers)
Wei: no Cavalry Archer, but with Xianbei Raider, Thumb Ring and Parthian Tactics; Wu: Cavalry Archer; Shu: Heavy Cavalry Archer
Got right: Romans Heavy Cavalry Archer (equites sagittarii)

findings.title: 5. The crossbow distributed the wrong way round
findings.detail:
The Crossbowman exists in 54 of the 56 civs; only the Bulgarians and the SPANISH lack it. The Spanish do, however, have Mounted Crossbowman and Heavy Mounted Crossbowman: crossbow on horseback yes, crossbow on foot no. This ignores the Catalan crossbowmen of Roger of Lauria's fleets (1280s, narrated by Muntaner), the Castilian ballesteros and the 32 crossbowmen (against 13 arquebusiers) that Bernal Díaz counts in Cortés' expedition of 1519. Rating: wrong.

FRANKS without Arbalester, although the crown kept the office of Grand maître des arbalétriers until 1534. TEUTONS without Arbalester, although the inventories of the Order's castles (Großes Ämterbuch) record crossbows in large numbers. BURGUNDIANS without Arbalester, despite the Flemish crossbowmen's guilds. The Viking Sagas update softened part of the problem: the Franks have Heavy Mounted Crossbowman and the UT Ordonnance Companies, which lowers the cost of mounted crossbowmen; the Teutons have Heavy Mounted Crossbowman; the Burgundians have Mounted Crossbowman. The gap in foot crossbows remains. Rating: stretched.

Meanwhile, the Aztecs, Incas, Mayans, Muisca, Tupi, Mongols, Malians and Ethiopians have Arbalester (unfounded).

Well distributed: Italians (Genoese Crossbowman); Portuguese (besteiros do conto); Chinese, Shu, Wu, Koreans and Vietnamese (Asian crossbow tradition); Khmer, whose UT Double Crossbows evokes the ballistae of the reliefs; Saracens.
examples: Spanish: no Crossbowman and no Arbalester, but with Mounted Crossbowman and Heavy Mounted Crossbowman
Franks: no Arbalester (mitigated by Heavy Mounted Crossbowman and Ordonnance Companies)
Teutons: no Arbalester (with Heavy Mounted Crossbowman)
Burgundians: no Arbalester
Arbalester: Aztecs, Incas, Mayans, Muisca, Tupi, Mongols, Malians, Ethiopians
Got right: Italians (Genoese Crossbowman), Portuguese, Shu and Wu

findings.title: 6. Invented siege identities and erased siege traditions
findings.detail:
CUMANS: they have the Siege Workshop and Battering Ram already in the Feudal Age, Capped Ram in the Castle Age, and also Siege Onager and Siege Ram. The Kipchaks were nomads with no siege tradition. Rating: unfounded.

CELTS: they are an “Infantry and Siege civilization”, with +25% attack speed for siege weapons, Siege Onager, Siege Ram and the UT Furor Celtica (+40% HP for siege weapons). The name evokes the classical stereotype of warrior fury, not engineering. The Irish and Scots of the 11th to 14th centuries were not siege specialists. Robert I (the Bruce) even razed the castles he took, such as Edinburgh in 1314, instead of garrisoning them. The only real support comes from James II's artillery in the 15th century (point 2), and that is precisely the piece the Celts do not have. Rating: stretched (in the draft, “unfounded”).

ETHIOPIANS (Torsion Engines, Siege Onager) and MALIANS (Siege Onager): unfounded. The SLAVS, also an “Infantry and Siege civilization”, with cheaper siege and Siege Onager: stretched.

The absences are ironic:
- BYZANTINES without Heavy Scorpion, despite the Roman-Byzantine continuity of bolt-throwers (the cheiroballistra; the toxobolistrai in the Taktika of Leo VI). Rating: wrong.
- ROMANS with Onager but without Siege Onager, when the very term “onager” is Roman military slang recorded by Ammianus Marcellinus (XXIII.4).

Well founded: Bulgarians with Siege Onager (capture of Mesembria in 812 with an Arab engineer; the Scriptor Incertus describes the engines Krum prepared against Constantinople in 813–814), Huns with Siege Ram (Priscus describes rams and towers at the siege of Naissus, c. 442), Mongols with Siege Onager (Chinese and Persian engineers), Saracens with Counterweights, Britons with Warwolf (Stirling, 1304) and the Indian civs with the Siege Elephant in place of the ram.
examples: Cumans: Siege Workshop and Battering Ram in the Feudal Age; Siege Onager; Siege Ram
Celts: siege bonus + Siege Onager + Siege Ram + Furor Celtica (stretched; only James II's artillery supports it)
Ethiopians: Torsion Engines + Siege Onager; Malians: Siege Onager
Byzantines: no Heavy Scorpion
Romans: with Onager but no Siege Onager (Ammianus Marcellinus XXIII.4)
Got right: Bulgarians Siege Onager (Krum), Huns Siege Ram (Priscus, Naissus)

findings.title: 7. The names of the final tiers (Paladin, Hussar, Halberdier, Champion) applied to the wrong periods and peoples
findings.detail:
The last tiers of the generic lines are named after specific, late types of soldier, and were then distributed for balance.
- PALADIN (10 civs; heavy cavalry with full barding) for the HUNS, CELTS and CUMANS: unfounded. By contrast, the SICILIANS, who represent the Hauteville Normans (whose cavalry won at Civitate, 1053), do not have Paladin, and the ITALIANS, home of the condottieri's men-at-arms, stop at Cavalier.
- HUSSAR (30 civs; 15th-century Hungarian-Serbian light cavalry, the name coming from the Hungarian huszár) for the Goths, Celts, Saxons, Burgundians, Khmer, Burmese, Wei and Wu: the name is anachronistic, the function is an acceptable abstraction.
- HALBERDIER (a 14th- and 15th-century polearm) for the Huns, Goths and Romans: anachronistic. The ITALIANS do not have it, despite the Italian polearm tradition (roncone, partigiana). For the Chinese, Shu, Wei and Wu, the Halberdier corresponds well to the ji, the Chinese dagger-halberd (faithful).
- CHAMPION for the MONGOLS and CUMANS, peoples whose strength was almost entirely mounted: unfounded. For the KHITANS it is stretched, but less serious, because the Liao had Chinese infantry. For the Celts, the Two-Handed Swordsman evokes the claymore (15th and 16th centuries): plausible.
- The KHITANS have neither Knight nor Cavalier, even though the game's own history text says that the core of the Liao army was the ordo cavalry, heavily armoured and armed with lance, bow, sword and mace. The Steppe Lancer and the UT Ordo Cavalry only partly compensate. Rating: stretched, with the game contradicting its own text.

The game has already solved this in other cases with substitutions: Savar, Winged Hussar, Legionary, Hei Guang, Iron Pagoda (which replaces the Knight for the Jurchens), Imperial Camel Rider and Imperial Skirmisher.
examples: Paladin: Huns, Celts, Cumans (but not Sicilians or Italians)
Hussar: Goths, Celts, Saxons, Burgundians, Khmer, Burmese, Wei, Wu
Halberdier: Huns, Goths, Romans (but not Italians)
Champion: Mongols, Cumans, Khitans
Khitans: no Knight and no Cavalier, against the game's own text (armoured ordo cavalry)
Got right: Chinese Halberdier = ji; Magyars with Hussar; Iron Pagoda in place of the Jurchen Knight

findings.title: 8. Navy: Huns and Romans with Galleon, “Greek fire” for almost everyone and caravels in Mexico
findings.detail:
HUNS with Dromon and Galleon: Attila's Huns never had a navy. Rating: unfounded. ROMANS (5th century) with Galleon: anachronistic.

SIPHONS: the tech (which gives Fire Ships an explosive charge) is named after the Byzantine liquid-fire siphon and is in 29 civs, including the Britons, Vikings, Teutons, Mongols and Mapuche. Constantine VII (De Administrando Imperio, ch. 13) orders that liquid fire be made only by the Christians of the capital and never be given to any other nation. For most of them, the name and the distribution are wrong. There are, however, nuances. The CHINESE and the JURCHENS have a basis, because the Wujing Zongyao (1044) describes a petroleum piston flamethrower. So do the SARACENS, through the naval use of naphtha. And the BULGARIANS, who do not have Siphons, are the ironic case: according to Theophanes, Krum captured siphons and liquid fire at Mesembria (812), although their use by the Bulgarians is contested.

CHINESE without Cannon Galleon, despite the Ming fleets and Poyang (1363): unfounded.

CARRACK: missing for the Britons (Henry V's Grace Dieu, 1418; Mary Rose, 1511) and the Danes, but present for the Aztecs, Incas, Mayans, Muisca and Mapuche. Rating: wrong.

SHIPWRIGHT: missing for the PORTUGUESE, the VIKINGS and WU (which has free Dry Dock), compensated by ship HP and cost bonuses (abstraction). The tech's name fails precisely those it most concerns. For the Ethiopians, Gurjaras and Magyars, Shipwright is stretched.

KHITANS and MALIANS with Cannon Galleon but no Galleon: internal inconsistency, as well as anachronistic.

Well founded: Byzantines with Greek Fire and Dromon; Koreans with Turtle Ship and Cannon Galleon (Choe Mu-seon at Jinpo, 1380); Wu with Red Cliffs Tactics; Lou Chuan for the Chinese civs; Longship for the Danes, Saxons, Varangians and Vikings; the Portuguese Caravel; the Turks with Galleon (the large Ottoman sailing ships, göke, of Kemal Reis at Zonchio, 1499; at Preveza, 1538, the Ottoman fleet was made up of galleys). Goths with Dromon is plausible (Totila's fleet at Sena Gallica, 551; Gothic raids across the Aegean in the 3rd century).
examples: Huns: Dromon + Galleon; Romans: Galleon
Siphons: 29 civs, including Britons, Vikings, Teutons, Mongols, Mapuche (against De Administrando Imperio, ch. 13); plausible for Chinese/Jurchens (Wujing Zongyao) and Saracens
Bulgarians: no Siphons, despite Mesembria (812)
Chinese: no Cannon Galleon
Carrack: missing for Britons and Danes; present for Aztecs, Incas, Mayans, Muisca, Mapuche
Shipwright: missing for Portuguese, Vikings and Wu
Khitans and Malians: Cannon Galleon without Galleon

findings.title: 9. Trebuchets: wrong chronology, with the Three Kingdoms case as an example to follow
findings.detail:
The traction trebuchet was born in China (the pao) and reached Byzantium via the Avars (siege of Thessalonica, 586 or 597, in the Miracles of Saint Demetrius). The counterweight trebuchet appears in the 12th century: al-Tarsusi describes it c. 1187 for Saladin, and the Byzantine priority (c. 1165) argued by Chevedden is contested. It only reached China in 1273, at the siege of Xiangyang, with the Muslim engineers Ismail and Ala al-Din.

The game gives the counterweight Trebuchet to 53 civs, that is, to all except Shu, Wei and Wu. That includes the Huns, Goths and Romans (anachronistic), the six American civs (unfounded) and the Khitans and Jurchens (anachronistic: the Liao fell in 1125 and the Jin used traction trebuchets at Kaifeng, 1232). The Huns also have a trebuchet accuracy bonus (unfounded). The Khitans have the Mounted Trebuchet, a game invention without basis (unfounded).

Irony: the Chinese, Jurchens, Khitans and Koreans do not have Mangonel. In many medieval sources, “mangonel” meant precisely the traction trebuchet (debated terminology), whereas the game's Mangonel is a torsion catapult. The Japanese Kataparuto is stretched, because the trebuchet was very rare in Japan.

The positive point is exemplary: Shu, Wei and Wu have Traction Trebuchet instead of Trebuchet. It corresponds to Cao Cao's “thunder carts” (pilizhe) at Guandu (AD 200), according to the Sanguozhi. Also faithful are the Britons' Warwolf (Stirling, 1304) and the Saracens' Counterweights.
examples: Counterweight Trebuchet: Huns, Goths, Romans, Khitans, Jurchens and the six American civs
Huns: Trebuchet accuracy bonus
Khitans: Mounted Trebuchet (invention)
Chinese, Jurchens, Khitans, Koreans: no Mangonel
Japanese: UT Kataparuto
Got right: Shu, Wei, Wu with Traction Trebuchet (Guandu, 200); Britons Warwolf; Saracens Counterweights

findings.title: 10. Fire Lancer, Rocket Cart and Rocketry: one of the best ideas, with dating errors
findings.detail:
The East Asian regional gunpowder branch is, on the whole, well founded.
- The fire lance is first attested at De'an (1132).
- The JURCHENS (Jin) used “flying fire lances” against the Mongols at Guide (1233) and zhentianlei (“heaven-shaking thunder”) bombs at Kaifeng (1232). The Fire Lancer, the Grenadier and the UT Thunderclap Bombs are therefore faithful. The Jurchen Rocket Cart is contested: some read the “flying fire” of 1232 as rockets. The Bombard Cannon was already dealt with in point 1.
- The Korean Rocket Cart corresponds to the hwacha (1409, improved in 1451): faithful.
- Chinese Rocketry is faithful. The Vietnamese Fire Lancer is plausible and is supported by the game's own text (gunpowder adopted by 1390).

The error lies with the KHITANS, who have Fire Lancer and Rocket Cart. The Liao dynasty fell in 1125, before the first attested fire lance, and there is no evidence of such weapons in the Western Liao (Qara Khitai, until 1218). The game's text states that the Liao gradually began to use Chinese gunpowder. That is believable for incendiaries (in the 11th century, the Song banned the sale of saltpetre and sulphur to foreigners), but not for fire lances or rockets. Rating: anachronistic.

The MONGOLS do not have Fire Lancer, despite having absorbed the Jin and Song gunners: a contested absence, depending on whether one considers the imperial phase or the Yuan phase.
examples: Khitans: Fire Lancer + Rocket Cart (Liao extinct in 1125; fire lance attested in 1132)
Jurchens: Fire Lancer + Thunderclap Bombs + Grenadier (Guide, 1233; Kaifeng, 1232), faithful; Rocket Cart contested
Koreans: Rocket Cart = hwacha (1409/1451), faithful
Mongols: no Fire Lancer (contested)

findings.title: 11. Three Kingdoms: the 3rd century with Galleons, printing and mass heavy cavalry
findings.detail:
Shu, Wei and Wu are 3rd-century AD civs that coexist with the 15th-century model: all have Galleon and Carrack, Wei and Wu have Hussar, and Wei has Block Printing (woodblock printing only appears in the 7th and 8th centuries; the printed Diamond Sutra dates from 868). All of this is anachronistic.

Correction to the draft: the Fast Fire Ship (Wei and Wu; Shu does not have it) is not anachronistic. Huang Gai's fire ships at the Battle of Red Cliffs (208), narrated in Zhou Yu's biography in the Sanguozhi, are the most famous naval episode of the period. For Wu, with the UT Red Cliffs Tactics, it is faithful.

Internal inversions: the three civs share the Hei Guang Cavalry, but it is WU, the riverine kingdom poor in horses, that gets +2 attack for the Hei Guang in the Imperial Age, as well as Cavalry Archer: stretched. WEI, the kingdom with the strongest crossbow tradition in the north, does not have Arbalester (Shu does): minor. The Heavy Hei Guang Cavalry, armoured cavalry as a mass unit, clashes with a fragment of Cao Cao's military orders quoted in the Taiping Yulan: Yuan Shao reportedly had 300 sets of horse armour and Cao Cao not even ten. Barding was rare in the 3rd century. Rating: stretched.

What it gets right: Traction Trebuchet, Lou Chuan, Tiger Cavalry (Cao Cao's Hubao guard), Halberdier as the ji, Arbalester for Shu (the repeating crossbow associated with Zhuge Liang) and Shu's War Chariot in place of the Scorpion.
examples: Shu, Wei, Wu: Galleon and Carrack; Wei and Wu: Hussar
Wei: Block Printing (printing only from the 7th century)
Wu: +2 attack for Hei Guang Cavalry + Cavalry Archer
Wei: no Arbalester
Heavy Hei Guang Cavalry vs. Cao Cao's note on the scarcity of barding
Correction: Wu's Fast Fire Ship is faithful (Red Cliffs, 208)
Got right:Traction Trebuchet, Lou Chuan, Tiger Cavalry

findings.title: 12. Norse regional units (The Viking Sagas): exemplary Varangian Guard, poorly distributed Mounted Crossbowman
findings.detail:
The VARANGIAN GUARD (Byzantines, Danes, Saxons, Varangians, Vikings) is a model of good distribution. The Byzantines created it, the Scandinavians were the recruits, and including the Saxons reflects the Anglo-Saxons exiled after 1066 (Orderic Vitalis). Rating: faithful. The SLAVS lack it, although the Guard was born from the warriors (traditionally about 6,000) whom Vladimir of Kiev sent to Basil II in 988. Since the Varangians civ now exists to represent the Norsemen of the Rus', the omission is debatable (stretched), not an error.

The MOUNTED CROSSBOWMAN is in 15 civs and the Heavy Mounted Crossbowman in 10. The faithful or plausible cases are the Spanish (ballesteros a caballo), Portuguese (besteiros a cavalo), Franks (with the UT Ordonnance Companies), Burgundians, Italians, Teutons (Teutonic Order), Poles, Bohemians and Sicilians (Angevin-Aragonese period), and also the Danes in the Valdemarian era. For the Britons it is stretched: English mounted archers used the longbow and dismounted to fight. For the Vikings, Varangians, Celts and Saxons it is unfounded, and the last three even have the Heavy Mounted Crossbowman.

The SAXONS have Knight, Cavalier and Heavy Mounted Crossbowman, but the Anglo-Saxons rode to battle and fought on foot. In the Maldon poem (991), Byrhtnoth orders the horses driven away. In 1055, when Earl Ralph made the English fight on horseback against their custom, the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the rout. At Hastings (1066), the English host fought dismounted. Rating: unfounded.

The VIKINGS with Cavalier: unfounded. The Saxons' Longship is plausible (clinker-built ships; Sutton Hoo).
examples: Varangian Guard: Byzantines, Danes, Saxons, Varangians, Vikings (faithful); Slavs without it (debatable, given the Varangians civ)
Mounted Crossbowman unfounded: Vikings, Varangians, Celts, Saxons (the last three with Heavy Mounted Crossbowman)
Mounted Crossbowman faithful/plausible: Spanish, Portuguese, Franks, Burgundians, Italians, Teutons, Poles, Bohemians, Sicilians, Danes
Saxons: Knight + Cavalier + Heavy Mounted Crossbowman (Maldon, 991; Hereford, 1055; Hastings, 1066)
Vikings: Cavalier

findings.title: 13. Romans: a mounted Centurion, a 5th-century legionary and a Galleon
findings.detail:
The CENTURION is cavalry in the game, but the centurion was an infantry officer, and in the 5th century the equivalent rank was already mostly that of the centenarius. The unit type is wrong; the command aura is an acceptable abstraction of leadership. The LEGIONARY as 5th-century elite infantry is stretched. The civ represents the Western Empire after 395, and the history text itself speaks of poorly paid, under-strength legions. Vegetius (late 4th or early 5th century, date debated) was already lamenting the decline of the classical legion.

Anachronistic: Trebuchet, Halberdier, Galleon and Block Printing. The absence of Siege Onager was mentioned in point 6.

What it clearly gets right: Comitatenses (the late Roman field army), the UT Ballistas and the Scorpion bonus, the Heavy Cavalry Archer (equites sagittarii) and the Dromon. The last of these is plausible, although the dromon is only well attested from the 6th century (Procopius).
examples: Romans: Centurion as cavalry (an infantry officer)
Romans: Legionary in the 5th century
Romans: Trebuchet, Halberdier, Galleon and Block Printing
Got right:Comitatenses, Ballistas, Heavy Cavalry Archer

findings.title: 14. Elephants: almost everything right, and the absences are weaker than they seem
findings.detail:
This is one of the best-handled areas.
- The Battle Elephant exists for the Bengalis (elephants of Gauda and of the Palas), Burmese, Dravidians (Chola), Khmer (Angkor reliefs), Malay (the elephants of Malacca in 1511) and Vietnamese: faithful.
- The Persian War Elephant evokes the Sasanians (Avarayr, 451; al-Qadisiyya, 636): faithful.
- The Armored Elephant and Siege Elephant of the four Indian civs, in place of the ram, are faithful: the spikes on the gates of Indian fortresses existed to counter elephants.
- The Khmer Ballista Elephant is directly based on the reliefs.

Review of the absences:
- HINDUSTANIS: they have neither Battle Elephant nor Elephant Archer, only Armored and Siege Elephant. For the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals this is stretched: Timur faced the elephants of Mahmud Tughluq at Delhi (1398), and the Ain-i-Akbari devotes a whole section to Akbar's elephant stables.
- GURJARAS: they have Elephant Archer, Armored Elephant and Siege Elephant. They lack only the melee elephant, which is consistent with Sulaiman the Merchant (851): according to him, no Indian prince had cavalry as good as the king of Juzr (Gurjara), and his camels and horses were numerous. It is a defensible abstraction. The claim that al-Masudi describes many Pratihara elephants has not been confirmed.
- ETHIOPIANS without elephants: defensible. Malalas describes the Aksumite king (Kaleb) on a platform drawn by four elephants (c. 530), but Cosmas Indicopleustes states that the Ethiopians did not know how to tame elephants, apart from one or two for royal display. Abraha's elephant (the “Year of the Elephant”, traditional date c. 570, contested) belongs to Islamic tradition and to Yemen.
- TATARS/Timurids: Timur used captured Indian elephants, for example at Ankara (1402). Minor absence.
examples: Battle Elephant: Bengalis, Burmese, Dravidians, Khmer, Malay, Vietnamese (faithful)
Hindustanis: only Armored/Siege Elephant (stretched: Delhi, 1398; Ain-i-Akbari)
Gurjaras: Elephant Archer + Armored/Siege Elephant, no Battle Elephant (defensible: Sulaiman, 851)
Ethiopians: no elephants (defensible: Cosmas Indicopleustes)
Got right:Khmer Ballista Elephant, Persians War Elephant

findings.title: 15. Camel line: broadly plausible, with exaggerations on the steppes
findings.detail:
The Camel Rider exists for 13 civs.

Faithful or plausible:
- Saracens, Berbers, Persians and Turks.
- Hindustanis: the generic Camel Rider is plausible (camels in the armies of Delhi and the Mughals). The Imperial Camel Rider is stretched: it is a melee unit, whereas the most characteristic Mughal camel cavalry was the zamburak or shutarnal, a swivel gun mounted on the camel (17th and 18th centuries). The draft said the opposite.
- Gurjaras: Sulaiman (851) mentions numerous camels; the Camel Scout is plausible.
- Byzantines: the late Roman dromedarii of the Notitia Dignitatum.
- Tatars: the Flaming Camel corresponds to Timur's stratagem against the elephants of Delhi (1398). It comes from the Zafarnama of Nizam al-Din Shami (1404), almost contemporary, and was amplified in the Malfuzat-i Timuri, of doubtful authorship; the details are uncertain. Rating: plausible.

The Cumans, Khitans and Mongols are stretched: they used Bactrian camels mainly for logistics, not as shock cavalry. Malians and Ethiopians fall between plausible and stretched, because the camel belonged mainly to the Tuareg and Saharan Berbers and to the lowland peoples.

The very mechanic of the camel as anti-cavalry has a classical basis: Herodotus (I.80) tells how the smell of Cyrus' camels routed the Lydian cavalry before Sardis.
examples: Faithful: Saracens, Berbers, Persians, Turks, Byzantines (dromedarii), Tatars (Flaming Camel; Shami, 1404)
Hindustanis: melee Imperial Camel Rider (the typical Mughal camel was the zamburak, with a cannon)
Stretched: Cumans, Khitans, Mongols (Bactrian camel used for logistics)
Gurjaras: Camel Scout (Sulaiman, 851)

findings.title: 16. Monastery and “writing techs”: the Latin Christian model applied to everyone
findings.detail:
The universal Monk and Monastery are an acceptable abstraction of religious influence. It is the distribution of some techs that fails.

BLOCK PRINTING (in the game, +3 conversion range) exists for Aztecs, Incas (no writing, with quipus), Mayans (painted codices) and Muisca: wrong. Also for Romans (5th century) and Wei (3rd century), before any printing existed: anachronistic.

The KHITANS do not have it, but the Liao dynasty printed its edition of the Chinese Buddhist canon (the so-called Qidan zang) in the 11th century. Printed fragments were found in 1974 in the wooden pagoda of Yingxian, which the game's own text mentions. Rating: wrong.

The TURKS do not have it either, which is accidentally consistent with the late adoption of printing in Arabic script (Müteferrika, 1727), although the idea of an Ottoman “ban” is contested.

The Huns' UT ATHEISM confuses paganism with atheism. It is an anachronistic concept for a poorly documented steppe religion: wrong.

What it gets right: Hussite Reforms (Bohemians), Inquisition (Spanish), the Armenian and Georgian Fortified Church, Mahayana (Pala Buddhist patronage, for the Bengalis) and Clerical Recruitment (Saxons).
examples: Block Printing: Aztecs, Incas, Mayans, Muisca; and Romans and Wei (anachronistic)
Khitans: no Block Printing (Liao Buddhist canon printed in the 11th century; Yingxian fragments)
Turks: no Block Printing (Müteferrika, 1727; “ban” contested)
Huns: UT Atheism
Got right:Hussite Reforms, Fortified Church, Mahayana

findings.title: 17. Universal anachronisms: Petard, Chemistry and the high-seas fleet for everyone
findings.detail:
Some pieces are in every tree and go unnoticed.
- The PETARD (56/56) is a gunpowder charge for blowing open gates, typical of the 16th century (Henry of Navarre at Cahors, 1580). It is available to Romans, Three Kingdoms, Huns and Aztecs.
- CHEMISTRY (56/56) is required for gunpowder, but it also gives +1 attack to the archers and towers of all civs, including those that will never have gunpowder.
- The War Hulk (56/56) and the Galleon (53/56) give a late-medieval high-seas fleet to almost everyone.

Rating: anachronistic. It is acceptable as an abstraction if the Petard is read as “sappers with incendiary charges”, and it can be fixed without touching balance by renaming by period (for example, “Sapper” for civs before the 15th century).
examples: Petard: 56/56 civs (16th century)
Chemistry: 56/56 civs
War Hulk: 56/56; Galleon: 53/56 (only Aztecs, Khitans and Malians lack it)

findings.title: 18. Regional names swapped between peoples
findings.detail:
Champi, the Quechua word for a star-headed mace, came to name the Champi Warrior, Champi Scout and Champi Runner units for the Tupi, Muisca and Mapuche as well, who spoke Tupi-Guarani languages, Chibcha and Mapudungun. Huaracas (from Quechua waraka, “sling”) is a Muisca UT. Rating: stretched, because the game uses an Andean term instead of a native name for each people.

The SHRIVAMSHA RIDER has an onomastic basis: the Chatsu inscription (of the Guhilas) says that the feudatory Harsha offered Mihira Bhoja horses of the Shrivamsha breed, able to cross “seas of sand”. The name is plausible; the projectile-dodging mechanic is unfounded.

Kamayuk, Ibirapema, Kona and Guecha are well-chosen native terms.
examples: Champi Warrior, Champi Scout, Champi Runner: Tupi, Muisca, Mapuche (Quechua term)
Muisca: UT Huaracas (Quechua waraka)
Gurjaras: Shrivamsha Rider (name with an epigraphic basis; invented dodge)

findings.title: 19. What the tree does well (so that the criticism is fair)
examples: Stable absent from the six American civs; Mapuche with Kona and Bolas Rider
Traction Trebuchet: Shu, Wei, Wu
Armored/Siege Elephant: Bengalis, Dravidians, Gurjaras, Hindustanis
Steppe Lancer: Cumans, Jurchens, Khitans, Mongols, Tatars
Varangian Guard: Byzantines, Danes, Saxons, Varangians, Vikings
Gambesons: Aztecs (ichcahuipilli)

debate_questions: Should a civ represent its peak or its whole time span? The Goths run from c. 250 to 711 (or to 1475, if we count Theodoro); the game's Persians run from the Sasanians to the Safavids, but their history text ends in 651; and the Gurjaras run from Mihira Bhoja to Maharana Pratap. Is giving gunpowder to the Goths worse or better than denying it to the Chinese?

Should the game's history text be each civ's 'constitution'? If so, the Vietnamese and the Burmese should have Hand Cannoneer, the Khitans should have generic heavy cavalry and the Jurchens should have Thumb Ring, because the game itself says so.

Is the design rule 'every civ needs a siege answer and an anti-unit answer' legitimate? What would an honest siege set look like for the Aztecs, who took cities with infantry, ladders and fire, not with trebuchets?

Is the problem with the Huns' Halberdier or the Goths' Hussar in the name or in the function? Would renaming the tiers by region (for example, Halberdier→Ji in the Chinese civs, Petard→Sapper before the 15th century) be enough to settle most of the complaints without touching the balance?

Should the regional units (Varangian Guard, Steppe Lancer, Fire Lancer, Mounted Crossbowman) be distributed by shared culture, by period or by networks of contact? If by contact, should the Slavs have the Varangian Guard because of 988, and the Bulgarians the Siphons because of Mesembria (812)?

Is an absence compensated by a bonus still a historical error? For example, the Portuguese without Shipwright but with tougher ships, or the Franks without Arbalester but with a cheaper Heavy Mounted Crossbowman.
If the Hindustanis received the Battle Elephant, what should they lose to keep the balance? And how far is it worth sacrificing history to competitive balance?

The Three Kingdoms (3rd century) and the Portuguese (16th century) play on the same map. Would a per-civ 'chronological ceiling' make sense, blocking technologies later than the civilization's end date? Which civs would become unplayable in the Imperial Age?

How should a game handle contested historiography? For example: the description of the 'chained horses' (guaizi ma) associated with the Iron Pagoda, which Deng Guangming considered a misreading of the Song sources; the Byzantine origin of the counterweight trebuchet (Chevedden); the Ottoman 'ban' on printing; or Timur's flaming camels.

Primary-source test: if every element of the tree had to cite at least one source (Procopius for Gothic cavalry, the De Administrando Imperio for Greek fire, Ammianus Marcellinus for the onager, Sulaiman for Gurjara cavalry), how many generic lines would survive?
Should the 'Celts' civ be Brian Boru's Ireland, the Scotland of Bruce, who razed castles, or that of James II and Mons Meg? The answer decides whether the 'Siege' identity is invented or justified.
proposals: Generalise the replacement mechanism that already works (Savar, Legionary, Winged Hussar, Hei Guang, Iron Pagoda, Traction Trebuchet, Champi) instead of removing units. For example: Traction Trebuchet for the Khitans and Jurchens too (in place of the Trebuchet and the Mounted Trebuchet); Huns, Goths and Romans without Trebuchet, with Onager and Scorpion as the top of their siege line.

Redistribute gunpowder. Remove the Hand Cannoneer and Bombard Cannon from the Goths and Malians; the Hand Cannoneer and Cannon Galleon from the Khmer; the Bombard Cannon from the Jurchens; the Cannon Galleon from the Malians and Ethiopians; the Elite Cannon Galleon from the Persians and Khmer; and the Bombard Tower from the Armenians. Give Hand Cannoneer and Cannon Galleon to the Chinese (for example, as 'Huochong'), Hand Cannoneer to the Vietnamese and Burmese (consistent with the game's own text) and Bombard Cannon to the Celts (Mons Meg). The Gurjaras keep late gunpowder (Gujarat Sultanate).
Give the Magyars a UT tied to the Black Army that unlocks arquebusiers (or the Hand Cannoneer in the Imperial Age), instead of Corvinian Army affecting only the Magyar Huszar.

Fix the crossbow: Crossbowman and Arbalester for the Spanish; Arbalester for the Franks, Teutons and Burgundians. The Mounted Crossbowman stays with the Spanish, Portuguese, Franks, Burgundians, Italians, Teutons, Poles, Bohemians, Sicilians and Danes, and is removed from the Vikings, Varangians, Celts and Saxons.

Fix horse archery: remove Cavalry Archer and Heavy Cavalry Archer from the Goths (Procopius), Khmer, Malay and Malians, and Parthian Tactics from the Khmer and Burmese; give Thumb Ring and Parthian Tactics to the Jurchens; in the Three Kingdoms, keep Wei's Xianbei Raider as the replacement and remove the Heavy Cavalry Archer from Shu.

Give the Battle Elephant to the Hindustanis (possibly without Elite, so as not to unbalance things). Keep the Gurjaras as they are (cavalry and camels, with Elephant Archer) and do not invent Ethiopian war elephants, which are poorly attested.

Review the siege identities: the Cumans lose the Feudal Age Siege Workshop in exchange for mobility and plunder. The Celts become an infantry and fortification civ, with Scottish artillery (Bombard Cannon) as their only strong siege piece and a Furor Celtica that gives the infantry a charge attack. The Byzantines get the Heavy Scorpion and the Romans the Siege Onager.

Create a dedicated American tree: replace Carrack, Galleon and Catapult Galleon with a line of war canoes (the large Maya canoes seen by Columbus in 1502); remove Arbalester, Trebuchet, Siege Onager and Heavy Scorpion (and keep the Mapuche Bombard Tower only as a late option); rename the economic technologies (Chinampas instead of Heavy Plow, Andenes instead of Crop Rotation, Huayrachina instead of Blast Furnace) and remove Horse Collar and Block Printing.

Clean up the navy: Huns without Dromon or Galleon; Romans without Galleon; Siphons for the Byzantines and the Bulgarians (Mesembria, 812), with renamed variants for the Chinese and Jurchens (the Wujing Zongyao flamethrower) and for the Saracens (naphtha), and a generic 'incendiary pots' technology for the rest; Carrack for the Britons; Shipwright for the Portuguese and Vikings (with their own bonuses reduced); Khitans and Malians without Cannon Galleon.

Small one-off fixes: the Centurion becomes an infantry officer with an aura; the Khitans receive generic heavy cavalry (or a replacement 'Ordo Cavalry') and Block Printing, and lose the Fire Lancer and the Rocket Cart; Wei and Romans without Block Printing; the Huns' UT Atheism is renamed (for example, 'Steppe Paganism'); the Hindustani Imperial Camel Rider becomes a camel unit with a swivel gun (zamburak); Varangian Guard optional for the Slavs.

Create a layer of regional names with no impact on balance. Each civ would have its own names for the generic tiers (for example, Halberdier→Ji in the Chinese civs; Hussar→'Light Cavalry' outside Hungary; Petard→'Sapper' before the 15th century) and native terms instead of 'Champi' for the Tupi, Muisca and Mapuche. This can be prototyped in a fork of aoe2techtree by editing data/locales/<language>/strings.json.

Use the repository itself as a debating tool: a script that exports from data/data.json a civ × unit/technology matrix (names are resolved via the LanguageNameId in data/locales/en/strings.json), with a rating column (faithful / plausible / abstraction / stretched / anachronistic / wrong / unfounded) and its source, and an alternative view on the site that colours each cell according to the rating. It would be the basis for a 'Historical Tech Trees' data mod on the Workshop.
verification_log: All inclusions and absences were re-checked with a script over data/data.json + data/locales/en/strings.json. Confirmed counts: Hand Cannoneer 23, Bombard Cannon 25, Cannon Galleon 35, Elite Cannon Galleon 20, Bombard Tower 18, Crossbowman 54, Arbalester 30, Mounted Crossbowman 15, H. Mounted Crossbowman 10, Cavalry Archer 31, Heavy Cavalry Archer 27, Paladin 10, Hussar 30, Siege Onager 15, Trebuchet 53, Siphons 29, Shipwright 27, Camel Rider 13, Petard 56.
Removed “Incendiaries” from the Goths' gunpowder list: in the game it is a Fire Ship technology (the ships explode when they sink), not gunpowder.

Corrected the Corvinian Army UT: it only swaps the Magyar Huszar's gold cost for food. The claim that the game “contradicts itself” was replaced by “partial selection” (stretched), and the figure of one arquebus for every four infantrymen in the Black Army was flagged as often repeated but of unclear origin.

Gurjaras: the game's history text does not centre only on the Pratiharas; it reaches Gujarat, Malwa and Mewar in the 16th century. Gunpowder moved from anachronistic to plausible (late phase: Rumi Khan, Chittor, 1535).

Gurjaras and elephants: it could not be confirmed that al-Masudi describes Pratihara elephants. Used Sulaiman (851) instead: unrivalled cavalry and many camels and horses. Noted that the Gurjaras have Elephant Archer, Armored and Siege Elephant. The absence of Battle Elephant became a defensible abstraction.

Ethiopians and elephants: Cosmas Indicopleustes says the Ethiopians did NOT tame elephants, except one or two for display, which contradicts the use the draft made of him. Used Malalas (four-elephant platform, c. 530) and marked the Abraha tradition as contested. The absence became defensible.

Added omitted gunpowder cases: Jurchens with Bombard Cannon (anachronistic), Khmer with Cannon Galleon and Elite Cannon Galleon, Armenians with Bombard Tower, Malians with Cannon Galleon but no Galleon.

Added the Burmese to the list of gunpowder absences (they lack Hand Cannoneer, even though the game's text mentions firearms and Portuguese gunners). Strengthened the Vietnamese case with the game's own text (gunpowder adopted by 1390).
Persians: noted that the game's history text covers only the Sasanians, up to 651. Land gunpowder became plausible for the Safavid phase; the Elite Cannon Galleon changed from “wrong” to “unfounded”.

Slavs: the game's text ends in 1240, so the absence of gunpowder became “contested (depends on scope)”. The absence of the Varangian Guard went from “wrong” to “debatable”, given that the Varangians civ exists.

Three Kingdoms: removed the Fast Fire Ship from the list of anachronisms (the fireships at Red Cliffs, 208, make it faithful for Wu; Shu does not even have it). Clarified that all three civs have Hei Guang and that the odd case is Wu's +2 attack bonus. Added Wei's Block Printing and Wei's lack of Arbalester. Noted that Wei has Thumb Ring, Parthian Tactics and Xianbei Raider (absence of Cavalry Archer reclassified as an abstraction).

Mapuche: corrected the generalisation “no cavalry in the Americas”; they have Kona and Bolas Rider via the Castle (faithful to the 16th century). The Bombard Tower went from unfounded to stretched (Marihueñu, 1554; the Lautaro legend in the game's text).

Eagle line (requested in the brief and missing from the draft): the Eagle Warrior is now only in the Aztecs and the Mayans. The Incas moved to the Champi; for the Mayans it is plausible (Chichén Itzá).

Mounted Crossbowman: corrected the list. The Britons, Bohemians, Italians, Poles, Sicilians and Teutons also have it; the Heavy Mounted Crossbowman is in only 10 civs (including Celts, Saxons and Varangians, but not Vikings). Updated the proposal accordingly.

Franks and Teutons without Arbalester: rating changed from “wrong” to “stretched”, because The Viking Sagas update gave them Heavy Mounted Crossbowman (and gave the Franks the Ordonnance Companies UT). Kept “wrong” only for the Spanish. Bernal Díaz clarified: 32 crossbowmen and 13 arquebusiers.
Celts: the siege identity went from “unfounded” to “stretched”, because the draft itself invoked James II's artillery (the only real support). Former point 5 reordered and lowered to moderate.
Siphons: added nuances (the Chinese flamethrower of the Wujing Zongyao, 1044; Arab naphtha) and the Bulgarian irony (Mesembria, 812, according to Theophanes; Bulgarian use contested).
Turks with Galleon: removed the justification “Preveza, 1538”, where the Ottoman fleet was made up of galleys; replaced it with Kemal Reis's göke at Zonchio (1499).
Huns with ships: rating changed from “wrong” to “unfounded”. Added the Romans' Galleon.

Imperial Camel Rider: corrected the claim that it “evokes the shutarnal”. The shutarnal or zamburak was a swivel gun mounted on a camel, and the Imperial Camel Rider is a melee unit. Flaming Camel: source identified (Shami's Zafarnama, 1404), with uncertain details.

Khitans: noted that the game's own text describes the ordo cavalry as heavily armoured (which reinforces the absence of Knight) and states that the Liao adopted gunpowder (credible only for incendiaries, not for Fire Lancer and Rocket Cart). Khitan Mounted Trebuchet rated as an invention. Clarified that the printed Liao Buddhist canon was a Chinese edition (Yingxian fragments, 1974).

Jurchens: Rocket Cart marked as contested. The absence of Thumb Ring and Parthian Tactics was reinforced with the game's text (“they fought mainly as mounted archers”). Debate on the Iron Pagoda corrected: Deng Guangming's thesis concerns the “chained horses” (guaizi ma), not the existence of the heavy cavalry.
Romans: added the Galleon and Block Printing to the anachronisms. Centurion clarified (the unit type is wrong; the aura is an acceptable abstraction). Dating of Vegetius marked as debated.
New finding 17 on universal anachronisms (Petard, Chemistry, War Hulk, Galleon), missing from the draft.

Corrected the summary (“Late Romans” moved to the 5th century, not the 3rd; “French” changed to Franks) and the reference to the translation-file path (data/locales/<language>/strings.json). Elephants severity lowered to minor; findings reordered (horse archery before the crossbow; siege moved to moderate).
